N° XXII. A Copy of a Narrative of the Voyage of £idds Captain William Kidd, Commander of the Adventure Pm^ies, Gaily, from London to the East Judies.

That the Journal of the said Captain Kidd, being violently taken from him in the Port of St. Marie's in Madagascar, and his Life being many times threatened to be taken away from him by Ninety-seven of his Men that deserted him there, he cannot give that exact Account he otherwise could have done; but, as far as his Memory will serve, is as followeth; viz.

That the said Adventure Gaily was launched in Castles Yard at Deptford, about the Fourth of December 1695; and about the latter End of February, the said Gaily came to the Buoy in the Nore; and about the 1st Day of March following, his Men were pressed from him for the Fleet; which caused him to stay there for Nineteen Days; and then he sailed for the Dowries, and arrived there about the Eighth or the Tenth Day of April 1696; and sailed thence for Plymouth; and, on the Twenty-third Day of the said Month of April he sailed on his intended Voyage; and, some Time in the Month of May, met with a small French Vessel, with Salt and Fishing Tackle on board, bouad for Newfoundland, which he took and made Prize of, and carried the same into Nczv York, about the Fourth Day of July, where she was condemned as lawful Prize: The Produce whereof purchased Provisions for the said Gaily, _ for her further intended Voyage.

That about the Sixth Day of September 1696, the said Captain Kidd sailed for the Madtras, in Company with one Joyner, ^faster of a Brigantine belonging to Bermudas, and arrived there about the 8th Day of October following; and thence to Boncrcista, where they arrived about the Nineteenth of the said Month, and took in some Salt, and stayed Three or Four Days; and sailed thence to St. Jago, and arrived there the Twenty-fourth of the said Month, where he took in some Water, and stayed about Eight or Nine Days; and thence sailed for the Capd of Good Hope; and, in the Latitude of Thirty-two, on the Twelfth Day of December 1696, met with Pour English Men of War: Captain Warren was Commodore; and sailed a Week in their Company; and then parted, and sailed to Tclere, a Port in the Island of Madagascar, and, being the re about the Twenty-ninth Day of January, came in a Sloop belonging to Barbadoes, loaded with Rum,

Sugar, Powder, and Shot, one French, Master, and Mr. Hatton, and Mr. John Batt, Merchants; and the said Hatton came on board the said Gaily, and was suddenly taken ill, and died in the Cabin: And, about the latter End of February, sailedTor the Island of Johanna, the said Sloop keeping Company, and arrived there about the Eighteenth Day of March; where he found Four East India M erchant-men outward bound; and watered there all together, arid staid about Four Days: And from thence, about the Twenty-second of March, sailed for Mehila, an Island Ten Leagues distant from Johanna, where he arrived the next Morning, and there careened the said Gaily; and about Fifty Men died there in a Week's Time.

That, on the 25th Day of April 1697, set sail for the Coast of India, and came upon the Coast of Mallabar, in the Beginning of the Month of September; and went into Carwarr upon that Coast about the Middle of the same Month, and watered there: And the Gentlemen of the English Factory gave the Narrator an Account, That the Portuguese were fitting out Two Men of War to take him; and advised him to put out to Sea, and to take Care of himself from them, and immediately to set sail thereupon;

..... about the 12th of the said Month of September; and the next Morning, about Break of Day, saw the said Two Men of War standing for the said Gaily; and spoke with him, and asked him, Whence he was ? Who replied, From London; and they returned Answ er, From Goa; and so parted, wishing each other a good Voyage:

And making still along the Coast, the Commodore of the said Man of War kept dogging the said Gaily all the Night, waiting an Opportunity to board her; and in the Morning, without speaking a Word, fired Six great Guns at the Gaily, some whereof went through her, and 13 wounded

wounded Four of his Men; and thereupon he fired upon him again; and the Fight continued all Day; and the Narrator had Eleven Men wounded: The other Por~ tuguese Man of War lay some Distance off, and could not come up with the Gaily, being calm; else would have likewise assaulted the same: The said Fight was sharp, and the said Portuguese left the said Gaily with such Satisfaction, that the Narrator believes no Pwtuguese will ever attack the King's Colours again, in that Part of the World especially: And afterwards continued upon the said Coast, cruising upon the Coast of Cameroone} for Pirates that frequent that Coast, till the Beginning of the Month of November 1697; when he met with Captain Hmo in the Loyal Captaine, an English Ship belonging to Maderas, bound to Surat, whom he examined; and, finding his Pass good, designed freely to let her pass about her Affairs; but, having Two Dutchmen on board, they told the Narrator's Men, That they had divers Greeks and Armenians on board, who had divers precious Stones and divers other rich Goods on board, which caused his Men to be very mutinous, and got up their Arms, and swore they would take the Ship; and Two-thirds of his Men voted for the same: The Narrator told them, The small Arms belonged to the Gaily, and that he was not come to take any Englishmen, or lawful Traders; and that, if they attempted any such thing, they should never come on board the Gaily again, nor have the Boat, or small Anns, for he had no Commission to take any but the Kings Enemies, and Pirates; and that he would attack them with the Gaily, and drive them into Bombay; the other being a Merchantman, and having no Guns, might easily have done it with a few Hands; and, with all the Arguments and Menaces he could use, could scarce restrain them from their unlawful Design; but at last I prevailed, and with much ado I got him clear, and let him go about his Business. All which the said Captain How will attest, if Jiving.

And that, about the 18th or 19th Day of the said Month of November, met with a Moors ship of about 200 Tons, coming from Surat, bound to the Coast of Mallabar, loaded with Two Horses, Sugar, and Cotton, to trade there, having about Forty Moors on board, with a Dutch Pilot, Boatswain, and Gunner; which said Ship the Narrator haled, and commanded on board; and with him came Eight or Nine Moors, and the said Three Dutchmen, who declared it was a Moors Ship; and demanding their pass from Surat, which they shewed; and the same was a French Pass, which he believes was shewed by a Mistake; for the Pilot swore Sacrament she was a Prize, and staid on board the Gaily; and would not return on board the Moor Ship; but went in the Gaily to the Port of St. Maries.

And that, about^the First Day of February following, upon the same Coast, under French Colours, with a Design to decoy, met with a Bengali Merchantman belonging to Suraty of the Burden of or 500 Tons, 10 Guns; and he commanded the Master on board; and a Frenchman, Inhabitant of Surat, and belonging to the French Factory there, and Gunner of the said Ship, came on board as Master; and, when he came on board, the Narrator caused the English Colours to be hoisted; and the said Master was surprised, and said, You are all English; and asking, which was the Captain ? Whom, when he saw, said, Here is a good Prize, and delivered him the French Pass.

And that, with the said Tw o Prizes, sailed for the Port of St. Maries in Madagascar; and, sailing thither, the said Gaily was so leaky, that they feared she would have sunk every hour, and it required Eight Men every Tw o Glasses, to keep her free; and was forced to woold her round with Cables to keep her together; and with much ado carried her into the said Port of St. Marie s; where they arrived about the First Day of April 1698: And, about the 6th Day of May, the lesser Prize was haled into the careening Island or Key, the other not being arrived; and ransacked and sunk by the mutinous Men; who threatened the Narrator, and the Men that would not

join with them, to burn and sink the other, that they miglv not go Home and tell the News.

And that, when he arrived in the said Port, there was. a Pirate Ship, called the Moca Frigate, at an Anchor, Robert Culliford Commander thereof; who, with his Men, left the same at his coming in, and ran into the Woods: And the Narrator proposed to his Men to take the same, having sufficient Power and Authority so to do; but the mutinous Crew told him, If he offered the same, they would rather fire Two Guns into him, than One into the other; and thereupon Ninety-seven deserted, and went into the Moca Frigate, and sent into the Woods for the said Pirates; and brought the said Culliford\ and his Men, on board again; and all the Time she staid in the said Port, which was for the Space of Four or Five Days, the said Deserters, sometimes in great Numbers, came on board the said Gaily and Adventure Prize, and carried away great Guns, Powder, Shot, small Arms, Sails, Anchors, Cables, Surgeons Chest, and w'hat else they pleased; and threatened several times to murder the Narrator, as he was informed, and advised to take Care of himself; which they designed in the Night to^effect; but was prevented by his locking himself in his Cabin at Night, and securing himself with barricading the same with Bales of Goods; and, having about Forty small Arms, besides Pistols, ready charged, kept them out; Their Wickedness was so great, after they had plundered and ransacked sufficiently, went Four Miles off to one Edzcard Welches House, where his the Narrator's Chest was lodged, and broke it open; and took out Ten Ounces of Gold, 40 Pound of Plate, 370 Pieces of Eight, the Narrator's Journal, and a great many Papers, that belonged to him, and the People of New York that fitted them out.

That, about the 15th of June the Moca Frigate went away, being manned with about 130 Men, and Forty Guns, bound out to take all Nations: Then it was tha$ the Narrator was left only with Thirteen Men; so that the Moors he had to pump and keep the Adventure Gaily above Water, being carried away, she sunk in the Harbour; and the Narrator, with the said Thirteen Men, went on board of the Adventure Prize; where he was forced to stay Five Months for a fair Wind: In the mean Time, some Passengers presented, that were bound for these Parts; which he took on board, to help to bring the said Adventure Prize Home.

That, about the Beginning of April 1.699, the Narrator arrived at Anguilla in the West Indies, and sent his Boat on Shore; where his Men had the News, That he and his People were proclaimed Pirates; which put them into such a Consternation, that they sought all Opportunities to run the Ship on Shore upon some Reef or Shoal, fearing the Narrator should carry them into some English Port.

From Anguilla they came to St. Thomas; where his Brother-in-law^, Samuel Bradley, was put on Shore, being sick; and Five more went away, and deserted him;v Where he heard the same News, That the Narrator, and his Company, were proclaimed Pirates, which incensed the People more and more.

From St. Thomas set sail for Mama, an Island between Hispaniola and Porto Rico; where they met with a Sloop called the St. Anthony, hound for Antegua from Curaso, Mr. Wm. Boulton.Merchant, and Samuel Wood Master: The Men on hoard then swore, they would bring the Ship no further: The Narrator then sent the said Sloop St. Anthony for Curaso, for Canvas to make Sails for the Prize, she being not able to proceed; and she returned in Ten Days; and after the Canvas came, he could not persuade the Men to carry her for New England; but Six of them went and carried their Chests and Things on hoard of Two Dutch Sloops, bound for Curaso; and would not so much as heel the Vessel, or do any thing; the Remainder of the Men not being able to bring the Ad-' venture Prize to Boston, the Narrator secured her id a good safe Harbour in some Part of Hispaniola; and left in the Possession of Mr, Henry Boulton of Antegua, Merchant,

Wm. Kidd.

Boston in New-England, Monday, 3d July 1699. Captain Wm. Kidd, by Command of his Excellency the Earl of Bellomont, having been notified and required to attend his Lordship in Council, at Six a Clock this Evening, at his Lordship's House, to give an Account of his Proceedings in his late Voyage to Madagascar, and Parts adjacent, and other Places, since his last Departure from England in the Adventure Gaily, with his Majesty's Royal Commission;

The said JVm. Kidd appeared accordingly, to the Summons served upon him, as above.

And, being demanded an Account of his proceedings, as above; he answered, That his Journal was destroyed, Vol. 13.

33

and made away, by his Company; but if his Excellency would please to grant him time for the same, he would prepare, and present his Lordship with, a Narrative thereof in Writing.

Being further demanded an Account of his Lading on board his Sloop now lying within this Port, and on board the Ship which he said he left at Hispaniola; saith, There is on board the Sloop; viz.

Forty Bales, containing Callicoes, Silk, Muslins striped and plain.

Five or Six Tons of refined Sugar, contained in Bags.

About 40lb. Weight in Dust and Bar Gold.

About 80 lb. Weight in Bar Silver.

All which, he saith, he purchased at Madagascar, with the Powder, Small Arms, and other Furniture, belonging to the Adventure Gaily, whereof he was late Commander.

And further saith, That, about Forty-two or Three Days since, he left a Ship on the South Side of Hispaniola in the Possession of Henry Boulton of Antegua, Merchant, and about Twenty-two Men; which Ship he brought last from Madagascar: And that there is oti board the same the several Goods following; viz.

About One hundred and Fifty Bales.

Seventy or Eighty Tons of Sugar.

About Ten Tons of Iron in short Junks.

About Fourteen or Fifteen Anchors.

Forty Tons of Saltpetre.

About Twenty Guns in the Hold.

Thirty Guns mounted, being the Guns lately belonging to the Adventure Gaily.

There is no Gold or Silver on board, that he knows

of.

Saith, He never romaged her.

The Ship is about 400 Tons in Burden, built at Sarrat by the Moors: All her Seams are rabbetted.

JVm. Kidd.

N° XXIV. The Depositions of Abel Owen Mariner, of full Age, late Cook of the Adventure Gaily, Captain JVm. Kidd Commander; and Samuel Arris Mariner, late Steward of the same Ship, of full Age; Depose and testify, as followeth; viz.

That the said Ship was launched at Deptford, at Castle's Yard, about the 4th Day of December 1695,: And that the said Ship came to the Buoy and Nore about the latter end of February; and about the First Day of March the Men were pressed from on board the said Gaily for the Fleet; and she was staid about Nineteen Days, and then sailed for the Demmes; and, about the Eighth or Tenth Day of April, arrived there ;and thence sailed for Plymouth; and, on the 23d Day of the Month of April 1696, the said Ship sailed from Plymouth; and sometime in the Month of May, met with a small French Vessel, bound for Newfoundland, which they took, and* made Prize of, and carried the same into New York about the 4th Day of July following; and the same was condemned there as lawful Prize: And that, about the 6th Day of September then also following, the said Gaily sailed for the Maderas; and thence to Bonavista; thence to St.Jago; thence to Teleix, and the Island of Madagascar; thence to Johanna; thence to Mehila, w here they buried about Fifty of their Men in the Month of May 1697; and thence sailed upon the Coast of India; and, returning back to St. Maries, the Ship was all along so leaky, that they feared she would have sunk every Hour; and that it required Eight Men, every Two Glasses, to keep her free; and were forced to woold her round with Cables, to keep her together; and, with much ado, kept her above Water, and carried her into the said Port of St. Maries.

The Five Deponents within-named did severally declare, That, whereas, in their within written Affidavits, they speak of the taking of Two Vessels, they do further explain themselves; and testify, That the said Two Vessels were Moorish Ships, and taken by them upon the Coast of India; One of them of Burden betwixt Four and Five hundred Tons, the other about Tw o hundred Tons: They surrendered to them without firing any Guns at them: The greater Ship came from Bengali; the lesser Ship came from Surratt: The smaller Ship was taken in November 1697; the greater Ship in February following: The Master, Gunner, and Boatswain, of the smaller Ship were Dutchmen, the rest of the Company were Moors, being about Forty in Number in the Whole; Iier Lading consisted of some Persian Silks, and other dry Goods, with some Horses: The Three Dutchmen afterwards took up Arms on board the Gaily: The greater of the Tw o Ships is the same that they lately left at Hispaniola: She had about Ninety Meh on board: She was commanded by an Englishmen named Jfright; the Mate and Gunner were Dutch; all the rest of the Company were Moors: She was mounted with Ten Guns; and laden with Bengali Goods.

The Deponents further say, They met with the Mocha Frigate at the Port of Saint Marie's; and the Company belonging to her took the Companies belonging to the aforesaid Two Ships, forcibly, from on board the Adventure Gaily; and Ninety of the Company belonging to the said Gaily there also left her, and entered themselves on board the saickMocha Frigate; having first plundered the Two Ships before-named, and taken out of them a 3

169-J-. January. And upon Consideration of the Means to root these Pirates out of those Seas, the East India Company proposed to the said Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, That Two or Three Fourth Rate Frh gates might be sent in March next for that End.

Whereupon Captain JVarren being sent for, he gave an Account of the Strength of the Pirates Ships at St, Maries; and proposed Four Ships of War as sufficient to suppress them.

February. The East India Company presented to the said Commissioners some further Advices about Pirates, which they had received from their Factors in the East Indies; unto w'hich they added, That the Pirates are so numerous in those Seas, that the Company is obliged to be at the Charge of sending Convoys with the Mogul!* Ships from Port to Port.

They also sent to the Board Mr. Henry JVatson, who gave in a Narrative of the Taking of Two Coasting Vessels in the East Indies, in August 1696, belonging to the East India Company's Servants there, by a Vessel called John and Rebecca, commanded by one John Hoar.

The said Account of vrhat Captain Kidd has done abroad, and what has been done thereupon.

The East India Company having, about the Month of August. 1698, communicated, to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, some Informations they had received from their Factors in the East hidies, of Piracies committed by Captain Kidd; circular Letters were thereupon sent to all the American Plantations, by the Secretary of State, giving Notice thereof; and strictly commanding all the Governors of the said Plantations, by tire Frigates there, and otherwise, to make Search for him; and to seize him, if he came within their Reach.

The First Advice received of Kidd's Return to America, was by a Letter from the President and Council of Nevis to the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Vernon, dated the 18th of May 1699; wherein they write, That Kidd being returned from Madagascar, in a large Ge-imesse Vessel, of about 400 Tons, with 30 Guns, but leaky, and the Men much in Distress for want of Provisions, he had, about Twenty Days before their Writing, touched at Anguilla, a small Island under that Government, where he tarried about Four Hours^; but, being refused Succour, sailed thence for the Island St. Thomas, belonging to the Crown of Denmark, and anchored off that Harbour Three Days; in which time he treated with them also for Relief; but the Governor absolutely denying him, he bore away further to Leeward; and, upon Advice thereof, the said President and Council of Nevis forthwith sent out his Majesty's Ship the Queenborough, then attending that Government, in Pursuit of him.

The said President and Council sent also afterwards to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, the Information of one Peter Smith a Dutchman, and an Inhabitant of the Island of St. Thomas, dated at Nevis the 27th of June 1699; by which, and other Advices since received from the Earl of Bellomont, it appears, That Kidd sailed from St. Thomas for the Island of Mona, lying between Porto Rico and Hispaniola; and there meeting with one Bolton, of Antegoa, and one Burt, of St. Thomas s, he sold them several Goods, and sent Bolton to Curasrn to fetch him Provisions: Which being accordingly done, he bought of Bolton a Sloop, and therein laded the best of his own Goods, and sailed towards New York; leaving the said Bolton, with Seventeen or Eighteen Men, in Trust with the Ship Quidah Merchant, one of the Ships seized by the said Kidd in the East Indies, and the Goods left in her.

The next Advice received of him was from Colonel Quart/, Judge of the Admiralty Court in Pensilvania, by Letters dated the Sixth of June; in which he writes, That Kidd was arrived in Delaware Bay, in a Sloop with about Forty Men, having with him a vast Treasure; and that he had sent his Boat on shore to the Horekills, where he was supplied with what he wanted; and from whence the People frequently went on board him.

After which it appears, by other Informations, That from thence he sailed into the Sound of New York, sending Word to his Friends at New Yo?'k of his Arrival; and that he stopt at Gardner's Island, and there put several Bales of Goods on shore, as some also into a New York Sloop, then lying the re; and landed others at Tar~ pmlin Cm; and that in Oyster Bay he took in one Emot, of New York, whom he carried along with him to Rhode Island, and there set him on shore.

Whilst Kidd staid there, or upon that Coast, Emot Voi. 13.

went to Boston to the Earl of Bellomont, telling him, Kidd1* That Kidd had left a great Moorish Ship he took io piracieli India, called the Quedah Merchant, in a Creek on the Coast of Hispaniola, with Goods to the Value of 30,000'/.; though his Lordship writes, That, upon a Computation of the Particulars afterwards given in by Kidd, they were judged to be worth 70,000 /.; And that he had bought a Sloop, in which he was come before to make his Terms; and had brought Goods with him in the said Sloop, which he believed would sell for about 10,000l.

He said also, That Kidd was very innocent, and would make it appear, that his Men forced him; locking him up in the Cabin of the Adventure Gaily, whilst they robbed Two or Three Ships; which he could prove by many Witnesses.

Hereupon the Earl of Bellomont answered Emot, That if Kidd could make his Innocency appear, he might safely come into that Port: And accordingly he wrote a Letter to Kidd, inviting him to come in; and assuring him,

That if his Case was as clear as he, or Mr. Emot for him, had said, then he might safely come in thither; and made no Doubt but to obtain the Kings Pardon for him.

This Letter his Lordship sent by one Campbell; and in Three or Four Days time, Campbell returned with Answer from Kidd, full of Protestations of his Innocency; and expressing his Design of bringing his Sloop into that Port.

Kidd came accordingly, and landed at Boston the First of July 1699; but, by his trifling Answers to the Earl of Bellomont and Council, upon several Examinations; by the Endeavours of his Friends Campbell and Livingstone to embezzle the Cargo on board the Sloop; by Intimation given of an intended Present; by Livingstone's peremptory Demand, That a Bond and Articles, which he has entered into as Security for Kidd, upon his undertaking this Expedition, should be discharged; and by his Threats, That unless those Securities were immediately given up, Kidd would never bring in the great Ship that he had left on the Coast of Hispaniola; his Lordship, finding it necessary to act more openly, caused Kidd, upon the 6th of July, to be seized, and committed to Prison.

This whole Matter was transacted by his Lordship, from first to last, with the Privity and Advice of the Council of the Massachusets Bay: And then Commissioners were appointed to take care of the Sloop's Cargo, and to make Inventories thereof; and other Directions given, for securing any Part that could be found of the Goods which had been put ashore on that Coast.

Having done this, his Lordship's next Care was to fit out a Ship to look after the Quedah Merchant, and secure the Goods that might be found in her; but, before that, could be done, he received an Account, viz. the 17th of the same Month of July, from one Captain Nicolas Evertse, That he had been at Curaçao, and saw several Sloops lading of the said Goods brought thither; and there understood, That the said Ship had been carried, by a Curassaw Master, into a Salt Lagon in the Island of St. Helena, to the South-east of Hispaniola; and that, in coming from Curassaw, and touching at the said Island of St. Helena, on the 29th of the foregoing Month, he himself saw the said Ship, the Quedah Merchant, on Fire, and almost burnt down, there being then Two Sloops at that Place.

Kidd being thus secured, such of his Men as could be met with were seized also; and, by the Informations of some of them, who had been witji him in the whole Voyage, it appears, That, about the Month of April 1696, he sailed in the Adventure Gaily from Plymouth to New York; and, in his Way, took a French Prize, which he carried in with him.

From New Yoi'k he sailed to Madera, thence to Bona-vista and St. Jago, where he took in Provisions, and proceeded to Madagascar: After that, having sailed to and again, and touched in several Places, he cruised off

Thence he sailed to Calicut; and, after Four or Five Days Stay, went a cruising upon that Coast; and there took a Ship of 150 Tons Burden, whereof the Master, and Three or Four Seamen, were Dutchmen, the rest Moors, laden with Cotton; which Ship he carried to Madagascar: This was done about May 1698.

Five Weeks after, he took the fore-mentioned Ship, the Quidah Merchant, of 400 Tons Burden, commanded by one Right an Englishmen; having on Board Two Dutch Mates, and One French Gunner; but the main dumber of the Crew were Moors; being in all about -Ninety Persons.

Kidd carried the said Ship into St. Mane's, near Madagascar; and there unladed the Goods, and shared them with his Company, they being then about 115 Men; who had, one with another, Three or Four Bales apiece for his Share; and Kidd had Forty Shares for his Part: The Bales contained Callicoes, Romalls, Muslins, and some Silk, flowered, and striped, and plain.

After the Sharing of these Goods, Ninety of the Company left Kidd, and went aboard the Mocha Frigate, then lying at St. Marie s.

Kidd, and the Men that remained with him, carried their Goods again aboard the Quidah Merchant, and run the Adventure Gaily on shore, she being very leaky, and set her on Fire; and; having procured some more Men at St. Marie's, came away in her for the West Indies, and arrived at Anguilla, as before-mentioned.

The Earl of Bellomont, in transmitting this Account of his Proceedings in relation to Kidd, gave further Intimation, at the same time, That he was not only fearful of the Escape of the Prisoners, having then before him fresh Example of the Escape of one Bradish{ another Pirate, with great Suspicion of the Privity of the Gaoler; but also that there are no Laws in that Country for the Punishing of Piracy with Death; and that the People, in all these neighbouring Parts, are so favourable to Pirates, by reason of the Money they brought and dispersed amongst them, that there could be no Expectation of any Justice against them there.

Upon which Advice, their Excellencies the late Lords Justices sent One of his Majesty's Ships to fetch over Kidd, and other Pirates, in safe Custody; together with their Effects that had been seized, and the Evidences that might be useful towards their Conviction here; in order to their being tried and punished here, according to Law: But it happened, as is said, that the said Ship, having met with Storms at Sea, and suffered such Damage thereby, that she could not proceed, is lately returned into Portsmouth.

A PETITION of the Mayor and Citizens of the Dee

City of Chester, was presented to the House, and Navigatioi read; setting forth, That the River Dee was heretofore navigable for Ships and Vessels of considerable Burden, from the Sea to the City of Chester; but, for want of sufficient Banks and Fences on the Sides thereof, against the Flux and Reflux of the Sea, the Channel is become so various and incertain, that the Navigation to the said City is almost lost; for Recovery whereof, the Petitioners are willing to submit to a Tax on all Lime and Coal that shall be unladed in the said City: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill to recover and preserve the Navigation of the said River.

And the said Petition, Minutes, and Report, are as follow:

The said Petition.

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of

England:

The humble Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading to the East Indies, Humbly sheweth,

That, of late years, great Numbers of vicious and ill-principled Men have set out several Ships, from Europe and the West Indies, on purpose to rob and seize the Ships of all Nations they can meet with in the Indian Seas; and, in pursuance of the said villainous Designs, have already committed so great Robberies and Outrages, that the Nations of those Parts, finding their Ships robbed, and Navigation interrupted, by Pirates under English Colours, and, in Truth, the greatest Part of them are Subjects of the Crown of England, have several times seized the Factories of your Petitioners, and put their Factors and Servants in Irons, to their great Detriment: Nor do your Petitioners yet know, whether the Mogul hath not seized all the Effects of your Petitioners in India, to make good the Damage his Subjects have sustained by the late Piracies committed by Every and others.

That your Petitioners have Advice, That several Ships are gone out, and more are fitting out, from our Plantations in the West Indies, on the same Designs; and, unless some Stop be put to these villainous Practices, your Petitioners have too great Reason to apprehend the Continuance of such Practices will so far exasperate the Indian Nations, that they will utterly destroy the Factors and Effects of your Petitioners, and totally forbid all Commerce between them and the English Nation.

That your Petitioners are, on their Parts, ready to do whatever they can to suppress their piratical Practices; nor will they spare any Cost effectually to put an End to these Violations of the Laws of all Nations, as far as they shall be enabled.

Your Petitioners therefore humbly pray, your Lord-' ships would please to impower the Petitioners Ships

and Officers to seize and take all Pirates infesting those Seas, within the Limits of the Company's Charter; and likewise to impower them to erect a Court of Admiralty in those Parts, to try and condemn such Pirates as they shall take; or in such other manner as your Lordships shall judge most effectual for suppressing and preventing the like Villainies in time to come.

And your Petitioners shall ever pray, &;c.

Ko. Blackborne, Secretary.

2d March

Report on the Petition of the East India Company, for erecting Courts of Admiralty there.

17 March. Sir Charles Hedges, Judge of the Admiralty, attended the Board; and acquainted them, That in case they do appoint a Vice Admiral at Bombay, or any other Place in the East Indies, he will thereby have Power to proceed against the Ships of such Pirates as shall be taken by the East India Company's Ships, seized on by the Powers given them by the Board, by virtue of a Commission under the Great Seal of England] and to send home the Persons in Custody.

5° December 99. A true Copy,

J. Burbhett.

The said Report;

Copy of a Letter from Sir Charles Hedges to the Lords of the Admiralty, dated the 8th March 1696.

Having, according to your Lordships Order of the 4th Instant, considered the Petition of the East India Company, relating to Commissions to take Pirates, and the Establishing of a Court of Admiralty for proceeding against them in the East Indies; it is my humble Opinion, That the most regular Way will be, for your Lordships to take a Commission under the Great Seal of England, giving Power to the Lord Admiral, or Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord Admiral of England, by Name, and for the Time being, to grant Commissions to any of the Captains of the East India Company's Ships, for the taking of Ships of Pirates; wherein it may be expressed, What Parts or Shares the King shall think fit to reserve to himself or bestow upon the Captors and Company.

And, to the end that legal Proceedings may be had in the East Indies, I humbly conceive, That your Lordships may be pleased to erect a Vice Admiral at Bombay, or any other Place that shall be thought expedient, in the same manner as is done in the West Indies; which being established by a Commission in the ordinary Form, that will be sufficient to impower such Vice Admiralty there, to proceed against Ships, as fully as any Vice Admiralty in England, or the High Court of Admiralty, can do:

And, as to the Persons, I think there is no Doubt but they may be sent home in Custody: But, whether it will be fit to try them there for their Lives, considering the Statute 28 Hen. VIII. Chap. 15. I must crave Leave to submit to the Gentlemen learned in the common Laws of the Land, and your Lordships further Consideration#

5 December 1699. A true Copy,

J. Burchett.

Sir Charles Hedges to attend the Board, touching his . Vol. 13.

Gentlemen,

MY Parliaments have done so great things for me, and I have, upon all proper Occasions, expressed so great a Sense of their Kindness, and my Opinion has been so often declared, That the Happiness of an English King depends upon an intire good Correspondence between him and his Parliament, That it cannot seem strange for me to assure you, That no Persons have ever yet dared to go about to misrepresent to me the Proceedings of either House; Had I found any such, they would have immediately felt the highest Marks of my Displeasure: It is a Justice I owe, not only to my Parliaments, but to every one of my Subjects, to judge of them by their Actions; and this Rule I will steadily pursue. If any shall hereafter attempt to put me on other Methods, by Calumnies or Misrepresentations, they will not only fail L ®f

Supply.

Papers

respecting

Piracies.

38 50 Decembris. 1699.

of Success, but shall be looked upon, and treated by me, as my worst Enemies.

Gentlemen,

I am pleased to see, by your Address, That you have the same Thoughts of the great Advantages which will ensue to the Kingdom, from our mutual Confidence, as I expressed to both Houses at the Opening of this Session. I take very kindly the Assurance you give me, of using your utmost Care and Endeavour to prevent and discourage all false Rumours and Reports, reflecting upon Me, and my Government; and I faithfully promise you, That no Actions of mine shall give a just Ground for any Misunderstanding between me and my People.

Mr. Secretary Vernon, according to Order, presented to the House the Petition of the East India Company to the Lords Justices: And

An Extract out of the Lords Justices Minute Book: And

A Copy of a Letter from the Privy Council to the Governors of the Plantations, for Apprehending of Pirates, and Suppressing Piracy.

And the Titles thereof were read.

And the same were as follow; viz.

The said Petition.

To their Excellencies the Lords Justices of England.

May it please your Excellencies,

The Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading to the East Indies, having received a letter, dated the 14th of August 96, from Mr. Yard, intimating, That there hath been Application made to your Excellencies, on behalf of One of the Persons that was on board the Ship Charles, alias Fancy, mentioned in your Excellencies last Proclamation, who, if he might have a Pardon, offers to come in, and discover his Knowledge in the whole Matter of the Piracy committed in India by the said Ship, and use his utmost Diligence for the Apprehending those other Pirates that were concerned on board the same; and to represent to your Excellencies, what we thought proper to be done in that Case; do humbly shew to your Excellencies, That there being Persons enough already in Custody, to prove the Matter of Fact, of which the rest stand accused; do therefore humbly conceive, with Submission to your Excellencies, That a Pardon to any other of the Criminals can be of no other Use, than upon the Terms in the said Proclamation mentioned; and the Government in India, where the Company's Affairs, occasioned by the horrid Villainies and Robberies committed by the said Pirates, are in a very deplorable Condition, being no otherwise to be satisfied, than by the Execution of Justice upon the Criminals.

And they do further humbly pray, That such of the Species of Gold, Silver and Jewels, as have already been, or shall hereafter be, seized in the Custody of any of the said Pirates, or of any other Persons, who cannot make a legal Title thereunto, may not be disposed of, but put into the Possession of the said Governor and Company, in order to be preserved for the Use of the Proprietors in India; that the Government there may see, That his Majesty here, as well as the said Company, have done their utmost Endeavours to seize the said Pirates, and to make Restitution to the Persons injured, as far as it is in their Power.

Signed by Order of the Governor and Company.

Ro. Blackborne, Secretary.

East India House,

20th Aug. 1696.

The said Extract, 20th Aug. 1696.

Present,

Lord Archbishop, Lord Steward,

Lord Privy Seal, Duke of Shrevsbury,

Lord Godolphin.

A Memorial, presented by the East India Company, against pardoning any of the Pirates, but such as should come in upon the Terms of the Proclamation; and, that what Money should be found belonging to the Pirates, might be put into their Hands, to be restored to the Owners in India.

Ordered, That it be brought to the Council, to be considered there.

The said Letter.

At the Council Chamber in Whitehall, the 27th Aug. 1696.

Present,

Their Excellencies the Lord Justices in Council. Lord Keeper, Earl of Mountague,

Lord Privy Seal, Earl of Tankci'ville,

Duke of Shrewsbury, Mr. Vice Chamberlain,

Lord Chamberlain, Mr. Chancellor of Exchequer, Lord Godolphin, Sir Henry Goodrich,

Mr. Boscazcen.

After our very hearty Commendations: Whereas their Excellencies the Lords Justices of England have received Information, from the Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading to the East Indies, That Henry Every, alias Bridgman, with divers other Persons, English and Foreigners, having run away with the Ship Charles the Second, alias the Pliancy, from the Port of Corunna in Spain, had committed several Acts of Piracy in the Seas of India and Persia; and, having afterwards left the said Ship at the Island of Providence, had shared the Plunder so by them gotten, and dispersed themselves: Their Excellencies have thereupon thought fit, by Proclamation in his Majesty's Name, to require all his Majesty's Admirals, Commanders, and other Officers at Sea, and all Governors and Commanders, and other Officers whatsoever, in his Majesty's Plantations, to secure and apprehend the said Henry Every, alias Bridgman, and other Persons named in the said Proclamation, and such others as were with them in the said Ship; d Copy of which Proclamation you will herewith receive. And whereas Information has been likewise given, That divers Pirates and Sea Robbers have, of late Years, gone from several Parts of his Majesty's Plantations in America to the Seas of India and Persia, and other remote Parts, upon the like piratical Designs; and that some of them have returned home pgain, and dispersed themselves in his Majesty's Plantations, with great Quantities of Gold, and other Plunder; We do hereby, in his Majesty's Name, strictly require and command you, forthwith, upon Receipt hereof, to cause the said Proclamation to be published within your Government: And that, for the Suppressing, as inucii as may be, all such evil Practices for the future, whereby the Trade of his Majesty's good Subjects in foreign Parts may be otherwise greatly disturbed, We do hereby, in his Majesty's Name, strictly charge and require you. and all his Majesty's Officers and loving Subjects, within your Government, to take all possible Care, and use all due Means, for the Seizing and Apprehending all such Pirates and Sea Robbers, and such as may reasonably be suspected for the same, either by reason of the great Quantities of Gold and Silver of foreign Coins they usually have with them, or by other probable Circumstances; and to cause them

to

to be strcightly imprisoned; and their Ships, Goods, and Plunder, to be kept in safe Custody; until, upon returning a full Account unto us of the said Persons, their Ships, Goods, and Plunder, with the Evidences relating to them, his Majesty's Pleasure shall be known and signified concerning the m: And so we bid you very heartily farewell.

From the Council Chamber at Whitehall, the 27th Day of August 1696.

Your very loving Friends, Romney, Tankerville,

Pere. Bertie, Ch. Mountague,

H. Goodrich, J. Boscawen.

A Petition of Thomas Ryder, Thomas Warner, and others, for and on account of themselves, and the rest of the Soldiers, Horse, Foot, and Dragoons, who were lately disbanded out of his Majesty's Service, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That notwithstanding the late Act of Parliament for Relief of the Army, their Agent, Robert Griffith, and several other Officers and Agents, have absolutely refused to state their Accounts: That the Petitioners can prove great Sums to be in Arrear to the whole Army, and great Abuses, to their utter Ruin, unless relieved by this House: And praying the House to inquire into their*Grievances, and give them speedy Relief therein.

A Petition of many of the Inhabitants of the Towns of Deptford and Chatham, in the County of Kent, many of which are Innholders and Victuallers, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the Beginning of the late War, the Petitioners entertained great Numbers of sick and wounded Seamen, by Order of the Commissioners appointed for that Purpose, at 12 d. per Day, promising the same should be allowed out of their Pay; and the Hospitals being then full, the Petitioners, by reason of such Subsistence, have run themselves in Debt for Three or Four Years together: And new Commissioners have discharged the Debts of the sick and wounded Seameh at all Ports of this Kingdom, from the 1st of

Vol. 13.

41

July 1698, to the 30th of December 1699; but the former Commissioners are in Arrear from the Year 1695, to the last of June 1698; alleging, That they have not Money to discharge the same; which make the Creditors of the Petitioners very severe with them, who have made away with all they had; and others have been forced to abscond from their Habitations, for Want of what is due to them:

And praying the Consideration of the House, in order to their Relief.

Ordered, That as well the late as the present Commissioners for sick and wounded Seamen do lay before this House, a State of the Debt due upon Account of that Service.

A Petition of the Commissioners appointed by Act of Exporting Parliament for preventing the Exportation of Wool, &c. w°o1* was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, being appointed by Act of Parliament, without any Fund, did, in 1698, take upon them, at their own Charge, to settle Officers in all the Maritime and Northern Counties; who did engage themselves in the said Service, without any Salaries, in Hopes their good Works would recommend them to future Consideration:

That they acted therein with good Success, and made many considerable Seizures, and gained divers Informations against notorious Offenders, and became more formidable to them, than other Officers formerly appointed for that Purpose: But for Want of Encouragement the Owlers have found Means to raise such powerful Interests v against the said Officers, that they have been put under all the Difficulties imaginable; sometimes their Seizures taken from them by open Force; sometimes by Replevin; and sometimes committed to Prison by Justices of the Peace, upon frivolous Pretences, when they have only acted in the Execution of their Offices: Of which the Petitioners being sensible, they petitioned his Majesty for a competent Supply to carry on the said Work; who referred it to the Lords of the Treasury: But the Petitioners could get no Report from them, and despair of getting any Assistance from that Board; so that, without the Aid of this House, their Officers, who have been at great Expence, and contracted great Debts, must be inevitably ruined; neither are they able to raise Money to condemn divers Parcels of Wool they have now under Seizure; nor to prosecute the Offenders: That, if the Petitioners were encouraged, they believe they can do much more, towards suppressing the Exportation of Wool, than any other Officers heretofore employed in that Business; there having been many Corruptions, and remiss Practices, in the subordinate Officers, to the Encouragement of Offenders: And that the Petitioners, proposing no Benefit to themselves, but for the common Good, hope, That if the House shall think fit to grant them some other Powers, and enable them to support their Officers, they shall give such Satisfaction for suppressing the said unlawful Practices, as that this House may have no more Occasion of thinking of other Methods for the suppressing the like Mischiefs for the future: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for that Purpose; and for reimbursing their Officers what they have expended in the said Service.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to consider, what has been done, upon the former Laws, against the Exportation of Wool, and for encouraging the Woollen Manufactures; and to report the same, with their Opinion of what may be necessary to be further done.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do examine what Proceedings have been upon the Commission in the said Petition mentioned; and report their Opinion, How far it is fit the Act, the said Commission is grounded upon, ought to be repealed, or made more effectual; and that all the Members that serve for the Counties of Southampton, Suffolk, and Cornwall, be added to the said Committee.

Importing A Petition of the Bailiffs, Wardens, and Assistants, of

Silks. the Company of Weavers, London, on behalf of themselves and Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That raw Silk from Turky, being chiefly the Product of our Woollen Manufactures, and Stuffs mixt with Wool and Silk, and Silks, exported, having, by divers Acts of Parliament, been encouraged, the Manufacturers are become very numerous, and have attained to such Perfection therein, that they equalize most Nations; and, till of late Years, by the vast Quantities of East India, Pet'sia, and China, wrought Silks and Stuffs, imported, are ruined, comfortably maintained their numerous Families and Dependencies; many ingenious Artists, who were a Help to others, being fallen to the Parish wherein they live; and divers have been forced to go into Ireland, and foreign Parts, for their Subsistence; so that the Petitioners apprehend, That the Weaving Trade will, in a short time, be wholly lost, unless some

speedy Stop be put to the Home Consumption of the said foreign wrought Goods: And praying the House to consider their deplorable Condition, and to grant them such Relief as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the State and Condition of the Trade of England.

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of Importing the Company of Silk-throwers of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners Trade chiefly consists in Throwing raw Silks, and preparing them for the Weavers, whose Trade is very much decayed, by reason of the Home Consumption of the Abundance of wrought Silk and Stuffs imported from India, and other Parts; and, by consequence, the Petitioners Trade, which was formerly computed to employ above 40,000 People, is in Hazard of being lost, to the Ruin of those Thousands; who are, for the most Part, reduced to the utmost Extremity: And praying, That some Provision be made for preventing the Home Consumption, if not the Importation, of those foreign-wrought Silks and Stuffs.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the State and Condition of the Trade of England.

Memorandum. That though the Bonds, taken upon Sights of Seven East India Ships arriving the last Summer, are not herein mentioned, the said Sights being not yet all completely perfected; nevertheless, inasmuch as those Ships imported within the Period of this Account for 1699, the Duties, arising on the same ought to be comprehended in the Produce of that Year; which Duties, upon examining the Quantities of the several Species, are computed to amount to 163,600 L; whereof about 35,000 /. will be applicable to the Customs: Which Addition will raise the Duty very near as high this Year, as ever it advanced to in any former Year.

The said Return of the Commissioners of the Customs to the Honourable the Commons of England, assembled in Parliament.

Custom House, London, 6th December 1699. The Commissioners of the Customs, in Obedience to the Orders of this Honourable House of the 29th and 30th of November last, directed the Comptroller General of the Accounts of the Customs, to draw out Abstracts of the Total Produce in London and the Out Ports, of the several Branches of Duties received at the Custom House, for the Years ending at Michaelmas 1698, md Michaelmas 1699; and also the like Accounts for the Years ending at Michaelmas 1687, and Mi-

chaelmas 1688; which are herewith humbly presented to this Honourable House; together with what appears, by the Books of the Exchequer, to have been paid in there on every respective Branch in the several Years: From comparing whereof, and of the Exportations distinctly in the several Years, which are also herewith delivered, the said Commissioners crave Leave humbly to observe, That, though the Revenue of Customs was higher in the Years 1687, and 1088; which arose visibly from the French Trade open at that time, than in the Years 1698, and 1699; in the former of which the Revenue had not found the full Effects of the Peace; yet that the Trade in these Two Years may be judged to be in a better State for the national Interest; inasmuch as the Duties upon Goods exported have exceeded the Accounts of the same in the former Years by 10,000l. a Year; which Increase of Exportation will answer to a very great Value in a foreign Market, towards the Advantage of this Kingdom, in the general Balance of Trade.

And, in farther Obedience to the said Order of the 29th, the said Commissioners crave Leave humbly to acquaint this Honourable House, That, upon the Observations they have made of the great Art and Industry that is daily used to import prohibited Goods, and clandestinely to import and land customable Goods, without Payment of the Duty, they have, for some time, had under Consideration the Heads of a Bill to prevent illegal and clandestine Trade in general, by setting it on a more equal Foot; and will beg Leave to offer the same to this Honourable House in a few Days; Which being what the Commissioners

missioners presume is expected from this Board, is most humbly submitted.

Walter Yonge, C. Godolphin,

Wm. St. Quintin, Sam.

T. Newport, Ite/z. Ovei'ton,

Robert Iienlcy.

And the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The late Duke of Holstein being dispossessed of his Country by the late King of Denmark; in the Year 1684; he was restored to it again by the Treaty of Aliena, concluded the 20th of June 1689.

The third Article of the said Treaty takes notice, That the Island of Eemcren, with the Lands and Baillages of Stcinhorst, Tremsbuttel, and Trittau, were mortgaged to the King of Denmark; and it was insisted on, That they should be restored to the Duke, free of all Incumbrances:

And, by the said Article, the King of Denmark agrees to the immediate Restitution of the Baillage of Trittau; but, as to the Island of Femeren; with the Baillages of Trems-buttell, and Steinhorst, it appearing, That the King of Denmark could not dispose of them, since they were in the Possession of his Brother, Prince George of Denmark~

That there might be no Obstruction, upon that Account, to the Settlement of Peace in those Parts; the Mediators took upon themselves to find out the Means, whereby the Prince of Denmark should have Satisfaction given him for his Mortgage, without having any Recourse for it to his Brother: The said Mediators did likewise undertake to procure the Prince of Denmark's Consent, That the said Island and Baillages should be restored to the Duke of Holstein, cigar of all Debts and Demands.

Memorandum. In the Act for 1,500,000 I. Bills there is a Clause, Page 132, That if the Aids or Supplies therein mentioned should be deficient to raise the said 1,500,000l.; such Deficiency should, in the first Place, be made good and supplied, out of any the Monies that should be raised by any Act or Acts of the then next Session of Parliament.

Bills, Page 521, it is enacted, That all the Bills which should not be cancelled by the Produce of the Funds or Supplies therein mentioned, by the 25th of March 1699, should be satisfied, as well by the Arrears of those Funds, as out of the Monies which should arise by any Aids to be granted in the then next Session of Parliament.

Humbly sheweth,

That there are several Cottages, and small Parcels of land, and other Premises, under small Rents, in several Counties, within the said Duchy and County Palatine, which have been out of Lease for some time; and being of small Value, nobody will be at the Charge of passing Leases thereof; by Reason of the double Stamp, and other Charges in passing thereof; and if some Care be not taken to let the same in time, those Rents may be lost, and the Premises concealed, to his Majesty's Loss and Damage thereby: To prevent which, And for that your Petitioner hath served his Majesty, and his Predecessors, near Twenty Years, in the said Duchy, and never had any Grant or Reward for his Services; Your Petitioner humbly begs your Lordship's Favour to grant him a Lease of the Premises, contained in a Paper hereunto annexed; Part whereof, being Reversions, though of small Value, yet together may compensate the Charges of passing the Lease of them with the others, and oblige your Petitioner,

A Petition of the Clothiers and Weavers of the Borough of Nezvberry in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, -and read; setting forth, That, since the Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures in Flanders, so great Stocks of Cloth remain upon the Petitioners Hands, that they are not able to employ their numerous W'ork-people; who are thereby reduced to very great Hardships: That by the many Advantages foreign Woollen Manufactures have, in the easy Price of Oil, Soap, and Dying-stuff, which adds to their cheap Workmanship, our Cloathing Trade is in Danger of being transplanted: And praying, That the Decay of our Woollen Trade maybe taken into Consideration; and that the Petitioners may be some way relieved in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom it was referred to consider what has been done upon former Laws against the Exportation of Wool; and for encouraging the Woollen Manufactures; and to report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Henry Boy sett, and several others, in be- Ditto, half of themselves, and a great many more disbanded and reduced Soldiers, or otherwise discharged, both Horse and Foot, who faithfully served his Majesty in the late Wars, and in the particular Regiments therein mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, when the Petitioners were severally discharged the Service, they demanded an Account of their Arrears, and the Horsemen their Horses, or Satisfaction, according to his Majesty's Orders; but, instead thereof, many were stript of their Cloaths, turned out without their Horse9, or any Account, and without a Farthing Subsistence to carry them home; and others forced by Threats and Punishments, to give Discharges in full for Subsistence, though they had not received it; and now after the Fatigue of a long War, not having wherewith to recover their Rights against their Officers by Law, they and their Families are in a starving Condition: And praying the House to take some speedy Course, That the Petitioners Officers may make up their Accounts, and pay what is justly due thereupon.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to w hom the Petition of Richard Nicholls, and others, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do take care, That the Soldiers be at no Charge, either to Solicitors, or otherwise, in relation to their petitioning, and attending this House.

A Petition of Captain Martin Lay cock, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner having spent his Blood, and Substance, in curing his Wounds, in the Service of this Government, and undergone as great Hardships as Fire, Water, Famine, Sword, and Imprisonment, can inflict; yet he has received no Recompence for it, though he had Two Orders for that Purpose, and an Order of the Treasury for 100l. per Annum Pension; nor so much as Half-pay, though in Service the 10th of September 1607, because his Name uas not upon the Muster-roll, and voted upon Half-pay by this House the 18th of April last; nor 668 /. 14 s. 81 d. stated by the late Commissioners for publick Accounts to be due to the Petitioner, before he went last into Flanders; nor 400l. due to* him as Executor to his Uncle Captain Beilby, for his Service in the Lord Douglass Regiment, though his said Uncles Burial cost 60/. by his Direction; by all which means, the Petitioner is run above 300l. in Debt, and his Family now in want of all Necessaries for this Life: And praying the House to grant him such speedy Redress in the Premises, as they shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the said Committee: And that they do particularly examine the Matter thereof'; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House, with all convenient Speed.

A Petition of Sir Henry Fitzharris Baronet, Grandson and Heir of Sir Edxcard Fitzharris Baronet, deceased, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in the Acts of Settlement of Irish Forfeitures there are several Provisions for the Restitution ofinnocent Protestants and Papists to their Estates; and the Petitioners Grandfather did clear his innocency; yet neither he, tior the Petitioner, were restored to the Estate of their Family; for which Reason the Petitioner did petition the last Par-Lament here, for Leave to bring in a Bill for restoring him to his paternal Estate, and to make Provision for his Mother and Sister; which was referred to a Committee; who reported, That the Petitioner had just Right and Title to be restored; but the House then having weighty Affairs before them, the Session ended before the House came to any Resolution thereupon: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for restoring him to his paternal Estate, and making Provision for his Mother and Sister

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same to the House, with their Opinion, Whether they conceive it fit that a Bill should be brought in, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

A PETITION of the Merchants, Clothiers, and other Traders in the Woollen Manufacture, in and about the Town of Leeds, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That since the Commissioners appointed by Act of Parliament, i° Gulielmi ct Maries, for putting the Laws in Execution for preventing the Exportation of Wool, did undertake the Management thereof, great Quantities of \v ool have been hindered from Transportation by the Diligence of the Commissioners Officers; but there being no Fund for discharging their Expence, the Commissioners are disabled from proceeding in the said Work; which, if a Fund were provided, would effectually stop the Exportation of Wool, to the great Advancement of the Woollen Manufactory Trade: And praying the House to raise a l and, by a Tax upon the Woollen Manufactures, or otherwise, as shall be thought fit, for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, who are to examine what has been done upon the former Laws against the Exportation of Wool; and for encouraging the Woollen Manufacture; and to report to the House their Opinion, what may be further necessary to be done.

A Petition of the Merchants, Clothiers, and other Expmtii Traders in the Woollen Manufacture, in and about the Town of JVakefcild, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That for many Years past little Care has been taken to prevent the Exportation of Wool, till, of late, the Commissioners appointed by Act of Parliament for that Purpose deputed several Officers; whose Diligence therein, for above 15 Months past, has greatly, and was further like to put a Stop to that pernicious Practice to the Woollen Manufactures; but, for want of a Fund for defraying the Charges necessary for so good a Work, the Commissioners are disabled from further proceeding in their said Trust, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and the Kingdom in general: And praying. That some Provision may be made for the encouraging the Agents employed in the said Undertaking, in such manner as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, who are to examine what has been done upon former Laws against the Exportation of Wool; and for encouraging the Woollen Manufacture; and to report to the House their Opinion, what may be farther necessary to be done.

tyskuch Mr. Carter reported from the Committee appointed to inspect the Journals of the House, for the last Session, what was done upon the Petition of John Goodall, and other Petitions relating to the Abuses of the Prisons of the Kings Bench and Fleet, and report the same to the House, That they had inspected the Journals accordingly, and collected thereout what had been done upon the said Petitions, and the Resolutions of the Committee, and afterwards of the House, thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That, on the Fourth Day of May last, Mr. Offley reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Vol, 13.

John Goodall, and the several Petitions of Mr. Lascoe'

Sir William Duncombe, Mr. Killigrav, Eleanor Smith John Praed, Thomas Hammersly, and Henry Caldecot, and Mr. Glover; were referred; and who were to inquire into the ill Practices and Abuses of the Prisons of the King's Bench and Fleet; the Matter as it appeared to the: said Committee, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That, upon the Petition of the said John Goodall, the Matter appeared as followeth:

Mr. Richard Day said, That, by Direction of Mr, Goodall, he caused John Kelson to be arrested in an Action for 2,800l.; who by Habeas Corpus removed himself to the Fleet Prison, where he was actually a Prisoner: That afterwards a Statute of Bankrupt issued against the said John Kelscn; and he was adjudged a Bankrupt by the Commissioners, Mr. Goodall the Petitioner having proved the said Debt before them; and Three of the said Commissioners, whereof the Informant was One, went to the Fleet, in order to examine the said Kelson, upon Oath, for a Discovery of his Estate; but, though he appeared before them, he obstinately refused to be sworn: Whereupon the said Three Commissioners, by Warrant under their Hands and Seals, dated the 4th of August 1697, and directed to the then Warden of the Fleet, did, by virtue of the said Commission, require and authorize the said Warden of the Fleet to detain the said Kelson in Custody, without Bail or Mainprize; since which, he has escaped without answering.

Thomas Leaky said, That he served Mr. Church, the , then Warden of the Fleet, with the said Warrant, the same Day as it bore Date; and Mr. Church owned, That the said Kelson was then his Prisoner.

In Answer to which, Mr. Ford, the now Warden of the Fleet, said, That he finds by the Commitment Books of the Fleet, that John Kelson was committed a Prisoner there, upon Mesne Process, the 31st of July 1697; but does not find any Entry of the said Warrant from the Commissioners of Bankrupt in any of the Fleet Books.

That he was sworn and admitted Warden of the Fleet on the 28th Day of September 1697; when he had an Indenture of Assignment of the Prisoners committed to his Charge, in Number about 100; but the said John Kcl* son is not named therein, nor was then in the Prison; neither does he know him, or ever saw him; nor knows what is become of him; but said, That since he was admitted Warden, he has superseded Goodall's Actions, and -produced the Supersedeas.

That he insisted, That the Commissioners of Bankrupts had no Power to charge the Warden of the Fleet with any Prisoners for a Contempt of their Demand; but he ought to be looked upon as a Criminal, and removed by Habeas Corpus to the County Gaol; and instanced the Case of one Gregory, a Bankrupt and Prisoner in the Compter, who brought Three several Habeas Corpus's to remove himself to the Fleet; and was as otten remanded to the Compter by the present Lord Chief Justice Treby.

That he further alleged, That the Warden cannot be charged with the Custody of any Prisoner, save by the Council Board, or Courts of Westminster-hall; for that a Justice of Peace cannot commit to the Fleet, much less Commissioners of Bankrupts.

Upon which, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner John Goodall has fully proved the Allegations of his Petition.

That upon the Petition of Mr. Lascoe, the Matter appeareth to be as followeth:

That Sir John James, and others^ was indebted to the Petitioner 1,400l. upon a Bond of 4,000l. Penalty: Upon which Sir John James was arrested, who turned himself over to the Fleet; and, in Trinity Term, 1697,

Sir John James was charged; and committed in Execu-

That, on the 16th Day of September 1697, Sir John James escaped, and was seen in Gerrard-street, near St. Anne s Church, W estminster, by Mr. Holden, the Petitioner's Attorney, and Mr. French; who asked him, What he did there ? He said, He was about his Business; and then voluntarily went with them to the Fleet; and they complaining of the said Escape to Mr. Church, the then Warden, he said, He had Security; but hoped no Kotice w ould be taken of the said Escape.

That, in Michaelmas Term, 1697, the Petitioner Mr. Lasco brought his Action of Escape against the said Mr. Church, and obtained Judgment thereon; and moved the Court of Common Pleas for a Sequestration; which was not granted, because the Judges thought the Petitioner could have no advantage thereby, by reason of the many Incumbrances that were upon the Office of the Fleet; since which the said Mr. Church is absconded; and as the Petitioner is informed. Sir John James hath, by Habeas Corpus, removed himself to the Kings Bench, from whence he hath also escaped.

Mr. Holding said, That the Door-keeper of the King's Bench told him, That Sir John James w as a Prisoner there; and Mr. Taylor, the then Marshal, told him, he should see Sir John James in Two or Three Days: After which, Holding went down again; but could not be admitted to see him. 1

That to this Petition Mr. Ford, the new Warden, answered, That he admits Sir John James was charged in Execution, as the Petition sets forth: That he was afterwards seen in Gerrard-street; and that Judgment was recovered against Mr. Church, as aforesaid; but that Judgment is referred to a Prothonotary, as irregular: And hopes it shall not be adjudged an Escape; the Prisoner returning the same Day, and a fresh Pursuit being allowed, by which he might have been taken.

That Sir John James was a Prisoner turned over to Ford, and was never, after the said 16th of September 1697, out of the Walls of the Prison, until he removed himself to the King's Bench by Habeas Corpus.

Mr. Gimbert, now Marshal of the King's Bench, said, That he was sworn Marshal, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, on the 29th of December last, when he had but One-and-thirty Prisoners committed to his Charge, or turned over to him, amongst which Sir John James is not named: But he has heard since his Admission, That Sir Jo. James wras a Prisoner to Mr. Taylor, the late Marshal; and that he suffered him to escape.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner Francis Lascoe has fully proved the Allegation of his Petition.

That after the said Verdict, and before Sevear could have any Benefit thereby, a late Act of Parliament passed, for the more effectual Relief of Creditors in Cases of Escapes; and for preventing Abuses of Prisons, and pretended privileged Places; wherein there is a Clause to vacate all Grants or Deputations then before made by Mr. Lenthall of the said Office, of which Smear declared lie had no Notice: And coming back to the Chancery, Smear's Bill was dismissed, because of the said Clause: That, since such Dismission, Seaver brought his Action of Covenant against Lenthall; and hath recovered 2,322 /. 17s. 6d. thereupon; as by Three several Judgments produced to the said Committee.

Sir William Williams also alleged, That Sevear had done all that the Law would allow, to do himself Right; and all that can be done, is only to confine Lenthall to his own House and Dominion; and can have no Satisfaction, without the Help of an Act of Parliament, though it has cost Sevear above 2,600l. as informed.

To prove which, he called John Stanley, Mr. Sevear s Attorney; who said, Mr. Sevear brought his Bill in Chancery, against Lenthall, Briggs, and others; and, before they answered, they preferred a cross Bill against Mr. Sevear; and those Suits, which the said Issue directed, and References to Masters, cost Mr. Sevear 1,500l. as he believes, besides what Costs he was at in prosecuting other Tryals at Law.

It appeared to the Committee, That George Moor had recovered Judgment against the said Mr. Lenthall, 30 Willi &$ Marice, for.2,025 /. for the Escape of Henry Paine, who was a Prisoner in Execution to Mr. Lenthall, when lie executed the Office of Marshal himself:

That Moor issued out an Elegit, and seized Part of Lent hall's Goods and Estate in Oxfordshire; which Goods were sold, and produced about 100l. besides Charges: But he was turned out of Possession of the Lands by Mr. Boulter, by virtue of a prior Incumbrance; and can have no Relief against Lenthalls Person, because those Persons, who have since exercised the Office of the Marshal of the King's Bench, have been favourable to Mr. Lenthall:

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That thepresent Offices of the Marshal of the King's Bench, and Warden of the Fleet Prisons, in respect of their Management, have been very prejudicial to personal Credit, and a great Grievance to the whole Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the many Incumbrances on the said Offices do cover those Prisons against Judgments in Cases of Escapes; whereby the good Intention of the late Act of Parliament for the Relief of Creditors is eluded, the Keepers of the said Prisons, for Bribes, continuing to suffer Escapes, and the Creditors left without Remedy for the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Habeas Corpus shall be hereafter granted for Removing of Prisoners, in personal Actions, to any of the Courts at Westminster-hall, in order to be turned over to the King's Bench or Fleet Prisons, but upon sufficient Cause shewn by the Defendant, or some Person for him, in Open Court, in the Presence of the Plaintiff or some Person authorized by him.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Way for preventing the Abuses of the King's Bench and Fleet Prisons is, by discharging the Incumbrances that are upon the said Prisons, by Sale of the said Offices, or otherwise: And that, for the future, neither of the said Offices should be liable to any incumbrance, except upon Escapes.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the present Offices of the Marshal of the King's Bench, and Warden of the Fleet Prisons, in respect of their Management, have been very prejudicial to personal Credit, and a great Grievance to the whole Kingdom.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the many Incumbrances^ on the said Offices do cover those Prisons against Judgments in Cases of Escapes; whereby the good Intention of the late Act of Parliament for Relief of Creditors is eluded, the Keepers of the said Prisons, for Bribes, continuing to suffer Escapes, and the Creditors left without Remedy for the same.

The Third Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by leaving out " but upon sufficient Cause shewn by the " Defendant, or some Person for him, in open Court, in the Presence of the Plaintiff, or some Person authorized by him;" and inserting, instead thereof, " and " if any Person shall be removed by Habeas Corpus, and " the Person so removed shall not be bailed, or totally €t discharged, that then the Person so removed shall be <c remanded to the Prison from whence he was brought :n And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Petition of a Multitude of poor Prisoners for Debt, (hat lie in the King's Bench and Fleet, for and on the behalf of themselves, and many Thousand other the like Prisoners in the several Prisons \n London-and Westminster, and Suburbs thereof, and in the many Prisons in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by the Abuse of the Coin, and the Tediousness of the late War, and many other inevitable Losses, (hey have been reduced to Poverty, and! imprisoned by their Creditors; where many of them have lain in a starving Condition many Years* to the Ruin of their Families, who, bad they been at Liberty, might have paid their Debts, and been useful to the Kiblick; but now are a great Burden to the same; the Prisoners in England being computed at 60,000 Souls, who chiefly subsist by lagging at the Grate of the Prisons; and, when that Charity faila, they starve, as weekly Examples' testify, to the Dishonour of this Protestant Kingdom, and Damage thereof, from many contagious Distempers, which oftentimes have their Beginning in Prisons: And praying the consideration of the House, That they may be relieved, either by causing them to be discharged, under such reasonable Conditions as shall be adjudged fit, or by some speedy Methods for their support and Maintenance, either from their Creditors, who detain them, or otherwise, as shall be found to be convenient; and that a Bill be brought in accordingly.

Ordered, That the Conskieration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report to the House what they do conceive proper to be done for the Petitioners Relief.

setting forth, That, notwithstanding the Resolutions of this House the 6th of February 1696; the Lord Coningsby and Mr. Foj's. A Petition of Charles Here ton, and others, Afasters of Ships of Newcastle, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is due to the Petitioners above 2,381/. for Transport Service, in 1693; and though they borrowed Aiouey at Interest, for victualling and carrying on the said Service, yet the Petitioners have received no manner of Satisfaction; for want whereof they are reduced to very great Streights: And praying, That Consideration may be had of their said Debts, so as they may be paid what is due to them.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.
