Irish And he acquainted the House, That the Report of the

Forfeitures. Commissioners was signed by Four of them; and was an Index to all the rest of the Books:

That they had the Misfortune, that Three of the Gen- tlemen that acted in the Commission with them;

The Earl of Drogheda, Sir Francis Brczvster, and Sir Richard Lecing, did refuse to sign it ;they having some Objections to 8or g Paragraphs in the Report; and therefore they would not sign, but with a Protestation to those 8 or Nine Paragraphs; but that the Four thought it not proper, that Three should sign to a Protestation against the rest, and so they ordered that Leaf, wherein they were named, to be cut out: And afterwaeds, the Report being made intire, the Four signed and sealed it, pursuant to the Act of Parliament, being a Quorum; and afterwards they desired the Three would do the same; but they refused it;

That they gave them a Day to consider of it; and they attended the Execution; and refused to sign it; and gave their Reasons; a Copy of which also he had ready to deliver in, with the rest, if the House pleased:

As also the Paper which was cut out, with the Earl of Drogheda's Name, and the other Gentlemens.

He also acquainted the House, That the Commissioners had sooner attended this House with their Proceedings in this Matter, their Commission being determined the 25th of October; but that the Matter was of so extraordinary Nature, so long, and so many Difficulties did attend it, that he hoped die Time they had taken, will not be ill construed; for that they lost no Time, they not being, one Hour in a Day, absent from the Duty incumbent on them.

And they hoped, That if any thing should be said to their Prejudice, the House will not harbour an ill Opinion of them; but will hear them: And then they doubted not but to give an Answer to the Satisfaction of the House.

And then he withdrew.

And the Report, being the 10th Book, was read.

And also the Memorial of Three of the Commissioners, and the cut Sheet of Paper, with their Names thereto, were also read.

A PETITION of the Wardens and Assistants of importing the Company of Worsted Weavers, in the City of Wrought Norwich, and County of Norfolk, on behalf of themselves, &c*

and others of the same Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners trade is very much improved in the Making all Sorts of Stuffs of English Wool, fit for all Sorts of Persons; and met with great Encouragement during the late War, by reason the East India Company did not import so many Indian Commodities as formerly: But now the Petitioners Trade labours under very great Difficulties; and will be in Danger of being lost, unless some Restraint be laid, or Stop put to the Importation or Consumption of the vast Quantities of Wrought Silks, Bengalis, and printed and stained Callicoes, daily imported from India, which are worn instead of our Manufactures: And praying the Consideration of the House, and Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the State and Condition of the Trade of England.

A Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, free Men, and chief Inhabitants, of the ancient To\yn and Port in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Harbour of is the only Harbour for Ships that the English have upon the Coast of Kent and Sussex, from the Downes to Portsmouth, Vol. 13.

which is above 100 Miles by Sea: It lies very convenient for Ships sailing from East to West in Stress of Weather; and lies opposite to Diep, and other Ports of France; and Ships of War, of considerable Strength, used to ride there, to hinder French Ships from infesting our Coast; and, besides, the Mouth of the Harbour is but 60 Fathom wide; so that a Fort might he built there, at a small Charge, which will hinder an Enemy from coming to annoy the Ships riding in Rye Harbour: That the Tide used to flow and reflow, near 24 Miles from the said Harbour, up the River Rot her; whereby small Vessels

used

68 16° — i 8* Decenthr 1699*

used to convey the Commodities of several Towns to the Town of Rye; which thereby had a considerable Trade; and the Fishery also was then much better than now: All which Conveniences and Advantages of the said Harbour . are in Danger of being lost, by reason that several Persons, of late Years, have inned several Acres of Land belonging to the said Harbour, and built Flood-gates, and made cross Walls, which hinder the Tide from its usual Flux and Reflux; whereby the Slub is stopped; and Seven Fathom Water, at Low-water Mark, is now brought to 3 Fathom, and yearly grows worse and worse; so that, unless some Care be taken therein, a Ship of Burden will not be able to come into Rye Harbour; And praying, That such Course may be taken for restoring the said Harbour to its ancient Goodness, as shall be thought fit; that so considerable a Harbour for the Benefit of the whole Kingdom may not be lost.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter; and report to the House, by what Means the said Harbour became so obstructed and decayed; and what they conceive is fit to be done in relation to the said Harbour.

A Petition of the many Prisoners in the County Prisons of England, particularly in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by Losses and Misfortunes, are detained in Prison for Ten times more than they owe, by the Contrivance of ill Attorneys, holding them to excessive Bail, and by outlawing them without Notice, to their utter Ruin; against which there is no Redress, but by a Suit at Law, which poor Prisoners are no ways able to undergo: That, by the late Composition Act, many hundred Prisoners in and about London were discharged; but the Prisoners in remote Parts did not know of the said Act, till the Time therein limited was past: So that the Petitioners are without Remedy, reduced to great Want, without the Relief of this JUouse: And praying, That Consideration may he had of their deplorable Condition: and some Remedy may be found out for their Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of VOL 13.

the Prisoners in the Prisons of the King's Bench and Fleet is referred.

The said Copy of his Majesty's Order of the 29th of May last, relating to Retrenchments in the Establishment of the Navy;

My Lords, Whitehall, 29th May 1699.

His Majesty commands me to acquaint you, That he would have you take into Consideration, and lay before him, what you think may be conveniently retrenched from the present Charge of the Navy; and particularly that you apply yourselves to consider what relates to Half-pay, or double Half-pay, pretended to by the Officers of the Fleet in time of Peace; and how far the same may be fit to be continued. I am, my Lords,

Your Lordships most faithful humble Servant,

A true Copy. Ja. Vernon.

The said Memorial concerning Retrenchments in the Navy, pursuant to his Majesty's Order of the 29th of May 1699.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England.

Memorial for their Excellencies the Lords Justices.

His Majesty's Pleasure having been signified to us, by the Right Honourable Mr. Secretary Vernon, the 29th of May last, that we should consider, and lay before his Majesty, what we think may be most conveniently retrenched from the present Charge of the Navy; and that we should particularly consider what relates to Half-pay, and the double Half-pay, pretended to by the Officers of the Fleet in time of Peace; and bow far tire same may be fit to be continued: And their Excellencies the Lords Justices.

U having

0

18 Decetnbris* A. 1699.

Kavy Esta* yUbmcaU

having lately signified their Pleasure to us, That, in pursuance of his Majesty's said Commands, we should consider of and prepare a Scheme to be laid before them, for lessening the Expences of the several Branches of the Navy: We do humbly report to their Excellencies, in the following Method, what we have already ordered to be retrenched since his Majesty's Pleasure was signified to us; and what other Heads have fallen under our Con- ' sideration for Retrenchments; Which we most humbly expect their Excellencies Directions in; viz.

We did, in the first Place, give Orders for discharging the Muster-masters at Yai'mouth and , whose

Salaries together amounted to 1.50 /. per Annum.

We have ordered ttye Navy Board to cause all possible Dispatch to be made, in the Finishing the new 5th Rate building at Kinsale; and that, so soon as the same is done, not only the Officers and Workmen now in Pay there be retrenched, but the Yards also, and Houses hired therein on occasion of the War, and the Hulks, Transport Vessels, and Stores brought away, and only the Person continued there, who now serves as Store-keeper and Clerk of the Cheque, to look after the King's Yard and Houses, and muster the Ships, which shall have Occasion, from time to time, to come to that Port; whereby the yearly Charge of about 1,500l. will be saved.

And, in regard it is intended the Squadron now in the Streights shall be called home, Orders will be given for sending from thence the Officers belonging to One of the Two Hulks, which Hulks are to be left with the Officers only of One, to do what is necessary for cleaning and careening the Squadron going against Sally; so that the yearly charge of 138/. will by this means be retrenched.

The Solicitor for the Affairs of this and the Navy Office having had 100l. a Year during the War, that Salary is retrenched; and he is to do the Duty of his Place for his Fees only.

As for the Charge, which his Majesty has been at upon account of the Officers, for managing the Affairs of the Register, and Sick and Wounded, we have ordered the Navy Board, according to their own Proposals, to cause the same to be performed by Members of their Board, not charged with any particular Branch of the Business of their Office, and the like Directions will be given for the carrying on by those Gentlemen the Business for collecting the Sixpences, according to Act of Parliament, from Seamen, towards maintaining the Hospital at;

by which Retrenchment, including the Instruments necessary to assist the Commissioners appointed for this Service, his Majesty will be eased of the Charge of more than 2,000 /. per Annum.

Having thus laid before their Excellencies the several Particulars, which we have already ordered to be retrenched for easing the growing Charge, which amounts to near 4,000l. per Annum, we pray Leave humbly to inentiotv some other Heads, which have been proposed by the principal Officers and Commissioners of the Navy for Retrenchments, together with our Observations thereon; viz.

1st. That of Secretary to the Fleet, in regard every Admiral,... is presumed, may reasonably expect to have the Choice of his own Secretary. Upon this Head, wc pray Leave to inform their Excellencies, That this standing Office of Secretary to the Fleet was approved of, and directed by his Majesty, and accordingly he was established, as well for Peace as War, at the Allowance of 450 /. per Annum for himself and Clerk: The then Board of Admiralty did think it advisable to recommend such an Officer, in regard not only of the Trust incident to the Employment, but that they might have more particular Accounts of all Transactions in the Fleet; and in regard it has heretofore happened, as possibly it may hereafter, that the Choice of such an Officer by the Admiral may sufficiently shew what Caution ought to be taken who is admitted to that Trust; and that the Expence thereof has often amounted, during the late War, to as much, or more than the Allowance to the present Officers: It is therefore most humbly submitted to their Excellencies,

whether this Office shall be retrenched, or continued as it is.

2. There is an Officer, who has, during the late War, and still does enjoy the Salary of 200l. per Annum, upon account of building Bomb Vessels for his Majesty; and though the Want of such an Officer may, at this time, in our humble Opinion, be dispensed with; yet, in regard he was appointed by his Majesty's special Warrant, we do humbly submit it to their Excellencies.

3. Another Person has, for many Years, enjoyed the Salary of 50/. per Annum, as Surveyor of the Woods in New England: His Business is, as he informs us, the Taking Care to preserve the Trees in those Parts fit for Masts; and he says, That in doing it, he yearly expends the Moiety of his Salary. The Navy Board acquaint us, That they do not remember any Benefit has accrued to the Navy by the Service of this Person; wherefore we shall only inform their Excellencies, That he holds his Employment under the Great Seal, and submit his Case to their Excellencies Pleasure.

4. As to what relates to the Sea Officers their being allowed double Pay while at Sea, and Half-pay on Shore, we have had under our Consideration what Alterations or Retrenchments may be made in that Particular; but it being a matter of such Consequence, as requires a very mature Consideration, !>efore any Opinion be given concerning the same, we shall accordingly weigh every particular Circumstance relating the reunto, with respect not only to the Good of the Service, but the comfortable Support of the Officers; and give their Excellencies our Opinion upon the Whole as soon as possibly may be.

And having thus laid before their Excellencies, not only the several Particulars already retrenched by us, but those also which have been offered to us for Retrenchments, with our Observations thereon, we pray Leave further to observe, That notwithstanding what has been, since the War, retrenched by the late Board, what has further been done therein by us, and what other Methods ought to be taken, for easing the present Charge, as far as it may consist with the Good of his Majesty's Service, the principal Officers and Commissioners of his Majesty's Navy have represented to us the Evils, which attend the Taking off the Assistants to the Surveyor, Clerk of the Acts, and Comptroller of the Victualling Accounts, as also the Reduction of the Salaries to the chief Clerks in the Ticket Office; inso much that they acquaint us, they should think it unanswerable in them, did they not represent it to us as a Retrenchment wholly unsafe for his Majesty both in his Service and Treasure, and for them in their Management thereof, while assisted by Persons labouring under Salaries so little adequate to the Trusts committed to them, or the Qualifications fitting them for the same: Whereupon we did, some Days since, direct those Gentlemen, That, in case their present Instructions were not sufficient to enable them effectually to carry on his Majesty's Service, they should propose unto us what they thought proper, with respect to the Adding no greater Charge to the Navy than was absolutely necessary; and they having thereupon recommended to us the Continuance of the Second Assistant to the Surveyor of the Navy at 150 /. per Annum, and the Assistants to the Clerk of the Acts and Comptroller of the Victualling at 300 /. per Annum each; as also the Salaries of the chief Clerk to the Comptroller of the Navy in the Business of Wages, and the Two chief Clerks of the Ticket Office, at 200l. per Annum each; we thought it our Duty humbly to acquaint their Excellencies, That, upon Consideration of the great Increase of Business in the late War, it was, on the repeated Instances of the Navy Board, thought for the Service to appoint Two Assistants to the Surveyor of the Navy, and to increase the Salary of the Comptroller's chief Clerk, and to the Two chief Clerks to the Ticket Office, that of the Assistant to the Clerk of the Acts having been an Office at the Salary of 300l. per Annum, as well before as during the whole Time of the late War: But, in regard the former Board did think it necessary intirely to reduce the aforesaid Assistants, and to retrench the Salaries of the

Thre«

11 W. III.

18° Decembris.

Three Clerks; and the Navy Board have since, in so pressing a manner, represented the Inconveniencies thereof, and the Necessity there is of restoring both the one and the other, we do most humbly report our Opinion to their Excellencies, That, in regard those Gentlemen are, by daily Experience, the most proper Judges what Assistance is wanting, to enable them to carry on the Business of their Office to the Advantage of his Majesty's Service, we cannot do otherwise than advise the restoring the afore-mentioned Officers, and the Salaries to the Clerks, lest otherwise the Discipline and Oeconomy of the Navy be. subjected to the Inconveniencies those Gentlemen are apprehensive of: We do most humbly submit the same to their Excellencies, for such Directions therein as their Excellencies shall think fit Dated at the Admiralty Office this 27th July 1699.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Foot Onslow Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Guildford in the County of Surrey.

A Petition of the Dean and Chapter of Westminster Westminster was presented to the House, and read; setting forth; Small L'ebu‘ That time out of tnind there hath been an ancient Court of Record, held every Three Weeks, within the City and Liberties of Westminster, for the Ease and Relief of such Persons as had just Cause of Action, for any Debt or Damages under 4 os.by Way of Summons, and Distress

of the Defendant's Goods, in case of his Noa-appearance:

But some Persons, unknown to the Petitioners, are endeavouring to pass a Bill in this House, for erecting and establishing a Court of Conscience within the City of Westminster, and Liberties thereof; which, the Petitioners are advised, will rather prove a Detriment to thfe Inhabitants than a Convenience; there being as speedy and easy Relief already in the said Three Weeks Court as can well be granted; and praying, That no such Bill may pass until the Petitioners be heard by Counsel*

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time*

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City and Liberty Di^ta> of Westminster was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That within the said City and Liberties there is an ancient Court, holding Piea of Debt and Damages under 40 s.in which there always was a speedy and easy Remedy for Recovery of small Debts, until lately the Proceedings of the said.....hath met with some Ob-

structions; and therefore Persons have been unwilling to trust for small Sums, for w ant of an easy Remedy for Recovery thereof; which hath greatly prejudiced the poorer Sort of People, who want small Credit for carrying on their Trades: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for removing the said Obstructions, and restoring the ancient Remedy in the said Court for the Recovery of small Debts.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for erecting and establishing a Court of Conscience within the City of Westminster, and Liberties thereof, be read a Second time.

Bristoll, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That it is found by Experience, that nothing tends more to the promoting the Strength and Wealth of the Kingdom than Trade and Navigation having Communication with Places that tend to maritime Ports: And the River Avon being capable of being made navigable from the said City to Bath, the Petitioners pray, That an Act may pass for that purpose.

A Petition of Sir Edward Mansell Baronet, Stephen Martha Str'mger, and others, Owners of the Ship Martha of Ship. Mar gam, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Ship was shipwrecked on Kenfigg Sands in 1698, where she was beaten almost to Pieces by the Sea; and bought, with her Riggings, for 301. by the Petitioners; and rebuilt with new Timber, new Beams, a new Deck, and 40 Tons larger than before; which cost above 800l. with her Rigging, and other Necessaries; but, she being a foreign Bottom, some Doubts have arisen, whether, by an Act for preventing Frauds, and regular ting Abuses, in the Plantation Trade, she is not prohibited to trade to or from any of his Majesty's Plantations or Colonies: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill to make the said Ship, a free Ship to trade and traffick to and from the Ports of this Kingdom, to any of his Majesty's Plantations or Colonies.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Edward Stradling, Sir Thomas Day, and Mr. Cox, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Mr. Eyres reported, from the Committee, to whom the Consideration of the Petition of the Clothiers, and Woollen Manufacturers, within the City of New Sarum, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands of poor Persons depending on them, was referred, the Resolution of the said Committee; which they had directed him to report to the House, which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Bill be brought in, to repeal an Act of Parliament made in the 9th and 10th Years of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for rendering the Laws more effectual for preventing the Importation of foreign Bone-lace, Loom-lace, Needle-work, Point, and Cut-work.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the said Report be recommitted to i the same Committee.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do inform themselves of the Allegations of the said Petition; and report the Fact, as it appears to the said Committee, with their Opinion what is fit to be done.

A Petition of several Makers of and Dealers in Bone-lace, made in Buckinghamshire, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Manufacture has been exercised several hundred Years in England\ end employs many Thousands in the said County; most whereof are Women and Children, who have no other Subsistence; and the repealing the Acts prohibiting the Importation of foreign Bone-lace will inevitably tend to the Ruin of the said poor People, although the same are no Prejudice to the Trade of the Woollen Manufacture, as the Petitioners are ready to prove: And praying, that they may be heard against the Repeal of the said Act.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the said Committee: And that the Petitioners be heard before the said Committee thereupon.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do inquire into the Value of the yearly Exportation of the Woollen Manufacture into Flanders, in the Time of Peace.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

I. The said Copy of the said Commissions to Captain Long, Captain Hunter, Captain Dampier, and Captain Haley.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England, Ireland, &c.

To Captain Richard Long, hereby appointed Captain of his Majesty's Ship the Rupert Prize.

By virtue of the Power and Authority to Us given*

We do hereby constitute and appoint you Captain of his Majesty's Ship the Rupei't Prize, willing and requiring you forthwith to go on board, and take, upon, you the Charge and Command of Captain in her accordingly; strictly charging and commanding all the Officers and Company of the said Ship to behave themselves, jointly and severally, in their respective Employments, with all due Respect and Obedience unto you their said Captain; and you likewise to observe and execute, as well the standing Instructions hereunto annexed, attested by our Secretary, as what further Order and Directions you shall from time to time receive of Us, or any other your super rior Officers, for his Majesty's Service: Hereof you, nor any of you, may fail, as you will answer the same at your Perils: And for so doing this shall be your Warrant.

Given under our Hands, and the Seal of the Office of the Admiralty, this 4th Day of December 1697, in the Ninth Year of his Majesty's Reign.

Henry Priestman,

By Command of their Lordships, Robert Rich,

JVm. Bridgman. Geo. Rook,

VII. The said Copy of Instructions of Captain Haley, of the Paramour Pink, for the finding out the Variation of the Needle.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England, Ireland, Sic. Whereas his Majesty has been pleased to lend his Pink the Paramour, for your proceeding a Second time with her, on an Expedition to improve the Ivnowlege of the Longitude, and Variation of the Compass; which Ship is now completely manned, stored and victualled, at his Majesty's Charge, for the said Expedition: You are therefore hereby required and directed forthwith to proceed with her,' according to the following Instructions.

You arc, without Loss of Time, to set Sail with her, and proceed to make a Discovery of the unknown South Lands between the Magellan Streights, and the Cape of Good Hope, between the Latitude of 50 and 55 South, if you meet not with the Land sooner; observing the Variation of the Compass with all the Accuracy you can; as also the true Situation, both in Longitude and Latitude, of the Ports where you arrive.

You are likewise to make the like Observations at as many of the Islands, in the Seas between the aforesaid Coasts, as you can, without too much Deviation, bring into your Course.

In your Return home, you are to visit the English West India Plantations, or as many of them as conveniently you may; and in them to make such Observations as may contribute to lay them down truly in their geographical Situation: And, in all the Course of your Voyage, you must be careful to omit no Opportunity of noting the Variation of the Compass; of which you are to keep a Register in your Journal.

You are, for the better lengthening out your Pro-VOL. 13.

visions, to put the Men under your Command, when you come out of the Chanel, to Six to Four Mens Allowance; assuring them, That they shall be punctually paid at the End of the Voyage.

You are, during the Term of this Voyage, to be very careful in conforming yourself to what is directed by the general printed Instructions annexed to your Commission, with regard as well to his Majesty's Honour, as to the Government of the Ship under your Command: And, when you return to England, you are to call in at

mouth, and, finding no Orders there to the contrary, to make the best of your Way to the Downes, and remain there till further Order. Dated at the Admiralty Office, the 12th of September 1699,

J. Bridgwater, Haversham,

To Captain Edmund Haley, Com- D. Mitchell. mander of his Majesty's Pink the Paramour, at Deptjaid.

IX. The said Copy of the Instructions to Captain Dampier, of the Roebuck, far making Discoveries in foreign Parts.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England, Ireland, &c. Whereas, upon some Proposals of your making Discoveries in foreign Parts, which may be of Advantage to the Publick, it hath been thought fit to appoint you Commander of his Majesty's Ship the Roebuck', and that you shall proceed with the said Ship upon the aforesaid Service: You are therefore hereby required and directed, forthwith upon your Receipt hereof, to proceed with her till you shall come near the Ca Hope, and from thence stretch away towards New Holland, and then to New Guinea, and Terra Australis: But in case, either with relation to the Seasons of the Year, or any other good Reason that shall occur to you, you shall think it may more conduce to the Service you are going on, to steer any other Course than what is before directed, you are hereby impowered and directed to do the same: And, in regard his Majesty is at great Charge in fitting out, and maintaining at Sea, the Ship you command for this Service, you are therefore to take especial Care, that your utmost Endeavours be used towards the discovering all such Things, in those Parts of the World where you shall proceed, as you shall judge may any ways tend to the Good of the Nation: And, to that End, you are to bring home with you some of the Produce of the Places you touch at, where you shall think it material: And you are likewise at Liberty to bring home some of the Natives, provided they are willing to come along with you: For the better enabling you to do the same, and to keep a Correspondence with the said Natives, we have, according to what you propose, given Orders for your being furnished with several Things you desire, and some other Trifles, to trade with them.

And whereas it may probably happen, That, during the Course of your intended Voyage, some of your Ship's Company may die, or that others may prove so disorderly as to make it necessary for you to part with them; We do hereby give you Permission to exchange such disorderly Persons with any Ship or Vessel of his Majesty's Subjects you shall meet with, in case the Master of such Ship or Vessel consent thereunto: But in case you shall, at any time, during your being abroad, meet with any of his Majesty's

Dolphin, &c. Ships, and Instructions for Discovt* ries.

88 ao° — 2i° Decembris. 1699.

Majesty's Ships, and that you shall not then have your Complement of Men, their Commanders are hereby required and directed, upon your Application, to spare you so many as conveniently they can: And in case you shall also have on board any Persons, that shall have endeavoured to cause any Disturbance in the Ship, so as that you shall think it for the Service, that they be removed . from her, the Commander of any such Ship or Vessel of his Majesty's is hereby further required to take them on board, and give you other Men in their Room, and to keep the said disorderly Persons in safe Custody till he returns to England, that they may be brought to Tryal, and punished, for their Offence: And as you are strictly to comply with what is before directed, as to such of your Ship's Company as shall misbehave themselves; so are you, before you sail, to make it publickly known, not only to all your Officers, but Men, that such as shall behave themselves well, and chearfully perform their Duty, in this Affair, which, it is hoped, may tend to the Advantage of the Nation, shall, at their Return, receive all fitting Reward and Encouragement.

You are, during your whole Voyage, to keep an exact Journal of your Proceedings, and of all Things remarkable, which shall occur to you; which, at your Return, you are to deliver, fairly writ, to this Board, under your Hand, and to no other; taking care to conform yourself to what is directed by the general printed Instructions annexed to your Commission, with regard as well to his Majesty's Honour, as to the Government of the Ship under your Command; except as to what relates to your Journal, as aforesaid: And when you shall find, that youv can make no further Discovery for the Good of the Nation, you are to take care not to put the King to any unnecessary Charge by staying abroad, but to return to England, as soon as may be, with the Ship you command, calling in at Plymouth; from whence, if you find no Orders there to the contrary, you are to repair to the Downes, and remain there till further Orders: And you are, by all Opportunities which you shall meet with, to send this Board an Account of your Proceedings: And, during the whole Term of your Voyage, you are to take particular Care not to annoy any of his Majesty's Subjects, or those of his Allies, but rather to give them what Assistance you can, without Hindrance or Prejudice to the Affair whereon you are employed.

And, for the better lengthening out your Provisions, you are to put the Men under your Command, when you come out of the Chanel, to Six to Four Men's Allowance; assuring them, That they shall be punctually paid for the same at the End of the Voyage. Dated at the Admiralty Office, this 30th of November 1698.

To Captain Dampier, Commander H. Priestman, of his Majesty's Ship the Roc- G. Rooke, buck: Downes. J. Kendall.

Sir Rowland Gwynn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to the said Committee, touching the Election for the County of Bedford; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; w'hich they had directed him to report to the House; and which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of William Duncomb and Thomas Bromsall Esquires, complaining of an undue Election, and Return, of the Lord Edward Russell and Sir Wm. Gostwick to serve for the County of Bedford:

That the ^Majority of the Poll was agreed to be with the Sitting Members.

But the Petitioners Counsel complained of an irregular Proceeding in Two Points:

1st, That Persons w'ho had voted for One of the Candidates, and afterwards came, and would have given their Second Vote for another Candidate, were denied their Second Vote.

2dly, That several of the Sitting Members Votes were gained by Treating.

That, upon the First Point, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if a Person, having a Right to vote for Tw o Members to serve in Parliament, shall give a single Vote, such Person hath not a Right to come afterwards, and give his Second Vote, during the said Election,

That, as to the' Point of Treating, the Counsel called several Witnesses:

John Green said, That he kept the Falcon Inn at Bedford; and that Mr. Hayes, formerly a Servant to Sir Wm. Gostwick, but now an Innkeeper at Bedford, took up his Inn for the Lord Russell and Sir Wm. Gostwick: That Mr. Blosse, Sir Wm. Gostwick's Servant, told the said Green} He should receive wrhat Money he could of the Freeholders, and Sir Wm. Gostwick would pay the rest: That, in August last, he went to Sir Wm. Gostwick's, to ask his Money: That Sir Wm. A PETITION of the Clothiers, and others con- Exporting f\ cemed in the Woollen Manufactures, residing in Wool, the Borough of Reading in the County of Berks, in behalf of themselves and thousands of Poor depending on them, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That, for many Years, most of the Petitioners Manufactures have been exported to Flanders, where they are now prohibited, by reason some of their Manufactures are prohibited here; so that they are setting up the Trade of making Cloth there, to the Impoverishing of the Petitioners, and the Ruin of many poor Families, who are become burdensome to the said Borough for want of Employment: And the Petitioners conceive, That the vast Quantities of Wool exported hath also very much conduced to the Decay of bur Woollen Manufacture; which might he prevented, if a sufficient Fund wrere provided, to delray the Charge of proper Officers, to put the Laws in Execution, for suppressing that Mischief: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, for the Encouragement of the Consumption of the English Woollen Manufactures in foreign Parts; and that the Laws, to prevent the Exportation of Wool, may be diligently executed.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Consideration of the Petition of the Clothiers, and Woollen Manufacturers, within the City of New Sarum} and others depending on them, is referred.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of Richard Nicholls, and others, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That within the said City, and Liberties thereof, there is an ancient Court, holding Pleaof Debts and Damages under 405.; which was an easy and speedy Remedy for Recovery of small Debts, until, of late, the Proceedings of the said Court have been obstructed; and Persons are unwilling to trust for small Sums, because they cannot recover them but at great Charge; whereby the poorer Sort of People, who have not ready Money, cannot be trusted for Goods to employ themselves in their Trades; whose Poverty thereby daily increaseth: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for removing the said Obstructions, and recovering the ancient Remedy by suit in the said Court.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Harcourt and Mr. Thursby do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

Mr. Carter reported, from the Committee, to whom it was referred to inspect the Journals for the last Sessions, what was done upon the Petition of John Goodall, and others, relating to the Abuses of the Prisons of the Kings Bench and Fleet, the Matter, upon the Petition of Jacob Massey, and others, touching the Escape of one Feiting, a Dutchman, as it appeared to the Committee; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio weth; viz.

That Mr. Grove, the Petitioners Counsel, opened the Petitioners Case as in the Petition; and alledged, That in case his Clients had proceeded as far as the Law would allow; yet, by the Practice of the Wardens of the Fleet in suffering Escapes, a Plaintiff is no nearer the Recovery of his Debt than when he commenced his Action; by reason that he must begin a new' Action of Escape against the Warden, if ever any Satisfaction is expected: And proceeded to prove the Matter of the Petition.

Mr. Rudge, the Petitioners Attorney, said, That in June last the Petitioner Massey told him, That he, and the rest of the Petitioners, had delivered to one FYitrng, a Dutchman, at the City of Paris, certain Diamonds, of the Value of 700 /. to be by him polished for the Petitioners; and that Feiting had run away with the Diamonds, and was come to England; and desired Mr. Rudge to advise him what was fit to be done therein: Upon which, Mr. Rudge advised an Action of Trover; and accordingly Feiting was arrested in London, at the Suit of the Petitioner Massey only.

That Feiting turned himself over to the Fled by Habeas Corpus: in obtaining which, he being brought before Judge Poxcell, the Informant prayed, in behalf of his Clients, That Feiting might be kept in safe Custody of the Warden of the Fleet; and the Judge strictly charged, That he should. And afterwards the Informant, while Feiting was in Custody, delivered at the Fleet Five several Declarations in Five Actions, at the several Suits of the Petitioners.

Since which, the Warden of the Fleet did own to the Informant, That Feiting had escaped from the Fleet: notwithstanding which, the Petitioner Massey proceeded in his said Action; and, upon a Writ of Enquiry of Damages, a Jury of Middlesex gave him 310/. Damages, besides Costs of Suit: But the Petitioner cannot charge the said Feiting in Execution, by reason of the said Escape.

Mr. Groce also called one Hall, a Witness, to prove the other Part of the Petition; which charges, That the Warden of the Fleet took 20 Guineas Consideration for the Escape of Feiting: But, his Evidence being only Hearsay, the Committee did not think fit to examine him.

To answer which Complaint;

Mr. Ford, the Warden of the Fleet, owned, That Feiting was his Prisoner as aforesaid, and is escaped; but that he took all the Care he could to prevent it, having heard that Feiting had formerly broke Gaol, for which Reason, he not only confined him within the Walls of the Prison, but set a Waiter over him Night and Day, and designed to remove him to the King's Bench; which Feitp ing hearing of, proposed to give Security by Four Persons, such as he believes the Sheriff would have accepted, for his true Imprisonment; who accordingly entered into a Bond of 2*oooo/. to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner's Father was seised of divers Manors and Lands; and, as he thought, upon the Marriage of his eldest Son William, sufficiently entailed the Barton and Demesnes of Hartraw, and other Manors, upon his Issue Male; and conveyed his Manors of Kingston, Seymour,

Upton, and Storminster, in the Counties of Somersett, Gloucester, and Dorsett, to Trustees for raising 2,400l. for Portions for his Three Daughters after his Death, with divers remainders over; and died: That had only One Daughter; and he suffered a Recovery of all, except the Barton and Demesnes of Hartrm, which stands

charged with his Wife's and Mother's Jointure, and barred the Remainders intailed; so that his Daughter goes away with all that Estate; and the other Premises settled to raise Portions for the Petitioner's Sisters, and his Mother's Jointure, are all that will come to him as Heir Male of his Family; and those being Western Manors, the Income will not pay the Interest of die Portions, the same being also mortgaged for 3,000l. raised to pay the said Portions; by which, and Debts contracted by the Petitioner, he is in a much worse Condition than his Sisters; though, if the said Western Manors were sold, they would yield a considerable Sum, more than sufficient to pay off the said Debt: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for the Sale of the said Western Manors, and Lands charged with the said Mortgage; and for laying out the Residue of the Money in a Purchase to the same Uses the said Manors and Lands are now settled.

A Petition of the Goldsmiths of the City and County of Exon, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by reason of a Clause in an Act of Parliament made in the 8th and 9th Years of his Majesty's Reign, for making a new Standard for Silver, the Petitioners cannot exercise their Trades; for that their Plate is liable to a Seizure for want of the Britannia Mark, which they are uncapable to fix, unless they incur the Penalty of the Law: And praying, That the said Clause may be repealed; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual preventing the melting down of the current Coin of this Kingdom: and also to prevent all Manner of Frauds and Abuses in the ^Silver Manufacture.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same to the Hoyse; together with their Opinion, what is fit to be done in relation to the Britannia Mark:

A Petition of Daniel Small and Christopher Fowler, Ditto. Trustees for the rest of the Proprietors of the Undertaking for bringing fresh Water into the City of Bristoll, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That in 1695, the Petitioners obtained a Grant from the Mayor, Aldermen, and Council of Bristoll, for laying Pipes and Aqueducts in their Streets; paying 150/. Fine, and 1661. 13*4 d.every Seventh Year for 200 Years:

And, as the most convenient Place from whence to bring the best Water, the Proprietors fixed upon Harmam Mills, on the River Avon, Five Miles from Bristoll, for which they paid 900l. Fine; and are to pay 9 per Annum, for 200 Years: That, in the 7th and 8th Years of the King, they had an Act of Parliament to lay their Pipes from Hannam Mills to Bristoll; and have expended hear 18,000 /. in the said Undertaking: But there is a Bill in this House, for making the said River Avon navigable from Bristoll to Bath, which will not only destroy the said Undertaking, without making the Proprietors Satisfaction, but also subject them to the several Actions of many hundreds of their Tenants, with whom they have covenanted by Leases, to supply them with Water: And praying the Consideration of their Case; and that they may be heard by Counsel, at the Bar. of the House, or be otherwise relieved, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; And that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the said Committee, thereupon.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Paili/Ts, and Burgesses of the Borough of in Lancashire,

was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Rye is the only Harbour for Ships from Dover to Portsmouth, where many Ships have been saved in Stress of Weather; and also lies opposite to Diep, and several other Ports of France; from whence also bhips of War used to go out, and prevent Privateers from infesting the Coast; and was capable of receiving his Majesty's whole Navy: But now the Harbour is so decayed by the Inning of Land, and making Flood-gates and Cross-walls, that the Slub stops, and the Harbourgrows yearly worse and worse; so that in few Years a Ship of Burden will not be able to get in; and, if some Care be not taken to remove the l lood-gates and Walls, this advantageous Harbour will be utterly lost: And praying, That such Course may be taken as may restore the said Harbour to its ancient Goodness.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Town of Rj/c is referred.

A PETITION of the Afayor, Burgesses, and In- Avon Navi-habitants, of the Borough of Church, was gation.

presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there was an Act of Parliament made in the 16th and 17th Years of King Charles the 2d, for making the River Avon navigable from Christ Church to New Sarum; and the Undertakers made several Attempts therein; bu^ finding no Advantage, though they did carry up some Barges, they desisted, till of late Years, they began again, but have not yet made the River navigable for any Benefit to themselves, or the Publick; nor the Haven near Christ Church any better than before: But now certain Persons in New Sarum claim a Right in the said Undertaking; and, by Colour of the said Act, and some Orders made by the Commissioners, demand many causeless and unreasonable Fines of the Petitioners, who have Lands contiguous to the said River, or have made use of the said Haven, as formerly; s© that the said Act, which was designed for the Benefit of the Country, hath and is like to turn to their Prejudice; and, as the Petitioners are informed, there is a Bill depending in the House for making the said Act more effectual, which is to give the Undertakers further Power to recover such Fines as they have or shall lay: And praying That they may be heard what they have to object against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Clothiers of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the late Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures abroad, being added to the many Difficulties the Cloathing Trade labours under at home, threatens the Overthrow of their foreign Trade, which is improved to the utmost abroad, when Men of all Occupations enter into the same here, to the Ruin of the Reputation of our Cloth abroad, and the Prejudice of the skilful Trader; and besides, they pay great Duties upon OU, Soap, and Dyeing Stuffs, when as Foreigners are freed from that Charge, and consequently can make their Cloth cheaper; and thereby discourage the Sale of our Cloth, and encourage the

A Petition of the Drapers, Clothiers, and Clothworkers, on behalf of themselves, and divers other Persons employed in, and subsisting by, the Woollen Manufacture in the Corporation of Salop, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That those Manufactures were so considerable to Salop, until the additional Duties upon Flanders Linen, and their Prohibition of our Woollen Cloth, That at least 1,500l. a Week was laid out therein; but since, there is not above 200l. weekly laid out; so that many Families, which used to be employed, are reduced to great Poverty, and become burdensome to their several Parishes: And praying the House to consider of such Methods as they shall think proper, for restoring and opening the Trade to Flanders, as the only Means to prevent the Calamities which otherwise must befal the Petitioners.

Dover A Petition of the Commissioners for the Repair of

Harbour. Dover Harbour, was presented to the House, and read;

setting forth, That the said Harbour is of great Importance to this Kingdom, not only in time of War, where a few Ships may command all Trade passing the narrowest Part of the Channel, and the Place where the Royal Navy, when in the takes in Provisions;

the only Victualling Office between Chatham and Portsmouth being at Dover; but also in time of Peace is a safe Harbour for Ships in Distress, which hath often happened; and the rather, because the French King is now, with all Diligence and Expence, making a Harbour at , the nearest opposite Port to Dover And praying the Consideration of the House, That some Methods may be taken for the Repair and Preservation of the said Harbour; which is so far run to decay, that, without the Assistance of the House, it will be irrecoverably lost.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same to the House,

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, RyeiiarUur. of the Borough of Portsmouth in the County of South

ampton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Harbour of Rye is the only Harbour for Ships the English have, upon the Coast of Kent and Sussex, from Dover to Southampton, which is above a Hundred Miles by Sea; and many Ships have been saved by putting in there from Storms, and Stress of Weather:

Resides, the said llarbourliesopposite to iXn'p, and several other considerable Ports of France, and Ships of War, of considerable Strength, used to ride there, to he ready to go in and out at any time, to hinder French Privateers from infesting our Coast: But now the said Harbour is so decayed, that it will not entertain above Twenty small Ships, which formerly would have received the whole Navy Royal; which is occasioned by the Inning of Land, and making Flood-gates and Cross-walls; and that yearly, by the stopping the Slubb in the Harbour, the same grows worse and worse; so that, in a few Years, a Ship of Burden will not be able to come in there, to the great Damage of Navigation and Trade; unless there be some care taken, that the Flood-gates and Cross-walls may be taken away, so as the Tide indy ilow and reflow as formerly: And praying, That the House will take some Course for restoring the said Harbour to its ancient G ood-ness, that so considerable a Harbour, for the Benefit of the whole Nation, may not be totally lost.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Town of Rye is referred.

To answer which Evidence, the Sitting Member's Counsel insisted,

That it would be hard to put the Sitting Member extempore to justify so many Votes as the Petitioners had excepted to: But they said, They should very much rely upon an Agreement made by the Candidates at the time of the Election; which Was to this Effect:

That none of the Candidates should be present; but there were to be Two Persons present on each Candidate's behalf, who were to determine, among themselves, what Persons were qualified to vote; and accordingly the Mayor was to direct the Clerk to set them down:

That none, who did not pay to Scotland Lot, should poll:

That none, who were paid for by the Parish, or received Alms, should have any Vote:

That only One Person should vote for One House. They further insisted,

That the Place of Polling was the same a9 usual; viz* in the Chamber; and that now, as formerly, they came up Stairs to the Chamber; and, when they went away, were let down by a Ladder into the Church-yard.

That, if any Riot or Disorder was, it was begun by Mr. Rayner, and his Party.

As to the Riot, they called

John Henly, John Scorer: Who said, They were Constables at this Election. Henly said, The Poll was taken at the usual Place, in the Chamber over the South Porch: That now, as at other Elections, they went up a Pair of Stairs, and went from the said Chamber, by a Ladder* into the Church-yard. The said Henly and Scorer said, They were placed to keep the South Door of the Church: That, before the Church Doors were shut up, the Voters were generally let in; and they were appointed to keep out the Rabble: But, after the Poll was over, Mr, Hern, and others of Mr. Rayner's Party, encouraged by Mr. Rayner at the Head of them, joining with some others without, endeavoured, by Violence, to force open the Door; and pressed upon Henly and Scorer in a most violent Manner; and One threw a Stone at Henly, and hit him on the Neck: And Scorer said, His Arms were like to be pulled from his Body; and that several Persons whipped off their Cravats, and put themselves into a Posture of Fighting; and cried out, A Rayner!

William Killinger said, That, almost at the End of the Poll, he heard some say, That Sir Francis Molineux, and all there, should not come down alive: That Joseph Gibson, and several others that voted for Mr. Rayner, had their Cravats off, and Sticks in their Hands, before the Election was declared: That he voted for Sir Fra. As to the Agreement;

Mr. Clay, Mr. Read, James Potter, Mr. Clarke, said, That it was agreed before the Poll, that none should have Votes but what were in the Towns Book of Assessment to the Poor:

And this Agreement was made by those they called the Triers, no One of them opposing it; and the Triers were Two Persons appointed on behalf of each Candidate, to see Things fairly carried on; none of the Candidates themselves being in the Chamber where the Poll was taken: And that, accordingly, they believed, several that lived Two in a House, who were for Sir Francis Mott-neux, were turned down, without giving their Votes; and several were turned dow n, because they were not in the Assessment Books: And Mr. Read said, when the Poll was over, Mr. Raynor asked Sir John Bolls, how it went: And Sir John Bolles answering, He had lost it by Two, Mr. Rayner bid him proclaim the other Two.

And, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all the Inhabitants within the Borough of Newark upon Trent, in the County of Nottingham, who pay, or ought to pay, Scotland Lot within the said Borough, have a Right to vote at the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Fra?icis Molineux Baronet is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Newark.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That John Rayner Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Newark.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, after the Word That," to insert the Mayor, Aldermen, and;"

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That the Mayor, Aldermen, and all the Inhabitants within the said Borough of Newark upon Trent, in the County of Nottingham, who pay, or ought to pay, Scotland Lot within the said Borough, have a Right to vote at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

The Second and Third Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the Clerk of the Crown do attend this House Tomorrow Morning, to amend the Return for the said Borough, by rasing out the Name of Sir Francis MolineuxBoxonet, and inserting the Name of John Rayner Esquire, instead thereof.

Ordered, That Edward Hobson, late Mayor of the Borough of Newark, in the County of Nottingham, for his irregular Proceedings at the Election for the said Borough, be taken into Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

But the Petitioners Counsel insisted, That the Sitting Member's Votes w ere gained by Promises of Places, and by sending great Quantities of Junk, to be made into Oakum by the poor People of Newport; which, the Petitioner s Counsel alleged, was on Purpose to gain himself Votes; which, they conceived, wrould vacate the Sitting Member's Election: And to make good the said Allegations, they called several Witnesses:

Mr. Mathews: Who said, Mr. Greenhill, the Sitting Member, being but little known in Newport, made use of Mr. Smith's Interest, who w?as Clerk of the Rope-yard: And that Mr. Smith, before the Election of my Lord Cutts and Sir Robert Colton, to serve for the said Borough, did propose Mr. Grecnhill; and that, if they would vote for Mr. Grecnhill} he would employ the poor of Newport, by sending over Junk: That Mr. Smith particularly pressing him, the said Mathezvs, he answered, He would be for him, if he could get a Recommendation from the Lord Cutts: And it was discoursed how to engage the Mayor, and the Corporation; and it was proposed to engage the then Mayor, by helping his Son to a Pursers Place, from which he had been before discharged; and the Corporation was to be obliged, by sending Junk for the Poor to pick: That, after, he received a Letter from Mr. Smith, dated the 28 July 1698; and writ in these Words following; viz.

Dear Sir,

I most humbly thank you for the particular Service you have clone me, in respect to Commissioner Greenhill, who is wonderfully pleased at the Letter you sent my Lord Cutts, on his behalf: He orders me to send his most humble Service to you, and let you know, That on Monday, about Four a Clock in the Afternoon, he will wait on, and give you his most hearty Thanks.

I am still to pray the Continuance of your Favour in this Affair; and that you will please to let Mr. Mayor know, that, for the Respect that is designed him by the Corporation, be will forthw ith make his Son John Purser of a Third-rate Ship; an Employment now-a-days hard to be gotten: And for my Brother Rookly, upon your Request to him, on his behalf, will immediately proceed to get him a very good Post; and also will do you, and the Tow n, any other Service that shall be desired of him.

The Commissioner has this Day wrote to the Earls of Orford and Scarborough, to request of my Lord Cutts his Recommendation to your Corporation, according as I hinted to you; and I hope, in few Days, to hear a good Account of that Matter: However, whether the Commissioner does obtain his Ends, or not, he assures me, that his Zeal to serve the Town will be not a Jot the less; and that now he will forthwith employ all the Poor.

I most earnestly beg your best Endeavours to promote his Interest, against he comes over; and will please cunningly to intimate the Commissioner's Design to serve the Mayor's Son, as also my Brother Rookley; which he positively resolves to do. I hope, by your prudent Management, the Commissioner will find from the Corporation, a civil and candid Reception; which will be most gratefully acknowledged by him to you all; particularly to yourself; as also by, Sir,

Your most faithful humble Servant,

IV. Smith.

Portsmouth Dock-yard,

28 July 1698.

I have sent the Coffee by the Bearer, Nurse Dart; which humbly prays your Acceptance.

My Service attends you, and my Cousins.

And the said Mathews said, That afterwards he received a Second Letter from the said Mr. Smith, upon the said Subject; which he. did not produce: And thereto

upon he went and acquainted the then Mayor with what Mr, Smith had wrote, concerning his the said Mayors Son, the Mayor's Wife being present; who said, The Good of her Son was more to them than any Parliament-man: And that afterwards Mr. Greenhill lav at the said Mr. Keblarright's; and he espoused his Interest: That afterwards Mr. Mathews discoursed with Mr. Greenhill about the Subject-matter of Mr. Smith's Letter; and told him, That if Keblewright's Son was not preferred, and Junk sent to the Town, he could not expect to succeed; but did not shew him Mr. Smith's Letter: And Mr. Greenhill said, it should be done: And that, about September, some Junk was sent, and so continued to be sent for Six or Seven Months, in the King's Boat; but he could not say, by the Commissioner's Means or Order: And that some of the poor People said, That they must have had Relief but for the said Oakum:

That John Read said, He wrould not have voted for Mr. Greenhill, but for the Preferment of his Brother, and the Importunity of his Sister; his Brother being promised to be head Carpenter of a Yard:

Weight remained at the lime of the Election; but lie could not say, by whose Order the Junk was sent; but it was brought in the King's Boat; but none had been sent since August last.

Mr. Robert Lee said. That Alderman Webb told him, That he would not promise his Vote till the Day df Election; but his Son had given It for Mr. Greenhill Mr. Greenhill having promised him a Place for his Son, which was worth 30/. a Year; and, in a little time, would be worth 50 or 601.

That the Counsel for the Sitting Member insisted, That taking it upon the Petitioner's Evidence, The Promise of Junk being made before the Vacancy, it was not within the Words of the Act of Parliament, nor within the meaning of the same; it not being given to the Voters:

That what Mr. Smith did, was without Mr. Greenhill's Privity;

That Mr. Keblewright was not Mayor at the time of Mr. Greenhill's being elected:

And that, instead of Promises on behalf of the Sitting Member, there were Promises and Threats made use of on behalf of the Petitioner: And called several Witnesses.

Mr. William Smith said, That there was a Want of Oakum in the Dock Yard at Portsmouth, occasioned by the poor People's refusing to pick it, they in War-time finding Ways better to employ their Time; and that formerly they have had Oakum sent to Portsmouth from Deptford, which costs the King 3s. id. per C. Weight picking, besides the Charge of carrying it to Portsmouth; whereas that picked at Neufort cost but 3*. 4d.: That formerly they had made use of Fareham, and other Places, for the Picking of Oakum: That, when he did understand the Lord Cults was elected for Cambridgeshire, he went over to Newport, and proposed Mr. Greenhill; presuming the Lord Cults would stand for Cambridgeshire, and decline Newport; and did say, the People of the Town might receive Benefit by the Picking ot Oakum; and that Junk was sent to Newport to Mr. Farrington, till it was contradicted: But it was Mr. Cowpers Office to direct it; and Mr. Greenhill was not concerned in sending it there:

That the Junk was carried in the King's Boat, with two Men, which were kept to look after the Buoys; and, when they could be spared from that, they carried the Junk:

That Mr. Keblewright's Son, and he, having been Clerks several Years together in the Dock-yard, he wrote him a Letter, to speak to Mr. Greenhill on his behalf: and accordingly he did speak to Mr. Greenhill, for his Letter, for young Keblerwright: But whether he had such Letter, Mr. Smith could not tell.

Mr. Francis Hosier produced an Account of 26 Tons and an half, sent from Deptfoi'd to Portsmouth, for the Year 1696, 97, and 98; and he said, It cost picking at Deptford 4$. per C.; which he supposes was sent to Portsmouth from Deptford, because they could not be supplied fast enough at Portsmouth.

Mr. Wm. Keblewright denied, That he had any Promise, that his Son should be made a Purser; or that he gave his Vote upon any such Account.

Mr. John Keblewright himself, being examined, said, That he was Purser of the Josiah in 1695; which being rendered unserviceable, he got a Certificate from the Officers of Portsmouth Yard; and, after a Year and Half's Attendance, was, by the Lords of the Admiralty, made Purser of the Nassau, his Father and Brother being Security for his Arrears; and that be had a Promise of being Purser, Two or Three Months before the Election: And he produced his Certificate, dated the 13 July 1694; and Warrant to be Purser of the Nassau, dated the 2d October 1699.

Mr. Edward Webb said, He never was offered any thing by Mr. Greenhill to vote for him; but voted for him out of Judgment: That he knows of no Clerk's Place, or other Place of Profit, that his Grandson has; nor is he like to have any, that ever he heard of.

John How said, That Mr. Acton came to Newport Vo l. 13.

some time before Christmas last, and sent for him, and Newport told him, my Lord Cutts had ordered him some Money, that was owing him, and desired his Vote; and, if he Election would give him his Vote, be should have his Money when he pleased: And accordingly he received Money of him twice; and Mr. Acton' promised him both my Lord s and his own Favour, if he would vote for him;

That afterwards my Lord Cutts came down, went ta Mr. Hales, and sent for him, and pressed him for his Vote; but, he not being willing to promise, my Lord asked him, What he would have: Who saying, He would have his Money, and his Bill signed; accordingly his Bill was signed: That my Lord bid him come the next Morning, which he did; and then my Lord whispered, and told him, That if his Wife, who was then with Child, was brought to-bed of a Son, he would take care of it as soon as he was able to go abroad.

But Colonel Dudley, being called in to confront John How,1 said. He was present all the time that How was with the Lord Cutts; and that he did not observe my Lord whisper hjm: That he desired his Account should be passed; and that he would use him as a Freeman, and a Burgess of the Town.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Henry Greenhill Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Newport, in the Isle of Wight.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Henry Greenhill Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Newport, in the Isle of Wight.

And then the House adjourned till -To-morrow Morning, Eight a Clock.

Common Council and Inhabitants, of the Borough of Weymouth, and Melcem Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That Rye is the only Harbour the English have upon the Coast of Kent and Sussex, for above 100 Miles; and lies very commodious for Ships of War, as well as Merchant Ships, either in War or Peace; whereby many Ships have been saved in Stress of Weather; but the said Harbour is in Danger of being lost by the Inning of Land, and making Walls cross the same with Flood-gates; whereby the Tide is checked; the Slub stopped, and the Harbour yearly worse and w orse: And praying, That some Course may be taken for restoring the said Harbour to its ancient Goodness.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said. Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Town of Rye is referred.

A Petition of John Key, late Captain in the Lord Strath-naver's Regiment, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That he raised a Company in the said Regiment, at his own Charge, on the Irish Establishment, which was since put upon the English Establishment; and the Petitioner served therein faithfully, till the latter End of 1696; w'hen he was deprived of his Command, without any just Ground; although there is a considerable Sum due to him, of which he can obtain no Account or Payment; whereby he, and his numerous Family, are reduced to great Distress: And praying, that he may be admitted to have Half-pay, or be otherwise relieved in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of Richard Nicholls, and others, is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, and of other the chief inhabitants, of the Borough of Newbery in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by reason of the Act for prohibiting the Importation of foreign Bone-lace, and the Prohibition of English Woollen Manufactures in Flanders, occasioned thereby, many of the chief Clothiers have quitted their Trades; and the Trade of those that carry it Still on, is so much lessened, that their Poor are greatly increased, for want of Employment: And praying, That the said Act may be repealed, their chiefest Trade being to Flanders.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to w hom the Petition of the Clothiers of Salisbury is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Corporation of Taunton in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners arc highly sensible of the great Advantage navigable Rivers bring to this Kingdom in general: And praying, That the Bill depending in the House, for making the River Avon navigable from Bristoll to Bath, may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That no Petition for or against the said Bill be received after this Day Sevennight.

Ifoolleo Ma* A Petition of the Clothiers of the County of Gloucester \vk\m, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Cloathing Trade is very much discouraged by the Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures into Flan-ders md Brabant; the Dearness of Dyeing Stuff, Oil, and Soap, consumed here, and the Drawback upon Exportation, chiefly by Foreigners; which will endanger the Supplanting of the Woollen Trade into foreign Countries, to the Loss of it here, by the Weakness of the Stock of Foreigners; it being our Advantage to encourage English Merchants, who employ far greater Stocks therein: And praying, That some Course may be taken for regaining the Trade to Flanda's and Brabant, and all Encouragement given to English Merchants to export our Woollen Manufactures thither; and that the Petitioners may be put on an equal Foot with their Neighbours in the Materials of Soap, Oil, and Dyeing Stuff.

Treaty of Altena} 20th June 1689.

NOTUM sit omnibus, qua ratione graves controversial, quae ab aliquo abhinc tempore inter suam Regiam Majestatem Daniae & Norvegi®, ac Domini Ducis Sleswicensis Holsati® Celsitudinem, agigat® fuerunt per solieitam meditationem Sacrae Caesarete Majestatis, ac sua-ruin Serenitatem Electoralium SaXoni® & Brandeburgi, in sequentes leges composit®, atque in perpetuum abolitae fuerunt:

1. Sit maneatque generalis amnestia, & reterna obli-vio, omnium illorum, quae hucusque ab utraque parte, earumve ministris, subditis, & adhaerentibus, invicem susccpta atque patrata fuerint; quorum nomine nemo utrinque ad reddendas rationes vocabitur, nec eadem cui-piam fraudi aut damnocedent: Vicissim, inter suam Regiam Majestatem Daniae & Norvegioe, ejusque h®redes. Sc in regno successores, ac Domini Ducis Sleswisencis Holsatiae Celsitudinem, ejusque successores, asterna atque insolubilis amicitia & unio, hoc ipso, restaurata atque stabilita sit.

2. Sua Regia Majestas Daniae & Norvegiae Celsitudi-nem suam Ducalem in omnes ipsius dictae Celsitudinis ditiones, terras, insulas, & bona; atque in specie in prae-dium Gottesgabe dictum, simul in ejusdemsoveraenitatem, regalia, jura collectarum, foederum, munimentorumque extruendorum & possidendorum; dcniqtie, in universum, in omnia ilia jura, eminentias, & qu®vis competentia, prout sua Celsitudo isthaec, ante & post pacem West-phalicam, & Rorealcm, usque ad annum 1675, obtinuit atque possedit; turn & quicquid suoe Celsitudini per pacificationem Fontisbellaquensem coinpetere potest; quarum pacificationum leges contentae, hoc ipso, iterum confirmantur: Nec minus sua Regia Majestas suoe Celsitudinis ininistros atque subditos in quaevis horum bona & pecunias creditas restituit.

3.
