A Petition oi William Rider Esquire, was presented to DealWate the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioner, works* and Edward Burdet Esquire, having found out a Way for the supplying the Town and Port of New Deal with fresh Water; which will be a great Service to the Inhabitants and Ships that have Occasion to water there; King James the Second did, by Letters Patents, dated 21 July, in the 4th Year of his Reign, grant them the sole fliberty and Power of building a Conduit Head, Wharf, and other necessary Buildings, upon the Beach of the said Town, for carrying on the said Work; and to dig the Highways, Streets, and Waste Grounds, of his Majesty:

And the Patentees were at great Charges, in causing Engineers to go from London to Deal, to view the Premises, and direct what was necessay to be done; and to treat with the Inhabitants, in order to the speedy completing of the said Work; but the Petitioner is informed, that one William Warner is endeavouring to advantage himself by the Petitioner s Discovery; and, for that End, hath begun a Work for bringing fresh Water to the Town of Deal; and hath obtained Leave of this House to bring in a Bill to bring fresh Water to the Town and Port of v Deal; which, if it should pass into an Act, will destroy the Rights and Privileges granted to the Petitioner by the said Patent: And praying to be heard by Counsel, before the said Bill do pass.

Ordered, That foe said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time: And that the Bill be read a Second time upon Friday Morning next.

Himbnrough A Petition of divers Gentlemen and Clothiers, Cloth-Company, workers, and others, principally concerned in the Woollen Manufactures, in Huddersfeild, and the adjacent Parts, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of our Woollen Manufactures was first begun, and successfully Carried on, by the Hamborough Company, to the Benefit. the whole Nation: But the Privileges of the said Company, have, of late, been infringed by Foreigners, who have already gotten a great Part of that Trade, especially to Holland; and the Whole is in Danger of falling into their Hands; which may be a Means of transplanting our Woollen Manufactures, by their Insight therein, to foreign Countries, where the same is already begun: And praying, That the said Company may be protected in their Privileges and Trade to Germany, only upon such Terms as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read a Second

time.

Ditto. A Petition of divers Gentlemen and Clothiers, in the Cloathing Town and Parish of Guisely, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Trade of exporting our Woollen Manufactures was first begun, and has been best managed for the Good of the Manufacturers, by the Hamborough Company: But of late Years, for want of a sufficient Support of the said Company, Foreigners have gotten so great a Share of that Trade, that the English Merchants are in Danger of the utter Loss of exporting our Woollen Ma-I nufactures to Germany, as they have for some Years, to

I Holland: And shouldthat Trade be intrusted in the hands

of Foreigners, it must lie under great Hazards of having Hardships put upon the Clothiers, and of being set up in foreign Countries, by their Insight of the Cloathing Trade: And praying, That the said Company may be established and protected in their Trade directly to Germany, under such Regulations as the House shall think fit, and that effectual Care may be taken to prevent the Exportation of our Wool.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read a Second time.

Ditto, A Petition of divers Gentlemen, Clothiers, Cloth-workers, and others, principally concerned in the Woollen Manufactures in Wakefeild, Horbory, Alverthorpe, and Ossett, in the West Hiding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Hamborough Company first attempted, and successfully promoted, the Exportation of English Woollen Manufactures, to the great Advantage of the Traders therein: But, for want of a sufficient Support, Foreigners have gotten so great a Share of that Trade, that the said Company is in Danger of being destroyed; and thereby that Trade is in Danger of being lost to England, either by the Weakness of their Stocks, or, by their Insight into the Manner of working our Cloth, the Carrying and Setting up the same in foreign Countries: And praying, That the Hamborough Company may be established and protected in their Privileges and Trade to Germany, to prevent the Mischiefs aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read ai Second time.

A Petition of divers Gentlemen, Clothiers, Cloth-dressers, and divers others, concerned in the Woollen Manufactures, in the ancient Cloathing Town and Parish of Bradford, in the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of English Woollen Manufactures was begun, and carried on, by the Hamborough Company, to the Advantage of all the Traders therein; But, of late, Foreigners have in-Vo*. 13.

fringed the Privileges of that Company, and gotten so great a Part of the Trade to Germany, that English Merchants are like to have no Part thereof; and thereby that Trade is in great Danger of being lost to England, by Foreigners Insight to the Working of our Cloth, and the Opportunity of exporting our Wool; and so the same may be carried into foreign Countries: And praying,

That the said Company may be established and protected in their Trade directly to Germany, under such Regulations as the House shall think fit; so as all his Majesty's natural-born Subjects may be admitted into the said Company; and that effectual Care may be taken to prevent the Exportation of Wool.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read a Second time.

A Petition of divers Clothiers* and others, depending Hamborough on the Woollen Manufactures, in the County of Suffolk, Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That heretofore the Hamborough Company did export a considerable Part of the Petitioners Manufactures into Germany: But of late Years, since Foreigners have been permitted to trade thither, the Petitioners Trade hath much declined; and, if some Provision be not made for supporting the said Company, that Trade will wholly fall, into the Hands of Foreigners; which will be very prejudicial to the Trade of the Woollen Manufactures in general: And praying, That the said Company may be supported in their Trade to Germany, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Serge-makers, and Wool-combers, Exporting of the Town and County of Southampton, was presented Wool, to the House, and read; setting forth, That formerly Licence was granted for exporting from Southampton to the Islands of Guernsey, Jersey, Alderney, and Sark, 3,300 Todds of Wool yearly, to be combed, one Moiety at Southampton: But, in the late King James's Reign, Sir Edward de Carteret obtained a Grant for exporting thither double that Quantity unwrought; which was also established by an Act of Parliament in the First Year of his Majesty's Reign; to the great Impoverishment of the Petitioners, for Want of Work: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the State and Condition of the Trade of England.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of Moreton, Hamstead\ Woollen and Parts adjacent, in the County of Devon, was pre- Manufacture, sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That their Woollen Manufacture Trade is very much decreased*since the Prohibition thereof in Flanders, where the same is set up, and great Rewards offered to draw our Workmen thither; which has much increased the Number of the Poor, who are driven to great Wants for lack of Work:

And praying, That some seasonable Remedy may be provided for the Petitioners Relief.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of the State and Condition of the Trade of England.

PETITION of Colonel Henry Holt, in behalf of Half paj Captain Thomas Holt, Captain John Pigott, Captain John Forster, Ensign Samuel Clark, Ensign Thomas Bisse, and Ensign John Horn, late Officers in the Regiment of Foot commanded by him in the West Indies, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Regiment was, on the i st of May 169.5, reduced from Thirteen Companies to Five; and the supernumerary Officers were, by his Majesty's Order, to attend the Service, and be subsisted, together with the Regiment, and preferred as Vacancies should happen: That the aforesaid Officers are all of that Reducement, who are not yet provided for; and are excluded the Benefit of Half-pay, as reduced before the 10th of September 1697; and thereby are incapable of Preferment on the Vacancies-which happen, though they are Englishmen, have a great Arrear of Pay due, and served long in a most unhealthy Climate, and undergone greater Hardships than those who have served nearer Home: And praying the House to consider the Case of the said Officers; and that they be allowed the same Benevolence of Half-pay, as is granted to the Officers reduced since the 10th of September 1697.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Blaize Gercaisot, a French Protestant Refugee, Lieutenant of Grenadiers, in the late Regiment of Foot, commanded by Colonel Saunderson, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner received the first Year's Half-pay; but some earnest Occasions calling him into Flanders, he there fell sick, and could not come over soon enough to be naturalized the last Session of Parliament; so that his Half-pay has been stopped: That the Petitioner is in the first Naturalization Bill of this Sessions; which has passed the House of Lords, and is now before this House: And praying, That his Half-pay may be continued, without which he and his Family must starve.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Dotyon A Petition of the principal White Paper-makers, on behalf of themselves, and the rest concerned in that Manufacture in England, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That they are arrived to a very great Perfection in the said Art, and employ Abundance of poor Families; but the Duty upon all foreign, except French Paper, is so low, and therefore such vast Quantities imported, that tends to the Destruction of the said Manufacture in England: And praying, That a Duty may be laid upon foreign Paper, with a Duty in lesser Proportion on English Paper, by Distinction and Enumeration of Reams, as shall be thought meet for the Preservation, and further Encouragement, of the said Manufacture in England.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply to be granted to his Majesty*

jjwnborough A Petition of the Traders in the Woollen and Cotton Manufactures of the Stocking Trade, in the Counties of Worcester and Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there being a Bill depending in the House for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company, the Petitioners say, that Experience shews, the Trade in the Woollen Manufactures does best flourish when left to its full Freedom, the many Buyers causing a current, and speedy Payment for their Commodities; the Consideration of which hath hitherto induced this House to discourage all Monopolies, as against Law, and destructive to the Rights and liberties of the Subject: And praying, That the said Trade may remain free and unrestraiued from the Interest of the Hamborough Company.

Vol. 13.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Cloth-buyers, Clothiers, Hamborough and other Traders in the Woollen Manufactures, in and Compaiy. near the Town of Wakefield, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the‘Petitioners find by the Votes of this House, that a Bill is brought in for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company: That Experience doth demonstrate, that when the Trade to Flanders was limited to the said Company only, it was very prejudicial to the Woollen Manufacture Trade of England in general; but, w hen that Trade was left to its full Freedom, it met wtith far greater En«i couragement, both at Home and Abroad: And praying,

That the said Trade may not be again reduced to the sole Interest of the Hambwough Company.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Clothiers, Ditto. Cloth-w'orkers, and other considerable Dealers in the Woollen Manufactures, at Halifax, and Places adjacent, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is a Bill depending in the House for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company: But the Petitioners find, by Experience, that the Trade in the Woollen Manufactures doth meet with greater Encouragement, both at Home and Abroad, when ?tis left to its full Freedom of Commerce; and that, when it was limited to the Hamborough Company, that Trade was generally prejudiced thereby: And praying, That the Trade of the Woollen Manufactures may remain free and unlimited.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of divers Gentlemen, Clothiers, and others, Ditto, in Batley, Hicmonwick, Birkenshaw, Heaton, and Ad-xcalton, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of our Woollen Manufactures was first attempted, and afterwards successfully carried on, by the good Management of the Hamborough Company, to the great Benefit of this Nation; but, for want of a sufficient Support of the said Company, Foreigners have gotten so great a Share of that Trade, that all English Merchants are in Danger of being excluded from the Trade to Germany, as they have been from Holland several Years; whereby our Manufactures are in Danger of being debased, and the Art of making them transplanted into foreign Countries: And praying. That an Act of Parliament may pass, for establishing and protecting the said Company in their Trade to Germany, under such Regulations as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Bill for the better Encouraging and Settling the Trade of the Hamborough Company be read a Second time.

grew, Esquires, in behalf of themselves and others, claiming under the Drainers of Lindsey Level, in the County of Lincolne, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in 1634, the Commissioners of Sewers, Lords, Owners, and Commoners of Lindsey Level, at a general Assembly, contracted with the Earl of Lindsey for draining the same; for which he was to have 24,000 r Acres, and be put into the Possession of 14,000 Acres for his own Use, as soon as he should have drained the Lands between Bourn and Kime Ea, and to have the other 10,000 Acres when the Whole should be drained; and the Contract was decreed by the Commissioners of Sewers, confirmed by the Royal Assent, and inrolled in Chancery; and the Earl took in Participants; and, at the Expence of 80,000 /. so effectually drained that Part between Bourn and Kime Ea, that the Sewers decreed 14,000 Acres to the said Earl, and ascertained the same: That the Proprietors thereof built thereon several good Houses; inclosed, and plowed, and sowed, a considerable Part thereof; and planted themselves and Families there, intending to drain the remaining Part of the Level: But the Inhabitants of the neighbouring Towns, taking Advantage of the National Troubles in 1641, riotously entered on the said 14,000 Acres, and destroyed all the Buildings, Fences, and growing Crops; and have forcibly held the same in common ever since, notwithstanding many legal and amicable Endeavours have been used to regain the same: And praying, That the Petitioners, and their Participants, may have Leave to bring in a Bill for confirming the said Decrees, and their Title under them to the said 14,000 Acres, Part of the said Level.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the said Petition be rejected.

A Petition of Lieutenant Charles Hubbelthome was Half-pj presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That his Father, Colonel John Hubblethome, served in English Pay in Scotland and in England many Years; and was afterwards slain in a Sea Engagement; and the Petitioner, upon the late Resolution, went over into Ireland, with Duke Schonberg, and served as a Lieutenant in the Earl of Meath's Regiment; where, in the first general Attack against Lymrick, the Petitioner was wounded through the Face and Tongue, and thought mortal; under which he lay in great Pain several Months, speechless; and, before he was thoroughly recovered, marched with the said Regiment into Flanders, and served there until he lost his Speech again, and contracted such an Illness, that he was forced to desire Leave to come over for England for Relief; and, in his Absence, another was put in his Post; and his Sickness being of a long Duration, occasioned his not applying sooner to the House: And praying, That, in Consideration of his Father's long and faithful Services, and the Petitioner's own Services, Sufferings, and Disabilities, he may be admitted into Half-pay, for his necessary Support, he having never had any Allowance.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Upon the Petition of Sir Edmund Bacon Baronet, and Wm. Johnson Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Thomas Felton Baronet, and Sir Charles Hedges Knight, to serve for the said Borough:

That the 1st Question between the Petitioners and Sitting Members, and determined by the Committee, w»as upon the Right of Election.

That the Petitioners Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Portmen, capital Burgesses, and Freemen, of the said Borough.

That the Number of the Portmen is Eight; the Number of the capital Burgesses is 12.

That the Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses only.

And it appeared by the Evidence, That the said Paper was Mr. Alexanders Hand, who was Town Clerk of Orford at that time the said Poll was mentioned to be taken. And

Mr. Nathanael Gooding said, That he found the said Pa^ per, about 14 Years since, among Mr. Copping s Papers, with the Town Seal; which Mr. Copping had been Mayor of Orford: That he had been a Member of the Corporation for Twenty Years and upwards, and never knew Freemen denied to vote; and that he had acted as Town Clerk in the Year 1680, when there happened an Election, at which Sir John Duke and Mr. Glemham stood Candidates: That he then called over the capital Burgesses and Freemen, and there was no Objection to the Freemen when called over; but they did not sign the Indenture of Return; yet owned there was no other Candidates nor Dispute about it: That at the Election soon after the Resolution, Sir Adam Felton being like to be out-voted, and he making Interest for him, sent for Simon Bredstrey and Richard Townsend, antient Freemen, w hom he kept private, in case there should be Occasion for them; and that Tho. and Joseph Hastings were the Occasion of sending for them; but there being no Occasion of them, he acknowleged they did not vote: That at the Election in 1695, the Freemen, as well as the capital Burgesses, were called over before the Election.

Simon Bredstry said, That he was at the Election in 1695, at which time he gave his Vote for Mr. Jeremy Copping, that lived in London; and that about Seven or Eight Years ago, Mr. llamond of Burford sent for him to give his Vote; and accordingly he did go to Orford; but did not vote, there being no Occasion for him.

Mr. Palmer, who had been Portman 15 or 16 Years, and John Marrett, who said he had been a Freeman ever since the Year 1680, said, They were present at the Eleo tion in 1680; and that the free Burgesses were called over at that Election, and held up their Hands, as well as the rest.

Mr. John Hook said, He had been at Three Elections since the Year 1680, when all the Freemen were called over, and voted.

Mr. John Stephens, who had been Freeman of Orford 40 Years, said, that he remembred, that the free Burgesses had joined with the capital Burgesses in several Elections; but he could name only One Election, which was that of the Earl of Disert and Mr. Glemham, when they were not opposed; nor did he ever know any Election controverted.

That it appeared by the Town Book, that John Marret was made free the Second October 1682.

That there was also read to the Committee, out of a Book of the Corporation, an Entry made at a Court held by the Mayor, Five Portmen, and Five capital Burgesses, on the 5th of February 1680, in these Words: Memorandum, quod eadem die, fyc. major et communitas

he could remember for 40 Years very well; and that he never knew any Persons elect but Mayor, Portmen, and 12 capital Burgesses; nor have the Freemen offered themselves, or been called over at such Elections, as the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses, are; and that he never knew Simon Bredstrey vote, or offer to vote at any Election.

Tho. Thurston, said, He had known Orford 20 Years, and has been at several Elections; and that the Right was in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses.; and he never knew Freemen called over, or offer to vote.

William Robinson said, That he was a Portman, and had been a Freeman of Orford 19 Years; and that the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgeses only; and that himself was a Freeman Nine Years, and never voted, nor never knew any Freeman offer to vote.

John Brady said, That he was a capital Burgess and had known Orford 47 Years being born and bred there, and that the Right w'&s in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses; and that he never knew Freemen offer to vote till the last Election.

John Tyes said, That he is a capital Burgess, and had known Orford 20 Years; and that the Right was in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses; and that he never knew Freemen vote, nor called over.

Mr. Edmund Foster, a Neighbour to Orford, said, That he had known Two or Three Elections; and that the Method was, that the Town Clerk, before the Election, called over the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses, and doited such of them as did appear; and that, at the Election in 1693, he dotted with Mr. Porter the Town Clerk; and that the Freemen are not called over: However, be acknowleged, that some of the Freemen would be in the Room, and upon the Naming of the Candidates would hallow and make a Noise at Elections.

Sir Charles Gandy said, That he had known Orford 20 Years, and had been a capital Burgess of Orford\ and had endeavoured to satisfy himself in the Constitution of the Town; and that they did assure him the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Portmen, and capital Burgesses: That he was present once when the Lord Discrt w as elected, and there was a great Confluence of People; but they were not distinguished by Freemen: However, he acknowdeged, for refusing the Office of Mayor, he had been discontinued for some Years.

Ordered, That the Clerk of the Crown do attend this House upon Monday Morning, to amend the Return for the Borough of Orford, in the County of Suffolk, by rasing out the Names of Sir Thomas Felton Baronet, and Sir Charles Hedges Knight; and inserting, instead thereof, the Names of Sir Edmund Bacon Baronet, and William Johnson Esquire.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Bill for taking off the Duties upon the Woollen Manufactures exported.

Wm. Lowndes. Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The House, according to Order, took into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition, relating to Dover Harbour, was referred:

And the said Report was read; and is as followeth; viz. Sir Henry Sheet's said, That all Seafaring Men are undoubtedly very sensible of the Usefulness of the said HarBour, when in Repair; the same being a Security for all Ships in Distress, whether driven by Storm from their Anchors in the Downes, or otherwise; but now it is, in a manner, become useless, being choaked up with Beach, Sand and Mud, and the Piers are very much out of Repair, inso much that they are in continual Danger of being lost; and should the Sea break in before they are repaired, the Harbour will be irrevocably lost.

That in the Year 1652, a Squadron of English Cruisers, of the 4th Rate, went into the said Harbour, and cleaned and victualled within the Piers, some of which Ships came in one Day, and went out the next; there being then Eleven Foot Water at Neap Tides, and Twenty-two Foot Water at Spring Tides; and since that, King Charles the Second ascribed a great deal of his Success, in his Maritime Wars, to the Service of the said Harbour, which is the most commodiously situated in the World; and, could the Publick but be made sensible of the Advantages the said Harbour might be improved to, no Cost would be spared to improve so good a Work, which will answer any Expence the Nation shall be put to, and which, he believes, might be a great Means to prevent a Maritime War, it commanding the narrow est Part of the Chanel:

That he has seen a Survey of the said Harbour, taken by Direction of the Lords of the Admiralty, about Two Years ago, which is a perfect Transcript of what he took about 15 Years since; and thinks there is no Doubt, if Money be provided, but that the said Harbour may be restored to its former Condition, if not better; the Port, by Art, being capable of yielding Two or Three Foot Depth of Water more within than ever it did, which is a very great Matter: And Sir Henry Sheers presented the annexed Estimate of the Charge, amounting to 30,100l. but said, That 6 or 7,000l. yearly will be a sufficient Sum to be expended in carrying on the said Work:

Vol. 13.

That when the Work, pursuant to the said Estimate* Dover shall be completed, the said Harbour, by the help of a Harbour* Backwater and the Sea, as he has conceived and designed it, the Backwater being now of very little Use, will cleanse itself from what the Sea brings in, and thereby preserve its Depth for ever, without, any future Expence to the Publick; which no artificial Port does, that he knows of, they being subject to be choaked up, and are a

constant.....to their several Princes and States, who are Masters of the like artificial Ports:

That the new Work of Masonry, by the said Estimate* designed on the North Side of the Haven, to be carried out some Distance into deeper Water, being designed as a Remedy to the future bringing in of the Beach, which has been all along the greatest Impediment to the Service of this Port, will add an Advantage to the Preservation of the Work against the Rage of the Sea, and cure that Evil for the Time to come; which is a Benefit the Port never yet enjoyed.

Mr. Breton said, That the Harbour is so choaked up, that the Packet Boat cannot come in but at Spring Tides; for which Reason, Captain Gibson, Commander of the Packet, lately besought the Commissioners of the Post Offi.ce, that the Mail might be delivered at Deale; for that the said Harbour was no longer safe, he having been like to be cast away, while waiting to get in: W hich was ordered actordingly.

Mr. Mackay, Manager of the Dover Packet, said, That the Packet has often been obliged to land the Mail from the Downes, for Want of sufficient Water to come into Dover Harbour: Though the Packet Boat draws but Six Foot Water; yet many Times there is not Three Foot Depth of Water in the Harbour; so that the Packet must many Times wait, till a Boat goes out to tell the Commander whether he may venture in or not, which is a very great Delay to Passengers, and the Mail; of which frequent Complaints w ere made: For which Reason, the Commissioners of the Post Office ordered the Mail to be delivered at Deal.

James Harvey, Master of the Packet betw ixt Dover and Ostend, said, That Dover Harbour is so bad, that he had often been obliged to land the Mail from the Downes; and that sometimes it is so shallow, that a long Boat cannot get in; and once he was forced to wait 48 Hours to get into the Harbour, though he had a fair Wind.

Mr. Bret ton said, That, within these 20 Years, he has known a Ship of 300 Tons, laden with Tobacco, discharge herself at the Port of Dover, which is now lost, and the Piers of the Harbour want great Repair; so that if his Majesty had not allowed 500l. Two Years ago, for their Support, upon the Report of Sir Cloudesly Shovell and others, who were at the said Survey mentioned by Sir Henry Sheers, and agrees with it; they had then been quite destroyed, as he believes; and if the Sea should break in before the Piers are repaired, the said Harbour, , which is the safest on all the Coast, is not to be recovered; so that many Merchant Ships in Distress, which might receive Succour from the said Harbour, will be utterly lost; many of which, every Winter, being driven in, very much shattered, without Cable or Anchors, where they unlade, and refit; which, in 20 Years last, has saved many Hundred thousand Pounds to the Merchants:

That in 1689, about Seventy Sail of Merchant Ships were driven into the said Harbour by Storm from their Anchors, without Cables; the which, at 2,000l. a Ship, being a moderate Computation, as he takes it, amounts to 140,000l.; and, in all Probability, would have fallen into the Enemies Hands, had it not been for the said Harbour; and that, about Years since, several Transport Ships, with Men, were forced into the Harbour, wffiich otherwise would have been cast away, as lie believes:

That heretofore the Port of Dover yielded a Revenue to the Crown of about 20,000l. per Annum for Customs; but for 12 Years past it has produced a very inconsiderable yearly Sum, through the Loss of their said Port and Trade; the w'hich, with Losses by Fire of a Farm-house Fff and

202

i 2* Fehrudrii. 1699

boyer Har- and Barn, Part of the Harbour Revenue, and Losses by the late War to the Inhabitants of Dover, has rendered them incapable of paying their Rents for the cleansing and repairing the said Harbour and Piers; for the doing whereof, there is a Revenue of about 300 /. per Annum; but not above 1,50/. per Annum is received of it:

That former Parliaments had such a Regard to the Service of the said Harbour, that, towards its Repairs, sever ral Acts passed in the Reigns of Queen Eliz. King James the First, and King Charles the Second, for laying a Duty upon all Ships and Vessels, that did or might receive any Advantage by the said Harbour; the last of which Acts expired about 38 Years since, and produced about 9,000 L in Seven Years time; but what the former Acts yielded, he does not know, or does it appear by the Books of the Harbour Revenue, several Leaves thereof being torn out that should shew the same.

He further said, That there is a very good Victualling Office at Dovciy with great Conveniencies, and the only Victualling Office between Chatham and Portsmouth, from whence the Navy Royal, when in the Downes, takes in Provisions; and where he believes, and has been informed, the King may victual cheaper than at London; which Office will become useless, in case the said Harbour be not repaired.

Mr. PapiUon said, That the Commissioners of the Victualling Office, on their Agent s Information from Dover, that the said Harbour was so cltoaked up, that his Majesty's Ships could no longer be supplied with Provisions from thence, have been forced to supply them from London, though on various Occasions, during the War, Dover supplied the main Body of the Fleet with Provisions for some Time; and believes it is capable of supplying 20 or 30 Sail throughout the Year, on fitting Notice:

That if there had not been a Victualling Office at Dover during the late War, the Fleet must many Times have met with considerable Disappointments, to the Prejudice of the Service; at was too plain, when that Port was not fully provided to answer the Wants of the Ships in the Downes, but were forced to wait for Provisions from London; which has frequently given that Delay, through the Incertainty of Wind and Weather to admit its going down, that it has been a great Prejudice to the Publick: Besides, they are subject to Miscarriages; and cost the King, besides Pilotage and Demurrage, 3 s. per Ton more than what is sent from Dover, as he believes.

Mr. Breton said, That upon the late Expedition by Sea before Dunkirk, the Fleet was supplied with Pilots from Dover; which has alw ays been a very great Nursery for able Pilots and Seamen, who have signalized themselves upon many Occasions, and are a great Help to the Fishery at Yarmouth; and that the Port of Dover maintained Five or Six Privateers during the late War, and took many Prizes; and many other Privateers also took Sanctuary there, because they could speedily be out and into Port again.

That he has heard by several Gentlemen that came from Calais, That the French King is making a Harbour there at a very great Expence.

Mr. Mackay said, That in August last he was at Calais; where he saw about 300 Men employed in making a Harbour; that they wrere making a Work to carry their Pier out below Low-water Mark, in Order to maintain 20 Foot constant Water within the Harbour, as the Captain of the Quay told him, which they thought sufficient for 4th or 5th Rates to go out and in, at any Time: And the said Captain further told Mr. Mackay, That the Money w*as raised for carrying on the said Work; and that it was intended to make the said Harbour as good and safe as Money and Art could possibly, although they have no Backwater.

That the Committee thought it for their Service to have the Opinion of Trinity-house, touching the said Harbour,

And accordingly, Sir Richard Haddock, Captain Atkinson, and several others of their Members attended; and

informed the Committee, That their Board were unanimously agreed, That Dover Harbour w'as of very great Use and Consequence to the Nation, and a general Advantage to Trade.

Sir Richard Haddock also agreed with Sir Henry Sheersy that in 1652, 4th and 5th Rates frequently went into the said Harbour, and cleaned, and victualledAnd added, That he saw Two 4th Rates come in and lie to the Side of the said Harbour, and in 48 Hours after went out cleaned: And also said, That the Dover Merchant, a Three-deck Ship of or 500 Tons, loaded in the said Harbour, and proceeded in her Voyage to Cadiz: And that the Victualling Office at Dover is of much less Use than formerly, and w ill become useless, if the Harbour be not speedily repaired.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the restoring the said Harbour of Dover to its former State and Condition, will be of great Service to the Nation, and Benefit to Trade and Navigation.

The Estimate, mentioned in the said Report, of the Charge of repairing and recovering the Harbour and Pier of Dover.

A Petition of several Merchants trading to Spaine was Clandcsiii presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Trade, notwithstanding the high Duties laid on French Goods, yet the Petitioners have cause to believe, divers Persons have found out a Way to evade the Law, by importing French Wines from St. Sebastian, Leghorne, Genoa, and other Ports, and entering and paying Duties, only as Spanish and Italian Wines, to the great Prejudice of the fair Trader, and this Kingdom in general; for that, unless this pernicious Trade be prevented, it will much lessen the Exportation of Commodities from England to Spain; which are chiefly vested into Spanish Wines brought hither; which the Petitioners cannot vent, by reason of the Importation of French Wines, as aforesaid: And praying, That such Means may be used for preventing the said unfair Trading, and for the Encouraging the Spanish Trade, as the House shall, think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, who are appointed to pre* pare, and bring in, the Bill for the better preventing unlawful and clandestine Trade.

A Petition of several Merchants of London trading to Ditto. Portugall was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That since the high Duties laid upon French Wines, there have been great Quantities of Wines imported into this Kingdom from St. Sebastian, and other Ports in Biscay, and the Streights; which the Petitioners believe to be French Wines, because that, till lately, no Wines were brought from thence, nor any such Wines made near these Places; yet they are entered, and pay Duties as Spanish or Italian Wines: That the Petitioners do yearly export great Quantities of Woollen Manufactures, Fish,

Lead, Tin, &c. to Portugall, the Returns whereof are chiefly their Wines; by which the Petitioners were considerable Losers the last Year, and are like to be greater this Year; for that since last Vintage several thousand Tuns of French Wines have been imported into England from Biscay, and the Streights; and greater Quantities are expected from thence, and the Streights: That this collusive Trade of bringing in French, under the Name and Duty of Spanish and Italian Wines, is not only prejudicial to the Petitioners, but the Nation in general; for that French Wines are not to be purchased without ready Money, but the Portuguese exchange for our Commodities; which advantageous trade must greatly abate, if the Petitioners cannot find Vent for their Wines: And praying the Consideration of the House thereof, that such Means may be used, for preventing the said national Mischief, as shall be thought meet.

A Petition of the Fishery, inhabiting the Town of Folkstone, in the County of Kent, a Member of the Cinque Ports, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, The said Town, within these 30 Years, is very much improved, and peopled by the Fishing Trade, who fish the whole Year throughout in the narrow Seas; but their chief Dependence is by fishing in MaCkrel and Herring Seasons, between Beachy Head and the North Foreland, with a Fleet of about Ninety Sail; whereby themselves, and many poor People in the Country, are relieved, and many able Seamen raised: That the Petitioners are much discouraged in their said Fishery, since the Peace, by the French of Diep and Bulloine, who catch on our Coast great Quantities of Mackrels and Herrings, and sell them at Sea to English Smackmen; thereby ruining the Petitioners Trade, and glutting their Markets, and under colour of fishing, and dealing with such Smackmen, many French Commodities are commonly imported, and Wool, and the Coin of this Kingdom, unlawfully exported: And praying, That such Provision may be made for Preservation of the Petitioners Trade, and encouraging the English Fishery, as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the Sale, within this Kingdom, of Fish taken by Foreigners in Foreign Vessels: And that Sir Philip Butler, Mr. Desbovery and Mr, Breaker, do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of several of the Gentlemen, Clergymen, Woollen and other Inhabitants, of the adjoining Counties of Mont- Manu‘ gomery and Merioneth, in North Wales, on behalf of faclures‘ themselves, and many others subsisting on the Woollen Manufactures in those Parts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Decay of Trade in the Woollen Manufactures is so visible with them, That their Poor daily increase; and those that make a shift to keep House are so reduced, that they cannot help to subsist their Fellow Christians and Tvades-folks in the Woollen Manufactures; the Cause whereof they chiefly ascribe to the additional Duty laid on Flanders Linen, and the Prohibition of our Cloth there: And praying the Consideration of the House, for restoring and improving the Trade of the English Woollen Manufactory.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the State and Condition of the Trade of England; and particularly to consider of the Encouraging and Improving the Manufactures of thi£ Kingdom.

A Petition of Robei't Broadnax, Lieutenant Colonel to the Broadnj Earl of Warrington s Regiment of Horse, was presented Petition to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner RecomJ was one of the Party, that joined with the late Earl of Warrington, at the time of his Majesty's Landing for out Deliverance; and being best skilled in military Discipline, had the chief Conduct of that Party; for the Promoting of which Service the Petitioner spent the greatest Part of his Fortune, and never received any Consideration for the same-; and afterwards he obtained a Commission to be Lieutenant Colonel of the said Regiment in the Service of Ireland, and was at great Expence to put himself in an Equipage for that Post; wherein he had not been Two Months, but he was cashiered, without any Fault, that he knows of, and sent Prisoner to England, without his Pay, his Horses and Servants being taken from him: And praying, That, by reason of his Losses and Disappointment, he being reduced to Want and Poverty, his Case may be taken into Consideration, and a Recompence for his Services and Losses appointed him.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Francis Cremick Esquire, and Mary his Wife, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bill depending in the House for vesting the real Estate of Joseph Gardner, and Sarah his Wife, in Trustees, to be sold, is prejudicial to the Petitioners, and ' to disinherit them, they being Co-legatees with their Bro-

thers and Sisters in the Will of their Father William Ridges Esquire, whose Estate the Premises to be sold was; and Charles Ridges endeavours to stifle a Settlement, w hereby the Petitioners are intitled to a Remainder of Part of the Lands in the Bill: And praying, That the Petitioners may be heard touching the Premises; and that James Ridges may produce the said Settlement.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

JWract' A Petition of several Aldermen and Burgesses of the ecUon‘ ancient Borough of Pontefract, in the County of 'York, in the behalf of themselves, and of the Majority of the Aldermen and Burgesses of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a late Election of John Bright Esquire, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, being declared void by this House, a Writ issued for choosing another Burgess: At which Election, on the First Instant, several of the Petitioners, who have a Right to vote, offered to vote for Robert Monckton Esquire; but Mr. Hastins Sayle, the Mayor, arbitrarily refused to accept them, and admitted others to vote for the said Mr. Bright, who had no Right: That, if the Petitioners Votes had been taken, Mr. Monckton would have had the Majority; but the Mayor had unduly returned Mr. Bright, in Wrong to the Petitioners, and Mr. Monckton, who was duly chosen: And praying Relief therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Colonel Baldwin Leighton was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was the first Commissioned Officer that appeared for his Majesty, and the Protestant Interest, in Ireland, upon the Resolution, and used his utmost Endeavours towards the rescuing that Kingdom out of Popish Hands; and, though great Solicitations were made to him, to continue in the Service of the late King James, with Promises of paying the Petitioner all his Arrears, amounting to near 1,000l. yet he attended his Majesty with the Address and Association of the Protestant Nobility and Gentry of Ireland\. before his Majesty's Accession to the Throne, and returned into Ireland with about 5.50 blank Commissions, and was made a Colonel himself; in which Service he suffered very great Losses: And there is due to him, for subsisting Ids Men, and his ow n Pay, the Sum ot 2,400l. besides his former Arrears: And praying, That he may have Half-pay as a Colonel, until his Arrears are paid, or he be otherwise provided for.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

An ingrossed Bill for the ascertaining the Measures of Beer and Ale, according to sealed Measures, to be kept in every Tow n, was read the Third time.

An iiigrossed Clause was offered, as a Rider, for marking of Glass and Eai then-ware Measures:

And the same was Tw ice read; and amended;

And then the same was read the Third time.

And the Question being put, That the Clause be made Part of the Bill;

It passed in the Negative.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered, as a Rider, That the Act shall not extend to the Colleges and Halls in the Universities:

And the same was Thrice read, and agreed to be made Part of the Bill.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Bill; Pr. 3. L. *, after " same," to insert " and the said " Standard Measures shall be delivered to every succeeding Officer

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and the Bill amended at the Table accordingly.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Bill; Pr. *, L. *, to leave out " One Penny per Quart,

" and so in proportion," and insert One Farthing per Measure

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and the Bill amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be, An Act for the ascertaining the Measures for retailing Ale and Beer.

Ordered, That Mr. Pierpoint do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the City of Exetei', and other the principal Citizens and Inhabitants of the said City, and County of the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners designing to make the River Exe navigable from the Sea to the said City, which will be of public Good to the Places adjacent, and increase his Majesty's Revenues there, have expended, for that Purpose, within 25 Years past, the Sum of 10,000l. and the further Sum of 11,000l. within the last Two Years; which

Sums are still owing from the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, who, of themselves, are not able to complete the said Work: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for raising Money for perfecting the making the River Exe navigable.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter; and report the same, with their Opinion therein to the House, whether it be fit, that a Bill be brought in according to the said Petitition:

And it is referred to Sir Edward Seymour, Sir Richard Cocks, Mr. ScobellMr. Clark, Mr. Gwynn, Mr. Carter,

Sir JVm. Drake, Mr. Vernon, Sir Walter Yonge, Sir Rowland Guy n, Sir Robert Davers, Mr. Harley, Mr. Lcrwther,

Sir Barth. Shower, Mr. Blaake, Lord Ranelagh, Sir JVa. Young, Sir Arth. Owen, Mr. Thornhagh; and all . that serve for the Counties of Devon and Cornwall: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Four a Clock, in the Speaker's Chambers: And are to have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of divers Gentlemen, Freeholders, Mer- Exe chants, Traders, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of IsavlSal101 Exon, paying Scotland Lot, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said City has enjoyed a flourishing Trade for many Years; which was greatly advanced by the Convenience the Citizens have had, for above 100 Years, by bringing their Goods imported from foreign Parts, by Barges and Lighters, to the said City: But the Chamber of the said City, being intrusted with the Disposal of its Revenues, have unadvisedly undertaken to enlarge their Chanels, through which the Lighters and Barges used to pass; and, for about 15 Months last past, have diverted the River out of its ancient Course, and totally deprived the Petitioners of their said Conveniency, to their very great Damage:

That the said Chamber, being disappointed in their rash Undertaking, have desisted from prosecuting thereof; and refuse to apply the Revenues of the saief City, w herewith they are only intrusted as Trustees, towards finishing the said Work, although they have sufficient for that Purpose; the same being, by their own Estimate, to be done for 5,000l.: But, by indirect Practices, the Chamber have procured a Petition to be signed to this House, by great Numbers of poor Inhabitants of the said City, who are no way liable to pay Rates or Taxes, desiring Leave to bring in a Bill to assess the Inhabitants of the said City towards completing the said Work; which Tax, as it is altogether unnecessary, so it will be very grievous to the Petitioners: And praying, That they may not be burdened with an unnecessary Tax; but that the Revenues of the City may be applied to make the said River navigable, as formerly it was.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the City of Exeter, is referred.

A Complaint being made to the House, That Mr. Privilege Stuteville, being summoned to attend a Committee of this Witness House, as he was going away from the said Committee, ^ouse.1 was taken up by Sir Talbot Clark and one Mr. Edmund Evans\ who detained him into their Custody, on Account of their being Bail for him;

Ordered, That the said Sir Talbot Clark and Mr. Evans do set the said Mr. Stuteville at Liberty.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty, towards the Payment of his Proportion of the Debt owing to the Prince of Denmark.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, for the Carrying on the Coinage of the Gold and Silver of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, for continuing the Contracts for circulating Exchequer Bills for One Year longer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards making good the Deficiencies of the Aid of Three Shillings in the Pound, granted in the Eighth Year of his Majesty's Reign.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards making good the Deficiencies of the Duty upon Paper and Parchment, granted the same Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards making good the Deficiencies upon Malt 'Pickets.

Resolved, 'I hat it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards making good the Deficiencies of the Quarterly Poll, grained in the Ninth Year of his Majesty's lieign.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards the Paying off the Debt due for Transport Service.

Resolxed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards the Payment of the Debt due to the Navy, and the Debt due for sick and wounded Seamen.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made therein, by adding, "and the Monies, to be raised, to be laid out in " Lands in this Kingdom, and settled upon the Prince

iC and Princess, and their Issue, according to the Marriage Agreement

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That a Supply be granted to his Majesty, towards the Payment of his Proportion of the Debt owing to the Prince of Denmark; and the Monies, to be raised, to be laid out in Lands in this Kingdom, and settled upon the Prince and Princess, and their Issue, according to their Marriage Agreement.

The rest of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his ^ebt due to Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, That his Majesty will please to use his Endeavours lo procure other Princes and States to pay their Proportions of the Debt due to the Prince of Denmark.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, Ways and resolve itself into a Committee of the w hole House, to ^leans* consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Memorandum. I cannot possibly give a perfect Account of all Grants since his Majesty's Accession to the Crown, pursuant to the Order of this Honourable House,.by reason several hath been within the Division of other Auditors, and not before me; and besides, there hath been lately several Rents claimed, as purchased of the Trustees for Sale of Fee-farm Rents within my Division; but, the Deed not being inrolled before me, I cannot give that Account of his Majesty's Revenue within my said Division which I ought or could do, if all Grants were inrolled in due Course accordingly. All which is most humbly submitted to this Honourable House.

Per Henry Shales, Auditor. I m

A PETITION of JVittiam Rider Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the late King Jams the Second, by his Letters Patents, did grant unto the Petitioner, and Edward Burdet Esquire, the sole Liberty and Power to erect a Conduit, Wharf, and other Buildings, upon the Beach of New Deal; and to dig the Highways, Streets, and waste Grounds, for laying Pipes, and bringing fresh Water to the said Town; which will be a great Advantage to the Inhabitants, and all Shipping resorting thither, where they have no fresh Water at present: But the Petitioner, who purpose th to supply the said Necessity from a River called foe. North Stream, it being the Opinion of able Engineers, that it cannot be done by Wrell-water, cannot effectually perform this Undertaking, without breaking up some small Part of the Soil of some Persons, lying between the Town and the said River: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill to enable him to perform and complete his Undertaking for bringing fresh Water to the Town of Deale.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir Robert Dovers do prepare, and bring in, the Bill.

A Petition of the Freeholders and others, of the Hundred of Brivton and Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surry, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have paid 4$. 6d. and 5$. 6 d. in the Pound, upon the two last 3 s. Aids upon Land, by reason many Persons, whose Estates were in Money, have since lost the same in Trade; others, who paid double, have complied with the Law, and now pay but single; and many others have removed out of the said Hundred and Borough; and many Families are impoverished by the great Fires in Bermondsey, and other Places; whereby the Petitioners are grievously burdened by the present Land Tax: And praying to be relieved in the succeeding Taxes.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty's Navy, Guards, and Garisons, and towards paying the Debt due to Seamen, and for other necessary Occasions, is committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Sir John Packington reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Sir Henry Fitzharris Baronet, was referred, That they had examined and considered the same, and had agreed upon Resolutions, winch they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Vol. 13.

Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same # *

That, upon Examination of the Allegations contained in the said Petition, it did appear, That the Estate of Sir Edward Fitzharris Baronet, the Petitioner's Grandfather, was, immediately after the Rebellion in 1641, granted to Robert Oliver Esquire, and others; who possessed themselves thereof; the said Sir Edward being neither outlawed, attainted, or convicted of any Crime:

That by the Act of Settlement and Explanation, made in the 17th and 18th Years of the Reign of the late King Charles the Second, it is, amongst other Things, enacted,' That the said Sir Edward Fitzharris, with several others therein named, their Heirs and Assigns, Should be restored unto their several and respective-Seats; as they should respectively choose, in Two Months after the Sitting of the Commissioners for examining the said Act* and of 2,000 Acres of Land thereunto adjoining, if they, or any of their Ancestors, or any in Trust for them, were seised of so much, upon the 22d of October 1641; subject nevertheless to the Proviso following; vis.

That if any Person or Persons shall, within the Space of Six Months, next after the Royal Assent to this Bill actually given, allege before the Lord Lieutenant, or other chief Governor or Governors of Ireland, and Council there, that the said Sir Edward Fitzharris huth committed any Massacre, Murder, or any such heinous Crime or Cruelty, upon the Persons of any of his Majesty's good Subjects; and shall prove the same by such Witnesses, or other Evidence, as the said Lord Lieutenant, or other chief Governor or Governors, and Council there, shall think good Proof; that then, and in such Case, it shall and may be lawful to and for the Lord Lieutenant, or other chief Governor or Governors there, by Order of the Council, to declare and adjudge him the said Sir Edward Fitzharris to be guilty of the Crimes and Cruelties so alleged and proved as aforesaid; and, upon such Declaration and Judgment, the said Sir Edward Fuzkarrisii and his Heirs, shall be, and are hereby made, incapable of any Benefit or Advantage in and by this present Act given, or of any Restitution as aforesaid; but shall remain and be, to all Intents and Purposes, in the same Plight and Condition as he or they would have been, if the said Sir Edward Fitzharris had not been named in this present Act: That there is a Clause in the said Act, for an Equiva-> lent to the Tenants in Possession:

That it appeared to the Committee, by an attested Copy' of an Order made by the Lord Lieutenant and Council of Ireland, the 25th Day of May 1666, That the said Robert Oliver exhibited a Petition at the Council Board, setting forth, That the Petitioner was able to prove the said Sir Edzcard Fitzharris guilty of *such Crimes, as would render him incapable of any Benefit by the said Act: To which Petition the Defendant Sir Edward did appear, and answer: And the Cause being, according to Appointment, then heard, in the Presence of both Parties, and their Counsel, and upon full Hearing thereof, and of such Witnesses or Evidences as were then produced, it was by the said Lord Lieutenant and Council declared, That no Proof, by Witnesses or other Evidences, had been produced before them, whereby they might be induced to declare and adjudge the said Sir Edward Fitzharris to be guilty of any Massacre, Murder, or such other heinous Crime or Cruelty, committed upon die Person of any of his Majesty's good Subjects:

A Petition of the Masters, and Keepers or Wardens, and Commonalty of the Mystery and Art of Brewers, of the City of London, and the rest of the Brewers in the Weekly Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That it is the Property of all Englishmen to be tried by a Jury; but that Right was taken away from the Petitioners by an Act of the 12th Car. 2di for granting certain Impositions upon Beer, Ale, and other Liquors; whereby all Forfeitures and Offences were to be heard by the Commissioners of Excise, from whom an Appeal was to be had to Commissioners of Appeals to be appointed by his Majesty, whose Judgment was to be final: That the Offences comprised in the said Act were but few, and the Forfeitures small; but, by several late Acts, very great Penalties are inflicted for small Offences, and a Moiety given to Informers: And although, by the last Acts, it is directed, That the Penalties shall be recovered by Information, &c. in Westminster-hall; yet Liberty is thereby given, that such Penalties may be recovered by such Ways as by the said Act; by which Means, there has not one Penalty been sued for at Westminster, as the Petitioners know of: That the Gaugers also charge the Petitioners with more than they ought, against which, the Petitioners have made Complaints; but the Commissioners of Excise will not hear or relieve them before Payment of the Duty, contrary to the Meaning of the said Act. as the Petitioners conceive: The Commissioners also refuse to appoint the Hearing of such Complaints against Overcharges in Course; whereby they often . many Months and Years unheard; but, upon Information of a Penalty, the same is forthwith heard, adjudged, and levied upon the Petitioners, who, at the same Time, have many Complaints depending of much elder Date; and though positive Evidence be given of such Overcharges, yet the Complainants are denied Relief: That many Times the Petitioners have Drink returned, which has paid the Duty; and they are forced to start, or put again into new Drink, then in the Tuns; which though done in Presence of the Gaugers, yet they charge the same again with the full Duty of Excise, for which the Petitioners are forced to pay double Duty: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for their Relief in the Matters aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table until the House shall resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of his Majesty's Revenue.

A PETITION of the Aldermen, Stewards, and Company of Tanners, within the City of Chester, on behalf of themselves, and others of their Trade, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bark of Trees, which is absolutely necessary for the tanning of Leather, is become scarcer than formerly, great Quantities being ground to Dust, made up into Casks, and exported to Ireland; which Practice, if continued, will ruin the Peiitioners Trade, and damage the Landed Men of England, by rendering raw Hides of little Value: And praying, That a Remedy may be provided against the Exporting of Bark into Ireland\

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Master Ropemakers in and about the City of London, on behalf of themselves, and several other Masters and Journeymen of the same Trade, belonging to the several Sea Port Towns of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by the late Practice of importing great Quantities of foreign Cordage, and Cable Yarn, the Petitioners are greatly impoverished, the Plantations, Which are chiefly supplied therewith, ill served, because it is not well wrought, and the Kings Duties diminished; all which is occasioned by the Drawback, being 5s. 7d. outward, and but 5s. 11 d. iuward Duty, per Hundred; so that the King hath but 4d. per C. Weight, which encourages the Merchants to import foreign Cordage; whereas, if the same were made in England, the Hemp pays 2$. 6d. Duty inwards, and the wrought Cordage 6d. outwards; and thereby the Petitioners would be employed, and the Plantations well served: And praying that the Drawback upon foreign Cordage, and Cable Yarn, may be taken off.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of W'fcys and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Twelve Governors of the Heredita- Frauds ments and Goods of the Church of Crediton, alias Kirton, Workr in the County of Devon, their Assistants and Guardians, incorporated by virtue of an Act of Parliament made anu a in the 10th Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for erecting Hospitals, Wrork-houses, and Houses of Correction, within the Town and Parish of Crediton, in the County of Devon; and for the better Relief of the Poor there; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there... many Hundreds of poor People in the said Parish employed in the Woollen Manufactures, some of which commit small Thefts, under the Value of 12d. and confess the same; who are thereupon committed to Prison, where they lie several Months, and their Families, during that time, are wholly maintained at the Charge of the Parish, and often return greater Thieves than before; and many are not prosecuted, for fear of bringing a greater Charge upon the toid Parish, so that they often proceed to commit greeter Crimes: And praying, That a Clause may be inserted in

one of the Acts now passing for the better Employing of the Poor, or some other Act, to empower such Corporation, or any of their Courts, to call before them any poor Person of their Parish, that shall be accused to have committed Petit Larceny; and if they confess the same, that the Corporation may be impowered to order such poor Persons to be sent to their House of Correction, and there be publickly whipped for the said Offence, without being sent to the common Gaol.

Mr. Speaker reported. That he having, with the House, attended his Majesty, on Wednesday last, with their Address of the 15th Instant, representing to his Majesty the Resolutions of this House of the 18th of January last, relating to the Grants of the forfeited Estates in Ireland; and that, to prevent any Mistake in reporting his Majesty's Answer thereupon, he had obtained a Copy thereof; which he read; and is as followeth; viz.

Gentlemen,

I was not only led by Inclination, but thought myself obliged in Justice, to reward those who had served well, and particularly in the Reduction of Ireland, out of the Estates forfeited to me by the Rebellion there.

The long War, in which we were engaged, did occasion great Taxes, and has left the Nation much in Debt; and the taking just and effectual Ways for lessening that Debt, and supporting publick Credit, is what, in my Opinion, will best contribute to the Honour, Interest, and Security, of the Kingdom.

Resolved, That whosoever advised his Majesty's Answer to the Address of this House, presented to his Majesty on Wednesday last, has used his utmost Endeavour to create a Misunderstanding and Jealousy betwixt the King and his People.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty belaid upon all Hops imported into Ireland, except such as are of the Growth of this Kingdom.

A PETITION of several Pursers, in behalf of them- Pursersofthi selves, and the rest of the aggrieved Pursers of his Navy. Majesty's Navy Royal, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Pursers are the only Persons that give Security to the King for the true Performance of their Trust; yet they are often injured by the Commanders taking what Provisions they please, and converting them to their own Use; which that they may the easier do, they often take the Pursers Instruments, and employ them in their own Service; and when Pursers have modestly asked their Commanders how they should be salved, they have been abused, beaten, and confined to their Cabins; by which and many other unwarrantable Methods, the Pursers cannot escape running into the King's Debt, to their utter Ruin: And praying the House to take their Case into Consideration, and relieve them therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Kelly is referred: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, to the House.

Carteret; w ho, in 1(381, for a valuable Consideration, conveyed East Jersey to the Petitioners, and others, their Heirs and Assigns: That in 1682, the said Duke confirmed the Petitioners Title to East Jersey, with all the Powers of Government, as fully as they were granted to him: And King Charles, by his Declaration, under the Great Seal of England, recognized the Petitioners Authority, commanding the Inhabitants to obey the Petitioners, as their lawful Governors: That the Petitioners have laid out great Sums of Money in settling Plantations at East Jersey, and by their Industry have laid the Foundations of a hopeful Colony there, which has, ever since its first Separation from New York, remained a distinct Province and Government; and had distinct Assemblies, and a Port called Amboy; but, upon unjust Complaints of some Inhabitants of New York, Attempts have been made to take away the Port of Amboy; and the Governors of New York have, by Force of Arms, boarded several Ships, and carried them out of Amboy to New York, to compel them to enter their Ships, and pay such Customs as were imposed by their Assemblies; though the Inhabitants of East Jersey are not subject to the Laws of New York, nor are any Customs payable for European Goods imported to East Jersey, or any other English Plantation, otherwise than by Laws made by the respective Assemblies of those Plantations: That the Petitioners, insisting on their Right, obtained from the Commissioners of the Treasury, Directions Vol. 13*

Colonel Granville reported from the said Committee,

That they had spent some time in the Consideration of the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

The House being informed, That a Crowd of People Riotous are got together, in a tumultuous and riotous Manner, Crowd about in the Palace-yard, Westmmster-hall, and Passages to th*House* this House;

Ordered, That the Justices of the Peace of Middlesex, and Westminster do go forthwith, and disperse the said riotous Crowd.

Ordered, That the Justices of the Peace of the City of Westminster do immediately attend this House, and bring the Constables with them.

The House being informed, That the Justices of Peace of the City of Westminster attended;

They were called in: And, at the Bar, Mr. Speaker, by Order of the House, acquainted them with the said tumultuous Riot; and that the House did expect, that they should go immediately, and disperse the same; and give the House an Account what they did therein; and that they do commit such as they found most active in the said Riot, and take care to prevent any such Riots for the time to come.

And then they withdrew.

Resolved, That the inciting and encouraging any Number of Persons to come in a riotous, tumultuous, or disorderly Manner, to this House, in order either to hinder or promote the passing any Bill, or other Matters depending before the House, being against the Constitution and Freedom of Parliaments, is a high Crime and Misdemeanor.

The House being informed, That one J. Dennis, hath incited the Seamen and Seamen's Wives to come in a riotous Manner to this House;

Ordered, That the said J, Dennis be, for the said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

The House being informed, That the Justices of Peace for the City of Westminster attended;

They were called in; and at the Bar, gave the House an Account, That they had taken care to disperse the said riotous Tumult

And then they withdrew.

The House being informed, That one James Gardner, had uttered very insolent Words, inciting the said Tumult against the Members of this House; and was seized by some of the said Justices Officers near the House;

Ordered, That the said James Gardner be sent for Ly the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, together with Mr. Braddon, who heard him utter the said Words.
