Mr. Brewer', according to Order, presented to VOL. 13.

the

That by several Assignments from the said Earl of Dover's Trustees, and lastly from the Petitioner Mr. Kent, by Indenture dated the 5th of July 1699, the Freehold' and Inheritance of the said Markets and Fair became vested in Sir Nath. Curson, and his Heirs, for the Consideration of 23,344 /. subject to an Equity of Redemption at any time within Ten Years.

That the Patentees, and their Assigns, quietly enjoyed the said Markets from the Time they were granted until the 13th of February last, w hen the City of London sued out a Scire facias, which is now depending, to repeal the aforesaid Grants, by virtue of a Charter granted to the

City

-Cattle Markets in the Haymarket.

233 28 Februar . 1699.

City of London by King Edward the Third, in Parliament, in the First Year of his Reign; wherein there is a Clause, That Ho Market should from thenceforth be granted infra septem leucas in circuitu civitatis pr(edict.:

That Sir Nath. Curson, and those under whom he claims, have been at great Charges in Building, Paving, and making other Conveniences, for the said Markets: And the Petitioners alleged, That the Suppression thereof will be a great Inconvenience to the neighbouring Villages, and all Inhabitants near the same.

To prove which, John Allen, Butcher, of Westminster, £aid, That he bought and sold Cattle and Sheep at the Hay market, on Mondays md Wednesdays, about 30 Years ago; and that, for 12 Years past, he and his Sons have bought Cattle on Tuesdays and Thursdays at Brookfield Market, which is made very convenient, at the Ciiarge of several Thousand Pounds; and if the same should be put down, it will ruin Thousands of People; who are supplied with Provisions from thence; and particularly the People of Southwark, Lambeth, Wandsor, Putney, Fulham, Chelsey, Westminster, and all Parts lying westward of London:

That Brookfield Market is also convenient for all Cattle coming out of the West of England, by reason they heed not be driven on the Stones to Smithfield Market; which oftentimes occasions the Flesh to be heated, and then it soon taints.

Peter Wych and Richard Steel, Butchers, of Newport Market, confirmed what Allen said in relation to Brookfield Market, for Six or Seven Years past.

Nozvel Kellet, of Westminster, Butcher, and Richard Steer, said, That they knew Cattle sold in the Hay market, about 35 or 40 Years ago, in Inns, being then few in Number; but the said Market being since removed to Brookfield, it is very much increased, and is a greater Conve-niency for the Butchers, near that End of the Town, to buy Cattle there, than at Smithfield; because driving them on the Stones from Smithfield often lames them, and many times they are frighted, and over-heat themselves, so that they must be immediately killed on a Friday, whilst the Flesh is hot, for Saturdays Market; and then the Flesh will not take Salt; whereby they have many times disobliged their Customers: And Steel said, He believed there are or 500 Sheep and Lambs, and about 200 Oxen, brought to Brookfield on a Market-day.

John Allen said, He would rather give Ten Shillings more for a Bullock bought at Broolfield Market, than he would for a Bullock of the same Value, bought at Smithfield; because they can buy on Thursdays at Brookfield, and kill the next Day, when the Flesh is cool; but if he buys at Smithfield, the Market is on Friday, and must kill the same Day, whatever Accident happens, or lose Saturdays Market

That there is not Room enough at Smithfield to hold the Cattle brought to Town in a Midsummer Quarter; for which Reason, there is as many, or more, bought at Islington, Newington, Paddington, Mile-End, and other Places about London, as are sold at Smithfield; and knows that one Holland, at Islington, sold 2,500 Sheep at one time, because there was not Room enough for them at Smithfield Market.

Charles Bettie, of Newport Market, Butcher, said, That, within these Four or Five Years, he has seen several Droves of Cattle driven from Smithfield to Knights-bridge, for want of Room at Smithfield, the Pens being all full.

John Allen said, That, for 12 Years past, he has seen Beasts, Sheep, and Lambs, driven from Smithfield for want of Room; and has observed Ten Droves at a time 60 driven away from Smithfield.

All the Witnesses agree, That Brookfield Market is very convenient for that End of the Town: And it was insisted, That the publick Good ought to be considered by the Legislative Power, who, upon all Occasions, have altered the Law as Occasion required; and the Establishment of Brookfield Market cannot so prejudice Smithfield Market,

as to reduce the Tolls and Rents to less than what they were at the time of the Grant to the City, the City and Suburbs being now as big again as they were then.

That, upon the Petition of the City of London, also referred to the said Committee, the Matter is as followeth; viz.

That King Edward the Third, in the First Year of his Reign, by Charter in Parliament, granted to the City of London, That no Market should be granted from thenceforth, within Seven Miles of the said City; which Char* ter was confirmed by Act of Parliament, reciting the same, in the Seventh Year of the Reign of King Richard the Second:

That till the Year 1636, no Market for live Cattle was attempted since the said Charter; but then one Dor-rell, and the Inhabitants of St. Giles s Parish, endeavoured to set up one near Hyde Park; and the City being heard thereupon at the Council Board, a Stop was put thereto, their Lordships declaring, That a Market there would be inconvenient and unfit, and contrary to the said Grants in Parliament:

That, about the 15th Car. 2di, the Grant to John Harvey and John Coell Esquires, was procured for Two Markets weekly, in the Hay market, as in the Petition of Sir Nath. Curson is alleged: But the Place being inconvenient, and but little used, the City did not oppose it: That afterwards some Persons endeavoured to obtain a Patent for erecting Tw o Markets in Conduit Mead, behind Albemarle House, in lieu of those at the Haymarket \ but the City, being informed thereof, entered a Caveat against the said intended Patent; and in March 1683, Sir John Coell, who was interested therein, petitioned the Council Board, That the Suspension might be taken off: But, upon hearing both Parties, on the Fourth of April 1683, the Suspension was continued, and the Patent stopped:

That soon after a Quo warranto was brought against the City; and, by Judgment thereon, they were dissolved, and their Liberties seized; and then, viz. in the Second and Fourth Years of the Reign of the late King James the Second, the Lord Dover obtained Tw o Grants, theoue for removing the said Markets from the Haymarket to Great Brookfield, and the other for changing the Days as in the Petition of Sir Nath. Curson, non obstante, that no Writ of Ad quod damnum had been executed or returned: That when the City Charter and Liberties were restored by the present Government, the City petitioned his now Majesty to be relieved against the said Grants; who ordered Sir Edward Ward, the then Attorney General, to examine and report the Fact:

And, at the Hearing before the said Attorney Gene-neral. Dr. Barbon appeared, and was heard; who claimed an Interest in the said Grants, and desired to try the Validity thereof by Law:

That on the 11th of April 1695, the said Attorney General made his Report to the King and Council; and was of Opinion, That the King might permit the City to bring a Scire facias, in his Majesty's Name, in order to try the Validity and Legality of the said Grants to Sir John Coell; which his Majesty was pleased in Council to order accordingly, as appeared by the Report:

That in 1695, the City sued out a Scire facias against the Heir of Sir John Coell; and Doctor Barbon, being then a Member of Parliament, insisting on his Privilege, put a Stop to any further Proceedings thereon during his Life; but after his Death another Scire facias was sued out against the Heir of Sir John Coell; and then an Appearance was*obtained ;' and the Defendants excepted to the Scire facias: On arguing whereof before the Lord Chancellor, the Exceptions were over-ruled, and the Defendants ordered to plead, which they did in Abatement, the last Term; because no Person is returned Tenant to the Market; and so the Matter depends in Chancery undetermined.

It was insisted, That Brookfield Market would much prejudice Smithfield Market, by lessening the Tolls there, and

will

12. W. III. .28° Februarii. ,233

will bring to decay St- Bartholomew's Hospital, whose Revenue chiefly ariseth out of the Rents and Fines of Houses adjacent to Smithfield.

It was also insisted, That there is a particular Act of Parliament, made in the 22d and 23d Years of King Charles the Second, for the preventing Frauds in the Buying and Selling Cattle in Smithfield, and for seizing such as shall be once bought there, and brought thither again to be sold; which will not extend to Brookfield Markets. And,

To prove that there is Room enough at Smithfield Market to receive all Sorts of live Cattle, to supply the City and Suburbs;

Mr. Wright, the King's Purveyor, and John Preston, Graziers, said, That there is Room enough at Smithfield for all the live Cattle that are brought to Town; and, as a Reason, said, That there w ere Three Market-days every Week, viz. Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays; and that Wednesday was omitted for want of Cattle, Two Market days being sufficient to supply the Occasions of the Town: That they have bought and sold Cattle and Sheep there these 30 Years, and never knew that any were drove back for want of Room, but sometimes to keep them for next Market-day, in Hopes of a better Price, when the Market has been low; but the Rounds in Smithfield, which will hold Thousands of Sheep, are not made Use of, though they might, if streigbtened for Room:

That they have bought Sheep at Islington on Thursdays, and sold them again at Smithfield on Fridays, for about 12 Years past; and others have done so long before; and often buy Sheep at Islington, not for want of Room at Smithfield, but to throw them into the Marshes to supply the Town in Winter; and for that, if they should be brought to Smithfield, they would be dirty, and 12 d. apiece worse than when bought clean.

Mr. Wright also said, That SmitMeld is big enough to hold all the live Cattle sold in the City and Suburbs, and

Seven Miles about; but not for all the Flesh Provisions Cattle expended within that Compass, if brought to Town alive; ^arkctB much whereof is brought to Town killed, and so sold in the several Markets of London, and the Suburbs; and much killed and sold in the Villages round about, that never came to Town.

JVHUam Cookson, Edward Yardley, John Buckston,

Salesmen, said. There was always Room enough at Smithfield for all the Cattle and Sheep brought thither; and that, for 30 or 40 Years past, they never heard any body complain for want of Room, the Market never being so full but that it would hold more; and if the Cattle sold at Islington, and other Places, were brought to Smithfield, there would be Room enough for them: And Cookson said, That he knows not of any Cattle sold any where but in the Market; but it would be better for the Butchers, and all Persons, to have all Cattle sold at Smithfield; from whence they may, with Care, drive their Cattle to this End of the Town without Damage; but sometimes a Bullock will be frighted and overheated, do what they can.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken in Consideration upon Thursday Morning next, in a full House.

A Petition of Baldwyn Leighton Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in 1689, the Petitioner, being informed of the great Abuses committed in the Fleet Prison, whereby the Publick suffered ' extremely, applied himself to his Majesty, in order to redress the same; who ordered the Petitioner to take out a Commission under the Great Seal, to inquire into the said Grievances: Which be accordingly did; executed it at his own Cost; and thereupon, by Inquisition taken in March 1689, the then Warden was found guilty of several Extortions, wilful Escapes, and other Oppressions; whereby the Office was forfeited to his Majesty in Fee, who granted the same to the Petitioner; which Grant passed the Privy Seal, but was stopt at the Great Seal, by a Caveat entered there; and the Matter was contested several Years, before the King and Council, the House of Lords, and this House; but by the Craft of the

Fleet Officers, the said Inquisition was quashed :-

That in May % 1698, the Petitioner sued another Inquisition out of the Chancery; and thereupon, in August following, the present Warden, IVm. Ford Esquire, was found guilty of many Misdemeanors, and thereby the Office was forfeited to Iris Majesty; to which Inquisition Mr Ford has pleaded, and traversed the Facts; to which the Attorney General hath replied, and joined Issue; and.

Vol. 13.

the Cause is set down to be tried at the King's Bench Bar, upon the 24th of April next: But there being a Bill in the House, for paying off the Incumbrances on the Fleet Prison, and for Dissolution of the said Prison, he is thereby like to lose all Benefit of his Trouble and Charge, unless relieved by this House: And praying the House to take his Case into Consideration.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Memorial was read.

And the said Memorial is as followeth; viz.

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

His Majesty, by his Letters of Privy Seal, bearing Date the 28th Day of February last past, having required your Lordships, amongst other Things, to call all the Receivers of the Land Revenue to make up and pass their Accounts to Michaelmas 1698; and I being nominated, by the same Letters of Privy Seal, to be the Receiver of the Debts and Arrears that shall be depending insuper, or otherwise, upon the Foot of such Accounts, do think it my duty humbly to lay before your Lordships the Pro* ceedings which have been made thereupon.

First, Your Lordships were pleased, by your Warrant, bearing Date the 24th. Day of March 1698, strictly to charge and require the respective Auditors of the said Land Revenue to call every the said Receivers to make up and pass their said Accounts; and to certify your Lordships, if any Failure or Neglect should be made by them, or any of them, in the Performance thereof: And, by the same Warrant, the said Auditors were required to to transmit Abstracts to your Lordships of the last declared Accounts of the said Revenues remaining with them respectively.

That some of the said Auditors have accordingly transmitted Abstracts of the last declared Accounts to your Lordships; but very few, or none, of the said Receivers, as I find, upon Inquiry, the Receivers of the Duchy of Cornwall excepted, do prosecute or attend the passing of their said Accounts; nor have the said Auditors certified to your Lordships the Persons failing or neglecting so to do: Wherefore I have taken from the said Abstracts the following Account, to shew your Lordships in what lamentable Backwardness most of the said Receivers are in their Accounts; to the end your Lordships may thereby judge of the Necessity of compelling them to expedite the passing of the same by such Means as your Lordship*. shall think fitting.

As for the several Counties of Hampskirey Somerset, Dorset, Devon, Gloucester, and Cornwall, which are under the Audit of Mr. Parsons; there has been no Return made from him to your Lordships concerning the same: But I am informed, That all, or most, of the Accounts for the Revenues within this District, are in good Forwardness for Declaration:

I take leave also humbly to acquaint your Lordships, That, in pursuance of the said Letters of Privy Seal, your Lordships have been pleased to direct Mr. Auditor Shales to call the Receivers of the Profits arising to his Majesty from the Estate of the late Lord Preston to an Account for the same; and, by a State made thereof, by the said Mr. Shales, which is hereunto annexed, it appears, there is due and owing to his Majesty, as well from the Tenants of the said Estate, as the Accountants, and others therein concerned, the Sum of 3,524/. 105. 2 id. besides 3,1/46/. 15 s. 0 d. for the Profits of the said Estate in Yorkshire, for the time it was in Lease to the Earl of Carlisle and Sir Geo. Fletcher; of which no Account is yet given: But I am informed by the said Auditors, that unless a more than ordinary Authority be used by your Lordships, to compel the Persons concerned in the receiving the Issues and Profits in the said Estate, whereof Mr. Reginald Harriot was Chief, to account for the same, his Majesty will, in all Likelihood, be defeated of the Monies owing to him from the said Estate; the said Mr. Marryot using and contriving all Manner of ill Practices and Devices for that Purpose; and wholly neglects and evades the passing or perfecting of any Accounts of the same.

Thus having laid before your Lordships a State of the Proceedings, which have been already made upon the said Letters of Privy-Seal, I do humbly submit the same to your Lordships, to take such further Measures, for the

more effectual performing of his Majesty's Pleasure sig- Crown nified therein, as your Lordships, in your great Judgment Lands* and Wisdom, shall think fit

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

In Obedience to his Majesty's Letters of Privy Seal, bearing Date the 28th of February 1698, and your Lordships dormant Warrant thereupon, I have endeavoured to deliver in States or Abstracts of all such Accounts of his Majesty's Land Revenue, as I find have hitherto been declared, for the respective Counties within my several Assignments; but do not find any declared Accounts for the Counties of Salop, Stafford, Worcester, and Hereford, since the Restoration of his late Majesty YdmgCharks the Second; which said Counties were lately in the Assignment of Sir Joseph Seymour Knight, deceased, as Auditor; and the Receipt thereof hath been for some Time past, and still is, in the Hands of one Mr. John Digby; and if any such Accounts have been declared, they are not delivered over to me amongst the other Writings belonging to the said Assignment, but remain still in the Hands of Mr. Reginald Marriot, who was Deputy to the said Sir Joseph Seymour: Therefore I must humbly crave your Lordships, strict Order for Mr. Marryot to deliver up the said Accounts, if any such there be; and also for Mr. Digby to hasten to account for the Time that he hath been Receiver of the said Counties: Which is most humbly submitted to your Lordships Consideration.

A Copy examined. Henry Shales, Auditor.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir John Hoskins and Sir Rob. Regard:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act to enable Dalby Thomas Esguire, to sell Lands in Islington, in Middlesex, settled on his^Marriage with Dorothy his Wife, as Part of her Jointurfc; he settling another Estate, of equal or greater Value, in lieu thereof: To which they desire the Concurrence of this House. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the ascertaining the Measure for retailing Ale and Beer, vitiiout any Amendment.

A PETITION of the Deputy Lieutenants, Justices of the Peace and several Gentlemen, and other Freeholders, and Inhabitants, within the County of Cardigan, on the behalf of themselves, and several Thousands of the Inhabitants, Clothiers, and Dealers in the Wool Trade, in the said County, and the Parts adjoining the reunto, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, for several Years past, the Petitioners have had considerable Trade in Wool, and the Woollen Manufactures; but that the same is now very much obstructed by several Persons employed as Officers to prevent the Exportation of Wool, by their seizing great Parcels thereof carrying to, and brought from, the Markets, and extorting several great Sums from Persons owning the same, though there never was any Wool exported from those Parts, or any Suspicion thereof: And praying Redress in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of

Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Aldborough, in the Couqty of York; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Table: Where the same was read and is as followeth; viz.

That the Petitioner upon the Hearing, did not controvert the Election of Sir George Cook:

That, upon the Poll, there was,

But the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That the Sitting Member's Votes were procured by Bribery: And called their Witnesses; viz.

William Pent it h said, That, about Three Weeks or a f Month before the Election, Sir Abstrupus Danby came to Aldborough, and sent for the Borough-men, and him amongst the rest; and told them, he had thought of a way to gratify the Town, if they w ould choose him Parliament*4 man; and that was, That he would give Two Loads of Coal to each Borough-man; and that he would send them Tickets, by which they should receive the same:

And accordingly he did receive a Ticket from one of Sir Abstrupus's Servants; who told him, They had been about to deliver Tickets to others; and accordingly he produced his Ticket, dated the 8th day of June, which, lie said, was a Week after the Date: He said, The Tickets were given only to Borough-men, and to them without Distinction: That afterwards it was noised about the Town, that this would be reckoned Bribery: And Mr. Johnson and Mr. Stavely, Two of Sir Abstrupus'9 Servants, desired his Ticket up again, because, they said, it might do their Master a Prejudice; but he refused to part with .:

That, about a Fortnight or Ten Days before the Election, Sir Abstrupus made use of his House to treat the Borough-men; and made use of his Fire and Candle; and he had of Mr. Johnson 21. 5s. for the same: But, after all, he said, he did not vote for Sir Abstrupus.

John Elly, Thomas Rawlins, Richard Smithson, all concurred in this, That Sir Abstrupus Danby was a Stranger to the Borough; but did, some time before the Dissolution of the last Parliament, come to Aldborough, and offer himself to serve for the said Borough in Parliament; and desired their Votes: And that Sir Abstrupus, upon that Occasion, told them, That he would give to every Borough-man, Two Load of Coal, and send them Tickets for them to go and receive the same: And accordingly, afterwards, he did send Tickets to all the Borough-men, having Votes, indifferently: And EUys Ticket was produced to the Committee, of the same Date with Pentithe s. None of the Witnesses could say, any Coals w ere delivered by virtue of the said Tickets; but said,

That some time after, and Ellys said, that io Days before the Election, Sir Abstrupus Danby, and his Servants, came to several Persons that had the Tickets, and told them, That it was feared those Tickets might do Sir Abstrupus a Diskindness; and therefore they desired the Tickets to be delivered up again; and told them, Sir Abstrupus w'ould do them as good a Kindness: And accordingly most of them were delivered up again; and neither Elly, Rawlins, nor Smithson, voted for Sir Abstrupus.

That which was particular in their Evidence was, Thomas Rawlins; who said, That Sir Abstrupus Danby told them, his House was upon the Road as they went for the Coals; and, if they would call there, they should have Entertainment as they went by:

And that Mr. Johnson, Sir Abstrupus s Steward, afterwards met him, and asked him to give his Vote for his Master; and pulled out an Handful of Money, and gave him 5$.; but he told the said Mr. Johnson he could not resolve him them: That, about a Fortnight before

' Richard Smithson said, That he not being present with the rest, when Sir Abstrupus made the Promise to the Burgesses of giving them Two Loads of Coals apiece, the said Sir Abstrupus came to his House, and desired his Vote; and told him, He should have Two Load of Coals, and a Ticket to fetch them by; which he had: ‘But afterwards Sir Abstrupus came to his Wife, and desired it again, and had it: And, about 10 Days before the Election, Sir Abstrupus met him, and told him, He would make it twice as good to him; and that, if he would give him his Vote, he would give his Daughter a George,

That Stocsaker, an Attorney, the Sunday before the Election, came to him, and desired his Vote for Sir Ab-ptrnpus; and told him, In that Case he would bear all the Charges of a Suit at Law he was engaged in, whether he won or lost.

And the said Stocsaker pretended to read a Letter to him, from his Mother and Brother-in-law; in which it was said, That, if he would vote for Sir Abstrupus, it should be better than One hundred Pounds to him; and Rawlins and Smithson said, That the said Mr. Stocsaker used to be much in Company with Sir Abstrupus, when he was in Town.

JVm. Pentith and Fra. Barraby said, That Mr. Morris, the Vicar of Aldborough, told them, He had offered Four Burgesses, who they named, but differed in their Evidence as to one of the Persons, to Mr. Tankrcd, if the said Mr. Tankrcd would give him 40 Pounds; Morris telling Pentith, That Mr. Tankrnl had put him to so much Charges in a Law-suit: But Mr. Tankrcd would not queept of him upon the said Terms; and went away angry from him.

Mr. Barraby said, That Mr. Morris made the same Proposal, touching the said Four Votes, for Mr. Ar-thington, who was also a Candidate.

And these Men being found in Sir Abstrupus s Poll, the Petitioners Counsel inferred, That Money was given for those Votes by Sir Abstrupus.

Rawlins also testified, That Mr. TVomble came to him, and desired his Vote for Sir Abstrupus; and told him, It w ould be kindly taken by the Lady Wentworth; and that he voted for Sir George Cook and Mr. Tankrcd; and had Notice to quit his Farm that he held of the Lady Went-worth; and George Lawton and JVm. Painter, who held Tw o other Farms under the said Lady, had likewise Notice, as he was told, to quit their Farms: But the said Rawlins could not say, these Notices proceeded from their voting in the said Election; only, he said, He believed it was so, because he knew no other Reason for it.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel, as to the Point of delivering the Tickets for Coals, called

Mr. Robert Stately: Who said, That he, on the 9th of June, did deliver to each Borough-man a Ticket for Two Wain-loads of Coals, with this Caution, That they should fetch them before the Dissolution of the Parliament; and . that, upon the delivering out of the Tickets, nobody was asked for their Votes, nor nobody promised them: That the last Parliament being near, in point of Time, to be dissolved, and no Coals having been delivered, it was thought it might be dangerous to let than continue out; and thereupon he called for the said Tickets; all which, except Six or Eight, were delivered ' up voluntarily, without any Promise of doing any thing in lieu of them; and all but Two of them signed a Note to make no Use of them, the Borough-men being willing no Prejudice should come to Sir Abstrupus Danby, and the *Town, by them.

Robert Turton said, That the Tickets for Coals were delivered out on the 8th of June; and he was present at the Delivery of them; and there was no Vote then asked, nor mention made of the Election: That no Coals were delivered by virtue of the said Tickets; and that they were called in again before the Dissolution of the last Parliament.

Mr. Thomas Johnson denied, That he ever gave Raw-

lins any Money upon the Account of the Election; but said, The 5«y. was given him on the 24th of May, for 1,5 Medals of old Coin which Rawlins had presented his Master with.

That Sir Abstrupus Danby treated the Borough-men at Pentys House, the 24th of June; and for the Use of his House, Linen, Fire, and Hay, by him then found, he, the said Mr. Johnson, did pay him Five and forty Shillings, which, at that time, the said Penty did think but indifferent Pay; and that he, the said Mr. Johnson, at that time, did not mention his voting to the said Pentyt nor knew that he had any Vote. - j

Rawlins, being called to confront Mr. Johnson, to that Point of Evidence touching the said Mr. Johnsons giving him 5 s. denied that ever he gave any Medals to Mr.

Johnson; but he gave them to one of Rippon: And at first, he said, That the said Person of Rippon did not pay him for them, but Mr. Johnson did: But, being asked again to that Matter, he said, Mr. Johnson told him, when he gave him the 5 s. That it was not for those Me* dais: Yet the said Rawlins acknowledged, That he had no Consideration for the said Medals.

As to Richard Smithson; it was opened by the Sitting Member's Council, That he had been guilty of Sheepstealing, and a Man of no Reputation: And they called Richard Scruton, who began his Evidence with relation to that Matter; but he was interrupted by the Petitioner's Counsel objecting to it, as not being proper Evidence, without shewing that the said Richard.....son was convicted for the same.

Richard Scruton said, That Rawlins, at the Election of Knights of the Shire at York, did swear, That he had 40 s. a Year Freehold; and that he, or his Father, never had any Freehold.

Mr. Robert Smithson, and Mr. John Brough, said, That Thomas Rawlins and Richard Smithson were Men of bad Reputation.

To the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury.

May it please your Lordships,

Upon the Decease of Mr. Auditor Phelips, your Lordships being pleased to refer the Accounts of that District to my Examination, I did, in order thereunto, receive from Mr. Marriot, the said late Auditor's Deputy, pursuant to your Lordships Commands, sundry Books of Inrollment, Records, Accounts, and Papers, relating to that Office; and, amongst the rest, the Accounts of Mr.

Smith, as Receiver of Norfolk and Huntingdon for Six Years, ended at Michaelmas 1686, declared by Sir John Ernie, then Chancellor of the Exchequer, 8° Decembris 1688.

And, upon the Perusal of the Account for the Year ended at Michaelmas 1681, a true Copy whereof is hereunto annexed, I find discharged not only divers Rents within the said Counties alleged to be sold, and amounting to 391 /. 9 s. per Annum; but also the Sum of 2,725 /.

17s. 8 id. Part of the Arrears in the preceding Account depending; for that they are alleged to be sold, as by a Schedule thereof.

Now the Accounts of this Revenue for sundry preceding Years, from whence these Arrears are brought,

And Mr. Marriott says the same.

To supply which Defect, I have taken a great deal of Pains, from the last Accounts and Records in my Custody, to draw out the Particulars of all the Rents in Charge before the Year 1660, hereunto annexed; taking notice of all such as appeared to be sold by Deeds inrolled in the aforesaid Office, of what is Parcel of the Queen Dowager's Jointure, and of those which Mr. receives at this

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, That it shall not extend to prejudice any Rights, Liberties, or Privileges, of Sir Wm. Glyiin Baronet, or any the Lords,

Owners, or Proprietors, of the Lands, Grounds, or Marshes, lying on the South Side of the main Chanel of the said River, or his or their Fishery in the same;

Another Clause was offered to be made Part of the Bill*

That all Coal, Lime, and Lime-stone, brought to the City of Chester for Sale by Land-carriage, shall be! brought to such Place as the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, shall appoint for the easier Collection and Payment of the Duties payable for the same:

And the same was twice read with Blanks: And the Blanks were filled up; and the Clause upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill,

That, in case the Chanel of the said River shall become so deep, as that at Low Water, w hen the Tide of Sea is out of, and no Flood of fresh Water in, the said River, the same shall not be fordable, betw een Blacon Point and Burtenhead, for the Mayor and Citizens to erect and employ Tw o sufficient and free Ferry-boats, for the publick Use of his Majesty's Subjects, to pass and repass, without paying any thing for the same:

And the said Clause was twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Upon the Petition of the Town of Hall faic;

William Swdhcliffe, Clothier for 30 Years, said,

That, before April last, they lived handsomely one by another; but since, many Thousands are ready to starve: 'Tis true, he still keeps up his Work, and employs a Thousand poor People at Four-pence a Day, to whom he formerly gave Six-pence per Day; but is not able to hold it long, unless he hath a better Trade:

That he dealt with Men who sent the Goods to Flanders, and sells the same Cloth now for Two-and-forty Shillings, that he used to sell for Six-and-forty Shillings.

Upon the Petition of the Clothiers of Ratchdale; Gabriel Garth side, Dealer in the Woollen Manufacture, said,

That, before the First Day of May, the Town of T&atclidak had a good Trade; but now have little; and have great Stocks lying on their Hands:

That he hath sold Clpth in Amsterdam, which, as he was informed, was sent into Flanders; and his Dealing was in several Sorts of Bays:

That the 'Jowp, about Two or Three Years ago, returned 1,500l. per Week,* and now they do not return above 500l. per Week:

That he hath known Goods entered at Hull, and shipped pff for Flanders:

That in the Town of Ratchddle, they formerly collected not above 7, qr 800l. a Year for the Poor; but by reason of the Decay o,f Trade, and Increase of their Poor, they were forced the last Year to raise 1,069/.

Upon the Petition of Salop;

Mr* Jeremiah Powell, Dealer in the Woollen Manufacture, said,

That formerly there was laid down Fifteen Hundred Pounds a Week for carrying on the Trade there; and, since the Prohibition, the Trade is abated 75/. per Cent.: That the Prohibition of the Flanders Lace is the Occasion of the Decay of their Trade:

That, when the Act was passing for the Prohibition of Flanders Lace, he was told by the Merchants he used to sell his Goods to, That they should buy no more Goods of him; for that the Act would cause a Prohibition in Flanders. Mr. Samuel Monk spoke to the same Effect.

Upon the Petition of the Lacemen of Buckinghamshire', Mr. Edward Purcell, Laceman, said,

That the Number of Workers is so great, that he cannot tell how many they are; but believes 3,000l. a Week is paid in ready Money, to the Bone-lace-makers in that County:

That formerly the Price at Five Shillings a Yard was reckoned extraordinary; but since the Act, they have some Lace of Six-and-thirty Shillings a Yard; and believes, shall be able to make as good as can be madq; and produced Two Pieces of 26 s. per Yard:

That the Improvement is both in Price and Quantity. That Children of Five Years of Age work upon Twopeny Lace.

Mr. Edward Hooton, Laceman, lives at Newport, and sells Lace, said,

That there are Thirty thousand Workers in Buckinghamshire; and that, before the Act, there was not Half so many; and their Trade is computqd at between 3 and 4,000l. per Week:

That he buys at Newpoi't, where there are i,3QO Workers, and sells in London:

That he keeps a Hundred Workers, and buys 40 or 50 Pounds worth of Lace in a Week:

That Lace is much dearer now than formerly; whereby the Poor is much encouraged; for that Lace, which sold formerly for 6$. a Yard, now sells for 10 s. a Yard; and a Child of Six or Seven Years of Age may earn Twenty-pence a Week:

That there are Men at Needs return 20/. per Week; and that the Increase of Trade hath beep since the Prohibition. Richard Gurney, Laceman, at Putnam in Hertford- Mr.e, said,

That he keeps 2 or 300 People at Work in Buckinghamshire, upon Bone-lace; but did not employ Half so many before the Prohibition.

John Smith, Laceman, said, That Sisters Thread pays 18 d. a Pound Duty: And that twice the Quantity of Lace hath been shipped off since the Prohibition as was before: That those Customers who used to write for Lace of a Yard, now write for Lace of 20s. a Yard:

That Flanders Lace used to pay no Duty in or out, but was always run:

That what he sends out himself, lie sends to Jamaica. Thomas Robinson, Laceman, said,

That in Buckinghamshire there are 200 Dealers in Lace, and about 150 of them come to London every Week; and, one with another, deal for Twenty Pounds a Week: That, within these Three Years, they are increased about 50 in Number:

That there is more Lace made now, than formerly; and lie takes more now in a Week, than in a Fortnight, within Three Years last past; but for the last Quarter of a Year the Trade hath a little fallen off:

That Men, Women, and Children, one with another, earn about Three Shillings a Week:

That a good Workwoman will earn Seven Shillings a Week.

Mr. Clerk, Dealer in Lace, said,

That there are One thousand and Eighty-one Persons employed in making of Lace in Salisbury; besides great Numbers in Places adjacent:

That he and his Partner send between Sixty and Eighty Pounds worth of Lace per Week, from Salisbury:

That, in the West of England, they now make Lace of 5/. or 6/. a Yard; where the best they made formerly was but 4/.: And he produced some Lace to the Committee, which was made in Dorsetshire, and cost above 3/. a Yard:

That 5/. Sterling, in Thread, makes a Hundred Pounds Worth of Lace; but generally, one Sort of Thread with another 15/. Sterling makes a Hundred Pounds Worth; and the finest Lace is made of Nuns Thread:

That, in the North of England, the Number of Workers are increased double what they were within these Two Years; and that there are, by Computation, at least 100,000 Men, Women, and Children, employed in the making of Lace within this Kingdom.

That, several Merchants appearing, the Committee thought fit to examine them: Who said as followed; viz.

Mr. Kent, Merchant, said,

That the Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures in Flanders commenced the First of May last; and the Occasion of such Prohibition arose from the late Act for the more effectual Prohibition of foreign Bone-lace, as he hath always heard from his Correspondents there;

That he and his Brother, before such Prohibition, have exported between Sixty and Seventy thousand Pounds worth per Annum, from the Port of London, and Port of Hull, of our Woollen Manufacture, and very little else, particularly in the Years 1697, and 1698; that is to say, Thirty thousand Pounds worth from Hull, and the rest from London:

That there was no Comparison between the Exports from England, and other Countries, to Flanders, though their Prohibition runs generally to all; for England exported Fifty Times as much as Holland and France; and believes they prohibited the Hollanders, by reason great Quantities of Goods went through that Country from England to Flande?'s:

That one Mr. Ververt was in England when the late Act for the more effectual prohibiting the Importation of Foreign Bone-lace was in Debate in the House of Commons; and said, If the Bill passed, when he went into Flanders, he would take care that our Woollen Manufacture should be prohibited there:

That he believes the People that were formerly employed. in the Linen Manufactures there, are nt>\v employed in the Woollen Manufacture.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there hath been a great Decay of the Woollen Manufacture of England, since the First of May 1699.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for rendering the Laws more effectual for preventing the Importation of Foreign Bone-lace, Loom-lace, Needle-work, Point, and Cut-work, hath been an Occasion of the said Decay of the Woollen Manufacture of England.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Encouragement of the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom, a Bill be brought in to repeal the said Act.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That there hath been a great Decay of the Woollen Manufacture of England\ since the First of May 1699.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Debate be adjourned;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That an Act, made in the Ninth and Tenth Years of his present Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for rendering the Laws more effectual, for preventing the Importation of Foreign Bone-lace, Loom-lace, Needle-work, Point, and Cut-work, hath been an Occasion of the said Decay of the Woollen Manufactures of England;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

The Third Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by adding " to commence Three Months after the Prohibition of the English Woollen Manufactures is taken off* " in Flanders

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill; for allowing the whole Reward of One hundred Pounds to such Person as shall discover and convict any Person of sending any Child, or other Person under thefr Government, into

Parts beyond the Seas, to be educated in the Romish Religion:

And the same was twice read and amended; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill,

That Protestant Children of Popish Parents may not, in the Lives-time of such Parent, for want of fitting Maintenance, be necessitated to embrace the Popish Religion, contrary to their own Inclinations:

And the same was twice read, with a Blank; which was filled up: And, upon the Question put thereupon, the Clause was agreed unto, by the House, to be mad*

Part of the Bill.

And the Letter was read; and is as followeth; viz. Sir,

Being bound upon a Voyage beyond Sea, which will hinder me from attendingtny Duty in the House this Sessions; and Sir Edmund Bacon and myself having a Petition depending before the Committee of Elections, about the Election for Orford; I humbly take the Liberty to acquaint you, That in case Sir Edmund Bacon and myself be declared duly elected for the said Corporation, that I do hereby make my Election to serve for the Corporation of Orford; which I request you to communicate to the House; that they make such Provision for having the Corporation of Aldborough, for which I likewise serve, represented, as is usual in such Cases. I am, Sir, Your most humble Servant,

That the further Duty to be laid on all wrought Silks,

That a further Duty belaid upon all Muslins imported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*,

A Petition of the Half-pay Officers was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, notwithstanding this House was pleased to appropriate the Half-pay for the Year 1699, they have not received any since September: And, praying, such Methods may be taken for adjusting their former Accounts, and present Payment of their Halfpay, that their present Necessities may be relieved.

Ordered, That, in the Clause of Appropriation to be brought into the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty for maintaining his Majesty's Navy, Guards, and Gari-sons, and towards paying the Debts due to Seamen, and for other necessary Occasions, there be Provision made, as well for the Arrears of Half-pay, as for the Half-pay this present Year.

Ordered, That Care be taken also in the said Clause of Appropriation, That the 300,000l. given for Guards and Garisons, be strictly and particularly applied for their Maintenance; and that no more Men be kept on Foot, than that Sum will actually and fully pay.

A Petition of Mary Duchess of Norfolk was pre- Duke of sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for putting an End to all Differences betw een the Duke her Uism*' Husband and herself, an Agreement, and Deeds pursuant to the same, were executed; whereby the Duke obtained his desired Advantage, and, hath fully enjoyed the Benefit thereof; notwithstanding which, apd without ever signifying any Dissatisfaction to or with the Petitioner, and w ithout any Notice or previous Proceeding in the ordinary Course of Justice, and to take from her that legal Trial in the Ecclesiastical Court, which by Law she is advised she is intitled to, did exhibit a Bill in the House of Peer# to dissolve his Marriage with the Petitioner, and to enable him to marry again; upon which the Proceedings were so very quick, Two Witnesses lately brought from beyond the Seas being forthwith examined against the Petitioner, and she charged with Facts supposed to be committed many Years since, and long before the said Agreement, could not be prepared to make her Defence, the Places of Abode of the Witnesses being yet not known to her; and the Petitioner hearing the said Bill is passed the House of Peers, and sent down for the Concurrence of this House: And praying to be heard by her Counsel at Law, and one Civilian, against the said Bill, before any Proceedings be had thereupon by this House.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read.

A Petition of Sir Edward Wills, and others, in behalf of themselves, and several other Inhabitants of the Parish of St. Martin's Orgars, London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by a Bill depending in this House, for confirming of a Lease of a Piece of Ground from the Rector and Churchwardens of the said Parish, for: Liberty to build a Church thereon, for the Worship and Service of God, in the French Tongue, according to the Usage of the Church of England, Leave is given to erect a Church in the Church-yard of the said Parish, contrary to several Acts of Parliament, and will be very prejudicial to the Petitioners: And praying to be heard against the said Bill, before the same doth pass.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read a Second time.

A Petition of Benjamin Smith was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is a Bill depending in this House, for Sale of the Estate of one Brian Janson, for Payment of Debts; upon which Estate the Petitioner hath a Mortgage; but does not find any Provision made for Payment thereof, by the Bill: And therefore praying to be heard by his Counsel, before the Bill do pass.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioner be heard by his Counsel, before the Committee, thereupon.

A Petition of several of the Justices of Ppace, Ministers, Churchwardens, Overseers of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of several Parishes in the Tower Hamlets, adjoining to the River of Thames, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That their several Parishes have of late been burdened with numerous Poor, from the Sailors Want of Pay, whereby their necessitous Families are, and will be, a continual Charge to the Petitioners: And praying the Consideration of the House, in the Case now before them, touching the Q's and R's set upon the Sailors Names in the Navy Books.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the Report from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and Commissioners of the Navy, touching Q's and IPs, be taken into Consideration.

Saturni, 22° die Novembris 1606, Sir George Moor reports the several Cases committed to the Committee.

New Members to be chosen in the Place of Sir Humphry Wynch, Sir Oliver St. John, and Sir Thomas Ridg-ttwy.

They considered, according to the Instructions given them; namely, of Sir Thomas Ridgway, Treasurer, Sir Humphry IVynch Lord Chief Baron, and Sir Oliver St. John, Master of the Ordnance in Ireland; whose Cases they conceive different from the Case of Ambassadors; for that, as they thought, their Patents were for Life, and therefore new to be chosen in their Places.

The late Precedent of Sir James Lee, advanced to the Place of Lord Chief Justice in Ireland remembred; in whose Place Mr. Alexander Chock was chosen for the Town of West bury, in Wiltshire.

Several Questions were made of every particular Case; and it was resolved,

That Warrants should be granted by Mr. Speaker for the Choice of New Members in the Place of Sir Thomas Ridgway, Sir Humphry Wynch, and Sir Oliver St. John, according to the Opinion of the Committee, and according to a former Precedent in the Case of Sir James Lee.

Ordered, That Warrants should issue for new Writs to elect for Places void, as in place of Sir Tho. Ridgway, for the County of Devon, in this Form; viz.

Whereas Sir Thomas Ridgway Knight, now Treasurer at War in his Majesty's Realm of Ireland\ was, at the First Session of this Parliament, elected and returned, into the Commons House of Parliament, one of the Knights of the Shire for the County of Devon; and being sithence, by his Majesty's Favour, advanced to the Place of Treasurer; It was this Day moved in the said House, Whether his Place of Knight of the Shire were void: Which^ upon the Question, was over-ruled; and ordered; That a new Writ should issue for the Choice of another Knight, in the room and place of the said Sir Thomas; for which this shall be your Warrant.

Directed, To my loving Friend Sir George Copping Knight, Clerk of the Crown in his Majesty's High Court of Chancery.

And for the rest in the like Form.

offer,

That his Majesty was pleased, by a Commission dated the 15th of May 1696, to appoint Commissioners for promoting the Trade of this Kingdom; and for inspecting and improving his Plantations m America, and elsewhere; with several Directions' and Instructions; the chief whereof are as follow:

To examine into, and take an Account of, the State and Condition of the general Trade of England, and of the several particular Trades into foreign Parts:

To examine what Trades are, or may prove, hurtful, and what beneficial, to this Kingdom; and by what means the advantageous Trades may be improved, and those that are prejudicial discouraged:

To consider by what means profitable Manufactures* already settled, may be further improved; and how other new and profitable Manufactures may be introduced:

To consider of proper Methods for setting on Work and employing the Poor, and making them useful to the Publick:

To inquire into the Condition of the Plantations, as w?ell with Regard to the Administration of Government there, as in relation to Commerce; and how those Colonies may be rendered most beneficial to this Kingdom:

To inquire tv hat naval Stores may be furnished from the Plantations; and how the same may be best procured:

To prepare Instructions for Governors; and to take Account of their Administration:

To examine the Journals of the Councils, and the Acts or Law's made by the respective General Assemblies, in order to his Majesty's Approbation or Disallowance thereof:

To require an Account of all Money given by the Assemblies for publick Uses; and how the same is expended:

And to make Representations and Reports to his Majesty, or the Privy Council, in Writing, as there shall be Occasion.

In pursuance w hereof, we have proceeded in the manner following:

Towards the Improvement of the Woollen Manufacture, and for hindering the Exportation of our un-wrought Wool, we did, in December 1696, represent to his Majesty, That Officers might be appointed by Land, on the Coasts of Kent and Sasser, to attend constantly upon that'Service; and to act in Concert with the Ships directed, by Act of Parliament, to cruise upon those Coasts, in order thereunto: And we did likewise propose, for the more easy Prosecution of Offenders, the Issuing of a Capias against them; which has since passed into a Law.

Upon Information that a W'oollen Manufacture was set up at Sada, near the Groyne, by the Encouragement of the Court of Spain; and ihat the Dutch Consul at the Groyne wras supposed to be a great Promoter of it; we procured such Orders, from time to time, from his Majesty to his Ministers in Spaine, and at the Hague, as, we hope, may have disappointed that Undertaking:

And, upon Advice of the like Attempt in Sweden, we have transmitted to his Majesty's Minister at Stockholm

12 W. III. 26° Martii.

such Memorials, as, we presume, will be useful to that End.

Upon the late Prohibition of our Woollen Manufactures in Flanders, we made an early Inquiry into that Matter, by his Majesty's Minister at Brussels; and, finding the Government of Flanders unwilling to treat thereof we gave our Opinion, as Occasion offered, That the absolute Repealing of our Act for prohibiting the Importation of Bone-lace from thence, without some provisional Conditions to be performed on their Parts, would tioways answer the proposed Design.

Having been required by his Majesty to take into Consideration the Trade of England and Ireland, how they stood in relation to each other, and how they might be improved to the Advantage of each Nation; we took that Occasion humbly to represent, That the most proper Means to divert the people of Ireland from applying themselves to the Woollen Manufactures, was, by giving them such Encouragement in the Manufacture of Linen, as might engage them heartily in it.

Nor have our Endeavours been wanting, by several Representations to his Majesty, and Considerations had of Bills transmitted from Ireland, to induce that Parliament towards passing such Acts, in reference to both Manufactures, as might be of mutual Benefit to both Kingdoms.

His Majesty having likewise referred to our Consideration some Proposals, made by Monsieur Crommelin, a French Refugee, long experienced in the Linen Manufacture, for the more effectual Establishment and Improvement of that Manufacture in Ireland; we humbly offered our Opinion, That.his Majesty would be pleased to allow 800 /. per Annum, for Ten Years, to pay the Interest, at Eight per Cent, of 10,0001, to be advanced by the said Crommelin, and his Friends, for the setting on Foot of that Manufacture; the said 800l. to be received, and issued out, by Trustees appointed by his Majesty to inspect the Employing of the said 10,000l.: And, his Majesty having been pleased to give Directions accordingly, the said Crommelin is lately gone to Ireland, in older to put his Proposals in Execution; and we have Reason to believe he will be able to make a considerable Advance therein.

Having further observed, that several of his Majesty's Plantations in America applied themselves to the Improvement of Woollen Manufactures in those Parts, for the Supplying of themselves and Neighbours, to the Hindrance of the Exportation of our English Manufactures; we prepared a Clause for the preventing thereof; which was presented to this Honourable House, and accordingly received, and enacted, the last Session of Parliament; and we have since understood, That the said Restraint has had a very good Effect.

The Turkey Company finding their Trade much prejudiced by the East India Company's seeking a Vent in Northern Parts of Persia for those Draperies, which, by their Charter, they are obliged annually to export; and his Majesty having referred that Matter to our Examination; we humbly reported our Opinion, That it would be inconvenient, that the East India Company should send any greater Quantity of Draperies into Persia, than they had done formerly; and that they ought therefore to vend the Draperies they are obliged to export, either in India, China, Japan, or elsewhere, at such Distance from those Places where the Turkey Company have usually traded, as may not cause any interfering betw een those Two Companies.

And, for the better preventing other more general Inconveniences apprehended from the East India Trade, we did also, upon another Occasion, humbly propose, That the Wearing or Consumption of the manufactured Goods of India, Persia, or China, made of Silk or Herba, or mixed with either of those Materials; as also of painted or stained Callicoes, and of all Handicraft-wares imported from those Parts; should be discouraged and lessened in these Kingdoms, and in his Majesty's Plantations.

VOL. 13,

For Encouragement of the Royal Lustring Company, Improve and the Establishment of that Manufacture here, we have raent of made several Representations of what we conceived ne- Tride* cessary to be done; divers of which Things have since been enacted.

Upon the Czar of Muscovy's coming into Holland\ we represented the State of Trade betw een Muscovy and England, and the Advantage this Kingdom would receive by the Importation of Tobacco into that Country, if permitted: Whereupon Instructions were sent to his Majesty's Embassadors at the Hague, to treat with the Czar's Ministers; which was done accordingly: And we afterwards represented the Necessity of enlarging the Russia Company, as has since been done by Act of, Parliament, in order to the better Improving of that Trade, and the Supply of Naval Stores from thence, as well as from Denmark and Sweden.

Upon Occasion of the late Treaty of Peace at Reswyck, a particular Account having been required from us, for the Information of His Majesty's Plenipotentiaries there, of what had been lost or gained in all his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations, since the Treaty of Breda until that time; w e accordingly prepared many particular Accounts, not only of what had been lost or gained, as aforesaid, but also of all Pretensions, and Grounds of Differences, between the French and us, with relation to eacii particular Plantation, as also to Newfoundland, Hudsons Bay, the Royal African Company, &c.; which were accordingly transmitted.

Since the Conclusion-of the Pease, we did also, by his Majesty's Directions, draw up many Memorials for the Use of the Commissioners appointed by his Majesty, to treat here with Commissioners from France, upon all such of the aforesaid Matters, as, by the Treaty of Reswyck, required any further Settlement.

The Regulation of Passes for Ships trading to the Mediterranean, and other Southern Parts, with respect to the Government of Atgier, being of great Importance to the Trade of his Majesty's Subjects into those Parts; we have, by his Majesty's Directions in several Representations, humbly offered our Opinion thereupon; as also concerning a Treaty with that Government, and likewise with the Emperor of Morocco, and relating to the English Trade at Tunis.

We have prepared a Draught of a Treaty of Commerce with Sweden, with such Articles as we conceive proper, not only to preserve the Trade and Vent of our Northern Draperies in that Country, but also to remove the many Difficulties that his Majesty's Subjects trading into those Parts have of late Years met with.

We have taken the like Care in a Draught of a Treaty of Commerce with France; and prepared such Memorials relating the reunto, as may be proper to be had in Consideration, whensoever a Negociation of that Nature shall be set on Foot.

We have, upon the Application of the Merchants of this City trading to Leghorne, represented to his Majesty the present Grievances, and further Apprehensions, that they, or their Correspondents there, lie under, in relation to die Privileges formerly granted to them, and other Strangers, by the great Dukes of Tuscany; and have thereupon proposed what may be of Use for their Ease and Security, and for the Advantage of England in that Trade.

To prevent Delays in determining Differences about Matters of Trade, we prepared a Bill for determining such Differences by Arbitration; which has since passed into a Law.

Our Report relating to the Rate of Guineas, and the Difference of Value between Gold 'and Silver, has been laid before this Honourable House, and approved of.

We have made Representations to prevent the Jews of Leghorn from trading in English Ships, thereby to enjoy the Privileges of the English at Alexandria', to prevent the Encroachments of the Consul at Rotterdam; and the Establishing of a Consul at the Madiras, independent on the Consul General at Portugal; and to promote the Assiento or Contract for supplying the Spanish JFesi Indies

6

Improvement of Trade.

300

with Negroes; not to mention many others upon private Cases in Matters of Trade.

In order to the Employing of the Poor of this Kingdom, and making them useful to the Publick, we have made divers Proposals, how we conceived that Work might be effected; and have lately, in pursuance of an Order of a Committee of this Honourable House, prepared a complete Abstract of all the Laws relating to the Poor, now in Force; together with the Draught of a Bill, whereby they may be all reduced into One Law; and laid the same before the said Committee.

We have made divers Representations for the Security and Improvement of the Newfoundland Trade and Fishery, ds well during the War, as since the Peace; and have constantly every Year examined into, and taken an Account of, the Course and Progress of that Trade; and now particularly formed Instructions, and Heads of Inquiries, to he given to the Commander of the Convoy appointed for that Fishery, for the due Execution of the late Act to encourage the Trade to Newfoundland\ for the better preventing Irregularities therein.

We have presented to his Majesty a general State of the Trade of this Kingdom, with Observations thereupon, how we conceive divers advantageous Trades may be improved, and prejudicial ones discouraged; a Copy whereof has been formerly laid before this Honourable House.

As to his Majesty's Plantations in America, we do further offer, That, within the Allegiance of the Crown of England, there are Twenty several Colonies, besides Hudson's Bay and Newfoundland, in which last Place there is no Governor; each whereof have their distinct Governments, Councils, and Assemblies, by whom particular Laws, and Rules of Government, are passed and enacted; some of which Colonies are governed by his Majesty's immediate Commission, and others by Proprietors and Charters.

The Business relating to these Plantations is managed by a constant Correspondence with all the Governors appointed by his Majesty's immediate Commission, and occasionally with all the rest; in the Course whereof they send us Journals of their Councils, Assemblies, and other publick Proceedings, with Accounts of all Things whatsoever relating to each of their Governments; all which are considered by us for the necessary Orders to be returned thereupon; and, more particularly, the many Acts or Laws of the several Assemblies transmitted from thence fall under our Examination; and, after our consulting his Majesty's Counsel learned in the Law', as to the legal Part, our Reports are made thereupon to his Majesty in his Privy Council, for his Royal Assent, or Disallowance thereof; with particular Regard to the Interest and Improvement of the Trade of England, as well as the Good of those Plantations.

We have, since our Constitution, prepared Draughts of Commissions and Instructions for all the Governors of his Majesty's Plantations.

We have, upon several Occasions, proposed to his Majesty the Appointing of Convoys for the Plantations, and of Ships of War necessary to attend and protect the Trade of those Plantations: And, upon the Complaints of the Inhabitants there, or Merchants in England, of Hardships in the Pressing of Men, and otherwise, by Captains of Men of War in those Parts, we have presented to his Majesty Regulations therein, which have had a good Effect.

Upon Information from the Officers of his Majesty's Customs in the Plantations, and others, of the Partiality of the People there, and more particularly in the Propriety Governments, in all Tryals upon the Acts of Trade wherein their private Interest is concerned, and of the Difficulties in the obtaining any Execution of those Acts in the former Method; we did represent the Usefulness of Courts of Admiralty in the Plantations: Upon which such Courts have been erected; and, where they have not been disputed, have proved of great Encouragement to legal Trade.

Being informed, by many Instances, of the great

j. 1700.

Countenance given to Pirates in some of the Plantations, and chiefly in the Proprieties, and Charter Governments, by fitting out their Ships from thence, and furnishing them with all Sorts of Provision and Ammunition, and receiving them, with their Plunder and Booty, at their Return, and acquitting them upon feigned Tryals; we did make several Representations thereupon; and proposed the Enacting of Laws there, for the Tryai and Punishment of Pirates, in Conformity to a Law heretofore passed ini Jamaica to that Effect: Which having been refused in the said Proprieties, and Charter Governments, we proposed, as the only Remedy for so great an Evil, the offering a Bill in Parliament for that Purpose; w herein we consulted Sir Charles Hedges, Judge of His Majesty's High Court of Admiralty; by whose great Care and Assistance such a Bill has been prepared, and is now lying before this Honourable House.

And, being further sensible of the great Irregularities in the Proprieties, and Charter Governments, not only in reference to illegal Trade, and Piracy, but otherwise, we have, upon several Occasions, represented the same to his Majesty: And an Act of Parliament having passed, whereby the Governors of those Plantations are obliged to have his Majesty's Approbation, for their acting in that Capacity; we required all the said Proprietors and Governments to present their respective Governors to his Majesty; and, in order to his Approbation of them, to give Security for their due observing the Acts of Trade, according to an Address presented tQ his Majesty, by the Right Honourable the House of Lords, for that Purpose: But all the said Proprietors here having declined to give any such Security; and only Two Charter Governments, viz. Connecticut, and Rhode Island, having lately done it in America; and not any one of those Governors being at present qualified by his Majesty's Approbation of them, as required by the said Act of Parliament; w^e do not see any thing, without some further Provision by Parliament; capable to reduce them to a more regular Conduct, and Compliance with their Duty, in reference to the Trade of England.

We have also, upon Occasion, represented the Misdemeanors, and ill Conduct, of some Governors of Plantations acting by his Majesty's immediate Commission.

We have made many Representations in Defence of his Majesty's Title to several Islands in America, claimed by foreign Princes; of which one is a Claim made by the Elector of Brandenburgh to the Island of New Tertholen, lying amongst his Majesty's Leeward Caribbee Islands; one made by the French King, to the Island of Sancta Lucia, lying amongst the Windward Caribbee Islands; one made by the French King, to the Island of Tobago, one of the Windward Caribbee Islands; and another by the Duke of Coitrland, to the same Island.

Having been required, this Session of Parliament, by the Right Honourable the House of Lords, to lay before their Lordships our Opinion, how consistent the Colony at Darien may be with the Treaties wdth Spain, and the Trade of this Kingdom; we did accordingly make our humble Report therein; which, we presume, was satisfactory, their Lordships having made an Address to his Majesty to the same Effect.

We have made several Representations relating to the "Boundaries between his Majesty's Plantations, and those of the French, upon the Continent, particularly in the North-eastern Parts of New England, where they have endeavoured to encroadi upon us both as to the Land and Fishery.

Upon Controversies that have happened between some of his Majesty's Colonies, and others, relating to their Boundaries; especially between his Majesty's Governments and Proprieties; and upon different Claims that have been set on foot to some whole Provinces, we have examined all their respective Titles; and the necessary Instructions have been given by his Majesty thereupon.

We have often represented the Necessity of preserving the Friendship of the Five Nations of Indians, which are a Barrier between his Majesty's Plantations and Canada, by

treating

treating them kindly, and shewing them a Force constantly maintained in New York, ready to protect them upon all Occasions.

We have applied ourselves to the promoting the Importation of Naval Stores from New England, and other his Majesty's Plantations; and for the carrying on so good a Design, his Majesty has been pleased, upon our Applications, to order the Navy Board to send Commissioners to New England, who have been likewise joined with Commissioners of that Colony, for the Viewing and Inspecting the Woods lying upon that Coast, for providing his Majesty's Navy with Masts, and other necessary Materials for Building of Ships, as also with Pitch, Tar, and Rosin, of which great Quantities may be produced in those Parts; and some Specimens of each, sent by the said Commissioners, are lately arrived, and now under the Examination of the Navy Board.

These being the chief Particulars about which our Time has been and is daily taken up, besides the frequent Applications of Merchants, and of the Persons concerned in the Plantations, with the constant Accession of the like Business; we thought it our Duty to lay as short an Account thereof before this Honourable House, as the Nature of each Particular would bear.

All which is humbly submitted.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he, with the House, did, on Saturday last, present to his Majesty their Address, That it will much conduce to the Service of his Majesty, and Good of the Kingdom, That Gentlemen of Quality, and good Estates, be restored and put into the Commissions of the Peace, and Lieutenancy; and that Men of small Estates b£ neither continued, nor put into the said Commissions: And that his Majesty was pleased to give a most gracious Answer, as followeth; 4'iz.

Gentlemen,

I am of the Opinion, that Men of the best Quality and Estates are most proper to he intrusted in the Commissions of the Peace, and Lieutenancy; and Directions shall be given accordingly.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the humble Thanks of this House be given to his Majesty, for his Majesty's said most gracious Answer.

Ordered, That the said humble Thanks be given to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty's Pleasure, when he will be attended by this House.

A Petition of the Half-pay Officers was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, on the 14th

308

2 Skin, " any."

5 Skin,

of Jlarch last, this House was pleased to vote, That the Petitioners should have their Arrears of Half-pay, and be continued therein for this present Year: And being apprehensive, that Provision is made, for Debentures to be given them lor their Arrears, thereupon the Half-pay to cease; all those who have no Estates, nor otherways provided for, must of Necessity be in a very deplorable Condition; which will be the Fate of most of the Petitioners, who have no other Dependence, but the Favour of this House, as a Reward for their Services: That several have been necessitated to contract Debts upon Credit of their Arrears, and others to sell the Half-pay for tin's present Year, upon passing of the said Vote: and, unless the House should continue their Half-pay, according to the said Vote, the Petitioners, and their Families, must perish for Want: And praying, That their miserable Case may be taken into Consideration, as to their Half-pay for this present Year.

London Poor. Mr. White reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for the better employing and relieving the Poor of the City of London was committed, That they had considered the Petitions of the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor of the several Parishes of St. Sepulchre'sr, St. Andrew'sHolborn, St. Bridget's alias St. Brides, and Part of St. Martins Ludgate, in the Ward of Farrington, without, London, and other Inhabitants of the said Ward, being accounted a Sixth Part of the City of London, and Liberties thereof; and also the Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Christ Church within Newgate, London; to them referred; and heard the Petitioners; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the former Petition;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it may be prejudicial to the Government of the City of London, in relation to the Poor, to have any separate Corporation erected within their Limits.

And, upon the latter Petition;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That nothing can be done upon the said Petition, without an Alteration of the whole Body of the Laws relating to the Poor.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Sir Richard Onslow reported from the Committee, to Woollen w'hom it was referred to draw up Reasons, to be offered Manufac-at a Conference with the Lords, touching the Amend- tures>*c-ment, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled,

An Act for taking away the Duties upon the Woollen Manufactures, Corn, G rain, Bread, Biscuit, and Meal, exported, That they had drawn up Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were twice read; and agreed unto by the House; and are as follow; viz.

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendment, made by your Lordships, to the said Bill, Press the 2d, L. 38. by Leaving out these Words, " or other sooner Determination, except for Nonpayment of Rent within " Three Months after the same becomes due and payable;" because all Grants of Offices or Duties, from the Crown, are subject to other Determinations than by Effluxion of Time, or for Nonpayment of Rent: And though the Commons may think it reasonable, to leave the Grants of the Subsidies, and Aulnage Duties, in the same Condition they are now in; yet cannot consent to continue the said Subsidies and Duties after the Patentees Interest therein shall be determined; whereas the Amendment, made by your Lordships, seems to continue the said Dutiesduring the Term mentioned in the said Grants, though the Right and Interest of the Patentees should be legally determined before the Expiration of that Term.

Ordered, That Sir Richard Onslow do go to the Lords, Conference and desire a Conference upon the Subject-matter of the^srl^d Wltil said Amendment. r
