MR. Shackerly reported from the Committee, to whom Ry# the Petition of the Mayor, Jurats, Freemen, and Harbour, chief Inhabitants, of the ancient Town and Port of Rye, in the County of Sussex-, and other Petitions relating to the Harbour at Rye; were referred; That they had considered the same, and heard the Petitioners; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, together w'ith the Matter, as it appeared to them, to the Hous^; w'hich lie read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

That the Committee having heard the Petitioners upon their Petition, and in order to prove the Allegations of the same; and to shew how the Rye Harbour became so obstructed and decayed, as now- it is; they produced several Books from the Commissioners of Sewers, shewing the Condition that Harbour was formerly in; and the Obstructions that have since been made thereto: And the Petitioners likewise produced several Witnesses in relation to the Premises, who gave their Testimony as follows; viz.

Captain

12 W. III. 6°dprilis, 3J5

Captain Wright said, That Captain Skwie came into the Harbour with a Fireship, which drew Eleven Foot Water, at the time of Beach-head Fight.

That the Hindrance of restoring it to the Depth of Water, as formerly, is the having so many Flood-gates; And that it is a very advantageous Harbour: And that there is no other Harbour to secure our Ships betwixt the Nesse and Portsmouth, which is about a Hundred Miles:

That when he went and viewed the said Flood-^ates, he found they took away the Strength of the Water from the Harbour, and hindered the Efflux and Reflux of the Tide; which has caused the Harbour to he chqaked up: That the St. Andrew has rid there in 2\ Foot Water: That it lies very useful to receive Ships that come from Haverdvgrace and Diep: That many a Ship w ould come in there, if there was Depth of Water: And that it is a very convenient Port for Ships to put in and clean, which they might do in Two Days, and put to Sea again.

Robert Cullpepper said, That before any Stops were made. Ships went up to Blackball; and that those Stops did much damage to the Harbour of Rye, so that, in a little time, the whole Harbour would be stopped up:

That if the Flood-gates and Crossrwalls were taken away, it would be as formerly; and that the nearer they come to the Harbour with Stops, the worse it is:

That he has seen Four Ships put in there, of about 60 Tons each, w ithout Anchor and Cable.

Mark Cheswtll said, That he w as born at Rye; He has known the Harbour 45 Years, and that it was, at that Time, a very good Harbour; and can remember when there could ride a Hundred Sail of Ships in the Harbour:

That he has knowfn about 45 Years since, it being in Oliver CrovncelTs Time, Ships ride against the Town of Rye at Low-water, then having Two Fathom and half Water:

That in the late War with the French it w'as much better than now; and that 20 Sail of Ships might come and ride within half a Mile of the Town:

That the last War, a Mile within the Harbour at High-water in the said Point, there was Eleven Foot Water: That the Cause of the Decay of the Harbour, is the making Cross-ways and Flood-gates cross the River Appledore, and Chanel through JVittersham Level:

That he can remember a Ship of a Hundred Tons, built at Appledore, being Six Miles above the Town, about Forty-five or Forty-six Yeare since:

That he knows not how long it is since the First Stop was made:

That Stops were made at Blackwall, about the Year 1646:

That, about Seventeen or Eighteen Years ago, he was, with his Hoy of Sixty Tons, which drew Nine Foot Water, as high as Blackwall, and hath unloaded there:

That the last Stop was made about Four or Five Years ago; and that all Sullage that comes in, rebounds back, and settles in the Harbour, and so choakes it up:

That one Captain Cadman went up to Stone, in the Isle of Omey, with a Ship of a Hundred Ton, and loaded there:

That he can remember a Dutch Man of War, of 40 Guns, came in there, and rid afloat, and loaded Guns there:

That at Spring Tid es it flows Four Fathom, and at Low-water not above a Foot and half, Two Miles without the Town, being a Fla t.

William Cheszoell sa id, That he can remember a Stop made about Five Years ago, and also of his Fathers Iloy going up to Blackball, and of her drawing Nine Foot Water; and that William Kirby was Master of the said Hoy:

And that he can remember Two or Three Fireships coming the re at the time of the Beachy-head Fight.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following; viz.

1 VpJ-. 13.

Resolved, That it b the Opauion of thb Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations, of their Petition,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Crossrwalls* Stops, and Flood-gales, se.t up ro the River of Rother, and Chanel through JVitterskam Levell\ and inning the said River and Chanefe and making Land of tfoMapie; and likewise Inning of Sea Wasts, which draw a eon&taut Influx and Efflux, to % caur the Harbour of Rye, have wholly hindered; the Navb gation of the said River and Chanel, and are tho Cairn of stopping up thq xaid Harbour.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That if the Stops in the Chanel through Ifittersham Lefoell shall be taken away, and Inside-walls made on both Sides of the Chanel, that it will restore the ancient Navigation of the River Rother> and make the Harbour of Rye a good Harbour again,

Mr, Rayner reported from the Committee, to whom Frame-work-the Petition of the Frame-work-knitters, inhabitingwith- kmtters-in the Counties of Nottingham, and Leicester, and Derby, and other Counties adjacent, and within the Town, and County of the Town, of Nottingham, on the behalf of themselves, and other Members of the said Trade, waa committed, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon hearing the Petitioners, and the Company of Framework-knitters; which he read in his Place,; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Beiyannn Green said, That the Company had then Charter granted them in the Year 1663:

That the Company obliges every Man, after he hath served his Apprenticeship, to copie to London, though never so far distant, to take up his Freedom; the Charge whereof is computed at Five Rounds, otherwise he cannot take an Apprentice, which is a very great Prejudice fp the poor Men of the said Trade; And that he knew 0113 Trueman, who came up to London upon that Account, ruined by the Expence, and not able *9 return hack again into the Country:

That, upon the Binding of an Apprentice, they pay to the Company in the Whole, 1 /. 2s. bd.:

That each Man, upon his Admittance into the said Company, pays 15^. and 6d- a Quarter:

That they elect Two Persons to be Stewards in Town, and Two in the Country; and, if they do not come up, they fine them 10/.:

That they chose one Thomas Godfry a Steward; who not complying, they sued him in the City, and got Judgment for 14/.; and put him in Prison for it: And the Money was paid by Collection of the Trade; he beipg so poor, that he could not pay it himself:

That they take 6 d, a Quarter of every Person using the Trade, without rendering any Account; which amounts to 300l. per Annum; and would maintain their Poor, if applied to that Use:

That the Company chose him Steward, and summoned him to make a Feast; but he refusing,' they fined biin 10/.; and brought their Action in London, which put him to 50L Charge:

That they have prosecuted several for their Fines, tP their great Prejudice; though, upon several Arguments in the Common Pleas, the By-law was over-ruled, abd held illegal; notwithstanding which they have chose others since.

James Shaw said, They forced him to come to £<P*-don, to take up his Freedom, which cost about 29 s.; and, together with the Charge of coming up, amounted to 5 L; and be was forced to work Half £ Year to get it up again;

That

u>

That he paid 15$. for his Admittance, and pays 6d. per Quarter.

Edward Staples said, They forced him to come up to London, to take up his Freedom; and took 13s. 4^ for his Admittance, and 1 /. 2 s. 6d. for binding an Apfc prentice:

That he pays 6 d. per Quarter.

Gregory WiUmotl said, That the Company having chose him Steward, he came up, and met the Master; who asked him, Whether he would fine ? He answered, He could not tell till he knew his Partner: And, asking *who he was, the Master refused to tell him; saying, He would have him fine; but he refused:

That he provided a Dinner, and went to the Hall; but the same was shut up, and nobody there to eat it; nor a Room to eat it in:

That there are 2,000 Persons, at least, in the Country, that pay 6d. per Quarter to the Company.

Mr. Roby Sherwin said, That the Company sued one Godfry for not standing Steward, after he was elected by them:

That they choose new Stewards every Year, and fine them 10/.; and, if they do not pay it, they sue them for it The Master, Wardens, and Assistants, appeared; and produced their Charter: By which it appeared, That King Charles the 2d, by his Letters Patents, bearing Date the 19th Day of August, in the 15th Year of his Reign, did ordain, That the Frame-work-knitters should be one Body Politick and Corporate, by the Name of the Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Society, of the Art or Mystery of Frame-work-knitters of the Cities of London and Westminster, and Kingdom of England, and Dominion of Wales: And thereby did authorize the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, yearly, upon the Feast of St. John the Baptist, to elect and choose One Master and Two Wardens; and also, at the same Feast, to elect and choose Assistants when, and so oft as, there should be any Vacancy: And did also impower the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, and their Successors, to make Orders for the Rule and Government of the said Master, Wardens, Assistants, and Society, in their several Offices, Function, and Business, touching and concerning the said Society; so as that the said By-laws were not unreasonable, and against the I^aws of the Land: And did also impower the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, under their Common Seal, to make Deputies; which Deputies shall have full Power and Authority, in such Place or Places, within the Kingdom of England, and Dominion of Wales, where such Deputy shall live, and within such Compass as in their Deputation shall be limited, to rule and govern all Persons using the said Art, according to the Powers in the said Letters Patents before expressed; and according to such By-laws as the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, shall, from time to time, make, in as ample Manner, to all Intents and Purposes, as the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants might do, by virtue of the said Letters Patents, within the said Cities of London and Westminster.

As to the First thing complained of; they said, That they did force such as were Apprentices to Freemen of London to come up to London, before they would admit him into their Company; though they lived never so far off:

That Persons free of their Trade are not obliged to be free of the City of London; and that they cannot make any free of the said City of London by their Charter, they being no Company thereof.

As to the 2d thing complained of; they did allow', That they take 15$. for the Admittance of any Person into their said Company: And, for their Justification, produced a By-law, which did oblige to pay, to the Company, ios. in lieu of a Silver Spoon; 2$. to the Clerk of the Company; 1 s. to the Beadle, and 2$. for the King's Duty; and that, if any one refuse to pay this Money, he shall forfeit 30$. to the Use of the Company.

' As to the 3d thing complained of; they did also admit of the taking of the 1/. 2$. 6d.: And said, the Particulars were as follow; viz. 10 s. to the Company, in lieu of a Proof-piece; 3$. 6tf.;to the Clerk of the Company, for Inrolling; 1 s. to the Beadle; 1$. 6d. to the Company, according to the Statute of Hen. the VUIth; 6 d. for Parchment; the King's Duty, 2s.; and, by the Orphans Act, 2 s. 6 d.

As to the 4th thing complained of; they admitted the taking the 2$. 6d.: And said, It Was pursuant to the Orphans Act; and that they took it of everyone, though they were not bound to Freemen of London.

As to the 5th tiling complained of; they pretended, That, by one of their By-law*s, they had a Power to elect Two Persons, living in the Country, to be Stewards, to make the Company a Treat upon Michaelmas-day; and* upon Refusal, to forfeit 10/.; though the Company did never attend the Lord Mayor on that Day.

As to the 6th thing complained of; they justified th6 Taking of it by virtue of a By-law, which did oblige all Persons to contribute a proportionable Sum of Money towards the obtaining of their Charter, as any other things necessary for the w'ell-being of the Company; provided that such Person or Persons be equally rated according to their Degree, Quality, and Condition; but no mention is there made of any Sum in particular: But denied, That the same amounted to near so much as in the Petition: And that they think 6d. a Quarter very moderate.

Sir Edward Seymour reported from the said Committee,

That they had drawn up Reasons to be offered at the said ' Conference; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerics Table: Where the same were-read; and agreed unto by the House; and are as follow; viz.

The Commons cannot agree to the Amendments, made by your Lordships, to this Bill; For that all Aids and Supplies, granted to his Majesty in Parliament, are the sole and intire Gift of the Commons: And as all Bills for the granting such Aids and Supplies begin with the Commons, so it is the undoubted and sole Right of the Commons to direct, limit, and appoint, in such Bills, the Ends and Purposes, Considerations, Limitations, and Qualifications, of such Grants; which ought not to be changed or altered by your Lordships.

This is well know n to be such a fundamental Right of the Commons, that to give Reasons for it, has been esteemed, by our Ancestors, to be a Weakening of that Right.

The Commons therefore leave the^ Bill, and the Amendments, with your Lordships; together with the ill Consequences that may attend the not passing this Bill.

Sir Rowland Gwyn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to the Committee, upon the Complaint of a Breach of Privilege against Christopher Lister i Esquire, by Sir Bazil Firebrasscy and others, arresting Edward Chandler, a menial Servant, and Under-keeper of the Walk, of the said Mr. Lister; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Matter of Fact w as opened by the Counsel to be thus;

That, upon tho 7th of May last, the said Edward Chandler was taken up in Enfield Chase by 15 or 16 Men, upon Pretence of Deer-stealing, and carried to Sir Baz. Firebrass his House, and there examined; and, after having i been carried to several Places, lie was at last brought to the St. Johns Head Tavern in Chancery Lane, where he was examined by the Recorder of London, and convicted of Deer-stealing, and by him committed to Newgate: That he was discharged from his Imprisonment by the Court of King's Bench, being brought before the Court' by Habeas Corpus; and was afterwards, viz. on the 1st Day of January last, taken up for the said Offence, and again committed to Newgate by Mr. Justice Monday; and in like manner, again discharged by the Court of King's Bench: And to prove the whole Matter, but especially the first Taking up of the said Edward Chandler, which, they alleged, was without a Warrant or Officer, the Counsel for Mr. Lister w ould have examined the said Edward Chandler himself; which they insisted upon to be reasonable in this Case, he neither being to get nor lose by any Examination of the Committee; and for the Necessity of this Sort of Proof, in this Case, the Matter not being capable of being proved otherwise.

1 On the contrary, the Counsel for the Persons complained of insisted, That he ought not to he admitted a Witness in this Case, having been convicted twice for so great an Offence as Deer-stealing; and for that his Evi- dence would tend to justify himself against the Convictions; and therefore that he would be concerned in the Consequence, which w as to ease himself: And said, That the said Edward Chandler was not discharged from those Convictions, but they were still under Consideration of the Court of King's Bench; and that they had a Warrant for the first Apprehending of the said Edzoard Chandler.

And that, upon hearing the Counsel on both Sides, the Committee came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Edward Chandler ought not to be admitted as a Witness in this Cause.

And the Counsel being called in again, and acquainted With the said Resolution; Mr. Lister's Counsel declared, That they depended on the Evidence of the said Edward Chandler, to make out the said Breach of Privilege; and, he being not to be admitted as a Witness, they could not advise their Client to proceed.

And they being withdrawn; the Committee came to this Resolution:

The House proceeded to the further Consideration of the Report from the Commissioners appointed to inquire into the forfeited Estates of Ireland.

other Estates and Interests in Ireland; and by a Land Tax in England, for the several Purposes therein mentioned.

Because the Reasons given by the Commons, against their Lordships Amendments, do no-ways relate to the Matter contained in the said Amendments:

Because, though there be nothing in the said Amendments relating to Aids and Supplies granted to his Majesty in Parliament; yet the Commons have thought fit to take Occasion thereupon to assert a Claim to their sole and entire Right, not only.. the granting all Aids in Parliament, but that such Aids are to be raised by such Methods, and with such Provisions, as the Commons only think proper: If the said Assertions were exactly true, which their Lordships cannot allow; yet it could not with good Reason, follow from thence, That the Lords may not alter or leave out according to their Amendments, when the saving the Estates of innocent Persons, and of such as have been outlawed after their Death, makes such Amendments necessary.

And the Lords think it unreasonable and urfjust to vest in the Trustees any greater or other Estate, than was in the forfeiting Person, or than the King may legally have; since thereby not only many innocent Persons, who come in by Descent, or Purchase, or other valuable Considerations, might suffer equally as Criminals, but 'tis possible that Men, who, with the utmost Hazard of their Lives, have been defending the Government, may forfeit as Traitors; and they cannot apprehend, that, by any Law of this Land, or by any Rule of Reason or Justice, any Person ought to be outlawed after his Death; since 'tis condemning a Man unheard, and allowing him no Opportunity of making his Innocence appear.

The I>ords admit the Resumption of the forfeited Estates in Ireland to be a Thing necessary, by reason of the great Debt due to the Army, and others, which they earnestly desire to see discharged; and are therefore very willing and desirous to give their Consents to any reasonable Bill the Commons shall send them up to that Purpose: But the Lords can by no means consent, That the Commons shall take upon them to dispose of any of the said Forfeitures to any private Persons; it being the sole and undoubted Right of the Crown, to be the Distributor of

lutions of the Eighteenth of January last, and of Monday last, relating to Grants, be read; and also that several Paragraphs of the said Report be read:

Mr. Speaker,

Resolved, That the House doth agree to a Conference, as the Lords do desire.

Sir Edward Seymour reported, That those who the House were pleased to command, had met the Lords at the Conference; and that it was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Lord President; who was pleased to open the Conference in this manner:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I shall not trouble you with any Reasons to introduce ‘this Conference: The Reasons that relate to the Differences between us are contained in a Paper; and I hope they are proposed in that manlier, as will tend always to the maintaining a good Correspondence between the Two Houses: Which Paper is as followed); viz.

The Lords do insist on their Amendments to the Bill for "granling an Aid to his Majesty, by Sale of the forfeited and of Parliaments, to give Aids, Supplies, or Grants, to any but the King only: And, as the contrary Practice is totally new and unprecedented; so, in Process of Time, it may become of the last ill Consequence to the Publick.

The Ixirds cannot agree to the Clauses, that create an Incapacity in the Commissioners or Managers of the Excise for sitting in this Parliament: Because the Qualification of Members to serve in Parliament is a Thing, if proper to-be meddled wdth at all, that hath been thought fit, by the Commons, to be in a Bill by itself; and the joining together in a Money- Bill Things so totally foreign to the Methods of raising Money, and to the Quantity or Qualifications of the Sums to be raised, is wholly destructive of the Freedom of Debates, dangerous to the Privileges of the Lords, and to the Prerogative of die Crown: For, by this means, Things of die last ill Consequence to the Nation may be brought into Money Bills; and yet neither the Lords, nor the Crown, be able to give their Negative to them, without hazarding the publick Peace and Security: And it seems a great Hardship to the Counties and Places who chose such Members, to deprive them of their Service, since they knew them to be Commissioners of Excise at the time they chose them; and since the Commons admit them to be proper Persons to serve either in Excise or Parliament, though not at the same time; so that there seems to be no other Reason of distinguishing these Commissioners, but what is common to all other Officers of the Crown; and the Question, whether such an Alteration may be convenient, must needs be a Doubt with the Lords, since the Commons have not been able, this very Sessions, "to satisfy themselves with the Bill, and the Considerations diey have entertained upon that Subject.

The Lords do seriously consider the Dangers.and Inconveniencies that are likely to happen by the Loss of this Bill,

12 W. Ill

By the KING.

A PROCLAMATION

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the speedy calling another.

WILLIAM R.

Prodama- WHEREAS We have thought fit, for divers im-tion for dis- portant and weighty Considerations, by and with the Ad-toent.Par* V1Ce Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to Thursday the Sixteenth of January next: We do, for that End, publish this Our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, of the said Parliament, are discharged from their meeting

323

upon Thursday the said Sixteenth Day of January: And to the Intent Our good Subjects may perceive the Confidence We have in their Affection, and how desirous We are to meet Our People, and have their Advice in Parliament, We do hereby make known to Our said Subjects, That, in respect of some Matters of the highest Importance to this Our Kingdom, We do intend to give Directions to the Keeper of Our Great Seal, for the Issuing out of Writs in due form of Law, for the calling a new Parliament; which shall begin and be holden at Westminster on Thursday the Sixth Day of February next.

Given at Our Court at Kensington, the Nineteenth Day of December 1700, in the Twelfth Year of Our Reign.

GOD save The KING.

THE Parliament meeting, pursuant to a Proclamation hereunto annexed, and to the Writs which had issued for that Purpose; the most Noble William Duke of Devonshire, Lord Steward of his Majesty's Household, came, about Eleven a Clock, into the Rooms belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons called the Inner Court of Wards, the usual Place, to administer the Oaths appointed to be taken by the Members returned to serve in Parliament: And Thomas Chute Esquire, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having delivered in a Book of the Names of the Members who had been returned; and Paul JodrcU> Esquire, the Clerk of the House of Commons, and Mr. Needier, his Clerk Assistant, and other his Clerks, attending according to their Duty; the said Lord Steward did administer the Oaths appointed, to several of the Members who appeared; and afterwards made a Commission, or Deputation, under his Hand and Seal, hereunto annexed, to several of the said Members, who had been sworn, to administer the said Oaths to the rest of the Members returned; who administered the same accordingly, to such others as appeared: And the Members being informed, That the Parliament w^s to be prorogued, by Writ directed to the Lords and Commons, they, without expecting any Message from the Lords, went to the House of Peers: Where the Writ for proroguing the Parliament until the Tenth Day of February Instant was read: Which is as followeth; viz.

And accordingly Mr. Speaker elect, with the House, Mr. Speaker went up to attend his Majesty, and to present their Speaker: approved of Who spake thus; vis. the KinS4

May it please your most Excellent Majesty,

THE Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, in Obedience to your Majesty's Commands have proceeded to the Election of a Speaker; and by their Direction, I am presented to your Majesty, as the effect of that Choice: At the same time I most humbly lay before your Majesty my own Insufficiency to discharge so great a Trust; and therefore do most earnestly beseech / your Majesty to accept my Excuse; and, that, the Publick may receive no Detriment from my Want of Ability,

I most heartily beg your Majesty will give your Commons an Opportunity to make a better Choice.

"Whereupon the Lord Keeper acquainted the House of Commons, That his Majesty was pleased to approve of the Choice they had made; and allowed of Mr. Harley to be their Speaker.

After which Mr. Harley replied;

May it please Your Majesty,'

SINCE your Majesty hath not been pleased to admit of my Excuse, it is my Duty to submit; and I do, in the first Place, with the utmost Thankfulness, acknow-lege the undeserved Honour your Majesty is pleased to confer upon me: And that I may the better discharge that great Trust which your Majesty, and the Commons, have committed to me, I am an humble Suitor to your Majesty, That none of my Failings, or Infirmities, may be imputed to your faithful Commons: And that your Commons may be better enabled to consider of the important Affairs that shall come before them, I do, in their Name, by humble Petition, lay Claim to all their ancient Rights and Privileges; and more particularly, that they may have Freedom from Arrests and Disturbance to their Persons, Estates, and Servants; -'Liberty of Speech, for the better Management of their Debates;

Freedom of Access to your Majesty's Royal Person, upon Occasion; and that the Proceedings of the House may receive a favourable Interpretation, and be free from all Misconstruction.

I have nothing more to add, but my hearty Prayers, and poor Endeavours, That the Consultations of the Parliament may tend to the Honour and Safety of your Majesty and your Kingdoms.

The House being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That his Majesty had been pleased to give his Approbation to their Choice of a Speaker: That he had laid claim, by humble Petition, to all their Rights and Privileges, and particularly to that of Freedom from Arrests, and Disturbance of their,

Persons, Estates, and Servants; Liberty ot Speech; and Freedom of Access to his Majesty's Person: And that the Lord Keeper did signify his Majesty's Pleasure, That they should enjoy all their ancient Privileges, as fully as any of their Predecessors.

And afterwards Mr. Speaker returned the House his hearty Acknowledgments for the great Honour they had done him, in placing him in that Chair; assuring the m,

That he would endeavour to discharge the Duty incumbent on him, uprightly, with all Impartiality, and Respect to the House, and every particular Member of it; hoping that they would consider his Weakness and Infirmities, and give him their Assistance and Support in doing his Duty; and that, in order thereunto, that they would keep the good Orders their Predecessors had established 4O for

And all that come are to have Voices: And they are to meet upon Friday next, at Five a Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker's Chambers; and sit every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, in the Afternoon: And they are to take into Consideration all such Matters as shall or may come in Question touching Returns, Elections, and Privi-t leges; and to proceed upon Double Returns, in the First Place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinions therein, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons that w ill question Returns, are to do it in Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee have Power to send for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are returned for Two or more Places, are to make their Elections by this Day Three Weeks, for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in Question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw, till their Returns are determined.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit but Two Counsel of a Side to be heard in any Case before them.

Resolved, That no Person be taken into the Custody Usual of the Serjeant at Arms, upon any Complaint of a Breach Orders, of Privilege, until the Matter of such Complaint hath been examined by the Committee of Privileges, and re-, ported to the House.

Resolved, That no Member have Privilege in any Case where he is only a Trustee.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election for any Member to serve in Parliament.

Declared, Nemine contradicente, to be a Standing Order of the House, That no Member of this House have any Privilege, except for his Person only, against any Commoner, in any Suit or Proceedings in Courts of Law or Equity, for any longer time than the House shall be actually sitting for the Dispatch of Business in Parliament.

The House being informed, That Samuel Shepherd Esquire, a Member of this House, hath been guilty of Bribery at several Corporations, in order to procure Members to be elected into this Parliament;

To which Mr. Shepherd being heard in his Place, and insisting upon his Innocency;

Resolved, That the Matter of the Charge be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Names of the Places, where the said Mr. Shepherd is charged to be guilty of the said Bribery, be delivered to him in Writing.

Ordered, That the said Matter be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Tuesday next come Three Weeks.

A Petition of Sir Charles Hedges Knight, and Sir Tho. Felton Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners were duly elected to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Or-ford, in the County of Suffolk, not only by the Mayor and Commonalty, but by the Freemen also; yet Henry Cooper Esquire, High Sheriff of the said County, with Intent to make a false Return against the Petitioners, delivered his Precept to one John Saunders; both whom knew well, that the Execution thereof did not belong to Saunders, as was adjudged at a TryaJ at Bar, last Michaelmas Term; and the said Sheriff did receive an Indenture from the said Saunders, importing, though untruly, that Sir Edmund Bacon and Sir Edward Turner were elected Burgesses for the said Borough; and returned them accordingly; he refusing an Indenture under the Corporation Seal, wherein the Petitioners are rightfully returned by the Mayor of the said Borough: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report The same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Vol. 13.

A Petition of John Gape Esquire was presented to the St. Albans House, and read; setting forth, That at the Election of Election. Burgesses to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford, Colonel Geo.

Churchill, the Petitioner and Joshua and Tho. Lomax Esquires, stood Candidates; where the said Joshua, by several illegal Practices, procured several Persons to vote for him, as well such as had a Right to vote, as such as had no Right; who, by the Mayors Permission, were admitted to poll, though objected against by the Petitioner; and, upon a Scrutiny, it appeared, That the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, beyond the said Joshua Lomax, and ought to have been returned with Colonel Churchill; but the said Mayor hath returned the said Joshua, in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as the House, in Justice, shall think meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections:

Prideaux, who then had a Majority of Thirty-three Votes; and, as a Continuance of his arbitrary Proceedings, got, last Michaelmas, a mean Taylor, that works fey a Groat a Day, and his Nephew's Servant, to be chosen Vianders; having once before gotten the said Servant, while a School-boy, to be chosen Viander: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and put a Stop to such arbitrary Proceedings, w hereby the Petitioners Rights and Liberties are perverted.

And the House taking Notice, upon the said Petition, relating to the Election for the Port of Sandwich, That Sir Henry Furnesse, a Member of this House, is concerned in managing several Aids and Duties granted to his Majesty; thereupon a Clause, in the Act made in the 5 th and 6th Years of the Reign of his Majesty and the late Queen Mary, for granting to their Majesties certain Rates and Duties upon Salt, and upon Beer, Ale, and Other Liquors, for securing certain Recompences and Advantages, in the said Act mentioned, to such Persons as shall voluntarily advance the Sum of Ten hundred thousand Pounds, towards carrying on the War against France, was read; whereby no Member is to be concerned in farming, collecting, or managing, any Monies, Duties, or Aids, granted to their Majesties, except as therein is mentioned;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, take into Consideration what Members are concerned in the said Clause.

Mr. Speaker reported; That his Majesty had been The King's pleased, upon Tuesday last, to make a most gracious sPeecJ^ Speech to both Houses of Parliament; and* that, to rei, ort 1 prevent Mistakes, he had desired and obtained a Copy thereof; which he read to the House, and is as followed!; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

OUR great Misfortune, in the Loss of the Duke of Gloucester, hath made it absolutely necessary, that there should be a further Provision, for the Succession to the Crown in the Protestant Line, after me and the Princess.

The Happiness of the Nation, and the Security of our Religion, which is oar chiefest Concern, seems so much to depend upon this, that I cannot doubt but it will meet with a general Concurrence; and I earnestly recommend it to your early and effectual Consideration.

The Death of the late King of Spain, with the Declaration of his Successor to that Monarchy, has made so great an Alteration in the Affairs abroad, that I must desire you, very maturely, to consider their present State;.

And I make.no doubt, but your Resolutions thereupon will be such, as shall be most conducing to the Interest and Safety of England, the Preservation of the Protestant Religion in general, and the Peace of all Europe.

These things are of such Weight, that I have thought them most proper for the Consideration of a new Parliament, to have the more immediate Sense of ' the Kingdom in so great a Conjuncture.

I must desire of you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, such Supplies, as you shall judge necessary, for the Service of the current Year: And I must particularly put you in mind of the Deficiencies, and publick Debts, occasioned by the late War, that are yet unprovided for.

I am obliged further to recommend to you, That you would inspect the Condition of the Fleet; and consider what Repairs or Augmentations may be requisite for the Navy; which is the great Bulwark of the English Nation, and ought, in this Conjuncture most especially, to be put in a good Condition; And that you would also consider, what is proper for the better Security of those Places where the Ships are laid up in Winter.

The Regulation and Improvement of our Trade is of so publick Concern, that I hope it will ever have your serious Thoughts; and if you can find proper Means of setting the Poor at Work, you will ease yourselves of a very great Burden, and, at the same Time, add so many useful Hands to be employed in our Manufactures, and other publick Occasions.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I hope there will be such an Agreement and Vigour, in the Resolutions you shall take upon the important Mattel's now before you, as may make it appear we are firmly united among ourselves; and, in my Opinion, nothing can contribute more to our Safety at Home, or to our being considerable Abroad.

Resolved, Nemine contradiccntc. That this House will, Kinj Tomorrow Morning at Eleven a Clock, take into Con- Spee sideration his Majesty's most gracious Speech to both 0005 Houses of Parliament.

Answer to The Message from the Lords Yesterday, of the Ad-Address. dress, being read; the same is as followeth; viz.

Vol. 13.

WE the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, return our most humble Thanks and Acknowledgments to your Majesty, for your Concern expressed for the Protestant Religion, in your gracious Speech; and your Care for its future Preservation, by recommending to our Consideration a further Provision for the Succession to the Crown in the Protestant Line.

We are highly sensible of the Weight of those Things your Majesty is pleased further to recommend to our Consideration; and therefore humbly desire you will be pleased to order all the Treaties that have been made between your Majesty, and any other Prince or State, since the late War, to be laid before us; that we may be enabled to give our mature Advice, when we are informed of all those Matters necessary to direct our Judgment.

And we further humbly desire of your Sacred Majesty, that you will enter into Alliances with all those Princes and States, u-bo are willing to unite for the Preservation of the Balance of Europe; assuring your Majesty, that we shall most readily concur in all such Methods, which may effectually conduce to the Honour and Safety of England, the Preservation of the Protestant Religion, and the Peace of Europe.

Mr. Secretary Vernon acquainted the House, That he intercepted was commanded by his Majesty to communicate to this Letter from House a Letter, which came very providentially to his p^of Hands, out of France, being a Letter from the Earl of Melfort to his Brother the Earl of Perth: And he delivered a Copy in at the Table, and the Original to Mr.

Speaker: And the said Copy was read, and is as followed; viz.

My dearest Brother, Friday, 18 Feb. 1700.

Since I promised to put in Writing what we had not Time to talk, fully of, I am set down to it in the Morning, that my Letter may be ready for the Messenger, if any call.

I told you all that I had heard at Versailles, and the favourable Audience I had of Madame de Maintenon; for which I beg it of you to return my most humble Thanks to the Queen, and beg of her to be so good as to thank Madame de Maintenon, and know from her what can be done in that Matter: It will be a great Charity in the Queen.

I told you, amongst other Things, the great Fleet the King intends to put out this Summer, the Orders being given, and the Money ready, the Stores full, and every one concerned active in their Stations: There is no Doubt but this Fleet will be Master of the Sea for some Time, if not for all the Summer; because the Dutch dare not stir till the English be ready; and they have long Debates yet before they can be in a Condition to act, if they have the Will; and it is a Question if they will have it at all.

The King never had so favourable a Conjuncture, if he can persuade this King, that his Affairs are really in the Circumstances they are in: But there is the Difficulty.

The King and Queen have more Authority with the King and Madame de Maintenon, than any other in the World can have: But that is not all: There should be some one acceptable to the Ministers, who should lay before them these Proofs their Majesties cannot enter into the Detail of, and explain the Reasons, make Plans and Memoirs by their Majesties Approbation, to convince them of the Necessity, and to shew the Easiness of restoring the King, the Glory it brings to their King, and the Advantage to Religion.

How this will be done, their Majesties are wise enough to consider; and I think it is not a Subjqct fit for me to enter upon: But their Friends in general, who know not the Half of what I know in this Matter, think that it will not be wfell done by a Protestant Minister, lazy in his Temper, Enemy to France by his Inclination, tainted with Commonwealth Principles, and against the King's returning by any other Power than that of the People of England^ upon Capitulation and Terms; who is suspected of giving Aim to the Compounders, if not worse.

That Mr. Caryl is qualified, no man doubts; but, in Society with the other, those w ho must be instrumental, will not trust him as he ought; so that, so long as the other is within Distance of penetrating the Affairs, they will never think themselves secure.

And yet the King has no such Game to play as by these very Persons who are thus diffident; namely, the true Church of England Party, the Catholicks, and the Earl of Arran: And I shall say something as to every one of

Intercepted Letter trom Earl of Lerih.

33 6 17° Februa A. 1700,

of them. The King cannot but be sensible, that the true Church of England Party, and their Principal Head, now, the Bishop of Norwich, has been silent of a long Time; and their Majesties may remember what Weight the Court of France laid upon their joining the King (I mean the non-swearing Clergy) in case of a Landing.

Therefore all Arts should be tried without JDelav, to get them to enter into Correspondence again; and every Impediment ought to be removed; I say, without Exception: And though sometimes it is of hard Digestion for Sovereigns, who ought to be obeyed without Reserve, to yield to the Humours of Subjects; yet Prudence should teach them, when they cannot, without hurting their A flairs, do what they would, to do what they can; and remember the Fable of the Dog, w ho lost the Substance for the Shadow.

Assurances from the Non-swearers, the soundest and venerablest Part of the English Church, would be of great L'se at this Time, to persuade France to undertake this great Affair: For, besides their own Example at a Landing, and their Preaching and Writing to the People, that their Religion was in no Danger; 'tis most certain, they know better than any others can,- what the Church of England in general would do for the Kings Service; and they being to run all the Hazard, would be better believed at the Court of Franceth&n any other, as I found by Experience.

As to the Catholicks, and others associate with them, unfortunately for the King, they were thought to have too much Inclination for me; and so have R en reckoned as useless to the King: But I must beg Leave to say, That Undertaking was the best Feather in his Wing, and was most thought so by him, and by the Court of France too, even to that Degree, that they pretended, if this and the other Article concerning the Clergy, could be made appear, they would concur with the King to invade England- They consisted of Seven Regiments of Horse and Dragoons; their Arms, Trumpets, Kettle Drums, Standards, See. were all ready, and are yet in Security; their Men were all listed, and their Officers chosen, and they had Twenty Horses to a Troop; which Troops lying at a Distance in a Horse Country, Twenty Horses would soon have mounted the rest.

Those who could not divine the Greatness, and the Use, of the Undertaking, blamed the Rashness of it; and even some Churchmen have not been disapproved for endeavouring undutifully, because contrary to the King's written Orders, to break the Design: But I desire you* now, for all this, to believe that you have not such another Argument to use to the Court of France as this: And if you could make it appear, as it might have been done some Years ago, I should have very good Hopes of this Summer's Work: Nay, let the King have what other Hopes, or even Promises, you please, from the Court of France, this is to be encouraged; and, if possible,1 to be put in the Circumstances it was in; for, if ever there be a Landing, in England to Purpose, it must be before they can be armed; and they cannot be armed before the Parliament come to a Resolution concerning the War; and considering the few Troops in England, suppose these Men to be no better than Militia, what a Diversion would it be!

It is not necessary forme to say any more of this Article, till I know whether their Majesties have as good an Opinion of this Undertaking as I have. If so, I shall shew what I think to- be done in it: If otherwise, I shall save the Pains.

As to the Earl of Arran, it would be of great Use to have an Understanding with him: He will have none

where-..... can pry; his All is at Stake; and he ought

to be wary with whom he ventures to deal.

I think it better for the King's Service, that the Court Party prevailed in the Manner they have done in the Parliament of Scotland, than that the Country Party should have got their Will: Opposition swells the Waters, to a Flood; and so long as the Country Party is not discouraged, they gain more Ground in the Kingdom than they

lose in Government; so that the Disaffection, to the Government will increase; and one may judge of the Nation in general, which is of another Temper than this pretended Parliament, or rather Presbyterian Rabble, ill representing the Nation; for since, even in it, there is such a Struggle against the Government, w hat would there be in a free Parliament, which the P* ... . of 0. ,. durst never hazard to call?

The Natioia then, at least a great Part of it, being disaffected to this Government, it is of the last Consequence, that E. Arran may know what to do in case of an Invasion of England; or in case he and his Friends be obliged, for Self-preservation, to rise for their own De-, fence.

The Army, who are, and ever were, well affected, are to be gained by Money; and a little goes a great Way with them.

The disbanded Troops would be engaged, and the Officers are well inclined.

The Places of Strength would be secured, and such as. can be put in Defence, without Expences, fortified,

To do all this, at least such a Part of them as can be begun with, a small Sum will serve; and he ought to have I lopes of it, and of the Command.

These being only Heads to be discoursed of, and much to be said x>f every Part, it is not thought, that this Letter can carry a final Conclusion; for it may be, upon Discourse, I might change my Mind, or be more eon-, firmed in, and see further.

This makes me insist again to you upon Two Things, as appearing to me absolutely necessary, to put Things upon a right Foot.

The First is the Removing of all Impediments out of the Wav, and sending all suspected Persons to Champagne or Burgundy, according to their Goust.

And the Second is of the last Use, both to their. Majesties and the Prince: Which is the establishing of such a Number, under no Qualification to talk of their Affairs in their Majesties Presence, with whom wfe can, freely converse and propose what may be for their Majesties Service.

As for the first; it w ill be for the King's Reputation, both at the Court of Rome, France, and with all his true Friends in England, for many Reasons.

As for the Second; it is according to Scripture, il la the Multitude of Counsellors th$re is Safety."

Nothing is so dangerous as first to determine what one will do, and then hear Reasons against it; and imitate the deaf Adder, who hearkens not to the Voice of the Charmer, let him charm never so sweetly: Reasons against a Resolution taken, offend; and the more Force they have, they offend the more; whilst, before the Resolution be taken, Reason has its effect, and the Determinations are not the Effects of Humour and Faction, but of Prudence and Justice.

If in any thing I fail, I will sw ear 'tis Want of Under-? standing, and not of Will; and I beg, that their Majesties may be persuaded, that it is not Humour nor Vanity, but their Service, I have in my View: Who am, my dearest Brother,

Most humbly yours.

There are no Letters from England, I expect, and atm promised.

I forgot to tell you, that the Conjuncture ought to be improved, so long as the Court of France have the-ill Opinion of the Prince of Orange s Treachery, discovered lately, in their Hands.

chequer Mr. Lowndes, according to Order, presented to the ! Bills* House, a Copy of the Lords of the Treasury's Authority to the Trustees for circulating Exchequer Bills: And the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Whereas we the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury, out of the Eighteen Persons elected by the Majority of Votes, at a general Meeting of the Subscribers, Contractors for the advancing Money for circulating the Exchequer Bills, not exceeding 1,500,000l. pursuant to an Act of Parliament, intituled, An Act for making good the Deficiency of several Funds therein mentioned, and for enlarging the capital Stock of the Bank of England, and for raising the Publick Credit, have chosen you, Bartholomezv Burton Esquire, Sir William Ashurst, James Bateman Esquire, John Knight Esquire, Sir Henry Furnesse, and Sir Joseph Hern, Trustees on the Part of the King; and you, Mr. Francis Eylcs, Sir Theodore Janssen, Mordecai Abbot Esquire, Mr. Gilbert Heathcote, Mr. William Sedgwick, and George Doddington Esquire, being elected by the Majority of Votes, Trustees on the Part of the Contractors:

We do hereby desire you to take the said Trust and Charge upon you; and, in order to the carrying on this Service, we direct you to choose a Book-keeper with an Assistant, a Cashier with Two or more Assistants, with such other Officers, and at such Salaries or Wages, as you shall think necessary, which shall be paid and defrayed by his Majesty.

We do also desire, that you do meet once every Week, at the least, and not less than Seven to be a Quorum, by whose Directions and Orders this whole Service is to be managed; and that Two of you do constantly attend every Day at the Place w here your Money is to be deposited, to execute such Orders as shall be given by the said Quorum, or the major Part of them; One of the said Two Persons attending each Day to be of those appointed on the behalf of his Majesty, and the other of those elected on behalf of the Contractors.

And we having, for the greater Ease and Convenience of the Contractors, directed that the First Fourth Payment should be paid into the Chamber of London, we do order you to remove the same to such Place in the Exchequer as we shall appoint for that Purpose.

And if, in the Management of this Trust, you do meet with any Difficulty, we direct you to apply to us, as there shall be Occasion. Dated at the Treasury Chambers in Whitehall, 7th Day of Mav 1697.

Cha. Mountague,

A true Copy: Examined per Ste. For,

Wm. Lowndes. Tho. Littleton,

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That he, with the House, did attend his Majesty Yesterday, with their Resolution of the 14th Instant: And that his Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I thank you for this Address, and your ready Concurrence to those great Ends therein mentioned, which I take to be extremely important to the Honour and Safety of England; and I assure you, I shall never propose any thing but what is for our common Advantage and Security.

Having this Occasion, I think it proper to acquaint you, That Yesterday I received a Memorial from the Envoy Extraordinary of the States General, a Translation whereof I leave with you: As to the First Part of it, I think it necessary to ask your Advice; and, as to the latter Part, I desire your Assistance.

States Cene- And that his Majesty had been pleased to put into his nil's Memo- Hand the said Memorial: Which he read to the House; rial# and is as follow'eth; viz.

The underwritten Envoy Extraordinary of the States General of die United Provinces has Order to represent to your Majesty, with great Respect, That their High and Mightinesses having considered, that their Delays in owning the Duke of Anjou for King of Spain were subject to sinister Interpretations, as if all their Aim had been to gain Time to put themselves into a Posture to make War, having thought themselves obliged to proceed to the acknowledging the Duke of Anjou without any Conditions, reserving to themselves to stipulate, in

Februani. 1703.

the Negotiation they are now entering upon, the necessary Conditions for securing the Peace of Europe; in such Negotiation the States are firmly resolved not to do any thing without the Concurrence of your Majesty, and the other Potentates concerned in the Preservation of the said Peace, as they have expressly declared to the Ambassador of France, The Underwritten has, in particular, the strictest Orders to give your Majesty the most positive Assurances that can be, that the States will not take any Step in this important Affair, but in Concert with your Majesty; praying, to that Purpose, that you will please to give your Minister at the Hague Instructions, and necessary Orders, to act jointly in this Negotiation; not to conclude any thing one without the other, and unless England and Holland shall equally find their Security; which, at the same time, tends to the Confirmation of the publick Quiet: But as it may so happen, that it shall not be possible to agree with France and Spain on reasonable Conditions; and so, the Negotiation being interrupted, the States should on a sudden be attacked by the numerous Forces that France has sent to their very Frontiers; they have ordered the Underwritten to represent to your Majesty the extreme Necessity they shall have, in so great a Danger, of the Assistance of England; and to desire your Majesty will be pleased to order the Succours, agreed on by the Treaty, to be in a Readiness; so that, if Occasion be, they may depend upon them. At London, February 170*1.

Persons dis- The House, according to Order, proceeded to take bled from into Consideration, what Members are concerned in the Clause of the Act, made in the 5th and 6th Years of the em ers. ]^e|gi1 of his Majesty and the late Queen, disabling Persons to be Members of Parliament:

And the Clause w as read.

And Sir Henry Furnesse, a Member of this House, being charged to be one of the Trustees for circulating Exchequer Bills, and to have acted under that Trust since he was a Member;

To which the said Sir Henry Furnesse, being heard in his Place, acknowleged that he was one of the said Trustees; and that he acted under that Trust since he was a Member; but that he conceived himself not to be within the said Clause, as being concerned only for the Subscribers Money.

And then he withdrew.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Sir Henry Furnesse Knight, a Member of the House of Commons, having, since his being elected a Member of this present Parliament, been concerned, and acted, as a Trustee for the circulating Exchequer Bills, is guilty of a Breach of the Act, made in the 5th and 6th Years of the Reign of his Majesty and the late Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for granting to their Majesties certain Rates and Duties upon Salt, and upon Beer, Ale, and other Liquors; for securing certain Recompences and Advantages, in the said Act mentioned, to such Persons as shall voluntarily advance the Sum of Ten hundred thousand Pounds, towards carrying on the War against France;

The House divided.

Treaty with Mr. Secretary Hedges acquainted the House, That his Holland. Majesty, according to their Address, had been pleased to give him Direction to lay before this House, Copies of the Treaty with the States General of the United Pro-winces, of the 3d of March 1677; and the Renewals thereof, since that time t And he presented the same to the House accordingly; viz.

A Copy of the Treaty of the 3d of March 1677, and the Translation thereof: And also, 4

A Copy of the Ratification of the 17th of August 1685, and the Translation thereof: And also*

A Copy of the Renewal of the Treaties of the 24th of August 1689, and a Translation thereof;

The Titles whereof were read:

And the said Translations are act follow; viz.

The said Translation of the Treaty of the 3d of March 1677.

Whereas the most Serene Ring of Great Britain, besides the strict Engagements he has already entered into with the States General of the United Provinces, for the Preservation of the Spanish Netherlands, and the Support of their common Interest of that Part of Europe, is very desirous to come, at the same time, into a perpetual defensive League with the said States, for the mutual Preservation of each other, their Subjects and Countries, against all those that should undertake to attack them, or molest or injure them in any wise whatsoever; And the said States, being likewise desirous, on their Part, to enter into the said perpetual Alliance of a: defensive Treaty with his Majesty, have given Power to Mr. Van Beuainghen, their Ambassador, with his Majesty, to treat and conclude the Said Alliance: His said Majesty having named on his Side, for Commissioners, Heneage Baron Finch, Lord High Chancellor of England; Thomas Earl of Danby, Lord High Treasurer of England; Henry Earl of Arlington, Lord Chamberlain of his Majesty's Houshold; Henry Coventry Esquire, and Sir Joseph Williamson Knight, his Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State: The said Commissioners, and the said Embassador after several Meetings and Conferences, have, by virtue of their respective Powers, Copies whereof are inserted at the End of these Presents, agreed and concluded that which followeth:

0.)

There shall be, ftrf the future, between the King, and his Successors, Kings of Great Britain, and his Kingdoms, on one, and the States General of the United Pro* tmees on the other Side, their States, and Territories belonging to them, and their Subjects reciprocally, a sincere, firm, and perpetual Friendship, and good Correspondence, as well by Sea as by Land, in all Things, and every where, both without and within Europe.

(2.)

Moreover, there shall be between his Majesty, and his Successors, Kings of Great Britain, and his Kingdoms, and the said States General, and their States, and Terri to* ties belonging to them, a strict Alliance and faithful Confederation for the mutual Preservation and Maintenance of each other in Tranquillity, Peace, Amity, and Neutrality, by Sea and Land; and in the Possession of all the Rights, Privileges, and Liberties, they enjoy, of have Right to enjoy, or which they have acquired, or shall obtain by Treaties of Peace, Amity, and Neutrality, heretofore made, or which shall hereafter be made, jointly, and in common Concert, with other Kings, Repub-licks, Princes, and Cities: Yet all this within the Extent of Europe only.

(3.)

And therefore they both promise and oblige themselves to keep not only all the Treaties, which his Majesty and the said States General have already made with other Kings, Republicks, Princes and States, which shall be exhibited by both Parties, before the Exchange of the

Vol. 13

Ratifications; but also all those which they shall make Treaty vitii hereafter, jointly, and in common Concert; and to de- Holland; fend, assist, and maintain, one another reciprocally in the Possession of the Countries, Cities, and Places, which at present belong, or hereafter shall appertain, as well td his Majesty, and his Successors, Kings of Great Britain, as to the said States General, by the aforesaid Treaties, in whatsoever Part of Europe the said Countries, Towns, and Places, are situated; in case, that in whatsoever is abovementioned, his Majesty, or the said States General, shall be disturbed, or attacked by any Hostility, or open,

War, by whom, or upon what Pretence, soever.

.(4.)

The reciprocal Obligation to assist and defend each other, is likewise understood for preserving and maintaining his Majesty, and the said States General, their Countries and Subjects, in all their Rights, Possessions, Immunities, and Liberties, as well of Navigation and Commerce, as in all other respects both by Sea and Land, which shall belong to them by common Right, or which* they shall acqhire by Treaties made, or to be made, as aforesaid against all Kings, Princes, Republicks; or States:

So that, it* in Prejudice of the said Tranquillity, Peace,

Amity or Neutrality, present or future, his Majesty, or the said States General, shall hereafter be attacked, or in any other Manner whatsoever disturbed in the Possession of the Dominions, Territories, Towns, and Places*

Rights, Immunities, and Liberties of Commerce, Navigation, or otherwise, which his Majesty, or the said States General, enjoy at present, or shall have Right to enjoy, by common Law, or by Treaties already made, or which shall be made as aforesaid; his Majesty, and the said States General, having Notice thereof, and being desired one by the others shall jointly do their utmost to stop any Disturbance or Hostility, and to procure Satisfaction for the Wrong and Injuries done to one of the Ailies.

(5-)

And in case the said Attack or Disturbance should be followed by an open Rupture, he of the Two Allies that shall not be attacked, shall be obliged to break, Two Months after the first Request of the Ally that shall already be in the Rupture; during \vbich time he shall do his Endeavours by his Ambassadors, or other Ministers, to mediate an equitable Agreement between the Aggressor or Disturber, and the Attacked or Disturbed: And, noU withstanding, shall in the mean time, give a strong Succour to his Ally, such as shall be agreed on by the separate Articles between his Majesty and the said States General; which, though there be no mention made of them in this present Article, shall be kept and observed as if they were therein inserted and written: However, after the Expiration of the said Time of Tw o Months, it shall be left to the choice of him of the Allies, that shall be in the Rupture, to continue to enjoy the Advantage of the said Succour, in case the Conjuncture of the Time, and the State of his Affairs, make him prefer the Effect thereof before that of an open Rupture of his Ally.

(6.)

The reciprocal Guaranty being in this manner settled and promised, when either of the Allies shall be attacked or disturbed; if the State of the United Provinces comes to be attacked, and shall be obliged to entef into an open War, his Majesty shall likewise be obliged to break with the Aggressor or Disturber, and to employ all his Power* and all his Forces by Sea and Land, and to join thtoi with those of the said States General* when it shall he thought convenient, in order to bring the common Enemy to an honourable, safe, and equitable Agreement with Great Britain, and the said United Provinces.

(7.)

And, in this case, the Forces of his Majesty of Great Britain, and of the said States General, shall act jointly and separately, according to what shall be then more particularly concerted between his Majesty and the said Stated General; who, together, shall advise and resolve upon the most proper Ways and Means to annoy the common Enemy, either by way of Diversion or otherwise* to the 4 T end

Treaty with lioiiaud.

20° Februarii. 1700*

end, as 'aforesaid, that he may the sooner be brought to an Agreement.

m (80.

The same that is contained in the Two Articles, which do immediately precede this, shall be performed by the said States, in case England shall be attacked or disturbed in the Manner aforesaid.

(9-)

When once the War is begun by both Allies, according to the present Treaty, neither of the Allies shall make any Cessation of Arms with him that is declared and owned for an Enemy, unless jointly, and by common Consent.

(10)

If it should happen, that a Negotiation should be entered upon, either to treat of a Peace, or a Truce for some Years; the same shall not be commenced by either of the Allies without the Participation of the other, and without his procuring at the same time, and as soon as to himself, the Liberty and Security requisite and necessary for sending his Ministers to the Place of Treaty; as also shall communicate constantly, and from time to time, all that shall pass in the said Negociation; and neither the one nor the other shall come to a Conclusion of the said Peace or Truce, without comprehending therein his Ally, and restoring him, if he desires it, to the Possession of his Country, Territories, or Places, and Enjoyment of the Rights and Immunities, which he held and enjoyed before the War; and without stipulating with the common Enemy, for his Ally, the same Rights, Immunities, Exemptions, and Privileges, as for himself; unless it shall be otherwise agreed between the Allies.

(n.)

It shall be permitted to him of the Allies that shall be attacked, to raise all Sorts of Men fit for War in the Dominions of the other, to serve in their Land Armies, provided it be done by Capitulations, such as both Parties shall agree upon between themselves.

(1:2.)

The Ratifications of this present Treaty shall be given in due Form, and exchanged on both Sides, within the Space of Four Weeks, from the Signing thereof

In Witness whereof, the said Commissioners, and the said Ambassador, have signed and sealed these Presents. Done at Westminster, the 3d March 167-^.

Separate Articles.

If the Case mentioned in the 5th Article shall happen, the said King, and his Successors, and the said States General, shall be obliged mutually to assist each other, as often as they are attacked or disturbed, as it is more at large expressed in the said Article, with Succours; viz. His Majesty of Great Britain the States General, with 10,000 Foot; and the said States General his Majesty with 6,000 Foot, w ell armed, under such Regiments, Companies, Colonels, and other Officers, as his said Majesty, and the said States, shall think fit, and judge most proper, for such an Assistance; and with Twenty Men of War, well equipped and provided: And the said Succour shall be delivered and maintained at the Cost of him that sends the same for the Service of him that shall be attacked.

(2-)

If the Necessity of Affairs make it judged and acknowledged, that the Succour promised and granted ought to be augmented, the said King, and States General, shall use their Endeavours to agree about it.

(3-)

The Succour which shall be sent shall be wholly under the Command and Order of him to ivhoin it is sent, to make use thereof, and to carry them to such Places as he shall think fit, by Water and Land, in the Field, at Sieges, for the Guarding of Places, and wheresoever his Necessity or Advantage shall require.

In Witness whereof, the Commissioners of the King of Great Britain, and the Ambassador of the States General, have signed and sealed these separate Articles. Done at Westminster, the 3d March 167-J-.

The said Translation of the Ratification of the 17th of August 1685.

James the Second, &c. We are willing to have it appear to all and singular who are, or may be, concerned, That whereas the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Netherlands, out of their Desire to renew and confirm Friendship with us, have sent to us Ambassadors Extraordinary; an Agreement has been made between them, and Commissioners appointed on our Part, with full Powers, Copies whereof are inserted at the End of this Treaty, the 17th Day of August 1685, at our Castle of Windsor, in the Manner following:

The High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Netherlands, having signified, that they very much desire, that all Treaties which have been made at divers Times and Places, hereafter particularly named, between the most Serene and Powerful Prince, Charles the Second, late King of Great Britain, of glorious Memory, and themselves the said States General, which are now in Being, and relate, as well to the Peace and good Understanding between the British Crown, and the States of the United Netherlands, as to the Liberty, Usage, and Security, of Commerce between the Subjects of either State, may be continued and confirmed anew'; and, to that End, have sent hither their Ambassadors Extraordinary, James Baron of Wassenaer, &c. Arnold de Citters, Everard deWcede, Lord of Dickvelt, &c.; and have made them their Commissaries and Deputies on this Occasion, and armed them with full Power and Authority:

The most Serene and Powerful Prince, James the Second, by the Grace of God, King of England, Scotland, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, &c. being moved with the same Desire of continuing and observing the ancient Friendship between the said Two Nations, and increasing the same by any advantageous Agreements and Conditions on both Sides, hath named and constituted on his Part, and armed them with the like Power and Authority, his right trusty and right wrell beloved Cousins and Counsellors, Laurence Earl of Rochester, High Treasurer of England; George Marquis of Hallifax, President of the Privy Council; Robert Earl of Sunderland, one of the Principal Secretaries of State; and Charles Earl of Middleton, the other Principal Secretary of State: The aforesaid Commissioners and Deputies, as well on the Part of the most Serene Prince, James King of Great Britain, as on the Part of the States General, having several times met and conferred together concerning the Premises, according to the Authorities and Powers given them on both Sides, Copies whereof are inserted in the End of this Treaty, have agreed and concluded,

That all and singular the Treaties here recited and named;

1st, The Treaty of Peace and Confederacy concluded at Breda, the -|4 July 1667;

2d, The Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, made at the same Place, and the same Day;

3d, The Treaty of Peace and Friendship, concluded at Westminster the -tV Day of February 167!.

And all and singular the Articles contained in the said Treaties, and any of them; shall from henceforth be continued for ever; shall be confirmed, and remain in Force, in the same Sense, a*?d to the same Purpose, as they were at first framed and concluded; and shall have and obtain, for the future, the same Force and Power as they ought to have had, or were supposed 16 have had, before; and that in as ample Manner and Form as they were at first conceived and concluded, and as if each particular Treaty, and every Article of those Treaties, were repeated and inserted in these Presents.

(2.)

The aforesaid most Serene Lord the King of Great Britain, and the aforesaid High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces, shall sincerely, and bona fide, observe all and singular the Heads agreed upon and confirmed by all and singular the Treaties recited and named in the foregoing Article, and cause the same to be observed by their Subjects and People; and shall not, directly or indirectly, do any thing to the contrary themselves, or suffer the like to be done by their Subjects or People; and they shall on both Sides, ratify and confirm, by Letters Patents, signed by their own Hands, and sealed with their Great Seals, the Confirmation of all and singular the aforesaid Treaties, now agreed on and concluded by their respective Commissaries and Deputies; which shall be conceived and drawn up in sufficient and effectual Manner; and shall deliver the same, or cause them to be delivered reciprocally, bona fidey really and effectually, within Four Weeks after the Date of these Presents, or sooner, if it may be. Done in the Royal Castle of Windsor, the 17th Day of August 1685.

The said Translation of the Renewal of the Treaties the 24th of August 1689.

Whereas after several Breaches of the Peace on the Part of France, the most Serene King of Great Britain, and the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Law Countries, are jointly entered into a War with the most Christian King; and the said

Lords the States General, having..... the Sieurs

Alexander Schimmelpemiinck Vander Oijey Lord of En~ gelenburg, Grand Baily and Disckgrave of the City and Majorality of Bokleduc; Nicolas IVitsen Burgomaster, Counsellor and Treasurer of the City of Amsterdam; William de Nassau, Lord of Odjick, Cortgene, Seijst, Drij-lergen, and Blichenburg, first Nobleman, and representing the Nobility in the Assembly of the States, and in the Council of the Province of Zeland; Arnold Van Citters, formerly their Ambassador in Ordinary in England; and Ever hard de JVeede, Lord of TVeede, Dickvelty & c. their Ambassadors Extraordinary to his Majesty of Great Britain; and having shewed their Desire by the said Ambassadors, not only to confirm all the Treaties of Amity and Alliance, which are subsisting between the Crown of England, and the said States General, but also to enter into other Engagements of stricter Alliance with his said Majesty, for the Maintenance, and reciprocal Preservation, of their Subjects, Countries, and States, and to reduce the most Christian King to a just and reasonable Peace, which may restore and confirm the Quiet and Tranquillity of Europe: And as the said States General have given Power to the said Ambassadors Extraordinary, to treat and conclude the said Treaty; his Majesty, being of the Vol. 13.

same Mind, and willing to concur in that Design, has Treaty with named for Commissioners, on his Side, Thomas Marquis Holland, of Carmarthen, President of his Privy Council; George Marquis of Halifax, Keeper of the Privy Seal; the Earl of Shrezosbury, and the Earl of Nottingham, his Majesty's Principal Secretaries of State; and Thomas Wharton Esquire, Privy Counsellor, and Comptroller of his Majesty's Houshold: The said Commissioners, and the said Ambassadors, after several Meetings and Conferences, have, by virtue of their respective Powders, Copies whereof are inserted at the End of these Presents, agreed and concluded that which followeth:

O')

There shall be, for the future, between the King of Great Britain, and his Successors, Kings of Great Britain, and their Kingdoms, on one Side, and the States General of the United Provinces, on the other, and their Dominions, Territories, and Subjects, reciprocally, a sincere, firm, and perpetual Amity, and good Correspondence, both by Sea and Land, in all Things, and in all Places, as well without as within Europe.

(2.)

And, for the better Security of this Friendship, and good Correspondence; and to remove all Difficulties between both Parties, upon what Pretence soever; it is agreed and covenanted between the said King of Great Britain, and the said States General, That all Treaties of Peace, Friendship, Alliance, and Confederacy, of Commerce and Marine, hereafter named and mentioned, shall be approved of, and confirmed, on both Sides; viz.

The Treaty of Peace and Alliance, concluded at Breda the |4 July 1607.

The Treaty of Navigation and Commerce, concluded at the same Time, and in the same Place; 1

The Treaty of Peace and Amity, concluded at Westminster the -rV February 1 674.

The Treaty of Marine, concluded at London the First October 1674; with a Declaration, explaining several Articles of the said Treaty, as also of the Marine Treaty of the n7Tth February 1674, concluded at the Hague the December 1675.

An Article for preventing and composing the Disputes which may happen between the East India Companies of England and Holland, concluded at London the -T March 1674.

The defensive League, concluded at Westminster the 3d of March 1674.

The Treaty of Concert relating to the English and Holland Fleets, concluded at Whitehall the 29th April 1689.

The Treaty for prohibiting Commerce with Trance, concluded at Whitehall the August 1689.

Whereas the said Treaties, and all and every the ArtF cles of them, are effectually approved of, and confirmed, by this present Treaty; and shall remain in their first Force and Virtue, as if they were here inserted Word for Word, as far as they do not contradict or derogate one from the other, or from this present Treaty: So that the Points and Matters, stipulated by a latter Treaty, shall be fulfilled in the Sense then agreed upon, without any Regard to an ancienter Treaty.

(3-)

Moreover, there shall be betwixt his Majesty, and his Successors, and the said Lords States General, and their Subjects and Ii habitants, reciprocally, a firm Alliance, and faithful Confederacy, mutually to preserve and maintain each other in Tranquillity, Peace, Friendship, and Neutrality, by Sea and Land, and in Possession of all Rights, Franchises, and Liberties, that they enjoy, or have Right, to enjoy, or which are acquired for them, or that they shall acquire by Treaties of Peace, Friendship, and Neutrality, which have been heretofore made, or shall be hereafter made, jointly, and by common Consent, with other Kings, Republicks, Princes, and Cities, but all within the Extent of Europe only.

(4.) And
