Treaty with Holland.

(4.)

And thus they promise and oblige themselves to maintain, reciprocally, not only all the Treaties which his Majesty, or his Predecessors, and the said Lords States General, have already made with other Kings, Republicks, Princes* or States, which shall be exhibited on each Side before the Exchange of the Ratifications, but also all those which they may make hereafter, jointly or by common Consent; and to defend, assist, and preserve, each other in the Possession of the Lands, Cities, and Places, which at present belong, or hereafter may belong, as well to his Majesty, and his Successors, Kings of Great Britain, as to the said Lords States General, by the said Treaties, in what Place soever the said Lands, Cities, and Places, are situated, in case that, in any thing above-mentioned, his Majesty, or the said Lords States General, should be troubled or attacked by any Hostility, or open War, by 6ny one, or upon ... Pretext whatsoever; in which case they shall act on each Side, according to what is agreed upon! in the abovesaid Treaty, concluded the 3d of March 167-J-.

(5.)

And whereas the said King of Great Britain, and the said States, are at present in War against the most Christian King; and as the said King of Great Britain, and States General, are under a reciprocal Obligation to assist, defend, maintain, and preserve, mutually each other, their Countries and Subjects, in their Possessions, Immunities, and Liberties, as well of Navigation as Commerce, and other Rights whatsoever, both by Sea and Land, against all Kings, Princes, and States* and particularly the said most Christian King; and for the better attaining to a just and reasonable Peace, which may re-establish the Quiet and Tranquillity of Europe; it is agreed between the said King of Great Britain, and the said States, That there shall not any Suspension of Arms, Truce, or Peace, be agreed on between any of the said Allies, and the most Christian King, or any other King, Prince, or State, whereby either of the said Allies may be molested or attacked, but jointly, and by common Consent.

(6.)

And whereas the said King of Great Britain and the said States General, have already entered into a Treaty of Concert for the employing their Forces this Year against the said most Christian King; it is determined and resolved, That they shall speedily agree upon other Articles and Conditions, in relation to the Numbers and Employing of their Troops, and Men of War, in such manner as shall be thought most convenient, to act with better Success against the common Enemy.

(7.)

It is further agreed between the said King of Great Britain, and the said States, That if, after a Peace is made with the most Christian King, jointly, and with common Consent, as it is above-mentioned, either of the Parties shall be attacked afresh by the most Christian King, or if either of the Parties shall be attacked by any other King Prince, or State; in such Case, the Treaty of Alliance and Guaranty above-mentioned, concluded the 3d Day of March in the Year 167^, between the Crown of England and the said States, which is also approved of, and confirmed by this present Treaty, shall subsist then in all its utmost Extent; and shall be executed in all its Points and Articles, as if the same, or a like Treaty, had been made anew, and since the Conclusion of the Peace with the said most Christian King; with this Variation only, that the War happening in the Case mentioned in the 4th Article of this Treaty, none of the said Allies shall make any Suspension of Arms, Truce, or Peace, with the said most Christian King, or other Aggressor, but jointly and by common Consent.

In this present Treaty shall be comprehended all Kings, Princes, and States, who shall be willing to enter into it before the Exchange of the Ratifications, or within Six Months after, with the common Consent of his Majesty, and the said States.

The present Treaty shall be ratified, and approved of, by the said King, and the said States, and the Letters of Ratification shall be delivered by the one and the other, in good and usual Form, within the Term of Six Weeks, or sooner, if possible, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing thereof.

InWitness whereof, his Majesty's above-mentioned Commissioners, and the Ambassadors Extraordinary aforesaid, by virtue of their respective Powers, have signed these Presents in their ordinary Manner of signing; and have caused their Coat of Arms to be set thereunto. Concluded at Westminster, the 24th Day of August 1689.

A Petition of Sir Francis Windham Baronet was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, Sir Philip Sidenham, and James Anderton Esquire, stood Candidates at the Election of Burgesses, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Ilchester, in the County of Somerset: But the said Mr. Anderton did, contrary to a late Act of Parliament, distribute and expend several Sums of Money amongst the Electors, by which Means he hath procured himself to be returned, in Prejudice to the Petitioner: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration.

Offered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath tampered with any Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or, directly or indirectly endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence; the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor: And this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any Cause before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offenders.

Mr, Speaker reported, That the House having yester- Answer to day attended his Majesty, and presented to him their Address. Address, his Majesty was pleased, thereupon, to give the gracious Answer following; viz.

Gentlemen,

I thank you heartily for the Advice you have given me, and your unanimous. Resolution to support and assist me in making good the Treaty mentioned in your Address:

And I will immediately order my Ministers abroad to enter into Negotiations, in Concert with the States General, and other Potentates, for the attaining of those great Ends which you desire.

Nothing can more effectually conduce to our Security, than the Unanimity and Vigour you have shewed on this Occasion; and I shall always endeavour, on my Part, to preserve and increase this mutual Trust and Confidence between us.

A Petition of several Burgesses of the Borough of Denbigh Holt, in the County of Denbigh, on behalf of themselves, Election, and other Burgesses of the said Borough of Holt, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by Act of Parliament, 35 Henry 8th, the said Borough, together with the Boroughs of Ruthin and Denbigh, are impowered to elect a Burgess for Parliament; to which Election, none but Burgesses have a Right to vote; and the Election of such Burgesses is, by an ancient Charter, vested in the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of Holt:

That on the 25th of August 1698, Tho. Warburton Esquire, then Mayor of Holt, did, 'without the Consent, and against the express Will, of the Bailiffs, and most of the Burgesses, make about 400 Foreigners and Strangers, brought thither by the Interest of Sir Robert Cotton, of Cheshire, Burgesses of Holt; in Opposition to which Proceeding, the old Burgesses did demand a Poll; but Mr. Warburton peremptorily refused it; and, on the 28th of September following, made above 400 more Foreigners and Strangers, brought thither by the like Interest, Burgesses, notwithstanding the like Opposition was made, though to no Purpose: That Edward Brere-ton Esquire prosecuted an Information in the Kings Bench, against the said Mr. Warburton, for his irregular Proceedings; which was tried at the last Salop Assizes; and a Verdict was given against him, upon full Evidence given by his own Witnesses; and yet Sir Robert Cotton, on behalf of his Son Thomas, did, at the last Election of a Burgess to represent the Petitioners, with Ruthin and 4 X Denbigh,

The House being informed, That the Commissioners Commii-for taking, examining, and determining, the Debts due to the Army, Navy, and for Transport Service; and also ArmyDd an Account of the Prizes taken during the late War; &c. attended at the Door;

And the said Report, or Account, and the Titles of; the other Papers and Accounts, were read;

And the said Report, or Account, is as followeth; viz.

An Account of the Proceedings of the Commissioners appointed by an Act of Parliament, made in the 11th and 12th Years of his Majesty's Reign, to take, examine, and determine, the Debts due to the Army, Navy, and for Transport Service; and also an Account of the Prizes taken during the late War; delivered in to the Honourable House of Commons, in Obedience to an Order dated the 24th Day of this Instant February 1700-1.

May it please your Honours,

Army.] According to the Directions of the said Act, we applied ourselves with all Diligence, in the First Place, to the stating and determining the Arrears of Pay to the Officers who have served under his Majesty, either for the Reduction of Ireland, or in the War against France.

In order whereunto we gave frequent Notices by Precepts, Letters, and public Advertisements, to the Colonels and Agents of the respective Regiments, forthwith to lay their Accounts before us; as will appear in the Scheme herewith humbly presented, marked (A.)

notwithstanding which, very few were brought to us before the First of September; but those that were, have been carefully examined and stated; and Certificates made by us for the Arrears thereof, to the Paymaster of his Majesty's Forces, within the Time limited by the Act, beginning with those whose Officers received Half-pay; of which Arrears we here present an Abstract, marked (B); wherein we have distinguished what is due upon the Account of Cloathing, what for Poundage, and what for the Royal Hospital at Chelsea.

And here we think it proper to observe, That, in the stating of those Accounts, we found several Sums of Money due to the private Soldiers, amounting to above 2,500 /.; which having no Power to certify, we took care to distinguish to the- Paymaster, that he might retain the same for the further Direction of Parliament.

And that this Honourable House may not want any Observation we have been capable of making, we have prepared, and herewith offer, an Account of the several Sums of Money arising from Respites taken oft, and other

Allowances

13 W. III.

£5° — 26° Febraaril.

Allowances made by Warrants, siilce the loth of April 1700; contained in the Paper marked (C):

As also a Comparison of the Difference between the Arrears delivered into Parliament by the Paymaster of his Majesty's Forces, and those brought by him to us; and between those, and the Arrears certified for; as will appear, marked?D.)

After the Time for certifying was expired, hoping to have made a greater Progress in the remaining Accounts, 'we renewed, our Letters, Precepts, and Notices, to the several Colonels, Agents, and Governors of Garisons, whose Accounts were not then brought in, to lay the same before us; some of whom complying the rewith, their Accounts have been examined and stated by us; others have Wrought them so imperfect, that we could not examine knd state them, till they were amended by the Colonels or Agents; to whom they were given back for that Purpose, and are not yet returned; though we have not been wanting to exert all our Power for their Assistance, where the same was found requisite or desired; others have lately brought in their Accounts, which are now under Examination; and the rest, notwithstanding all the Notice given, have not yet brought in any; a List of all which is contained in the Paper marked (E.)

Navy.] The Result of the Inquiries which wre have been hitherto able to make into the Debt of his Majesty's Navy Royal, on the 31st of December 1700, we humbly present under the several Heads in the Paper marked (F.)

Transport] We have examined and stated the Accounts, brought before us, of the Principal Money due for Transport Service, which were not before adjusted and determined by Act of Parliament; and have issued out Debentures, for the said Debt, to all Persons u ho have applied to us for the same; and are ready to deliver out the rest, when the Persons concerned shall call for them; the slate of which Debt will appear in the Abstract marked (G.)

Prizes.] We have sent Precepts and Letters, and had several Conferences with, and Promises from, the present Commissioners for Prizes, to lay before us an Account of all Ships and Goods taken, and condemned as Prize, during the late War; notwithstanding which, we have not been able to this Day to obtain any sort of Return thereto: But that we may be found, as we hope, to have pursued the proper Methods for attaining the Ends of our Commission in this Affair, we humbly offer a Copy of our First Precept to them, marked (H.)

Nor could we supply their Defect by the Applications we made to several other Officers, so as to come to any Knowledge either of the true Number or Nature of Prizes taken, or of the Disposal of them, or any Part of their Proceed, whereby we might give any Satisfaction therein to this Honourable House.

To all which we humbly crave Leave to add an Account of the Sums of Money received from the Exchequer, and otherwise, by the respective Treasurers of his Majesty's Navy, Paymasters of his Armies, and Cashiers of the Ordnance, betw een the 13th of February 1688, and the 24th of December 1699, amounting to near Forty-two Millions; which will appear in the Paper marked (I); above one Half whereof has not yet been accounted for before the Auditors of the Imprests.

Tho. Morice, (S. L.)

S. Atkins, (S. L.)

Tho. Lister, (S. L.)

JVnu Farrer, S. L.)

Geo. Langton. (S. L.)

The other Papers to which the Report refers, with the Report also, are bound up with other Papers and Accounts of this Session.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, at Eleven a Clock, take into Consideration the said Report, and Accounts.

A Petition of Christopher KilUam Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That his Father, being seised in Fee of several Lands, devised the same to Trustees, for 21 Years, for Payment of Debts, and raising Portions and Maintenance for his younger Children; Remainder to the Petitioner and his Heirs, in Tail Male: That the said Estate is insufficient to perform the Uses of the Will: But the Petitioner, being desirous the same should be performed, has given new Securities for the said Debts and Legacies; and is willing, that another Estate, whereof he is seised in Fee, should be also sold with the aforesaid Lands, to pay the said Debts and Legacies, which will eat out the same, by incident Charges, and Interest, if not assisted by an Act of Parliament; the Petitioner being willing, that the Remainder of the

last said.....be settled, as an Equivalent, to such Uses

as are mentioned in the said Will: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for Sale of the said several Lands, to pay Debts, and raise Portions and Maintenance, and for settling Lands according to the said Will.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Scobell and Mr. Fortescue do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Mercers, Drapers, Grocers, and other the Traders, within the Borough of Malton; and several of the Gentlemen and Freeholders of several Towns nigh thereto, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Malton is a great trading Market Town in Yorkshire, situate upon the River Darwent, which runs into the River Ouze, and is capable of being made navigable; and will thereby be a great Ease and Advantage to the Petitioners, and other neighbouring Towns; who now are forced, at very

?*eat Charges, to carry and re-carry their Goods many files by Land: And praying Leave to bring in a Bill for making the River Darwent navigable, at the Charge of such Gentlemen as shall undertake the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Palmes and Sir John Kay do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the poor distressed Prisoners for Debt, in the Prisons of the Kings Bench and Fleet, on behalf of themselves, and many Thousands more in the several Prisons and Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are in a miserable Condition, by reason of their long Confinement; and if not speedily relieved, must inevitably perish, and their Wives and Children come to the Parish: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for relieving the Petitioners from their Confinement.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Prisoners in Ludgate is referred.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt in the Gaol D^ton of Rothwell, for the Honour of Pontefract, in the West Petill0D* Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are above 60 Prisoners for Debt in the said Gaol; who, with their Wives and Children, are, by their long Confinement, ruined, many of them being likely to perish, there being no Allowance for Prisoners; many of whom have been substantial Housekeepers, and might have paid their just Debts, had they had their Liberty; but are kept confined merely to gratify the Malice of some Creditors, who know the Petitioners have offered the utmost in their ] Power towards their Satisfaction, and have no Intent to > avoid Payment of their Debts: And praying, That some Relief may be found out for the Petitioners.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Prisoners in Ludgate is referred.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to Corrupting prevent the Embracing and Corrupting of Juries: And Junes-that Sir Richard Cocks, Mr. Birch, and Mr. Dolben, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Coffee, Tea, Hawkers, and Pedlars.

The Duties on Coffee and Tea are granted until May 1701; and those on Hawkers and Pedlari until 24th June 1701; to pay the Interest for the Irish Transport Debt 5 the Principal only of which Debt, being payable by the forfeited Estates in Ireland; there will be a deficiency to pay the Interest, unless the Lands be speedily sold, or those Duties continued.

Then the House, according to Order, proceeded to the Hearing of the Merits of the Election for the Town and Port of fVinckelsea, in the County of Susses, upon the several Petitions of Robert Austen Esquire, and John Hayes Esquire.

And the Counsel were called in, both for the Petitioners, and for Thomas Newport Esquire, and Robert Bristow Esquire, the Sitting Members: And the Counsel were beard; and divers Witnesses were examined on both Sides.

And then, the Witnesses, and Counsel, withdrew.

And then the said Mr. Newport and Mr. Bristow were heard in their Places.

And then they withdrew.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Thomas Newport Esquire is duly elected a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the Town and Port of Winchelsea, in the County of Susses;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Robert Bristow Esquire, is duly elected a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Robert Austen Esquire is duly elected a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion being made, and the Question being put, That John Hayes Esquire is duly elected a Baron to serve in this present Parliament for the said Tow n and Port of Winchelsea;

It passed in the Negative.

Declared, That the late Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea is a void Election.

Resolved, That John Dunmall, Agent of Robert Bri-stow Esquire, is guilty of Bribery in the late Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea.

Vol. 13.

Ordered, That the said John Dunmall be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Resolved, That Mr. Edward Martyn, Mayor of the Town and Port of Winchelsea, is guilty of Threats, and indirect Practices, in order to procure an Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea.

Ordered, That the said Mr. Edward Martin be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Ordered, That no Warrant do issue this Session, for electing any Members to serve for the said Town and Port of Winchelsea.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, That he will please to order, That the said Mr. Edward Martin be turned out of all Employments in his Majesty's Customs.

And the House being informed, that the Commissioners of Accounts, and Commissioners of Prizes, attended, according to Order; they were called in: And, they being at the Bar, the said Report, or Account, and Precept, and the Scheme, were again read to them.

And the Commissioners of Accounts delivered in an Account of their Proceedings with the Commissioners of the Prize Office, 'in relation to the Business of Prizes: which was also read; afc$l is as followeth; viz.

1700. As soon as wdflhad given Notices, and sent out our Precepts and Letters, to the Officers of the Army, as we were directed by the Act first to do; we entered upon that Part of our Duty which relates to the taking an Account of the Prizes taken during the late War, and of the Proceed thereof; and upon the 20th May, made Inquiry, who were the present Commissioners thereof.

Ma*2' A Precept was considered of, and prepared.

30. And sent away.

31. Delivered to Mr. Paschall, one of the Commissioners.

June 3d. Mr. Paschall, and Mr. Buckeridge, their Accountant, being called in; he acquainted the Board, That he had received their Precept of the 30th of May; and was come to shew, That they were not able, from the Books kept in their Office, or otherwise, to make a Re- . turn to several Particulars in the Schemes sent to them in the Precept: Which being called for, he instanced in Two or Three: To which he was told, That the Schemes were drawnuponan Expectation, that their Books aodAccounts were kept in good Order and Method; and then they must be enabled to do it; there being none of them demanded without good Reasons, some of which were shewn in the Debates of the Board with him: At least he said, They would comply as far, and as soon, as they could; and in a few Days, lay before the Board, in Writing, their Reasons why they could not comply with the Whole.

June 29th. Mr. Buckeridge came from the Commissioners for Prizes, and brought a Paper, which, he said, contained Reasons, why the Commissioners could not comply with some Part of the Precept, which they received from this Board: Upon which the Board told him, They thought the Precept, which they s^nt, very well grounded; and that it was the Business of their Office, to have kept their Books and Entries in such a Method, as to have been able to answer the same: But, since they could not, the said Paper w as returned him, with Directions, That, with the Return the said Commissioners do make, they signify under their Hands, That they are capable of sending nothing more.

July 2d. Mr. Brucer came to the Board from the Treasurer of the Prize Office, and desired to be informed, what was required of them by the Precept; acquainting the Board, That Mr. Buckeridge was able to have answered any thing that should be demanded of them, he having their Accounts in his Custody; as also, that Mr. Buckeridge always knew what Specie each Ship was sold for, whether Bank Notes, Exchequer Bills, or ready Money; and that the Treasurer, when any Sum was to be received, always had recourse to the Board, to know what they sold for, and in what Specie it was to be received; but that he did not say this, to shew any Unwillingness to obey the Precept: Upon w'hich he was directed to give Mr. Buckeridge Notice to come to the Board, and to attend at the same time himself, that they might receive the Instructions of the Board together.

12. Mr. Brucer, from the Treasurer of the Prize Office, laid before the Board a Specimen of their Accounts, to know whether it would answer Expectation: Which being perused, the Scheme sent by this Board was likewise looked over; and he was acquainted, That the Board expected, that the Return, to be made to the Precept, should be according to the Particulars of that Scheme; and recommended it to him, to consult with Mr. Buckeridge,\k\e Accountant to the said Office; so that the Whole might be answered accordingly: Which lie promised to do.

August 20th. Mr. Buckeridge ordered to attend.

16th. Mr. Paschallone of the Commissioners for Prizes, came and acquainted the Board, That he w as not in Town when the Precept from this Board came to their Office; but he was in Hopes, last time he had attended this Board, that it was agreed to give them till Michaelmas; which he now desired: That he had employed more Hands, and did not doubt but to be ready at that time: To which he was answered, That this Board had set a Time by their Precept, and never altered the same, nor designed so to do: That the Time drew' near for the Meeting of the Parliament, who would expect an Account from this Board of that Matter. Then he promised to bring what was ready done, to 9ee if the Board could receive and proceed upon it: But failing to do it, a Third Precept w as agreed on, and sent, as follows:

By, &c.

October 29th. Having received no Return to our Precept, notwithstanding the several Assurances you have given us, here, that your Accounts should long since be laid before us; we do hereby require a full Return to our former Precepts, on or before Friday the 1st of November next, or your Reasons in Writing, under your Hands, for your not complying the rewith. Given under our Hands, at York Buildings, this. 29th of October 1700.

To John Parkhust, &c.

November 1st The following Letter was received from them in Answer thereto.

We, the Commissioners for Prizes, having received ail Order from you, to lay before you our Accounts in a Method you then prescribed; and we having promised it should he performed by Michaelmas Day last; this is humbly to give you our Reason why we have not performed our Promise. We have endeavoured, with all Diligence possible, to have complied with your Order; but having long before dismissed all our old Clerks, though we have taken the best we could meet withal, yet they have been so dilatory and negligent, and made so many Mistakes, that much of it is to tye done over again; by which means, we are become much behind hand in time: Now we are ready, as we are always willing, to lay before you our Accounts, in the Method they were kept by us; which if you think fit to accept of, your own Clerks will inform you of the Tediousness and Difficulty of such a Work put into a new Model: However, we shall not scruple our Pains; but, if you please to have Patience, we

shall, in a short Time, and with all the Expedition imaginable, lay them before you, perfected in the Method you have prescribed. We are

Your most humble Servants,

John Parkhurst, John Paschall. November lith. And, on the 11th, this Answer returned:

Gentlemen,

We are sorry your Clerks have been so dilatory and negligent, and made so many Mistakes, as you mention in your late Letter; and cannot guess, what sort of Method your Accounts should be kept in; that a Form prescribed by us, so essential, as we conceive, to the giving such Information to the Parliament, as we have Reason to believe they will expect from us, should create you so many Difficulties: For we ourselves are satisfied, without receiving any Information from our Clerks therein, That if the Accounts be kept in such a Method, as we doubt not Gentlemen of your Skill in Business would direct, there would be no other Tediousness or Difficulty, than the transcribing them into the Method we desired. Upon this Occasion, we cannot but observe to you, That more than Half the Time allowed us by Act of Parliament is now elapsed; and therefore we think ourselves obliged, again to press you for a Return to our Precept with all possible Expedition. We are, Gentlemen,

Your humble Servants,

‘ W.F.T.L.T.M.S.A. To the Commissioners for Prizes.

Your most humble Servant,

December 5th. Mr. Buckeridge ordered to attend.

7. Mr. Buckeridge, of the Prize Office, attended; and was put in Mind how far the Time was elapsed, in which it was expected their Accounts should have been brought in; To which he said, lie had been very ill, otherwise they had been in great Forwardness; but that no Time should be lost; and he hoped they would be finished by Christmas.

Feb. 19th. The following Certificate w;as sent in a blank Cover to the Commissioners, &c.

I do hereby certify, That Mr. Buckeridge, who, I am informed, has been Accountant General to the Prize Office, is at present so very ill, that I look on him as unable to make up Accounts, which, he says, would have been completed in Three or Four Days; but still, I hope, that, in a Week's Time, he may be able to apply himself to Business, and to finish the before-mentioned Accounts.

Richard Blackmore.

Prayers.

A P E T1TIO N of the Gentlemen, and other the most Woollen substantial Inhabitants, of the Towns and Parishes Manufac-of Milverton, Wellington, and Places adjacent, within tures* the County of Somersett, as well on the behalf of themselves, and many Hundred more of the like Quality, as of the Serge-weavers, and Worsted-weavers, in those Parts, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That the Persons concerned in the said Callings are more numerous than any other; and many unskilful Persons, who, for a little Money, have just learned to weave, have not only brought a Discredit to the said Trade, but themselves and Families are become chargeable to their several Parishes, when their Masters turn them out of Employment, such Persons having never served Apprenticeships to the said Trade: And praying, That the House will redress their Grievances, in such Manner as shall be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufactures.

Mr. Lowndes also, according to Order, presented to Auditors 7 the House, the Auditors Fees for the Accounts of the Fees-Navy Forces and Ordnance: Navyand

And the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. Ordnance -

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Bur- CCOUnU* gesses, assembled in Parliament.

In Obedience to an Order of this Honourable House, dated the 21 Instant; we do humbly lay before this House an Account of the Fees claimed by us, and allowed, for passing the annual Accounts hereafter mentioned: wherein we take Leave to set forth a short Scheme of the Method used by us, in examining and auditing the said Accounts; viz.

For auditing the Accounts of the Treasurer of the Navy, our Allowance is 25 /. for every Hundred thousand Pounds accounted for by the said Treasurer; which abates or increases, according to the annual Charge of the Navy.

The said Allowance was granted to the Auditors, by Letters of Privy Seal of the late King Charles the Second, dated the 24th of December 1678, grounded on a Report thereof, made by the Honourable Charles Bertie Esquire,

Sir Cha. Harbord Knight, and John Lawrence Esquire, to whom the Consideration thereof was referred by the Duke of Leeds, then Lord High Treasurer of England; and confirmed by Letters of Privy Seal of the late King James the 2d, dated the 23d December 1686.

In the examining and making up this Account for Declaration, we observe this Method; viz.

1st, We adjust the Charge, by transferring, and charging over all the Supers, from the Foot of the preceding Account, to the Account for the present Year.

2dly, We examine the Exchequer Charge, with an Imprest Certificate, signed by the Auditor of the Receipt, and Clerk of the Pells.

3dly, We examine and cast all the Rates of old unserviceable Stores, sold by the Navy Board, and other Parts of the voluntary Charge, signed by the Commissioners of the Navy.

In the Discharge is contained, all the Bills for Stores of all Kinds, bought for the Use of the Navy, being entered at large, and the Quantities and Rates thereof particularly set forth; which are all examined and cast by us: The said Leiger-book likewise contains the Salaries of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, and principal Officers and Commissioners of the Navy, their Clerks, and others, attending the Business of the Navy in London, and the several Yards, together with the Wages of Ships

and

13 W. III. I. Mart367

and Yards; all of which we examine, and compare with former Accounts, to prevent double Allowances.

Lastly, We take care to set Insuper, at the Foot of the Account, all Persons who have had any Money Imprested to them for the Service of the Navy; and discharge the said Supers, when they have cleared their Accounts; which done, the said Leiger is reduced under proper Heads, and drawn up in the Form of an Exchequer Account; and, after that, Three times ingrossed for Declaration.

For the annual Accounts of the Forces, is allowed us, ... virtue of his late Majesty's Letters of Privy Seal, and several Warrants under his now Majesty's Royal Sign Manual, 20,?. for every Troop of Horse, and Company of Foot, with their Officers, which shall, from time to time, be mustered, and serving in his Majesty's Guards and Ga-risons, or otherwise, in his Majesty's Pay or Service.

In the stating, examining, and making up, of which Account for Declaration, we observe this Method; viz.

The Accountant's Leiger is signed only by himself; and therefore every Article of it to be vouched.

The Charge we compare with the Imprest-roll, and such other Authorities, by which any Money is issued to the Accountant.

The Discharge we compare with the several Muster-rolls, which are some Thousands, his Majesty's Warrants and Establishments; in examining whereof, besides the very great Trouble of computing the number of Officers and Soldiers in each Troop and Company, which are mustered at least Six times in a Year, we examine and compute each Man's different Pay with the Establishment; deduct all Respites, and compare the net Pay with his Majesty's Warrants, and the Acquittances of the Parties appointed to receive it: So that, besides the Trouble of computing each Man's Pay, and comparing it with the Establishments; there are few Articles in this Account, have less than Five Vouchers belonging to it, which are all examined: When the Account has been thus examined, it is then reduced under proper Heads, and drawn into the Form of an Exchequer Account, which is Three Times ingrossed for Declaration.

For the annual Accounts of the Treasurer, and Paymaster of the Ordnance, wherein is included the Accounts of the Armoury, and of the Tents and Toyls, our Allowance is 240/. per Annum; which has been annual y allowed by the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury ever since the Year 1672: In the stating whereof, we examine the Quarter Books for Salaries of the principal Officers of the Ordnance, and their Clerks, of the several Store-keepers, Fire-workers, Gunners, Labourers, and others; and compare them with former Accounts, to prevent double Allowances: We likewise examine all Payments made upon Debentures, signed by the principal Officers of the Ordnance, for all Sorts of Stores relating to the Ordnance, for Workmanship, Repairs of Forts, &c. and cast the particular Rates therein; and take care, that the Payments be all duly executed; and, lastly, set Insuper, at the Foot of the Account, the several Persons that have had any Money imprested to them for the Service of the Ordnance, in order to their accounting for the same; and discharge the Supers standing out in former Years, and vacated in the present Year: And, when the Account has been thus examined, it is then reduced under proper Heads, and drawn into the Form of an Exchequer Account; and Three Times ingrossed for Declaration.

For Prizes, no Accounts have been brought to us; nor are any Allowances settled for taking those Accounts.

Herein we have humbly represented to this Honourable House a true Account of the Fees allowed to us for examining and auditing the Accounts before-mentioned; and humbly hope, your Honours will take into your Consideration the great Trouble, Care, and Trust, in the faithful Discharge of our Duties; as also, the great Charge we are at to our Deputies and Clerks, Rent of our Offices*, Taxes, Stationary Wares, and all other Incidents borne by us out of the said Allowances i Which considered, we humbly hope the Allowances made us will not appear unreasonable,

Vol. 13.

All which is humbly submitted to this Honourable

House.

Memorandum: The Right Honourable the Earl of Orford, late Treasurer of his Majesty's Navy, has delivered into our Offices, Accounts to the last of December 1696; whereof the Tw?o first Years are declared; the 3d lies before Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer for Declaration; and the rest, being but newly brought to us, are under Examination.

The Right Honourable the Earl of Ranelagh, as Paymaster of his Majesty's Forces, his Accounts to the 31st of December 1690, are declared: His Account, to the 31st of March 1692, is before the Chancellor, for Declaration: And no other Account of that Office is before us.

The Honourable Charles Bertie Esquire, late Paymaster of the Ordnance, has accounted to the 30th of June 1697: All which Accounts are declared: And no subsequent Accounts of that Office are yet brought to us.

B. Bridges,

T. Done.

There is due, and claimed, for every intire Account declared at the Treasury, the Sum of Thirty Shillings; which, according to ancient Custom, is divided between the Secretary and his Clerks.

And the said Account and Abstract are as follow:

The said Account of what Progress is made in passing the said Accounts.

The Lord Falkland was Treasurer of his Majesty's Navy, to the Third of April 1689; For which Time, all the Ships and Yard Books, paid by his Lordship, are made up and adjusted in order to be brought to Account; but the said Leiger is not yet brought to the Navy Board, to be examined and signed.

The Earl of Orford succeeded; and all his Lordship 8 Leigersare signed, and passed, by the Navy Board, from his Commencement, to the last of December 1 696.

And all the Ships and Yards Books paid by his Lordship in the Year 1699, to the End of his Lordship's Treasurership, are likewise made up, and adjusted, to be brought to Account in his Lordship's Leiger for that Year.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for the preserving the Peace and Happiness of this Kingdom, and the Security of the Protestant Religion, it is absolutely necessary, a further Declaration be made of the Limitation and Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line, after his Majesty and the Princess, and the Heirs of their Bodies, respectively.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee;

That further Provision be made for Security of the Rights and Liberties of the People.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by adding, after " Religion," these Words, " by Law " established

A PETITION of William Ryder Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the late King James the 2d, by Letters Patents, did grant unto Edward Burdet Esquire, and the Petitioner, the sole Power and Liberty to erect a Conduit-head, and other Buildings upon the Beach of New Deale; and to dig open the Highways, Streets, and waste Grounds, for laying Pipes, and bringing fresh Water to the said Town: The Interest of which Patent is also, by Mortgage, vested in the Petitioner; who hath been at Expence to Engineers, to view and contrive how to effect the said Work; which will be a great Advantage to the Town, and all Shipping coming to the , Downes; but the same cannot be performed without breaking up some Grounds belonging to private Persons: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable him to proceed in so good and necessary an Undertaking.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord Marquis of Hartington, and Sir Robert Davers, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of the Serge and Worsted-weavers, or other Woollen-weavers, living in or near the Town of Creditor1, in the County of Devon, on behalf of themselves, and others concerned in the said Woollen Manufacture; and also, of the Gentlemen and others inhabiting in or nigh the said Town and Parish; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a great Number of poor People are solely subsisted by Employment in the said Manufactures; which are come to great Discredit abroad, by reason that Persons exercise the said Trades, who never served their Apprenticeships thereto; and, if not speedily remedied, the Loss of the said Trades may be endangered, the same being thereby much decayed, and the N umber of the Poor increased: And praying, That Care may be taken to prevent

A Petition of William Horton Esquire, and Samud Rams<M Treaplaud Doctor of Physick, Trustees to Thomas Ranisden ^Statt Esquire, deceased, and of Samuel Ramsden Gentleman, Brother of the said Tho. Ramesden; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth: That the said Thomas Ramsden died about 29th January 1697, leaving an Infant Heir, and an Estate of about 700l. per Annum, charged with Two Jointures, and about 5,000l. Debts; by his Will, directing his said Trustees by Mortgage, to raise Money to pay his Debts; but they cannot find any Person to lend such a Sum on the Security of the Estate, by reason of the Jointures; and Infancy of the Heir, about Four Years of Age; so that it is conceived most for the Heir's Advantage by the Petitioners, and all his Relations, to have some Part of the Estate sold to discharge the said Debts, which otherwise will eat out the whole Estate; but the same, by reason of the said Infancy, cannot be done without an Act of Parliament: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Sale of such Part of the said Estate, as will raise Money to satisfy the said Debts.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Conyers, and Sir John Kay, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of divers Traders in and about CovenC King's Bench Garden was presented to the House, and read; setting p"fs^et forth, That the Petitioners are very sensible of the many r s Difficulties Trade lies under, by the ill Practices of the Kings-Bejich and Fleet Prisons; which is become a mere Licensing Office to all fraudulent Dealers; whereby all the Laws in being, to confine any Person, are insignificant; which manifestly tends to the Ruin of all personal Credit: That this House, the last Session, came to several good Resolutions for remedying those Abuses; but, by reason of the many Prorogations, did not perfect the same:

And praying, That some Methods may be found out for the redressing of the said Grievances.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner, in the proceeding in the Evidence, offering to produce Witnesses to prove the Confession of several Voters, that they had Money given them for their Votes;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member objecting against such Evidence;

The Counsel withdrew upon that Point, Whether Evidence shall be given of such Confessions.

Resolved, That the Counsel be permitted to give Evidence of the Voters Confession of Bribery.

And the Counsel were called in again: And they proceeded with their Evidence: Which being gone through on the Petitioner's Side;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded with their Evidence.

And Mr. Clayton, the Mayor of Grimsby, being offered as a Witness on his Part; who being objected against by the Petitioner s Counsel, as being a Person, charged in the Petition, and proved to be concerned in paying Money to the Voters;

A Petition of divers Inhabitants of the Borough of Hertford, in the County of Hertford, in behalf of themselves, and several other Inhabitants of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Mayor of Hertford did, at the late Election of a Burgess to represent the said Borough, in the room of Tho. Fihner Esquire, deceased, permit several pretended Freemen, who were arbitrarily, and contrary to their Charter, made so in the First of the late King James the 2d, to poll at the said Election; by means whereof, although Wm. Monson Esquire had the Majority of legal Voters for him, he hath unduly returned Richard Goulston Esquire; in Prejudice to the Rights of the Petitioners; who complained to the Parliament held in the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, of the like Proceedings: But the then Mayor, and several of the Aldermen, promising to desist from those Practices for the future, the Petitioners prosecuted their Petition no further: Yet the now Mayor, and some of the said Aldermen, have again violated the Rights and Privileges of the said Borough: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, and Relief therein.

A PETITION of the Wool-combers, in and about Woollen Ma* the City of Peterborough, was presented to the nufacture. House, and read; setting forth, That great Numbers of Persons of all other Trades have intruded into the Petitioners said Trade, so that they cannot get a Livelihood, as they formerly used to do; many of such Intruders taking 14 or more Apprentices to work for them a Year or Two, and then they work as Journeymen, to the Ruin of such as have legally served Apprenticeships to the said Trade:

And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the said Trade of Wool-combing, under such Penalties as the House shull think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufactures.

A Petition of the Masters and Workmen of the Art Ditto, and Trade of Wool-combing within the City of London, and Bills of Mortality, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That divers Persons, for many Years last past, got a good Livelihood by the said Trade; but, of late, vast Numbers of unskilful Persons have intruded into the said Trade, made bad Goods, and then are forced to sell them at an under Rate; whereby they have impoverished themselves, many of them falling to their respective Parishes for a Maintenance; which Mischiefs, if not timely prevented by some Law, will be the Ruin of the Petitioners, and the said Trade: And praying.

That a Bill for regulating the said Trade may pass into a Law; whereby Multitudes of poor Families, within the Bills of Mortality, may receive Employment.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufactures.

A Petition of Robert Steyner Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Proprietors of the several Freehold Estates within the Borough of Droitwich, in the County of Worcester, have ever had a Right of electing Members to Parliament for the said Borough; the Ma jority of whom did, at the last Flection there, offer their Votes to the Petitioner; but the Bailiffs of the said Borough refused to take them, and have returned Philip Foley Esquire as a Burgess, to the Petitioner's great Wrong: And praying Relief therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the Twelve Governors, Assistants, and Guardians, for the better Relief of the Poor of the Town of Crediton, alias Kirton, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are many lewd and disorderly idle Persons in this Kingdom, and particularly in Crediton, who commit small Thefts, under 1 2d.Value, and other Misdemeanors, and on Examination, confess the same; and then they are committed to Bridewell, or the common Gaol, where they continue several Months; during which time their Families are wholly maintained by the Parish where they live; and commonly such Offenders return out of Gaol greater Thieves than before, the Parish fearing to prosecute them, because of bringing a further Charge upon themselves: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to impower Corporations, constituted by Acts of Parliament, to call before them such Persons as shall have committed small Thefts and Misdemeanors, and punish and keep them to Labour.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more speedy Punishment of certain Offences in Work-houses, or Houses of Correction, erected, or to be erected, by Act of Parliament, for the better Relief of the Poor: And that Mr. Hoblyn and Mr. Northmore do prepare, and bring in, the same.

A Petition of Joseph Bruxby was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the great Fall of the Revenue of Excise has chiefly been occasioned through the Want of Skill and Judgment of the late and present Commissioners for Management thereof, who know not how to instruct or contradict their inferior Officers in the

.....relating to the Brewing Trade; inso much that the King has been frequently cheated of the Exciseof 50 Bar- rels in 70 of Strong Drink, Three times a Week, in many Brew houses: That the Petitioner can demonstrate how the Excise may be improved at least 100,000l. per Annum, if not Two; which will be advantageous to the Government.

Resolved, That the Petition be rejected.

Whereas, in and by an Act of this present Parliament, made in the Third Year of the Reign of their present Majesties King William and Queen Mary, intituled, An Act for granting an Aid to their Majesties, of 1,651,702/.

18r. towards the carrying on a vigorous War against France, it is Provided and Enacted, That no Fees should be demanded or taken by any Officer of the Exchequer, or of any Officers thereof, for the Receiving or Issuing any of the Monies granted by the said Act, or any other Act of this presdht Parliament, for the Aids and Supplies to their Majesties, but such ancient and legal Fees, as shall be allowed by the Lord Chief Bdron, and Barons of the Coif of the Court of Exchequer, to be such, and not otherwise: And that the said Chief Baron, and other Barons, are thereby required to present a Table or Schedule of the said Fees to the Lords and Commons assembled in Parliament, at the next Sessions to be holden for this or the next succeeding Parliament.

In pursuance therefore of the said Act of Parliament, we have called before us the Officers of the Receipt of Exchequer, and received Informations of the Fees demanded or taken by the said Officers, for the Receiving and Issuing the aforesaid Monies; and upon Hearing of them, and Consideration of the whole Matter, w'e do allow the Fees mentioned in the Tables or Schedules hereuuto annexed, and no other, to be ancient legal Fees; and from henceforth to be demanded and taken, by the said Officers, for the receiving and issuing any of the Monies aforesaid: And we do present a Table or Schedule of the said Fees, so allowed, as aforesaid, to the Lords and Commons assembled in Parliament, according to the said Act of Parliament.

Tythe of A Petition of divers Ministers of the County of liad-ore. was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners residing on their Benefices in that Part of Derbyshire where there are Lead-mines, have a just Right to a Tythe of Lead-ore gotten in their respective Parishes; which Right hath been tried and adjudged in all the Courts of I-aw and Equity, and confessed by the Body of Miners upon Oath: And the Petitioners Predecessors did, for many Ages past, until very lately, receive Tythes of Lead-ore, or Composition for it; and divers Noblemen, Gentlemen, and Clergymen, the Petitioners Neighbours, having the same general Right, do all of them, at this Day, receive the like Tythes; notwithstanding which, and the many Records the Petitioners can produce of their said Right, the said Miners joining in one' common Purse, have, upon all Opportunities,..... to promote Multitudes of chargeable and vexatious Suits against the Proprietors of this Tythe, sometimes taking Occasion, from the Death, Change, or Poverty, of the Incumbent, to with-hold the same from the Successor, whose Predecessor, at great Expence, had recovered the same, and by creating as many Suits as there are Parishes, Places, or Proprietors; by which, and such-like vexatious Methods, the Petitioners are kept out of their just Rights, and are not able to follow so many chargeable vexatious Suits: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for preventing Multiplicity of vexatious Suits; and for settling and ascertaining the said customary Tythe, according to the Tenor, Equity, and Establishment of divers Decrees in Chancery, grounded on solemn Tryals at Common Law.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for preventing Multiplicity of vexatious Suits; and for settling and ascertaining the Tythes of Lead-ore in the County of Derby: And that the Lord Marquis of Sir John Cotton, and Mr. Dolben, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

of the Country, and Expedition of our Business, we did, on the 9th of December last, further publish, That we would from the 7th Day of January, bear and determine all Claims on the same Estate together; beginning with the private Estate: By which means we shall dispatch more Claims in less time; they depending much on the same Title, and frequently the same Deeds and Witnesses; And as we clear Estates, we may thereby put them into a Method of Sale: We have and do sit Tour Days every Wreek on hearing Claims; the Multiplicity of other Business being more than sufficient for the other Two Days: There has been posted already 1,133 Claims, about 800 whereof are heard and determined, many of which we found to contain several distinct Claims on different Titles and Estates: Those posted, and not heard, are postponed for want of Prosecution, or at the Claimant's Request: So that it will be impossible, with our utmost Industry and Application, to determine all the Claims within the Time limited.

13. Several of the Grantees of Debts have not complied with the Act, in paying the Monies by them received into the Exchequer, on or before the 24th Day of August; whereby they have forfeited double the Value.

14. Several other Grantees have neither paid the Rent-charges, or other Rents, issuing out of the Estates granted, nor the Interest of Mortgages, or other Securities, affecting the same, pursuant to the said Act, on or before the First of November; by which means, the Debts are increased to double the Money lent, and lie as an heavy Charge on the Lands, every Day giving fresh Instances of this kind: We therefore think it our Duty, humbly to lay this Matter before your Honours, for your Directions herein.

15. The Number of Discoveries already lodged amount to 600; but we are not able to make any Conjecture how valuable they are, not having lime to hear them till after the 25th of March.

16. We have made Inquiry into the Wastes committed on the forfeited Woods in this Kingdom; which we find very considerable: The Trespassers, that are able, we shall punish; but most of the Destruction has been by the ordinary People of the Country, who are unable to make Satisfaction, or so much as answrer the Expence of our Witnesses.

17. Great Arrears of Rent out of the forfeited Estates and Interests not granted, have incurred since the 13th of February 1688; and before the 2d of November 1699 > which are neither paid to his Majesty, nor are we intitled to demand them; and which will never be discovered, unless invested in us, with due Encouragement to such as shall discover and pay them.

18. We hope it will not be thought presuming, if we humbly represent toyour Honours some Instances, wherein, we conceive, we are not impowered to execute our Trust to the best Advantage of the Publick: By the present Provision of the Act, all Arrears of Rent due from the 2d of November, or which shall hereafter become due; all Penalties, Fines, and Forfeitures; all Debts due to forfeiting Persons; and all Bonds entered into for Security; are to be sued for in the Name of the King's Attorney General: We apprehend, many Debts of this kind may become due near the Expiration of our Commission, when there will not be time left us to recover them: Besides, we do humbly acquaint your Honours, That so many of the People of this Kingdom are so interested in the Forfeitures, that we have not hitherto thought it advisable to submit any thing to their Determination: We therefore do, with all Submission, lay it before your Honours, whether the Placing the last Result and Determination of these Matters in the Trust be not for the publick Service.

19. There is one other Part of the Act, which though 'jve apprehend may not want Explanation; yet because we find an Opinion industriously spread here, which may tend to the Discouragement of Purchasers, we think it our Duty to mention it to your Honours: The Construction put upon die Vesting Clause, FoL 8. is, That nothing

is vested in us, but what the forfeiting Person had; so that he that has any Demand to, or out of, any of the said forfeited or other Estates or Interests, expects to be at Liberty, w>hen our Commission is ended, to prosecute that Demand in the Courts here, though they have entered no Claim: Which Construction, we humbly conceive, may make the Claiming Clause of little Use: And, lest it should, in some Measure, frustrate the Ends of the Act, we lay it before your Honours; and submit it to your Consideration, how far the Validity of our Sales in general shall be left to be controverted any where, under any Pretence whatsoever.

20. We conceive also, that our not having Power, by the Act, to punish the Contrivers, Aiders, and Abettors, of false Claims, as well as the Claimants themselves, has been an Encouragement to Persons of Interest and Wealth, to procure Claims to be entered in the Names of insolvent People; whereby the Intention of the Act is defeated.

21. We do, further, humbly crave Leave to represent to your Honours, That if some Provision was made for enabling the Persons, having the Remainders, after the forfeited Estates for Lives, to mortgage their Interests, for the purchasing such Estates for Lives, they would become the best Purchasers; and that, in case such Persons, so in Remainder, were restrained from barring the forfeited Reversions vested in us, that the said Reversions would be more valuable than now they are; by reason of some Opinions prevailing here, that such Reversions may be barred by common Recoveries: And that if we had Power to accept and take Assignments, or Discharges of Incumbrances, claimed and allowed, as so much Monies for the Purchase of other Lands, most of the Persons having such Incumbrances would be the fairest Purchasers; which may increase the Number of Bidders, lessen the Burden of Interest, and expedite the Sales.

22. We were of Opinion, That the Quit and Crown Rents, issuing out of the forfeited and other Estates and Interests, vested in us, tvere, by Unity of Possession in his Majesty, extinguished; and that, in our Hands, they were not liable to such Rents, by the Words and plain Construction of the Act, that they shall be sold discharged of all Arrears: But the Commissioners of his Majesty's Revenue being advised, that the said Estates were chargeable with Quit and Crown Rents, during their Continuance in our Hands; we were willing, and did, for the Ease and Quiet of the Tenants, permit them to collect the said Rents in the usual Manner, and deposit them in the Exchequer: We do therefore most humbly represent this Matter to your Honours, for further Directions, whether these Rents shall be applied towards the Discharge of the publick Expence of this Kingdom, or go in Ease of the Subjects of England; and be applied, as Part of the Fund allotted by the said Act, to the Uses therein mentioned; such Rent amounting to about 5,000l. per Annum.

23. We think it incumbent on us to lay some few Cases before your Honours, as Objects of Compassion; and wherein the Provisions of the Act are, as we conceive, short of your Intentions.

24. The Lady Baroness Dowager of Upper-Ossory did claim the Benent of a Clause in the Act, for confirming a Grant from his Majesty, of a Maintenance to her, out of her late Husband's Estate, not exceeding 80 /. per Annum; And there being no Grant; but only a Letter from his Majesty, in order to a Grant; we humbly conceive, she is not so within the Letter of the Act, as to have an Allowance of her Claim: We have continued her in Possession, and chose rather to represent her Case, than disallow her Claim;

25. Captain James Rock is under the same Circumstance; only with this Difference, That, since the Act, his Grant is passed the Seals; and, as we humbly conceive, may want Confirmation.

26. The Grant of Francis de la Rue, made upon the most valueable Consideration, and intended to be 400l. per Annum, by reason of the Adjudication of some Persons within Articles, whose Estates were comprised in his

Grant,

Sir Rowland Gwyn, according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared, touching the Election for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of John Gape Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return 01 Joshua JLomax Esquire, to serve for the Borough of St. Albans:

That the First Question, between the Petitioner and Sitting Member, was, the Right of Election; the Petitioner insisting, That the Right of Election was in the Mayor, Aldermen, Freemen, and such Ilousholders only as paid Scotland Lot; the Sitting Member insisting, That'th© Right of Election was in the Mayor, Aldermen, Freemen, and all Housholders, whether they paid Scotland Lot, or no.

And thereupon the Committee proceeded to examine several Witnesses.

The First Witness examined to that Point was,

Mr. Edmund Aylworth, the Town Clerk: Who said, That ne had lived in St. Albans about Thirty Years, and had known the several Elections for Twenty Years: He said, He believed that those who did not pay Scotland Lot had, during that time, voted; but the Reason was, That they were so tumultuous, that there was no opposing them, and they had always been marked with a Quare: But the same had never been contested, because of the great. Majority of one Side: However, he acknowledged, That Freemen had a Right to vote, whether they paid Scotland Lot, or no.

That, to maintain the Right of the Housholders at large, several Witnesses were produced on behalf of the Sitting Member; viz.

John Tisdale: Who had known St. Albans above Fifty Years.

John Lee: Who had known St. Albans Forty Years.

John Howard: Who had known St. Albans Sixty Years, and had been at several Elections: Who testified, That not only those who did pay Scotland Lot, but those that received Alms, have all along, to their Knowledge, voted without any Exception: But Mr. Lee said, They had been excepted to.

That the Counsel for the Petitioner did not think fit to call any other Witnesses, as to the Matter of Fact; but insisted upon it, That, by the Law of the Land, and in reason, those that did not contribute to the Charge of the Borough ought not to elect Representatives in Parliament for the same.

Whereupon the Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, is in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Freemen, and such Housholders only as pay Scotland Lot.

That the Committee having come to this Resolution, the Sitting Member's Counsel yielded the Majority to be with the Petitioner; but insisted, That, by Bribes and Treats he had procured the Majority; and was thereby rendered unqualified to sit in the House: And thereupon, they called several Witnesses; viz.

John Beeson, Jos. Eaton, Nath. Tibbs, Tho. Chandler;

Vol. 13.

The Substance of whose Evidence was, That Beeson, Eaton, and Tibbs were at Chandlers House the Monday before the Election, the Election being on Wednesday then following, and there were Mr. Thomas Gape, the Petitioner s Brother, and John Bernard, who desired their Votes for the Petitioner: That Beeson had fis. given him by Mr. Tho. Gape: That Eaton, on condition he would vote for the Petitioner, was promised, That my Lord should give him what he should desire in Reason: That Tibbs had Two Sixpences of Mr. Gape: That they staid at Chandlers till next Morning; and that Mr. Gape and Mr. Bernard paid the Reckoning, which came to Eight or Nine Shillings: However, they voted for Mr. Lomax: At the same time Chandler acknowledged, That, about a Week before the Election, he had drawn Drink to the Value of Forty Shillings, at tw:ice, for Mr. Tho. Lomax, the Sitting Member's Brother, w ho was a Candidate at the said Election: That he did not know, That Mr. Tho. I.o-max made an Interest for his Brother; but said, That Bee-son, Eaton, and Tibbs, and others, drank of it; of whom some voted for one Party, and some for another.

Mary Bouton, Thomas Lee, testified, That Mr. Foiher-gill, Mr. Gapes Nephew, made an Interest for Mr. Gape; and that Mr. Fothergi/l told the said Mary Bouton, That, if her Husband would vote for Mr. Gape, he would deliver up an old Lease of a House which her Husbahds Father bad bought of one Pooley: However, her Husband voted for both the Lomax's.

Thomas Someifield said, That, the Night before the Election, Mr. Gape's Nephew, Mr. Marson, came to his House, and asked him, Who he was for ? That he answered, He was for Mr. Lomax; but the said Marson replied, He had better poll for his Uncle, and then demanded a Guinea for a Gun, that the said Somerfield had of Mr. Marson's: But withal, told him, That if he would not poll at all, he, the said Marson, would have nothing for it: That accordingly he did not poll; and he met Mr. Marson afterwards; who told him, he was very well satisfied.

Mary Springatts&\d, Mr. Fothergi/l came to her House and told her, if her Husband would vote for Mr. Gape, her Husband should have as great a Share of Gawens Charity as any: And accordingly, he did vote for Mr. Joshua J*omax and Mr. Gape, but had not voted for Mr. Gape but for that Promise: She acknow ledged her Husband had received nothing, and did not pay Scotland Lot.

Jos. I*acker said, That Mr. Fothergill spake to him to be for Mr. Gape; and that he received 10 s. Charity Money given to the Town; which he did, as he guessed, receive upon the Account of his Vote: That he did vote for Mr. Gape and Mr. Lomax; but he acknowledged, That he did not pay Scotland Lot, nor was free of St. Albans.

Anne Harrop said, That she was, about a Week before the Election, with Mr. Gape, for some Part of the Charity Money: That Mr. Gapes Son told her, there was some left in the Mayors Hands; and asked her Husband's Vote for Mr. Gape; to which she replied, she did not know but hefr Husband might vote for him: And thereupon, he went and told his Father, who sent her Half a Crown by his Son; and afterwards, he sent his Son to her not to speak of it; for there was no more left: And the said Harrop said, That one Townsend: s Wile had it at the same time: And Townsend's Wife, being called in, confirmed the same: But it appeared, That Harrops Husband was admitted to live in the Parish by Certificate; and that Townsend did not pay Scotland Lot.

Henry Beech said, That he went to Richard Martin; and told him he would vote for Mr. Gape, if he could

pick

Limitation and Succession of the Crown.

pick up 20 and Martin said, His Business should be done: And that old Mr. Gape asked his Voice for his Son; and said, If he would give his Son a Voice, he should have Part of the Charity Money: And, accordingly he ordered him 10 s. which he received of the said Martin; and afterwards told him, That Mr. Lomax could do him no Kindness, but we can: But he acknowledged he did not pay to Scotland Lot.

)Vm. Butler was examined: Who said little more, than that the Earl of Marlborough was present at the Election; but he did not observe, that he meddled in it.

For the Petitioner, it was insisted, That there was very irregular and indirect Practices, on the other Side: And called,

Mr. John Fothergill, a Clergyman: Who said, That the Mob were so rude, they were ready to pull off his Gown, and insulted him in the Streets, when he went to speak on the behalf of Mr. Gape: That Mr. Gapes Friends, upon the Scrutiny, proved Twelve who voted for Mr. Lomax to have no Right; but the Mayor said, Those Things ought to be tried above: That the Mob threatened the Mayor in case he returned Mr. Gape; and put up these Verses on his House:

" If you return Lomax, we'll be still as a Mouse:

" If you return Gape, then down comes your House.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Joshua Lomax Esquire is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Gape Esquire is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of St. Albans.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Declared, That the said Election for the said Borough of St. Albans is a void Election.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County of Hertford, in the room of Joshua Lomax Esquire, whose Election is declared to be void.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of that Part of his Majesty's Speech, which relates to the Succession.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Conyers took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Conyers reported from the said Committee, That they had made a further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

Memorandum: The several Years Accounts above-mentioned, to the 30th of June 1697, have been annually made up, examined, and passed, by the Office of the Ordnance; and the same, with the proper Vouchers, all delivered up to the Auditors; and the said Accounts declared by the Lords of the Treasury; and the Accountant's Quietus had thereupon for his Discharge, without any Privy Seal obtained to supply the Wants of due and regular Vouchers, as may be certified by the Auditors.

The Two other Accounts, for the Years ending the 30th of June 1698, and the 30th of Junfe 1699, are made up, and lie before the Board of Ordnance for their Examination; and to be sent to the Auditorsj with the Vouchers thereunto belonging, to be by them examined, in order for a Quietus to be had for the full Discharge of this Acountant.

Charles Bertie.

A Petition of Cixarks Goreing Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and Sir Robert Fagg, stood Candidates at the late Election of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Steyning, in the County of Sussex, in the room of Sir John Fagg, deceased.: That the said Sir Robert, by Bribery, and many illegal Practices, did endeavour to get a Majority of Voices for him; but the Petitioner had the Majority of legal Votes for him, and he ought to have been returned; yet the Constable of the said Borough, being.threatened and over-awed by the said Sir Robert Fagg, hath returned him, in Prejudice to the Petitioner: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.
