That the Committee having taken the Ekamination of several Persons, the same is as followeth*:

Mr. Thomas Waller, attending, according to Order, produced a Letter, dated the 17th of December 1700, from one William Clifton, his Uncle; wherein, amongst other Things, is written;

" I have a Person that is suitable fora Member to serve " for your Town of Bramber: I will fling away 100l. or <c such a Thing, unknown to him: If you can be his " Friend, I can fling 200l. into the River of Bramber

Mr. Waller said, He never answered the said Letter; nor ever asked Clif ton who the Person was he had recommended; he looking upon him to be a dangerous Man.

That Clifton was present and busy about the Election, and told him he took it unkindly he had never answered his Letter.

That the said Clifton being summoned to attend the Committee, the Serjeant's Messenger, who went to serve him with the Order, acquainted the Committee, That Mr, C/ftons Landlady told him, That Mr. Clifton had left his Lodgings the Friday before; and that she had heard since, that he wras gone into Scotland.

Mr. Harvey said, That he, being at Bramber at the Election, was in Mr. Clifton's Company there; and that Clifton shewed him a Letter, which he said he had received from Mr. Millman, by the Hands of one Mr. Alexander Cutting; which said Cutting was directed, by the said Letter, to apply himself to Clifton for to/.; and Clift oh w as to place it to the Account of Mr. Shepherd.

Mr. Cutting said, That he did receive a Letter from Mr. Millman, the Week after Christmas last, to carry to Mr. Clifton; and that he was to apply himself to Clfton for. 10/. for which Sum he had given Mr. Millman a Note, when in Town; and believes the Money was to be placed upon Mr. Shepherd's Account* had it been paid; but Clfton pretending he had not Money, the said Cutting brought back the Letter to Mr. Millman, and had his Note delivered to him again:

That Clifton told him, That Mr. Millman was to have 100l. for his Interest in the said Election.

Mr. William Millman, attending the Committee, said,

He did write a Letter to Mr. Clfton at Bramber, and sent it by Mr. Cutting, who was to have received 10/. of Clfton, Cutting having given him a Note for so much here; but that there was no Direction to place the same to the Account of Mr. Shepherd.

And, being asked to pfoduce the said Letter, he said,

That one Mr. Perris, of the Sik Clerks Office, advised him to bum the same; which he did do about the beginning of last Week, because there was an Indorsement thereupon, which, he believes, was w ritten by Clifton, and

signed

Martii.

Charges of Bribery at Bramber Election.

400

signed S. S.; which Indorsement he thought would have done Mr. Shepherd a Prejudice; but that he had kept a Copy of the Letter without the Indorsement; and produced a Paper, which he said imported such Letter.

But the said Mr. Harvey confronting him, said, That Letter was not a true Copy of the Letter he saw Clif ton had from Cutting, because the Direction of placing the i 0/. to the Account of Mr. Shepherd was omitted.

Mr. Millman, upon his further Examination, said, That, upon the 27th Day of December last, Mr. Martin, a Member of this House, came to him, and desired him to go with him to a Coffee-house; which he did: And in a private Room up Stairs in the Coffee-house, was Mr. Samuel Shepherd; which Mr. Shepherd, applying himself to Mr. Millman, told him, He knew the great Interest he had at Bramber; and therefore desired he would recommend a Gentleman he should propose to him; but refused then to name him, but desired the Recommendation might be by Letter, and that he would leave a Blank for the Name therein; which he did do: And Mr. Shepherd afterwards told him, the Gentleman he had his Recommendation for, was one Mr. Paschall, and his Name was put into the Blank of the Letter which was sent to Mr. Clifton:

That Mr. Shepherd told him, he had hired the said Cutting a Coach to go down to Bramber about the said Election, and had put 20 Guineas into his Pocket:

But that Clifton having written to Dolby Thomas, who communicated the same to Mr. Shepherd, That he found there was Money to be spent, and that it would cost 2 or 300l. more; Mr. Shepherd said, That as he had given Clifton Money already, he would not send him any more, nor go on any further in the Election.

Mr. Millman said further, That he having an Account from Cutting of the said Election, who told him, That Mr. Asgill had not fair Play; and that the Town would petition the House against the said Election; and that he had gotten a Petition drawn;

Upon which Mr. Shepherd came to Mr. Millman, and desired he would put a Stop to the Petition, because, he said, it would make a Clamour; and that Mr. Millman did stop the same accordingly:

That, upon Saturday the 1st of March, at Night, he was sent for to meet Mr. Shepherd at the Blue Posts; where was Mr, Shepherd, his Two Sons, Mr. Martin, Dalby Thomas, and one Mr. Lawton; which Mr. Lawton proposed a Method of Interrogation and Answ ers, upon a Supposition there should be an Examination of the said Letter; and told him, That he might say. That as he was sitting in a Coffee-house, a Gentleman came to him, a Stranger, and told him, He had heard of what Interest he had at Bramber; and therefore desired he would give him such Letter of Recommendation:

To which Mr. Millman making Answer, That Mr. Clifton would be able to contradict such Proposition;

He was told, Clifton could not come in; for he was gone upon a Commission into Yorkshire:

And Mr. Shepherd several times desired him not to mention his Name upon any Examination; and that, if he would stand Buff, they could make nothing of the said Letter:

That when he told them, He must speak the Truth, if he was examined, they upbraided him with being fearful and timorous:

That they had several Meetings upon Mr. Shepherd's Desire; and was to prevail upon Mr. Millman not to take Notice of Mr. Shepherd's Name upon any Examination: That, upon Mr. Millmaris applying himself to Mr. Dodd for Advice in the Premises, in case of an Examination, Mr. Dodd advised him to tell the whole Truth.

That, upon the Examination of other Letters, produced to the said Committee, there appeared to be one from the said Mr. Cutting to Mr. Millman, dated the 2d January 1700; whereby, among the rest that stood for Candidates, he writes, " And your Friend, which is not here;'* and

A. iqoo.

further writes, " Here is Money brought down, and, I " believe, delivered amongst your Tenants."

And Mr. Cutting, who wrote the Letter, being asked to explain the said Letter; he said, He believed the Contents to be true, because those Tenants refused to vote for Mr. Stringer, but did so for Mr. Owen, who was a perfect Stranger to the Borough; which occasioned his Supposition of their being bribed.

That, by another Letter from the said Cutting to Mr. Millman, dated January the 4th, Twelve a Clock at Night, 1700 $ wherein is written, " I have Two Votes " promised, which is their own Houses: I have promised c< them 10/. apiece to mend their Houses: It has cost me " 13/. already: I hope you have returned me Money:

" It is too late to send a Messenger on purpose."

Mr. Cutting said, The Meaning of that Letter was, that Mr. Millman told him, That, if he sent a Messenger, he would return him 100l. to repair the Tenants Houses; and that was no Bribery; but that Money was not sent, because Mr. Millmaris Interest miscarried.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That there hath been many indirect and corrupt Practices, in order to procure an Election at the said Borough of Bramber.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That there hath been Endeavours and tampering with Witnesses, in relation to the Evidence to be given, concerning the corrupting the Electors for the said Borough of Bramber.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person whatsoever, that is not a Native of England, Scotland, or Ireland, or of the Dominions thereunto belonging; or who is not born of English Parents beyond the Seas; although such Person be naturalized, or made Denizen; shall be capable to be of the Pnvy Council, or a Member of either House of Parliament, or to enjoy any Office or Place of Trust, either Civil or Military.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person whatsoever, that is not a Native of England, Scotland, or Ireland, or of the Dominions thereunto belonging; or who is not born of English Parents beyond the Seas; although such Person be naturalized, or made Denizen; shall be capable of any Grant of Lands, Tenements; or Hereditaments, from the Crown, to himself, or any other in Trust for him.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, upon the further Limitation of the Crown, in case the same shall hereafter come to any Person not being a Native of this Kingdom of England, this Nation be not obliged to engage in any War for the Defence of any Dominions or Territories not belonging to the Crown of England, without the Consent of Parliament.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committefe, That whosoever shall hefeaftgr Come to the Possession of this Crown, shall join in Communion with the Church of England, as by Law established.

6. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That ho Pardon be pleadable to an Impeachment in Parliament.

7. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Person who shall hereafter come to the Possession of this Crown, shall go out of the Dominions of England, Scotland, or Ireland, without Consent of Parliament.

Sir Rowland Gwyn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, upon the Double Return for the Borough of Banbury, in the County of Oxon; and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee have inspected and examined the Matter of the Double Return for Banbury.

That, upon Inspection of the Record, they find, That Charles North Esquire is returned by one Indenture; and that John Dormer Esquire is returned by another Indenture.

That, in Banbury, at present, and at the time of the Election, and for about Two Years last past, there have been Two contending Mayors; and which of them Two was the proper Officer to make the Return, was the Question before the Committee.

That this Fact was agreed on by both Parties, That Mr. Thorp was Mayor of Banbury, and died before his Year was up; viz. the 25th of February 1698; but the* Question in Dispute was, which was his lawful Successor.

That the Corporation, by Charter, consists of Twelve Aldermen, Six Capital Burgesses, and Thirty Assistants; and the Mayor is to be chosen out of the Aldermen; that is-to say, upon the annual Choice of a Mayor, the Alder-imu, Capital Burgesses, and Assistants, have a Right to

vote; but if a Mayor die within a Year, then his Successor tpr the remaining Part of the Year is to be chosen by the Aldermen and Burgesses only.

That Mr. North's Return Being affixed next to the Writ, his Counsel first began to maintain his Return, which was by John West senior; whose Succession to Thorp they derived thus: That, after the Death of Mr. Thorp, one Welshman was chosen Mayor for the succeeding Part of the Year; to him succeeded John West junior; and to John West junior succeeded John West, senior; who made the Return of Mr. North.

That to make out Mr. West senior s Title of Mayor, the Counsel for Mr. North first proceeded to make out who had the Right of electing the Mayor of Banbury: And, for that, they produced their Charter of Confirmation, 6* Jacobi y which says, That the Mayor, Aldermen, Capital Burgesses, Chamberlain, and Assistants of the Borough of Banbury, sive major pars eofum, de tempore in tempus, in perpetuum, perpetuis futuris temporibus, authoritatem et potestatem habeant, et habebunt, atinu-atim, et quolibet anno, in die Lunoe, qui primo et proxime evenerit, accident, et contigerit, in mense Septembris, eli-gendi et nominandi, et quod eligere et nominare possint et valeant unum de alderamannis burgi pnedicti fore et esse majorem burgi pnedicti, to continue from Michaelmas Day following for One whole Year; and that the Mayor, so elected, before he be admitted to execute his Office, sacramentum corporate coram ultimo majore proedecessore suo, seu ejus deputato, aut seniore alder-inanno, et cseteris aldermannis, et capitallibus burgensi-bus burgi praedicti, vel tot eorum, qui adtunc interesse voluerint, in et supra quodlibet festum sancti Michaelis Arehangeli, proximum post electionem et nominationem suam, pvaestabit: And the Charter further provides, That if the Mayor shall die within a Year, or, for just Cause, be removed, Quod tunc et toties bene liceat £t licebit resi-duis de aldermannis burgi praedicti, et capitalibus bur-gensibus burgi pracdicti, adtunc superviventibus vel re-manentibus, pro tempore existentibus, vel majore parte eorundem, unum alium de aldermannis pnedicti burgi in locum et officium ipsius majoris burgi praedicti sic mori, vel amoveri, contigentis, eligere et preeficere, secundum ordinationem et provisionem in his pnesentibus^dedaratas:

i3 W. III.

13° Ma

et quod ille sic electuS et praefectus in officio iftajoris burgi praedicti, officium illud habeat et exerceat, durante residuo ejusdem anni, sacramentum coporale in forma prasdicta prius prasstante; et, si nullum deputatum fecerit tunc succedat in ejus locum, officium, et authoritatem, senior aldermannus dicti burgi, pro tempore domi existens* ad faciendum et exequendum omnia et singula, quae dictus major, si prassens fuerit, exequeretur aut faceret The Charter also grants, That the said Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, shall for ever have and hold a Court of Record, in every Week throughout the Year, coram majore burgi praedicti, vel ejussufficiente deputato, ac uno also aldermanno burgi praedicti, necnon recordatore ejusdem burgi pro tempore existente, vel ejus sufficients deputato, et duobus capitalibus burgensibus burgi praedicti, vel aliquibus tribus eorum, quorum major, vel ejus deputatus pro tempore existens, unum esse volumus.

That the Counsel for Mr. North also produced a Copy of By-laws, made, amongst other Things, for the regulating the Elections of Mayors; by which By-laws it is provided, That, at the Choice of every Mayor, the Mayor for the Time being, or his Deputy, or senior Alderman, shall call unto him the next senior Alderman, and junior Alderman, and senior and junior Burgess, who shall separate themselves from the rest of the Company, and go into the little Chamber, and, by most of their Voices, shall agree upon One of the Aldermen to stand to succeed to be Mayor for the Year following; which Alderman, so agreed upon, shall depart into the minor Chamber, and there remain till he be called; Whereupon the Mayor for the Time being, and all the Aldermen and Burgesses, Chamberlain, and Assistants, shall proceed by Voices ta the allowing, or disallowing, the said Choice, in manner following; viz. Every one of the said Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, Chamberlain, and Assistants present, shall openly give his Voice to the said Choice affirmatively, dr negatively, to be taken by the Chamberlain, or Town Clerk; and if the more Part of the said Assembly shall dislike erf the said Alderman proposed, then the Mayor, Two Aldermen, and Two Burgesses shall, proceed to the Naming of some other Alderman, who shall be tried in like manner; and so* continuing the same Course, until; One shall be agreed upon to be one of the Aldermen to stand in Election to be Mayor of the said Borough for One whole Year, from the Feast of St. Michael the Archangel then next following; which being done, the like Course shall be taken for the Naming of One other Alderman, One of which shall be elected Mayor for the Year following, as aforesaid: And then the Mayor, Alder-iften, Burgesses, Chamberlain, and Assistants present, shall openly give their Voices which of the Two shall be Mayor for the Year following, according to the Letters Patents, upon the Penalty of forfeiting 20.?.

That the Right of electing Mayor being thus made Cut by the Charter, and By-laws; Mr. North's Counsel proceeded to the making out of the Fact; That Mr. John West was, at the time of the Return, rightful Mayor: And, for that, they called,

Mr. Philip Styles senior, the Town-Clerk: Who testified, That Mr*. Thorpe died on Saturday the 25th of February was Two Years; and that the eldest Alderman, upon the Death of a Mayor, has Power to act; who summoned the Aldermen and Burgesses to meet together the same Day; and about Ten of them did meet; amongst others, Mr. Reynolds, who was for going to an Election that Night; but at last it was agreed to meet next Night, at Five a Clock; and it was then ordered, That all who had a Right to elect, should be summoned to attend; and accordingly Eight of them met at the eldest Alderman's, Mr. Richard JVheatlys, in Gowns; and then they went to the Tow n Hall, and rung the Bell, to give Notice: That some were out of the Way, and some would not come: That after they had stayed some time, they went to an Election, and had Five Nominators, according to the By-laws, and did elect Mr. Welshman for the remaining Part of the Year, who was sworn by the senior Alderman: That Eight voted for Mr. Welshman, and Nine kept aw ay; But, however, he conceived the , Vol.13*

major Part appearing to have Power to elect; and, upon Banbury Search in the Books, had found 16 or 17 Instances of a Election. Mayor elected without the Majority of all that had a Right to elect: That, the first Monday in the Month of September following, they sent the like Summons, and elected and swore JohwWe&t junior; arid; the First Monday in last September, they did, in like mannery elect and swear John Wtst senior; who returned Mr. North: And that the Ensigns belonging to the Office of Mayor have; ever since Mr. Thorp's Death, been in their Possession successively.

Mr. Styles senior further said, That after the Aldermen and Burgesses are summoned, and meet,* to electa Mayor, he never knew them depart without masking an Election; and the Reason they proceeded to elect Mr. Welshman on the Sunday following the Death of Mr.

Thorp, was, because a Court was to be held next Day, which ought to held by the Mayor; and though theseniov Alderman does act in Court as Deputy Mayor, he never knew him act upon the Death of a Mayor*

Thomas We/jord, Serjeant at Mace, said, That the same Day that Mr. Thorp died, there were Ten. or Eleven met at his House; and some of them proposed to go ta an Election immediately, but some of the Seniors thought it would be better next Day, but agreed it must be then, because of the Court; and that was to be held on Monday; and accordingly, some of them said, They would take Notice of it: However, he went to every one of their Borises afterwards, and summoned them as at all other times; and in like manner summoned them upon the Choice of Mr. West junior, and Mr. West senior.

That the Counsel for Mr. Dormer insisted, That where there is a Corporation aggregate, every Act of the Corporation that is obliging, must be done, not only by the major Part present, but by the major Part of the Whole; and instanced in the Case of Dean and Chapters; and that the By-laws could not alter the Manner of Election appointed by Charter, which says, shall be by the Ma<* jority of the Corporation; and that Mr. Reynolds and Mr.

Samuel West were elected by such a Majority; and that it was not pretended, that the Mayors, under which Mr.

North's Return was made, had such a Majority: They farther insisted, That the senior and junior Alderman and Burgess was always understood of such as appeared: That the Matter of Welshman's Election was heard before the Council; and another Election directed by them, and called

Mr. Styles junior, who acted as Town Clerk under Mayor Sam. West, and Mr. Clark: Who said, after Mr.

Thorp's Death, Mr. Reynolds was elected for the remaining Part of the Year; Nine appearing at that Election; and he was sworn before the Recorder, and other Aldermen: And that, the First Monday in September following, Mr. Samuel West was elected Mayor by 26 present; and, last September, the said Mr. West was again continued Mayor, by the Votes of 11 Aldermen and Burgesses, and 18 Assistants; but the senior Alderman was not present; and that Mr. Sam. West had also his Officers, arid kept Courts; and had the Books of the Corporation, and the Seal of the Corporation: And Mr. Styles said further,

That, upon the Choice of a Mayor to succeed another dying within the Year, he never knew them make use of Nominators.

John Stokes said, That he had known several Elections, at which the senior Alderman has not appeared, and the next senior Alderman has acted.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution following; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Charles North Esquire is duly returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Danbury, in the County of Oxon*

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into further Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom it was referred to examine into the Matter of a Letter that was written down to Bramber, to corrupt the said Borough, in the last Election of Members there.

And Mr. Stringer acquainted the House, That, since the Report made, there was come to his Hands the Original of a Letter, a Copy whereof is mentioned in the Report; and he delivered. the same in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To Mr. Thomas Waller, at Bramber near Steyning, in Sussex.

Mr* Waller,

I writ to you last Night, to desire you and the Tenants not to oppose Mr- Asgill, if he stands; but I likewise desire my Tenants would give me their Votes for the other Representative: I understand the Houses are much out of Repair, and I have desired the Bearer to view them, in order to make them tenantable, to the liking of the Tenants. As to the approaching Election; if you find that Mr. Asgill is not like to prevail; then I desire you will promote my Interest, and the Interest of my Friend, who Mr. Clifton shall name unto you, being John Paschall Esquire, so that he and myself may be chosen; wishing you, and all my Tenants a happy Christmas, and merry New Year, and expecting to hear from you: And am Your Friend at Command,

Inner Temple, Wm. Milman.

27 December 1700.

A PETITION of the Masters add Workmen of the Woollen^ Art and Trade of Wool-combing, of the Borough tiufccuira. of Leicester, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, for many Years past, got a good Livelihood for themselves and Families, by their said Trade; which, of late, is very much prejudiced, by ignorant Persons falling into this Trade, who make iU-wrought Goods, and are constrained to put them off at under Prices; which Mischiefs, if not timely regulated by some good Act, will shortly ruin the said Trade: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Law* in being, relating to the Woollen Manufactures.

A Petition of the Masters and Journeymen of the Ditto. Mystery, Art, or Occupation, of Wool-combing, of the Town and Borough of Cirencester, in the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That many Thousands of Persons have been well maintained by the said Employment, which is much fallen to Decay of late, by reason that many wtyo were never bred up in the said Trade, it not being within the Statute, intermeddle therein, upon Pretence of setting the Poor on Work; though it is only to put off their own Commodities to them at their own Prices, instead of Money, to the Ruin of the said Trade, and the poor People so employed: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, that none may use the Trade of Wool-combing, but such as have served Seven Years Apprenticeship to the same; or that their Grievances may be otherwise redressed, as the House shall think meet Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufactures.

A Petition of the- Merchants, Clothiers, and others, Traders in the Woollen Manufacture, in and about the Town of JValce/ield in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Exportation of Wool is of very bad consequence

to all Dealers in the Woollen Manufactures; for the Preventing whereof, Commissioners were appointed by an Act of Parliament, made in the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, to put the Laws in Execution against the Exportation of Wool; who took upon them the said Trust, and deputed several Officers in several Parts of the Kingdom, who were very diligent in their Places, and hindered the Exportation of Wool, in great measure; but, by reason there was no Provision made, by the said Act, to recompense the Commissioners for their Pains and Charges, which wfere very great, they are discouraged and disabled from proceeding in the said Service: And praying, That, for the better Encouragement of the said Commissioners, and their Officers, some Provision may be made for them, in such manner as shall be thought fit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

The said Copies were read by the Clefk; and are act follow; viz.

The Copy of Proposals made to the French Ambassador, by Mr. Stanhope.

.. Translation.

Whereas his Majesty the King of Grectt Britain, and the Lords the States tleneral of the United Provinces, concluded, on the 25th of the Mohth March, of the last Year 1706, a Treaty of Partition with his most Christian Majesty, for preventing Troubles and a hew War, which there was great Reason t6 apprehend, upon the Death of the King of Spaine without Issue; and that, amongst other Things, the thief Prospect of the high Contractors in this Affair was, to preserve the Peace and general Tranquillity of Europe, and ‘to establish the particular. Security of his Majesty's Kingdoms; it is manifest, That although his most Christian Majesty haS thought fit to accept the Will of the late King of Spaine, departing from the Partition: yet his Majesty of Great Britain ought not to lose the Effect of that Treaty; but should obtain, at least, the Intention of the Treaty; to wit, the Peace, and general Tranquillity, and his particular Security, by some Equivalent, or other Means: And, to this End, Mr. Stanhope, the King of Great Britain's Envoy Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the said Stated General, is ordered to propose to the Count D'Avaux, his most Christian Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, the following Points and Articles:

That, to preserve the Peace, and general Tranquillity, ppoti which a great Part of the particular Security of the King of Great Britain's Dominions depends, his Imperial Majesty shall be invited to enter into this Negotiation; and, that he be contented, and have reasonable Satisfaction given him, for his Pretensions to the Succession of Spaine; which were regulated by the Treaty of Partition: And that his Imperial Majesty shall be admitted and included in the Treaty, which the King of Great Britain, and the States General, shall make with the most Christian King, and the Crown of Spaine:

That his most Christian Majesty, within a certain time limited, and that as short as possible can be agreed on, shall withdraw all Troops from the Spanish Netherlands, without leaving any of them there; and that it shall not be lawful for him ever to send them thither again; but that, for the future, there shall be kept in the said Sixmkh Netherlands, except in the Places of Surety, which shall be mentioned in the following Article, only Spanish and Walloon Troops, or of the Countries in Subjection to the Spanish Monarchy, exclusive of all others, under the Oath, and in the Pay of Spaine; and not any Troops of his most Christian Majesty, directly or indirectly: Provided nevertheless, That it shall and may be lawful for the King of Great Britain, and the Lords the States General, to send some of their Troops for the Defence of the said Netherlands, when they shall be thereto required:

That, for the particular Security of the Dominions of the King of Great Britain, the Towns of Ostend and Newport shall be yielded up, and entrusted to his Majesty s sole Custody, together with their Ports, Castles, and Citadels, and all the Forts and Works of the Fortifications thereto belonging, all in the Condition they now are; with Power to put in, and keep there, such Garisons, either of his own Troops, or those of his Allies, whom his Majesty should require for that Purpose, and as he shall find convenient; And that it shall not be lawful for France or Spaine to put the least Garison therein; or to raise behind, or round about, the said Towns, Ports, and Fortresses, any other Forts, Lines, or Works of Fortification; or to do any thing whatsoever, that may VojL. 13.

farm. 4*1

occasion any Prejudice to the Guard of the said Towns Papers and Fortresses, and hinder the Effect thereof: , respecting

That it shall be in the Power of the Kino; of Great Britain to augment, lessen, and change the Garisons of the said Tow ns and Fortresses, as often as he shall think fit; and to send thither Victuals, Ammunition, Arms, Materials for Fortifications, and generally whate ver shall he thought fit and necessary for the Service of the Garisons and Fortifications, without being hindered in the least, either by Sea or Land, directly or indirectly:

That the King of Great Britain shall have the full Command and Authority over the said Towns, Ports,

Castles, and Fortresses; where he shall have Garisons and Commanders, such as he shall think fit, saving, and without Prejudice to, the Rights and Revenues of Jhfc Crown of Spaine over and in the said Tow ns: ,

That, moreover, it shall be lawful for the King of Great Britain to fortify, and repair the Fortifications of, the said Towms, Ports, and Fortresses, as he shall judge fitting; and, generally, to do every thing which he shall find necessary for their Defence:

That no Kingdoms, Provinces, Towns, Territories, or Places belonging to the Crown of Spaine, as well within as without Europe, ' and, especially, no Towns,

Places, or Lands of the Spanish Netherlands, shall be yielded or transferred; neither shall they devolve or come to the Crown of France, by Gift, Purchase, Exchange,

Contract of Marriage, Succession by Will, or abintestato, or by any other Title whatsoever; and that they shall not any w*ay be subjected to the Power, or be under the Authority, of the most Christian King:

That in the States and Kingdoms of the Spanish Monarchy, as well within as without Europe, and consequently in the Spanish Netherlands also, the Subjects of the King of Great Britain shall remain in the Enjoyment of all the Privileges, Rights, Freedoms, and other Advantages, as well in respect of their Navigation, Commerce, and free Use of Ports, as in any other Thing which they have, or ought to have enjoyed, till the Death of the late King of Spaine; so that every Thing whatsoever, except what shall be otherwise agreed on by the Treaty to be made, shall be left in the Condition it was, at the Time of the late King of Spain's Death:

That all the Treaties of Peace and Commerce, and other Conventions between England and Spaine, shall be ' renewed, or taken to be renewed, in such manner as shall be agreed on, so far forth, as they shall not be altered by the Treaty that shall be made:

Further, That the Subjects of the King of Great Britain shall enjoy, in all the Kingdoms, Dominions, Towns,

Places, Bays, and Harbours, of the Crown of Spaine, within and without Europe, the same Privileges, Rights, and Franchises, as also all the Immunities and Advantages, w'hich the Subjects of the most Christian King, or any other Princes or Potentates, do enjoy; as well as those that shall be granted them, and which they shall enjoy for the future:

That, on the Part of France and Spaine, a solemn Promise shall be made, of the strict Observation of all these Points in general, and of every one of them in particular:

That that Treaty which shall be made on that Subject, shall have the Guaranty of such Kings, Princes, and Potentates, as either of the high Contractors shall desire; and that in the firmest manner that they can invent, and agree on:

All this with a Reservation to amplify those Points in the Negotiation, as far as shall be thought necessary for the Explanation of the true Sense and Intention thereof; as also to prevent all manner of Dispute.

' The Report of the Heer Van Essen, and other the States General, deputies for the Foreign Affairs, was read:

4 Whereupon, and according to their Resolution of the . 1 ith instant, importing a Commission, they have weighed and deliberated, how, and in what manner, they should , proceed in the Negotiation, which they were to enter upon with Count D'Avau.v, the French King's Ambassador Extraordinary, concerning the general Peace, and the Safety of their State: And, after due Consideration,

it was resolved, That, in Concert with Mr. Slanhope, his Majesty of Great Britain's Envoy Extraordinary, the following Points should be proposed, in a Conference, to the said Count D'Avauv:

Whereas the King of Great Britain, and the States General of the United Provinces, have concluded a Treaty of Partition with the French King, on the 25th of March 1700, in order to prevent Troubles and Disturbances which might arise about the Succession of the late King of Spaine, in case he should die without Children; and that therein, amongst other Things, the chief Aim of the Parties concerned was, the Preservation of the general Quiet and Peace of Europe, and the particular Safety of this State: Wherefore it is evident, That the French King, by accepting the Will of the King of Spaine, as contrary to the aforesaid Treaty, cannot deny the States General the Effect of the aforesaid Treaty; but that, at least, by some Equivalent, or other Means, he ought to make good what they proposed to themselves tby the said Treaty; viz. the aforesaid general Quiet and Peace, and particularly the Safety of this State: And therefore the States General do require, That, in order to establish the general Quiet and Peace, in which consists chiefly their Safety, the Emperor ought to have reasonable Satisfaction and Content given him, in his Pretensions about the Succession of Spaine, which were regulated in the aforesaid Treaty of Partition; and that he may be admitted and included in the Treaty which England and Holland is to make with France and Spaine; and consequently to be invited to this Negotiation:

% That the King of France shall, within such time as shall be agreed on, draw his Troops out of the Spanish Netherlands, and not to leave any of them there, or send any thither at any time hereafter; but that, for the future, there shall be in the said Spanish Netherlands, except such Places named for Security in the following Articles, no other Troops, but what are either Spaniards, Walloons, or of the Low Countries, being under Command of the King of Spaine, and belonging only to him, and having taken an Oath to him, and being in his Pay; and no French, either directly or indirectly; but if the King of Spaine shall desire any Troops of England or Holland, for the Defence of the same, they shall be admitted:

That, for the particular Safety and Tranquillity of the States, there shall be delivered unto them, and they shall take Possession of, the Towns, Places, and Forts, of Venlo, Rocrmonde, Stcevenswaardt, Luxembourg, Namur,

Charleroy, Mons, Dendermonde, Damme, and St. Donaas, with the Castles of the said Towns and Places belonging, together with all the Forts, Fortifications, and Works, about or near them, in the same Condition as they now are; and they shall have Power to put and keep in them such Garisons, both of their own Troops, and their Allies, as they shall think fit; and that neither France nor Spaine shall, in the least, put. any military Forces into the said Towns; and shall not raise any Forts or Strongholds about or near the said Towns, Places, Castles, and Forts; nor shall do any thing that may in any-wise hinder or lessen the Effect of the aforesaid Possession:

That the States General shall have Liberty to augment, diminish, or change, their respective Garisons in the aforesaid Towns, Places, Castles, and Forts, as they shall judge proper; and to send thither Provision, Ammunition, Arms, Materials for Fortifications, and all that shall be useful and necessary for the said Garisons and Fortifications; and that, for transporting the same, and the said Garisons, there shall always be a:free Passage through the Spanish Territories, and over their Risers, both going and coming, without the least Hindrance or Molestation, either directly or indirectly:

That the States General shall have the:full.Command over such Towns, Places, Castles, and Fortsj inta which they have put Garisons, under such Governors and Commanders as they shall think fit; so that it be not any Prejudice to their former Rights, Privileges, and Revenues of the King of Spaine, in those Towns and Places:

Further, That the States shall have Power to fortify the aforesaid Towns, Places, Castles, and Forts, in their Possession; and to repair the Fortifications thereof; and to do all and all manner of Things which they shaltfcbink fitting for their Defence:

That no Dominions, Provinces, Towns, Territories, or Places belonging to the Crown of Spai?ie, m\im or without Europe, and particularly* not any Towns, Places, or Countries, of the Spanish Netherlands, shall be given up, or delivered to, or shall devolve or. come to the Crown of France, either byway of Gift* Sale, Exchange, Marriage, Inheritance, or Will, or ab intestate, o^by what Title soever; nor shall the same, any otherwise whatsoever, be put under the Command or Jurisdiction of France:

That the Subjects and Inhabitants of the States shall continue to enjoy all such Rights, Privileges, and Immunities, and other Advantages, in the Dominions and Territories of Spaine, in, and out of Europe, as also in the Spanish Netherlands, in the Navigation, -Commerce, and Freedom of the Ports, and all others, which they lwve enjoyed, or should have enjoyed, till the Death of the late King of Spaine; and consequently, that all Things whatsoever, except what shall be otherwise agreed on by-the Treaty to l)e made, shall remain in the..same Condition as they were, when the said King of Spaine died:

That the Treaty made between Spaine and Holland at Munster in the Year 1648, as also all other Treaties find Conventions, since that, concluded, between 'Spaine find Holland, shall be renewed in the best manner both Parties can agree upon; so far forth as they shall not be altered by the Treaty to be made:

Further, That the Subjects and Inhabitants of the States shall have and enjoy, in the Countries, Towns, Places, Bays, and Havens, of the Crown of Spaine, both within and without Europe, the same Privileges, Liberties, and Rights, together with the Immunities find Advantages, as the Subjects and Inhabitants of France, or those of other Princes and Potentates, do there enjoy, or hereafter shall be permitted to enjoy:

That the Observation of the aforesaid Points in general, and of each of them in particular, shall be solemnly promised by the Kings of France and Spaine, their Heirs and Successors:

That the Treaty to be made hereupon shall have the Guaranty of such Kings, Princes, and Potentates;v a3 either Party shall thereto desire; and that in the firmest manner that they can devise:

Reserving to themselves a Power to enlarge the aforesaid Points in the Negotiations, as shall be necessary for a further Explanation of the true Meaning of the sarme, and to prevent all Differences for the future.

And the Heer Van Essen, and other the States Deputies for the foreign Affairs, are hereby desired and commissioned to notify the Premises to Count D'Avaux; and enter into Conference and Negotiation with him, concerning the same.

This agrees with the aforesaid Register.

War in Ireland and Flanders, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That after Disbanding of the said Regiments, upon the Petition of the Petitioners to the Treasury, which was referred to the Lord Coningsby, he reported, That the Petitioners had no Accounts made up by their Captains; and the Captains say, They cannot get Accounts from the Colonels, according to the Directions of a late Act of Parliament, they have placed so many unwarrantable Deductions on the Head of Subsistence, that the Petitioners, and the Captains, Arrears are reduced to little or nothing; whereupon the Petitioners applied to the Commissioners of Accounts, who sent for the Captains, who owned, that there were Arrears due to the Petitioners, and desired the Commissioners to examine and determine the Accounts between them and the Colonels; but the Commissioners finding, that the said Regiments could not expect Debentures, being disbanded, and paid by the Government, they thought themselves not authorized to meddle therewith; so that the Petitioners remain remediless, in great Distress, for want of their just Dues; nor have they had any Consideration for their Cloathing, Two Years wanting: And praying, That the House will take their Case into Consideration, and relieve them therein.

A Petition of Ann Rosell, the Widow and Relict of Gervas Rosell Esquire, deceased, and Mother and Guardian of Gervas Rosell, an Infant, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That Thomas Rosell, the Petitioner's Husband's Father, being seised in Fee of several Lands in Nottinghamshire, of about 250 I per Annum, did, by his Will, devise the same to Trustees, for Payment of Debts, and raising above 2,600 I. for his younger Childrens Portions, they being all now living: That, Thomas dying, the said Premises descended to the said Gervas, who likewise subjected the same to the Payment of his Debts; and further, for answering a Jointure to the Petitioners, and for Maintenance of, and Portions for, his Two Daughters, to be ascertained by Trustees, named in his Will: That the said Lands are frequently overflowed by the River Trent, which breaks down the Banks, and requires a considerable Sum to keep the same, and Waterworks, in Repair; for the doing whereof, and discharging other Branches of the said Trust, the acting Trustee took up, at Interest, several Sums of Money upon the Premises, and died, leaving the same unpaid, and without appointing any Maintenance, or Portions, for the Daughters of the said Gervas; and the Trust is now vested in his Second Son, who is young, unable to manage, and refuses to act, or receive the Rents, and has actually released the said Trust; and the said Estate will soon be swallowed up with Interest, and other incident Charges; so that the Petitioner, and the Children of Thomas and Gervas Rosell, must be inevitably ruined, unless relieved by an Act of Parliament: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for vesting the said Estate, or so much thereof as will pay off the Debts and Incumbrances to which the same is liable, and make Provision for the Daughters of the said Gervas, in Trustees, to be sold for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord Marquis of Hartington, and Mr. Leigh, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Resolved, Ncniine contradicente, That the Thanks of this House be given to Sir Edward Seymour Baronet, a Member of this House, for the great Service he hath done the Publick, in detecting the Bribery and Corruption, which hath been practised in the Elections of several Members to serve in this present Parliament.

And Mr. Speaker gave him the Thanks of the House accordingly, as followeth; viz.

Sir Edward Seymour,

The House has had a long Examination of several corrupt Practices, tending to the Destruction of the Constitution: They are sensible the Discovery thereof is owing to your Resolution, to your Love of the Publick; and is brought about at your Charge, and by your Conduct.

Tis an Honour, Sir, to you, that you are descended from Ancestors, who have been successful in commanding Armies and Fleets of this Kingdom, and from a Protector of the Realm: But 'tis your personal Honour, that you have protected even the Constitution of this Place.

As the House has expressed their Zealand Indignation against those who have endeavoured to undermine and ruin the Foundation of our Liberties; so they are desirous, at the same time, that your Name may stand upon Record, as being the Means, by which 'tis brought about: Vol. 13.

4X5

Therefore they have commanded, That the Thanks of this House be given to you, for the great Service you have done the Publick, in detecting the Bribery and Corruption, which hath been practised in the Elections of several Members to serve in this present Parliament.

Whereupon Sir Edward Seymour spoke to the Effect following; viz.

Mr. Speaker,

The Honour I have received this Day, is sufficient to gratify the greatest Ambition, and the greatest Endeavours any Man is capable of, in order to the public Service, which was the only Inducement that occasioned me to undertake it: And I am extraordinary happy, that Success has crowned my Endeavours so far, as to entitle them to your Approbation: I must say, that I am indebted to several particular worthy Gentlemen, who have given their Assistance in this Matter; and that the great Honour you have been pleased to do me this Day, will be so great an Ornament to my Escutcheon, that it will wait upon me to my Grave.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Supply, Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Conyers took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Conyers reported from the said Committee, That they had made a further Progress in the Matter to them referred; and had directed him to move, That they may have Leave to sit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday next, after his Majesty's gracious Message considered, resolve itself into a Committee of the w hole House, to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Woollen Ma- A Petition of the Masters and Journeymen of the Art nufacture. and Mystery of Wool-combing, within the Town and Borough of Chulmkxgh, in the County of Devon, wa3 presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That divers Persons, for several Years last past, in Cholmley, and the adjacent Parishes, have, and do make it their Endeavours to destroy the said Art of Wool-combing, by 1 the irregular Management of divers Farmers, Shopkeepers, and others, who are of different Trades and Calling; and yet set divers People to Work, that never were bound or served Apprenticeships to the said Art, as the Law directs, under feigned Pretences of employing the Poor; although, by it greater Poverty ensues; they giving little or no Money for their Labour, only Goods and Commodities, at their own Rates; by Means whereof, the Petitioners Trade is undervalued, and under-sold by such Interlopers in Trade; so that the Master Workmen cannot subsist, and the Journeymen can scarce get Bread; and must unavoidably be brought to extreme Want, if not speedily relieved by some good Law for the better regulating the said Art; which may be a great Improvement to the Woollen Manufacture, and a Means to employ the Poor in general: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to redress the Inconveniencies arising by Persons exercising the Art and Mystery of Wool-combing, who have not served their Apprenticeships therein.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufacture;

It passed in the Negative.

A Petition of John Mitchell, John Pozvney, Charles Aldxcorth, William Smith, and Richard Topham, Esquires, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for the Enlarging of Windsor Park, the Petitioners conveyed to his now Majesty certain Freehold and Leasehold Lands; in Consideration whereof his Majesty by Letters Patents, did grant to the Petitioners other Lands in Windsor Parish; which being of something greater Value than the Lands conveyed by the Petitioners, they paid the Overplus in Money: And praying, That they may have proper Savings inserted in the Bill to resume the Grants of Lands, and other Revenues, since the 6th Day of February 1684; and applying the same to the Use of the Publick.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whoie House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of John Oliver, and others, on behalf of themselves, and alt others, that served in the Regiment of Horse, commanded by the Honourable Colonel Francis Langston, in the Reducing of Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in 1688, his Majesty, of his Bounty, gave to each Man in the said Regiment 31 Days full Pay, which was paid them, and afterwards stopt out of their Subsistence; and in 1692, they received another Bounty from the Queen; which is since charged as Part of their Subsistence: That, in 169 2, the Regiment was broke; and the Colonel hath signed a full Discharge, in the Pay Office, for the said Regiment, entire to the 1st of April 1692; and hath cleared with the Commission Officers for their own Pay, and accounted with his own Troop, and paid them in Part, and gave w Note under his Hand for the rest: That the Petitioners, Who were in the Five other Troops, have had no manner of Account, either from the Colonel or Captains, though all possible Endeavours have been used to obtain the same by their several Complaints to this House, and Application to the Commissioners of Accounts: And praying. That they may be relieved in their just Complaints, by Such means as the House shall.....most proper and

1700.

expedient; the said Colonel designing to go for Ireland, very speedily.

Ordered, That it he referred to the Commissioners of Accounts, to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and to report the Fact to this House.

A Petition of several Troopers, late belonging to Cap- Army tain De la Fond's Troop, when Major to Colonel indsor s Deduction Regiment of Horse, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the said Major hath made several unwarrantable Deductions out of the Petitioners Subsistence, amounting to 14/. a Man, besides the Offreckonings, and Horses detained at Disbanding; for all which the Petitioners cannot obtain any Satisfaction, though often demanded; and praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

A Petition of the Clothiers of his Majesty's Army Army was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That beUctum the Petitioners are possessed of certain Army Debentures for their Debts, made out by the Commissioners of Accounts; which Debentures are to be satisfied by Sale of the forfeited Estates in Ireland: And the Petitioners ought thereby to have been paid before this time, or have had Liberty of purchasing the said Estates; but, as yet, I they have not received their Debentures for the greatest 1 Part of their Debts, nor Power of purchasing the said Estates; And the said Debentures, carrying no Interest, are at a very great Discount; whereby the Petitioners Credits and Stocks are under great Hardships:

And praying, That such as have not received Debentures may be relieved touching the same; and that on all the Debentures there may be such an Interest, as the House shall think reasonable.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the w hole House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

1 sented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the

5 Petitioner's Father, by Deed, charged a considerable Part

s of his Estate with a Rent-charge of 200l. per Annum to

i his Wife, and 2,000 /. for his Daughters Portions; by

s which the Petitioner's Estate is so much lessened, that he

is become liable to great Debts, which he is utterly unable to pay, as also his Sisters Portions, without the Assistance of an Act of Parliament; he having in 1695, so settled his Estate upon his Marriage, that he cannot dispose of the same, but reserving a Power of letting Leases for Lives upon Fines: That his Wife is willing to relinquish a considerable Part of ber Jointure for the Benefit of the Petitioner^ Family: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioner to charge some Part of the Estate with the Sum of 3,000 L for the Payment of his Debts, and his Sisters Portions, and the transferring his Power of making Leases to Trustees for applying thO Funds towards raising the said Money.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Stanley and Mr. Hysham do prepare, and bring in the same.

troy De* A Petition of the Officers of His Majesty's Army, was jataiti. presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are intitled to certain Debentures for their respective Debts, by virtue of an Act of Parliament for appointing Commissioners of Accounts; which they ought to have had by the time limited by the said Act; and which were to be settled by Sale of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, or by purchasing thereof before this time; but the Petitioners have not yet received their Debentures, nor Power of purchasing the said Estates: And praying that the said Debentures may carry Interest; and that the Petitioners may be relieved touching the same.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Non-commission Officers, Corporals, Anon. Trumpeters, and private Centinels, reduced, discharged, and disbanded, out of his Majesty's Army, since the happy Conclusion of the Peace, who served in the Reducing of Ireland, and in the Low Countries, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are several Sums of Money due to the Petitionerg for Subsistence, and Off-reckonings, for which they cannet bring their Officers to account, notwithstanding their many Complaints to this House, and an Act of Parliament made in the 10th and 1 lth Years of his Majesty's Reign, for that Purpose: That the last Session of Parliament, an Act passed for appointing Commissioners to state and determine the Debts due to the Army, &c.; and the Petitioners applied to the Commissioners for Relief, who declared, that, for want of the Word u Soldier," in the said Act, they had no Power to compel the Colonels to account with their Captains, nor the Captains with their Soldiers; by which Means, the Petitioners are still unrelieved i And praying, That they may be relieved in their just Complaints, and their Officers compelled to account, and pay them what they have received for their said Service.

Ordered, That it be referred to the Commissioners of Accounts, to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and state the Fact to this House.

A Petition of Jane Barkstead, Widow' and Relict of BarksteadV Francis Barkstead, late Citizen and Mercer of London, Nat* deceased, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was the Daughter of George Gill, and was born at Lyons in France, but sent over into England very young, about 30 Years ago, and married the said Francis Barkstead, who was an Englishmen, who died about Seven Years since, leaving Three Infant Children, to whom he, by his Will gave a Third Part of his Estate, and made the Petitioner Executrix; who proved the Will, and put out her Children's Money at Interest, upon Securities, w'hich have been approved by the Court of Chancery: That the Persons who borrowed the said Money are ready to pay it in; but are advised, that the Petitioner, being a Foreigner, cannot reassign, or make a good Title, without being naturalized: And praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for naturalizing the Petitioner, and vesting several Securities, for Part of her late Husband's Estate, in her; so that she may be enabled to take in, and let out, her own and her Children's Money, as there shall be Occasion.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Ward and Mr. Gulston do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Woollen A Petition of the Merchants, Clothiers, and other Tra-

Manufucture. ders in the Woollen Manufacture, in and about the Town of Halifax, in the County of was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by Act of Parliament made in the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, Commissioners were impowered to put the Laws in Execution against the Exportation of Wool; who employed several Officers, and were at great Trouble and Expence, for that Purpose; by means whereof, they are much disabled in the Management of so great a Concern; and, unless some Fund be granted to the said Commissioners, they will be forced to lay aside their said Trust, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and all Traders in the Woollen Manufactures: And praying, That a Fund may be raised for the better Encouragement of the said Petitioners.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws in being, touching the -Woollen Manufacture.

A PETITION of Robert Steynor Esquire was pre- Running sentedtothe House, and read; setting forth, That the Salt.

Laws hitherto made, to secure the Duty payable on Salt, are daily eluded by the Officers, Makers, and Carriers, of Salt, within the Borough of Droitwichin Worcestershire, to the Value of 10,000l. per Annum Loss to his Majesty, and the fair Dealer's Loss of Trade; not only because the Officers have the sole Pow er of seizing Salt, passing before Entry; which if all other Persons had, half so much would not be run, and it would save his Majesty half the Number of Officers; but also, for that the Justices of Peace of the said Borough arc great Makers of Salt, and take upon them to try all Causes relating to the Running of Salt, and excuse each other their Friends and Relations, who are also great Dealers in Salt: And praying, that some effectual Care may be taken to prevent the Running and Smuggling of Salt, either by a Bill, or any other Way, as shall be thought fit.

A Petition of the Clothiers of Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, notwithstanding this Kingdom is at great Charges in maintaining Vessels and Men to prevent the Exportation of Wool; yet, within these Two Years, many Thousand Packs of Wool have been exported into France, and other foreign Parts, through the Connivance, as it is feared, or great Neglect, of the Commanders of those Vessels; to the great Decay of the "Petitioners Trades: And praying, That effectual Care may be taken to prevent the evil Practices in Transporting of Wool, and to maintain the Woollen Manufactures of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, who were appointed to inspect the Laws in being, relating to the Woollen Manufacture.

Matter, touching the Election for the Borough of Orford, in the County of Suffolk, as it appeared to the said Committee; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the

House; which he read in his Place; anil afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir Charles Hedges and Sir Tho. Felton, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Edmund Bacon Baronet, and Sir Edward Turner Knight, to serve for the Borough of Orford:

That the Matter, as it appeared before the Committee, was thus:

That the Petition sets forth, That the Petitioners are duly elected to serve for the said Borough of Orford: And complaining, That Henry Cooper Esquire, High Sheriff' of Suffolk, with an Intention to make a false Return, delivered his Precept to one John Saunders, to whom the Execution thereof did not belong; which the said Sheriff and Saunders well knew, by a solemn Tryal at Bar, in Michaelmas Term last; and afterwards did receive an Indenture, importing, though untruly, that Sir Edmund Bacon and Sir Edward Turner Baronets were elected Burgesses for the said Borough; and has returned the same, and refused a Return of the Petitioners from the Mayor of the said Borough.

That the Fact appeared to be thus:

In Orford are Two Persons who pretend to the Office of Mayor, Thomas Hastings and John Saunders: On the 26th of December, Mr. Edmund Foster went to Orford, where the High Sheriff lived; and acquainted tiiin. That Mr. Hastings was the Mayor of Orford, and expected the Precept: And, on the 30th of December, he wentto Orfot d\ to John Saunders, and told him, he hoped, lie would not meddle with the Precept; and did leave with the High Sheriff and John Saunders, a Copy of a Verdict, at liar, against John Morgan: And Mr. Foster said, That he was present when the Verdict was given, which was upon the Point, Whether Morgan was the real Mayor: Mr. Foster could not say but he demanded the Precept of the Sheriff, before the Sheriff had the Writ: But one Thomas Fnnch testified, That Mr. Hastings did demand the Precept of Mr. Saunders, after it came to Town; but he refused to deliver it*

That it further appeared to the Committee, That&tffl-ders, having the Precept, gave Notice, That the Election would be the 10th of January; and accordingly, upon the 10th of January, went to the Town-hall, and there the Sitting Members were elected: That after Mr. Saunders, and those with him, were come out of the Town-hall, Mr. Hastings, and several of the Freemen, went into the Town-hall; and there the Petitioners were elected, by about the Number of 58.

That the Petitioners Counsel insisted, That they could make it appear, That John Sannders was not the lawful Mayor, the said Saimders claiming under Morgan.

To w'hich Point the Committee did not think fit to hear them.

But it not being pretended, that publick Notice had been given of the Time of the said Election by Hastings, neither ever had he the Precept; and it also appearing, that no Person protested against Saunders Proceedings while he was in the Town-hall, or any one demanded a Poll of him;

The Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Edmund Bacon Baronet is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Orford, in the County of Suffolk.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Edward Turner Knight is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Orford.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Merits of the Election for the said Borough be recommitted;

It passed in the Negative.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Com-VOL. 13.

mittee in the said Resolution, That Sir Edmund Bacon Baronet is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Orford, in the County of Suffolk.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time:

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Sir Edward Turner Knight is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Orford.

Memorandum: The Fourth of the said Seven Accounts was made up for Sixteen Mouths, the Accountant being Earl of directed so to do, by a Warrant signed by his Majesty, and countersigned by the then Lords of the Treasury, Raoelagh's dated the 11th Day of September 1689 Which Warrant t^es Notice, That, by reason of the Interruption Accounts, of the Musters from November 1G88, to May 1689, the Payments to the Forres had been, for that time, so intermixed, that it would be most convenient for all Persons concerned, that the said Accounts should be made up for Sixteen Months; viz. From the First of January 1687, to the last of April 1689, from which time the New Establishment was to begin: And, by the said Warrant, the Fifth of the said Accounts is directed to be made up for Eight Months; viz. from the First of May 1689, to the last of December following; so that the said Fourth and Fifth Accounts take in Two Years; viz, from the First of January 1687, to the last of December 1689.

Memorandum also, That the Seventh of the said foregoing Accounts is made up for 15 Months; viz, from the First of January 1690, to the last of March 1692; because the great Establishment of the Forces which brought most of the Regiments that had served in thereducing of Ireland, under the Accountants Care, begins from the First of April 1692.

The said State of the Poundage, and what was deducted of it by the Accountants within the time of the foregoing Account; viz.

By the several Establishments which took in the whole time of this Account, being Six Years and Three Months, ending as aforesaid, the last of March 1692, the Account* ant was directed to deduct as usually, Twelve-pence out of every Twenty Shillings paid by him to the Forces, &c.; of which One Third Part was, by the Warrants directing the said Deductions* to be applied to the Exchequer Fees, and to the Paymaster of the Forces for the Time being; and the remaining Two Thirds were to remain in the said Paymaster's Hands upon Account* to be applied either to the Use of the Royal Hospital near Chelsea, or towards the lessening the Charge of the Establishments, according to Directions: But from the First of April

1692, when the great Establishment of the Forces began* which brought most of the Regiments that had served in the_reducing of Ireland, under this Accountant's Care; and which amounted to 1,143,183/. 10 s. 11 d. per Annum; the Third of the Poundage, applicable by the former Establishments, as aforesaid, to the Exchequer Fees* and to the Paymaster of the Forces for the Time being* was entirely extinguished; and the whole Poundage was left to his Majesty's Disposal; who was pleased to grant this Accountant, out of it, a settled Salary of 3,000l. a Year, being what was then allowed to the Treasurer of the Navy.

As to the Two Thirds of the Poundage deducted from the First of January 1685, to the last of March 1692* which amounted to 136,622 /. 19$. 2 d. this Account* ant hath accounted for the same, in manner following:

The Earl of Nottingham reported from the Lords Committees appointed to draw up, q,nd state, the Facts, as to the Treaty now in Debate.

That the Committee had met, and thought it proper to set down such Facts as appeared to them; viz.

1st, That, by the Treaty of Partition, Naples, Sicily, &c. were: to be given to the Dauphin.

2d, That the Emperor was not a Party to the Treaty, though principally concerned.

3. That no Minister of the States General met with the Plenipotentiaries of England and France, as was re-

K* ed by the Powers at the making of the Treaty in don.

4. That there were no Instructions in Writing to our Plenipotentiaries, though the Powers were unlimited; and that, if there were verbal Orders given, yet it appears not to us they were considered in any Council.

5. That the Treaty, when perfected, was not considered in any Council before it was ratified.

6. That it appears, that the Warrant for Ratification was countersigned by one of the Plenipotentiaries.

7. That the Treaty was transacted and signed, and the Great Seal affixed to it, during the Sitting of a Parliament.

Then the House, upon Consideration of the First Head in the said Report, agreed to the same, with the Alteration following; viz.

Instead of " given to," read " put into the Hands of." Then the Second Head was read.

After Debate thereupon, the Question was put, Whether this Paragraph shall stand.

It was resolved in the Negative.

Dissentient',

1. Because it is manifest by the Treaty itself, that the Matter of Fact is true.

2. Because the Emperor, as we conceive, had been the most proper to have been treated with on this Occasion; for it was more prudent and safe to have treated with the Emperor to have restrained the Pretensions of France, than with France to lessen the Dominions of the House of Austria; which, in its full Strength, and in Conjunction with the most considerable Powers of Europe, and with the Expence of more than Sixty Millions Sterling to our Share, was scarce able to withstand the Arms of France.

3dly, But, admitting that the Emperor was not the most proper to be treated with; yet, to prevent the Umbrage which might be taken by uniting too many Dominions under one Prince, especially such a Prince, as, without any Additions, was formidable to all Europe; yet, of all others, the Emperor was the most improper to be left out of such a Treaty; for he was most concerned in it; and our Ministers could not, or at least did not, sufficiently support his Interests, or the just Balance of Europe: But, on the contrary, as we are informed by One Lord, who signed this Treaty, it was concluded against the express Desire of the Emperor.

3 Head. That no Minister of the States General met with the Plenipotentiaries of England and France, as were required by the Powers at the making the Treaty

in London.

After Debate, the Question was put, Whether this Paragraph shall stand.

It was resolved in the Negative.

Dissentient',

1st, Because the Truth of this Proposition is Reason enough for asserting it; and it must certainly be of fatal Consequence, if Ministers, without any Directions by Instructions in Writing, shall presume to act contrary to the very Commission that impowers them: And, in this Case, the Assistance of the Dutch Minister was the more necessary, because the Emperor was no Party to this Treaty; and the States General are more immediately concerned than we are, to promote his Interests.

2dly, Because, if this Treaty was concerted wit h the Dutch Ministers in 1699, before his Majesty's Return into England, as was asserted by One of the Lords who signed it afterwards in London; then,

1st, This Treaty was made by those who had no i\u-thority to transact it; for the Power was not granted by his Majesty till the Second of January following.

2dly, As they acted without Power, so without Instructions too in Writing; which never was practised iin any former Transaction abroad.

Lastly, We conceive, That neither of the foregoing Facts ought, in Reason, according to the Method oJ Parliament, to be ordered to be omitted; because, till the Committee had formed the Address, pursuant to the Or* der, it was impossible to know what Use should be made of those Facts; for as they might have been improperly applied, and then would have been justly rejected, so there might have been so great Use made of them, and so opposite to the Design of the House in the intended Address, that it will be improper to omit them.

Jovis, 20° Martii

The Earl of Nottingham reported from the Lords Committees appointed to state Matters of Fact upon the Treaty of Partition, and to draw an Address thereupon, That the Committee had accordingly drawn an Address, to be presented to his Majesty: Which was read; and, with one Amendment, agreed to, as follows; viz.

We your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords. Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, having read and considered the Treaty *700,

made with the French King, together with the separate and secret Articles which your Majesty hath been pleased to communicate to us, do, with all Humility, represent to your Majesty, That, to our great Sorrow, we find the Matters thereof to have been of very ill Consequence to the Peace and Safety of Europe: For, besides the Occasion it may have given to the late King of Spain to have made his Will in Favour of the Duke of Anjou, if this Treaty had taken Effect, the Prejudice to your Majesty and your Subjects, and indeed to all Europe, by the Addition of Sicily, Naples, several Ports in the Mediterranean, the Province of Guypuscoa, and the Duchy of Lorraine, had been not only very great, but contrary to the Pretence of the Treaty itself; w'hich was, to prevent any Umbrage which might betaken, by uniting too many States and Dominions under one Head.

And, by all the Informations we have yet had of the Progress of this fatal Treaty, we cannot find, that the verbal Orders and Instructions, if any were given to your Majesty's Plenipotentiaries, were ever considered in any of your Majesty's Councils; or that the Draught of this Treaty was ever laid before your Majesty at any Meeting of your Council; much less, that it was advised or approved by any Council, or Committee of Council.

We therefore think ourselves obliged, in Duty to your Majesty, and Justice to our Country, most humbly to beseech your Majesty, that, for the future, your Majesty will be pleased to require and admit, in all Matters of Importance, the Advice of your natural-born Subjects, whose known Probity and Fortunes may give your Majesty, and your People, a just Assurance of their Fidelity in your Service; and, in order hereunto, to constitute a Council of such Persons, to whom your Majesty may be pleased to impart all Affairs, both at home and abroad, which may any way concern your Majesty, and your Dominions: For, as Interest, and natural Affection to their Country, will incline them to wish the Welfare *md Pros-. perity of it much more than others, who have not such Ties upon them; and as their Experience and Knowlege of their Country will also render them more capable, than Strangers, of advising your Majesty in the true Interests of it; so we are very confident, that, after such large and repeated Demonstrations of your Subjects Duty and Assetion, your Majesty cannot doubt of thei^ Zeal in your Service, nor w'ant the Knowledge of Persons fit to be employed in all your most secret and arduous Affairs.

And since it appears, That the French King's accepting of the King of Spains Will is a manifest Violation of this Treaty; we humbly advise your Majesty, in future Treaties with the French King, to proceed with such Caution, as may carry along with it a real Security.

It being proposed to send to the House of Commons for their Concurrence to the said Address;

And Debate thereupon;

The Question was put, Whether this Address shall be communicated to the House of Commons for their Concurrence.

It was resolved in the Negative.

Dissentient',

Rochester, JV. Oxon, Devonshire.

1st, Because we conceive, That the last Clause in the Address does necessarily imply a War, and That a very long one, by reason of the Extent, unintelligible, at least to us, of real Security, and the great improbability of obtaining any Terms of that Kind: And since this necessarily implies great Supplies, which cannot be granted without the House of Commons, we think their Concurrence in this Address absolutely necessary; and that'tis very improper for us to desire That of the King, which, for want of such Concurrence of the Commons, we conceive his Majesty will not think fit or prudent to grant.

2dly, We conceive all the other Parts of the Address very fit to be communicated to the House of Commons; for upon the Success of it depends the future Happiness of this Nation: And as we cannot doubt of the Readiness of the Commons to join in any proper Measures towards it; so we think their Concurrence in it vill highly contribute towards the obtaining a gracious Answer from his Majesty: And we cannot but think it reasonable, that the Advice of the whole Nation, assembled in Parliament, should be made know n to his Majesty upon this Occasion.

3dly, Having desired the House of Commons to permit Mr. Secretary Vernony a Member of their House, to come to a Committee of Lords, to inform them of some Matters relating to this Treaty; we apprehend, that the House of Commons may think it extraordinary, and not suitable to the good Correspondence which is highly necessary between the Two Houses, not to acquaint them with the Things which had come to our Knowlege, partly by the Information of their own Member.

4thly, And having been otherwise informed of some Transactions, relating to this Treaty, between the Earl of Portland and Mr. Secretary Vernon, by Letters, of which we have not had a full Account; we think it may be very useful to the Publick to communicate this Address to the Commons, who have better Opportunity, than we have had, of inquiring into this Matter; which seems to be yet in the Dark; and which their own- Members may help to explain to them.

Leeds, Normanby, De Longueville,

Nottingham, Bath, Weymouth,

Granville, Abingdon, Jeffries,

Craven, Guilford, Hunsden,

Thanet, Willoughby, N. Durtsme,

Kent, Scarsdale, Tho. Rojftii,

H. London, Carnarvon, Poulett.

The Serjeant at Arms being called upon to give an Account of what he had done in Execution of the Orders of the House, for the Taking of Mr. William Adye and Mr. William Clifton; he acquainted the House, That his Messengers had been at the said Mr. Adye s and Mr. Clifton s Houses, and searched for them; and that, at Mr. Adye s House, the Messenger was informed, That the said Mr. Adye had not been at home for Ten Days; and could have no Account where he was; and that, at the said Mr. Clifton's, the Messenger was informed, That the said Mr. Clifton was gone into Holland; so that neither of them can be apprehended.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will please to issue his Royal Proclamation for the apprehending the said Mr. William Adye and Mr. William Clifton; promising a Reward for the same.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House, as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council.

Mr. Weld attending in his Place, according to Order;

The Petition of Sir Paid Pindar Baronet, presented to the House Yesterday, was read; setting forth, That the Petitioner's Father and Mother died about Eleven Years since, leaving the Petitioner, an Infant of about Nine Years of Age, a real Estate of 1,200 /. per Annum, and a very considerable personal Estate, which the said Mr. Weld has managed and received as the Petitioners Guardian: That the Petitioner is advised to call his Guardian to an Account; who, being a Member, has declared he will not insist upon his Privilege: And praying, That the House will give Leave for the Petitioner to proceed against the said Mr. Weld, to call him to an Account for what he has received as the Petitioner's Guardian.

To which the said Mr. Weld being heard, declared he did not insist upon his Privilege.
