A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Common Council, and chief Inhabitants of the City of Norwich, and County of the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That it is found by Experience, that the erecting a Court of Conscience in the City of London, for determining all Matters of Debts or Actions, under the Value of 40 s. hath been of great Advantage to the poorer Sort of Inhabitants thereof: That the City of Norwich is very populous; and many poor Inhabitants therein, for want of the like good Establishment there, are often prosecuted in vexatious Suits, and imprisoned for small Debts; the Charges whereof, many times, amount to more than the Debt; whereby whole Families are ruined, the Gaols filled with miserable Debtors, and the Parish Charges increased for their Support: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for establishing 41 Court of Conscience at Norwich, as it is in

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Blqfield, Sir Jacob Ashley, and Sir Samuel -

chston, do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Speaker, also acquainted the House, That he, with Answer to the House, did Yesterday present to his Majesty their Addre*. Address: And that his Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer;

Gentlemen,

I am glad you are pleased with my communicating to you the State of the Negotiations I have entered into, pursuant to your Address: I shall continue to inform you of the Progress that shall be made in them, and be always willing to receive your Advice thereupon j being fully persuaded, that nothing can contribute more effectually to the Happiness of this Kingdom, and the Peace of Europe, than the Concurrence of the Parliament in all my Negotiations, and a good Understanding betw een me and my People.

Which Articles and Sailing Orders, are as follow: —

The other Four being entered in the Journal of the 4II1 of December 1699.

Articles of Agreement, made this 10th Day of October

169.5, between the Right Honourable Richard Earl ! of Bellomont, of the one Part; and Robert Leving-ston Esquire, and Captain William Kidd, of the other Part.

Whereas the said Captain Kidd is desirous to obtain a Commission as Captain of a private Alan of War, in order to take Prizes from the Kings Enemies, and other* wise to annoy them: And whereas also, certain Person* did some time since depart from New England, Rhode,

Island, New York, and other Parts in America, and elsewhere, with an Intention to become Pirates, and to commit Spoils and Depredations against the Law of Nations, in the Red Sea or elsewhere, and to return, with such Goods and Riches a* they shall get, to certain Places by them agreed upon; of which said Persons and Places the said Captain Kidd hath Notice, and is desirous to fight with and subdue the said Pirates, as also all other Pirates, with whom the said Captain Kidd shall meet at Sea, in case he be employed so to do: And whereas it is agreed between the said Parties, That, for the Purposes edoresaid, a good and sufficient Ship to the Liking of the said Captain Kidd, shall be forthwith bought, whereof the said Captain Kidd is to have the Command: Now these Presents witness, and it is agreed between the said Parties:

1. The said Earl of Bellomont doth covenant and agree, at his proper Charge, to procure from the King's Majesty, or from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, as the Case shall require, One or more Commissions, empowering him the said Captain Kidd to act against the King's Enemies, and to take Prizes from them, as a private Man of War, in the usual Manner; and also to fight with, conquer, and subdue Pirates; and to take them and their Goods, with such other large and beneficial Powers and Clauses in such Commissions, as may be most proper and effectual in such Cases.

2. The said Earl doth covenant and agree* That within*

Three Months after the said Captain Kidd's Departure

from

2 80 Martii.

ij W. III.

from England for the Purpose in these Presents mentioned, he will procure, at his proper Charge, a Grant from the King, to be made to some indifferent and trusty Person, of all such Merchandizes, Goods, Treasure, and other Things, as shall be taken from the said Pirates, or any other Pirates whatsoever, by the said Captain Kidd or by the said Ship, or any other Ship or Ships under his Command.

3. The said Earl doth agree to pay Four Fifth Parts, the whole in Five Parts to be divided, of all Monies which shall be laid out for the buying such good and sufficient Ship for the Purposes aforesaid, together with Rigging, and other Apparel and Furniture thereof, and providing the same with competent Victualling, the said Ship to be approved of by the said Parties; and the said other Fifth Part of the Charges of the said Ship to be paid by the said Robert Levingston and William Kidd.

4. The said Earl doth agree, That in order to the speedy buying the said Ship, and in Part of the said Four Parts of Five of the said Charges, he will pay down the Sum of 1,600l. by way of Advance, on or before the 6th Day of November next ensuing.

5. The said Robert Levingston and Captain William Kidd do jointly and severally covenant and agree, That on or before the said 6th Day of November, when the said Earl of Bellomont is to pay the said Sum of 1,600l. as aforesaid, they will advance, and pay down, 400 I. in Part of the Share and Proportion which they are to have in the said Ship.

6. The said Earl doth agree to pay such further Sum of Money, as shall complete, and make up, the said Four Parts of Five, of the Charges of the said Ship's Apparel, Furniture, and Victualling, unto the said Robert Levingston and William Kidd\ within Seven Weeks alter the Date of these Presents; and, in like manner, the said Robert Levingston and William Kidd do agree to pay such further Sum as shall amount to a Fifth Part of the whole Charge of the said Ship, within Seven Weeks after the Date of these Presents.

7. The said Captain Kidd doth covenant and agree to procure, and take with him, on board the said Ship, One hundred Mariners or Seamen, or thereabouts, and to make what reasonable and convenient Speed he can, to set out to Sea with the said Ship; and to sail to such Parts or Places where he may meet with the said Pirates; and to use his utmost Endeavour to meet with, conquer, and subdue the said Pirates, or any other Pirates; and to take from them their Goods, Merchandizes, and Treasure; also to take what Prizes he can from the King's Enemies, and forthwith to make the best of his Way to Boston in Neiv England; and that without touching at any other Port or Harbour whatsoever, or without breaking Bulk, or diminishing any Part of w hat he shall so take or obtain* on any Pretence whatsoever; of which he shall make Oath, in case the same shall be desired by the said Earl of Bellomont; and there to deliver the same into the Hands or Possession of the said Earl.

8. The said Captain Kidd doth agree, That the Contract and Bargain which he will make with his said Ship's Crew, shall be, No Purchase, no Pay; and not otherwise: And that the Share and Proportion which his said Crew shall, by such Contract, have of such Prizes, Goods, Merchandizes, and Treasure, as he shall take as Prize, or from any Pirates, shall not, at the most, exceed a Fourth Part of the same; and shall be less than a Fourth Part, in case the same may reasonably and conveniently be agreed upon.

9. The said Robei't Levingston, and Captain Wm. Kidd, do jointly and severally agree wdth the said Earl of Bellomont, That in case the said Captain Kidd do not meet with the said Pirates, which went from New England, Rhode Island\ New York, or elsewhere, as aforesaid; or do not take from any other Pirates, or from any the King's Enemies* such Goods, Merchandizes, or other Things of Value, as, being divided as herein after is mentioned, shall fully recompense the said Earl, for the Monies by him expended in buying the said Four Fifth

Vo l. 13.

445

Parts of the said Ship and Premises; that then they shall refund and repay to the said Earl of Bellomont the wrhole Money by him to be advanced, in Sterling Money, or Money equivalent thereunto, on or before the 25th Day of March, which shall be in the Year of our Lord 1697; the Danger of the Seas, and of the Enemy, and Mortality of the said Captain Kidd, always excepted: Upon Payment whereof, the said Robert Levingston and Captain Kidd are to have the sole Property in the said Ship and Furniture; and this Indenture to be delivered up to them, with all other Covenants and Obligations thereunto belonging.

10. It is agreed between the said Parties, That as well the Goods, Merchandizes, Treasure, and other Things, which shall be taken from the said Pirates, or any Pirates, by the said William Kidd, as also all such Prizes as shall be by him taken from any of the King's Enemies, shall be divided in manner following; that is to say, Such Part as shall be for that Purpose agreed upon by the said Captain Kidd, so as the same do not in the Whole exceed a Fourth Part, shall be paid or delivered to the Ship's Crew, for their Use; and the other Three Parts to be divided into Five equal Parts, w hereof the said Earl is to have, to his own Use, Four full Parts, and the other Fifth Part is to be equally divided between the said Robert Levingston and the said Wm. Kidd; and is to be paid and delivered, them by the said Earl of Bellomont, without Deduction or Abatement on any Pretence whatsoever: But it is always to be understood, that such Prizes as shall be taken from the King's Enemies, are to be lawfully adjudged Prize, ill the usual manner, before any Division, or otherwise intermeddling the rewith, than according to the true Intent of the said Commission, to be granted in that behalf.

Lastly, It is covenanted and agreed between the Parties to these Presents, That in Case the said Captain Wm. Kidd do bring to Boston aforesaid, and there deliver to the Earl of Bellomont, Goods, Merchandizes, Treasure, or Prizes, to the Value of 100,000l. or upwards, which he shall have taken from the said Pirates, or from other Pirates, or from the King's Enemies; that then the Ship which is now speedily to be bought by the said Parties, shall be and remain to the sole Use and Behoof of him the said Captain Kidd, as a Reward and Gratification for his good Service therein.

Bellomont.

Memorandum: Before the Sealing and Delivery of these Presents, it w^as covenanted and agreed by the said Earl of Bellomont, with the said Robert Livingston Esquire, and Captain William Kidd, That the Person to whom the Grant abovementioned in these Articles shall he made by his Majesty, shall within Eight Days at the most, after such Grant has passed the Great Seal of England, assign and transfer to each . of them the said Robert Livingston Esquire, and Captain William Kidd respectively, their Heirs and Assigns, One full Tenth Part (the Ship's Crew's Share and Proportion being first deducted) of all such Goods, Treasure, or other Things, as shall be taken by the said Captain Kidd, by virtue of such Commission as aforesaid: And the said Grantee shall make such Assignment as aforesaid, in such Manner as by the said Robert Livingston Esquire, and Captain William Kidd, or their Counsel learned in the Law, shall be reasonably devised and required: And then these Presents w*ere sealed and delivered, the Sixpenny Stamp being first affixed, in the Presence of us, Martha Bi'eken,

John Maddocke,

The said Sailing Orders.

London, 25th February 169^.

Captain William Kidd'

You being now ready to sail, I do hereby desire and direct you, that you and your Men do serve God in the best Manner you can: That you keep good Order, and good Government, in your Ship: That you make the best of your Way to the Place and Station where you are to put the Powers you have in Execution: And, having effected the same, you are, according to Agreement, to sail directly to Boston in New England, there to deliver unto me the Whole of what Prizes, Treasure, Merchandizes, and other Tilings, you shall have taken by virtue of the Powers and Authorities granted you: But if, after the Success of your Design, you shall fall in with any English Fleet bound for England, having good Convoy, you are, in such Case, to keep them Company, and bring all your Prizes to London, notwithstanding any Covenant to the contrary in pur Articles of Agreement. Pray fail not to give Advice, by all Opportunities, how the Gaily proves; how your Men stand, what Progress you make; and, in general of all remarkable Passages in your Voyage, to the Time of your Writing. Direct your Letters to Mr. Edmund Harrison. I pray God grant you good Success, and send us a good Meeting again.

Bdlomont.

Order of the 12th of March instant, by which they were to lay before this House an Account of their Proceedings for the Improvement of Trade, since the 21st Day of March 1699, being the Time of the Delivery of their last Account.

And the Title thereof w as read:

And the Answer is as followeth; viz.

In Obedience to the Order of this Honourable House, dated the 12th of this instant March, requiring from us an Account of our Proceedings for Improvement of Trade, since the 21st of March last; we humbly offer,

That we did then represent to the Honourable House the Powers and Authorities committed to us by his Majesty; whereby we are directed to examine, and take an Account of, the State of Trade; and to do what in us lies, for the Encouragement thereof, in giving the Merchants, and others concerned, all the Satisfaction and Dispatch we can in their Business, from time to time; as also to make constant Inquiries into the Conditions of his Majesty's Plantations in America, as well with regard to the Administration of Government, as in relation to Commerce; and how those Colonies may be kept in good Order, and rendered most beneficial to this Kingdom; to prepare Commissions and Instructions to Governors; and to examine the Journals and Proceedings of the several Councils and Assemblies, and all the Acts and Laws made by them, in order to the Amendment, Approbation, or Disallowance thereof; to correspond with all the said Governors, and other Officers, in the publick Administration; and to make Representations to his Majesty, or the Privy Council, of what may occur to us upon the Heads or Matters aforesaid; wherein a considerable Part of our Time has been continued to be taken up, since the said Month of March last: The chief Particulars whereof, and of other incident Business, we shall now lay before this Honourable House, in the shortest Method we are able, referring ourselves, for a clearer Deduction of several Matters transacted by us, and under our daily Consideration, to our former lleport, given at that Time.

The French Ambassador having presented to his Majesty a Memorial, complaining of the Royal African Company's trading into the River Senegall, and of their hindering the French from trading up the River Gambia; we thereupon heard the Company: And, finding that they deny their Trading up the River Senegall, and assert their Right to the sole Trade up the River Gambia, we represented the same to his Majesty, for Answer to the said Ambassador's Memorial; and offered, that the Trade along the Coast ought to be kept free, and common to both Nations.

In further Reference to that Trade, a Complaint having been made to his Majesty in Council, by Mr. William Bird and others, of the Seizure of their Ship, called the William and Jane, by the French, about Port Adally\ on that Coast of Africa, where she was trading with a Licence from the Royal African Company, according to the late Act of Parliament; were presented to his Majesty the Company's Right, and constant Trade on that Coast; humbly proposing, that his Majesty would be pleased to

insist

13 W. III. 29° M447

insist upon the Restitution of the said Ship and Damages, and to give such further Orders, as should be thought lit, to prevent the like Violences for the future.

The Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, having Understood from his Majesty's Consul at Algiers, by his Letter of the 13th April last, that the Dey of that Place had given no longer Time, than till September following, for all Ships belonging to his Majesty's Subjects to be provided with Admiralty Passes, which had been discontinued during the late War; insisting upon the Treaty made with them the 10th of April 1682; and declaring, That after that time, such Ships as should be met by their Cruisers, not being furnished with Passes in the Form required, would be seized, and carried up to Algici'S', by which means the Plantation Ships, those to Newfoundland, and others employed in long Voyages, would have been in great Danger; and his Majesty having thereupon required us to consider and settle the Method of granting Passes to the Ships of his Majesty's Subjects, tradingin the Way of the Algerines; we humbly reported to his Majesty the State of that Matter, not only in relation to the Forms of such Passes, but more particularly to the Places whither they should be sent to the Persons who might be intrusted with the Distribution thereof, and to the Directions and Instructions to be given to such Persons in the Execution of that Trust: And we humbly proposed, that the most pressing and effectual Means might be used with the Government of Algiers, to enlarge the Time that had been limited by that Government: All which having been accordingly directed, Passes were sent to the several Persons appointed to distribute them; and the Government of Algiers was prevailed with to prolong the Time for One Year more; xiz. till the End of September next; by which Means the Navigation of his Majesty's Subjects have been preserved from that Danger.

Memorials from Mr Broughton, his Majesty's Consul at Venice, relating to the Trade of Fish and Currans, between England and the Venetians Dominions, having, by his Majesty's Order, been referred to our Consideration; we consulted the Merchants trading in those Parts; and reported what we found to be the State of that Trade, not only with relation to those Two Commodities, but to the whole Trade between England and the Venetian Dominions in general: And we further set forth the Inconveniences and Hardships that, we bad been informed, the English Merchants, trading in those Parts, do lie under.

Differences having arisen between the English Merchants residing at Lisbon, and the Judge Conservator of the English Nation there; and the Merchants of London trading to Portugal having thereupon applied to his Majesty, that he w ould please to interpose with the King of Portugal, for the Removal of the said Conservator; we gave Ins Majesty the necessary Informations in that Matter; and humbly proposed what we judged most for the Ease of the Merchants, and the Advantage of that Trade.

A Vessel, called the Bedford Gaily, belonging to A

Owners, having been seized at Madagascar, by Pirates, in Combination of some of the said Ship's Company; we did, at the Owners Desire, represent the Case to his Majesty; and Letters, prepared by us for his Majesty's Royal Signature, were thereupon dispatched to the Governors of the Plantations, for securing the said Ship and Men, and proceeding against them according to Law.

An Act of Parliament having been made, in the last Sessions, for the more effectual Suppression of Piracy; wherein it is provided, That Commissions be passed, either under the Great Seal of England, or under the Seal of the Admiralty, for the Tryal of Pirates in the Methods directed by the said Act; we did immediately represent to Iris Majesty the Necessity that those Coirfmissions should be dispatched: And his Majesty having thereupon directed them to be passed under the Great Seal; we further humbly offered our Opinion upon the Form which had been prepared by Mr. Attorney and Mr. Solicitor Vol. 13.

General: And, having consulted both the Old and New Improvement East India Companies, we settled with each of them, to ol Ira(ii* what Persons and Places those Commissions might be fitly directed in those Parts: And soon after, we also laid before his Majesty a List of the Persons and Places to which the like Commissions might be directed in his Majesty's Plantations in America; All which having accordingly been done, and the said Commissions being passed ana sent, we prepared Letters for his Majesty's Royal Signature, to the respective Governors of those Plantations, for sending hither all Accessories in Cases of Piracy, w ho, by the said Act, are not to lie tried beyond the Seas.

And having since been required by his Majesty to consider of the Draft of a Proclamation, that Had been pre* pared, for encouraging the Apprehending and Convicting of Pirates, in reference to the Time fit to be allow, d them to come in, and make Affidavit, as thereby directed; we offered to his Majesty divers Considerations relating to Pirates: Upon which his Majesty was pleased to issue his late Proclamation of the 6th Instant.

There is a constant Return of Business every Year relating to the Trade and Fishery of Newfoundland:; and, from the Commodore of tlfe last Convoy, we received an Account of the Course and Progress thereof, with particular Respect to the Execution of the late Act of Parliament to encourage that Trade, in Answer to what was given him in Charge; and we have prepared other Instructions and Dispatches to the Commodore of the Convoy now going thither, for the rectifying several Abuses, and making further Inquiries into the State of the Trade and Fishery of his Majesty's Subjects there, and into that of the French in those Seas.

We have likewise taken again into Consideration the properest Methods of employing the Poor; but having, the last Session, represented to the House, That, for the making the Poor useful, and not burdensome, to the Publick, we had made divers Proposals, how we conceived that Work might be best effected; and having tdso, in pursuance of an Order of a Committee of the House at the End of the last Session, prepared an Abstract of all the Laws now in Force relating to the Poor, together with the Draught of a Bill, whereby they might be reduced into One Law, and laid the same before the Committee; we found, that we could not make a further Progress on that Subject, until this Honourable House shall have proceeded thereupon.

As to his Majesty's Plantations in America, we have made several Representations in Defence of his Majesty's Right to such of them as have been at any time claimed by the French, or other Foreigners; and having formerly set forth his Majesty's Title to the Island of Tobago, One of the Caribbe Islands in the Neighbourhood of Barbadoes, we have since offered to his Majesty such Considerations as put a Stop to the Design 01 some Persons here, who, under a Pretence of an Agreement with the Duke of Courland's Envoj, were contriving to settle the said Island under the Title and Protection of that Prince; and have thereby prevented the great Prejudice such a Settlement would have caused to the Island of Barbadoes, and the Trade of this Kingdom.

Having also formerly, in a Report to their Excellencies the Lords Justices, represented his Majesty's Right of Sovereignty over the Island of Sta; Lucia in the same Neighbourhood; and Directions having accordingly been given to the Governor of Barbadoes for maintaining the same: Upon which, the French Ambassador complained to his Majesty of those Proceedings; and insisted upon the Fi'ench King's Right to that Island; we again laid before his Majesty a full Deduction of his Majesty's Title to the said Island, in Answer to the French Pretensions.

The said Ambassador having likewise presented to his Majesty a Memorial, complaining of a Design alleged by him to be carrying on by some of the Inhabitants of Barbadoes, in order to the Settling of the Island of Domi* nico, another of the Caribbe Islands; and having therein questioned the Right of the English to the said Island,

duly subservient and useful to England; we have humbly offered our Opinion, That the Charters of the several Proprietors and others, intitling them to a Right of Government, should be reassumed to the Crown, and these Colonies put into the same State and Dependency as those of his Majesty's other Plantations, without further Prejudice to every Man's particular Property and Freehold; which, we conceive, cannot otherwise be well effected, than by the legislative Power of this Kingdom.

Upon Occasion of several Complaints relating to the Administration of Justice in Barbadoes, we have given Directions for the more regular Holding of the Courts of Justice in that Island, and transmitting to us such Account of their Proceedings, as will tend to the Reforming of all Neglects and Irregularities in those Courts: We have also prepared Letters for his Majesty's Royal Signature, which have accordingly been dispatched, containing particular Commands to the Governor and Council of the said Island; for redressing all Miscarriages of that kind, and preventing Complaints of the like Nature.

And a Petition having been presented to his Majesty by the Agents of that Island, and other Persons having an Interest there; wherein they set forth the present Condition of that Island; and pray, That the Duty or Impost of 4f per Cent, arising the re upon all dead Commodities exported from that Island, may be applied to the Reparation of the Forts, and other Uses; we laid before his Majesty the State of that Matter, expressing particularly the several Grounds and Considerations upon which the said Duty was given, and the Application that has been lately made thereof to the Uses mentioned in a late Act of Parliament for granting to his Majesty certain Duties, for the necessary Expence of his Majesty's Houshold, and other necessary Occasions: Further representing to his Majesty, That the Inhabitants of Barbadoes have expressed great Zeal, and been at considerable Expence, in his Ma-imperfectly: ~ jestys Service, during the late War; and that the said

Upon a Controversy between his Majesty's Province of New York and the Charter Government of Connecticut Colony in New England, relating to their Boundaries; we examined the Pretensions of both Sides; and reported to his Majesty the State thereof, together with Draughts of Letters for his Royal Signature, and an Instrument proper for the determining and settling those Boundaries.

We have, on many Occasions, represented to his Majesty, as we did likewise, in our last Report, to the late House of Commons, the State of such Plantations in America, as are under the Government of Proprietors and Charters; and how inconsistent these Governments are with the Trade and Welfare of this Kingdom:

That these Colonies, in general, have no ways answered the chief Design, for which such large Tracts of Land, and such Privileges and Immunities, were granted by the Crown:

That they have not conformed themselves to the several Acts of Parliament for regulating Trade and Navigation, to which they ought to pay the same Obedience, and submit to the same Restriction, as the other Plantations, which are subject to his Majesty's immediate Government; though, on the contrary, in most of these Propriety and Charter Governments, the Governors have not applied themselves to his Majesty for his Approbation, nor have taken the Oaths required by the Acts of Trade; both which Qualifications are made necessary by the late Act for preventing Frauds, and regulating Abuses in the Plantation Trade:

That they have assumed to themselves a Power to make Laws, contrary and repugnant to the Laws of England, and directly prejudicial to our Trade, some of them having refused to send hither such Laws as they have there enacted; and others having sent them, but

tj W. III. $9° Martii. ' 449

done with regard to the present Circumstances of that Province s From all which we are expecting a good Effect.

And having therein referred the Subject of Masts, and other Ship Timber, to be considered apart, because of the Relation it might have to other Plantations as well as to New York) we soon after laid before their Excellencies a separate Report thereupon; setting forth the State of his Majesty's Woods in those Parts; the great Waste and Spoil that is daily committed in them, by converting Oaks and Pines of the largest Dimensions into Pipe Staves and Deal Boards; the great Consumption likewise of Timber by a Trade to Spaine and Portugall, which is not prohibited by Law'; and the Advantages that may be drawn from those Woods to England, if there was a due Provision by Laws, which we accordingly proposed to be made; and having thereupon received his Majesty's Directions, we prepared a Letter for his Royal Signature to the Earl of Belbmont, requiring him, That he would use his Endeavours with the Assemblies there to pass Acts proper for that End; or, in case he could not prevail with them to do what is requisite, that he would report particularly what may be fit to be done here: Which Letter has been sent to his Lordship.

The Northern Frontiers of the Province of New Yw'k being the most advanced of any of his Majesty's Plantations towards Canada, and the chief Security of the neighbouring Plantations against an Enemy depending upon the Preservation of those Frontiers, which that Province is not alone able to provide for, we have, upon several Occasions, represented what seemed to us necessary for that Service; and particularly upon an Information from the Earl of Belbmont that all the Colonies of New England were alarmed, and under great Apprehensions, from the Intelligence given them, on all Sides, of a general Insurrection and Rebellion intended by the neighbouring In-(Hans, unto which they had been secretly instigated by the indirect Practices and malicious Insinuations of the French of Canada; and that our Five Nations of New York Indians were corrupted by those Artifices, and seemed inclining to shake off their Dependence on the Crown of England\ and to associate with the other Indians in that Insurrection; we humbly offered, That a Supply of Money might be sent towards the Building and Repairing of Forts in the Frontiers of New York, together with Presents for our Five Nations of Indians in those Parts, and Recruits for the Forces there.

We further humbly proposed to his Majesty, That the other Colonies which are so much concerned in the Security of those Frontiers, should be required to contribute, towards the Building and Repairing of their Forts, a certain Sum, in reasonable Proportions, according to a Scheme that we laid before his Majesty, together with Letters for his Royal Signature; which have accordingly been dispatched.

And his Majesty has been pleased, out of his Royal Bounty, to give 2,500 /. towards the Charge of Forts; to send Presents for our Five Nations of Indians, to the Value of 800 /.; and to recruit the Soldiers at New York, who were but 1 So, with Men from hence to make them up 400.

The Defence and Security of the Plantations in general being a Matter of the greatest Importance to the Trade of this Nation, we have not confined ourselves to what relates to the Province of New York, but have also, in Two other Representations, laid before his Majesty the State of all his Plantations, both in the Islands and in the Continent of America, with particular Relation to the Forts, Fortifications, and Stores of War, now there; and what may be further necessary for the Defence of those Plantations with regard to the present Conjuncture: Which Representations, or any others afore-mentioned, we are ready to lay before this Honourable House? when the same shall be required; and to explain more at large such Particulars therein, as have fallen under our Consideration, in reference to Trade, and the Security of his Majesty's foreign Dominions.

A Petition of several Persons, on behalf of themselves and many others, who advanced to his Majesty 564,7001. on the Credit of an Act of Parliament made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of his Majesty's Reign, for granting to his Majesty certain Rates and Duties on Stone, Glass, and Karthern Ware, Coals and Culm, for the Term of Five Years, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners did lately petition this House, shewing, That their said Fund was taken from them without their Consent; and that they are left destitute of any Security for Repayment of their Money: Which Petition was referred to the Committee of the whole House, for a Supply to his Majesty; who reported their Resolution; to which the House disagreed, with Intent, as the Petitioners hope, to make them some effectual Provision for discharging the said Debt: And praying, that their deplorable Case may be again taken into Consideration, and, if the House think fit to grant them the Continuance of the Duties on Coals and Culm for a sufficient Term of Years, after the Expiration of the Time granted by Act of Parliament to others; or else to make the Petitioners other effectual Provision for the Payment of so just a Debt, and Interest

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, That he will please to give Order, that Captain may be proceeded against according to Law'.

the County of Worcester, was presented to the ManufaC House, and read; setting forth, That, though many good tures' Laws had been made to prevent the Exportation of Wool; and the Government hath been at great Charges in maintaining divers Vessels for that Purpose; yet, through the Neglect or Connivance of those concerned in those Vessels, as it is feared, many thousand Packs of Wool have, within these Two last Years, been exported into France; which Practice hath much decayed our Woollen Manufactures, and, if not speedily prevented, will destroy the same, and consequently ruin the Manufactures: v And praying, That Inspections may be made into the Transporting of Wool; and that effectual Means may be used to prevent the same for the future, and to maintain the Good of the Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom.

The Resolution of the States General, 4th April 1701, "about Succours.

The Translation of the Envoy of the States Generals Memorial, March the 30th 1701.

And the said Message was read by Mr. Speaker; and is as folio we th; viz.

William R.

HIS Majesty having received an Account from Mr. Stanhope, his Envoy Extraordinary at the Hague, That the French Ambassador there had declared to the Pensionary, that the King his Master had no other Answer to return to the Demands made by the States General of the United Provinces, than that he is ready to renew and confirm the Treaty of Rysuick, it being alljhe Security the States are to expect; and that he has no Orders to give any Answer to his Majesty's said Envoy; but, if his Majesty has any thing to demand, it may be done by his Ambassador at Paris, or to the French Minister at London; and that he has no Commission to treat with any but the States: And his Majesty having also received Two Resolutions of the States, and a Memorial from their Envoy here, relating to the Ships they are sending to join his Majesty's Fleet, and the Succours they desire may be hastened to them, by virtue of the Treaty made the 3d of March 1677: His Majesty has thought fit to communicate the Whole to this House, that they may be particularly informed of the present State of Affairs abroad, where the Negociation seems to be at an End, by the positive Answer the French Ambassador has given to the States: Which his Majesty recommends to the serious Consideration of this House, as a Matter of the greatest Weight and Consequence; and desires that they will give his Majesty such Advice thereupon, as may be for our own Security, and that of the States General, and the Peace of Europe

Kensington, the 31st Day of March 1701.

And the Titles of the said Extract, and Translations, were read.

And the said Extract, and Translations, are as follow;

viz.

The said Extract.

The Sieur Councillor Pensionary Hcinsiits has reported to the Assembly, That the Count dAvau.r, Ambassador Extraordinary of the most Christian King, came to him to let him know, that the Courier he had sent into France with the Propositions delivered to him by the Deputies of their High and Mightinesses, concerning the Preservation of the publick Peace, and the Security of these States, being returned, has brought Orders to the Count dAvaux, to tell the Sieur Councillor Pensionary, That his most Christian Majesty, to shew his Inclination for Peace, was ready to renew the Treaties of Ryswiek, made in the Year 1697; and that the said Count d'Avaux had desired him to make Report thereof, and desire an Answer thereupon as soon as possible: Whereupon, Deliberation being had, it was thought good, and agreed, to require and give Order to the Sieur A Essen, and other Deputies of their High and Mightinesses for foreign Affairs, to impart and communicate the same to Mr. Stanhope, Envoy Extraordinary of his Majesty of Great Britain, and to enter into Conference with him thereupon.

Extract of the Register of the Resolutions of the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Lore Countries.

Monday 4th April 1701.

After previous Deliberation, it has been thought fit, and is concluded, to require and commission the Sieur dEssen, and other Deputies of their High and Mighty Lordships for the foreign Affairs, to enter into Conference with Mr. Stanhope, the Envoy Extraordinary of his Majesty of Great Britain; and to represent to him, that as soon as their Lordships iliad Notice of the Demand made by him the said Mr. Stanhope, in another Conference, in the Name, and by the Order, of his said Majesty, that they would give the necessary Orders for fitting out the Ships of War that his Majesty might require, in case of Necessity, for his Assistance, according to the Treaties between his said Majesty and their High and Mightinesses, they immediately took care to have the said Ships equipped, so that they are, at this time, most of them ready: That their Lordships have given Orders to the Admiralties, to send those Ships, with the first fair Wind, to their Rendezvous, in order to join his Majesty's Fleet: That their Lordships having on their Side prayed his Majesty, by the Sieur Gcldtrmansen, their Envoy Extraordinary, that he w ould be pleased, in Consideration of the present J uncture of Affairs, to have in Readiness the Succour agreed on by the Treaties to be sent hither to the Assistance of their Lordships, in case they were attacked, they had understood, with great Satisfaction, the good Disposition his Majesty was in to perforin the Treaties, and consequently to send them the Assistance demanded: The Case now happening, and their High Mightinesses seeing daily more Troops approaching to their Frontiers, and the Preparations for War that are making in their Neighbourhood, they cannot but apprehend their Country may suddenly be assaulted; and that, in such Case, the time might be too short to bring over hither the said Succours with so much Expedition as Necessity might require: And as their High and Mightinesses did not only give Directions immediately for fitting out the Men of War required by his Majesty, but also ordered them to set Sail forthwith, to join his Majesty's Fleet; they hope, for the Reasons before-mentioned, his Majesty will make no difficulty to send them likewise, immediately, the 10,000 Men for their Assistance, by virtue of the Treaty of the Third of March One thousand Six hundred and Seventy-seven-eight: And therefore the said Deputies shall desire the said Mr. Stanhope to employ his good Offices, that the said Ten thousand Men may be sent hither, and the 'sooner the better.

The said Translation of the Envoy of the States Generals Memorial, March the 30th, 1701.

The underwritten Envoy Extraordinary of the States General of the United Provinces has received Orders to represent, with very great Respect, to your Majesty, That your Minister at the Hague having, on your Majesty's behalf, demanded, that the Ships of War, wherewith they arc obliged, by virtue of the Treaties, to assist your Majesty, might be forthwith equipped, they had immediately given the necessary Orders for that Purpose; so that most of the said Vessels are actually ready, with Directions to set Sail, and join your Majesty's Fleet, with the first fair Wind.

Their High and Mightinesses having also, on their Side, desired of your Majesty by the Underwritten, That you would be pleased, in Consideration of the present Juncture, to have in a Readiness the Succours stipulated by the Treaty of the Third of March 1677-8; and having, with

Seat Satisfaction, understood your Majesty's favourable isposition in that Matter; they have given Orders to the Underwritten to represent anew to your Majesty, That the Preparations for War daily increasing in their Neighbourhood, as well as the Number of Troops which approach their Frontiers, they think there is just Reason to apprehend they shall suddenly be attacked; in which Case, your Majesty's Succours could not arrive so soon as Necessity might require; which obliges them to desire your Majesty to send to them, without any further Delay, the Ten thousand Men stipulated by the said Treaty: And they the rather hope for it, since, on their Part, they have not only made ready the Ships of War which they are obliged to furnish, but have also actually given Order for their joining your Majesty's Fleet.

London, March 30th, 1701.

It appearing by your Lordship's Journal, That your Lordships have received Information of some Transactions between the Earl of Portland and Mr. Secretary Vernon, relating to the Partition of the Spanish Monarchy, the Commons, having the said Matter under their Consideration, desire your Lordships will be pleased to communicate to the Commons, what Informations your Lordships have had of any Transactions relating to any Negotiations, or Treaties of Partition, of the Spanish Monarchy, by Letters or otherwise; and the Commons are fully assured, That your Lordships will readily concur in assisting them in this Inquiry, which they conceive absolutely necessary for the Safety and Honour of this Kingdom, and the Preservation of the Peace of Europe.

Sir Rowland Gwyn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, tire Matter, touching the Election for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petitions of George Morley Esquire, and of several Inhabitants of Hindon, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Reynolds Calthrop Esquire, to serve for the said Borough of Hindon:

That the Candidates, at the said Election, were Sir James Howe, Mr. Calthrop, and the Petitioner: But the Election of Sir Janies Hemet was not drawn into Question.

Upon the Poll there was, for

Mr. Calthrop - - 70.

Mr. Morley - - 62.

That the Petitioner insisted, That the Right of Election was in the Bailiff, Burgesses, and such Inhabitants only, fis pay Scotland Lot: The Sitting Member insisted, That the Right of Election was in the Bailiff, Burgesses, and Inhabitants not receiving Alms.

The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That the Law did exclude such from voting in Elections, who were not contributory to the common Charge of the Borough: And called,

Edward Lamb: Who said, That himself, his Father, and Grandfather, were born in Hindon; and that he had heard his Father and Grandfather say, That Parliament-men were to be chosen by the Lot and Scot Men; but acknowledged, that, during his time, the Inhabitants at large had voted.

That the Petitioner's Counsel produced Three Indentures of Returns; viz.

2 and 3 PA. and M.

1 Eliz.

43 Eliz.

Which mention, That the Bailiff and Burgesses had elected.

That tire Counsel for the Sitting Member insisted, That Hindon was a Borough by Prescription; and that Burgesses and Inhabitants are synonimous Terms; and that all the Inhabitants had a natural Right, unless the other Side could shew the Usage to the contrary: And, to prove the Usage to be with the SittingM ember, they called,

Robert Garrat: Who said, He had known the Elections of Parliament-men for Hindon for more than 40 Years; and that all the Inhabitants w ho did not receive Alms, have, during his time, voted in such Elections.

That the Committee, having considered the Evidence, and what had been argued by the Counsel of both Sides, came to this Resolution;

Rcsohed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Tliatthe Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hindon is in the Bailiff, Burgesses, and such Inhabitants only as pay Scotland Lot.

The Poors Rate for the Borough of Hindon was produced: And it appeared, that the Petitioner had the Majority of Voters who paid Scotland Lot.

The Sitting Member's Counsel insisted, That several Persons who had voted for the" Sitting Member had been formerly in the Poors Rate, and were of Ability, and ought to have been inserted in tire Rate; and therefore prayed they "might be allowed to them as good Voters; find offered to call Evidence as to Fact:

But that the Committee were of Opinion that they

were excluded by the former Vote, and.....not think fit to hear Evidence touching that Matter.

And, upon the whole Matter, came to these Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Reynolds Calthrop Esquire is not duly elected a Bur-

gss to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of indon, in the County of Wilts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee

That George Morley Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Hindon.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That it be re-committed.

Ordered, That the Matter, upon the Re-commitment, be heard before the Committee of Privileges and Elections upon this Day Three Weeks.

Resolved, That the Resolution, Yesterday, of the Address tot* Advice of this House, given to his Majesty, be presented presented by to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council.

But the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That the Assessment was made in favour of the Sitting Member.

And, as to that Matter, it appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Seward, Mr. Caleb Powell, Mr. Spencer, Richard Vaughan, and Mr. Clark;

That the Lew n, or Poors Rate, is made about Easter: And Seward and Powell said, Several were left out of the present Lewn, that were in before; and that neither Mr. Harley nor Mr. Colt was present when it was made; but the Magistrates of the Town appeared to be Friends of Mr. Colt's, and the Assessors signed the Lewn between Twelve and One a Clock at Night: And it was likewise testified, That, upon Complaint, some were put in; and afterwards Mr. Harley signed the Lewn.

That Mr. Harley desired a Copy of the Lewn of Mun the Overseer; which he allowed Mr. Harley's Man to write; but, before he had finished it, the said Mun took the Lewn from him, and refused to let Mr. Harley have a Copy, without paying Five Shillings, which, he said, was his Fee for it: That, afterwards, Caleb Powell demanded a Copy of the Lewn, producing the Order of the Committee for it; but Mun said, He did not value the Order, and he should not have it: Yet afterwards Mun came to Mr. Powel's House, desiring to speak with him in the Morning; and he, being a-bed, bid his Wife ask the said Mun his Business; and, if he had the Lewn, to leave it; but Mun went away, and did not leave the Lewn.

That, as to the Matter in relation to the Window Tax, it was insisted, by the Petitioners Counsel, That, by the Statute for laying a Duty upon Houses, the Dwelling-houses of such Persons, as, by reason of their Poverty, are exempted from paying to Church and Poor, are discharged from the Duties granted by that Act: And that the Magistrates of Leominster had, to gain Votes for Mr. Colt, excused 52 Persons from paying to the said Tax: And, for that, they called Mr. John Burt: Who said, He was Deputy Surveyor of the Window Tax last Year at Leominster; and that, about August was Twelve-months, be had charged 52 Persons Vo L. 13.

ham, Mr. Thompkins, and Mr. Thomas Price the Town Clerk; of which Persons Names he delivered in a List.

Justice Bangham, and some others, sent for him by the Serjeant of the Town, and asked for his Vote for Mr. Colt; and asked him if he paid to the Light-money; to which he answered, that he did: The said Justice Bangham said, He would ease him of it, if he would vote for Mr. Colt.

William Davis said, That Mr. Colt asked him for his Vote; and he told him, He had promised it: Afterwards Mr. Colt and Mr. Bangham, and he, were together; and Mr. Bangham asked him for his Vote; and Mr. Colt said, There is Ten Shillings Light-money to pay, and now is the Time to help yourself, and, if you have Occasion, make use of me: However, he acknowledged he had but Five Windows, and was never charged to that Tax. Royal A Petition of the Company of the Royal Fishery of

Fishery. England was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That King Charles the Second, by his Letters Patents, dated in the 29th Year of his Reign, did grant unto the Petitioners, and their Successors, divers Privileges and Immunities, for Encouragement of their Undertakings: That the said Company have, ever since, been at great Expence, and Loss of Time, in building and fitting out of Ships to Sea, and in employing and breeding up of several able Seamen: But, forasmuch as the said Company are convinced, as well by their own Experience and Losses, as from the Success others have heretofore had in pursuing the said Trade of Fishing, that the same cannot be carried on, and made considerable, in England, without further Privileges and Immunities, and an Exemption of the Duty of Salt spent upon Fish, as in Times past: And praying a speedy Consideration of the Premises, and an Encouragement of the said Trade.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do consider of the most effectual Means to promote the Fishery Trade of England; and report the same to the House: And it is referred to Sir Rowland Gwynne, Mr. Bromley, Sir Robert Davers, Mr Taylor, Mr. Verney, Sir Samuel Bernardiston, Mr. England, Mr. Fuller, Mr. Prideaux, Sir Fr. Colonel Byerly reported from the Committee appointed Hospitals, to inquire into the Abuses committed in the Revenues of &c. Hospitals; and report their Opinion, how the same may be remedied for the future; That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Abuses committed in the Management of all Grants, Gifts of Tenements and Hereditaments, and other Augmentations, limited or appointed for charitable Uses, proceeds from the undue and irregular Management of the same, by the Neglect of taking due Surveys of all Hereditaments or Augmentations given for such Uses; which may be redressed by appointing a better and more proper Method of Visitation, or inspecting the Revenues and Management of Hospitals or Charities.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Lord Chancellor, or Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, for the Time being, upon Application from the Justices of the Peace, at their General Quarter Sessions,

A Petition of several of the Inhabitants of the City of Rochester, in the County of Kent, on behalf of themselves, and many others, Inhabitants of the said City, and Places adjacent, who have quartered and entertained sick and wounded Seamen', was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in October 1697, there was due to the Petitioners, on that Service, upwards of 13,000l.; which, by Two several Payments since, is reduced to near 7,000l.; the Want whereof hath rendered the Petitioners uncapable of providing Quarters, or other Entertainment, for the sick and wounded Seamen for the future: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Uratred, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply to be granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of the Merchants trading to the English Plantations in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That great Abuses are practised on his Majesty's Subjects, by Societies of ill Men, who, by Insinuations and Promises, betray them to go as Servants to the Plantations; and also others, that offer themselves to go as Servants, with Design to embroil the Persons concerned, and get Money of them; whereby great Trouble often happens to Merchants, and Owners of Ships: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for Prevention of all evil Practices; and for the better Security of Merchants, Owners and Commanders of Ships, in the Transportation of Servants to the English Pantations in America.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Yates, Mr. Harley, Sir Edward Seymour, Sir Jeff. And also a Paper, although not signed by the Earl of Portland\ yet was laid before their Lordships by him.

And that there were some Questions asked by the Lords: To which there was this Answer:

At the Beginning of the Summer of the Year 1699, when I was in Holland, at my Country House; and when the King would have me concerned in the Negotiating of this Treaty with the Emperor, the French King, and the States; being very unwilling to meddle with Business again, from which I wa^ retired; before I vrould engage myself,

I advised with my Friends in Holland', and writ into England to Mr. Secretary Vernon, as my particular Friend, Whether it was advisable for me to engage in Business again? To which Mr. Vernon answered, inSubstance, That this would not engage me but for a little while: That I being upon the Place, and generally acquainted with the foreign Ministers, it would be easier for the King, and propercr for me to be employed in it, than any body else, that must be otherwise sent for on purpose.

The Earl of Portland being desired by the Lord Somers, tv ith the Leave of the House, to declare, if he pleased, Whether the Lord Somers s Name was mentioned in the Letter he received from Mr. Secretary Vernon;

The Earl of Portland declared, That if he had remembered any such Thing in the Letter, and not inserted it in the Paper which he had delivered to the House, he should have thought he had deceived the House.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Repbrt be adjourned until Tomorrow Morning.

Upon the Petition of Charles Goreing Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Robert Fagg to serve for the Borough of Steyning:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms:

That upon the Whole, there was,

For Sir Robert Fagg, 33.

For the Petitioner, 30.

But that the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That they should take off so many from Sir Robert Faggs Poll, as would make the Petitioner a Majority:

And that they also insisted, That there was Treating and Bribery on behalf of Sir Robert Fagg:

That there was at the time of the Poll, excepted to* of those that voted for Sir Robert Fagg, 8; viz. Nicolas JVolgar, Mich. Longmore, John Finch, Samuel Cox,

John Balcombe senior, John Read, George Goddard, and John Milks:

And that there was, at the time of the Poll, excepted to, of those that voted for the Petitioner, 4; viz. JValted Parson, Nicholas Killick, Richard Hedger, and Jl alter Hilman:

That there is at Sleyning a Charity called the White Horse Charity, which is 5/. a Year, received by certain Trustees, and lefttotheDistribution of the Churchwardens:

And a Certificate w'as produced, under the Hand of James Chat ten, Churchwarden, dated the 27 th of March last; by which it appeared. That at Easter last, John Grovesi John Bancombe senior, John Read, John Heasman, John Finch, John Mills, Thomas Glover, Geo. Goddart, had received of that Charity.

Jos. Mamer said, That Nicholas JVolgar lives in Part of a House divided about Six or Seven Years ago: That jVillet had the other Part: But it was acknowledged, That JVolgar is Headborough, and pays to Church and Poor:

Jos. JVarner and Grome said, That Samuel Cox has a House and Mill out of the Borough, where he lives; but it is acknowledged, That he had a House of his own in the Borough, with some Goods in it: That Cox was Overseer, in respect of his living out of the Borough; and was excused from the Rate about Four Years ago, at his Request: However it was acknowledged he was in the present Rate for the said House, as an empty House; and Grome said, He intended to ask for it.

That, as to Threats und Bribery;

Walter Parsons said, That he, and Several others, he Relieves, to the Number of above 20 Electors, were at Sir Robert Fagg's the Evening before the Election, being asked to go thither by John Read, John Balcombe senior, and Mr. Charles Fagg; where there was Beef and Mutton, and other Provisions for40 Men; bathe said, They had no Discourse about the Election.

Nic. Killick said, He was present at Sir Robert Fagg's^ at two Entertainments: One was at the time spoken of by Parsons; and the other was about a Week before the Election, when there were about 13 Voters: And John Ready at both times, asked him for his Vote for Sir Roben Fagg; and told him, If he did, he should have Work at 12 d. a Day, besides Meat and Drink: And Paching told the said Killick, If he would be for Sir Robert Fagg, he should have aNaile of Beef, and a Loaf, every Week: And Littington told him, If he would vote for Sir Robert Fagg, there would be two Rings, one for him, another for his Wife.

Thomas Mitchell said, he had a great many Offers by John Read and Littington, on account of Beef and Bread: And Littington told him, if he w'ould vote for Sir Robert Foggy he and his Wife should each of them have a Ring.

That the Counsel for the Sitting Member said, They would justify their own Votes, and take off Eight from the Petitioners Poll: But they proceeded fitst upon the Point of Bribery: And called John Pat chin: Who said, That Mr. Goreing came to his Shop, and agreed to give him a Guinea for a Gun: And afterwards he, said Patching met Mr. Goreing, and asked hiiri fof the Guinea: Upon which Mr. Goreing asked, How many Guineas he should give him to stand plum: And he, said Patchin, answering Five, Mr. Goreing' put his Hand in his Pocket, and gave him a double Louis-d or for a Coffee-mill, and his Vote, in Part of Five Guineas; but he never promised Mr. Goreing his Vote; And one Wallis told him, He had Occasion for a good Jack; and he would give him 5/. more for it, if he would vote for Mr. Goreing.

Thomas Grover said, That he was at Mr. Hunt's, and Mr. Goreing called him away: But Mr. Hunt told him, That Mr. Goreing would give him Four4 Guineas for his Vote: And Mr. Goreing said, What you say, I will stand to.

Richard Hunt denied, that he offered Grower any thing for his Vote; but said Mr. Goreing desired him to offer Thomas Grover Four or Five Guineas for his Vote; which he told Grover.

John Finch said, That Mi4. Grover, Three Days before the Election, promised him Two Guineas for his Vote; and that there was Half a Dozen Bottles of Wine drank at his House, at Mr. Goreing's Charge: And that. who drank of it but himself, voted for Mr. Goreing: But he said, Finch w as excepted to by Mr. Goreing, at the time of the Poll, as having no Vote in the Election.

John Double said, He see Mr. Goreing give some Money to Nicholas Gillick, which he heard Gillick's Wife afterwards say was 40 s.; and at the same time Mr. Goreing gave Gillick s Child Half a Crow n.

Longmore said, That Mr. Goreing, on the Election Day, came to him, and desired his Vote; and said, He had Work to do; and if he would vote for him, the said Mr. Goreing, he should have it all; and should have 5/. beforehand, if he questioned his Pay: And that, Three Or Four Days before the Election, he drank W'ine and strong Drink with Mr. Goreing, and did not pay.

A Petition of the freeholders and Miners within the j. Five Parishes of Ashover, Matlock, Darley, Bonsall, and Carrington> in the County of Derby, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by a Petition preferred to this House, by divers Ministers in the County of Derby, for Leave to bring in a Bill for preventing vexatious Suits; and settling the Tythes of Lead-ore there; it is suggested, That there is a Custom in the said County for the Payment of Lead-ore in Kind to the several Parsons, Vicars, Owners of Rectories Appropriate or Impropriate, or other Proprietors, in the said County; and that the same hath been generally acknowledged by the Owners of Lead-mines through the said County; and that* the same hath been confirmed by Decrees in Chancery and Exchequer, and Verdicts at Law'; and that, by the same Verdicts, the said customary Duty is found to extend to the whole County: That the Petitioners do affirm there was never any Tythe Lead-ore, or Composition for the same, paid for any the said Five Parishes abovesaid, within the Memory of Man; and that, when several of the Predecessors of the present Parsons or Vicars of the said Five Parishes have sued in the Exchequer and Duchy Courts for Tythe Lead-ore, upon Suggestion, that there was a Custom to pay Tythe of Lead-ore, Tryals at Law have been directed to try the Custom, and Verdicts passed against the same, and the Bills in the said Courts dismissed: That there hath been no Suit depending for Tythes these 20 Years: That if the Bill should pass into an Act, it w'ould Vox.. 13.

Sir Rowland Gwyn reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, touching the Complaint of a Breach of Privilege in arresting John Carter, Servant of Sir Edward Seijnwur Baronet, a Member of this House; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow'; viz.

That the Committee had examined the said

John Carter: Who testified that Mr. James Buckly, and his Father, before the last Election of Burgesses to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Totnesse, had threatened him, if he opposed his Interest, that he should be arrested in an Action of Scandalum Magnatum, at the Suit of the Duke of Bolton: That, accordingly, since the Election, the said James Buckley had sent for Two Writs against him; and he was actually arrested upon the 27th Day of March last: That he was arrested by the said John Whitborough: Who told him, He must carry hini through the Town Prisoner; and then he was to have Three Guineas, or otherwise he was to have but One: And that he was carried Prisoner through the Town; and Whitborcrw afterwards told him, He had received Three Guineas: And the said John Cart cr further said, That he had served the Lady Seymour; and since her Death, hath served Sir Edward Seymour as his Bailiff, and collects his Rents, and has a Salary.

And that the Committee came to these Resolutions;

Vol. 13.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, '

That John Whitborow, of Exon, Bailiff, having arrested John Carter, a menial Servant to Sir Edzvarcl Seymour Baronet, a Member of this House, during the Privilege of Parliament, is guilty of a Breach of Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That James Buckley junior, an Attorney, being concerned in the arresting of John Carter, a Servant to Sir Edward Seymour Baronet, a Member of this House, during the Privilege of Parliament, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

At Loo, the of August 1698.

I imparted to you, before I left England, rlh?X\n France there was expressed to my Lord Portland some Inclination to come to Agreement with me, concerning the Succession of the King of Spain; since which, Count Tul-lardhdOh mentioned it to me; and hath made Propositions, the Particulars of which my Lord Portland will write to Vernon, to whom I have given Orders not to communicate them to any other beside yourself; and to leave to your Judgment, to whom else you would think proper to impart them; To the End T might know your Opinions upon so important an Affair, and which requires the greatest Secrecy, if it be fit this Negotiation should be carried on, there's no Time to be lost; and you must send me the full Powers, under the Great Seal, with the Names

the Commission one Day. I have put the Seal to it without expecting the Return of the Warrant which Mr. Secretary sent; begging of your Majesty, that it may be soon transmitted to myself, or to Mr. Secretary, so as it may not be known but that I had it in time. You wilt be pleased to observe, that Two Persons, as the Commission is drawn, must be named in it; but the Powers may be executed by either of them; I suppose your Majesty will not think it proper to name Commissioners w ho are not English, or naturalized, in an Affair of this Nature.

I pray God give your Majesty Honour and Success in all your Undertakings! I am, with the utmost Duty and Respect,

Sir,

Your Majesty's most dutiful, and

most obedient SubjecLand Servant

The Commission is wrote by Mr. Secretary; and I have had it sealed in such a manner, that no Creature has fee least Knowledge of the Thing, besides the Persons already named.

Sir Rowland Gwynne, according to Order, reported, from the said Committee, the Matter touching the said Election, and the Resolutions of fee Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at fee Clerk's Table; Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir Wiltoughby Hickman Baronet, complaining of an undue Election of Thomas While Esquire, to serve for the Borough of East Retford:

That

That the First Thing that came in question before the Committee, was, the Right of Election:

The Petitioners Counsel insisted, That the Right was in the Burgesses being Freemen at large; the Sitting Members Counsel insisting, That the Right was only in the Freemen resident within the Borough.

Upon the Poll, there was,

For the Sitting Member, 24.

For the Petitioner, - 17.

That the Petitioner, as to the Right of Election, called several Witnesses:

William Bunby said, That Sir Edward Ncvill, though not resident, voted above 14 Years ago, and in several Elections, and continued an Alderman: That his Brother Richard Bunby continued Auditor, and did vote when not resident:

That Razcson was out of Town above a Year and Day, and voted at last Election, and had been a Soldier for 3 Years; however it was acknowdeged, That his Wife lived in Town: That William Gabitus voted, a Dozen Years ago, in the Election of an Alderman, or junior Bailiff; and Robert Mason voted the last Election before this.

Laurence King said, That, in King Charles the 2d s Time, John Ryley had lived above a Year and Half out of Town, at JVheatly; and.was sent for to vote; and his Vote was not questioned.

JVm. Moody said, That William Atkinson continued Alderman when he lived out of Town, and has voted for Officers; but himself had lived out of Town Twenty Years.

That the Petitioners insisted further, That the nonresident Burgesses were only excluded by an Order of the Corporation.

And they produced an Order, in an ancient Book, made by the Bailiffs and Aldermen, by which several Persons, not resident within the Borough, are, by Name, disabled and exempted from giving of any Voices at or for any Election or Elections whatsoever: And, in the same Order, it is order&d, established, and decreed, by the Bailiffs, and the Aldermen, That if any Burgess or Burgesses of the said Borough shall, at any time then after, remove his or their Dwelling or Dwellings forth of the Liberties of the said Borough, and so shall continue the same for the space of One whole Year; that then all and every such Burgess and Burgesses shall from thenceforth be and stand likewise disabled and exempted from giving of any Voice or Voices at or for any Election or Elections whatsoever within the said Borough.

That the Sitting Members Counsel insisted, That the Non-residents had no Vote: And called,

Richard Brownlowe; who was Apprentice at East Retford in 51:

William Jessop; who had known East Retford 46 Years: And,

Marmaduke Cotton; who had known East Retford 40 Years:

And they said, That they took the Custom of East Retford to be, That if any Freeman w as absent a Year and Day, he did lose his Right to vote: And Jessop also said, That there was some Order to that Purpose.

And Brownlowe said, he was denied his Vote, being not resident, though he lived but Half a Mile off Ret-t ford: And Cotton said, That one Popple could never have a Vote, though he lived within a Quarter of a Mile of East Retford.

That the Committee, bpon considering the Evidence, and the Order that was produced, came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of East Retford, in the County of Nottingham, is as 'well in the Burgesses non-resident, as in the Burgesses resident, within the said. Borough.

That the Petitioner then proccded to give Evidence of such Persons w>ho had a Right, and would have voted for the Petitioner, and were refused:

And by the Town Books, it appeared, That Richard Vo l. 13.

ff ll/iam Nicholls said, That Joint Leary was the eldest Son of a Freeman; and was sworn by William Popple-welly the junior Bailiff:

.And that drew' on another Question, of the Qualifications that intitled any Person to his Freedom; the Petitioner s Counsel insisting, That all the Sons of a Freeman, and all such as had served an Apprenticeship, had a Right to their Freedoms: The Sitting Member's Counsel did not controvert the Right by Service; but insisted, That no Person had a Right by Patrimony, but the eldest Son born after his Father was a Freeman.

And thereupon the Petitioner's Counsel called several Witnesses:

JVm. Bunly said. That himself, and Robert Mason, were both younger Sons of Freemen, and, as such, were made free about 11 Years ago.

Thomas Aloody said, lie w as the Second Son of a Freeman, and served an Apprenticeship at Mansfield\ and that he, and his Two younger Brothers, were made free by his Father's Copy, paying the Court Fees.

William Aloody, the eldest Son, was called: And eon* firmed the Testimony of Thomas Aloody: And said, That William Smithy the younger Son of a Freeman, was made free; and that he never knew any Freeman's Son denied,-paying the Court Fees.

That as to the Persons so intitled, and refused;

William Nicholls said, That Martin Colton junior is the only Son of a Freeman: That Robert Ready John Hodgkin, are the eldest Sons of Freemen: That Thomas Boncfant, John Colton, and Savile Atkynsony were the Sons of Freemen; and besides that, Savile Atlcynson, has been an Apprentice: That Boncfant and Colton had demanded their Freedoms, and w>ere sworn by Poppleivell, the junior Bailiff, in 98; and that all the rest of them had, some Years before this Election, demanded their Freedoms, and w^ould have voted for the Petitioner at the Election:

That it w'as testified, That there w as a Court held since Michaelmas; but Nicholls said, These Persons durst not offer themselves then, because they had been before threatened to be laid by the Heels, if they did; and one of them, particularly Tho. Bonifanty was committed; but it w as the Election before this.

Martin Colton said, That John Stevenson and Thomas Ryley had served him 7 Years as his Apprentices, and had demanded their Freedoms, and were denied: The Objection to Stevenson was, That, by a Covenant in his Indenture, he was to serve the London Carrier as a Porter, as he did before he was bound Apprentice; and accordingly he did attend the said Carrier once a Week, as his Porter: The Objection to Ryley was, That the Indentures, by w'hich he claimed his Freedom, were out so long before he asked his Freedom, that they gave a Suspicion.

That there was also Thomas Clarke, w ho had served as an Apprentice Five years to a Freeman, wrhen his Master died; apd it was testified, That there was no other of that Trade in Tow n.

And it was said, That these Persons wrould have voted for the Petitioner.

That then the Petitioner's Counsel proceeded to give Evidence of indirect Practices:

That it did appear, That at this Election, the Doors were shut, and none but the Freemen resident admitted to be present.

That, as to the Right and Manner of making free; John Reynolds said, That the Manner of making free was, That such who desired their Freedom, come to the Bailiffs, and make their Request; who bid them acquaint the Aldermen with it; and then, if the Aldermen condescended, next Court they were admitted to their Freedom: That he had known the Corporation between 30 and 40 Years; and no younger Son, to his Knowledge, as such, has been made free. That then the Sitting Member's Counsel called Witnesses to the Point of Bribery:

Rebecca Holland said, That a Week before the Election, Mr. Nicholls sent to her Husband to drink a Glass, of Ale with him; and that John Greathead, of Worksoppe> told her, That if she could persuade her Husband to vote for Sir Willoughby Hickman, he would give him 10/..; and that Greathead told her, Mr. Nicholls had sent him to know if her Husband would vote for Sir Willoughby Hickman; and said, She might have Twenty Guineas: And that Mr. Nicholls asked her, if her Husband did not deal in wild Leather; and told her, If her Husband would be for Sir Willoughby Hickman, he should have the Income of Three Parks: That she told her Husband of it the Night before the Election; but her Husband did actually vote for Mr. White and Mr. Thornhagh.

William Holland said, That, the Saturday after Christmas, John Greathead told him, He might have Money as-well as the rest; and, if he would vote for Sir Willoughby Hiclcman, he would give him 10/. and afterwards lie invited the said Holland to his House; and told him, He had told Berry all; and if he would be for Sir Willoughby, he might have 10/. home with him.

Nicholls said, If he would vote for Sir Willoughby, lie should have it; and Luke Fryth told him, He might have the Close, if he would vote for Sir Willoughby, with 40 or 50 L to put him into Stock; which is now taken by another.

Nicholls, and offered Aloney again; and they put their Hands in their Pockets, but did not shew him any Money.

Thomas Razvson said, He was threatened if he voted for Mr. Thornhagh and Mr. White, he should be arrested: and that he did vote for them, and was arrested Three Times the Election Day.

Mr. Bromley reported from the Committee, to whom it Mas referred to draw up an Address, upon the Resolutions Yesterday, and upon the Debate of the House, to be presented to his Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is* as followeth; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

WE, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects* the Commons in Parliament assembled, do humbly crave Leave to represent to Your Majesty the great Satisfaction we have, from our late Inquiry concerning the Treaty of Partition, made in the Year One thousand Six hundred Ninety-eight, on which the Treaty in the Year One thousand Six hundred Ninety-nine was founded, to see Your Majesty's great Care of your People, and this Nation, in not entering into that Negotiation without the Advice of Your English Counsellors; and find, That John Lord Somers, on whose Judgment Your Majesty did chiefly rely in that so important Affair, did, in Concert with Edward Earl of Orford, and Charles Lord Halifax, advise Your Majesty to enter into that Treaty, of so dangerous a Consequence to the Trade and Welfare of this Nation; and who, to avoid the Censure which might justly be apprehended to fall on those who advised the same, endeavoured to insinuate, That Your Majesty, without the Advice of your Council, entered into that Treaty; and under Your sacred Name to seek Protection for what themselves had so advised: Of which Treatment of Your Majesty, we cannot but have a just Resentment: And, that they may be no longer able to deceive Your Majesty, and abuse Your People, we do humbly beseech Your Majesty, That you will be pleased to remove John Lord Somers, Edward Earl of Or ford, and Charles Lord Halifax, from Your Council and Presence for ever; as also William Earl of Portland, who transacted these Treaties, so unjust in their own Nature, and so fatal in their Consequences to this Nation, and the Peace of Europe.

And the Address being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made, by adding " And we humbly crave Leave, upon this Occasion, to " repeat our Assurances to Your Majesty, That we will " always stand by, and support, Your Majesty, to the " utmost of our Power, against all Your Enemies, both " at home and abroad And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, Nemine contradicente.

And another Amendment being proposed to be made, by adding these Words, " And to prevent the ill Consequences that seem to threaten the Peace of Europe, " and the Interest and Trade of this Nation, by the present Union of France and Spaine-,"

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Words be added;

The previous Question was put, That that Question be now put: And The House divided.
