The Answer of Edu ard Earl of Orford to the Articles of Impeachment against him was, according to Order, read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Answer of Edward Earl of Orford to the Articles exhibited against him by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of England, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against the said Earl, for high Crimes and Misdemeanors supposed to be committed by him.

'1IIE said Earl, saving to himself all Advantages of Exception to the said Articles, and of not being prejudiced by any Words, or Want of Form, in this his Answer; and saving to him all Privileges and Rights belonging to him, as One of the Peers of this Realm; for Answer to the said Articles, humbly suith,

To the 1st Article,

That lie having, for several Years, rendered lira Majesty his utmost Service and Duty as a good and loyal Subject ought to do, his Royal Majesty was graciously pleased, upon several (>ccasions, to take notice of the same; and out of his wonted Bounty, and of his free Will, was pleased to give the said Earl Two Grants; one whereof was n reversionary Grant, for Years, of some Houses, depending then upon a precedent Estate for about 29 Years; which being a reversionary Interest at so great a Distance, although the said Earl thankfully received the same from his Majesty, as his Grace and Bounty, yet the same was of no great Value; and the other of them was a Grant of the Remainder of a gross Sum, amounting to about 2.000l. a Year, for Five Years; which are the only Grants of any Manors, Messuages, Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, or Sums of Money whatsoever, which he or any in Trust for him, hath had from his Majesty; and which said Two Grants his Majesty was graciously pleased, after many Years Service, freely to bestow upon him the said Earl, without any Surprize, sinister or indirect Means; of the said Earl in obtaining the same; and which Grants, he humbly conceives, were not unusual in like Cases: The accepting whereof, he humbly hopes, w'as not anjr Violation of his Duty, or of any Trust in him the said Earl reposed.

2. To the 2d Article,

The said Earl answereth and denied), That he, at any time, converted to his own private Use any publick Money issued to him for the Service of the Navy; or that he the said Earl ever procured or had any Privy Seal, or Privy Seals, to discharge him from accounting for the! same; but saith, That he the said Earl did make up, and, upon Oath, pass his Accounts for the Monies imprest to him for the Service in this Article mentioned; which Account was legally declared, and passed, upon very strict and great Examination, by the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury; and he the said Earl hath his Quietus cst, in due Course of Law, upon the same: But the Commissioners of the Victualling Office, making soma unusual Objections to Part of the said Account, concerning some Provisions furnished to the Fleet, by the said Earl, in the King of Spains Dominions; although the same w ere truly and really had and spent by the Seamen in the Fleet, and paid for by him the said Earl; and which Objections, in like Cases, had not been made, or stood upon, nor could be reasonably expected; his Majesty was pleased to direct and order a Privy Seal, to dispense with the Form in that Particular; but the said Earl did make no Advantage to himself thereby, nor was his Majesty, or the Government, in the least defrauded therein; it appearing, upon a very strict Examination, that less Rates were allowed for the said Provisions, than had been allowed before in like Cases, or; as the said Earl is informed, hath been since allowed: And, to the latter Park of the said Article, saith, That, for the Monies by him received, as Treasurer, or Receiver General of the Navy, he hath already delivered in his Accounts; and is ready to perfect the same, according to the ordinary Method; some of them lying ready with the Auditors, to be declared; and the rest of them being made up, and delivered in to be examined, in order to be passed: And saith. After just Allow ances had, he does not believe he shall appear to be indebted upon the said Accounts; and also denies, that any Persons are Sufferers for want of their Dues, in respect of the said Accounts; or that the publick Service is or hath been any-ways discouraged or discredited thereby, as in the said Article is alleged.

3; To the 3d Article the said Earl answereth, and denies, That he received any Monies whatsoever from the King of Spaine, or -any other Person, as in the

' Article

13 W.'HI. 16°

Article is alleged: And saith, That what Wine, Oil, or other Provisions were received from the King of Spainc, or any others, for the Fleet, were duly delivered, and distributed amongst the Officers and Seamen thereof: And denies he did convert the same to his own Use, or did imbezzle any of the Provisions, or reckoned them, or any Part of them, as bought with the Money allowed for furnishing the Navy with fresh Provisions: And does deny that the said Earl did enjoy any Otiices inconsistent in their Nature, as he is advised, one with the other, or which were, or ought to be, Checks one upon the other; or that he anyways secured, or pretended to secure, himself from rendering any Account to the Publick, by any Office or Offices whatsoever; or that he is guilty of the Breach of any Laws, to his Know lege, by executing any Office or Offices, or ever executed the same, to the Dishonour of his Majesty, or to the Prejudice of his People, as in the said Article is alleged.

4. To the 4th Article the said Earl answereth, and saith, He believes that the Prizes taken in the late War were appropriated as by the Act of Parliament in that behalf is provided; but denies that he did at any time sell or dispose of any Vessel or Vessels, or their Ladings, or Cargo, taken as, or under the Pretence of Prize, by any of his Majesty's Ships of War, without Condemnation, or judicial Proceedings; or converted the Monies arising by Sale of any Vessel or Vessels, or their Lading or Cargo, taken as, or under Pretence of, Pi ize, by any of his Majesty's Ships of War. to his own Usi; but, on the contrary, did, from time to time, in his Station, give Orders, that the Prizes taken should be carefully preserved, without lmbezzlement, and duly proceeded against, and the Produce answered as the Law directs: And therefore humbly insisted). That the Publick hath been no-ways endamaged, or the Debts of the Nation increased, by any Neglect or Default of the said Earl.

5. To the 5th Article the said Earl saith, That the F.ust-India Company, about the beginning of March iG96, did apply to the Admiralty hoard, ot which the said Earl was One, to impower their Ships and Officus to seize and take all Pirates infesting the Seas within the Limits of their Charter; and likewise to erect a Court of Admiralty in those Parts, to try and condemn such Pirates as they should take: Upon which Application, the Board of Admiralty did take Advice, and were informed they had no Authority to grant the same: And denies he the said Earl ever discouraged or rejected the Company's Request therein, unless it were by telling them, that the Admiral*., hv Law, could not grant the same: And denies that the Company was ever denied letters of Marque ui common Form, to the Knowledge of the said Earl: And saith, as to the Matter of Kidd, in this Article mentioned, he was gone upon his Expedition about 12 Months before that Time: And as to his Commission, and the Grant, in the said Article mentioned, the said Earl humbly conceives, and is advised, the same were not contrary to Law; but, sure he is, the said Expe-pedition was intended for the publick Good and Service: And saith, The said Kid.I hath no Powers and Instructions from the Board of Admiralty, other than the ordinary and common Letters of Marque, the Contents whereof are common, and well known to the Merchants: And the said Earl doth deny, that he knew the said Kidd to be of ill Fame and Reputation; but in case the said bath committed any Piraeus, he the said Kidd is answerable, and ought to answer, for the same, he never being ordered by the said Earl so to do; nor had he ever any the least Encouragement given him by the said Earl, or any other, to his Knowledge, to expect or hope for any Protection therein, in any illegal Action done or committed by him.

6.To the 6th Article the said Earl saith, lie believes it to be true, that there was a horrid and barbarous Plot and Conspiracy against his Majesty's Sacred Person; and that there was an Apprehension of an immediate Invasion; but the said Earl hopes no Neglect of Duty in his Station can be imputed to him, to prevent the same: And as for the Ship Duchess, which was, amongst many Vot. 13.

Mail. 545

others, armed and equipped in Defence of the Realm* the said Earl saith, That the Men, in the said Article mentioned to he taken from on board her, were but spine of the very Persons that were just before taken on board Captain Kidd, and returned, by their own Consent, on board Captain Kidd again, not being above 20 in Number: And saith, all Fears of the Invasion were then over, and at an end: And denies that the same was intended to weaken, or did weaken, the said Ship, or the Navy Royal; or that the said Seamen, so returning on board the said Kidd, were levied or provided at the Expence of the Publick; or did return, or were put, on board the said Kidd against their own Consent, or to the Prejudice of the publick Security; or that the Ship Duchess was thereby endangered, if she had been attacked, as in the said Article is a Hedged.

7. 'To the 7th Article the said Earl answereth, and denies that he did, by Misrepresentation, or otherwise, obtain or procure a Grant or Order for his Majesty's Ship Dolphin, to be employed in a private Voyage or Undertaking, but what was done therein, was done after the Peace concluded, and by his Majesty's Command, at the Instance and Request of other Persons, and not of the said Earl, but contrary to his Opinion; nor was the said Earl any-way concerned in Interest therein, till after his Majesty's Orders were given about the said Ship; and then, and not belore, some of the Persons concerned in the said Adventure desired the said Earl to take some Shares therein, the Number whereof he doth not remember, which the said Earl accordingly did; but humbly insists that his Actings therein were not contrary to his Duty, or the Trust in him reposed, or the Debts of the Nat.ii m thereby increased.

8. To the 8th Article the said Earl answereth, and

denies, that, at any time, w hile he commanded the Navy Royal, he did, through Neglect or Contempt of Orders, unnecessarily hazard, or expose to Danger, the said Navy: And also denies, that, upon any Opportunity of taking or destroying the Ships of the King, he did, contrary to Advice, or in Disobedience to Orders, neglect to do the same: And also denies, that he did suffer or permit any of the French King's Ships to return into their own Harbours, when he had Opportunity to prevent the same; and humbly insists, he is not guilty of any Neglect or Omission of his Duty herein; nor did expect, in this Particular, to be charged therewith, considering his Services rendered against the French Fleet.

9. To the 9th Article the said Earl saith, He believes it to be true, that his Majesty hath been engaged in several Alliances with several Princes, and particularly with the Emperor, in the Year 1689; and that the End cf those Alliances w as, to prevent the Grow th and Power of France, and to secure this Kingdom, and its Allies: But the said Earl does deny, that lie did advise his Majesty'to enter into the Treaty of Partition charged upon the said Earl in this Article; and, so far as the said Earl was*anyways acquainted therewith, he objected to, and gave his Opinion against, the same.

10. To the 10th Article the said Earl answereth, and saith, That, true it is, his Majesty w as pleased to employ and intrust him in the several Offices and Stations in this Article mentioned for several Years, as his Majesty's Occasions required, although not for all the Time in the said Article mentioned: And hopes, and humbly insisted) upon it, that he the said Earl did, from time to time, according to his Duty, and the Trusts in him reposed, discharge the said Offices and Employments with Loyalty, Faithfulness, and Zeal, to his Majesty, and his People.

And, having thus laid his Case before your Lordships, he the said Earl doth humbly insist, and answer lo the said Impeachment, and ail and every the Articles aforesaid exhibited against him, That he is not guilty of all or any the Matters or Things by the said Articles charged, in Manner and Form as the same are therein and thereby alleged against him; and that the Matters by him before set forth to be done and transacted, or any of them, were not done or committed by him the said Earl

The said Articles were read, Article by Article; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be Articles of Impeachment of high Crimes and Misdemeanors against the said Lord Somers: And the same are as follow; viz.

Articles exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesees, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of England, against John Lord Sommers Baron of Evesham, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against him for liiiih Crimes and Misdemeanors.

1st, THAT a Treaty and Alliance between Leopold the Emperor of Germany, and the States General of the United Provinces, was made and concluded, in the Year of our Lord 1689, upon their Consideration of the Greatness of the common Danger which then threatened all Christendom, from the exccsive Power of France, and the unconstant Faith of the French in the Observance of Treaties; w hereby it was agreed, That there should be and remain for ever, a constant, perpetual, and inviolable Friendship, and good Correspondence, between his Imperial Majesty and the States General: That each of them should be obliged to promote the other's Interest; and, as much as in them lay, prevent all Damages and Inconveniencies to each other.

That, during the Continuance of the War, there should hot be only a defensive, but also an offensive, Alliance between the said Parties, by virtue whereof, they should both of them act in an hostile Manner, with all their Forces, by Sea and Land, against the French King, and such of his Allies as should refuse to separate themselves from him:

That, after the War should be ended, and a Peace concluded, there should remain between his Imperial Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, and the States General, a perpetual defensive Alliance against the Crown of France, and its Adherents:

That, if the Crown of Frame should again attack either of the said confederate Parties, at what Time soever the same should be done, they should faithfully assist each other:

That his Imperial Majesty, and the States General, should at all Times, by all Mcaus, and with all their Forces, protect and defend all the Rights of each other, against the Crown of France and its Adherents:

And other Provisions were thereby made for their mutual Security, as well during the Continuance of die War, as after the Conclusion of a Peace.

Thgt certain separate Articles were also, at or about

A. 1701;

that time, made; whereby the States General maturely considering that France had openly declared in several Courts, That, notwithstanding the most solemn Renun-tiation, diey continued their Pretensions, by Force of Arms, to assert, for the Dauphin, the Succession of the Spanish Monarchy, in case the King of Spain should die without Issue; and also considering what a Blow their State would receive, and what a Prejudice might happen thereby to the publick Affairs and Quiet; did promise, That, in case his said Catholick Majesty should die without lawful Issue, they would, with all their Forces, assist his said Imperial Majesty, or his Heirs, in taking the Succesion of the Spanish Monarchy, lawfully belonging to that House, together with its Kingdoms, Provinces, Dominions, and Rights; and in their obtaining and securing the quiet Possession thereof against the French, and their Adherents, who should directly or indirectly oppose that Succession; and, with Force, repel the Force which should be brought against them:

That, at the Instance of the States General, in pur-' suance of the said Treaty, and separate Articles, our most gracious Lord and Sovereign his most Excellent Majesty King William the Third was invited to enter into the Alliance of the aforesaid Treaty, and into the Agreement of the said separate Articles, and thereupon, for restoring and preserving the publick Peace and Quiet, did afterwards, in the said Year of our Lord 1689, enter into, and, under the Great Seal of England, accept, approve, and ratify, and, in the most solemn Manner, engage and promise religiously and inviolably to observe the same, without violating the said Treaty, or separate Articles, in any Article, or suffering the same, to the utmost of his Power, to be violated:

That in the Year of our Lord 1698, a Treaty was projected and contrived in France, to be set on Foot between his Majesty, the French King, and the States General; for a Partition of the Spanish Monarchy; whereby many large Territories thereunto belonging, were to be allotted and delivered up to France:

That the Tenour and Design of the said last mentioned Treaty, whilst the same was in Negotiation, was communicated to the said John Lord Somers, then one of the Lords Justices of England, Lord Chancellor of England, and Onp of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council: That the said Lord Sommers, well knowing the most apparent evil Consequences, as well as the Injustice, of the said Partition, did not, according to the Trust and Duty of his said several Offices, dissuade, or endeavour to obstruct, its taking Effect; but, on the contrary, having neither Regard to his Majesty's Honour engaged by the said Treaty with the Emperor and States General as aforesaid, to the Trade and known Interest of this Kingdom, or the Peace of Europe, did advise his Majesty to enter into the said Treaty; and did so far encourage and promote the same, that the said Treaty was concluded, and ratified under the Great Seal of England, then in the Custody of the said Lord Sommers-, and thereby the Kingdoms of Naples ami Sicily, the Places depending on the Monarchy of Spain situate on the Coast of Tuscany, or adjacent Islands, comprehended under the Name of Porto Herculo, Orbitello, Tehvnone -

14. That the said John Lord Somers, to the great Oppression of the Subjects, and contrary to Magna Charta, and divers good Statutes of this Realm, and in manifest Breach and Violation of his Oath as Lord High Chancellor of England, hath, in several Causes depending before him, by many extraordinary Methods, and unwarrantable Practices, for several Years, delayed Proceedings in the said Causea; and, by colour of his Office, hath made divers arbitrary and illegal Orders, in Subversion of the Laws and Statutes of this Realm; and hath, of his own Authority, reversed Judgments given in the Court of Exchequer, and without calling before him the Barons of the Exchequer to hear their Informations, and the Causes of their Judgments, as the Statute, in those Cases, expressly directs; assuming thereby to himself an arbitrary and illegal Power: And hath declared and affirmed, in publick Places of Judicature, That particular Subjects might have Rights and Interests, without any Remedy for Recovery of the same, unless by Petition to the Person of the King only; or to that Effect: Which Position was highly dangerous to the legal Constitution of this Kingdom, and absolutely destructive to the Property of the Subject.

And the said Knights, Citizens* and Burgesses, by Protestation, saving to themselves the Liberty of exhibiting, at any time hereafter, any further Articles, or other Accusation or Impeachment, against the said Lord Somers; and also of replying to his Answers, which he shall make unto the said Articles, or any of them; and of offering Proofs to all and every the aforesaid Articles, and to all and every other Articles, Impeachment, or Accusation, which shall be exhibited by them, as the Cause shall, according to the Course of Parliament, require; do pray, That the said John Lord Somers may be put to answer the said Crimps and Misdemeanors; and that such Proceedings, Examinations, Tryals, and Judgments, may be thereupon had and given, as is agreeable to Law and Justice.

Sir Humphrey Mackworth, according to Order, reported Publick from the Committee, to-whom it was referred to receive Debts. Proposals for paying off the publick Debts, and advancing the Credit of the Nation; and report the same to the House; That they had received a Proposal from the old East India Company; which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Bur- Old Fast gesses, in Parliament assembled: , Com'

THE Governor and Company of Merchants of London trading into the East Indies, in a General Court assembled, do humbly represent, That this Company, having been possessed of the East India Trade above an Hundred Years; and having, at their very great Expence, during the said Time, procured Grants, Privileges, Immunities, and Revenues, in India; and having purchased and erected several strong Forts, Factories, and Settlements; all which are absolutely necessary for the Preservation and carrying on the Trade; and humbly conceiving, That the said Trade will be best carried on, to the Advantage of the Nation, in One general joint Stock, exclusive of all others: To which End, and for that this Company are desirous to manifest their Zeal for the publick Service;

They do therefore humbly propose,

That this Company having advanced the Sum of Three hundred and Fifteen thousand Pounds, in pursuance of an Act for raising Two Millions upon a Fund for Payment of Annuities after the Rate of 8/. per Centum per Annum; and for settling the Trade to the East Indies; and the new East India Company having advanced One Million Six hundred and Sixty-three thousand Pounds; and several private Traders the Sum of 22,000l.; making in all Two Millions; for which' the Publick now pay 8/. per Centime

Sending A Petition of the Joyners, Cabinet-makers, Fan-Models makers, and Japanners, in and about the City of London, abroad. in behalf of themselves, and many others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, by their great Labour and Industry, have attained to the curious Arts of Cabinet-making, Japanning, and Fan-making, to excel the most remote Chinas, or Indian: That there are several poor Artificers of this Kingdom employed in the said Works; and there are great Quantities of several Sorts of Commodities of the Growth of Turkey, Russia, and Barbary, and other foreign Parts, expended by the Petitioners in the said Arts, to the Increase of his Majesty's Customs, and Advantage of the Woollen Manufacture: That there are many Persons, minding only their own private Gain, and designing to ruin the Handicrafts of this Kingdom, take all Opportunities of disclosing the said Arts, by sending Models or Patterns abroad to India, and other Places: And praying, That this House will take their deplorable Case into their serious Consideration, and afford them Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir Robert Legard and Mr. Geiy:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for preventing any Inconveniencies that may happen by Privilege of Parliament, with some Amendments: To which they desire the Concurrence of this House. Also, They are commanded by the Lords to acquaint this House, That their Lordships having been desired by the Earl of Orford, that a Day may be appointed for his speedy Tryal, their Lordships, finding no Issue joined by Replication of this House, think fit to give Notice thereof to tins House. Also,

They are commanded by the Lords to acquaint this House, That they having, on the First Day of April last, sent up to their Lordships an Impeachment against William Earl of Portland, for high Crimes and Misdemeanors, and having also, on the 15th Day of the same Month, . Vox*. 13.

impeached Charles Lord Halifax for High Crimes and Misdemeanors; and there being as yet no particular Articles exhibited against the said Lords; their Lordships think themselves obliged to put this House in mind there* of; which, after Impeachments have so long depended, is a Hardship to the Persons concerned, and not agreeable to the usual Methods and Proceedings of Parliament in such Cases.

And then the Messengers withdrew;

Ordered, That the said Amendments to the Bill, inti- Privilege of tilled, An Act for preventing any Inconveniencies that Parliament, may happen by Privilege of Parliament, be'taken into Consideration upon Saturday Morning next.

Resolved, That this House will send an Answer to the Answer to said Messages* relating to the said Impeachments, by Lords Mes* Messengers of their own. 5aSes*

And the Messengers w^ere called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

Mr. St. John reported from the Committee, to whom Estates given the Petition of Lewis Gerard, and several others con- to super-ccrned with him, proposing a Discovery of Lands given stiUous Usee* to superstitious Uses, was referred, That they had heard the Petitioners; who not only produced several Witnesses to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, but also an Inquisition taken by virtue of a Commission under the Great Seal of England; whereby several Manors, Lands,

Tenements, and Mortgages, therein mentioned, of a considerable Value, were found to be given, and belong, to foreign Seminaries, and other Popish superstitious Uses:

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for the encouraging the Discovery of Estates given to Popish superstitious Uses.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for encouraging the Discovery of Estates given to Popish superstitious Uses: And that Mr. Sit. John, Sir Rowland Gxvynne, and Mr. Carterdo prepare, and bring in, the same.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to them, That they do provide in the Bill, That the said Estates be applied for the Benefit of Greenwich Hospital.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction also, That they do provide, That all Grants of the said Estates from the Crown be vacated.

Ordered, That Sir Cha. Bloys, Mr. BlofeUd, Mr. Kemp, Enfield Mr. Holmes, Mr. Freeman, Mr. Cesar, Mr. Trtdenham,

Mr. Carter; and all for Essex; be added to the Committee, appointed to inquire, by what Methods and Means such great Waste and Destruction is made in his Majesty's Chace at Enfield.

A Petition of several Colonels of the Army, in behalf army of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, Cloathing. and read; setting forth, That, upon the raising of a Regiment, Cloathing is immediately provided, and to be paid by a Deduction of some Part of the growing Pay, at the Year's End: That Cloathing is always provided for the complete Number of the Establishment, without regard to Defectives, by Loss in Service, or otherwise:

That, in December 1697, near a Third-part of every Rc-

5jment was reduced; and in February following, several legiments were intirely disbanded; and all the Men, by the King's Orders, were to take their Cloaths away; though the same could not be paid for till April following;

That, by a late Method of Accounting at the Pay Office, the Cloathing Part of the Pay, as well as the Subsistence, x is stopped, upon all Respites for defective Men; and no Credit given for the Cloathing Part, but to the very Day the Men were reduced, or disbanded; by which means, the Fund for satisfying the Tradesmen, who furnish the Cloaths, falls short; who have, on that account commenced Suits, and obtained Verdicts in Law, against the Colonels, who contracted with them for the Cloaths on the Regiments Account: And praying, That they may have such Relief, as this Honourable House shall think fit.'

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That out of the Produce of the several Subsidies, Duties, and Branches of the Revenue, appropriated to the Service of his Majesty's Houshold, the Sum of 3,000l. weekly, to commence from Christmas 1700, be applied for the Service of the Year 1701: And that the Surplus, after 600,000 /. for the Civil List satisfied, be appropriated to the Use of the Publick.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made, by leaving out "3,000," and inserting " 3,700" instead thereof:

And the same was, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House. i

Another Amendment was proposed to be made, by leaving out " Year 1701," and inserting "Publick" instead thereof: And the same was, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made, by leaving out " and that the Surplus, after 600,000 /. for " the Civil List satisfied, be appropriated to the Use of " the Publick:" And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made, by adding " and that the Residue of the said Subsidies and " Duties be applied to the Use of his Majesty's Houshold " and Family, and other his Majesty's Occasions:" And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended, That out of the Produce of the several Subsidies, Duties, and Branches of the Revenue appropriated to the Service of his Majesty's Houshold, the Sum of 3,700l. weekly, to commence from Christmas 1700, be applied to the Service of the Publick; and that the Residue of the said Subsidies and Duties be applied to the Use of his Majesty's Household and Family, and other his Majesty's Occasions.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty,

That they have Power to make the said 3,700l. weekly, a Fund of Credit.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Discharging the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards Seamen. delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee directed the Secretary of the Admiralty to attend them; and to lay before them what Orders were given for discharging the Seamen from the Fleet; and what Orders were given for the Payment of the Bounty-money to the Seamen.

The Committee also directed the Commissioners of the Navy to lay before them what Orders they had received from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty for paying the Seamen their Wages, and Bounty-money.

Accordingly, the Secretary of the Admiralty attended them; and delivered in to the Committee, from the Lords of the Admiralty,

1. The Reasons for discharging the Seamen from the Fleet, and not paying them on board their Ships:

2. Copies of Orders from the Lords of the Admiralty to the Navy Board, about paying Wages, and Bounty-money, to Men discharged from the Fleet:

3. Copies of Orders from the Lords of the Admiralty to the Flag Officers and Captains, about discharging Men from the Fleet:

4. Several Precedents for reducing Men from his Majesty's Ships, without paying them their Wages at the tmie of such Reduction.

There was also laid before the Committee a Copy of the Order of the Commissioners of the Navy, received from the Lords of the Admiralty, for solliciting for Money to pay the Seamen ordered to be discharged from the Fleet, for reducing their Complements; with Copies of their Letters to the Treasurer of the Navy; and other Proceedings thereupon.

All which Papers are submitted to the Consideration of the House, the Committee having no other Power than to inquire into the Reasons, how the Seamen came to be discharged without being paid.

The said Papers are as follow;

Admiralty Office, 8* May 1701.

IN pursuance of the Directions of a Committee of the Honourable House of Commons, appointed to inquire ' into the Reasons, how the Seamen came to be discharged from the Fleet without being paid, there is herewith delivered to the said Committee, Copies of what Orders have been given by the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty for discharging the said Men, and paying them their Wages and Bounty; but, since there was nothing, but Exchequer Bills, to pay them, that it was very uncertain when they could be reduced to Money, and altogether impracticable to pay the Men with the said Bills, by reason of the small Sums due to each Man, it was not thought convenient to send the said Bills to the Place where the Men were discharged, but rather to pay them their Wages, and Bounty, in Town; which is now doing, and to their full Satisfaction: To which may be added, That since the Ships in Sea Pay in April last did require upwards of

28,000 Men, and that there was actually borne on them 26,000, it was judged adviseable to begin with this Reduction, that so a good Strength might be kept at Sea the Winter Months, without exceeding 15,000 Men, one Month with another, the Year round; and, had not this Method been taken, these Men, which, generally speaking, are Land-men, would,- in all Probability, have been kept near Three Weeks longer in Wages and Victuals; which would have cost the Government near 300l. a Day: And to shew, that it has been the common Practice, not only to reduce the Complements of Ships, but even not to pay the Men, so reduced, before the Payment of those Ships they served in, there is herewith delivered as many Precedents thereof, as the Shortness of Time would admit; by one of which, in January 1697-8, it will appear, That the Men of the whole Fleet then in Pay, except some few Ships bound on foreign Voyages, were reduced to their lowest Complements, and no Provision made for paying the said Men, till such time as the Ships they were discharged from were paid.

By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England, Ireland, &c.

Memorial to his Majesty.

THERE being no more than 780,000l. in Prospect for the Sea Service this Year, which will maintain but

15,000 Men, one Month with another, for the 13 Months; we do most humbly inform his Majesty, That there is now about 26,000 Men in Pay; and that, if the Ships employed at home are brought to their lowest Complements, it will reduce them to about 24,000 Men: That, if that Number be kept up all the Month of May, there can be no more employed than 16,000 in the Month of August: If the said 24,000 Men are kept in Pay the Month of June, then there can be no more than 16,000 Men employed in July and August; and 10,000 Men from the First of September to the First Day of January following; which will bring each Month in the Year to 15,000.

Admiralty Office, 26° April 1701.

Pembroke, Mitchell, Churchill. By Command of their Lordships,

J. Burchett.

Admiralty Office, 31st March 1701.

Gentlemen,

WHEREAS we have given Orders for the discharging from his Majesty's Ships all such Men, who, either through Sickness or otherwise, are altogether unfit for his Majesty's Service at Sea; and directed, That each Captain shall transmit to your Board, attested by himself, and signing Officers, an exact List of the Names of such Men as they do so discharge, who were entered by or before the 28th Day of this present Month; we do hereby desire and direct you to take particular Care, that, upon Appli-, cation made to you by any Persons contained in the said Lists, the Allowance of Bounty promised by his Majesty's Royal Proclamation to an ordinary Seaman, be made unto them for the maintaining them in their Travelling to their respective Habitations. We are

Your affectionate Friends, Navy Board. G. Rook,

D. Mitchell, G. Churchill.

Gentlemen. Admiralty, 17th Feb. 94;

YOUR Letter of the Fifth Instant to our Secretaries, together with the Copy of one from the Commissioners of the Victualing, having been communicated to this Board; This is to acquaint you, in Answer thereto, That it is the JEtna Fireship at Plymouth, and not the Blaze, which is to be fitted for foreign Service; and that the Ships directed to be fitted for the Streights, and foreign Service, are to be victualled for their Middle Number of Men: And we do hereby desire and direct you to cause their respective Complements of Men to be reduced to their Middle Number, and to order the Commissioners of the Victualing to victual them accordingly. By the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of England, Ireland, &c.

WHEREAS we did, some time since, direct, That Lists should be prepared, and Sent to the Navy Board, of all such Men as voluntarily entered themselves to servfe in his Majesty's Fleet, from the 26th February last, the Date of his Majesty's Royal Proclamation, to the 26th of March following, and have been discharged by reason of Sickness, or other Incapacities for Service; and whereas we are informed by the Commissioners of the Navy, That, in the Lists which have been sent to them by the Captains, there are inserted some pressed Men, and others that have been discharged for Preferment: You are therefore hereby required and directed forthwith to give Orders to the respective Captains of his Majesty's Ships in the Fleet, as they shall come in your Reach, to send, as soon as possibly may be, to the Navy Board, Lists only of such Volunteers who entered within the aforesaid Time, and have since been, or shall be, discharged by reason of Sickness, or other Incapacities, in order to the paying them the Bounty promised by his Majesty's Proclamation; and that they do not insert in the said Lists any pressed Men, or any Volunteers that have been, or shall be, discharged from their Ships intirely out of the Service. Dated this 15° April 1701.

Haversham,

A Petition of George Harrison, William Aldred, Abraham Vol, Zacheus Skingley, and other the Tradesmen in Colchester, w'as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Woollen Manufactures in and about the said Borough are so considerable, that the Poor of the said Town, for Weaving, and of the Country 20 Miles round, for Spinning, have their Dependence thereon: That, for Supply thereof, Wool is weekly conveyed from London by common Carriers; and, after due Preparation, thence to Spinners in the Country: That the said Carriers, by reason of bad Weather, and divers Accidents, cannot make their weekly Returns, without sometimes exceeding the Hours limited by several Acts for preventing the Exportation of Wool; nor the Petitioners send to their Spinners in the Country, without doing the same: That the common Carriers of this Town have not been known, in Man's Memory, to carry any Wool for Exr portation; notwithstanding which, certain Persons, deputed by the Commissioners in the said Acts appointed, have, of late, presumed to seize , the Wool carrying to Spinners, and several Bags of Wool brought from London in Waggons; which, by the badness of the Weather only, had exceeded a few Hours appointed by the said Acts for their travelling in: That the Persons deputed had no Reason to suspect, that the said Wool was carried with any Intent to be exported, the Horses being out of the Waggons when the Seizure was made: Which Practices, if continued, will be a great Discouragement and Detriment to the Petitioners: And praying, That Consideration and Relief may be had in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee to whom it is referred to consider of the Laws relating to the Woollen Manufacture.

That the several Ridings, where the Wood is cut down, contains 28*6 Acres, all wooded, without Plains, which make, of Woodland-measure, 580 Acres:

That 73 Loads and an Half of Bark now lie in the Chace: That several Ridings are almost cleared, and the-Trees and Wood carried away:

Samuel Mitchell further says, That in one Riding, he counted 400 Oaks cut down, and only 9 of the least and worst were left standing.

Charles Wilford, Keeper to Sir Bazil Firebrace, says, That in cutting and falling the Trees in Enfeild Chace, no Regard has been had to any Ridings: That they havO gone into all Parts of the Chace for the best Trees: That they are cut off above-ground, the Stools covered with Moss in many Places, that they might not be discovered, and not any grubbed up:

That, on Wednesday the 14th Instant, about 9 in the Morning, he disturbed the Workmen, as they were falling the Trees, and told them of the Votes of this House; they went with him to one Moson, Mr. Westlake's Kinsman, and Shelly; who answered to the Votes, They signified nothing without an Act of Parliament; and that they would go on: And though the Order for stopping the cutting was with them about an Hour afterwards, the Workmen continued cutting till 6 at Night.

William Bosgrave says, Five of the Workmen told him, They worked all the next Day till 6 at Night, cut down and barked.

Sir Humphrey Mackworth reported from the Committee, to whom the several Petitions of Cavendish JVeedon Esquire, and others, relating to the new Way out of Chancery-lane into Lincoln s-inn-felds, was referred, That they had examined the Matter thereof, and had come to several Resolutions; w'hich they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee having examined the Allegations contained in the said Petition of Mr. JVeedon, it appeared, That, by an Act made the last Sessions of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the speedy and effectual making a convenient Way out of Chancery-lane to Lincoln's-innfolds, and Places adjacent, a Tax w as given for making the said new Way before the 25th Day of March, then next ensuing; viz. The Sum of Two Shillings and Six-pence a Quarter upon all Hackney Coaches within the Bills of Mortality; and the like Sum upon Cars, Carts, Tumbrels, and Drays, within the several Parishes of St. Giles in the Fields, St. Andrew s Holbourn, St. Clement Danes, St. Dunstan's in the West, and St. Bride's, for the Term of Six Years; with Liberty to borrow Three thousand Pounds, at Six Pounds per Cent, per Annum, the better to expedite the said Wray:

Vol. 13.

That the said Tax on the said Coaches amounts unto Three hundred and Fifty Pounds per Annum; and the Carts, Cars, Tumbrels, and Drays, to Ninety-three Pounds per Annum; in all, Four hundred and Forty-three* Pounds per Annum; but, deducting the Charges in collecting the same, the clear Product of the said Act is Four hundred and Thirteen Pounds per Annum; which, at Six Year$ End, in all, amounts to the Sum of Two thousand Four hundred Seventy-eight Pounds:

That, by the said Act, Eighty-nine Feet of Jackanapes-alley was granted to be sold towards the said Way; which is accordingly sold for One hundred and Five Pounds; and the Materials of the old Houses were sold for Sixty Pounds: So that the whole Value given by the said Act is Two thousand Six hundred Forty-three Pounds:

That the Petitioner Mr. Wcedon, to serve the Publick, effected the said new' Way Six Mouths sooner than the Time limited by the said Act: And it appeared, to the Committee, that he underwent very great Trouble, Charge, and Hazard, in executing the said Act, when other the Commissioners would not venture to join in the same:

That the Committee also having examined the Allegations contained in the Petition of Shem Bridges and John Thornicroft Esquires; as also of Jane Dring, an Infant, on behalf of herself and Tenants; it did appear, That the said Mr. Bridges and Mr. Thornicroft were, by the said Act of Parliament, to be paid for their Houses, that were to be pulled down for making the said new Way, the Sum of Two thousand Six hundred Pounds; That no Person being willing to lend any Money upon the said Act, the Petitioner Mr. IVeedon, and Two other of the Commissioners named in the said Act; viz. Mr. Atwell and Mr. Turner; assigned the said whole Tax, and Jackanapes-altey, in Mortgage, to Mr. JVotton and Mr. Tawnesend, in Trust for Mr. Bridges and Mr. Thornicroft, for the Sum of Two thousand Six hundred Pounds; whereby they claimed Interest for the said Two thousand Six hundred Pounds; which amounts to the Sum of Seven hundred Ninety-six Pounds, or thereabouts: But the said Act being deficient to make good the same; and the said Mr. Bridges and Mr. Thornicroft being willing, Mr. JVeedon, who had nothing left but the Sixty Pounds for the said old Houses, to carry on the said Way, as also all other Persons, should be satisfied their Damages on account of the said Way> having agreed to wave their Interest; which being deducted, there appears due unto the said Mr. Bridges and Mr. Thornicroft, upon the said Act, the Sum of Two thousand Six hundred Pounds for their Principal, and Seventy-two Pounds for their necessary Charges they have been put unto by reason of the said Act;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioner Mr. JVeedon, and the other Petitioners, have fully proved the Allegations contained in their said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the new Way made out of Chancery-lane into Lincoln s-imijHelds, pursuant to, and by the Authority of, the late Act of Parliament, is of great Benefit and Advantage to the Publick: And that the Deficiency of the said Act, amounting to the Sum of One thousand Five hundred and Five Pounds Seven Shillings and Seven-pence, ought to be made good.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Deficiency happens, by reason there are not a sufficient Number of Cars, Carts, Tumbrels, and Drays, charged by the said Act of Parliament.

The Answer of the Lord Somei's to the Articles of Impeachment exhibited against him was, according to impearh-Order, read; and is as followeth; viz. meat.

The Answer of John Lord Somers, Baron of Evesham, to the Articles exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in the Name of themselves, and of all the Commons of Fmgland, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against him, for high Crimes and Misdemeanors supposed to be by him committed.

THE said Lord Somers, saving to himself all Advantages of Exception to the said Articles, and of not being prejudiced by any Words, or Want of Form, in this his Answer; and also saving to himself all Rights and Privileges belonging to him, as One of the Peers of this Realm; for Answer to the said Articles, humbly saith,

1. To the First Article, That, he believes, the now Emperor of Germany, and the States General of the United Pi'ovinces, being, in the Year One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine, engaged in a War with France, a Treaty and Alliance was concluded between them; and a separate Article then made, to the Effect in this Article mentioned; and that his Sacred Majesty did afterwards enter into, ratify, and approve, the same; to which Treaty, separate Article, and Ratification, for more Certainty thereof, he referreth himself: And further saith,

That, in the Year One thousand Six hundred Ninety-and-eight, his Majesty, before he left England, was pleased to tell him, That some Intimation had been given to the Fail of Portland, when in France, that the French King.inclined to come to an Agreement with his Majesty concerning the Succession to the Crown of Spain; and afterwards, in August One thousand Six hundred Ninety-and-eight, his Majesty being then in Holland, and the said Lord Saniers at Tunbridge Wells, by his Majesty's Permission, for Recovery of his Health, Mr. Secretary Vernon communicated to him a Letter he had then receive^ written by the Earl of Portland, by his Majesty's Order; wherein it was mentioned, that Count Tallard, who was then Ambassador from the French King to his Majesty,

had declared, an Accommodation might be found out in relation to the Succession of Spain, in case of that King's Dehth; and that his Majesty had sounded France upon what Terms an Agreement might be made; and the Conditions were near of this Nature; viz. That the Electoral Prince of Bavaria should have the Kingdoms of Spain, the Indies, the Loiv Countries, and all that depends upon the Spanish Dominions, except the Kingdom of Naples and Sicily, Sardinia, the Province of GuypuScoa on this Side of the Pyreneans, Fontarabia, and St. Sebastian, Finally and the Places in Tuscany, of which Spain then stood possessed; in Consideration of which France was absolutely to renounce the Right it pretended to the Succession of Spain; and Milan was to be given to the Archduke, Second Son to the Emperor; and that his Majesty commanded the said Mr. Secretary to speak to him, the said Lord Somers, touching that Matter; and that his Lordship should discourse it with those he thought he might trust with that Secret; which to keep with the utmost Care was, by the said Letter, mentioned to be of the highest Importance: And, at the same time, the Lord Somers received a Letter from his Majesty, signed by himself, intimating, that Count 7h//r/rrfhad made some Propositions touching an Agreement with his Majesty, concerning the Succession of the Kingdom of Spaine, the which the said Earl of PortlandvtovAA write to Mr. Secretary Vernon, to the end his Majesty might have some Opinions upon that Affair, which required the greatest Secrecy, and in which no Time was to be lost, if that Negotiation were to be carried on; and, for that End, his Majesty thereby commanded the said Lord Somers to send full Powers to him, under the Great Seal of England, with Blanks for the Names of Commissioners to treat with Count Tallai'd; which his Majesty, by the said Letter, was pleased to say, he believed, might be done secretly, that none, but the said Lord Somers, and Mr. Secretary Vernon, and those to whom the said Lord Somers and Mr. Secretary should communicate it, might have Knowledge thereof; and that the Clerks, who were to write the full Powers, might net know what they were; or to the like Eftect: And the said Lord Somers did immediately return the Earl of Portland's said Letter to Mr. Secretary Vernon, and desired him to communicate the Contents thereof to the Earl of Orford, and the now Lord Hallifax, Two of the then Lords Justices, who, as he was assured, were then in Town; and also to such others as they and Mr. Secretary Vernon should think fit; who, in regard of the Kings Command to have that Affair kept a Secret, thought fit to impart it to the Duke of Shrezt}shury only, as the said Mr. Secretary afterwards acquainted the said Lord Somers; and, some time afterwards, the said Lord Hallifax came down to the said Wells, and Mr. Secretary Vernon coming thither also about the same tim$, they and the said Lord Somers had discoursed together concerning the said Proposal: And the said Lord Somers, by Letter dated the Eight-and-tw'entiethof August One thousand Six hundred Ninety-and-eight, did, as his own Thoughts, and as what he apprehended to be the Result of their Consideration, humbly represent to his Majesty; First, That the Entertaining of such a Proposal, as was mentioned by Count Tallard, seemed to be attended with many very ill Consequences, if the French did not act a sincere Part; but that they were soon at Ease as to any Apprehension of that sort, being fully assured, his Majesty would not act, but with the utmost Niceness, in an Affair, wherein his Glory, and the Safety of Europe, was so highly concerned: That the Second Thing the y considered was, the very ill Prospect of what w'as like to happen upon the Death of the King of Spain, in case nothing was done previously towards the providing against that Accident, w'hich seemed probably to be very near, the King of France then having so great a Force in such a Readiness, that he was in a Condition to take Possession of Spaine before any other Prince could be ready to make a Stand; that his Majesty was the best Judge whether that was the Case, w'ho was so perfectly informed of the Circumstances of all Parts abroad; but, so far as related to England^ it would be want of Duty not . Vo l. 13.

to give his Majesty tins clear Account, That there was a Lord Somers* Deadness and Want of Spirit in the Nation universally, so Impcach-as not at all to be disposed to the Thoughts of entering intp ment* a new War; and that they seemed to be tiredout with Taxes to a Degree beyond what w7as discerned, until it appeared upon the Occasion of the then late Elections; that That was the Truth of the Fact; upon which his Majesty would determine what Resolutions were proper to be taken t The remaining Consideration was, What would be the Condition of Europe, if the Proposal took place ? but of That they thought themselves little capable of judging; but, it seems, that, if Sicily was in the French Hands, they would be intirely Masters of the Levant Trade; that, if they were possessed of Fivall, and those other Sea Ports on that Side* w'hereby Milan would be intirely shutout from Relief by Sea, or any Commerce, that Duchy would be of little Signification in the Hands of any.Prince; and that if the King of France had possession of that Part of Guypuscoa, which is mentioned in the Proposal, besides the Ports he would have in the Ocean, it did seem, he would have as easy a Way of invading Spaine on that Side, as. he then had on the Side of Catalonia: 13ut it was not to be hoped, that France should quit its Pretensions to so great a Sue-; cession, without considerable Advantages; and they were assured his Majesty w ould reduce the Terms as low as could be done, and make them, as far as was possible in the then present Circumstances of, Things, such as might be some f oundation for the future Quiet of Christendom, which all his Majesty's Subjects could not but be convinced was his true Aim; and, if it could be brought to pass. That England might be some way a Gainer by that Transaction, whether it was by the Elector of Bavaria, who w'as the Gainer by his Majesty's Interposition in that Treaty, his coming to an Agreement to let the English into some Trade to the Spanish Plantations, or in any other Manner, it would wonderfully endear his Majesty to his English Subjects.

That it did not appear, in case the Negotiation should proceed, what was to be done on his Majesty's Part, in order to make it take place; whether any more was required, than that the English and Dutch should sit still, and France itself was to see it executed; and, if that were so, what Security ought to be expected, that, if by their being Neuters, the French should be successful, they w ould confine themselves to the Terms of the Treaty, and not attempt to make further Advantages of their Success?,

And the said Lord Somers suith, That, after the Writing of his said Letter, he had no Account whatsoever, nor heard any thing, of the said Treaty, or knew or heard, whether the same was proceeded upon, or not, until towards the latter End of September following, when he was acquainted by Mr. Secretary Vernon, that he had received an Account, that a Treaty, relating to the Succession of the Crown of Spaine, had been adjusted, concluded, and sign: ed, by the Commissioners named by his Majesty for that Purpose, and the Ambassador and Plenipotentiary of the French King: And the said Lord Somers doth deny, that the said Treaty of Partition, or any Proposition for such Treaty, or the Transaction thereof, was communicated to him the said Lord Somers; nor was he acquainted with the same, or the Design thereof, or any other Matter relating thereto, at any other time, or in any other Manner, before he was told of the Concluding and Signing thereof, as aforesaid, than as is herein before-mentioned to be done by his Majesty, as aforesaid, and by his and the said Earl of Portland's Letter herein before-mentioned: And the said Lord Soma's doth deny he did, at any time whatsoever, advise his Majesty to enter into the said Treaty, or any way encourage or promote the same; but, having made the Objections before-mentioned, in his said Letter to his Majesty, against the Propositions so communicated to Kim as aforesaid, and clearly laid open such Thoughts and Observations as occurred to him upon the said Matter, he did thereby, as he conceived, fully and faithfully discharge his Trust, and the Duty, incumbent on him: And the said Lord Somers further saith, That afterw ards Mr. Secretary Vernon did acquaint him, that be had recceived, by his Majesty

Warrants to the Trustees to contract, for the said Rents; and such Contracts were, pursuant thereunto, made; and such Grants of the said Rents were passed, as in the said Article is mentioned; and the Money, mentioned in such Contracts, was, for the Perfecting of his Majesty's said intended free Gift, discharged by Tallies struck for that Purpose: And the said Lord Somers saith, The said Contracts were not intended or designed to make the Grantees of the said Rents appear to be Purchasers; but the said Lord Somers always acknowledged he received the said Grants of his Majesty's Bounty; and, he humbly conceives, it was lawful for him so to accept the same.

9, 10. To the Ninth and Tenth Articles the said Lord Somers saith, That, after his Majesty had given such Direction to the Lords of the Treasury for granting Fee-farm Rents, and other Rents, to the yearly Value aforesaid, for the Benefit of the said Lord Somers, and his Heirs, and after Warrants were signed by the Lords of the Treasury to the said Trustees, for making Contracts for conveying Rents of the said yearly Value, for the Benefit of the said Lord Somers, it did appear, that the said intended Contracts and Grants could not be perfected; for that neither the Lords of the Treasury, nor the said Trustees, were sufficiently informed what Fee-farm Rents, or other Rents, remained undisposed of; so that the whole Benefit of his Majesty's intended Bounty would have been lost, without. Information could be granted of such particular Rents: And the said Lord Somers being informed, that Reginald Marriott, and John Digby, in this Article named, were the most likely, if not the only, Persons capable to give Information therein, Application was made to them for. that Purpose; and the said Marriott and Digby, being so applied to after the said Warrants of his Majesty, and the said Lords of the Treasury, were executed, as aforesaid, did refuse to give any Account of such Rents, unless they might have, as a Reward for their so doing, Rents amounting to near a Fourth-part of such Rents, whereof they should give such Account, 'conveyed in Trust for. them, in such manner as in the said Article is mentioned; which the said Lord Somers did, as he conceived, he lawfully might, it being only to his own Loss and Prejudice, comply with; not in order to any such End as is suggested in the said Article, but that he plight perfect

the Grant before designed and appointed to be made to Lonj SomeiV him by his Majesty of his own free Will, and not at the Imp?ach-said Lord Somers's Solicitation; the Discovery of any of ment* the said Rents not being made by the said Marriott and Digby, or any other Person, till after the said Warrants of his Majesty, and the Lords of the Treasury, as aforesaid; and accordingly the several Grants, in this Article mentioned, were made to Hancock and Warner, in Trust for the said Marriott and Digby, as was affirmed to the said Lord Somers: And the said Lord Somers saith, There was not any Sum of Money paid as the Consideration of the Grants of the said Rents; but the Contracts were made, and the Payment of the several Considerations thereof were discharged, in the Manner, and for the Reasons, herein before set forth; and were not colourably. or fraudulently contrived, in Deceit of his Majesty, or Elusion of the said Acts of Parliament.

11. To the Eleventh Article the said Lord Somers saith,

He believeth, that several of the Rents, mentioned to be granted in Trust for him, as aforesaid, had been before granted to other Persons by the said Trustees; and that others of them were not in the Power of the said Trustees to grant; which was, and is, very much to his Prejudice: And believes the game were inserted by mistake^ Informations given touching the same, and not out of any Design; and the like Mistakes have frequently happened in other Grants of other of the said Rents: And denies, that, to his Knowlege or Belief, any of the said Rents, so granted for his Benefit, were ever united or annexed to the Castle of Windsor for any Purpose whatsoever; or that any Oppression or Vexation hath happened to any of his Majesty's Subjects, by Reason of the Granting of any of the said Rents, and, as he believes, little or no new Charge to the Crown.

12. To the Twelfth Article the said Lord Somers saith,

That, his Majesty having designed, of his Bounty to him the said Lord Somers, and his Heirs, Fee-farm and other Rents, to the annual Value in the said Grants mentioned; and the said Trustees having covenanted, as was usual for them to do, that they had not njade any former or other Grant or Conveyance of the said Rents, or any of them; and Three hundred Forty-seven Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three-pence Farthing per Annum of the said Rents, so granted as aforesaid, having appeared to be granted before, or not to be grantable, by the said Trustees, or not leviable on Surrender of such Rentp; the said Trustees, by Warrant of the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury, who were thereunto sufficiently authorized, in Lieu and Satisfaction of the said Rents, and Arrears thereof, and in Discharge of the Covenants of the said Trustees, did, the Twenty-first Day of October One thousand Six hundred Ninty-and-nine, grant diver? other Rents, amounting to the yearly Value of Three hundred Ninety-one Pounds and Three-pence Halfpeny, to,

Richard Adney, and his Heirs, as in the said Article is mentioned, which were not so granted, as if the said yearly Rents of Three hundred Forty-seven Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three-pence Farthing had been bona fide, purchased, but was in Lieu and Reprize for the same as granted of his Majesty's Bounty, for the Benefit of the said Lord Somers, and his Heirs, as aforesaid; which, he conceives, might be, and was, lawfully done.

14; To the Fourteenth Article the said Lord Somers saith, He did not delay any Proceedings in any Cause or Causes depending before him, as Chancellor of England, longer or otherwise than as the Circumstances and Justice of each Cause required; but did, to the very manifest Impairing of his Health, constantly apply himself to the Dispatch of the Causes depending belore him: And denies that he did ever make, by colour of his Office, any arbitrary or illegal Order, to the Subversion of any Lawr or Statute of this Realm; or did ever assume to himself any arbitrary or illegal Power; or ever reverse any Judgment given in the Court of Exchequer, otherwise than as is warranted and allowed by the Law, and in the Presence of the Barons of the Court of Exchequer, who were always present in the Court of Exchequer Chamber when their Judgment were examined, as the Statute in such Cases directs: Nor did ever deliver in any Court of Judicature, or other Place whatsoever, any Position whatsoever dangerous to the legal Constitution of the Kingdom, or destructive to the Property of the Subject, as is charged by the said Article.

And as to all other Matters and Things in the said Articles contained, and not herein before particularly answered unto, the said Lord Somers saith, he is not guilty of them, or any of them, in Form as the same are charged upon him in and by the said Articles; and humbly submitteth himself to your Lordships Judgment.

AN ingrossed Bill for the better settling and preserving the Library kept in the House at Westminster, called Cotton-house, in the Name and Family of the Cottons, for the Benefit of the Publick, was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered, as a Rider, That, for the bettet securing and preserving the said Library, all Grants or Devises whatsoever of any the Manuscripts, Memorials, Medals, or other Rarities, in the said Library, in the Schedule now remaining in the said Library, shall be void; and that, within Six Months after any Library-keeper shall undertake the said Office, he shall cause another Schedule to be made in Parchment, as well of the Names and Titles of all Manuscripts, and other Papers and Records there, as of the Pages and Folios, and cause the same to be irirolled in Chancery, without Fees:

And the same was thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to be made Part of the Bill.

Then the several Amendments following were proposed to be made to the Bill; viz.

Pr. 2. L. 2. leave out " thereunto annexed;' and insert " now remaining in the said Library

Pr. 3. L. 30, and 31. leave out "* " and insert " in the said Schedule:*

And the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and the Bill amended at die Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: and that the Title be, An Act for the better settling and preserving the Library kept in the House at Westminster, called Cotton-house, in the Name and Family of the Cottons, for the Benefit of the Publick.

Ordered, That Sir Bartholomew Shower do cany the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence thereunto.

Ordered, That the Thanks of this House be given to Sir John Cotton, for his great and generous Benefaction to the Publick: And that Sir Bartholomew Shower and Mr. Topham do give him the Thanks of this House accordingly.

The Petitioners Council objected to John Esquire, and Giles Yard Esquire, as honorary Freemen; because the Oath of honorary Freemen is different from that of a trading Freeman; the Oath of the latter obliging them to perform the Duties of the Corporation, which is not mentioned in the Oath of an honorary Freeman.

That the Petitioners Counsel also objected to Five; viz. William Cock, John Manoioay, John Clarke, Francis

And the Short of that Case is this: Mr. Whitrow was Mayor of Dartmouth, and died within his Year: Mr. Whitrowe had been sworn by Mr. Bully, that was Mayor before him: After the Death of Mr. Whitrowe, Mr. Bully, swore Mr. Sykes Mayor; but Mr. Rocket, being a Candidate for the Mayoralty, and thinking himself aggrieved, the Day before Michaelmas, when Mr. Sykes was at London, broke open the Guildhall, and kept Possession: And afterwards brought a Mandamus for Mr. Bully to swear him Mayor; which Mr. Bully refusing to do, and making a Return, That Mr. Rockett was not duly elected,

viz the eldest Son for oa. Sd. Fine, and the Apprentices for I o s. Fine:

That the Petitioners Counsel also produced several Entries, in their Books, of Persons made free, as the Mayor Freemen; viz.One Person by a Mayor: But there was no Instance of that Kind since the Year One thousand Six hundred and Seventy-two:

That the Sitting Members Counsel admitted, That it had been formerly the Practice for the Mayors to make, each of them. One Freeman; but, since the Constitution of One thousand Six hundred Seventy-two, that Practice had been discontinued.

Upon the Petition of Frederick Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of the Lord William Port let, and George Rodney Bridges Esquire, to serve for the City of Winchester:

That the Petitioner's Counsel owned, That they had no Instructions against Mr. Bridges' Election.

But the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That there had been indirect Practices by the Sitting Member, the Lord William Powlett; and that they should also take off several from his Lordship's Poll: And they called,

Richard Good: Who said, That he was Mayor of Chester the last Year before this, and also Under Sheriff of the County of Southampton; but he had the Under Sheriff's Office by the Recommendation of the Duke of Bolton, who, at the same time, engaged him not to make any Freemen of Winchester without his Approbation: However, it was acknowleged, That the Duke of Bolton had not proposed to the Aldermen to make Mr. Chute and Mr. Pitt free; and it was opposed by Mr. Perdue and Mr. Sharpe; they saying, It was against the Duke's Interest: Mr. Good also said, That Mr. Tilney had settled

a Renefaction on the City in the same Year, the Nature of which was, to lend Money to some poor Tradesmen for a certain Time, without Interest: And that, the same Year, he did make Mr. Woodroffe, and Mr. Tichborne free:

And that afterwards Mr. Bridges came to him, and told him, He had a Letter from the Duke; and that he called him Knave, and said, He had very much disobliged tlife Duke, by making Persons free against the Duke's Interest; and that the Duke would be his Ruin.

And Mr. Good further said, That he had received Letters out of the Isle of Wight, That Colonel Lee would not employ him as Under Sheriff, because he was out of the Duke's Favour: That afterwards he was restored to the Duke's Favour; and the Duke wrote a Letter to Colonel Lee, on the said Mr. Good s behalf; but Colonel Lee said the: Letter came too late.

Mr. Matt hex. 0 Imber, the present Mayor, said, That

he had been Mayor several times; and that, a little before Michaelmas last, the Duke desired him, That he would not make any Person free without his Approbation: And he ivas desired to oppose the making free of Mr. Chute and Mr. Sturt; which accordingly lie did,

because he had promised the Duke: But it was acknowleged, That the Duke had not proposed any to him to be made free: And Mr. Imber further said, That the Recorder asked him, if the Under Sheriff's Place would be suitable to him; and he reckoned it was so proposed, to engage him to oppose the making of Mr. Chute and Mr. Pitt free: And that the Recorder came to him,

after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, and desired him to send the Serjeant to the Members of the Corporation, to desire them to attend the Duke, at his House, in the Afternoon:

That accordingly the Serjeant went: And he, coming to wait on the Duke, found a great Number of the Corporation there; and the Duke pressing him for his Votes, he told his Grace, He hoped he did not expect both his Votes: That they had Wine there; but Mr. Bridges said He would not drink, unless it was upon the Recorder's Account: That, desiring to make his Brother free, he was told, He must ask the Duke's Consent: To which he replied, shall I not make my Brother free, who may leave my Family 1,000l. ?and, accordingly he did make him free: And that, waiting on the Duke the Election Day in the Morning, his Grace desired him not to go to the Election, till Major Morgan came to Town; That, at the Election, the Duke of Richmond said to Colson and Clerke,

Upon the Complaint made to- toe House, That Edward Oliver junior, Thomas Terry, John and

George Briggs, have entered upon the Lands of James Herbert Esquire, in the County of Kent, and taken away Copperas Stones from off the same, in Breach of the Privilege of this House:

That the Committee have examined several Witnesses-in relation to that- Matter; v

John Kennard said, That he knew toe Estate where the Stones were picked; and that lie held the Ground of Mr. Herbert; and that his Father, and himself, had paid Rent for it Eighteen Years to Mr.

Mr. Gustavus Mell said, That he received Rent for Mr. Herbert, of Kennard, for the said Ground and had sold the Stones for Mr. Herbert several Years: That he had forewarned the Persons against Picking off the Copperas-Stones from Mr. Herbert's Ground; and did know in fact, that they were carried away; but could not speak, as to the Persons complained against, lie not being present when the Fact was done.

Stephen Taplin said, That himself, and Goodman-Terry's Wife and Family carried toe Stones from Mr. Herbert's Ground, and mixed them with the Stones on. Mr. Guidott's Ground; and that Thomas , John Terry, and George Briggs, were present when die Stones-were carried from Mr. Guidott's Ground, and put into the Boat.

Mary Milksted said. That Taplin, and Goody Terryt and herself, carried Stones off Mr. Herbert's Ground to Mr. Guidott's: That Goodman 'Terry knew his Wife picked the Stones off Mr. Herbert's G round; for that he had seen them do it several times; and lie paid for the picking of some of them no longer ago than the 15th of May last

Mary Kinsfoot, said, She had seen Goodman Servant and Children gather Stones from Mr. Herbert's Ground within Six Weeks.

Stephen Taplin, said, That Edward Oliver s Hoy, which carried away the said Stones, lay against Mr. Herbert's Lands.

Charles Waste said, That, by virtue of a Power given him from Mr. Herbert, he seized these Stones to Mr. Herbert's Use, upon Mr. Herbert's Manor; but he did not know upon whose Ground; and discharged them from taking away the said Stones.

Edward Gilbert said, That he had seen Captain Son and Daughter pick them; and they were afterwards carried away by Captain Terry to Oliver's Hoy, in Carts.

Henry Addis said, That he had rented the Profit of these Stones of Mr. Herbert, for his Master's Use; and that he paid on the First Lease, Fifty Pounds a Year, and, on the Second Lease, Sixty Pounds a Year; both which Leases were expired.

Mr. Mell said, That he had sold these Copperas Stones-

for Two hundred Thirteen Pounds a. Year, clear of all Charges.

That the Counsel for the Persons complained against, insisted, That, upon the Evidence given, it appearing that these Stones carried away were mixed with Mr. Guidott's, the Property of them all became Mr.

Guidott's; and that they had forewarned the Pickers-to take Stones from Mr. Herbert's Ground: And called,

Edward Metham: Who said, That Mr. Guidoit, about Three Years ago, did forewarn Taplin and Milsted not to pick any Stones from Mr. Herbert's Ground.

Elizabeth Kennard said, That this Freight had been gathering almost Twelve Months; and that she heard Stephen Ten-y, Two Years ago, forewarn Taplin and Milksted from picking any Stones off Mi-. Herbert's Ground.

A Petition of divers Officers, Clothiers, and others, willing to purchase forfeited Estates in Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners being interested in Arrears of Pay, and Cloath-ing the Army, and also possessed of Transport Debentures, Malt Tickets, and other Species, directed by Act of Parliament to be taken in Payment for the Purchase of the said Estates; which, to dispose of at the present Discount, would ruin many of the Petitioners; That it seems very difficult for the Petitioners to become single Purchasers, with their separate Effects, not only in respect of the great Trouble and Expence each Person must be at, in making particular and distinct Purchases, but that Purchases can never be found, suitable either to the Abilities of the Petitioners, or to the Species they are separately possessed

A. 1701.

of: Therefore the Petitioners, and others, are desirous to become joint Purchasers, and have subscribed about Two hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds, and deposited the greatest Part thereof in the several Species aforesaid:

That they are sensible many Difficulties may arise, and attend such joint Purchasers, in regard the same must be taken in Trust; whereby they will not be so capable of disposing their respective Estates, of sue, or be sued, as if they were impowered to act in a politick Capacity: And praying, That Leave may be given for bringing in a bill for an Incorporation, for the Purposes aforesaid; with such Powers and Limitations as- this House shall think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Lord Cutts do prepare, and bring in, the same.

Mr. Bromley reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up the Articles of Impeachment, and who w ere to consider of the Messages from the Lords, relating to the former Impeachments, and inspect the Precedents of Messages in relation to former Impeachments, and report the same to the House; That they had considered the said Messages, and inspected the Precedents: And that they had drawn up an Answer to the Message from the Lords, the Twenty-first Instant; and had directed him to report the same to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

IN Answer to your Lordships Message, of the Twenty-first Instant, the Commons have prepared a Replication to the Earl of Orford's Answer to the Articles of Impeachment of high Crimes and Misdemeanors, exhibited against him; and, at present, defer bringing it up to your Lordships, because, in the Tryal of the several Impeachments now depending, the Commons think it most proper, from the Nature of the Evidence that will be given at the said Tryals, to begin with the Tryal of the Impeachment of John Lord Sommers, of high Crimes and Misdemeanors.

And, as to your Lordships other Message, the Commons take it to be without Precedent, and unparliamentary; they, as Prosecutors, having a Liberty to exhibit their Articles of Impeachment in due time, of which they, who are to prepare them, are the proper Judges: Vol. 13.
