From the House of Commons, 31* Maii 1701.

Sir,

THE House of Commons having taken Notice of the Absence of several of their Members, I am commanded to acquaint you with it, that you may give immediate Summons to all the Members of this House, Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, within your County, to attend their Service in Parliament on Monday the Ninth Day of June next, notwithstanding any Leave for Absence; the House of Commons intending to proceed further, with all Severity, against all such of their Members, as shall then neglect their Attendance: And you are to give an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereupon, unto,

Sir,

Your humble Servant

A Bill for preventing Frauds &nd Abuses in the Duties upon Salt; and for collecting the same with less Charge to the Publick; was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time upon Tuesday Morning next.

The House being informed, That the Trustees for the Irish Forfeitures in England were at the Door;

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Paper relating to their Proceedings upon the Petitions to them referred: And the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Buf-gesses, in Parliament assembled;

May it please your Honours,

IN Obedience to your Orders of the Nineteenth of this instant May, requiring us to state Matters of Fact only, on the several Petitions relating to the Irish Forfeitures; and to report the same to your Honours; and that we should, with all Expedition, from time to time, transmit our Reports on the said Petitions respectively to the Clerk of this Honourable House;

We have, with utmost Diligence and Duty, pursuant to the said Orders, examined the several Facts, on such of the said Petitions as were delivered us, in such manner as we were capable of examining the same; and, where the Facts were within our Knowledge, and whereof we had certain Proof, we have reported the same accordingly.

As to other Matters, whereof the Proof lies in Ireland, and we could only hear ex parte, without administering an Oath, we have laid before your Honours such Proofs thereof, as have been offered us; and have annexed thereto such Affidavits, and other Papers, as the Petitioners produced before us, and affirmed to be true; which we have made Part of the Report, to the End your Honours may be duly apprised of the Evidence*, w hereon we have grounded our respective Reports.

We further crave Leave to acquaint your Honours, That we have given Copies of our Reports to such of the Petitioners as demanded them, that they might have an Opportunity of making further Proof of the Allegations of their Petitions; and to prevent your Honours receiving any Complaints, that we kept them in Ignorance of the Contents thereof.

All which is humbly submitted, &c.

II. Sheres,

Fra. Annesky, John Trenchard.

And then they withdrew.

And the House proceeded to take into Consideration what is proper to be done in relation to the said Petitions, and Reports thereupon.

And the Question being put, That the said Words be added to the Question;

The House divided.

A Petition of Jonathan Langley Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner raised and rommandeda Company of One hundred Men in the Regiment commanded by the Honourable Colonel Francis Russell, late Governor of Barbados; and served in that Island from the first going over of the said Regiment, being First Captain; and for great Part of the Time, was obliged to support his own Men out of his own Pocket and Credit, Returns being very difficult and uncertain, by reason of the late War with France; and was twice taken Prisoner by the French in his Return, and lost that little he had got by that troublesome Voyage; and, procuring the Ship, in which he was taken, to be ransomed, was, under God, the Instrument of preventing both the West-India and Virginia Fleets from being made Prisoners by the French, by giving seasonable Advice to their Excellencies the then Lords Justices: And praying he may be inserted in the List of Officers in Half-pay, to commence from the Disbanding of the said Regiment; and be otherwise considered for his Services and Losses, as shall be thought most fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to w hom it was referred to inspect the Papers relating to Half-pay, shall be made.

A Petition of William Adams Gentleman was presented Pitt®, to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was appointed Ensign to Captain Lodozcick Carlisle his Company of Foot, in the Regiment commanded by the Right Honourable the Earl of Drogheda, in Ireland, the Sixteenth of September One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine; and served therein till the said Regiment was broke: That the Petitioner's Brother, Lieutenant Thomas Adams, w as slain in the said Regiment at the Siege of Carrickfergus in Deland; to whom there was, and is yet, due the Sum of Thirty-eight Pounds Five Shillings, both for his Pay, and also for furnishing his Company with Stockings and Shoes: Which Monies are due to the Petitioner, as Heir and Administrator to his said Brother:

That the Petitioner hath, ever since, served his Majesty as a Volunteer, in Hopes of Preferment, both in Flanders and England, and now belongs to his Majesty's Regiment of Foot Guards: That by virtue of his Commission, he humbly hopes, he is within the Intentions of the House for Half-pay, until otherwise provided for: And praying,

That he may be inserted in the List of Half-pay.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom it was referred to inspect the Papers relating to Half-pay, shall be made.

A Petition of Captain William Folchier Despierres was Ditto* presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner served his Majesty, in Scotland\ as Captain in the Regiment of Foot commanded by the Honourable Sir William Douglas as Colonel, from the Time of the first raising that Regiment, until the Tenth of December One thousand Six hundred Ninety-seven: That having had no Allowance, nor Half-pay, he hath contracted Debts for his Subsistence: And praying the House to grant,

That he may be inserted in the List of Officers, and intitled to Half-pay, until otherwise provided for.

Resolved, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report of the Committee, unto whom it was referred to inspect the Papers relating to Half-pay, shall be made. \

Equity

Equity of Redemption of the Premises to his Wife and Executrix: Whereupon, the said Smith did afterwards, for a further Sum paid to her, purchase of her the same; and was put into Possession thereof: That, Two Years after Smith's Purchase, the said Lands were extended, upon a Recognizance of One thousand Six hundred Pounds, which Bromhall had, about Thirteen Yearn before the Purchase, entered into for Security of Money given to a Charity; and, upon that Extent, the said Smith was forced, in the Year One thousand Six hundred Eighty-three, to pay to one Edw. Kinmston Esquire, Four hundred Twenty-five Pounds more; upon which, the said Recognizance, by a Decree of the Court of Chancery, was assigned to Smith: That, Bromhall being, in his Life-time, and at his Death, seised of the Inheritance of the Office of Warden of the Fleet, the Prison-houses and Shops thereunto belonging, which were affected by the said Recognizance; but were by him pre-mortgaged to one Henry Norwood Esquire; Smith thereupon exhibited his Bill in Chancery against the said Norwood, and others, to have the said Four hundred Twenty-five Pounds, and Interest, paid out of the said Office; and, in One thousand Six hundred Eighty-five, Smith obtained a Decree to redeem Norwood\ who had the First Mortgage, and to have all Smith's said Money, and Demands, out of the said Office, after Nomood was Satisfied his Mortgage^money: That, in One thousand Six hundred and Ninety-two, there being a Bill in this House, % vhich passed into an Act, for Sale of the said Office and Houses, on behalf of the Heir of the said Bromhall, Smithy upon his Petition, had his Claim to the said Office and Houses saved to him in the said Act, by a Proviso therein: That also, in One thousand Six hundred Ninety-six, there being another Bill in this House, which passed into an Act, for the more effectual Relief of Creditors, in Cases of Escapes; and for preventing Abuses in Prisons, and pretended privileged Places; the said Smithy upon his Petition, had his, his Heirs, Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, Claim to the said Office and Houses particularly saved to him, and them, by a Proviso in that Act: That the Petitioners are informed, there is now a Bill depending before the House, to regulate the said Prison of the Fleet; in which there is no saving Clause for the Petitioners Right, as they are informed: And praying the y may have a saving Clause in this Bill, as they have had in former Acts of this Kind; or other Relief, as shall be thought fit.

King's Bench A Petition of the Clothiers, and others, Traders in the and Fleet Woollen Manufacture, on behalf of themselves, and divers others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners having sustained great Losses, by the ill Practices of the Marshal and Warden of the Kings Bench and Fleet; and understanding, that there is a Bill depending in this House, for regulating the said Prisons; which, the Petitioners humbly conceive, will be of great Advantage to the trading Part of the Kingdom: And praying the House will pass the same, with such Amendments as shall be thought fit.

ships let the Cohimoni know, That they will proceed to the Tryal of any of the impeached Lords, whom the Commons should be first ready to begin with, so as there may be no Occasion taken from thence for any unreasonable Delay in the Prosecution of any of them: And further to acquaint them, That, having searched their own Journals, they do not find, that, alter a general Impeachment, there has ever been so long a Delay of bring- > ing up the particular Articles of Impeachment, sitting the Parliament; and therefore the Lords do think they had Reason to assert, That it was a hardship to the Two Liords concerned, especially after their Lordships had put the House of Commons in mind of exhibiting such Articles; and not agreeable to the usual Proceedings in Parliament: And as the Lords do not controvert what Right the Commons may have of impeaching, in general Terms, if they please; so the Lords, in whom the Judicature does intirely reside, think themselves obliged to assert, That the Right of limiting a convenient Time for bringing the particular Charge before them, for the avoiding Delay ia Justice, is lodged in them.

The Lords hope the Commons, on their Part, will be as careful not to do any thing that may tend to the Interruption of the good Correspondence between the Two Houses, as the Lords shall ever be, on their Part: And the best Way to preserve that, is, for neither of the Two Houses to exceed those Limits, which the Law and Custom of Parliament have already established. Mr. Brewer reported, from the Committee, to whom Army Debts,

the Petition of several Colonels of the Army, in behalf of themselves, and others; and also the Petition of Colonel William Seymour, Sir Harry Dutton Colt, Administrators to Colonel Edward Dutton Colt, Colonel Harry Mordmit, and Colonel Thomas Brudeneil, on behalf of themselves and the rest of the Officers of the Four late Marine Regiments, were referred; the Matter as it appeared to the said Committee; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That upon hearing the Petitioners, and several Persons by them produced to make good the Allegations of their Petition:

It appeared to the Committee, That, upon the raising of a Regiment, Cloathing is immediately provided; and, for the Satisfaction of Tradesmen, who furnished the same, a Minute was made in Council, That the Cloathing Part of the Pay should be paid to the Year's End, although the Regiments should happen to be disbanded sooner:

That Cloathing is always provided for the Number of the Establishment, without any Regard to Defectives by Loss in Service, Sickness, Desertion, or otherwise:

That, in November and December One thousand Six hundred Ninety-seven, near a Third Part; Twelve Drummers, Twelve Serjeants, Twelve Corporals, and Two hundred and Thirty Men, were reduced out of every Regiment; and, in February following, several Regiments were intirely disbanded; w hereby the Fund for Cloathing ceased, and thereby a great Deficiency in that Payment happened; for that, at the Pay Office, they make na Allowance for Cloathing, any longer than the Men are upon the Muster-rolls.

And the great Discount upon publick Payment, at that time, increased the Deficiency of the Cloathing Part of the Pay; for that many of the Clothiers offered to cloatho for Half the Price in ready Money, as on the Tallies had from the Treasury:

That the House, by their Votes of the 27th of April 1699, having thought fit to allow* Half-pay to such Officers as were in the Regiments at the time of Disbanding, who were not cleared, nor any way provided for; That the Petitioner never received any Pay, neither Subsistence, nor otherwise; and there being a considerable Arrear due to him, and he being omitted in the Establishment for Half-pay: And praying, the House would be pleased, as n he is intitled to Half-pay. by the Votes aforesaid, to order,

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of Dutieso» the Society of Merchant Adventurers within the City of Bristo/l, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners being informed a Bill is brought in, proposing to restrain the Refining of Rock Salt; which, they humbly conceive, may tend to bring that Commodity into a Monopoly, and further advance the extravagant Price thereof, to the general Prejudice of his Majesty's Subjects, but especially to the Navigation and Trade of this City; and occasion more Ships belonging to this, and the Ports of this Channel, to victual in Ireland:

And praying, the House will take into Consideration the great Disadvantage that will accrue to this City, and the Trade and Navigation thereof, in case the Price of Salt shall be further advanced, by a Combination of the Refiners.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

xci&e Freuen Esquire, Gilbert Whitehall, and Robert William-

EYdiiie. S0)}^ in of themselves, and many Thousands more,

who are intitled to annual Rents, or Sums payable out of the hereditary Revenue of Excise, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Encouragement of an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of King Charles the Second, his said Majesty became indebted to the Petitioners, several Goldsmiths, and others, above Thirteen hundred thousand Pounds; in Lieu and Satisfaction whereof, by Letters Patents, in the

Twenty-ninth Year of his Reign, did grant, out of the hereditary Revenue of Excise, to each of the Patentees, their Heirs and Assigns, annual Rents, or Sums, for near Eighty thousand Pounds per Annum, after the Rate of Six per Cent, for ever, or till the Principal Sum, together with Arrears of Rent, should be paid to whom it should belong: That the said yearly Rents, or Sums, were paid to Lady-day 1683; ^ie Proprietors not obtaining further Payments, there is Eighteen Years Arrears of Rent due at Lady-day 1701: That, after Ten Years Prosecution of the Cause, in tJie several Courts of Law, by the Petitioner Williamson, the said Patents have, in the most solemn Manner, been affirmed to be a good Title; and that those yearly Rents, or Sums, and the Arrears thereof, ought to be paid out of that Revenue of Excise:

That all the Proprietors, under those Patents, have the very same Right and Title to their respective annual Rents, or Sums, and the Arrears thereof, out of the hereditary Excise, as the said Williamson hath; and, upon the like Process in Law, it is presumed, they may all obtain the like Justice; but it appears by the Votes of the 23d of May, that this House is intending to dispose of great Sums of Money, arising out of the Revenues mentioned in the Act for his Majesty's Houshold, &c.: And praying, That their legal Rights and Properties, in the hereditary Revenue of Excise, may be preserved, as the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to which the Petition of Thomas Hodges Esquire is referred.

A Petition of the Proprietors of Brine Salt, and Manufacturers thereof, and Inhabitants in and about Nampt-wick, in the County Palatine of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have been, and are, extremely discouraged by such Advantages given to Salt Rock, and the Salt made thereof, as tend to impair the Revenue, and ruin the Manufacture of Brine Salt, by not being under the same Limitations at the Pit, by Allowances in the Drawback, and Weight, exceeding the Brine a Third-part, though productive of better Salt, by importing and selling foreign Salts in England by Measure, and, in Ireland, both foreign and English Salt; the foreign there paying no more Duty than the English; which, if applied Weight for Weight, exceeds all other Salt in Cleanness, and Cure both of Flesh and Fish; and by so many and great Discouragements, the Petitioners, with Thousands more, are extremely impoverished: And praying, That for the general Encouragement of the said Manufacture of Salt, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to apply such Remedy as shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ditto. A Petition of the Refiners of Rock Salt, within the City of Bristoll, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners being informed, a Bill is brought in, proposing to restrain the refining Rock Salt; which, is conceived, will tend to the creating a Monopoly of that Commodity, to the Prejudice of his Majesty's Subjects, by further increasing the Price of Salt, and the Ruin of the Petitioners, and many Hundred Families in this Kingdom, who have erected very considerable Works for refining Rock Sait, and who wholly depend thereon: And praying, That the House will take the Petitioners into Protection, that they may not lose the great Sums of Money they have expended in erecting 'Works, and be deprived of the Benefit of their Trade, by which they support themselves and Families.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

toto. A Petition of Philip Doubt, John Adams, and Robert JVren, Inhabitants in the Borough of Bideford, in the Vol 13.

County of Devon, Refiners of Salt made from Rock, w as presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the greatest Part of the said County is furnished with Salt made of Rock: That it gives Content, and saves and cures Flesh and Fish, as well as Salt made of Brine; s That, in case the Use and Making of Rock Salt should be prohibited, it would be very prejudicial to all the Country, because the Brine Salt Men formerly did, and probably will again, if it be in their Power, make them pay pay Four times dearer than the Price current now; and will consequently cost at least Nine-pence,-if not Twelve-pence per Bushel, to the Country, more than now they pay; besides great Waste in bringing white Salt by Water, sometimes Fifteen or Twenty per Cent, more than Rock; and the Petitioners have been at very great Charges in erecting Houses, and providing Utensils, to refine Salt from Rock, having been encouraged by former Acts; so that, if the Making or Use of Rock Sait should be pro-, hibited, any otherwise than now it is, it will tend and bey not to the Petitioners great Loss only, but Damage of the Country generally; and many poor Men employed, and their Families, would be Sufferers thereby: Andi praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises, and order ..... the Continuance of refining Salt from Rock, in regard it manifestly tends to publick Good; and let it stand on the same Foot as it now doth.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the working People and Labourers, on Duties on behalf of themselves, and several others, employed in Salt, the Making of Salt from Brine, inhabiting in the Counties of Durham and Northumberland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, for some Months, have been reduced to a very deplorable and indigent Condition, by reason that the Saltworks in the Counties aforesaid were unemployed, and great Decay in the Salt Trade: That they being incapable of being employed in other Business, and having no other Subsistence; and they, and their Families, which consist of some Thousand of the poorest People, had undoubtedly starved and perished, if not relieved by the Proprietors of Salt, and other the Inhabitants:

And praying the Consideration of the House, and to redress the great Wants they are subject to, and lie under.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of Jonathan Case, John Blackbome, Samuel Brockcnborough, and Daniel Peek, Gentlemen, on behalf of themselves, and several others, Proprietors of Hock Salt, and Refiners of Salt from Rock, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in a Bill now depending before the House, for preventing Frauds and Abuses in the Duties upon Salt; and for collecting the same with less Charge to the Publick; there is a Clause to prohibit the Refining of Salt from Rock above Distance from the Pit, under colour to prevent Frauds in relation to the Duty: By passing this Clause, the Makers of Salt from Brine-springs and Sea-water will entirely engross the Salt Manufacture, and thereby ruin the Rock Salt Refiners; who, through the Encouragement of late Acts of Parliament, have been erected; and will be so far from increasing, that it will diminish, the Duty, by raising the Price of Salt, and lessening the Consumption thereof; And praying, That, by their Counsel, they may be heard against the said Clause, before the same do pass.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Jonathan Case, John Blackbome, Samuel Brockcnborough, and Daniel Peck, be heard before the said Committee, by their Counsel, upon their said Petition;

It pasted in the Negative.

Ordered, That the Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Amendments, made by the Lords, to the said Bill, be taken into Consideration.

Mr. Harcourt reported from the Committee appointed proceeding to draw up Articles of Impeachment; and who were to on the Im. consider of the Message from the Lords the Fourth of PeachraeDl* June instant; and to draw up what shall be offered at a Conference with the Lords, upon the Subject-matter of the said Message; That they had drawn up the same accordingly; and had directed him to report the same to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read twice; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and is as followeth; viz.

The Commons have desired this Conference, upon your Lordships Message of the 4th of June, in order to preserve a good Correspondence with your Lordships, which Will always be the Endeavour of the Commons, and is at this time particularly necessary, in order to bring the impeached Lords to a speedy Tryal: And because the Messages, which your Lordships have thought fit to send to the Commons, and the Answers thereunto, seem not to tend towards expediting the Tryals, which the Commons so much desire, but may rather furnish Matter of Dispute between the Two Houses; the Commons therefore choose to follow the Methods formerly used, with good Success, upon the like Occasion: And, for the more speedy and easy adjusting and preventing any Differences, which have already happened, or may arise, previous to, or upon, these Tryals; the Commons do propose to your Lordships, That a Committee of both Houses be nominated, to consider of the most proper Ways and Methods of proceeding on Impeachments, according to the Usage of Parliaments.

Ordered, That Mr. St. John do go to the Lords, and Conference desire the said Conference. desired.

delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and are as follow; viz.

Articles exhibited by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled, in Maintenance of their Impeachment against Charles Lord Halifax, t)f High Crimes and Misdemeanors.

1. WHEREAS several Persons, contrary t6 their Duty and Allegiance to his Majesty, and his late Royal Consort, of ever-blessed Memory, traiterously adhering to their Majesties Enemies, did levy and maintain, within their Majesties Realm of Ireland, a desperate and bloody War and Rebellion against their Majesties; and were, by his Majesty's Conduct and Courage, at the great Expence of his English Subjects, reduced to their due Obedience to the Crown of England ': And whereas, upon the Fourth Day of April in the Year of our Lord One thousand Six hundred and Ninety, it was resolved by the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, That a Bill should be brought in to attaint all Persons guilty of Rebellion in Ireland, or elsewhere, against their Majesties King William and Queen Mary; and to enact and declare their Estates to be forfeited, and to be sold, for the Reducing of that Kingdom: And whereas his Majesty, in his gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, did, upon the Fifth Day of January One thousand Six hundred and Ninety, 'assure them, That he would not make any Grant of the forfeited Lands in Ireland, till there should be another Opportunity of settling that Matter in Parliament, in such manner as should be thought most expedient: And where-ias the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled, by their humble Address to his Majesty, upon the Fourth Day of March One thousand Six hundred Ninety-two, did humbly beseech his Majesty, That, according to the Assurance his Majesty had been pleased to give them, no Grant might be made of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, till* there should be an Opportunity of settling that Matter in Parliament, in such manner as should be thought most expedient; to which his Majesty was pleased to give a most gracious Answer; whereby, and by many other Endeavours of the Commons in the following Sessions of Parliament, it appears, That what has since been declared by Act of Parliament, was the continued Sense of the Commons of England, That it was highly reasonable, that the forfeited Estates of Rebels and Traitors in Ireland should be applied in Ease of his Majesty's faithful Subjects of the Kingdom of England: And whereas it was the apparent Duty of every Officer or Minister of State to have had so much Regard to the Resolutions and Address of the House of Commons, to the publick Grood, and his Majesty's Honour, as to have dissuaded and prevented, as much as in them lay, the procuring or passing any Grant or Grants of the said forfeited Estates in Ireland; yet Charles now Lord Haiti fax, then the Honourable Charles Montague Esquire, being a Member of the Honourable House of Commons, One of the Lords of the Treasury, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and One of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, hath, since the aforesaid Fourth Day of March One thousand Six hundred Ninety-two, presumed to advise, pass, or direct the passing, a Grant to Thomas Railton Esquire, in Trust for himself, of several Debts, Interest, Sum and Sums of Money, amounting, in the Whole, to the Sum of Thirteen thousand Pounds, or thereabouts, due, owe-ing, and which ought to have accrued, to his Majesty, by reason of the Attainders, Outlawries, or other Forfeitures, of the respective Persons for whom the same were entered on Record; whereby he hath much contributed to the Contracting great Debts upon the Nation, the Laying heavy Taxes upon the People, hath highly reflected on his Majesty's Honour, and failed in the Performance of his Trust and Duty.

2dly, Whereas, by an Act of Parliament, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of his Majesty's Reign, in-12

tituled, An Act for granting an Aid to his Maj^ty, by Sale of the forfeited and other Estates and Interests in Ireland, and by a Land-tax in England, for the several Purposes therein mentioned, it is, amongst other things, enacted, That all and every Person or Persons whatsoever, who had, by virtue of any Grantor Disposition from his Majesty, or from his Majesty and the late Queen, received, for his or their own Use or Benefit, any Debt or Debts, or Sum or Sums of Motley whatsoever, due front any Debt Or Debts of any forfeiting Persons, mentioned or described in the said Act, or from any Person or Persons subject or liable to the Payment of any Sum of Money whatsoever to any of the said forfeiting Persons* should be, and they are thereby declared to be* respectively liable, and are required to repay every such Debt or Debts, Sum or Sums of Money, whatsoever, so by him, her or them, respectively received, into the Receipt of his Majesty's Exchequer in Ireland, on or before the Twenty-fourth Day of August One thousand Seveii hundred: And whereas the said Charles Lord Hally fax had, before the Making of the aforesaid Act, procured for Thomas Railton Esquire, in Trust for himself, a Grant of several Debts, by Judgments and otherwise, to several of the said forfeiting Persons, amounting to the Surn of Thirteen thousand Pounds, or therea bouts, forfeited to his Majesty by the Attainder, Outlawries, or other Forfeitures, of the respective Persons to whom such Debts were originally due; and, by virtue of the said Grant, the said Lord Halifax actually received, to his own Use, the Sum of One thousand Pounds, Part of the before-mentioned Sum of Thirteen thousand Pounds; which said Sum of One thousand Pounds the said Charles Lord Halyfax ought to have repaid, before the said Twenty-fourth of August One thousand Seven hundred, into the Receipt of his Majesty's Exchequer in Ireland, as by the Act he was required to have done; yet the said Charles Lord Halifax did not repay the said Sum of One thousand Pounds, as by the said Act he was required to do; but has hitherto, in Contempt of the Act, refused or neglected to repay the same; which Neglect or Refusal of him the said Charles Lord Halifax to repay the said Sum of One thousand Pounds, is a manifest Wrong to his Majesty, and the! Publick, and a Misapplication of that Sum to other Uses and Purposes than by the Act it is appropriated, and ought to have been applied.

3dly, That the said Charles Lord Halifax, being a Member of the Honourable House of Commons, One of the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord Treasurer of England, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and One of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, not contented with the many Employments, and Places of Honour, bestowed upon him by his Majesty, nor with the large and excessive Gains by him made by the Incomes and Profits arising from such Offices aftd Preferments, did, in Opposition to w hat he wrell knew to be the true Interest of England, and contrary to his Oath as a Piivy Counsellor, and his Duty as a publick Minister, at a time when the Nation was engaged in a tedious and expensive War against France for preserving the Balance and LiJ berties of Europe, and under such heavy Debts, as, without laying unsupportable Taxes on the People, were impossible to be satisfied, advise, procure, and assent, not only to the Passing of divers Grants to others in England and Ireland, but did obtain, and accept of, several beneficial ones to, or in Trust for, himself: Which said Practices of him the said Lord Halyfax were a most notorious Abuse of his Majesty's Goodness, a gre.it Breach of his Trust, and a very high Vexation and Oppression of his Majesty's other Subjects.

4thly, Whereas, by the Common Law, and by many Statutes and Ordinances of this Realm, it appears to have been the great Care of our Ancestors, that the King's Forests should be preserved, and, in particular, the Timber therein growing, for the Building and Repairing of the Navy Royal, which has ever been accounted, as it undoubtedly is, the great Security of this Realm: And whereas Charles Lord Halyfax was, in the Year of our

13 W* III g° JuniL 6ot

Lord One thousand Six hundred Ninety-seven, One of the Commissioners of the Treasury, Chancellor of the Exchequer* and One of his Majesty's Privy Council, and obliged, as well by repeated Oaths, as by the Duty he owed to his Majesty, and his Country, to have advised* consulted, and promoted, such Matters and Things as should, or at least were most likely to redound to his Majesty's Honour, and the Nation's Safety; yet the said Charles Lord Halyfax, not regarding the Laws and Ordinances of this Realm, nor his said Duty to his Majesty, and the Publick, but pursuing his private Interest, did, by Letters of Privy Seal, bearing Date on or about the Sixth Day of May, which was in the Year of our Lord One thousand Six hundred Ninety-seven, the Kingdom being then engaged in an expensive War, and the Debts of the Nation requiring the best and most frugal Management, procure from his Majesty a Grant to Henry Segar Gentleman, in Trust for himself, of the Sum of Fourteen thousand Pounds, of so much scrubbed Beach, Birch, Holly, Hazle, Thorns, and Orle, as should, by Sale, raise the said Sum of Fourteen thousand Pounds, to be fallen in . his Majesty's Forest of Deem, in the County of Gloucester, within the Space of Seven Years time, from the Twenty-fifth Day of December One thousand Six hundred and Ninety-seven; under colour of which Grant, Beach of a much greater Value, great Number of Saplin Oaks, which might, and would, have been serviceable to the Realm, and also many Tons of well-grown Timber, fit for the present Use of the Navy, have been cut, and fallen, and sold, and disposed of, for the Benefit of the said Lord Halyfax*.

5*th]y, Whereas there is not any thing that so much conduceth to his Majesty's and the Nation's Honour and Safety, as the due Ordering and Management of the King's Treasure, and the public Revenues, for the Receiving and Issuing forth of which the Wisdom and Policy of this Nation has provided and appointed several and distinct Officers, with beneficial Salaries, in order that they may be a Check to each other, and that no Loss may accrue to his Majesty, or the Publick, by the Corruption, Unskilfulness, or Negligence, of any particular Officer; yet he the said Charles Lord Halyfax, being One of the Lords of the Treasury, when, by the Death of the Honourable Sir Ro-hert Howard, the Office of the Auditor of the Receipts, and Writer of the Tallies, became vacant, not regarding the ancient Constitution, and approved Methods in ordering his Majesty's Treasury, and the publick Revenues, did grant, or procure to be granted, to Christopher Mount* ague Esquire, the Brother of him the said Charles Lord Holy fax, and then one of the Commissioners of the Excise, the said Place and Office of Auditor of the Receipts, and Writer of the Tallies; which said Grant was so made and procured by the said Lord Halyfax, in Trust, as to the Profits thereof, for himself; so that, from and after the Passing of the said Grant, he the said Lord Halyfax was, in Effect, at the same time, One of the Commissioners of the Treasury, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Auditor of the Receipts, and Writer of the Tallies, and enjoyed the Profits of the said several Offices; w'hich, by the Constitution of the Treasury, are manifestly inconsistent, and never were, or ought to be, trusted in the same Person; the Making and Procuring of which said Grant by him the said Charles Lord Halyfax, as aforesaid, was a manifest Violation of the established Course and Constitution of the Exchequer, a Breach of his Trust, of evil Example, and tended very much to the great Loss and Prejudice of his Majesty, and the Publick, by opening a Way to all manner of corrupt Practices in the future Management of the Revenues.

6thly, Whereas a Treaty and Alliance between Leopold the Emperor of Germany, and the States General of the United Provinces, was made, and concluded, in the Year of our Lord One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine, upon the Consideration of the Greatness of the common Danger, which then threatened all Christendom, from the excessive Power of France, and the unconstant Faith of the French in the Observance of Treaties i whereby it

was agreed, there should be, and remain for ever* a con- Lord stant, perpetual, and inviolable Friendship, and good Cor- HallifaxV respondence, between his Imperial Majesty and the States Impeach-General; That each of them should be obliged to pro- roent‘ mote the other's Interest; and, as much as in them lay, prevent all Damages and Inconveniences to each other:

And whereas certain separate Articles were also, at or about that time, made and annexed to the aforesaid Treaty; whereby the States General, maturely considering, that France had openly declared, in several Courts, That, notwithstanding the most solemn Renunciation, they continued their Pretension, by Force of Arms, to assert, for the Dauphin, the Succession of the Spanish Monarchy, in case the King of A^wshould die without Issue; and also considering, what a Blow their State would receive, and what Prejudice might happen, thereby to the publick Affairs and Quiet; did promise, That, in case his said Catholick Majesty should die without Issue, they would, with all their Force, assist his said Imperial Majesty, or his Heirs, in taking the Succession of the Spanish Monarchy, lawfully belonging to that House, together with its Kingdoms, Dominions, and Rights; and in their obtaining and securing the quiet Possession thereof, against the French, and their Adherents, w ho should, directly or indirectly, oppose that Succession; and, with Force, repel the Force which should be brought against them:

That, at the Instance of the States General, in pursuance of the said Treaty, and separate Articles, our most gracious Lord and Sovereign, his most Excellent Majesty King William the Third, w as invited to enter into the Alliance of the aforesaid Treaty, and into the Agreement of the said separate Articles; and thereupon, for restoring and preserving the publick Peace and Quiet, did afterwards, in the said Year of our Lord One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine, enter into, and, under the Great Seal of England* accept, approve, and ratify, and* in the most solemn manner, engage and promise, religiously and inviolably, to observe the same, without violate* ing the said Treaty, or separate Articles, in any Article, or suffering the same, to the utmost of his Power, to be violated:

That, in the Year of our Lord One thousand Six hundred Ninety-eight, a Treaty was projected and contrived in France, to be set on foot between his Majesty, the French King, and the States General, for a Partition of the Spanish Monarchy; whereby many large Territories thereunto belonging, in case of the Decease of the King of Spain, w ithout Issue, were to be allotted and delivered up to France:

The Tenour and Design of which last mentioned Treaty, w hilst the same was in Negotiation, w as communicated to the said Charles Lord Halyfax, then One of the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord Treasurer, Chancellor of the Exchequer, and One of his Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council: That the said Charles Lord Halifax, well knowing the most apparent evil Consequences, as well as the Injustice, of the said Partition, did not, according to the Trust and the Duty of the said several Offices, dissuade, or endeavour to obstruct, its take-ing Effect; but, on the contrary, having neither Regard to his Majesty's Honour, engaged by the above-mentioned Treaty with the Emperor and the States General, to the Trade and known Interest of these Kingdoms, or the Peace of Europe, did advise his Majesty to enter into the said Treaty; and did so far encourage and promote the same, that the said Treaty was concluded and ratified, under the Great Seal of England: Which said Treaty was evidently destructive of the Trade of this Realm, a Breach of the former Treaty, made with the Emperor in One thousand Six hundred Eighty-nine, dishonourable to his Majesty, highly injurious to the Interest of the Protestant Religion, and manifestly tended to disturb the general Peace of Europe by altering the Balance of Power therein, and strengthening France against the good Friends, and ancient Allies, of our Sovereign Lord the King.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir Richard and Mr. Grey:

Mr. Speaker,

We are commanded, by the Lords, to acquaint this House, That, in Answer to the Message of the House of Commons, of the Fourth Instant, the Lords say, by their Message sent on the Third, wherein they declare themselves ready to proceed to the T rial of any of the impeached Lords, whom the Commons should be first ready to begin with, they have given a full Proof of their Willingness to comply with the Commons, in any thing which may appear reasonable, in order to the speedy Determining of the Impeachments now depending: And therefore, as the Lords conceive the Commons had no Occasion to begin any Dispute on that Head, so their Lordships are careful to decline entering into a Controversy, which seems to them to be of no Use at present.

The Lords think themelves obliged to assert their un-undoubted Right to appoint a Day for the Trial of any Impeachment depending before them, if they see good Cause for it; w ithout any previous Signification from the Commons of their being ready to proceed; which Right i6 warranted by many Precedents, as well as consonant to Justice and Reason; and their Lordships, according to the Example of their Ancestors, w ill always use that Right with a Regard to the equal and impartial Administration of Justice, and with a due Care to prevent unreasonable Delays.

This being the Case, The Lords cannot but wonder, that the Commons, without any Foundation for it, should make use of Expressions, which, as their Lordships conceive, have never been used before by one House of Parliament to another; and which, if the like were returned, must necessarily destroy all good Correspondence between the Two Houses.

The last Part of the Commons Message being, in Effect, a Repetition only of their former, of the One-and-thirtieth of May, to which the Lords have already returned a full Answer, their Lordships think it not requisite to say more, than that they cannot apprehend with what Colour their calling upon the House of Commons to send up Articles against Two Lords, whom the Commons have so long since impeached in general Terms, can be said to tend to the Delay of Justice: And therefore, as the Lords think the Commons ought to have forborne that Reflection, so i 1

their Lordships, in saying no more upon the Occasion of this Message of the Commons, think they have given a convincing Proof of their Moderation, and of their sincere Desire of preserving a good Correspondence between the Two Houses; which is so necessary for the publick Security, as well as doing Right upon the Impeachments. Also,

That the Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Apsley'i Act for the better Performance of the last Will of Henry Apsley Esquire, deceased, without any Amendments.

A Petition of the Provost and Corporation of Money- Moneyer's ers was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, Company. That the Petitioners, for these several Hundred Years last past, have been incorporated into a Company, or Body Politick; and, in all that time, have made good, and are obliged to answer, all Gold and Silver committed to their Chaise: That, upon any Expedition of Coinage,

..... were and are forced to take to their Assistance great Numbers of strange Men, as Fifty or an Hundred, and sometimes Two or Three Hundred, or more, for the forwarding the Business of the Mint, and Service of the Publick; for all which the Petitioners are answerable: That the Petitioners have frequently been most notoriously abused by some Servants, and their Accomplices, who, under Pretence of seeing the Coinage, have robbed the Petitioners of great Sums of Money; so that, upon modest Computation, ..... have, at the last great Coinage, and since, lost above Six thousand Pounds:

That several of them, for such Robberies, have been prosecuted and convicted, and have afterwards obtained the Benefit of the Clergy; and that, notwithstanding such Punishment, such Robberies are often committed: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises; and to order, That Leave be given to bring in a Clause, to be added to some Bill, for making such Crimes Felony, w ithout Benefit of Clergy.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting several Duties upon low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction; and continuing several additional Duties upon Coffee, Tea, Cliocolate, Spices, and Pictures; and certain Impositions upon Haw kers,

Pedlars and Petty Chapmen; and the Duty of Fifteen Pounds per Centum upon Muslins; and for improving the Duties upon japanned and lacquered Goods; and for continuing the Coinage Duty for the several Terms and Purposes therein mentioned; is committed.

Sir Humphrey Mackworth reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for qualifying Justices of Peace was committed, That they had made several Amendments to the Bill; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally jmt thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

A Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to except some Counties out of the Act:

And the same was twice read with Blanks; and the Blanks were filled up:

And then the Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, to exempt Barristers at Law out of the Bill.

And the Question being put, That the Clause be brought up to the Table:

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, for Commissions of the Peace to be made gratis:

And the same was twice read; and amended; and afterwards agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Sir Rmvland Gwyn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Town of Nottingham; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Uppn the Petition of Robert Sacheverell Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of George Gregory Esquire, to serve for the Town of Nottingham:

That the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Mayor, Freemen, and Freeholders of 40 s. a Year.

It was also agreed, That the eldest Sons of Freemen, by their Birth; the younger Sons of Freemen, who have served Seven Years Apprenticeship whether in Nottingham, or elsewhere; and also Persons as have served Seven Years Apprenticeship to any Freeman of Nottingham; were well intitled to demand their Freedom.

That, upon the Poll, there were,

For the Sitting Member Mr. Gregory 558.

For the Petitioner - - - 534.

But the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That they should, by taking off from Mr. Gregory's Poll, and adding to their own, make themselves a Majority: And they also insisted, That there had been several ill Practices by the Sitting Member, in procuring Votes.

And, First, the Petitioner's Counsel proceeded to give an Account of such Persons as had a Right to their Freedoms, and had been denied to be made free; and would have voted for the Petitioner, and were refused: And they called,

Sam. Smith: Who said, That John Stevens did.serve JVm. Pery, a Freeman of Nottingham; and had demanded his Freedom Thirty or Forty times within these Two or Three Years last past:

That JVm. Lever ton had served Henry Brown, a Freeman; and had demanded Three times within a Year and an Half; but was refused, because he had waited upon a Gentleman out of Town Part of his Time:

That Nathnael Wild had served a Freeman; and demanded his Freedom Three Years ago; and was refused, because he lived out of Town:

Vol. 13.

That Edward Gunthorpe had served his Father, a Freeman; and demanded his Freedom Five Months before the Election; and was refused, because he was under Age:

That William Dunn had served one Bridges, a Bricklayer; and had demanded his Freedom Five Months ago, and before that, and was refused:

That John Brudsley was Apprentice with his Father; and had demanded his Freedom several times Five or Six Months ago; and was refused, because he lived in the Country:

That Sam. Anthony had served William BrinkJiurst; and was refused Five Months ago, and before, because he lived out of Town:

That JVm. Chamberlain had served his Father; but it was acknowleged he had been condemned for Horsestealing:

That Samuel Roberts was Apprentice to Thomas Figures; and demanded his Freedom Five Months before 'the Election; and was refused, because he did not produce his Indentures:

That Francis Pettison was the Second Son of a Freeman, and served his Father; and was' refused, because his Father lived out of Town: 1

That Tho. Burden served Thomas Bonny; and was refused, because he was married, although it was after his Apprenticeship:

That Joshua Skinner served John Iodin; and was refused, because his Master lived out of Town:

That John Weston served Geo. Kenning; but w as refused, because his Indentures were looked upon a fraudulent:

That Francis Sister served Benjamin Ryley; but was refused, because he served Part of his Time out of Town:

That Alexander Cormorick served Richard Redbour; but was refused for the like Cause:

That Stephen Longstone served Jeffery Lichman; and was refused, because he lived out of Town:

That JVm. Bartram was refused for the like Cause: That John Staples served John Clerk; but was refused, because his Master was not free, though he follows aTrade in Town:

That Daniel Noble served Thomas Goddard; and was refused for the like Cause, though Tho. Goddard's Name wras taken on the Poll:

To prove Soloinon Baker and John Baker were free, he produced the Copy of their Burgess Oath; which, Smith said, was usual to deliver to them at the time of (he making free:

That John Roberts served Joshua Walker; but w as refused, because his Master was not free:

That George Burton served Christopher Hooke; but was refused, because he was married:

That John Mabbott, the Son a Freeman, served John Pywell; and was refused, because he lived out of Town: That Stephen Ragg follows the Trade of a Carpenter in Town, and has voted several times:

That John Winter served Hugh Smith, Plasterer, and follows the Trade of a Plasterer; and was refused, because, Part of his Time of his Apprenticeship, he had been in the King's Service:

That William Crofts was a Freeman; but it w'as acknowleged, that he was disfranchised:

That William Blackstone is a reputed Burgess, and hath frequently voted:

That Patricius Goodall is a Freeman by Purchase: That William Roe is free; but lives out of Town: That John Sand ifer always enjoyed the Privilege of a Freeman; and his Apprentice's Vote was accepted.

That Gervase Sully, William Nicholson, and Joseph Hawkins, are reputed Freemen, and have frequently voted.

And Mr. Smith said, That these several Persons would have voted for Mr. Pierrepoint and Mr. Sacheverell, and were refused; and that several of them were asked who they w ere for, before they were refused:

Parsons said, That he hqd engaged hirnself to be for Master Pierrepont, and Mr. Sacheverell: And that Samuel Rickards, who solicited Votes for Mr. Gregory, desired his Vote for Mr. Gregory; and told him, He should have the Advantage of having \ol. of the Coventry Char rity lent him: That the said Parsons insisted to have ,5/. down: Mr. Rickards gave him a Note for it; and he accordingly received it: But it was acknowleged, That the 5/. was to be repaid when he received the 10/.; and that Thomas Wright was bound with him for it.

That he had 55. of one Hallom, to swear, that Ned Brazen, an Agent of Mr. Sacheverell, had given him 5 s.; but did not promise so to do, though he received the Money:

Mr. Harcourt reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up Articles of Impeachment, That they had, according to Order, drawn up an Answer to the Message from the Lords Yesterday; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was twice read; and, with an Amendment, agreed unto by the House; and is as followed; viz.

THE Commons in Hopes of avoiding all Interruptions and Delays in proceeding against the impeached Lords, and the many Inconveniencies, which might arise thereby, having proposed to your Lordships, at a Conference, That a Committee of both Houses might be nominated, to consider of the most proper Ways and Methods of proceeding on Impeachments, think, they might justly have expected your Lordships Compliance with their said Proposition, instead of your Lordships Answer to their Message, of the 4th Instant; which they Yesterday received: In which Answer of your Lordships, though many Matters of great Exception are contained, a suitable Reply whereunto would inevitably destroy all good Correspondence between the Two Houses; yet the Commons, from an earnest Desire to preserve the same, as well as to give the most convincing Proof of their Moderation, and to shew their Readiness to bring the impeached Lords to speedy Justice, at present insist only on their Proposition for a Committee of both Houses,

f Mr. Pierrepont,

I Mr. Scobell:

103.

to settle and adjust the necessary Preliminaries to the Tryals; particularly, whether the impeached Lords shall appear, on their Tryals, at your Lordships Bar, as Criminals; whether, being under Accusations of the same Crimes, they are to sit as Judges, on each others Tryals, for those Crimes; or can vote in their own Cases; as we find, by your Lordships Journals since their being impeached, they have been admitted to do: Which Matters, and some others, being necessary to be adjusted, the Commons cannot but insist on a Committee of both Houses to be appointed for that Purpose; their departing from which would be giving up the Rights of the Commons of England, known by unquestionable Precedents, and the Usage of Parliament; and making all Impeachments, the greatest Bulwark of the Laws and Liberties of England, impracticable for the future.

Ordered, That Mr. Harcourt do carry the said Answer to the Lords.

As to the Proposal of the Commons, That a Committee of both Houses should be appointed, to consider of the Ways and Methods of Proceedings on Impeachments; their Lordships cannot agree to it:

I. Because they do not find, that ever such a Committee was appointed on Occasion of Impeachments for Misdemeanors; And their Lordships think themselves obliged to be extremely cautious in admitting any thing new in Matters relating to Judicature.

2dlv, That although a Committee of this Nature was agreed to upon the Impeachments of the Earl of Danby, and the Five Popish Lords, for High Treason; yet it was upon Occasion of several considerable Questions and Difficulties, which did then arise; And their Lordships do not find, that the Success in that Instance was such, as should encourage the pursuing the same Methods again, though in the like Case; the Lords observing, that, after much Time spent at that Committee, the Disputes were so far from being the re adjusted, that they occasioned the abrupt Conclusion of a Session of Parliament.

3tlly, Their Lordships are of Opinion, That the Methods of Proceedings on Impeachments for Misdemeanors are so w ell settled by the Usage of Parliaments, that they do not foresee any Difficulties likely to happen; at least, none have been yet stated to them: And all the Preliminaries, in the Case of Stephen Goudett, and others, which was the last Instance of Impeachments for Misdemeanors, were easily settled and agreed to, without any such Committee.

4tbly, The Lords cannot but observe, That this Proposal of the Commons comes so very late, that their Lordships can expect no other Fruit of such a Committee, but the Preventing of the Tryals during this Session.

The Lords assure the Commons, That, in case any Difficulties shall arise in the Progress of these Tryals, which their Lordships do not foresee, they will be ready to comply with the Commons in removing them, as far as Justice, and the Usage of Parliament, will admit.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

Upon Examination of the Charge against Mr. Eduard Whitacre, for the Bailing and Escape of Mr. Henry Bolton, the Matter of Fact appears as followeth; viz.

By the Warrant of Commitment from Mr. Secretary Hedges it appears, That Bolton was accused, upon Oath, for confederating with Captain William Kidd for Piracy on the high Seas; which Warrant is marked (A); and is as followeth; viz.

(A) Whereas Henry Bolton is accused upon Oath, for confederating with Captain William Kidd, who is now a Prisoner in Newgate, for Piracy by him committed upon the High Seas: These are, in His Majesty's Name, to command and require you to receive into your Custody, from the Marshal of the Admiralty, the said Henry Bolton, and him safely to keep, until he shall be delivered by due course of Law: And'hereof fail not, as you will answer the contrary at your Peril.

Given under my Hand and Seal, this 30th Day of December 1700.

C. Hedges.

The Committee proceeded to examine into the Matter of the Presentment by the Grand Jury, High Sheriff, and Justices of the Peace, for the County of Southampton, against Mr. Whitacref dated the 26th of July 1700: Which said Presentment, with several Reasons for making the same, was laid before the Committee; and is marked (B); and is as followeth; viz.

By the Grand Jury, and Justices of the Peace, at the Assizes held at Wintcn, for the County of Southampton, July 26th 1700.

At the present and late Assizes held here for the said County, there have been several Prosecutions against Offenders, for notorious Thefts and Embezzlements of his Majesty's Naval Stores; and finding the Prosecutions* generally laid, have proved very irregular, to his Majesty's

geat Disservice, and to the Dissatisfaction of the whole ounty 2

We under-written, attending the said Assizes, to discharge our Duty, are of Opinion, That the Prosecution, and Management of the Tryals, upon the barbarous Murder of one Harris, and the Thefts that attended that Matter the last Assizes, and the Indictments now brought before us for several Abuses further discovered, relating to the notorious Practices of Purloining and Robbing of his Majesty's Stores at Portsmouth, and Timber in the New Forest, in a Succession of Years last past, are, by the Solicitor, Mr. Whitacre, either managed corruptly or ignorantly; whereby Opportunity hath been given for the Guilty to evade Justice, and bar the further Discovery of those pernicious Practices; the Consequences of which, we humbly desire, may be considered; and that the Reflections laid on our County, for want of Vigilance to detect such Crimes, may be removed, and fixed in the right Place.

GRAND JURY.

John St. Barbe, Geo. Stanley, Rich. Cobbe, Arthur Hyde, Will. Bishop, Tho. Dozvse, Richard Marks, IVm. Knapton, Jos. Hinxsman, Robert Cranston, Wm. Fisher junior, Edward Hooper, Jos. Lisle, Jos. White, Will. Bozcerman, Andrezv Smith, John King, John Goodyer.

Several Reasons which induced the Grand Jury, High Sheriff, and Justices of the Peace, for the County of Southampton, at the Assizes held at [Vinton, to make their Presentment against Mr. Whitaker, the 26th July 1700.

Article 1st. At Lent Assizes 1700, several Persons ' were indicted for embezzling his Majesty's Stores 2 at

13 W. III. ii° Junii.

at Portsmouth, and for murdering one Harris, who had discovered the same; but, by the irregular Management of the Prosecutions, several of them escaped Punishment; particularly David Aldridge, that had, by such Methods, got a very considerable Estate; and, as it appeared at the Tryals, was Principal in all those wicked Practices; but, by a sudden Artifice, he was tried first for the Murder, contrary to the positive Advice and Desire of Commissioner Greenhill, and Mr. Whitacre's Promise; where the Evidence, which after appeared upon other Indictments, was wanting, and he found guilty ex post facto; and a poor indigent Fellow', that was employed by him, being convicted as Principal, Aldridge was acquitted, with a slight Burning, though he had Three several Verdicts afterwards for Felony; the Indictments for which was observed to be against him only as accessary to the Embezzlement, when, at the TryaJs, the Evidence was full to have proved him Principal in several Burglaries; there being one Christopher May convicted upon the same Evidence, and was reprieved, and illegally bailed, before pardoned.

Article 2. One Daniel Lawrence was indicted for the same Crimes; but escaped, by Mr. Whit acre s Neglect, in not preparing the Evidence: And, in another Case, Three or Four Men were arraigned upon an Indictment drawn by Mr. Whitacre; who made so great a Mistake in Time, that what the Witnesses had to say, could not affect the Prisoners upon that Indictment; and were thereby acquitted.

Article 3. That one Moses House informed against White and Whitman, for cutting out the Marks of the King's Timber, in the New Fai'est, and setting their own Marks in the same, and carrying of it away for their own Use; but, instead of being made Prosecutor, was, the same Assizes, indicted for Facts of the like Nature; whereby to give White and Whitman, being rich Persons, Opportunity to escape, by taking of Houses Evidence; but House was tried at the Summer Assizes following, and was acquitted; the Prosecution appearing malicious.

Article 4. Summer Assizes 1700, one Ste. Carpenter Vas indicted for Felony and Burglary, in robbing his Majesty's Stores: The Evidence before the Grand Jury did not come up to find the Bill, as drawn, but would amount to a Misdemeanor: The Jury applied to Mr. Whitacre, and told him, That Bill would be found Ignoramus; but that the Fellow ought not to escape without Punishment; he refused to give any other Assistance then, but would refer it to the next Assizes; upon which the Jury sent to Commissioner Greenhill, who referred them to the Informations in Mr. Whitacre's Custody; upon Examination whereof, a new Indictment was brought, and other Witnesses sworn; upon which the Bill was found, the Person tried, convicted, and hanged; who, by Mr. Whitacre s Method, might have escaped.

Article 5th. Another Indictment was brought against one Whitman, for cutting the Mark out, and stealing of his Majesty's Timber in the New Forest; The Evidence sent up, were Two Peckhams;. but could say nothing to the Indictment against Whitman; but against one White; and House, which was to have been the Witness, was left out; upon which Mr. Whitacre was sent to, and a Bill desired against White, as well as Whitman; but he refused to do it; saying, He did not care whether the Bill was found or not; upon which Sir Robert Smith was sent for, who bound the Persons over; and told the Jury, That Mr. Whitacre had Informations by him, that would fully affect both White and Whitman; and thereupon a new Indictment was brought, without Whitacre'$ Knowledge, and the Witnesses sworn; upon which the Grand Jury found the Bill; but was quashed in Court by Mr. Whit-acre, and the Matter referred to the next Assizes after; where, by the Care of the Justices, a new Bill was preferred, and found; but, by this means, the Offenders gained a Year's time, to traverse; and it was observable, that those Persons were great Companions with Mr. Whitacre all the Assizes.

Article 6th. Several other Matters, relating to other Vol. 13.

Assizes, where Prosecutions seemed to be baffled, are Conduct of omitted; which might justly aggravate a Censure on Mr. Whitacre Whitacre's Management, especially as to his Delaying of Tryal from one Assize to another, and then being re* ltI moved to be tried in London; and the frequent Discouragement shewn to the King's Witnesses, with the vast Expence, it was observed, the King must be put to in these Prosecutions: And to see Tryals of such Importance, that respected Punishment for a most barbarous Murder, and the future Safety and Preservation of his Majesty's Stores and Timber, all managed in a Method for the principal Criminals to escape from Justice, gave a universal Dissatisfaction of the whole County, and a just Suspicion, that the same must proceed from Bribery and Corruption, or from Ignorance and Neglect, in Mr. Whitacre; he being the Officer intrusted with those Prosecutions; the Grand Jury thought themselves bound in Duty to put a Stop to such Proceedings, by making the said Presentment, in Conjunction with the High Sheriff, and Justices of the Peace, for the said County.

John St. Barbe

Robert Smithy E. Chute.

Mr. Whitacre was heard to that Part of the Presentment, which relates to the irregular Prosecuting, and Escape, of David Aldridge: And said, That he had full Examinations given him, before he went to the Assizes at Winton; and that he advised with Mr. Solicitor General, and the King's Counsel, upon all the Indictments; but desired he may refer, for Answer at large, to his Answer,

fiven in to the Commissioners of the Admiralty, to that Vosecution, dated the 25th of February 1701: Which Answer was laid before the Committee, and marked C; and is as followeth; viz.

Paragraph of Mr. Whitacre's Answer, relating to Aldridge.

ANSWER.

That I must agree with these Gentlemen, that, in my Judgment, that Method, that was taken, did contribute to Aldridge's Escape; for he being indicted as accessary, before and after the Facts, of Felony, in stealing the King's Stores, it would have been a mighty Weight and Load on him, both as to the Court and the Jury, if, after Conviction for those Offences, he had been tried for his being accessary before and after to the Murder. There were several other Reasons, too long to be mentioned here, to proceed that Way: And I must say, if I had consented- to the Method that was taken, and is now conn plained of; nay, had I not opposed it to the utmost, the Proceeding in the Method complained of; and had I not pressed, and insisted^to observe the Method those Gentlemen rightly observe should have been taken; I should be guilty, not of Ignorance only, but give the Gentlemen, who complain, just Cause to say, of Corruption: But E do affirm, That I pressed it; and so did Two of the Counsel, who were Counsel for the King upon that Occasion only; and they did advise and desire it: But this Method was opposed by the King's Serjeant, and by him only, there being then no other of the King's sworn Counsel: They were, and I was, and must be, directed in such Prosecution; and I was governed by the King's Serjeant, and did not dare to do otherwise; and so* against my . Will, against the other Advice of the Two Counsel, who were not the King's sworn Counsel, only Counsel for that OccasionAldridge was tried-, upon the Indictment for the Murder first: For the Truth of this, I appeal to the other Two Couusel; and, because One of them may be thought too favourable towards me, I appeal to Mr. Pratt, the other Counsel, since made a Serjeant, for the Truth of what I assert: I have no Reason to believe, but the.Kings Serjeant will: own this his Advice; and that it was upon his Advice and Direction the Tryal against Aldridge proceeded in the Method it did; b»it since the Method hath proved so false a Step, it will not be reasonable to put it upon any other Determination than the Affirmation of those Two Counsel, who were 7 S positively

Chndnct of Wtmacre, Admiralty Solicitor.

positively for trying Aldridge on the Indictments for Felony first: And all I shall further say in this Matter, That, if I did, in the least, mention, propose, or agree to, the trying Aldridge first on the Indictment for Murder, any otherwise than by being obliged, by the King's Serjeant's Advice and Direction, so to proceed, I am ready to own what Imputation shall be laid upon me, be it never so black and severe.

And further says, That the Method of Tryal was wholly directed by Mr. Serjeant Darnell Mr. Serjeant Darnell said, That Mr. Whit acre came to him, on a sudden, a little before the Tryal came on; and that the only Question he asked him, was, Whether the Indictments against Williams, for the Embezzlement of the Stores, or against Williams, for the Murder, should be tried first? And that Mr. Whitacre never asked the said Mr. Serjeant Darnell whether the Indictment against Aldridge, for Murder, should be tried first; or any Question about the Tryal of Aldridge:

And the Question about Wilfiams, as above, was asked the said Mr. Serjeant, just as they were going on to the Tryal, and not before:

That the King's Counsel were never asked to consult together about any of the Tryals; nor was Mr. Serjeant Darnell acquainted by Air. Whitacre, that any of the other Counsel differed from him in Opinion; nor was there any Indictment preferred against Aldridge, a Principal, for any Offence; but, upon the Evidence,#it did appear, that Aldridge was Principal, and ought to have been so indicted in all the Indictments:

That, by his Breviate, there appeared several trivial Matters 01 Charge, relating to Williams, for Embezzlements, and little or no Evidence: And having observed, that Mr. Whitacre often prosecuted Persons for very frivolous and insignificant Matters, not fit to be prosecuted; to the Dissatisfaction of the Country, and to the King's great Charge and Expence; which, he thought, tended to the Damage of other Prosecutions;

That, upon these Considerations, and Mr. Whit acre's Question to try Williams for the Embezzlements before the Murder, he was jealous there was some Trick intended to bring off the Murderers; and therefore, as the Matters stood, and upon such Information as he was possessed of, he did advise Mr. Wkitaci'e to try the Murder first against Williams, before the Embezzlements against Williams, the Murder being of the greatest Consequence; and for that Aldridge was only indicted as accessary in all the Indictments: But when the Tryals came on, there did sufficient Matter appear to the Court, to have indicted and convicted Aldridge and others, which escaped, as Principals in Stealing of the Kings Stores; and, if he had been rightly and fully instructed, must have advised the same; and do lay the Blame on Mr. Whitacre's Management.

Mr. Serjeant Darnell desired Mr. Whitacre might be asked for all the Indictments, Informations, and Briefs, about these Prosecutions.

Mr. Whitacre answered; That he had them not with him. /

Answered, That he never did -advise with him before the Indictments were found.

He was asked, If he did consult with the King's sworn Counsel, in all the Kings Causes:

Answered, He did not.

A Sum of 1/. 6 s. &d. charged in his Account for Counsellors Fees, was dipped on by Chance: And Mr. Whitacre, being asked to whom it was given;

Answered, He believed, to Mr. Smith. Associate to the Clerk of Assize of the Home Circuit.

He was asked, If he was a Counsellor;

Answered, No.

Mr. Hunt said, That, at the Assizes held at Winchester in March 1700, there was a great Want of Jurymen; and, being the re present, was returned to be'of the Jury on the Tryal of one David Aldridge, indicted for Murder of one John Harris; and upon several other Indictments, for embezzling his Majesty's Stores: That the said Jury, being agreed to find the said Aldridge guilty, as accessary to the Murder after die Fact committed, and of the Embezzlements; and, being so agreed, were permitted to go to an Inn, to refresh themselves; and, in parsing from the Hall to the Inn, he observed a Person, to him then unknown, whose Name, lie since understands, wal Gauntlett, call aside one John Biskopp, who was One of the said Jury; awd, shortly after, the said Bishopp came to this Examinant, and told him, That they might hate Forty Guineas to bring off the said Aldridge; which thi9 Examinant refused to accept.

This Examinant further safth, That whilst they xvtrt refreshing themselves in the said Inn, he observed several of the Jurymen, one by one, to go out of the ftdom; who, returning, would not stand to their Verdict they formerly agreed; which occasioned a further Debate; but, at last, they were prevailed with to stand to theif Former Verdict:

That, about Christmas last, one Evans came to him at Petersfield, and sent for him to the White Hart Inn, and asked him, if he were of the Jury that tried Aldridge; winch this Examinant acknowledged: That Evans asked, what Guineas were offered: This Examinant said, lie was offered Forty to bring off Aldridge; and Evans asked, by whom: He said, he could not tell; but Evans persuaded him to go to Winchester; and that he found the Person, who offered the Money, was Gauntlett.

- Thomas Wilshaw Esquire, One of the Principal Officers and Commissioners of his Majesty's Navy, informed the Committee,

That, about August 1691, he being the Commissioner of his Majesty's Navy at Portsmouth, Mr. William Cooper, Store-keeper of the Dock-yard, made Complaint to him, That he missed several Quantities of Pitch and Tar out of the King's Stores: Upon which strict Inquiry was made into the Matter; and, by the Care that was taken, Discovery was made of a great Gang of Thieves, consisting of Wa/tchmen and Workmen, that belonged to the King's Yard, which frequently robbed the Stoies: And, upon Examination, some of the Persons confessed the Fact; particularly Thomas Podd and John Hows; and that* they

were employed to steal the same by Henry Berry, who Conduct of bought the said stolen Goods of them: These Informa- Wlnucre* tions were sent to the Navy Board; and Mr. IV hit acre w&s Solkuor^ appointed to prosecute: But, instead of prosecuting the 1 ° ‘ real Offenders and Criminals, several of them were made Witnesses, and all the rest escaped without being brought to Tryal; and the Prosecution turned against the said Mr. fVilsharVy and several of the Officers of the aforesaid Yard, by whose Care these Thefts were discovered, as guilty of the very same Crimes which the Thieves bad confessed, and were accused of; That, by a general Information, mixed with the real Embezzlers, they were tried at the King's Bench Bar, after about Two Years Dependence; and, by a Special Jury of Hampshire Gem-tlemen, were acquitted: And the Court, blaming very much the Prosecution, ordered a Noli Prosequi to stop further Proceedings against the said Mr. Wilshaw, *and other of the Officers, who were prosecuted on Two Informations; which Noli Prosequi all the Criminals took the Advantage of, and were never afterwards prosecuted for the said Offences: That it cost the said Mr. Wilshaw 300l. for his own Part, to justify his Reputation under this Prosecution; and that his Majesty's Service was greatly endamaged by it, being in the Heat of the late War, when the whole Fleet was chiefly fitted at Portsmouth.

Mr. Richard Hale declared to the same Effect about the said Discoveries, Confessions, Prosecutions, and Acquittals; and that some of the Offenders were made Witnesses, and the rest never tried.

Mr. Jetcell attended; and informed the Committee, That, about llie Twelfth of January One thousand Six hundred Ninety-five, Captain Smith, Commander of his Majesty's Ship Dumvich, riding off Shoreham, received Informations, That Stores were embezzled from the said Ship: That' he went ashore, to make Search after the same; and called to his Assistance the Officers of the Customs at that Port: That they found some of the said Goods upon one Chatfeild, who confessed the same: That the Master and Boatswain were accused of the Embezzlement; and were secured, by the Captain, on board the said Ship; and Notice of the whole Matter given to the Admiralty: That the Prosecution was referred to Mr. who

ordered the Custom Officers to prepare Evidence against the Assizes; which they did: But Proceedings were stopped by Mr. Whitacre; and the Master and Boatswain sent for to London; their Informations received against the Captain; he turned out; afterwards prosecuted; and they made Witnesses against him for the very same Stores which they themselves had embezzled:

That, whilst this Matter was depending, he did, with much Difficulty, and with Consent of the Admiralty, proceed to prosecute the said Officers at his own Charge; and, although some of his principal Evidence was kept from him, by an unreasonable Method, at the Procurement of Mr. Whitacre, he proceeded to Tryal; where appearing full Proof, Chatfeild, and the Master and Boatswain, confessed the Fact; but Mr. s Son, their

Counsel, pleaded the benefit of the Act of the 16* Car. Ildi, which confines the Prosecution to be within Twelve Months after the Fact committed; and that the Reason they were not prosecuted within the Time, was, through Mr. Whitacre's Delay; and that, by this Means, Chat -

feild, and the other Criminals, escaped; and the Captain, and his Witnesses, utterly ruined by the violent and tedious Prosecution.
