last: And the Petitioners met; but the said Portreeve did not: And John Granvill Esquire, John Hicks Esquire, and also John Williams Esquire, Nephew' to the Portreeve, stood Candidates: But Nathanael Tingcomb, the Portreeve's Brother, who had w rongfully got the Precept, took upon him the Execution thereof; endeavouring to hinder the Major from acting in his Office, and arbitrarily, contrary to the Determination of the last House of Conn mons, touching Elections, rejected divers legal Votes for Mr. Granvill and Mr. IJicks, and allowed many unqualified Persons to vote for Mr. Williams; and committed many other illegal Practices for him: notwithstanding which Mr. Granvill and Mr. Hicks were duly elected, and the Petitioners executed an Indenture for returning the m: But the said Nathanael refused to deliver the Precept to the Mayor, to annex it thereto; by reason whereof the High Sheriff would not accept the said Indenture from the Petitioners; and the said Jonathan Tingcomb batli falsely returned the said Mr. Williams, instead of Colonel Granvill, with Mr. Hicks; to the great Injury of the Petitioners: And praying Relief in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of several Burghers of Appleby, in the County Appleby of Wtestmoreland, in behalf of themselves, and divers other the Burghers of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the Election, and after the Teste of the Writ, for Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, several unlawful Practices were used to gain Votes for Genas Pier-point and James Grahme Esquires, w hereby they gained a Majority; but the Petitioners conceive, that Wharton Dunch and RickardBrathwait Esquires w ere duly chosen for their Representatives: And praying, That the House w ill take the Premises into Consideration.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of Joshua Lomax Esquire, was presented to Sl Alban's the House, and read; setting forth,. That, at the Election ElectioD* of Burgesses to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of St. Albans, in the County oS Hertford\ the Petitioner, and John Gape junior, Esquire, with others, stood Candidates; and many illegal Practices were made use of, on behalf of the said Mr. Gape, at the said Election, to the Petitioners Prejudice: And praying the Consideration of the House therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Attainting Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for the the Pw-Attainder of the pretended Prince of Wales.

Mr. Speaker left foe Chair.

Sir Rowland Gwynn took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Rowli nd Gwyn reported from foe said Committee,

That they had gone through foe Bill; and made some Amendments thereto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be made Tomorrow Morning-

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, Answer to foat their Address of Saturday last having been presented Address-to his Majesty, his Majesty was pleased to return his

Thanks

Thanks to the House for their Address; and to say, That he will take care of what they desire therein.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for reviving and continuing the Act, intituled, An Act for the appointing and enabling Commissioners to take, examine, and determine, the Debts due to the Army, Navy, and for Transport Service; and also an Account of the Prizes taken during the late War; is committed; That they have Power to receive a Clause, That the Commissioners may take the Accounts of the Majors of Brigades.

Sir Charles Hedges, according to Order, presented to the House, a Bill for the further Security of his Majesty's Person; and the Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line; and extinguishing the Hopes of the pretended Prince of Wales, and all other Pretenders, and their open and secret Abettors: And the same was received.

The Bill was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time upon Thursday Morning next.

A Petition of Major General William Steuart was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in Consideration of Seven thousand Five hundred Pounds, due to the Petitioner for Arrears of Pay, and contingent Charges in Spain and Ireland, his Majesty did grant the Petitioner forfeited Lands in Ireland, of Light hundred Pounds per Annum; who thereupon released his Majesty from the said Debt; but, by the late Act of Resumption, the same Lands are taken from the Petitioner; in whose Favour a Clause was inserted in the said Act, That when any Person had taken any Grant in lieu of any Sum of

Money due from his Majesty, and had released the same, such Person should be intitled to such Debt, as if no Release had been given: In pursuance whereof, his Majesty, by Warrant, distinguishes the contingent Charges from the Arrears of Pay, and ordered the same to be paid; which amounts to Three thousand Nine hundred Sixty-two Pounds Seven Shillings and Four-pence: That the Petitioner produced the said Warrant to the late Commissioners of Accounts; but they said, They had no Power to allow any Warrants, or give Certificates for Money that did not appear to be due by the Establishment:

That the last House of Commons did admit a Clause, in the Petitioner's Favour, into the theri Bill for stating the Accounts of the Army,&c.: And praying, That the Commissioners of Accounts may have the necessary Powers to allow him a Certificate, that he may have Satisfaction for the Money due to him, as aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for reviving and continuing an Act, intituled, An Act for the appointing Commissioners to take, examine, arid determine, the Debts due to the Army and Navy* and for Transport Service; and also an Account of the Prizes taken during the late War; is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee* that they do consider of the Contracts for Transport Service; in the Year 1693.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee, That, of the Eighteen thousand Three hundred and Twenty-eight Men, that are to he raised to make up his Majesty's Quota of Forty thousand Men, to act in Conjunction with the Forces of his Allies, Eight thousand Three hundred and Twenty-eight be his Majesty's natural-born Subjects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee, That, of the said Eight thousand Three hundred and Twenty-eight Men, Five thousand be Foot, Two thousand Horse, and One thousand Three hundred and Twenty -eight Dragoons.

Januarii. 68;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the said Horse, Foot, and Dragoons, the Regiments in Pay in England and Holland shall be filled up to the Numbers they were in the late War.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the remaining Ten thousand Men, to complete the Quota of Forty thousand Men, be Foreigners, consisting of Nine thousand One hundred and Eighty-eight Foot, and Eight hundred and Twelve Horse and Dragoons.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House their Return to the Two Orders of the 16th Instant in the Papers following;

The Receiver General of the Customs his Account of the Payments into the Exchequer on the several Branches of the Customs, between Christm 1700, and Christmas 1701:

Th6 Comptroller General of the Customs his Account of the gross Produce. in the Port of London, between Christmas 1700, and Christtnas 1701:

An Account of all Goods imported from India, not rated in the Book of Rates;

An Account of Goods imported from other Places, besides India, not rated in the Book of Rates:

And then they withdrew.

And the Titles of the said Accounts were read.

And the said Return, and Two First Accounts, are as follow; viz.

The Return.

To the Honourable the Commons of England, in Parliament assembled:

IN Obedience to an Order of this Honourable House, of the 16th Instant, requiring the Commissioners of the Customs to lay before this House an Account of the Names of all Goods imported and exported, mentioned in the Book of Rates to pay Custom ad; we have caused to be extracted, out of the Collectors Books, the Names of such Goods, which, for not being mentioned in the Book of Rates, have been admitted to pay Duty, according to the Value sworn by the particular Importers on their respective Entries; which is what, we humbly presume, may answer the Intention of the House in that Order: Which Extracts are digested, by Alphabets, in Three Accounts hereunto annexed, for easier Observation; viz.

1. An Account of Godds imported from India, hot rated in the Book of Rates:

2. An Account of Goods imported from other Places, besides India, not rated in the Book of Rates:

3. An Account of Goods exported from this Kingdom* not rated in the Book of Rates.

And, in further Obedience to another Order of this Honourable House, of the same Date, requiring an Account of the gross and net Produce of the Customs, distinguish* ing the several Branches of them, for the Year ending the 25th of December last; we have caused the Receiver General of the Customs to draw out, in an Account hereunto annexed, the total Payments into the Exchequer, as well from the Receipts of the Out Ports, as in London, on the several Branches under our Management, between Christmas 1700, and Christmas 1701: But we crave Leave to observe, That the Account of the total gross Produce cannot be yet completed to the Books

from the Out Ports, for the last Quarter, being not yet sent up; but we will take care to get them in as soon as possible: In the mean while, we have annexed an Account of the gross Produce of the Port of London, in the said Year, as it is laid before us by the Comptroller General of the Customs: On which last Account, we must, nevertheless, observe, that the East India Company's having a Privilege to take out Bills at Sight on their Entries, and the Collector being not chargeable with a determinate Sum till those Entries are perfected, there may be several Ships standing out, the Duties whereof, with regard to the Importation, ought to be reckoned within the gross Produce of that Year; but cannot yet be brought to a regular Account till the Sights are perfected; which happens to be the Case every Year.

All which is humbly submitted.

Ben. Overton, C.

Sam. Clark, T. Newport,

A. Maynwa

The House being informed, That Two of the Irish Trustees attended, according to Order;

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House several Reports from the Trustees, on several Petitions to them referred, with a Schedule of them; and acquainted the House, That they expected other Papers Tomorrow, or Friday; and hoped they should be ready to give the House Satisfaction in all the Matters desired of them.

A Petition of the ancient Company of Woolstaplers, Fcltmongers, Manufacturers of Wool, in the City of London, and Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by Act of Parliament, made in the First Year of the Reign of King William and Queen Mary, divers Commissioners were appointed to prevent the Exportation of Wool; who, unknowingly, deputed, for that Purpose, divers necessitous and broken Persons, who committed many violent Actions upon the trading People in the Woollen Manufactures, by seizing Wool bought at common Fairs, as going Home to be manufactured; and Wool brought from adjacent Towns, as going to London, to be used there; and seizing Wool passing from Staplers Houses to the Inns, when sold to Clothiers, extorting at least 1 o s. per Pack for Passage; all which was proved before the said Commissioners, who discharged such their abusive Officers, who yet lie lurking about, and prey upon the Goods of Traders, upon Pretence that the Wool is carried at undue Hours, contrary to the Act of 13th and 14th Caroli Secundi; and thereby seize the same in the Carriers Hands, that keep their constant Stages; to the great Oppression of the Subject, and Prejudice of the Trade of the Woollen Manufactures of England: And praying Consideration thereof, and Relief touching the same.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt, that lie close confined in the Sheriffs Ward at Bodmyn, in the County of Cornwall, and in the behalf of many Thousands of their Fellow-sufferers in all the Prisons of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by inevitable Losses and Misfortunes, by the late War, and Alteration of the Coin, and otherwise, the Petitioners were reduced to Poverty, and thrown into Gaol by their Creditors, who know they are not able to pay their Debts j and yet keep the Petitioners confined in Prison; whereby they are rendered less capable of paying their Creditors; and might be serviceable to the Publick, if they had their Liberty, who otherwise must perish for Want: And praying, That Consideration may be had of their sad and necessitous Condition.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, till the Bill be brought in for the Relief of poor Prisoners for Debt.

Supply. Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported, from the

Committee of the whole House, who were to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

1. Resolved\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Twelve Battalions of Foot, now in Service in Holland, be made to consist of Thirteen Companies in each Regiment.

2. Resoboed\ That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Companies shall be made to consist of Sixty private Men in each Company.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Remainder of the Fifteen thousand Foot shall consist of Thirteen Companies in each Regiment, and Sixty private Men in each Company,

4. Resoboed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Regiments of Light Horse be recruited to Fifty-nine private Men in each Troop, including Servants.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be Three Regiments of Dragoons, consisting One of Eight Troops, and Two of Six Troops, and each Troop of Fifty-four private Men.

Upon the Petition of Irby Mountague Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of John Comyns Esquire to serve for the said Borough of Malden:

That, upon the Poll taken by the Bailiffs, the Numbers were;

For the Sitting Member Mr. Comyns - 141

For the Petitioner - - - - 129

That the Right of Election was agreed in the Freemen dot receiving Alms or Charity.

And the Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That several Persons, who were Freemen, and had a Right to vote in this Election, and did actually vote for the Petitioner, were not put down in the PqII; and also, that the Bailiffs had acted in a partial Manner in favour of the Sitting Member:

That the Persons refused by the Bailiffs to be put down on the Poll, were 30.

And as to these 30 Persons it appeared, by the Evidence of

William Coe, and Ralph Backnall, That they were all Freemen, and were called over, as such, by the Town Clerk; and voted for the Petitioner: But Three of them did vote for the Petitioner and Mr. Fitch; and Two of them voted for the Petitioner and Mr. Comyns: The Vol. 13.

7°7

Objection, as Mr. Coe said, to 24 of them, was, That Malden they had received Corn of the Gift of Mr. Charles Election. Mountague, now Lord Halifax; to Four, for receiving Alms; and to Two others; viz. Mr. Wiseman, as a Person in Debt, and to Peter Tilbrook, because, it was pretended, he had borrowed 51.: But he offered to swear he had not done it; and said, He was promised 20L to vote for Mr. Comyns.

And Mr. William Coe, being examined, on behalf of the Petitioner, as to the Matter of Distribution of Corn, gave tins Account; That, in the Year 1699, several Neighbours did write to Mr. Mount ague, now Lord Halifax, That, Corn being dear, by reason of the Exportation thereof, there were like to be Tumults in the Town by the poor People; and, in November, he Waited upon his Lordship, and told him to the same Effect: Whereupon his Lordship expressed his Willingness to do what was proper for him to do; and gave Orders to dispose of Wheat to the poorer Sort on the Christmas-day then following; which he did; and repeated the following April: That he did deliver the Corn without any Distinction, only with respect to the Poverty of the Persons: That he did not consult the Overseers of the Poor, or the Magistrates of the Town, about the Distribution of it; he having been Overseer himself, and knowing the People of the Town; That the whole Quantity was Two Load; which was delivered out by One or Two Bushels to a Man: That he could not say particularly to whom he delivered the Wheat; but, he believes, the whole 24 refused, upon that Account, had not received it: But, he said, He had given none after April 1700: That, after the 30 had polled for Mr. Mountague, the Town Clerk asked the Bailiffs, If he should put them down on the Poll; and the Bailiffs were against their being put down; and that, though these were not polled for the Petitioner, some, that had received the Corn and polled for the Sitting Member, were set down now; and 17 that received this Corn, did come to vote at the Election 1700; but there was no Poll, there being no dispute.

That the Petitioner's Counsel also examined as to other Practices: And they called,

Robert Chadd: Who said, That he, and Mr. Gibson, and Mr. Cockrell, being together, Gibson desired his Vote for the Sitting Member; and the said Chadd answering,

He was minded to vote for the Petitioner, Bailiff Cockrell bid him make much of his Licence; for he should have no more: However he acknowledged he voted for the Petitioner; and nobody had since demanded his Licence; but the Time for renewing Licences is not yet come.

Richmond testified, That he had heard Bailiff Taverner say, after the Election, That if the Sitting Member had but Six Votes, he would return him: And if they came to a new Election, the Petitioner should not be chosen; for they had made 35 free, and would make it strong enough to carry whom they pleased.

Lemuel Bradley said, Some were talking with Bailiff , Taverner, That the Petitioner would be a Parliament Man; and Mr. Taverner said, He should not: He knew a Trick worth Two of that

That the Counsel for the Sitting Member insisted, That the Persons who had received Corn, were disabled from voting, either as it might be considered to be an Alms, or a corrupt Practice to procure their Votes: And to that Matter they called, v

Thomas Stace: Who said, That about Two Years ago.

Wheat was distributed by Mr. Coe and his Man: That he saw 40 come away with it in about Four Hours time; which Wheat was carried away by the Freemen and their Wives: That the Election before the last, some Wheat had been delivered out; viz. to John Marsh, Four Bushels and to William Norman, Two Bushels; and that Marsh voted for the Petitioner at this Election: That he did not hear Mr. Coe say for what Purposes he delivered the Wheat; nor does he know that Wheat was denied to any:

But the said Stace asked several, viz. James Hubert, William Perkins, and Rob. Osborne, that had received the

John Cooke said, There was Treating at his House, on the Petitioner s Account, by Order of Mr. Coe, the same Night the Petitioner came down; and he was directed to draw Drink till about 11 a Clock at Night; for they did not know but the Writ might bear Teste after 12: And his Bill came to between 10 and 11; but he

was never asked for his Vote; but voted only for the Petitioner: He is not paid his Money, but expects it from Mr. Mountague.

John Day said, That the same Day, Mr. Coe bespoke a Treat at his House; and it continued till about 11 a Clock: He said, He was to treat all the Freemen in general, and only they; and the Reckoning came to about 7 or 8/.

William Wells said, That the Day before the last Election, Willimn Coe gave him 19^.; whereof Nine was for Two Bushels of Wrheat, he having had no Share in the Wheat Two Years ago; and 10 s. was for his Vote at the last Election: And that Coe bid him not let anybody know of the 10 s. for it would make the Election void: He voted for the Petitioner.

That the Right of Election was the point controverted; the Petitioner's Counsel insisting, That the Right of Election was in the Inhabitants of the Borough, not receiving Alms; the Sitting Member's Counsel insisting, That the Right was as well in the Burgesses or Freemen, as in the Inhabitants.

Another Matter controverted between the said Parties was, Supposing the Freemen.to have a Right, how the Persons ought to be qualified, who are made free ? The Petitioner's Counsel insisted, That Hertford was a Borough by Prescription; and that the First Charter granted . to the said Borough was primo Marias:

That the Petitioner s Counsel, to prove the Usage of the Borough, also called several Witnesses:

Henry Sweeting, aged 81 Years: Who said, He had voted for Parliament Men 50 Years ago: And the First time honorary Freemen were admitted was, when Sir Thomas Feild and Sir John Gore were chose: That he remembered Sir Tho. Fanshaw and Sir William Lemon's Election before that; and then never heard any voted, that was an honorary Freeman; but, since that time, they have all along been admitted.

John Hill, aged above 70 Years, said. He had known Hertford 50 Years; and he did not remember any Persons were made free, but the Inhabitants, till within about 40 Years.

John Hanscomb said, He served his Time in Hertford, and came to live there about 30 Years ago: He said also, He purchased his Freedom; and voted at last Election.

For the Sitting Member it was insisted, That Hertford was as well a Corporation by Prescription, as a Borough by Prescription; and that the Right of Election was in Vox- 13*

the Freemen of the Borough in general; and that such Hertford Right could not be restrained by any Charter: Election.

And they produced several Instances, out of an old Towm Book, to prove, that Persons living out of the Bo-rQugh, as well as Inhabitants, had been made free there of; viz.

One, of 19 January 1596; by which it appeared, That John Famake, of Hatfield, having requested, that he might serve Hertford with Beer, and to have Access thereto; it was granted to him, paying 10 s. a Year:

Another Instance, of 14th of March 1598; which is an Order of the Corporation, That the Brewer Thorogood^ of Hatfield, and some others, should be distrained for occupying their Mysteries and Trades, before they had agreed for Freedoms:

Another Instance, 7th May 1600; by which it appears, That John Cordell, of Cheshunt, common Loader, desired to be admitted a Freeman of Hertford; and was, admitted and sworn, for to sell Salt and Fish in the time* of Lent, for a certain Sum agreed on, and paying 12 d. for every Quarter:

Another Instance, of 13 August 1606; by which it appeared, That Tho. Borcham, of Broxborne, Shoemaker, was admitted a Freeman, paying 26 s. 8 d.:

Another Instance, of 25 November 1612; by which it appears, That Henry CockriU, of Cheshunt, did purchase his Freedom.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel also produced several Returns to Parliament; viz.

Three of Car. I.; by which it appears, that the Mayor,

Steward, Assistants, Burgesses, and Town Clerk, did elect:

The Return is under the Common Seal:

And Two other Returns of 13 °Car. 2 di; bywhich it appears, That several Gentlemen joined in these Elections.

That the Sitting Members Counsel also called several Witnesses to the Usage:

Sir Henry Chancey: Who said, He had been Recorder of Hertford, and came to live there at Michaelmas 1669, and continued there till November 1681; and had attended at every Election, but the Two last: And Sir Henry said, That all Freemen, as well those by Redemption, as others, always voted at Elections of Parliament Men: And that Sir William Cowper, when he first stood, carried it by those Freemen: And that he found a great many Gentlemen made free before he knew the Town; and believes there were 40 made free in King James's Time.

Rich. Bridgman said, He had known Hertford ever since 1665, and never knew any honorary Freemen refused or scrupled, though they lived out of Town: That the Petitioner himself has voted for Sir Wm. Catvper, though he lived at Brockborne: And that the Freemen by Redemption take the same Oath with others: That honorary Freemen do not concern themselves in any other Business of the Town, than Elections.

And that, upon this Evidence, the Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Right of electing Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hertford is not in such Persons only as are Inhabitants, Housholders of the said Borough, not receiving Alms; and in such Freeman, who, at the time of their Freedom granted to them, were Inhabitants of the said Borough, or of the Parishes thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Right of electing Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hertford is in all the Freemen, and also in all the Inhabitants, being Housholders, and not receiving Alms.

These Resolutions being passed, the Counsel were called in, and acquainted with them: And the Counsel for the Petitioner was asked, If he had any thing further to say for his Client? Who answered. That, the Right of Election being thus determined, he had nothing further to offer for his Client.

And thereupon the Committee came to this Resolution;

A PETITION of Edward Ilildeyard Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner hath lately invented Two several Instruments, for the Improvement of Navigation; One called a spherical Quadrant, the other a Calculator; whereby all Mariners may more plainly direct the Course of a Ship than by any Method yet practised; and may also thereby compute the Way that such Ship hath made; which will be of great Advantage to all Navigators: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for his Encouragement in the Invention of the said Instruments.

The said Copies were read; and are as follow; viz.

The Copy of the Letter.

Gentlemen, . Dublin, 23 December 1701.

IT is the Opinion of our Friends in England, who have an Opportunity to make the best Judgment of Things, That, if the King be rightly applied to, it may be in his Majesty's Power to procure us a Relaxation of the Grievances which the Act of Resumption hath brought upon us: They therefore have taken care to meet frequently, to consult of proper Methods; and have imparted their Thoughts to us: We have followed their Advice, and have made it our Business to have the Sense of the Nobility and Gentry here concerning the same Affair.

The Result of all the Consultations both there and here, and our unanimous Opinion, is, That the best and only Way is, for all the Counties in this Kingdom to represent our Grievance, and implore his Majesty's Favour and Assistance.

The Parchment inclosed is the Tenor of all the Addresses that we have sent to other Places: That which we intreat from you, and our good Friends of your County, as we have from worthy Gentlemen, and true Lovers of their Country, in all other Counties of Ireland, is, That you will, with all your Interest, recommend this Address at the next Quarter Sessions: The easiest and most concise Method will be, to have it read publickly, and signed by the Justices of Peace, Grand Jury, Clergy, Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of your County: When it is sent up hither, which pray do with all imaginable Expedition, due Care shall be taken to have it sent, and' presented to his Majesty, by acceptable Hands. The Service you will do to your Country, and the Obligations you will lay on the Protestants of this Kingdom, will be so great, that it will be needless^ to say, by way

of Incitement to you, that your Care in this Affair will greatly obligfe

Your affectionate Friends and Servants,

Meath, Invhiquin, Abercorn, Blesinton,

Hen. Tichborne Gus. Hamilton, K id. B rosier, Rob. Adare, John Cony, John Davys,

J. Lassaduel, Tho. Carr, Hen. Tomson, Tho. Burdet,

Donal Brien, Fran. Butler, Hen. Davys, Arth. Shaeiiy John Dillon, John Or ms by. Hen. Westenra, William Crow, Matth. Bridges, Rob. Johnston, Blany Toxvnley, Arthur Davys, Edw. Wing/teld, B. Butler,

Tho. Ash,

Da. Freight on, James Cony James Tvphm, U rn. Connelly Mann. Coghili, Sam. Dopping, Cha. Campbell, Da. Golborn, Rich. Owen, Jo. Winslanly Geo. Merefeili.

As soon as you have got this signed, let it be returned to M. Coghili, or W. Connolly, who will take care to transmit it to proper Persons in England, to present it to the King.

The said Address:

To the King's most Excellent Majesty,

The humble Address of the Nobility, Justices of the Peace, Grand Jury, Clergy, Gentlemen, and Freeholders, of the County* of West-Meath, at their General Quarter Sessions held at the

Day of 1701.

YOUR Majesty's faithful and loyal Subjects the Protestants of this Your Kingdom of Ireland, lying under such Pressures, by means of the late Act of Resumption, and of the Execution thereof, that they apprehend the

----- Protestants of this Kingdom, who have all of them,

to the utmost of their Power, been most forward and zealous for Your Majesty's Interest, and instrumental in reducing this Kingdom to its Dependence upon the Crown of England, must be the unavoidable Consequence of the Execution of that Act, do humbly fly to Your Majesty's Protection; and pray, That Your Majesty, the Restorer of their Religion, Rights, and Liberties, would once again be pleased to take their distressed Condition into Your Princely Consideration, and, by such Methods as to Your Majesty shall seem expedient, and their present Circumstances, and the Justice of their Cause, do require, apply suitable Remedies to the severe Burden under which they lie.

The deplorable Condition of very many Families, who always adhered firmly to the Interest of Your Majesty, and the Crown of England, and the general Discouragement that Act has given to the Protestant Interest of this Kingdom, constrain us, Avitli all Humility, to lay before Your Majesty, That the Act being intirely framed and passed in England, the real Truth of our late Circumstances could not be known: Hence we have Reason to complain,

1st, The Persons, who chiefly receive any Benefit or Favour by this Act, are the Papists of this Kingdom; and, among them, principally those, who, to the last, opposed Your Majesty's Arms and Interest: And, besides many other particular Favours to Irish Papists, all those, who, by Your Majesty's Grace, obtained the Reversal of their Outlawries, have the Benefit of those Reversals confirmed to them; and are, by this Act, restored as well to their Estates, as to their Blood, when most of the Grants made to the Protestants are re-assumed:

2. That the Improvers, and poor Husbandmen, who, by several Proclamations issued by Your Majesty* Order, were encouraged and required to betake themselves to their Tillage, to repair the Desolation wrought by the War, and prevent a Famine, are, by it, deprived of all the Benefit of their Labours, and the Charges of their Improvements:

3. That those, who purchased under Patentees, are generally Protestants, who, in their Dealings for these Estates, acted agreeably to the then known and established

Laws

13 W. III. 30 — 40 Februarii. 719

Laws of these Kingdoms; though now, by a Law made c.v post facto, they find themselves in the Condition of forfeiting Persons:

4. That the ill Consequence of this Act, and the Execution of it, do not only affect the Purchasers of forfeitures, but your Majesty's other Subjects here, who are wholly unconcerned in those Titles, and disquiet the whole Kingdom; for, some of the Trustees having declared in Court their Opinion, That, what Land soever they shall think fit to sell, it shall never after be controverted, whether that Land was the Estate of a forfeiting Person, and, in consequence of that, vested in them by the Act; but that their Sales, whatsoever they are, are confirmed by the Act, and past Controul: Your Majesty's Subjects of this Kingdom are sensible, that, if this Opinion prevail, the whole Property of Ireland depends upon the arbitrary Wills of the Majority of the Trustees:

5. That the Power given to the Trustees is so arbitrary and unlimited, that all Persons, under colour of Discoveries, or upon other Pretences, are liable to be summoned to appear before them, and to attend their Pleasure:

6. That the Act is a great Discouragement to Protestant Proprietors to, lay out Money in Improvements, upon account of the Uncertainty of Tilles to Estates here; it being construed not only to subject Titles, established by Judgments and Decrees of the highest Courts of Law and Equity here, to the Re-examination of the Trustees; but, in express Terms, defeats a Title confirmed by an Act of a Parliament legally convened, and held under Your Majesty, within this Kingdom:

7th, That the whole Scheme of the Act, and the Manner of the Execution of it, depresses... discontinues the Protestant Interest of this Kingdom, and encourages the Popish; of the Danger of which, we, who have felt the Effects of it, must alw ays be apprehensive; but more particularly now, when the Papists, throughout the whole Nation, by the Insolence of their Behaviour, shew, that the Acknowledging of the pretended Prince of Wales by the French King, or some other Dependence, has raised their Expectations to a great Height

We are persuaded, that the Parliament of England were in no sort apprised either of the Hardships, or dangerous Consequences, of the Act; and are sensible that the whole Act is grounded upon gross Misinformations given them concerning the Value of the Forfeitures; which were represented, by the Persons intrusted with that Inquiry, to be at least Four times the Value of what they will be found to amount to We will not affirm, that this was done wilfully, or to serve private Ends; but we must say, and can make it plain beyond Denial, that all Proofs offered to them in their Inquiries, though never so plain and evident, were by them disregarded and rejected, when they tended to lessen the Value of the Forfeitures, and deprive them of an Handle for making their exorbitant Report.

And we must add, that the Expences to which this Kingdom hath already been put, in Attendance upon the Trustees, with Counsel, Witnesses, in Fees to their Officers, &c. ,* the Salaries of the Trustees themselves, and of near Relations to some of them; and other Officers put into Employments, with great Allowances, under them; with other Charges winch the Act has occasioned to this Kingdom; if cast up, will exceed the utmost that the Act, even as now executed, can produce: Such a Sum might, without Grievance or Complaint, have been laid equally upon the Forfeitures in Ireland; and thereby the Publick might have received some Benefit, and this Kingdom not have groaned under a Burden, which nothing but the last Necessity forces her to complain of in this manner: Something of this kind may yet be done, though not near to what might have been, before the Country was so impoverished by the Means of the Act.

May it please your Majesty to suffer us, upon thisOc-sion, to assure Your Majesty, That Your Protestant Subjects of this Kingdom are so sensible of the inexpressible Favours they have received from Your Majesty, and of Your tender Care of them, that nothing can ever shake -their Faith and Duty to Your Majesty; and that, what-

Vol. \3.

ever the Malice of their Enemies may, for private End.«jt or ill Designs, suggest to the contrary, no Inducements whatsoever can prevail with them to endeavour to make; or to wish, themselves independent of, or not subject to the Crown of England; and that none of Your Majesty's Subjects of any of Your Dominions will, upon all Occasions, shew a more forward and ready Zeal to maintain and defend, against all Opposers whatsoever, Your Majesty's Sacred Person, and Government, the Protestant Religion, the Laws, Liberties, and the Right, of the Crown of England' than Your Majesty's Protestant Subjects of Ireland.

Ordered, That the Earl of Abercome, arid James Tbp+ ham Esquire, do attend this House upon Thursday Sevennight.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Mercuriii 4° die Februarii;

Anno 130 Willielmi Teitii.

Woollen A Petition of the Governors of the Dutch Bay-hall,

Manufdc- and also of the Bay-makers, Say-makers, and Perpetuana-

Uucs‘ makers, in Colchester, was presented to the House, and

read; setting forth, That many Thousands of People in and about Colchester are employed in the Woollen Manufactures; for the Managing whereof great Quantities of Wool are weekly bought at London, Buckinghamshire, and other inland Counties, and brought to Colchester, and is weekly carried to Spinners, many whereof live Thirty Miles off: That certain Persons, deputed by Commissioners appointed by Act of Parliament to prevent the Exportation of Wool, have seized great Quantities of the Petitioners Wool, as passing backwards and forwards, in the way of their Trades, under Pretence of being carried at Hours contrary to the said Act, notwithstanding the Petitioners never did, or endeavoured to, export Wool: And those Seizures tend to the Discouragement and stopping the said Trades; for that the Petitioners cannot make their weekly Returns, especially in short Days, and bad Roads, without exceeding the Hours limited by the said Act: And praying, That some Expedient may be found out for permitting the Petitioners to bring their Wool from London, and other Places, and carrying it to Spinners; and for bringing home Yam; without restraining them to the said Hours; yet continuing the Laws in Force to prevent Exportation of Wool or Yarn.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws relating to the Woollen Manufacture; and to consider of the best Methods for regulating and preventing the same.

Ordered, That the Bill for the better preventing Bri- Bribery at bery and Corruption in Elections of Members to serve Elections, in Parliament, be read a Second time upon Tuesday Morning next.

A Petition of the Clothiers of his Majesty's Army for the Y'cars One thousand Six hundred Ninety-eight, and One thousand Six hundred Ninety-nine, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners cloathed the Army on the Off-reckonings of those Y'ears, not doubting but the same woidd be effectually paid; but they have been out of their Money ever since, without any Interest; and those Debentures, given out pursuant to a late Act of Parliament, are above 40/. per Centum Discount: And the greatest Part of the Petitioners, w hose Accounts are not yet stated, are in a worse Condition, by reason of the Uncertainty of the Time and Manner of Payment; which is so great a Grievance, that it hath reduced the Petitioners to great Necessities: And praying, That they may have Interest on their Debentures; or be otherwise relieved, in such manner as shall be thought fit.

Mr . Blatliwait, from the Commissioners of Trade and Improve-

Plantations, presented to the House an Answer to their Orders, directing them to lay before this House an Account of their Proceedings, for the Improvement of Trade, since their last Account laid before this Mouse; and also the State of the Plantations, with relation to Trade, and their Security; together with the Names of the present Governors of the Plantations.

And the Title thereof was read:

And the said Answer and State areas follow'; viz.

The said Answer:

IN Obedience to an Order of this Honourable House, dated the Nineteenth of the last Month, requiring us to lay before them an Account of our Proceedings, for the Improvement of Trade, since our Account given in the Twelfth of March last; and in further Obedience to an Order of the Thirty-first of the last Month, requiring us to lay before this Honourable House the State'of the Plantations with relation to Trade, and their Security, together with the Names of the present Governors of the Plantations; we humbly take Leave to represent,

That, in pursuance of his Majesty's Commission for promoting the Trade of this Kingdom, and for inspecting and improving his Majesty's Plantations and Factories in America, and elsewhere, we have continued to apply ourselves to the Care of those Plantations, in relation to their Government and Commerce: And there being, within the Allegiance of the Crow n of England, Twenty several Colonies, besides Hudsons Bay and A Newfoundland, in which last Place there is no Governor; each of which have their distinct Governments, Councils, and General Assemblies, by whom Laws, and Rules of Government, are passed and enacted; some of which Colonies are governed by his Majesty's immediate Commission, and others by Proprietors and Charters; with these Governments, and particularly those under his Majesty's especial Direction, we have managed a constant Correspondence; in the Course whereof, the said Governors have sent us Journals of their Councils, Assemblies, and other publick Proceedings, with Accounts of all Matters whatsoever relating to their respective Governments; ajl which have been considered by us, and the necessary Orders returned thereupon: More particularly, the Acts of the several Assemblies, transmitted to us, have been examined; and our Reports have thereupon been made to his Majesty, in his Privy Council, for his Royal Assent, or Disallowance: In all which we have, according to our Duty, had especial Regard to the Interest and Improvement of the Trade of England, as well as to the Good of the Plantations.

We have prepared the necessary Orders, Commission, and Instructions, for Brigadier Selwyn, whom his Majesty has been pleased to appoint Governor of Jamaica: We have prepared the like Dispatches, Commission, and Instructions, for the Lord Cornbury, whom his Majesty has been pleased to constitute Governor oi New York: And, his Majesty having though fit to separate the said Government of New York from that of the Massachuscts Bay in New England, and to appoint Colonel Dudley to be Governor of the Place last mentioned, we have likewise prepared his Commission for that Government.

His Majesty having, by one of his principal Secretaries of State, directed us to prepare a Commission, and Instructions, for MitfordCrow Esquire to be Governor of Barbadoes, we have accordingly prepared his Commission .-In all which Commissions, and other Dispatches, we have 8 X made

We did then further represent, That the great Variations and Changes, which have happened in Trade since foe Year 1660, did require, that a new Book of Rates should be framed, which, we humbly conceive, should be done, and offered to the Consideration of this Honourable House, as the most effectual Way to remove many Difficulties, which our particular Trades lie under, occasioned by the Alterations, which have happened in the Price of most Commodities since the Year 1660, our Neighbour-N ations having taken great Ad vantages on several Branches of our Trade, by many Commodities being charged too high, and others too low: And we have also suffered much by the Importation of many manufactured Goods, and Handicraft Wares, which hinder the Consumption of our own: Also the fair Traders are discouraged by foe Corruptions, which have grown up with Time, in the Management of foe Re-exports, Debentures and Drawbacks:

Newfoundland.] Upon the sending a Convoy, this Year, to Newfoundland, under the Command of Captain Gray-don, we gave him several Heads of Inquiry relating to the Trade and Fishery of those Parts; with particular Regard to the late Act of Parliament for the better Regulation thereof: We likewise gave such Heads of Instructions to Mr. Larkin, before-mentioned, as we conceived proper, with relation to that Trade, and have, from them, received Accounts; the chief Particulars whereof are as follows:

That, in general, the Inhabitants have not a due Regard to the several Regulations for the more advantageous Management of the Fishery; it being found, that, Northward of St.John, as far as Carbonier, and to the Southward, as far as Ferry land, the Trees are ruined, and the Woods destroyed, as much as before the late Act.

That the Admirals, and Masters of Ships, do not exactly observe the Rules prescribed by Act of Parliament: That, as to the Admirals keeping Journals and Accounts, there are few of them capable of doing it, as the Law directs:

That the Admirals, before the 20th of August, will hear some Complaints; but after that time, none are made to them; they being generally the greatest Offenders themselves:

That the Vessels from New-England supply the People of Newfoundland with Provisions, Bread, Beef, Pork, Flour, Peas, Butter, Boards, and great Quantities of Virginia Tobacco:

That the European Commodities, carried to Newfoundland by the Masters of English Ships, are as follows; Vox. 13.

From France, Brandy, Wine, Salt, Linen, Cantas, Paper, Hats, and Silk:

From Spain, Wine, Brandy, and Iron: And,

From Portugal, Wine, Brandy, Salt; Oil, and Linen: All which Goods are sold, or trucked, with the Traders from New-England, for Tobacco, Sugar, and other of the enumerated Commodities, which they carry to foreign Parts; so that, at the latter end of the Year, the Masters are wholly taken up in the Management of that illegal Trade, which might, in some measure, be prevented, had the Officer or Officers, commanding his Majesty's Ships, Power, like that of a Custom-house Officer, to seize such Goods:

That the New-England Traders seldom depart the Country, till the Men of War are first sailed; and then they carry with them Numbers of Handicraftsmen, Seamen, and Fishermen, whom they entice thither, in Expectation of great Wages:

That the Masters of Ships are very negligent in bringing their Men Home; whereby they save the Charge of their Passage; and those Men, so left, are enticed, and carried, to New-England:

That the Reason, why the New-England Men do fish upon the Coast of Newfoundland, besides their illegal Trade, is, that they may get those Men from thence; they having otherwise a more advantageous Fishery on their own Coast.

Against which Irregularities, we humbly offer, That a further Provision be made by some Bill, that shall pass this Honourable House, relating to Trade.

We take Leave to add a short Account of the State of the French Trade, and Fishery, in those Parts.

Their Trade in Furs, upon Newfoundland, is very inconsiderable; and their Fishery is managed all by Ilshing Ships, without making use of Sack Ships, or By-Boats, as the English do.

Their Plantations there do not increase; nor are they of any other Use than for preserving the Boats, Craft, and Goods, left by the Merchant Ships for the succeeding Vo \ age.

They fish upon the Banks in Placentia Bay, and upon the North-east Coast of Newfoundland.

Placentia is the only Place of Strength they have in the* Country; which is daily fortified, and well furnished with Ammunition; and had new Supplies this Year; there being Three Companies of Foot, with Thirty Men in each Company.

They have the Fish a Month sooner in Placentia Bay, make their Fish with greater Dispatch, and leave the Country much sooner, than our People; and, consequently, may supply any Market they please before us.

To tiiu Bank they send yearly a considerable Number of Ships, to fish there; who arrive about the Tenth of June, and depart the latter End of August.

State of Defence of the Plantations.] As to the Security of his Majesty's Plantations, we did, on the 10th and 25th of January 1700-1 humbly lay before his Majesty the State of the several Forts, and Fortifications in his Majesty's Colonies and Plantations in , and of

other Particulars necessary for the Defence of the same; and thereupon, for his Majesty's further Information, did, by his Majesty's Command, write to the several Governors, directing them to dispatch to us, with all Diligence, perfect Accounts of the State of Defence of the Plantations under their Government, and of the Stores and Materials of War there wanting, that we might report to his Majesty what might be required from the several Plantations, and 'what may be fit for his Majesty to do for their Defence: And, having thereupon received Answers from several Governors, and further considered the Condition of those Parts, with relation to the present Conjuncture, we have lately represented the same to his Majesty; and do humbly lay before this Honourable House,

That Newfoundland is of great Importance to this Kingdom, by reason of its Trade and Fishery: That the Place of chief Strength in it is John's Harbour', whidi is now fortifying by his Majesty's Order; the Garison

Improvement where no regular Government hath ever been established, of Trade. the great Disorders amongst them have now inclined the Proprietors to make Application to his Majesty, to accept of a Surrender of their pretended Right to Government, and to put them under a Governor appointed by his Majesty's immediate Commission; which Matter is now transacting, and a Form of Surrender returned from his Majesty's Attorney General, which the said Proprietors are to execute.

The Province of Pensilvania is likewise without Fortifications, and in no State of Defence; nor has any Progress been made therein by the Proprietor, notwithstanding our Instance to him on that Subject, by Order of the Ixirds Justices.

His Majesty's Provinces of Maryland and be-

ing large Territories, and lying open by great Rivers, cannot so well be secured by Foitifications; but in both those Provinces, there is a well-regulated Militia, and Places of Rendezvous appointed for any Occasion: But we understand, that, at present, they are in want of a Supply of Small Arms and Ammunition.

The Provinces of North and South Carolina are under Proprietors, who do not take due Care to put that Country into a State of Defence, notwithstanding their being so exposed by the Neighbourhood of the Spaniards: We therefore have judged it necessary to the publick Service, that the said Proprietors be quickened, by an immediate Order from his Majesty, to perform their Duty herein, until some other Provision be made.

The Bahama Islands lying before the Gulph of and in the Way of all Ships that come from the Havanna, and the Bay of Mexico, it is of great Consequence to his Majesty's Service, that they be preserved from an Enemy. They belong to Proprietors, who ought to take care of them; but we have not been able to dispose those Proprietors to such Compliance, as was proper for his Majesty's Service therein. The Governor has lately desired some Force to keep the Fort there, built for Thirty-two Guns; which being of immediate Concern to the Proprietors, it is necessary that they be obliged to take some speedy Care therein.

In the Bermuda Islands there are Five little Castles; Three of which, lying at the Entrance of the easiest Passages to those Islands, are most considerable; where many of the Platforms being decayed, the Guns unserviceable, and Stores and Ammunicition wanting, a Supply of such Stores have, upon our Representation to his Majesty, been lately sent. Captain B, his Majesty's Commander in Chief in those Islands, has prevailed with the Assembly to pass an Act for repairing their Forts and Platforms; and has caused Trenches to be cast up in all Places where an Enemy may most probably attempt to land; so that, we hope, thereby, and the Company of Foot, which his Majesty has likewise sent thither, that Government is now iu a good State of Defence.

As to Jamaica, we laid before his Majesty, in our Report of the 25th of January 1700-1, the Importance of that Island, with Draughts and Plans of the necessary Fortifications, and several Considerations and Proposals relating to the Defence of each Part thereof; and his Majesty has since been pleased to commissionate Brigadier Selwyn to be Chief Governor there: Upon which Occasion, his Majesty sent thither Two Regiments of Foot, with Stores and Ammunition, for the Defence of the said Island; and, upon the Arrival of Colonel Selwyn there, w e expect to hear from him what Reinforcement of Men, and other Materials and Requisites of War, will be further wanting for the Security of that Island, and putting it into a Posture of offending an Enemy from thence; this Island lying, as it were, in the Centre of the Spanish Indies, and of the French Settlements.

Sir Williatn Beeston, his Majesty's late Governor of that Place, gives us an Account, That he had yet no News of his Majesty's Squadron, under the Command of Vice Admiral Bembow; but that he was credibly informed, That, about the Twentieth of September, Twenty-six Sail

were seen to Windward of Martinico, and the People of Jamaica supposed them to be French; which had engaged him to the putting the Island into as good a Posture of Defence as he could: That he has finished several small Works near Port-Royal, and caused the Bays, where most probably an Enemy may land, to be intrenched; he has further, by the Resolution of a Council of War, fortified the Town of St. Jago with a good Trench, regular Works, and Bastions; having Five hundred Negroes daily on those Works, at the Expence of the Island.

As to the Leeward Islands, at St. Christopher's, there is a Fort, called Cleoerly-Point Fort, where Twenty Gun9 are mounted; Brimstone-Hill Fort, where there areTwelve Guns, and a small Platform, where is Six Guns: There being also Thirty Pieces of Cannon brought out of the French Part of this Island during the late War, Colonel Codrington has given Directions for the mounting and placing them, with all Speed; which being done, he conceives, that there is not Occasion, at present, for more Artillery there; nor does he specify any further Want of Materials relating to the Defence of that Island; but represents the Danger of it to be greater than any other, by reason of the French being possessed of One Half, and the Fate of it likely to be decided upon the breaking out of a War, as hath formerly happened.

At Antegoaare several little Forts and Platforms. The

Governor proposes the sending of Twenty long Sakers, which may serve as well against the Indians as any other Enemy; as likewise, the building a small Fort at Parham, for which he desires Twelve Guns. He would also make a new Platform in another Place, where Privateers, in time of War, and unlawful Traders, in time of Peace, are very busy. He further adds, the great Want of Small Arms in this Island.

At Nevis, Colonel Codrington represents the Want of new Carriages for the Guns; and desires, further, Four long Sakers, Six Guns Twelve Pounders, and Six Eighteen Pounders, with a sufficient Quantity of Shot for them, and Five hundred Saker Shot for the Guns already in the Fort and Platforms, together with Twenty Barrels of Cannon Powder; his Majesty having been lately pleased to order Six hundred Firelocks to be sent to this Island, for as many Matchlocks returned from thence.

As to Mountsei'rat, the Governor represents the Island as able to defend itself; but fears a Danger from within, by an Insurrection, as happened upon breaking out of the last War; most of the Inhabitants of that Place being Papists.

His Majesty has, in these Islands, a Regiment of Foot, lately sent from Ireland; which wants to be strengthened, being of the lowest Complement.

The Island of Barbadoes, to the Windward, is naturally fortified by Rocks; and, for Defence of the Leeward Side, which is most exposed to an Enemy, there is now a Trench of Seven Feet broad, and Five Feet deep, all along the Coast; and, behind that, a Breast-work of loose Sand, about Six Feet high, and Three Feet broad at the Top: There are also, on that Side, several Redoubts; and at Bridge-Town, Two Forts, one at the Entrance of the Road, and the other within; which are the Defence of that Town and Road.

We have received from the Lord Grey, since his Arrival, a Memorial of what may be necessary for the Defence of this Island: That, upon a strict Survey of the State of the Fortifications, made by himself, and Commissioners appointed for that Purpose, he found, in Twenty-nine Forts and Batteries, Three hundred and Eight Guns of several Sorts; viz. Two Demi Cannon, Seventy-five Culverins, One hundred and Eight Demi Culverins, One hundred and One Sakers, and Twenty-two Minions; several of which were unserviceable: That most of the Forts and Batteries were out of Repair; his Lordship offering his Opinion, upon Consultation with the most experienced Inhabitants of the Island, That there be sent thither, at least One hundred great Guns, of Twelve Feet long, together with a suitable Proportion of Shot,

and

13 W. III. 5° Februarii. 729

and all other Ordnance Stores needful for them. He further says. That there is a Want of Small Arms and Shot.

Upon which Occasion, we humbly take Leave to inform this Honourable House, That the Inhabitants of this Island have, at all times, built their own Forts, and kept them in Repair at their own Expence; and have furnished themselves, for the most part, with Small Arms; but, at present they complain of their being deprived of the Revenue of 41 per Centum, raised within that Island for their Fortifications, and other publick Uses; and of their being weakened by the great Expence they were at in assisting the Leeward Islands, during the late War; for which they desire a Compensation: But, as to such a Number of great Guns, as may be proper, with a due Proportion of Shot and Ammunition, as by them desired, we humbly conceive, they must be sent from England.

The Company of Merchants trading to Hudson's Bay, having a Factory in those Parts, represent, That they can no way be safe, unless some Care be taken by his Majesty of their Security, which they have particularized to us.

Cautions, given them herein, have not met with due Com- improve-pliance, several Governors and Lieutenant Governors, not ment of qualified according to the late Act of Parliament, having Trade-been appointed by those Proprietors, even since the last Session of Parliament, we cannot but continue in the same Opinion, that it may be very expedient, for the Ends above mentioned, and particularly for the mutual Defence of the Plantations, that the' Charters of the several Proprietors and others, be, by the Legislative Power of this Kingdom, reassumed to the Crown; and that these Colonies be put into the same State of Dependency as other his Majesty's Plantations, without Prejudice to any Man's Property or Freehold; which, as it will greatly contribute to the Welfare of his Majesty's Subjects in those Parts, and to the Advantage of this Kingdom, is hereby humbly recommended to the Consideration of this Honourable House; together with the several other Particulars before enumerated; as most effectually tending to the Security of his Majesty's Plantations, and the Encouragement of Trade.

Names of the present Governors of his Majesty's Plantations in America.

Which Demands, made by the several Colonies and Plantations before-mentioned, we conceive to be chiefly in View of a present Defence: But, in case of a War, we arc humbly of Opinion, That a greater Quantity of Stores, and Materials of War, will be wanting; and that, in the principal and most considerable of those Plantations, it will be necessary, that there be Magazines of Ordnance Stores, of all Kinds, as well for the Defence of each respective Place, and of the Colonies adjoining, as for an-noving the Enemy; who will be very watchful and active, in this Conjuncture, to take Advantage against any of his Majesty's Plantations, which are of so great Importance to the Trade and Welfare of England.

We are also humbly of Opinion, That there be a like Provision there of Naval Stores, and Credit for his Majesty's Ships of War; which have often lain very long useless in Harbour in those Parts, by reason of their Want of Necessaries for refitting; which has been of great Prejudice to his Majesty's Service; the Safety of his Majesty's Dominions in America depending chiefly on the naval Force to be sent thither at proper Seasons, which may secure that Trade, and encourage the Planters, who will otherw ise be apt to desert their Settlements.

Laws contrary and repugnant to the Laws of England, and directly prejudicial to Trade: That by raising and lowering their Coin, to their particular Advantage, and to the Prejudice of other Colonies, by exempting their Inhabitants from Duties and Customs, to which the other Colonies are subject, by harbouring Servants and Fugitives, and thereby encouraging the Desertion of his Majesty's Standing Forces in those Parts, these Governments tend greatly to the undermining the Trade of the other Plantations: That these independent Colonies do turn the Course of Trade, to the promoting and propagating Woollen Manufactures, proper to England, instead of applying their Endeavours to the Production of such Commodities as are fit to be encouraged in those Parts:

The Committee examined into the Circumstances of this Matter: And she gave an Account, how she made Two Affidavits relating to it; the fatter being, to supply the Defect of Time, not mentioned in the First; but, it being not strictly to this Matter, I only mention it in general.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel insisted, That the Petitioner had more who received Alms, that voted for him, than there was of that Sort, who voted for the Sitting Member: That they would justify the Sitting Member in relation to the ill Practices charged upon him, and prove several ill Practices by the Petitioner: And called several Witnesses.

As to the Guinea given in Evidence to be spent at Marshal's House, the Chequer; the Sitting Member called,

John Marshal himself: Who said, That Mr. B/isse, upon Marshall's taking that House of Mr. B/isse about Three Quarters of a Year before, did promise to give him something for House-warming; which Promise he renewed several times: That, on the Thirteenth or Fourteenth of November, accordingly, he gave him a Guinea, which the said Marshall gave to his Wife: That, at the Time spoken of by the Petitioner's Witnesses, there were several others present, as well as Freemen and some of them went away without paying; and one said, He

would pay when he had Money: But the said Marshall denied that any Money was spent on the Account of the Election; and said, That Mr. B/issc told him, If he did draw any Drink on his Account, it would be as much as his Election was w orth.

Tho. Moor also said. That, about a Week before the Election, he was sent, by Mr. Blisse, to several Publick-houses, to forbid Treating.

The next Thing the Sitting Member's Counsel applied themselves to, was, to disqualify some of the Petitioner's Voters.

Zac. Cvllison said, That John Farringdon received Alms t)f the Parish; and he had given William Corford Monies Four or Five times, blit not weekly; and the last Time was Half a Year since:

That James Howard received Half a Year ago, being in Prison; and not since he had his Liberty; but his Wife had received weekly the Year before:

That Benjamin Gregson was dumb; but it was acknowleged he did buy and sell:

And that John Baptist is a Foreigner; but it was acknowleged he followed the Trade of a Barber in Maidstone.

That the next Thing the Sitting Member's Counsel proceeded on, was, a Charge of Bribery, by or on the behalf of the Petitioner: And called,

John Heley: Who said, That he came to London some time before the Election; and got the Names of about Ten Freemen, and returned to Maidstone, and acquainted Mr. Colcpeper with it: That, before the Election, he had Occasion to go to London again; and Mr. Colepeper bid him get those Freemen down, and use his own Means: That Mr. Colepeper also drew a Bill upon my Lord Colepeper for 40 I. which he desired the said Heley to bring dowrt with him; but he ignorantly gave to the said Ten Freemen in London from 1 o to 25 Shillings a Man, to bring them down: He said, He did desire their Votes for Mr. Colepeper; but Two or Three of them turned Cat-in-J>an, and voted for Mr. Blisse.

David Cops lick, one of those Freemen who lived in Southwark, said, He received of Heley Twenty-four or Twenty-five Shillings.

Oliver Simons, another of those Freemen, acknowleged, He received 20 s.of the said Heley, and voted for Mr. Colepeper, otherwise he would have voted for Mr. Blisse.

Richard Leder: That, on the Thirteenth Day of November, Mr. Colepeper laid down a Guinea, at the Castle in Maidstone, to be drank; and that the said Leder, and other Freemen, drank of it: He said, Mr. Colepeper desired their Votes; but he voted for Mr. Blisse.

William Ward said, That Mr. Colepeper, Four or Five Days before the Election, gave to Daniel Comber, 10 to bs spent amongst the Freemen; and he also gave 10#. to Henry Ward, upon the same Account.

Tho. Symonds said, That Mr. Colepeper, about Ten Days before the Election, gave him 5 to spend among the People: And that one Catlin told him, That Mr. Cole-

r gave him 20s. for his Vote: Symonds voted for Blisse.

George Ward said, That Mr. Thomas Colepeper, at several times, put into his Hands the Value of Two Guineas, to drink at several times; and told the said Ward,

If he would vote for him, the said Ward should get 20/. a Year by his Trade; and, if he was turned out of the House he then lived in, he should live in a House of Mr. Colepepers.

The next Head the Sitting Member's Counsel proceeded to, was, that of Libels and Reflections by the Petitioner.

William Wcrwsden produced a Letter, with a printed Paper in it, which, he said, was brought to his House by a Person unknown, and brought to him by his Man:

And Mr. Taylor said, The Letter was Mr. Thomas

Colepeper & Hand: And the said printed Paper was read; and is called; A Letter to the Freeholders and Freemen of England.

William Thacker said, That he was sent by Mr. Tlwmas Colepeper to Dr. Smith, for some Papers; and he brought away with him about Five Quires, and delivered the same to his MasterAnd, the next Day, several Freemen, that came to his Master, when they came from him, brought down Papers with them.

And, one of those Papers being produced, it appeared to be the same Paper with that received by Mr. Wowsden, in Mr. Colepepers Letter: And

William Thacker said further, That, upon Sunday the Sixteenth of November, Dr. Smith, Mr. Thomas Colepeper, Captain White, Captain Robinson, and Mr. Hamilton, dined at Sir Thomas Colepepers; and, amongst other Discourse one said, That Mr. Joh How had delivered an Address to his Majesty, and that his Majesty had received him with a particular Favour: Whereupon Dr. Smith said,

It was a devilish Lie, and the Party would say any thing; *' but they must outlye them.

He also gave an Account of some Discourse at Mr. Colepepers House, at Dinner, in relation to what Mr. Blisse had said to Mrs. Wattl; and how at first it was reported, that Mrs. Wattle would not stand to it: After* wards he heard she was willing to do any thing to sene Mr. Colepeper, but would not take away Mr. Blisse's Life: And that, they being talking about that Matter, one said.

If Mr. Blisse would have quitted his Interest, Mrs. Wattle would not have sworn to it: And Mr. Colepeper said. She would not: And the said Thacker gave an Account of several other Circumstances; which, not being directly to the Election, and difficult to be collected, I refer to the Memory of Gentlemen of the Committee, which was very well attended.

Tho. Swinnocksaid, That Mr. Francis Brook desired of

Dr. Smith, that he would be kind to his Neighbours:

And Dr. Smith said, That the tumultuous Proceedings at the Election were a great Matter in Mr. Petition; and they must make a Riot of it, or it would go against Mr. Colepeper in the House.

John Wylett said, That Thacker, when he served Sir Robert Guildford, pretended to be a Roman Catholick, and went not to Church.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions;

A Petition of John Mapas Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, being about Ten Years of Age, was outlawed for High Treason in Ireland, although he never had any Civil or Military Employment, or was any-ways concerned in the late Troubles there; nor was ever intitled to any Estate, real or personal, save only as Heir apparent to his Father, who is seised of an Estate in Fee-simple, and may dispose thereof as he pleases; and who is, by reason of the said Outlawry, which cannot be reversed but by Parliament, now upon settling the same upon others, although the Petitioner forfeited nothing, as appears by the Trustees Books: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for reversing the said Outlawry; the Petitioner having committed no Offence against the Government.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, to be considered with the other Petitions relating to the said forfeited Estates.

R1 solved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the Supply granted to his Majesty, an Aid, not exceeding Four Shillings in the Pound, for One Year, be laid upon all Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments.

2. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Fifty Shillings per Centum, for One Year, be laid upon the Value of all Stock in Trade.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Twenty-five Shillings per Centum, for One Year, be laid upon all Money at Interest.

4. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Four Shillings in the Pound, for One Year, be laid upon all Annuities, Pensions, and yearly Stipends.

5. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Five Shillings in the Pound, for One Year, be laid upon all Salaries, Fees, and Perquisites, of Offices Ecclesiastical and Civil.

To the King's most Excellent Majesty,

The humble Address of the Lord Mayor, Sheriffs, Commons, and Citizens of the City of Dublin, in Common Council assembled.

Great Sir,

WE, your Majesty's most dutiful Subjects of this City, with all Humility, presume to lay before your Sacred Majesty the great Pressures we, with the rest of our Protestant Fellow Subjects, lie under, by the rigorous Execution of the late Act of Resumption, and the unsupportable Charge occasioned, thereby to great Numbers of your loyal Subjects, who were wholly unconcerned in the late Forfeitures in this Kingdom.

Nothing less than the Ruin of many thousand Protestant improving Tenants, Purchasers, and others, which will immediately follow the further Execution of that Act, could force us to give your Majesty the least Interruption, by our Complaints, at a time when the most weighty Affairs of Europe are under the Consideration of your Majesty, and your great Council.

But we apprehend, Great Sir, that we should fail in that Regard we ought to have for the Protestant Interest of this Kingdom, should we omit representing to your
