May it therefore please Your Majesty to take our distressed Condition into Your Princely Care; and to give us Relief herein, as to Your Majesty shall seem proper for the Removal of so great a Burden.

And give us Leave, on this Occasion, to assure Your Majesty, that we will, at all times, shew a ready Zeal to maintain and defend Your Majesty's Person and Government, the Rights and Liberties of the Imperial Crown of England, against all Opposers whatsoever. In Testimony whereof, we have caused our Common Seal to be hereunto affixed, this 16th Day of January, in the Year of our Lord 1701.

To the King's most Excellent Majesty.

The humble Address of the Nobility,. Justices of the Peace, Grand Jury, Clergy, Gentlemen, and Free^ holders, of the County of Dublin, at their General Quarter Sessions held at Killmainham, the 16th Day of January 1701.

YOUR Majesty's faithful and loyal Subjects, the Protestants of this Your Kingdom of Ireland, lying under such Pressures, by reason of the late Act of Resumption, and of the Execution thereof, that they apprehend the Ruin of the Protestants of this Kingdom, who have all of them, to the utmost of their Power, been most forward and zealous for Your Majesty's Interest, and instrumental in the reducing this Kingdom to its Dependence upon the Crown of England' must be the unavoidable Consequence of the Execution of that Act, do humbly fly to Your Majesty's Protection; and pray, That Your Majesty, the Restorer of their Religion, Rights, and Liberties, would once again be pleased to take their distressed Condition into Your Princely Consideration, and, by such Methods as to Your Majesty shall seem most expedient, and their present Circumstances, and the Justice of their Cause, do require, apply suitable Remedies to the severe Burdeu under which they lie.

The deplorable Condition of very many Families, who always have adhered firmly to the Interest of Your Majesty, and of the Crown of England, and the general Discouragement that Act has given to the Protestant Interest of this Kingdom, constrains us, with all Humility, to lay before Your Majesty, That, the Act being intirely framed and passed in England, the real Truth of our Circumstances could not be known: Hence we have Reason to complain,

That the Persons, who chiefly receive any Benefit or Favour by this Act, are the Papists of this Kingdom; and, amongst them, principally those, who, to the last, opposed Your Majesty's Arms and Interest: And, besides many other particular Favours to Irish Papists, all those, who, by Your Majesty's Grace, obtained the Reversal of their Outlaw ries, have the Benefit of those Reversals confirmed to them; and are, by this Act, restored as well to their Estates, as to their Blood, when most of the Grants made to Protestants are, by the said Act, re-assumed: That the Improvers, and poor Husbandmen, who, by several Proclamations issued by Your Majesty's Order, w ere encouraged and required to betake themselves again to their Tillage, to repair the Desolation wrought by the War, and prevent a Famine, are, by it, deprived of all the Benefit of their Labour, and the Charges of their Improvements:

That, those who purchased under Patentees, are generally Protestants, who, in their Dealing for those Estates, acted agreeably to the then knowm and established Luws of these Kingdoms; now, by a Law made ex post facto, they find themselves in the Condition of forfeiting Persons:

That the ill Consequences, of this Act* and the Execution of it, do not only affect the Purchasers, but Your Majesty's other Subjects here* who are wholly unconcerned in those Titles* and disquiet the whole Kingdom: For, some of the Trustees having declared in Court their Opinion, That, what Lands they shall think VOL. 13.

fit to sell, it shall never afterwards be controverted, w hether that Land was the Estate of a forfeiting Person, and, in consequence of that, vested in them by the Act; but that their Sales, whatever they are, are confirmed by the Act, and past Controul; Your Majesty's Subjects of this Kingdom are sensible, that, if this Opinion prevail; the whole Property of Ireland depends upon the arbitrary Wills of a Majority of the Trustees:

That the Power given the Trustees is so arbitrary and unlimited, That all Persons, under colour of Discoveries, or upon other Pretences, are liable to be summoned to appear before them, and obliged to attend their Pleasure:

That this Act is a great Discouragement to Protestant Proprietors to lay out Money on Improvements, upon account of the Uncertainty of Titles to Estates here; it being construed not only to subject Titles established by Judgments and Decrees of the highest Courts of Law and Equity here, to the Re-examination of the Trustees; but it, in express Terms, defeats a Title confirmed by an Act of Parliament legally convened, and held under Your Majesty, within this Kingdpm:

That the whole Scheme of the Act, and the Manner of the Execution of it, depresses and discountenances the Protestant Interest of this Kingdom, and encourages the Popish; of the Dangers of which, we, who have felt the Effects of it, must always be apprehensive; but more particularly now, when the Papists throughout the whole Nation, by the Insolence of their Behaviour, shew, that the Acknowledging of the pretended Prince of Wales by the French King, or some other Dependence, has raised their Expectations to a great Height.

We are persuaded, that the Parliament of England were in no sort apprized either of the Hardships, or dangerous Consequence, of this Act; and are sensible, that the whole Act is grounded upon gross Misinformations given to them concerning the Value of the Forfeitures; which w ere represented, by the Persons intrusted with that Inquiry, to be at least Four times the Value of w hat they will be found to amount to We will not affirm, that this was done wilfully, or to serve private Ends; but we must say, and can make it plain, beyond Denial, that most Proofs offered to them in their Inquiries, though never so plain and evident, were by them disregarded and rejected, when they tended to lessen the Value of the Forfeitures, and deprive them of a Handle for making their exorbitant Report.

And we must add, that the Expences to which this Kingdom has already been put; in Attendance upon the Trustees, with Counsel, Witnesses, and in Fees to their Officers, &c.; the Salaries of the Trustees themselves, and of near Relations to some of them; and other Persons put into Employments, with great Allowances, under them; with other Charges which the Act has occasioned to this Kingdom; if cast up, will exceed the utmost that the Act, even as now executed, can produce: A considerable Sum might, without such Grievance or Complaint, have beeu la idEqually upon the Forfeitures in Ireland-, and thereby the Publick might have received some Benefit, and this Kingdom not have groaned under a Burden, which nothing but the last Necessity forces her to complain of in this manner: Something of this kind may yet he done, though not near to what might have been, before the Country was so impoverished by the Means of the Act.

May it please Your Majesty to suffer us, upon this Occasion, to assure Your Majesty, That your Protestant Subjects of this Kingdom are so sensible of the inexpressible Favours they have received from Your Majesty, and Your tender Care of them, that nothing can ever shake their Faith and Duty to Your Majesty; and that, whatever the Malice of their Enemies may, for private Ends, or ill Designs, suggest to the contrary, no Inducements whatsoever can prevail with them to endeavour to make, or so much as to wish, themselves independent of, or not subject unto, the Crown of England; and that none of Your Majesty's Subjects of any of Your Dominions will, upon all Occasions, shew' a more forward and ready Zeal to maintain and defend, against all Opposers whatsoever, Your Sacred Person, and Government, the Protestant 9 D Religion,

A Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Company of Distillers of London, on behalf of ilhemselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners distil Brahdy from many Thousand Quarters of Corn which is unfit for brewing; but are greatly discouraged by several unskilful Persons setting up the Trade of making and selling English Brandy, who are under no Regulation or Inspection, and have brought a Disreputation upon all Brandies, and strong Waters; and many Persons also run French Brandy, and under-sell the Petitioners, who pay a Duty of Six Shillings per Gallon for the same; by which means, and by reason of a Clause in a late Act of Parliament, for laying a Duty on low Wines, and Spirits of the First Extraction, for obliging all Persons that sell Brandy, or strong Waters, by Retail, to take Licences, the Petitioners Trades are become very contemptible, and much decayed: And praying that the House will give them such Relief in the Premises, as shall be thought fit.

A Petition of Gerrard Lowther Clerk, and Anne his Lowther'* Wife, was presented to the House, and read; setting Estate, forth, That Sibill Lowther, the Petitioner Gerrard"s Mother, was possessed of a Farm called Coleby Leathes, near Appleby, in the County of Westmoreland, held, by Lease for Twenty-one Years, of the Dean and Chapter of Carlisle; which was devised to her by her Husband Christopher Lowther, deceased; and assigned over to the Petitioner Gerrard by his Mother, who had renewed the same; but subject to pay her Debts and Incumbrances, which are near the Value thereof; That the Petitioner Gerrard, not knowing the said Estate to be so high charged, did, on his Marriage with his Wife, agree to settle the same, with other of her own Estate, upon her, and her Issue; and have since had Two Sons, to whom the Petitioner is Guardian:

But the Profits of the Premises will never pay the Debts of Sibill, and the growing Interest will swallow up the whole Estate; so that it is conceived, by all Parties concerned, that a Sale thereof will most conduce to their Advantage: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to vest the Estate late, of Doctor Christopher Lowther in Trustees, in order to the Sale thereof, for Discharge of the Debts thereupon.

A Petition of the Lords and Gentlemen of the County Salt Palatine of Chester, and the Grand Jury at the Quarter Sessions for the said County, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by the clandestine Use of Rock Salt in Specie; the selling foreign Salt by Measure; the Advantages given in Weight, and Drawback Bonds; and by other Allowances, which the Brine Salt wants; the Petitioners very sensibly find the Ruin of the Brine Manufacture, the Beggaring of many thousand Families, who, before these Frauds, got a comfortable Subsistence: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, for the general Encouragement of the Brine Salt Manufacture.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the whole House.

Roger Jones, and //ij/er,

said. That they have been frequently obliged to take Coc-quets, and give their Bonds below, when they have not brought above 60 Quarters of Corn; nay, when they have'brought but 20 or 15 Quarters, they have been obliged so to do; '

And that, notwithstanding the y have made good Returns from the Custom-house here to the Ports below, to be annexed to their Bonds, according to the Conditions thereof; yet, upon the Officers returning their Bonds up to the Exchequer, they have Process issued out against them; and have thereupon been forced to take out fresh Bonds, or be prosecuted; and, upon such Prosecutions, have been put to or 5 Charge; although their Returns were duly delivered to the Officers below, who make use of so slight a Way of annexing the Returns to the Bonds, only by a Bit of Thread through Two Pin-holes at the Edge of the Bond, whereby the Returns are often lost; and, when the Officer pleases, it is but paring off the Edges of the Bond, and then there remains no Sign that the Returns were affixed; whereby the Obligors, though they have duly performed the Bonds, become liable to the Exchequer Prosecutions: To prevent which, they must, at least, renew their Returns; which some- times cost them 17 or i8«. notwithstanding their duly clearing their Goods before.

Tho. Soccutg said, That they usually make their Voyages once a Week, or in a Fortnight at furthest; and are forced to take Cocquets every Voyage, which generally costs them 11 s. besides the Danger of their Returns being not annexed to their Bonds; and so are liable to Prosecutions; which proves a great Grievance to them, and a Discouragement to their Employment.

Maurice Atkins: That, about Thirty Years ago, it was usual to bring Com from Sandwich to London only by Transires, without giving any Bonds, or taking out

Cocquets; those Matters having been imposed upon them since that time; and used them to pay for their Transires is. 2d. apiece: But that now they arc forced to take Cocquets, and enter into Bonds; for which they pay 5 s. 6 d.at the Port where they lade; and 3 s. for put-

ting the same into the Custom-house; before they can have the Lord Mayor's Bill to deliver their Goods; and 6 d. for their Return, to be annexed to the Bond, when they go back to the Port where their Bonds lie.

Richard Rogers said, That, when he brings a Hundred Quarters, or above, of Corn from Esses, he is forced to take a Cocquet, and give Bond to the Collector of the Customs below; for which he must pay there 7 s* 2 and 2$. 6 d.for putting the same into the Custom-house;

A Petition of Michael Harvey Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That Antony Henley Esquire, and the Petitioner, stood Candidates at the last Election of a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Melcomb-Regin the County of Dot'set: And the said Mr. Henley, or his Agents, by Bribes and Entertainments, did procure divers Electors to vote for him, in Wrong to the Petitioner, and the Inhabitants of the said Borough: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the same, with their Opinion therein, to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor and Citizens of the City of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, by reason of the clandestine Use of Salt Rock in Specie; the Sale of foreign Salt by Measure; the Advantages given in Weight and Drawback Bonds; and the various Opportunities of Fraud in the Exportation of it, and imposing it on the Buyer for Brine Salt; the Petitioners are very sensible of the Ruin of the ancient Brine Manufacture; to the Decay of the Revenue upon Salt, and many Thousands, who got a Livelihood thereby: And praying, That the House will apply such Remedies, as may be for the general Encouragement of the Brine Manufacture.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for regulating the Frauds and Abuses in die Salt Duties is committed.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Gwyn, and Sir Hemy Dutton Colt, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

A Petition of the Vice Chancellor, Masters, and Cam Scholars, of the University of Cambridge, as also of the Navigation. Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, of the Town and Borough of Cambridge, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Rivers running from Cambridge to King's Lynn heretofore were great and navigable Streams for Barges and Vessels; whereby the said University, and Parts adjacent, were well served with Coals, Fish, Salt, and other Commodities, at reasonable Rates; but, for want of sufficient Banks, Stanks, and Sluices, for keeping up the Water in the shallow Places, the said River, in divers Places between Cambridge, and a Place about Seven Miles below, called Clayhive, is so silted, and grown up, that the said Navigation will be wholly lost, if not timely prevented: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for cleansing and digging the Shallows of the Rivers running from the University and Town of Cambridge to King's Lynn; and for making and erecting Sluices, and other Engines, on the said River; whereby the Navigation and Commerce of the said Town may be recovered and preserved.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Sir John Cotton, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, who were to consider further of Ways and Means for r.vi-'ng the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they tiad directed him to report to the House; which lie reau in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the ClnVs Tabic: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duty upon Malt be Six-pence per Bushel.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be granted to his Majesty from the Ninth of March One thousand Seva n hundred and One, to the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Three.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Duty be laid upon all Mum made or imported.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be after the Rate of Tew Shillings per Barrel.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty upon Mum be granted to his Majesty until the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Three.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Duty be laid upon all Cyder and Perry which shall be made for Sale, to be paid by the Retailer thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duty be after the Rate of Four Shillings per Hogshead.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Duties be granted to his Majesty until the Twenty-fourth Day of June One thousand Seven hundred and Three.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question se.orally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

That the Counsel for Sir Christopher Hales insisted,

That the Right of Election was in the Freemen of Coventry not receiving Alms, or Charity.

The Counsel for Mr. Neale insisted, That the Right was in all Freemen, whether they received Alms or no.

And the Committee, having heard what was alleged on both Sides, came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Freemen of Coventry receiving Alms, or Charity, have no Right to vote in the Election of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry.

That it was agreed by the Counsel on both Sides, That no Person could be a Freeman of Coventry, but by serving Seven Years Apprenticeship, within the City of Coventry, to one and the same Trade.

That the Counsel for Sir Chr. Hales alleged, That they should take off several that had polled for Mr. Neale-, and should prove ill Practices by Mr. and his

SirCAr. Hales Counsel alledged, That they could justify most of thqir Voters; but, they thought, there was no Occasion to trouble the Committee with it.

That the Hearing of this Cause having taken up Seven Nights; and the Evidence, relating to the Disqualifying and Justifying of Freemen, being very particular; it is conceived more proper to refer to the Minutes taken at the Committee, than to transcribe the same, and fill up the Journals with a long Report; which, after the Determination of the Election, can be of no Use.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee, That Sir Christopher Hales Baronet, is duly elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City of Coventry.

The first Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the Freemen of Co* ventry receiving Alms, or Charity, have no Right to vote in the Election of Ciuzens to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That Sir Christopher Hales Baronet is duly elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City of Coventry.

Ordered, That the Clerk of the Crown do attend this House Tomorrow Morning, to amend the Return for the City of Coventry, by taking off the Return, by which Henry Neal Esquire is returned a Citizen to serve for the said City.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the House do now adjourn;

A Petition of William Yarnold Gentleman, on behalf Newcastle of himself, and others, the Proprietors.and Undertakers upon Tine concerned in supplying the Town of Newcastle upon Tine Waterworks* with fresh Water, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, made in the Tenth Year of his Majesty's Reign, for the better supplying the Town of Newcastle upon Tine with fresh Water; and by a Lease made by the Mayor and Burgesses, as expressed in the said Act; the Petitioner has, at great Expence, brought sufficient fresh Water to serve the said Town, from a Place called The Zone, in the County of Durham, about Four Miles from Nerw-castle; and the High Sheriff of Durham hath held Three several Inquisitions to inquire what Damages the Owners of the Lands, through which the said Water is conveyed* have sustained thereby, as the said Act directs; which Damages the Petitioner hath fully paid and satisfied: And praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to confirm the said several Inquisitions and Lease, for the better bringing and continuing of the Water to the said Town, and ascertaining a due Satisfaction to the Owners of the Lands, through which the Water runs, for what Damages they may sustain, for the future* by that or any other Watercourse brought by the Petitioner to the said Town; and for the better Continuance and constant supplying the same with fresh Water.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr.

Carr and Mr. Lambton do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

A Petition of the Officers and Clothiers of the Army, j and Proprietors of the Debt of the several Transport Forfeitures. Services, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That great Part of the Petitioners Debts consist of small Sums; which renders it impossible for them to make separate Purchases of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, wherein the said Effects are made payable in the Purchases; so that the Petitioners will be forced to sell, to the moneyed Men, at intolerable Discounts, unless permitted to purchase in a joint Stock: That, last Year, the Petitioners obtained a Subscription for purchasing the said Forfeitures, of near 500,000/* and had Leave to bring in a Bill pursuant thereto; and now doubt not but to get Subscriptions for purchasing the Whole of those Estates, at reasonable Rates: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for taking Subscriptions for purchasing the Whole of the forfeited Estates in Ireland, on such Terms as may be agreeable with the Wisdom and Justice of the House.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the Fact to the House:

A Petition of /ZirgA Totterdell, of the Island of Jamaica, Gentleman, in behalf of himself, and others the Traders and Planters of the said Island, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Assembly of the said Island, which represents the Body of the Commons there, and consists of Thirty-five Persons, of which the Petitioner was One, being convened in June last, did enter into the Consideration of some Hardships put upon them in point of Trade, and Misapplication of the publick Money of the said Island, by the then Governor, Sir William Beeston, and Council of that Island, endeavouring to redress those Grievances; but, instead of Encouragement, they met with Threats and hard Words from the Governor: And the Assembly finding no Likelihood of Redress, they passed a Vote to apply themselves to this House for Relief; which the Governor so resented, that he immediately prorogued them; and, soon after, dissolved them by Proclamation; setting forth that Vote as One of the Reasons for the Dissolution: That, upon the said Prorogation, the Speaker, and Majority of the Assembly, drew up an Address to this House; setting forth Part of their Hardships, by Violation of the Laws, the Discouragement of their Trade, and Misapplication of the publick Money: Which Address they ordered the Petitioner to present to the House; a Copy whereof is annexed to the Petition; And praying the House to take the Grievances of the said Island into Consideration, and relieve them therein.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of William Freeman Esquire is referred; And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the Fact to the House.

A Petition of Thomas Hodges Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, and many others, being very much oppressed by the Maladministration of Justice in Barbadoes, under the Government of the Lord Grey, did, in December 1700, complain to his Majesty in Council thereof; who referred the Examination thereof to the Commissioners of Trade; with Direction, That they should report to his Majesty what they conceived fit to be done therein; That the Petitioner hath attended the said Commissioners for about a Twelvemonth; hath proved the Truth of his Complaint, and shewn the Maladministration of Justice; and hoped they would have made such a Report to his Majesty, as the Petitioner might have had some effectual Relief thereby; but they have lately made such a Report, as covers the Truth from his Majesty, and has effectually hindered the Petitioner from any Relief: That the Petitioner is ready to prove the several Articles annexed to the Petition, which do contain several Heads of the said Complaint: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

And the said Mr. Hodges was called in, to the Bar, to own the said Petition: And he owned the same accordingly; and declared, he was ready to make good the same.

Ordered, Thai the Consideration of the said Petition

be referred to a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter; and report the same to the House:

And the Trustees in Town, Mr. Annesley and Mr. Hooper, were called in; and examined; And they presented to the House a Memorial:

Which was read: and is as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled;

The humble Memorial of Francis Annesley and James Hopper, Two of the Trustees for the forfeited Estates in Ireland.

THAT the Trustees have used their Endeavours to improve your Estates, vested in them, to the best Rent that could be got for the same: In order whei eunto, they

appointed

14 W. III.

25* — 26° Fehruani.

Appointed Receivers and Surveyors, who have, upon Oath, viewed the Same; and made their Returns of the real Values of the said Estates, if to be lett for a Term of Years, amount-

ing to

I3M96

105,372 15 74-

Wherfeas the present Rent of the Year 1701, is no more than Their Computations proceeding from the Values of other Persons Lands, of equal Value, contiguous to those forfeited: But the Reasons they give the Trustees, why the forfeited Estates do not yield as much as the Estates of such private Persons, are,

1st, That several of the said Estates are in Lease for Terms of Years yet to come, which are allowed by the Trustees, and cannot yet be raised.

2dly, That several Gentlemen are now in Possession of a considerable Part of the said Estates, and will pay what they please; and nobody will take them over their Heads at a greater Rent, because they are sure to incur their Displeasure, for the Prospect of stnail Gain, which is to continue but for One Year; the Trustees not having thought fit, without your Honours Directions, to set them for a loriger Time.

3dly, Because no Tenant is able to improve Lands, which he holds for One Year only, to that Advantage as he would do, if he might enjoy them for a certain Term of Years.

4. That the Number of Acres appear, upon the Survey, to be considerably more than the old Proprietors knew them to be, or are returned to be in the Civil Downe, or Stafford Survey.

5. That the most unprofitable Lands, returned by those Surveys, are since improved, and made most profitable.

For which Reasons, the Trustees are humbly of Opinion, That, if your Honours would approve of their setting such of the said Estates, as are now out of Lease, to the best Advantage, for a certain Term of Years, alj those Inconveniences would be obviated, the Rents raised equal in Value to their adjacent Lands; whereby the annual Income of your Honours Estates would be greatly improved; and the Persons intending to be Purchasers, who are already alarmed with the false Suggestions of the Trustees taking Advantage of the Tenants in Possession, who could not easily remove their Stock, to rack them to an Overvalue, would more chearfully buy the same, and very considerably advance their Price for them, and induce Strangers, who can have no Knowledge of their Values but from their yearly Rent, to become Purchasers.

The Trustees thought it their Duty, and accordingly directed us, humbly to present this Matter to your Honours, for your immediate Directions therein; because, if not set before May next, the Year will be at an End; and it will take some time to give public Notice of such a Resolution.

Fra. Annesley, James Hooper.

And then they withdrew.

Ordered, That the Trustees for the forfeited Estates in Ireland do lay before this House an Account of the Claims made by the Irish Papists; and do distinguish how many have been allowed by them, of Estates whereof the Papists were not in Possession before the Act of Resumption, or decreed or adjudged to them by any Court of Law or Equity in Ireland.

Resolved' That, notwithstanding the Complaints and Clamours against the Trustees for the forfeited Estates in Ireland, with relation to the Execution of the said Trust, it does not appear to this House, but that those Complaints are groundless.

Resolved, That the said Memorial be taken into Consideration upon Saturday Morning next.

The said Abstract of Orders received by Edtv. Den* neston.

Triday, July 18th, I acquainted the Board, That* pursuant to their Order, I had searched the King's Brewhouse; and what Quantity of Strong Beer I had found* appears in the next Paper.

Saturday the 26th, The Board ordered me to go with Captain Betchinden to the Commissioners of the Victualing Office, to acquaint them with the evil Practice, by the Service at his Majesty's said Brewhouse; which I did accordingly.

Tuesday the 29th, I acquainted the Board, That the Commissioners of the Victualing Office had desired me to attend them on Thursday following; for they designed to examine the Servants, relating to my Report* The Board directed me to acquaint the Commissioners of the Victualing, That it was their Opinion, That it was a Fraud upon the Revenue of Excise; and that they would examine the Offenders at their own Board; which was accordingly done.

I also acquainted Mr. Hore, That my Masters, the Commissioners of Excise, desired he would let me knoW where to find him, when they should have Occasion to send for him.

Tuesday, August the 5th, The Board ordered me to go to the Victualing Office, and get a List of the Servants Names belonging to the said Brewhouse; and ordered them to attend the Board of Excise on Friday following: Which they did; and were there examined, relating to the said Fraud.

A PETITION of the Master Clothworkers in and Woollen about the City of London, on behalf of themselves, Manufke* and very many poor People employed under them in the turg§* Working and Dressing of rough Cloth, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, of late Years, there has been great Quantities of rough and undressed Woollen Cloths exported out of this Kingdom, to be dressed in foreign Parts; the which Practice, if not timely prevented, will be the Ruin of the Petitioners Trade:

And praying, That a Duty may be laid upon all rough and undressed Cloth exported.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to inspect the Laws relating to the Woollen Manufacture; and to consider of the best Methods for regulating and improving the same.

Mr. Moor, according to Order, reported from the Ms* Committee, to whom the Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Company of Distillers of London, on behalf of themselves, and others, was referred,

That they had considered the Matter to them referred; 1

and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: v

Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Distil* lers Company, have Power, from time to time, to inspect \ all Spirits, made of malted Corn, within the Limits of their Charter, to see that the same are made good and merchantable; and, otherwise, that the Offenders may be prosecuted for their Offence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committees,

That the Running of French Brandy is a great Discouragement to the Distillers; and hinders the Consump* tion of English Corn.

Besotted, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Clause in the Act, made in the Twelfth and Thirteenth Years of his Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for granting to his Majesty several Duties upon low Wines, or Spirits of the First Extraction, &c. whereby it is enacted, That no Person shall sell Brandy, or other distilled Liquors, by Retail, but such as shall be thereunto licensed and allowed in the same manner as common Alehouse-keepers, under the Penalties and Forfeitures therein mentioned; is a great Hindrance to the Consumption of English Brandies.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill upon the said Resolutions.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in upon the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Moor, Sir Henry Dutton Colt, and Mr. Carter, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

VOL. 13.

HIS Majesty, being at present hindered, by an unhappy Accident, from coming in Person to His Parliament, is pleased to signify to the House of Commons, by Message, what he designed to have spoken to both Houses from the Throne: His Majesty, in the First Year of His Reign, did acquaint the Parliament, That Commissioners were authorized, in Scotland, to treat with such Commissioners as shall be appointed in England, of proper Terms for uniting the Two Kingdoms; and, at the same time, expressed his great Desire of such an Union: His Majesty is fully satisfied, that nothing can contribute more to the present and future Peace, Security, and Happiness, of England and Scotland, than a firm and entire Union betwixt them'; and lie cannot but hope, that, upon a due Consideration of our present Circumstances, there will be found a general Disposition to this Union. His Majesty would esteem it a peculiar Felicity, if, during His Reign, some happy Expedient for making both Kingdoms One might take place; and is therefore extremely desirous, that a Treaty for that Purpose might be set on foot; and does, in the most earnest Manner, recommend this Affair to the Consideration of the iHouse.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Thursday Morning next, take his Majesty's most gracious Message into Consideration.

A Petition of the Poor distressed Prisoners for Debt, in the County Gaol of Leicester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have been a long time in the said Gaol, by reason of their extreme Poverty; where they are ready to starve, for want of Food and Raiment; and are in no way able or likely to be freed from thence, except by the Compassion of the House: And praying, That their deplorable Condition may be taken into Consideration, and they be relieved.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Relief of poor Prisoners for Debt is committed.

to the House, and read; setting forth, That there is a Bill depending in the House for regulating the Frauds and Abuses in the Salt Duties, which is to ascertain the Bushel of Rock and Foreign Salt: That, if the said Bushel should be diminished, it will prevent the Refining of Rock Salt, which is a great Advantage to the Petitioners, and has reduced the Price of White Salt to Half its former Value; and employs a great Number of poor Persons, and Shipping, in conveying the same to many Parts of England; and now is extending its Trade to , and the Baltick Seas: And praying, That the said Bushel may not be diminished ;p and that they may have Debentures allowed for exporting Rock and White Salt upon Affidavit, as now is used; and not be obliged to bring Certificates before they have their Debentures, which will be a great Hindrance and L03S of the said Trade.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of William Bourn, Robert Palmer, and Salt Duties. Thomas Ellams, Masters of Three Fish Barks belonging to the Town and Port of Hastings, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That, in June 1700, the Petitioners took in 30 Weight of Salt at Nerecastle, which they spent in curing

11,000 Cod-fish, caught in the North Seas, and sold at and about Newcastle; of all which they made Affidavits; and hoped, their Bonds, given upon Taking in of the Salt, would have been delivered up to them as usually; but the same is refused them, unless they will pay the Duty of the Salt, which is as much as the Value of the Fish caught in that Voyage: And praying the Reljef of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for regulating the Frauds and Abuses in the Salt Duties is committed.

A Petition of the Mercers, Grocers, Linen and Wool-Trade. len Drapers, Wet and Dry Salters, and Haberdashers, within the Borough of Pontefract, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That a great many Persons have, for several Years,- presumed to use the said , Trades, within the County of York, without serving

Seven Years Apprenticeship, contrary to the Statute, 5° Eliz.; under which Hardships and Discouragements the Petitioners have long laboured: And praying Relief therein.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

SilkSpinning A Petition of the poor distressed Twisters of Silk, Engines. Silver, and Gold, was presented to the House, and read;

setting forth, That the Petitioners are reduced to a most deplorable Condition, through the Use of Engines for the Spinning of Silk, Silver, and Gold; One of which Engines, with One Pair of Hands, being able to work above Twelve Quills of Plate, when the Petitioners cannot work one'single Quill, without employing Five Pair of Hands; which i3 a vast Prejudice to the Petitioners Trade, and is a Means to take Work out of the Hands of the Poor; especially in Cripplegate Parish, where they must want Bread, for want of Employment: And praying, That the Use of the said Engines may be suppressed.

Resolved, That the said Petition be rejected.

A Petition of Joan Bury Widow, Relict of Humphry Bury, late of Collator1, in the County of Devon, Esquire, deceased, on behalf of her Son, an Infant, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in One thousand Six hundred Seventy-five, the said Humphry did settle upon Trustees several Lands and Tenements, Coni Devon, in Tail Male; creating a Trust for Two hundred Years for raising Portions for his younger Sons, and Daughters; and, in One thousand Six hundred Ninety-five, by his last Will, appointed a further Trust for raising One thousand Two hundred Pounds for his Daughters: But, before the said Settlement, the Premises were charged with a Mortgage, whereupon there is now due about Two thousands Pounds: That the said Humphry left One Son Thomas, an Infant, about Ten Years of Age; during whose Infancy the Mortgage-money will much increase; and also Christian, One of his Daughters, who is of Age, is. intitled to receive her Portion: And it will be more for the Advantage of the said Infant, that Part of the Premises be sold for Payment of the said Mortgage and Portion, than to be raised out of the Profits of the said Estate: And praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable Trustees to make Sale of Part of the said Humphry Bury* Estate, for paying off the said Mortgage, and Portion.

A Petition of the Right Honourable Isabella Countess of Roscommon, of the Kingdom of Irelandwas presented to die House, and read; setting forth, That Wentworth Earl of Roscommon, the Petitioners late Husband, deceased, made a Conveyance, by way of Sale and Mortgage, to the Earl of Tyrconnell, of divers Lands in Ireland, which he looked upon only as a Security; and devised the Equity of Redemption thereof to the Petitioner, and her Heirs: That the said Conveyance was made after the Petitioners Marriage; yet she did not join therein, nor do any Act to debar her of her Right to Dower, or by virtue of the said Will; and the Earl of Tyrconnell forfeiting his Interest in the said Estate to his Majesty, the same became vested in the Trustees appointed by the late Act of Resumption, before whom the Petitioner entered her Claim; which they have allowed; and she is in the Receipt of a Third Part of the Profits of the said Estate: But the Countess of Tyrconnell having obtained Leave of this House to bring in a Bill to reverse the OutlawTy against her, she has not only brought in a Bill for that Purpose, but also to establish and put her into the Possession of the said Estate claimed by the Petitioner, without any Regard to the Petitioner's Title thereunto: And praying, That she may be heard, by her Counsel, before the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed, in order that her Right may not be prejudiced by the said Bill.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

And being returned;

Death of King William, and

Address of Condolence.

MR. Secretary Vernon acquainted the House, That the Queen's Majesty, in Council, had commanded Accession of him to acquaart this House, That it hath pleased God to Queen Anne, take to his Mercy our late most Gracious Sovereign King William, about Eight a Clock this Morning: And that the usual Orders were given for proclaiming her Majesty, according as hath been accustomed, at Three a Clock this Afternoon.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to the Queen, to condole with her Majesty upon the sad Occasion of the Death of our late most Gracious Sovereign; and to congratulate the happy Ac-<^ssion of her Majesty to the Throne; and to give her Majesty Assurance of the utmost Assistance of this House to support her Majesty on the Throne, and to maintain her Alliances for preserving the Liberties of Europe, and reducing the exorbitant Power of France: And that this House will effectually maintain the publick Credit of the Nation.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up the said Address.

>Uen Ma- Sir Henry Dutton Colt reported from the Committee, «tares, who were appointed to inspect the Laws relating to the

Woollen Manufacture; and to consider of the best Methods for regulating and improving the same: That they had considered the several Petitions to them referred; and had directed him to report the Matter, as it appeared to them, to the House; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, upon Consideration of the several Petitions touching the Serge and Worsted Weavers, to them referred, do find, That the Matters therein alleged are true; but yet are of Opinion, That the said Trade ought to be free, and not restrained, according to the Prayer, of the said Petitions.

Also, upon Consideration of the several Petitions of the Woolstapiers of London and Southwark, and the Manufacturers of Colchester, complaining of the Abuses committed by several Persons deputed by the Commissioners appointed, by Act of Parliament, to prevent the Exportation of Wool, the Committee do find, That several of the Officers employed by the said Commissioners have been guilty of many corrupt and indirect Practices, to

Vo l. 13.

the great Oppression and Discouragement of the Manufacturers of Wool.

Several Instances of which Abuses appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of the Persons following; viz.

David Picket informed the Committee, That one John Hughes and William Haling did seize Seventeen Bags of Wool in November last, between Six and Seven a Clock at Night, at Butt Wharf, which came from Kingston, and was consigned to a Dealer in Bamaby-street in Southwark; and extorted from the Owner 221, as appeared by a Receipt under the Hafed of the said Wm. Haling*

Bay, Whiting said, He went with Picket to the said Haling, in order to get the Wool discharged: And Haling demanded Twenty-one Guineas for the same; which was paid him: But Hughes, hearing thereof, was very angry that the Wool should be discharged for that Sum; and refused at first to consent to it.

Tho. Child said, That he paid Forty Shillings for the Reckoning at the time when the Wool was discharged.

William Haling owned before the Committee, the Receipt of the One-and-twenty Guineas; but said, He acted by the Direction of Hughes, who received above Six Pounds of that Money: And that Mr. Jones received 10$. Mr. Haines 5 s. and the rest was spent in Charges about the Seizure.

John Hughes was called in; and produced his Deputation from the Commissioners: And said, That he acted pursuant to the Act of Parliament for preventing the Exportation of Wool: That the said Wool was seized at Ten a Clock at Night, and therefore a lawful Seizure: Said, That he was not concerned in making the Agreement about the Discharge of the said Woof neither did he receive the Twenty-one Guineas; but owned, that William Haling paid him 5 /. Part thereof.

Mr. John Denton informed the Committee, That, in November last, he had a great Quantity of Wool seized at Arundell in Sussex, in the Carrier's Hands, w'hich was entered in the King's Books at the Port of Arundell: And John Dean, the said Mr. Denton's Factor, entered into a Bond of 2,000l. to the King, that the said Wool should not be transported, but lie brought to London; notwithstanding which, one Enoch Hurley, Cha. Jones and Tho. Brains, seized the same in the King's Officers Hands: And they offered to release it, if Mr. Denton would give them 30/.; but, he refusing the same, the Wool is still detained, to his great Damage: That he has often demanded his Wool; and offered to go to a Tryal for the same in the Court of Exchequer; which they promised to do, but never gave him any Notice of a Tryal; and have often offered to deliver up the said Wool, if he would give them Money.

Mr. Thomas Brayne, one of the Officers, insisted upon the Legality of the Seizure; and said, The Officers are ready and willing to try the same with Mr. Denton in the Exchequer.

Sam. Lewin Esquire said, That he had Seven Packs of Wool seized in the Middle of Cheapside, in November last, about Six a Clock in the Evening, going to the King's Arms at Holboum- Bridge, to Froom Carrier in Somersetshire: The said Wool was seized by Spencer and Bland, whose Deputations have been taken from them for several corrupt Practices and Abuses by them committed in several Parts of England.

Mrs. Rainer said, That she had Three Packs of Wool seized in Holbome going to Leadenhall Market, by Spicer and Webster, who extorted from her 30$. for the Discharge of her Wool.

Richard Peak said, That he had Four Packs of Wool seized in Holborne, going to leadenhall Market, by the said Spicer and Webster, who extorted from him 40 s.

Richard Middleton said, That he had Four Packs of Wool seized by the said Spicer and Webster*, at Charing-cross, at Twelve a Clock at Noon, which was going to Leadenhall, Market and they extorted from him 30$. for the Discharge thereof.

784 9° Mar tit.

- Woollen Ma- Abraham Vole, the Colchester Carrier, said, That, in n urtures. December last was Twelvemonth, one Jones and White seized One-and-twenty Bags of Wool at his own Door at Colchester; and that he paid Mr. and Jones 301.

to discharge the same: That it was near Ten a Clock at Night before he came in with his Waggon, by reason of an Accident which happened upon the Road with his Horses.

Mr. Brayne said, As to the said Twenty-one Bags of Wool, the same was seized at Ten a Clock at Night, and that it was a lawful Seizure; and a Writ of Appraisement was issued out according to Law: That several Gentlemen attended the Lord Chief Baron, to complain of this Seizure; and his Lordship ordered a new Writ of Appraisement: And accordingly the Wool*was appraised at 30 /. as a Dividend to the Officers that seized the same; which Appraisement was returned, and the Money paid to the Officer, according to Law.

Abra. Vole, the Colchester Carrier, said, That he hath several times given to one Francis Sutton .5 s. at a time, to suffer his Waggon to go unmolested; and, if the Carriers refuse to give them Money, then their Waggons are stopped, till such time as the Carriers will comply with their unreaspnable Demands.

Rich. Arnold, a Carrier, said, That very often the Carriers, by reason of Accidents upon the Road, either by breaking of their Waggons, or their Horses dying, or otherwise disabled, upon the Road, are forced to be out with their Waggons beyond the Hours limited by Act of Parliament for their carrying of Wool; and, when any Accident of that Nature happens, several Persons, pretending to be Officers, do seize their Wool, and extort Money from them.

Nathanael Lawrence Esquire, of Colchester, said, That several Persons, pretending to be Officers, do extort great Sums of Money from the Traders, who cannot carry their Wool to the Spinners, to be worked up, but immediately it is seized, under Pretence of exporting the same: That he had a Parcel of Wool seized coming from Stourbridge Fair, and he was forced to pay 41, to get the same discharged:

That he has committed some of these pretended Officers to Goal, for taking Money from Persons, in order to release Wool.

John Hughes, one of the Officers, said, That there are great Quantities of Wool bought up at Stourbridge Fair, and, under(pretence of being carried to Ipswich, and other trading Places, is conveyed away to France; and that several Persons are now under Prosecution for the same.

That there were several Proposals offered to the Committee, to prevent the Exportation of Wool; and, amongst others, one from Mr. John Purchase, a Wool-merchant, who proposed a general Registry ol all Wool throughout the Kingdom.:

And the Committee, having considered of the same, came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the most effectual Way to prevent the Exportation of Wrool, is, to establish a general Register of all Wool that shall be grown in this Kingdom.

That the Committee also, upon Consideration of the Proposal of the Woolstaplers of London and Southwark, came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opiiiion of this Committee, That one Way to prevent the Exportation of Wool, is, to prohibit all Wool from being water-borne on any Rivers leading to the Sea.

Resolved, That, &c. That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill pursuant to these Resolutions.

The First Resolution being read a Second time;

And the Question being put. That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the most effectual Way to prevent the Exportation of Wool, is, to establish a general Registry of all Wool that shall be grown in this Kingdom;

It passed in the Negative.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That one Way to prevent the Exportation of Wool, is, to prohibit all Wool from being water-borne on any Rivers leading to the Sea;

It passed in the Negative.

Colonel Granville reported from the Committee ap- Address of pointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to her Condolence. Majesty, That they had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mast gracious Sovereign,

WE, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons in Parliament assembled, having a deep and true'Sense of the great Loss the Nation has sustained by the Death of our late Sovereign Lord King William the Third, of glorious Memory, who, under God, was our Deliverer from Popery and Slavery, humbly crave Leave to condole with Your Majesty, and express our Sorrow on this sad Occasion.

Your Majesty's Accession to the Throne, which we most heartily congratulate, and your known Zeal for our Religion, and the Government, as by Law established, gives us a certain Prospect of future Happiness; moderates our Grief; and engages us unanimously to assure Your Majesty, That we will, to the utmost, assist and support Your Majesty on that Throne where God has placed You, against the pretended Prince of Wales, and all Your Enemies:

And, since nothing can conduce more to the Honour and Safety of Your Majesty, and Your Kingdoms, than maintaining inviolable such Alliances as have been made with the Emperor, the States General of the United Provinces, and other Potentates, for preserving the Liberties of Europe, and reducing the exorbitant Power of France, we do assure Your Majesty, That we are firmly resolved, to the utmost of our Power, to enable Your Majesty to prosecute that glorious Design: And, that all Your Subjects may rest in a full Assurance of Happiness under Your Majesty's Reign, we will maintain the Succession of the Crown, according to the Limitation in the several Acts of Settlement; and effectually provide for, and make good the public Credit of the Nation.

The said Address being read a Second time;

The several Amendments following, were proposed to be made therein; viz.

Alter " made," to insert " or that her Majesty shall " think fit to make ;"

And, after " Crown," to insert " in the Protestant " Line:"

And the same were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House dothiagree u-ith. the Committee in the said Address, so amended; which is as followeth; viz.

Sir RowlandGwyn, according to Order, reported, from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the City of Norwich; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were ftad; and are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Thomas Havers Esquire, One of the Sheriffs of Norwich; and also upon the Petition of Peter Thackei* Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Robert Davy Esquire, to serve for the said City of Norwich:

That the First thing the Committee proceeded on, was, the Right of Election: And the Right not being controverted either by the Petitioner or the Sitting Member; but allowed to be as in the following Resolution; the Committee for the better Settling of the Right came to this Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of electing Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Norwich is in the Freeholders, and such Freemen only of the said City as are entered in the Books, and do not receive Alms or Charity.

That, as to the Matter of the Return, upon Inspection of the Record, it appeared to be thus:

That there are Two Sheriffs of Norwich: The present Sheriffs are, Mr. Nall, and Mr. Haiers the Petitioner:

I he M rit was delivered to Mr. Havers, who afterwards delivered it over to Mr. Nall.

That it was admitted, That Mr. being an

2

Attorney, had all along done the Business of the Under Sheriff as well for himself as Mr. Havers the other Sheriff: That in this Case, Mr. Nall signed the Indenture, by which the Return was made; and Mr. Havers refused to sign it; and that Mr. Nall, as is usual for Under Sheriffs, subscribed Mr. Havers' Name, as well as his own, to the Indorsement of the Writ; importing, That the Execution of the Writ appeared by the said Indenture annexed; and then carried the same, and filed it with the Clerk of the Crown: That Mr. Havers, being not satisfied with the Return of Mr. Davy, brought up with him an Indenture; signed by several Inhabitants, and himself; importing the Return of Mr. Clark, and Mr. Thacker; and, after the Writ so returned by Mr. Nall had been filed, offered the same to the Clerk of the Crown, to be affixed to the Writ? to make a double Return; but the Clerk of the Crown, having had a perfect Return before, did not think fit to annex the same to the Writ:

But that the Matter chiefly in Difference between the Parties, in relation to the Petition of Mr. Havers, was about the Declaring of the Election, and refusing a Scrutiny:

And, to that, Mr. Havers' Counsel called several

Witnesses:

Mr. Matthew Coates said, He saw the Books sealed up by both the Sheriffs, as he believes, in order to a Scrutiny.

Mr. Edxo. Lock said, That, the Day after the Election, he was desired to go along with Mr. Sheriff Havers, to open the Books; and when they came to Mr. Sheriff Nall's House, they found the Books open.

Mr. John fViggot, Mr. Bernard Tooley, Mr. Thomas Lombe: The Substance of whose Evidence was; That the Election was on Wednesday the 26th of November last: That the Poll being cast up the next Day, there was a Scrutiny demanded, and consented to, by all Persons: That, on Friday, when they met in the Chamber,

to proceed in the Scrutiny, a Dispute arose about the adding one Cartwright to Mr. Davy's Poll; and thereupon

Sheriff Nall said, He would declare Mr. Davy to be duly lected; which Mr. Havers protested against: That, afterwards, Mr. Sheriff Nall, and Mr. Havers, went into the Court, and Mr. Sheriff Nall declared Mr. Clark and Mr. Davy duly elected: That Mr. Sheriff , though in Court, did not give his Assent to such Declaration; but disagreed to it; yet, notwithstanding, Mr. Sheriff Nall proceeded to prepare, and, with several others, to sign an Indenture for the Return of Mr. Clai'k and Mr. Davy; and offered the same to Mr. Sheriff Havers to sign; which Mr. Havers refused to sign.

And, upon this Fact, Mr. Thacker's Counsel argued. That the Election w as not well declared, nor the Return well made.

That the Question, as to Cartwright, was, Whether he came soon enough to be polled: And, as to that; Mr. Havers' Counsel called,

Mr. Sam. Crombe: Who gave an Account, That there was appointed a distinct Place, and a Bool:, for the taking each Candidate's Poll: That it was agreed, for the more certain concluding the Poll at the several Books, at the same time a certain Signal should be given for the shutting up the Books: That, an Hour and more before the Books were shut up, a Proclamation was made for all Persons to come and poll within an Hour: That they set their Watches; and that the Books were not shut up till 2 or 3 Minutes after the Hour expired; and, after the Books were shut up, Mr. Cartwright came to Mr. Davy's Poll, and desired to be polled for him:

That then Air. Thacker's Counsel, who were the same Persons retained by Air. Havers, proceeded to the Merits of the Election: And Air. s Counsel

insisted, That their Client had the Majority of qualified Votes.

Poll at the last Election; and said. That he, and the senior Bailiff, had equal Power; and that the Precept for this Election was delivered to him, and he gave a Receipt for it; and that he himself proclaimed the Day of this last Election; and his Partner joined with him.

That it was insisted by Sir Cha. Hedges' Counsel, That some indirect Practices had been used to gain Votes for Mr. BaintonAnd they examined some Witnesses:

77/o. Fowler gave an Account, That Stephen Blake, One of the Voters for Mr. Bainton, w'as at London at the time of the Dissolution, and came home to Caine on Wednesday before the Election: That he did not stay at home; but went to Mr. Haskins's, who was the Steward that returned Mr. Bainton, and kept a Publick-house; and there was kept by Force: He acknowledged he had a Warrant to arrest the said Blake; but, he said, Weeks the Attorney had promised him he should not be arrested till the Election was over: Fowler said also, That Haskins solicited Votes for Mr. Bainton:

He also said, that, upon Discourse with Walter Dole-man, and another Man, who was a Carpenter, before the Election preceding this last, they declared, They would not be for Mr. Bainton, but on account that he Would get their Debts paid, which were owing from a Kinsman of Mr. Bainton s: And before th e

Dissolution of last Parliament, said, He had received 50 /. the Remainder of his Debt.

Tun. Seager said, That, after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, Blake said, He would be for Sir Charles Hedges, and make what Interest he could for him.

Rich.Seager said, That, since the Dissolution of the last Parliament, he went to Walter Doleman, and desired his Vote for Mr. Chivers; and Dolcman answered,

That Mr. Bainton had paid him all his Money, and he Would be for him: That he was invited by Mr. Haskins, on the Election-day, to Dinner; and told, It should Cost him nothing: And that Mr. Bainton was there upon several Days.

John Laiidrick said, That, the Election before this Mr. Haskins bid him look into a Paper in the Window, and there was Ten Guineas; and, if he would vote for Mr. Bainton, he should have them: He said, He did see Guineas there; but could not tell how many.

That it appeared also, That Blake was, after he came down, at Normans, One of Mr. Bainton s Voters, at the drinking a Bowl of Punch.

That the Counsel for Mr. Bainton insisted, That the Returns had been all along made under the Common Seal: And they called some Witnesses:

Mr. Haskins said, That he had known 40 Years, and Four or Five Elections; and that the Returns were always made by the senior Steward: That Blake, when he came from London, went first to his own House on the Wednesday; but, hearing the re were Writs out against him, sent to him the next Day, to advise with him; and, on the next Day, being Friday, came to his House, to be safe: That there was 100 /. Action against him: That Mr. Bainton s Friends, who came to see him, paid their Club; and Blake himself paid for what he had at his House:

He said, That the Town have 150?. at Interest, which Interest is given among poor Tradesmen; and that one Landrick, who voted for Sir Cha. Hedges, received some of that Money; but he could not say it was the last Year.

Blake himself, being examined, said, He was, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday Nights at Haskins's, and paid for what he had: He said, There was no Force upon him; but he understood there was a Writ against him at Sir

IJungerfords Suit; and was at Mr. Haskins', because he was afraid of an Arrest: And denied he promised to be for Sir Charles Hedges before he went down: lie said,

The Head Stewards commonly made the Return, and, in the Town-business, had a casting Voice.

That they produced the Precept the last Election, which was to the Steward in the single Number: And the Under Sheriff said, The Reason was, he did not know, There were two Stewards.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Charles Hedges is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Caine, in the County of Wilts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Echo. Bainton Esquire is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Caine.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the said Election for the Borough of Caine is a void Election.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ, for the electing a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Caine, in the County of in

the place of Sir Charles Hedges Knight, and Edward Bainton Esquire; whose Election, upon their double Return, is declared to be void.

Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read iu his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow;

viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of several Witnesses, That Mendez de Breta is the Daughter of Jacob Mendez de , a Jew Merchant, Jiving in the Parish of St. Andrew Under shaft; and that, upon her being baptized and converted to the Christian Faith, the said Jacob her Father disowns her for his Child, and refuses to allow her any Maintenance; so that the Parish of St. Andrew Undershaft, in Compassion to her deplorable Condition, have, since her embracing the Christian Faith, allowed her a Maintenance, suitable to her Quality and Degree.

To prove which, several Persons of very good Repute, Inhabitants of the said Parish of St. Andrew and the other Parishes in the Petition mentioned, were examined; viz.

Maty Mendez de Breta said, That she is about Eighteen Years of Age, and was born at Scvill in and that

Jacob Mendez de Breta, her Father, lived with her Mother Eleven Years as her Husband, and had several other Children by her said Mother: That, soon after her Father came into England, he sent for her from Spain, and always

owned her for his Child; and that he kept her in very decent Habit, provided plentifully for her, sent her to the Dancing School, and allowed her an Education suitable to his Degree and Quality: That she, being convinced of her Error by living in the Jewish Religion, hath lately embraced the Christian Faith; and was, about the Month of May last, baptized by Mr. Tiwrold, a Minister of the Church of England; since which, her Father, Mr. Jacob Mendez de Breta, disowns her for his Child; and now, and for some time past, refuses to allow her any Maintenance; and that she never was disowned till after her Conversion:

That, being afraid of her Father's Anger, she applied herself to Sir 1 'ha.Abney, then Lord Mayor of London, for Protection; who ordered the Churchwardens of St. Andrew Undershaft to provide for her; and that she has been ever since very decently maintained at the Charge of the said Parish:

That her said Father, refusing to allow her a Maintenance, was bound over to the Sessions at Guildhall; and there the Justices made an Order for him to allow her 20 a Week for her Maintenance; but the said Order was set aside by the Court of King's Rend), as she is informed.

Mr. Shelton, of St.James Duke's Place, said, That he is a near Neighbour to the said Mr. Jacob Mendez de Breta; and has known the said Mary his Daughter from a Child: That she was always cloathed very well, like a Merchant's Daughter; and ever taken, esteemed, and called, as his Daughter.

Mr. FItoroid,a Minister of the Church of England,

said, That, after he had examined the said Mary Mendez de Breta, and being fully convinced of the Sincerity of her Conversion, did, by Direction of the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, baptize her; and that, as he was

performing his Function, a Person, unknown to him, but supposed to be a Jew by his Complexion, came into the Church, and, observing what was done, and being enraged thereat, sw ore and cursed, and wished the Church might fall, and they.. buried in the Ruins thereof: Whereupon Endeavours were made to apprehend him; but he made his Escape.

Mr. Mason, of St. Andrew Undershaft, at whose House the said Mary Mendez de Breta hath lodged ever since she hath been baptized, said, That the said Mary is a Person of a modest Behaviour, and, as he verily believes, a devout Christian; and that she hath constantly attended upon Divine Service.

Mr. Franshaw, a very noted Jew, being examined concerning the Temper and Disposition of the said Jacob Mendez de Breta, said, That he is a very cholerick and troublesome Person.

Vol. 13.

Mr. Adams said, That Mary Mendez de Breta was arrested some time since for some Stuff Cloaths that she had before she came from her Father, in order to oppress her, as he believes, by the Contrivance of her said Father, by reason of her Conversion.

Mr. JViggins said, That there was great Precaution used to prevent Mr. Jacob Mendez de s seizing the said Mary his Daughter; which, they feared, was intended, in order to send her beyond Sea, or otherwise misuse her.

Mrs. Duncombe said, That she hath been very conversant in Mr. Jacob de Mendez' Family for Eleven Years past; and that the said Mary was owned, esteemed, and ever taken, as his Daughter.

Mrs. Micclethwaite declared to the same Effect; and that she hath seen the said Mary cloathed as a Merchant's Daughter.

It appeared also to the Committee, by the Parish Books, That the said Mary was, from time to time, inserted therein; and that her. said Father paid to the Poll Tax for her, as his Daughter.

Mr. Bates said, That Mr. Jacob Mendez de Breta, the very last Year, was a Collector of the Tax for Births and Burials; and that, in the same Book that the said Jacob was so nominated a Collector, he was therein charged for his said Daughter.

John Rogers Gentleman produced the Book of the Capitation Tax; wherein the said Jacob Mendez de Breta was assessed for 2,oooo/.; and that, in the said Parish of St. Andrew Undershaft, the said Jacob Mendez is esteemed a Person w orth 5 or 6,000 /. at least.

Mr. Jacob Mendez de Breta, being present, was admitted to answer to the Charge against him; and being asked by the Committee, Whether the said Maty was his Daughter, said. He could not tell: That he never cohabited with the said Maty's Mother; nor ever had any other Wife than she he now has.

The said Jacob Mendez, being also asked, Whether the said Mary Mendez had any Brothers or Sisters, said, He knew not; but said, That the said Mary, with Two or Three more Children, were laid at his Door; and that he took them in, and maintained them, purely out of Charity.

The said Mr. Mendez de Breta, being further asked. Flow became to own her for his Daughter, and suffer her to be entered in the Parish Books as such, said, That he never owned her for his Daughter; but used her as his Servant: That she never sat at Table with him; nor ever allowed her any other Cloaths but such as he allowed his other Servants: That if she was entered in the Poll or Capitation Tax, as his Daughter, it was without his Know ledge or Consent.

To prove which, he called several Witnesses; vis.

Judith Pacheca, a Jew, and Slave to Mr. Mendez de Breta, said, She had lived with him 14 Years as his Slave: That the said Mrs. Mary Mendez came to her Master's in Portugal a Year after he was married; and she always looked upon the said Mary Mendez as a Servant; and the said Mary lay with her, and wore such Cloaths as she did; and used to call Mr. Jacob Mendez Master; and there was no Difference made between the said Mary and the rest of the Servants.

Mary Marwick said, That she had known Mr. Jacob Mendez de Breta several Years; and used to call Mr. Jacob Mendez Master: That she was alw ays looked upon as a Servant; and never sat at Table with Mr. Mendez, but with the other Servants.

Eliz.Chichester said to the same Effect.

But it appeared to the Committee, by the Testimony of Mr. Joseph Bagshaw, and several of the chief Inhabitants of the Parish of St. Andrew Undershaft, That the said Maty Warwick was a Person of very ill Repute, and of scandalous Life and Conversation

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions; viz.

A Petition of the Agents, Planters, and Merchants, concerned in, and trading to, the Island of Barbadoes, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That there is a Duty of Four and an Half per Centum on the Commodities of the said Island, exported thence; which was granted by an Act of the said Island in September 1663, for the Reparation and Building of Fortifications, and defraying all other public Charges incident to the Government there; which has been collected by Officers appointed by the Commissioners of the Customs in England, and applied to other Uses; whereby the Fortifications are run very much out of Repair, and other publick necessary Works are unbuilt, and their Magazine unprovided; so that, in case of a War, the said Island, and all other the Sugar Plantations to Windward of Jamaica, would be in Danger of being lost, if an Enemy should attack it; which would be a vast Loss to England: And praying, That the said Duty of Four and an Half per Centum may be applied to the Uses for which it was given, in order to the Defence and Security of the said Island.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, to be considered by the House.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Seven Years, and was made free by Popplewell.

John Leary said, That John Stevenson and Thomas Rylcy each served Seven Years to the same Master, within Two Doors of him:

That George Popplewell gave Seven Pounds for his Freedom:

That John Colton, William Thompson, and John Goodall, are the eldest Sons of Freemen; but he could not say they were born after their Fathers were made free:

That Thomas Colton and Steph. Hodgkin served Seven Years to their respective Fathers:

That William Woodhead served Seven Years to one Moody, a Butcher.

Wm. Smith said, That John Colton, Thompson, John Goodall, Tho. Soresby, were the eldest Sons of Free-pen; but could not say whether their Fathers were free before their Sons were born.

That Thomas Calton, Rich. Bonefont, Step.

William Goodall, William Woodhead, served in the Town as Apprentices; but they could not say whether they 'were bound by Indentures.

That they also proved by a Witness, That Martin Calton demanded his Freedom several Years:

That John Hodgkin, John Goodall, Tho. Bonefont, Tho. Soresby, John Calton, Tho. Calton, Sav'd Atkinson, Rich Bony font, John Stevenson, Steph. Hodgkin, Tho, Ryley, Wm. Goodall, Tho. Clark, William

Thompson, had demanded their Freedoms.

That, as to their offering to poll, the Petitioners Counsel called

William Nicholls: Who said, That John Leary, Geo. Popplewell, Martin Calton, John Calton, John Hodgkin, Wm. Thompson, Tho. Bonefont, John , John Colton, Tho. Calton, Sam. Atkinson, Rich. John

Stevenson, Steph. Hodgkin, Tho. Riley, Win. Goodall, Tho. Clark, William Woodhead, offered to poll for Sir Willoughby Hickman and Mr. Levinz, and were refused: And Thomas Soresby, who would have polled for Sir Willoughby Hickman and Mr. Thornhagh, was also re-

fused.

That the Petitioners Counsel also insisted, That the Sitting Members voted for themselves.

To which it was answered, That Sir Willoughby Hickman voted for himself.

That the Sitting Members Counsel also insisted, That they should take off some of the Petitioners Votes, on account of Charity:

That Mr. Popplewell had no Right to make any free, being himself disfranchised:

And that the Persons, said to have a Right, had not demanded their Freedoms at a proper Time:

And called several Witnesses:

James Mason said, That William Buttry had received 2 s.for several Years, and particularly the last Year, of Wharton's Charity:

That Martin Calton received of Clark's Charity: He said, He did not see it paid; but he finds his Name entered in the Book of the Account of Wharton's Charity.

William Booth said. That William Buttry had 2 s. a Year paid him several Years: That he had seen it given to his Wife the last Year but one.

John Hodson said, That, about a Week before the Election, Mr. Nicholls came to him, and desired his Vote for Sir Willoughby Hickman; and Mr. Levinz should help him to a Place of 20 or 30/. a Year; and Mr., Levinz should give him some Money: And Mr. Nicholls, at his going away, gave him a Crown.

Wm. Jessopsaid, John Johnsons Father is not free; and he was bound to one that was not free.

Wm.Skelton said, That John Leary's Father was asked to swear that his Son was made free; and lie refused to do it.

John Wallier said, He heard Martin Calton say, He could have his Freedom if he would; but he would vote for Parliament-men without it; and he would save hi* Money to buy Cloaths.

Skelton said, That John Calton did not serve a Freeman; but was put to one of the Waits of the Town, who died after Carletonhad been with him Two Years.

Savill Atkinson's Indenture of Apprenticeship to Tho. Shelton was produced, dated 15 October 166S; and, by Certificate, it appeared, that the said Shelton was buried 27 January 1672: But it was testified, on behalf of the Petitioners, That there was no other of that Trade in Town:

That, as to John Stevenson, it was testified, That, though he was Apprentice to one Calton, a Shoemaker, yet lie served the Huntington Carrier; but it w as by ton's Consent.

Edw. Jackson said, He was Bailiff last Year; and that Tho. Riley never demanded his Freedom of him.

Wm. Booth said, That Thomas Riley produced a Pair of Indentures, dated in \66o; but the Date was rased, and made 1670:

That Mr. Popplewell was disfranchised; and his Disfranchisement, 1 lth April 1699, w as read; which was by the Bailiffs and Aldermen subscribing that Disfranchisement.

John Reynolds said, That the Freemen, whereof Evidence was given that they demanded their Freedom, came to an improper Court; the Court they applied to being a Court Baron.

Mr. Serjeant Selby insisted, That Popplewell was not w'ell disfranchised; for such an Act ought to be by the Corporation.

Mary Cozens said, That Mrs. Moody sent for her on Wednesday before the Election, and desired her Husband's Vote for 'Six Willoughby Hickman, and Mr.; and

said, She would lay down 71, and she the said Cozens should take it up: That Cozens told her Husband; who said, He would be a Freeman: And afterwards she told Mrs. Moody of it; who said, If she could prevail with her Hftsband, she should have 10/. before they went into the Hall to give their Votes.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to these Resolutions;
