Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Tho. White Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of East Retford.

Sir John Bolles reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for the rebuilding, and keeping in good Repair, the Pier of the Town and Port of Whitby, in the North Riding in the County of York, was committed, That they had made several Amendments to the Bill; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were once read.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned until Friday Morning next.

A Petition of the poor Prisoners for Debt in the Sheriff's Ward for the County of Devon, in behalf of themselves, and all other suffering Brethren, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners have, for several Years, languished in Prison, being unable to pay their Debts; and having nothing to subsist on, if the Charity of well-dispo6ed Christians should fail, they must inevitably starve, if not relieved by the House: And praying, That the House will take their deplorable Condition into their Consideration, and give them some Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Relief of poor Prisoners for Debt is committed, be made.

A Petition of Arthur Bush and Peter Partington, in behalf of the Protestant Purchasers and Improvers, under the Earl of Athlone, on the Estate of the late Earl of Limerick, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners are employed by the said Purchasers and Improvers, and conceive the Bill depending in the House for the Relief of Maria Eufemia Countess of Limerick, and Thomas Earl of Limerick, with relation to the Irish Forfeitures, is greatly injurious to the said Purchasers and Improvers, and contrary to the Intention of the House: And praying, That they may have such Provision made in the said Bill, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Petition be referred to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Sir Henry Dutton Colt reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for Sale of Part of the Estate of Stephen Soame Gentleman, and Dorothy his Wife, and for applying the Money raised thereby for the Payment of his Debts, and for the Portions of Mary Soame and William Scame, Two of his younger Children, was committed, That they had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consents to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee; and that the Committee had made several Amendments to the Bill; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be'Ingrossed.

Mr. Harley, according to Order, reported, from the

Committee appointed to examine into the Matter of the Complaint of a great Abuse committed in her Majesty's Brewhouse St. Catharine's, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

That the Committee had examined into the Matter; and find it to be as followeth; viz.

Charlesllore informed the Committee, That he had been a labouring Servant in the said Brewhouse about Five Years, from which he was discharged in January last was Twelvemonth: And that, in June last, he acquainted an Officer of the Excise, that there was great Abuse committed at the said Brewhouse, by taking Ten, Twelve, or more Barrels, of the First Worts, out of every Brewing of Sea Beer; which, in Winter, was generally Four times a Week, and, in Summer once a Fortnight, or Month, as Occasion required: That those Worts were taken publickly by the Servants of the Brewhouse, who are Sixteen or Seventeen in Number; their Allowance, as they say, being a Gallon or Twoa-piece per Day, which they have conveyed into their particular Cellars; and thinks it is impossible they should drink so much Beer, though he cannot say they sold it: And said, it was always the Custom for the Servants to drink the Worts, but the Bakers drank only the common Sea Beer:

That he has cleansed Ten or Twelve Barrels of the First Worts of a Brewing several times, of Sea Beer, by the Order of U'iltiam Marshall, the Head Brewer there, as the Servants Btcr, which was carried into their several secret Places; which the Excise Officers never found out, till I lore told them: But when they brewed Petty Warrant Beer, there was not taken above a Firkin or Two out of a Brewing:

That he has heard Pursers say, They would sell the Kings Beer; which though he cannot say they did, yet John Tomkins, a Lighterman, and Tho. , Waterman,

who used to carry the Beer on board the King's Ships, have returned the empty Casks the same Tide: And said, That he never informed the Commissioners of the Victualling of die Matters aforesaid; but told ouc Mr. Dernriston, an Excise Officer, of it; who laid it before the Commissioners of Excise; where I lore had sworn it.

Mr. Edw. Denniston,a Surveyor General of the Excise,

said, That, long before he knew , the Informant was a Surveyor of the Division within which the said Brewhouse stands-; and, making his Surveys, he found a great Disproportion of the Worts between the Backs and the Tons; and ordered the Excise Officers to be watchful of the Frauds he suspected; acquainting the Commissioners of the Excise, from time to time, of such Disproportion; of which he had made an Entry, the Seventh of February One thousand Seven hundred, in his Leidger: That it must proceed from some unfair Practice of the Servants, there being missed One hundred Twenty-nine Barrels and Two Firkins in the F'ive Brewings following; viz.

All Strong Beer, and in Quality, worth 183. or 20 3* per Barrel; Twenty-six of them being new, and One Guile, in the Opinion of all the other Officers to his Assistance, who tasted and tried the same:

But that there was in Mr. King's Cellar, about Four Barrels of common Brewers Beer, of 40 s. per Barrel; a Copy of which Report he delivered to the Commissioners for Victualling:

That there is a continual Miss of the Worts, as appears by their Leidger-books: And that they keep as exact Accounts of the King's Brewhouses, as of the common Brewers; and can charge them, if... . could prove Salts of the Drink; which the Commissioners of Excise could not do: But the Servants of the said Brewhouse still continue the same Practice; notwithstanding that he went, by Order of the Board of Excise, and acquainted the Commissioners of the Victualling the rewith:

That he was ordered, on the Fifth of August last, to go to the Commissioners of the Victualling, for a List of the Servants Names belonging to the said Brew house j which he had: And they attended the Commissioners of Excise; and were examined accordingly:

That this Want of Worts is, when they brew Sea Beer; for, when they brew Petty Warrant Beer, it then answers to a F irkin; it being so small, that it is not w orth the Servants while to run it; the Six last Brewings in Petty Warrant being such; and then all answered very well: That Captain Francis Davison told him, He could buy. Beer cheaper at the King's Brewhouse, by 183. or 193. per Tun, than either at Newcastle or London: And that he, at that time, had a Tun and a Half on board, which cost him but 4.53.

Betij. Wilks, Brewer, said, That he deals with the Danes

and Swedes for Beer: And the Masters of Ships have bought Three and Four TunS at a time of the King's Beer; some of the Butts were emptied into the Master's own. Casks, and others were sold, with the King's Casks, for Half the Value: And asking the Master how he got the Beer, whether from the King's Brewhouse, or of a Purser, he refused to tell him: Ajnd that the Informant said, He had lost near 3001, a Year in his Trade by this Practice.

To answer this Complaint;

Mr. Moor, the Clerk, William Marshall, the Brewer, and other Servants of the Brewhouse, attended the Committee; and were examined: And claiming a Right to take of the First Worts for their own drinking; denying any Sale, or other Embezzlement of the Beer; or that M r. Denniston w as ever denied Leave to search, or had any ill Language from them, but the Keys as soon as he 0 jU . called

and sometimes hut a Barrel; and that the Beer is so bitter, that they must keep it a Month or Six Weeks before they can think it: And that the Servants Allowance continues all the Year round; though, in the Summer they brew but once a Fortnight, or once a Month, as there is Need.

Marshall &du\, That if there were Thirty-two Barrels of l>e- r found by Mr. Denin the Places aforesaid, yet some of them were not full; and that they were of several Guiles; particularly Six Barrels behind tire Third Square, which was for the Bakers drinking, and was but common Sea Beer; and Two other Barrels, to make up the Mens Complement, wereof several Brewings:

1 hat he, hearing that Complaint was made to the Commissioners of Excise, touching Embezzlements of the Beer at the said Brewhouse, went to them, desiring that they would send their Officers to see the Beer drawn off tire Backs into the Tuns, as often as they pleased, and observe how they answered one another; but no Officer came for that Purpose, as he knows of.

John Dolly said, That he had been a Servant in the said Brewhouse near Eleven Years; And tlratwhen Mr. Dot niston searched the House, there were Six or Eight of the Barrels discovered by him, then working, which wereof the Second or 'third Wort, for the Bakers Use: And that, when they brew but seldom, they take more than when they brew Three or Four times a Week; and never took above Three Barrels and an Half at a time, and sometimes but a Barrel in a Week.

The Commissioners of Excise acquainted the Committee, That they, having received an Account of great Abuses committed in the King's Brewhouse, ordered Edw. Den niston to endeavour to discover the same: That, upon the Report made to them by they sent him to

acquaint the Commissioners of the Victualling with it; and desired them to send their Servants to the Excise Office, to be examined: But there being no proof of any Sale, they examined no further, but ordered to acquaint the Commissioners of Victualling the rewith.

That the Commissioners of the Victualling Office acquainted the Committee, That, upon the Information given them by Din niston, they inquired into the Matter: And said, They did what they could to detect the said Fraud; and, in order thereunto, examined the Servants of the Brewhouse touching the same: Who denied the taking away any Worts but u hat was for the Use of the Servants, as had been usually practised: That they sent their Officers to examine the Beer found by Mr. Denniston; who wereof ()|)inion, That the said Beer was not worth above i tf or l 2 s. per Barrel: That he never gave them any further Account of the same: That the Commissioners desired Dennistto be present when they examined the Servants of tire Brewhouse; but that he was not there, though tlicy gave him all possible Encouragement to find out any Abuse; and desired him to inform then: if lie found any, which he promised to do: And further said, That it is the Duty of the Clerk of the Brewhouse, to see that the Drink be of its full Strength.

Mr. Mitchell, Secretary to the Victualling Office, said, That Mr. Denniston was at the Victualling Office that Day the Commissioners examined the Servants of the Brew-house; but Denniston went away, saying, He did not think it proper for him to stay, the Commissioners of Excise intending to examine the Matter: And that he desired Denniston to give the Victuallers an Account of the same; but knows not that he came again, but for a List of the Servants, or that he was ever summoned after:

That Mitchell, and others, tasted the Beer the same Day that Denniston complained; and it seemed to them to be l o or 12 s. Beer; and it was all the same as be tasted, as the Servants informed.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That there hath been a great Abuse committed in her Majesty's Brewhouse at St. Catharines, by drawing off the First Worts; to the Defrauding of her Majesty, and Prejudice of the Seamen.

MR. Clayton, according to Order, reported, from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants trading to the English Plantations in America was deferred, the Matter, as it appeared, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That they had examined the Matter thereof; and find the same, upon Information of several Witnesses, to be as followeth:

Mr. Perry, Merchant, said, That there are many ill Persons about Town, who make it their Business to be troublesome to Merchants, and Masters of Vessels, trading to the Plantations, upon Pretence of procuring them Servants and Workmen to be transported thither: And although such Servants and Workmen have sworn before a Justice of Peace, that they are npt married, nor any other Person's Servant; and have bound themselves at a certain Office, for that Purpose, called the Plantation Office; yet, afterwards, the Merchants, and Masters of Vessels, have been often prosecuted as Persons that have trepanned, or enticed away, such Servants from their former Masters, or from their Wives and-Families: So that though it is absolutely necessary, that the Plantations should be supplied with Servants and Workmen; yet there are so many Tricks, and troublesome Suits, that Merchants cannot safely agree for them, nor the Masters of Vessels carry them to the Plantations:

That there are Persons who pretend to come out of the Country for Employment, and bind themselves at the said Office as Servants; and, when cloathed, and gotten on board, some of their own Gang go and search for them, and afterwards sue the Merchant, or Master of the Vessel, for Kidnappers, when they themselves, are the Persons, merely to extort Money from them, by way of Composition:

That, last Year, a Woman came to Mr. Perry, and complained, That her Husband was kidnapped away in a Ship of his; and therefore he must keep her, and her Four Children; and she brought several of her Parishioners, and made a very great Clamour; threatening to sue Mr.

Perry;upon which he wrote away immediately to the Master of the Ship, which, by Accident, was Wind-bound at Cowes, to put the WOman's Husband on Shore; and,

as good Luck was, the Master received the Letter, and discharged the Man; but Mr. Petry lost all his Passage-money, and what was laid out in Cloaths; notwithstanding such married Man had sworn before a Justice of Peace, that he was a sjngle Man, and had fairly bound himself as a Servant at the said Office:

That, about Two Years since, one Daniel Walts was bound in a Voyage to Virginia, to carry Servants thither: That the Servants were all examined, and produced their Indentures at Gravesend, according to Custom; after which, a Man came on board to search for his Servant, whom he found, whose Name was Moor; but had bound himself by the false Name of; That, after

Watts returned from his Voyage, Moors Master arrested Watts, on a Capias in Withernam, and committed Prisoner to Nezi'gate; and the said Master demanded a Hundred Guineas for the Loss of his Servant: That Watts offered him Sixty Guineas; which not being accepted, the said Master prosecuted Watts in the King's Bench; where

200 — 219 Martii.

A. 1701.

Seven or Eight Motions were had; but the Plaintiff delayed his Declaration, thinking to bring Watts to his Terms rather than lose ft Voyage he was then bound in; but Watts petitioned the then Lord Keeper, from whom the said Capias issued, who granted a, Supersedeas thereon; yet he lost his intended Voyage, was imprisoned, and spent a great deal of Money; though he was only employed, as Master of the Vessel, to carry the Servants as Passengers; and knew not the said Servant, nor that he had a Master; and was to have but Six Pounds for his Passage:

That, about Three Terms since, a Trial was had at Guildhall against a Merchant, who had contracted with a Wheelwright, that seemed to be Four or . Five-and* twenty Years of Age: who bound himself at the said Office, and sw ore himself to be free from Servitude: The Action was brought by a Wheelwright of St. Albans, who declared, That the young Fellow was his Servant; and Judgment was given against the Defendant for 401.; and believes it cost him near 40/. more.

That, about a Fortnight since, a young Fellow bound himself at the said Office, by a false Name; and the Person, to whom he was bound, is now committed a Prisoner in Newgate; and the Merchant, for whose Service

he was bound, is threatened to be sued; and great Composition is demanded.

Mr. Braddle, Merchant, said, That Watts is not the

only Person that has suffered by Imprisonment; but one Wi/lmore, a Merchant of considerable Substance, was utterly ruined by Imprisonment, and Prosecution on a Capias in Withernam.

That they had many other Instances of the Hardships they labour under, which they had many Merchants ready to prove; but the Committee did not think it necessary to examine any further.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following; viz

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to prevent vexatious Suits for taking on board, and transporting Servants to the English Plantations in America:

And that Mr. Clayton do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

Sir Rowland Guyn reported from the Committee ap- Oath of

pointed to consider of the Oath in the late Act for the Abjuration, further Security of his Majesty's Person, and the Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line; and for extinguishing the Hopes of the pretended Prince of Wales, and all other Pretenders, and their open and secret Abettors; and what Variations are necessary to be made, by reason of the unfortunate Death of his late Majesty; That they had considered the Matter to them referred; and had made the Variations which they conceive necessary; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

The OATH.

I A.B. do truly and sincerely acknowlege, profess, testify, and declare, in my Conscience, before God and the World, That our Sovereign Lord King William is lawful and rightful King of this Realm, and of all other his Majesty's Dominions and Countries thereunto belonging:

And I do solemnly and sincerely declare, That I do believe, in my Conscience, That the Person pretended to be Prince of Wales during the Life of the late King James, and, since his Decease, pretending to be, and taking upon himself the Stile and Title of, Kingoi Englaby the Name of James the Third, hath not any Right or Title whatsoever to the Crown of this Realm, or any other the Dominions thereto belonging: And I do renounce, refuse, and abjure, any Allegiance or Obedience to him: And I do sw ear, That I will bear Faith and true Allegiance to his Majesty King William, and him will defend, to the utmost of my Power, against all traiterous Conspiracies and Attempts whatsoever, which shall be made against his Person, Crown, or Dignity: And I will do my best Endeavour to disclose, and make known to his Majesty, and his Successors, all Treasons, and traiterous Conspiracies, which I shall know to be against him, or any of them;

And I do faithfully promise, to the utmost of my Power, to support, maintain, and defend, the Limitation and Succession of the Crown, against him the said James, and all other Persons whatever, as the same is, and stands limited, by an Act, intituled, An Act declaring the Rights and Liberties of the Subject, and settling the Succession of the Crown to his Majesty, during his Majesty's Life; and, after his Majesty's Decease, to the Princess Anne of Denmark, and the Heirs of her Body, being Protestants; and, for Default of such Issue, to the Heirs of the Body of his Majesty, being Protestants: And as the same, by one other Act, intituled, An Act for the further Limitation of the Crown, and better securing the Rights and Liberties of the Subject, is, and stands limited, after the

Decease

Decease of his Majesty and the Princess Anne of Denmark, and for default of Issue of the said Princess, and of his Majesty, respectively, to the Princess Sophia Electress and Duchess Dowager of Hanover, and the Heirs of her Body, being Protestants: And all these things I do plainly and sincerely acknowledge, and swear, according to these express Words by me spoken, according to the plain and common Sense and Understanding of the same Words, without any Equivocation, mental Evasion, or secret Reservation whatsoever: And I do make this Recognition, Acknowlegement, Abjuration, Renunciation, and Promise, heartily, willingly, and truly, upon the true Faith of a Christian. So help me GOD.

Mr. Dormer, according to Order, reported, from tfiq Holder's Committee, to whom the Petition of Samiiel Let belief, Escape from John Denew, William Richardson, send Simon Lebland, on Fleet Pnw*' the behalf of themselves, and very many other Merchants in England, and in foreign Parts, Freighters and Insurers in the: Cloudesly Gaily; complaining of the Escape of John Holder, of London, Merchant, out of the Prison of the Fleet:where he wqs scharged,. by the Lord Chief Justice Holt, for a Contrivance in taking out the Goods, and afterwards burning the said Ship, upon which he had made great Insurances; was referred; the Matter, as it appeared so them; which they had directed him to report t;o the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

That the Committee had examined the Matter thereof, and find the same to be as followeth; viz.

That to the First Part of the Petition, relating to John Holder, Owner of the late Cloudesly Gaily;

William Suck/cy, Mariner, informed the Committee,

That, in March 1699, John Snapcs, Commander of the Holder Frigate, came to him, and told him, That Mr.

John Holder, of London, Merchant, desired to speak with him, intending to make him Commander of the Cloudesly Gaily, for a Voyage to Cadiz, Genoa, and Leghorne, and so Home agaiu; But Suck/ey replying. That he was. in Expectation of another Ship; Snapes said, That this Voyage would be most for his Advantage; and that he should go in the Holder Frigate, in Company thither, also: Thereupon the Informant went to Holder, and agreed to accept the Command of the said Gaily; and accordingly Bills of usual Notice were put up at the in

Name; and then Holder told the Informant, That they had or would make great Assurances upon the said Ship, and her Loading, and take up great Sump of Money on Bottomry, and Merchants Goods on Freight; and had contrived and designed to bum the said Ship at Sea, and make Advantage thereof for themselves;

That he entered into the said Confederacy with Holder and Snapes; for which he was to have 1,500l.; and der gave him Three Notes under his Hand, amounting to that Sum, payable within Twelve Months after; which Notes he produced to the Committee: And the same"

Day Holder gave him secret Orders for carrying on the said Contrivance, consisting of 26 Articles; and afterwards sent him inclosed, by Letter to under his Hand, additional Instructions:

That they prevailed with Suckley to sigu false Bills of Loading for Goods and Jewels that w ere never put on board; particularly 135 Pigs of Lead, 48 Hogsheads of Sugar, a Box of Jewels of 1,400l. Value, several Bales of Goods of many other Merchandizes: And also that after Goods have been shipped, he has altered the Marks by Holders Order; particularly 19 Casks of Wax, for which Holder had given a Bill of Lading to Mr

That Holder, Snapes, and Suckley, borrowed 900l. upon their Bottomry Bond: And Holder said, That he had secured to the Value of 16,000 /.

That he sailed from London, freighted with divers Merchants Goods of a considerable Value, and arrived at Cadiz, and there also gave false Bills of Lading; and took into the Amount of 18,000 Pieces of Eight, besides much Plate, of divers Merchants, on Freight; for Genoa and leghorne; and then sailed from in Company of the Holder Frigate, on their said pretended Voyage; but, by the Way, at Sea, before they arrived at the Port, to which they were consigned, great Quantities of the most valuable Goods put on board the Clotulesly Gaily nt London, and all the Pieces of Eight, and Plate, were, by Holder and Snapes, taken out of the Gaily, and put on*board the Ship Holder Frigate; and afterwards the said Gaily was set on Fire by one Robert Acres, w ho was Mate of

Nic. JValker said, That he was Quarter-master of tire Clcktdttly Gaily at the time she was burnt, which was on the goth of October 1699: That Robert the Mate, came running upon the Deck, and said, The Ship was on fire, end gave the Signal; upon which the Informant proposed to the Men, to carry Water, and endeavour to pot it out, there appearing only some Smoke at a great Distance from the Powder-room, and he offering to go and throw the Powder overboard; but Aci'es was against it, and ordered the Long-boat to be put out, and put therein the best of his Cloaths; and the Men also went into the Boat; but he would not suffer them to put any thing in her; and then they followed the Holder , which

liad left the Gaily Three Hours before; and the Fire burned 10 or 12 Hours before it reached the Powder-room; so that, if the Holder Frigate had staid, probably, great Part of the Goods might have been saved: And said, Me sawr Si tapes alter the Marks on several Goods taken out of the m.id Gully, after they were put on board the Holder Frigate.

Sir A/ illiam /ledgessaid, That there was Insurance made

at Cadiz, for 12,000 Dollars, upon the

for 2,900 whereof he subscribed for himself and Partners; and that, after the burning of the Gaily, he was required to give Insurance for the Musters of Ships; which, before, was unusual, and never demanded of the Merchants, and brought a great Discredit upon the English there.

Mr. Radbarn esaid, That he insured for 500 Dollars on the same Policy with Sir; and was at

Cadiz when the said Gaily was burned; which brought such a Disgrace upon our Merchants there, that, when they applied to the Italian Brokers to get them Freight for Italy, as usually, they replied, That they had such an Instance in the Cloudesly Gaily, as never to trust an Englishmen more.

Mr. Gideon said, That he has been employed to search the Insurance Offices at London and Bristol!, in this Matter; and finds, by the Policies in both Places, that there where 1 (5,000 /. insured upon the Cloudesly Gaily.

Mr. Hales, an Attorney, said, Tlrat some of the Insurance-money has been recovered by; but

hopes, he shall put a stop to further Matters of that Nature.

That, to prove the Second Part of the Petition, relating to the Warden of the Fle Prison; Mr. Hales said, That, on the 5th of this Instant March he served Mr. Dixon, the Clerk of the Papers of the said Prison, with the Lord Chief Justice Holt's Warrant, directed to the Warden of the Fleeor his Deputy; that the Warden was not within, as informed; requiring them to detain and keep John Holder, then in his Custody, in sure and safe Custody, for his Offence, in assisting, contriving and directing, the wilful burning of the Cloudesly Gaily, by Robert Acres Mate thereof, and whereof the said John Holder was Owner, until he should be discharged by due Course of Law': And Dixon then owned, That Holder was a Prisoner, and in Custody; and that he would take care, and secure him: And that Dixon always acted for the Warden as his Agent:

That he had another Warrant from my Lord Chief Justice Holt before this; which he did not think effectual; and therefore procured the above-said Warrant.

Mr. Jacob Kyzersaid, That, on the Sixth of March instant, in the Morning, he and Mr. met Mr. Dixon, with the above Warrant in his. Hand; and then Voi. 13.

827

Dixon owned, That the said Holder was a prisoner; and the Turnkey also said so: Upon.....Kyzer asked to

see Holder; but Dixon denied to shew him; saying, The Warden was out of Town; but if he w'ould come in the Afternoon, he might have an answer; and Kyzer threatening to complain to the House of Commons, Dixon said, Pugh! He did not care for the House of Commons. That, accordingly he went in the Afternoon; and then they said, He was not a Prisoner; and the Turnkey said. He lodged somewhere in the Old David Grill: That he went with Mr/ to the

Fleet, and met with the Warden, and asked for Holder; upon which the Warden bid them go to Dixon; he did all his Business; and he himself knew nothing of the Matter: Whereupon Grill told him, That Holder was his Prisoner; and that, if he did not produce him, he should hear of it in the House of Commons.

That, to answer this, Mr. Ford, the Warden, said, He did not know of Holder's Offences; if he had, he should have had more Care of him; but that he only stood committed to him the 4th of February last, in Discharge of his Bail, in Three or Four Actions, which amount to about 120/.

That he takes his Office to be in the Nature of a Sheriff's Office, where Bail is allowed; and that be has taken the same Person's Security for Holders Imprisonment, as the Sheriff had taken to the Actions, sufficient to answer the same, as he believes; and hopes, he shall not be answerable for more than his Commitments:

That he thinks my Lord Chief Justices Warrant to be unusual: To charge him with the Custody of Holder, there ought to have been a Habeas Corpus to have brought him before his Lordship; and then he would have removed him to a criminal Prison, more proper than the Fleet:

That he was out of Town, when the Matters were transacted; and when lie came, referred them to Dixon: That the Petitioners Agent searched for Holder upon the First Warrant, and took up one Mr. Bird for him; and thereupon Holder has taken the Alarm, and is gone aw ay; but hopes to take him again: And alleged, That, by the Act 8* Willidmi3tii, for regulating Prisons, the Person asking for a Prisoner in order to charge him, ought to demand a Note, under the Hand of the proper Officer, That he was a Prisoner; which, in this Case, was not done.

And the Committee taking Notice, that the Security Bond being of boo/. Penalty; and executed by William Bird, and Thomas Bush a Tipstaff to the Fleet',

The Warden owned, That Bush was his Tipstaff; but said, Mr. Bird was no Prisoner; but believes him to be a responsible Alan: and was the Person taken upon the said Warrant.

And Air. Dixon denied he spoke the Words mentioned by Kyzer touching the House of Commons.

And that, upon the whole Alatter, the Committee came to the Resolutions following;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have Fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Holder, by procuring false Bills of Loading, and making fraudulent Insurances in England, and foreign Parts, on the Cloudesly Gaily, and by contriving and directing the wilful burning of the said Ship, after the Goods of Value were taken out of the same, is guilty of a villainous Practice, highly dishonourable to the Nation, and prejudicial to the Trade thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That William IVeedon Ford Esquire, Warden of the Fleet, by suffering the said John Holder to escape, after he was legally charged in his Custody for the said Offence, is guilty of a notorious Breach of his Duty.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

And that, afterwards, her Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament: And that, to prevent any Mistake in reporting the same, he had desired, and obtained, a Copy thereof: which he read to the House; and is as followed); viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am very well pleased to have given My Assent to the Act for the taking the publick Accounts: Nothing is more reasonable than to give the Kingdom the Satisfaction of having those great Sums accounted for, which were raised to carry on the late War; especially when it is necessary for our own Safety, and the Support of our Allies, to continue great Taxes.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you My kind and hearty Thanks for continuing to Me, for My Life, the same Revenue you had granted to the King: I will take great Care it shall be managed to the best Advantage; and, while my Subjects remain under the Burden of such great Taxes, I will streighten Myself in my ow n Expences, rather than not contribute all I canto their Ease and Relief, with a just Regard to the Support of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown. It is probable the Revenue may fall very short of what it has formerly produced: However, I will give Directions, That One hundred thousand Pounds be applied to the publick Service, in this Year, out of the Revenue you have so unanimously given Me.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The present Posture of Adairs Abroad, as well as the Season of the Year, obliges Me to put you in mind of giving all possible Dispatch to the publick Business.

That which made the Difference of the Poll, was; In the Poll produced by the Petitioner, there were put down William Stockin and Richard James for the Petitioner; who were not put down to him on the Poll produced by the Sitting Member: And there was omitted, in the same Poll, to Mr. Mason, the said William Stockin, and the Bailiff's Vote; which were put down to him on the Poll produced by the Sitting Member.

The Matters endeavoured to be made out, as well by die Petitioner, as by the Silting Member, were, Bribery, and the making good a Majority upon the Poll.

The Evidence w as as follows:

The Petitioner's Counsel called several Witnesses; Robert Wollaston, said, That Mr. llanmer, 'Mr.Mason's,

Brother-in-law, told him, That the late Earl of Jicld, had, by his Will, left in his Hands 1001, and, if he would vote for Mr. Mason, he should have as great a Share as any one; and that Mr. Hanmcr made an Interest for Mr. Mason: Wollaston said, He was examined as a Witness, at the Hearing of the Merits of the last Election.

Geo. Winton said, That Mr. Mason met David Adams in the Street the Day before the Election, and told him, If he would vote for him, he should have the House, and Three Closes he then possessed, Rent-free: And, the same Day at Night, he told the said Adams, That, if he would come up to London, he would get him a beneficial Place: And that David Adams told him, He was in Ar-rear of Rent, and Mr. Mason had promised him to set it off: George Winton, being afterwards examined the next Night the Committee sat, said, That Mr. Mason offered him Five Guineas, if he would give him his Vote.

Eduard Minton said, That old Mr. Mason sent for him Tw o Days before the Election, and told him, That, if he would vote for his Son, he should have his House Rent-free, and Part of tool, left by the late Earl of Macclesfield: He acknowleged, He never had Possession of the House; and that, since Mr. Mason had lett it to another.

Edward Minton said, That, on the Christmas Eve last he heard John Waters say, That he would never have voted for Mr. Mason, but that he had 5/. for his Vote: He said, He was a Witness at the Hearing of the Merits of the last Election.

Walter Coneing said, That Isaiah Hoggin, on the Saturday before the Election, came to a House where the said Coneing was; and he said, That Isaiah Hoggin told him, He had no Money, but was to have Three Closes for his Life, after old Mr. Alas oris Death, paying 12 a Year; but he was to vote for the Sitting Member in the mean time: He said, He was a Witness against Sir Gilbert Gerard at the last Hearing of the Merits of the Election for the said Borough, but not against Mr. Mason.

Jos. Comyns said, That, at Night, after the Election was over Wm. Adams told him, He had seven Pounds, to vote for Mr. Mason; and desired him not to divulge it: He acknowleged Adam was in Drink: And that the said Adams came the Night after the Election, and denied it; and said. He had only a Promise of 40& of the late Earl of Macclcsfcild'sMoney.

That Wtn. Stockin, who was the contested Vote between Mr. Mason and Mr. Walcot, said, as he was going up tire Hall, 1 hat, which Way he gave his Vote, be was to have 51.

That the Petitioner's Counsel, in the next Place, proceeded to except to some Persons on Mr. Masons Poll, as receiving Charity: And called,

That Thomas Bright senior, Scrivener, his Wife had received of the same Charity:

That Samuel Richards, or his Wife, had received of the same Charity.

As to William Stoclin-, it was testified by the said Richard Wollaston, That the said Stockin was put dow n upon Three Polls: That Stockin, being called, and asked who he was for, answered twice. For Mr. Walcot and Mr. Bret: But the Bailiff, pretending he did not hear, asked him again; and then he gave his Vote for Mr. Bret and Mr. Mason, without going out of Court

That the next Thing the Petitioner's Counsel proceeded on, was, to add to their Poll: And they called,

Richard Wollaston, Robert Wollaston, Walter Coneing: Who said, That Samuel James had voted formerly for Sir William Brownlxnct: But it was acknowleged, that he lodged in the Town as a hired Servant, and was a Sort of a travelling Person.

Walter Coneing said, ThatThomas Waters was his Bedfellow; and he himself was a Housekeeper in Bishop's Castle.

That it was admitted by the Sitting Member's Counsel, That the said James and Waters did offer to poll for the Petitioner; but they denied that they had any Votes.

That the Sitting Member's Counsel first applied themselves to answer the Petitioner's Evidence: And they called,

Robert Mason, John Jones, and William Stockin: Who gave an Account, That Stockin did once, and but once, name Mr. Walcot's Name, by Mistake; and presently retracted, and gave his Vote for Mr. Bret and Mr. Mason: And Robert Mason said, That Samuel James was no Inhabitant; John Jones said, That the Bailiff did give his Vote for Mr. Bret and Mr. Mason.

Charles Bright said, That, after the Election was over, he discoursed with Robert Wollaston: Who said, He had no Business at London; and swore he had nothing to say against Mr. Mason, or any concerned for him.

Charles Jones and Robert Owen said, That, on the Thursday before the Election, they heard Edward,

one of the Petitioner's Witnesses, say, That if Mr. Mason was elected, Three or Four of them would come up and turn him out, right or wrong: And Robert Owen testified, That Wm.Minton, another of the Petitioner's Witnesses, said, That Mr. Mason should never sit in the House.

Charles Jones, Fran. Colbach, said. That they were at Morris Pugh's when Geo. Winton and Adam were there: And Colbach said, He was nearer to Mr. Mason than Minton: And they did not hear Mr. Mason' make any Promise to Adams, in Case he would vote for him: And Colbach and John Holmes said, That Adams had promised his Vote for Mr. Mason, before Mr. Mason came to Town: Jones said, That Adams told Mr. Mason, He had voted for him before, and would vote for him again.

John Holmes said, That David Adams has held his House Three Years at Lady-day of old Mr. Mason, paying 9/. a Year; and Adams paid 31, in Part of Rent, at Christmas last:

That Mr. Mt/son did not come down till the Day before the Election; and declared, He would not speak to any of the Mintons.

Josiah Hoggin said, That lie held Lands of old Mr. Mason; but that the Sitting Member had nothing to do with the Estate, unless his Father did please to give it him: And that all that voted for Mr. Mason, except Two Nortons, had promised to be for Mr. Mason, before ha came to Town.

Thomas Bright, Hugh Mason, and Fran. Colebach, Said, That Samuel James and Thomas Waters were not intitled to any Vote; for that he lived at Colebach, and not in Bishop's Castle.

A Message from the Lords, by Sir Robert Legard and Mr. Gery:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Lands and Tenements of Mountague Earl of Abingdon in Trustees, to be sold, and purchasing other Lands, of equal Value; and limiting the Lands to be purchased to the same Uses as the Lands to be sold are limited: To which they desire the Concurrence of this House. And also,

Have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the Lands of Henry 'Pawittt, a Lunatick, in order to make suitable Provision for him, his next Heir, and nearest Relations: To winch they desire the Concurrence of this House. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Amendments, made, by this House, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for Confirming and Settling of divers Charities given by the last Will of Job Marston Gentleman, deceased. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for Relief of Dorothy Baroness Dowager of Upper Ossory, and Captain James Roche, with relation to the Irish Forfeitures, without Amendments. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Sale of the Manor of Attingham, in the County of Salop; and settling a Farm, called Silly'hall, and a Moiety of the Manor of Temple Lawnic, in the County of Worcester, of better Value, in lieu thereof, without Amendments. Also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for charging the Estate late of William Adams Esquire, deceased, with Portions and Maintenance for William Adams and Elizabeth Adam, his younger Children, without any Amendments.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Conyers, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to w hom the Bill to declare the Alterations in the Oath appointed to be taken by the Act, intituled, An Act for the further Security of his Majesty's Person, and the Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line; and for extinguishing the Hopes of the pretended Prince of 1Vales, and all other Pretenders, and their open and secret Abettors; and for declaring the Association to be determined; was committed; the Amendments which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same wrere once read throughout; and then a Second time, one by one; and all of them, except Clause A. upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Clause A. being read a Second time, That such Members of either House of Parliament, who had taken the Oath according to the Form agreed upon in each House, should not be required again, in respect of their being Members of either House, to take the said Oath during the Continuance of that Parliament;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Amendment;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Clause being offered, to be added to the Bill, That no Member of either House of Parliament, who had taken the Oath according to the Form agreed upon in each House, be obliged to take the Oath again during the Continuance of that Parliament, in respect of their being Members of either House, or in respect of any Commission or Place held or enjoyed at the Time of taking the said Oath;

The same was twice read; and amended; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

The Lord Fairfax, according to Order, reported from DamaJ the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Encouragement fafc of an Invention of damasking, striking, and fixing, Colours into all Sorts of Stuffs and Cloth; and raking and embossing Flowers of various Colours on the same; was committed; to w'hom several Petitions were referred, with Direction, That they should make a special Report thereupon, before they proceeded upon the Bill; Rat they had considered the several Petitions to them referred, accordingly; and had directed him to report the Matter, as it appeared to them, to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read-; and is as followed; viz.

i. Upon the Petition of Sir Thomas Cudden Knight, and many others concerned in beautifying Stuffs with hot Rolls:

Air. Nic. Clark allegeth, That the Petitioners have used the Trade of Printing, Damasking, Striking, Flowering, of Stuffs and Cloths, for above Forty Years: and that there was a Patent granted the 36 Car. 2 di, for doing the same; and that the Petitioners have worked 3,000 Cloths a Year, after the same manner, but not in Colours.

Air. Pocklington alleged the same as Air. Clerk; and did insist, the Word Embossing was not in the Patent mentioned in the Bill.

It

I ANN;

17° Aprilis.

u was allowed by the Parties prosecuting the Bill, That the Word Embossing was not in their Patent; and that their Patent was of a contrary Nature to that of the Petitioners, dated 36° Car. 2cli, by reason the Words of their Patent was for damasking, striking, and fixing, Colours into Leather, all Sorts of Stuffs, Cloths, Velvets, and Hair, on both Sides.

Mr. Hen. Burnaby allegeth, That the Printing and Damasking of Stuffs is no new Invention; and that he hath known it practised for about Twenty-six Years; and that he hath done it himself, but not in Colours.

Mr. Tendall likewise said, That he has known Printing apd Damasking to have been an Art used Time out of mind; but did never see any so embossed, and mixed in Colours; and did own to one Mr. Hancock, That the said Invention was ne\v, and ought to be encouraged; but did further object, That the said Art was in too few Hands.

2. And that, upon the Petition of the Woollen-drapers of London and Westminster;

That there did only appear, on the behalf of the Woollen-drapers, one Mr. Molinmx: Who allowed the Intention of the Bill to be good; but objected against the Patentees buying and selling Cloths: And praying, they might have a Clause to prevent the same; as likewise a Clause, That no unreasonable Prices might be imposed upon doing the same; and that the same might be done cheap:

That the Parties concerned in the Bill did agree, That whatever Cloths Mr. Molineux, or other Drapers, or any other Persons, should bring unto them, they would do them as cheap, and reasonable, as can be desired; and are willing to admit of any Clause for that Purpose.

3. And that, upon the Petition of Thomas Plomer, and others, Traders in Wool about the City of London, and Westminster;

That there did only appear, on the Petitioner s behalf, one Mr. Smith: Who said, He did not come to oppose the Bill in general; but did allow the Invention to be a good Invention; but said, If the said Invention was to be managed by so small a Number of Persons, it might be very prejudicial to them: That he likewise produced a Piece of flowered Shag, which was done by the Press; which, he alleged, had *been used and practised by the Weavers for many Years; which employed many Thousands of People; as likewise many other things of the same Nature: And prayed, That they might have a Saving as to what related to their Trade: And also produced a prior Patent for preparing Crapes, and all Sorts of Stuffs and Silks in Flowers, Ramages, and Figures, before they be dyed, which appears after the Dyeing of them by the Dyers.

The Persons concerned in the Bill did agree, that the Weavers might have a Clause for the saving such Right as they have in the Premises.

4. And that, upon the Petition of Robert Parker, and others;

Robert Parker junior said, He was the first Inventor of Embossing; and that his Father and he taught Mr. Watts, One of the Patentees; and produced a wooden Print, or Pattern: And further said, That he and his Father were the Persons that brought the raised Work to Perfection; but said. This was not above Four Years since.

Mr. Walton said, That he made the said Wooden Prints, or Patterns, about Four Years ago, for the said Mr. Parker, senior and junior.

Mr. Mathews, being examined by the Petitioner's Counsel, did declare, He was not interested in the said Patent; but was the first Inventor of the Embossing Trade; and that the said Parker, the Petitioner, was his Servant; but was not capable of doing his Business; for which Reason he turned him out of his Service. He also produced a Waistcoat of flowered Cloth, in Colours; which was the first Works, and was the Occasion of procuring his Patent; which he has long since parted with, and his Interest in; and the said Patent bears Date in or about the 14th of December, in the Seventh Year of his Vol. 13.

late Majesty's ..... which was long before the said Damasking Parker could pretend to any thing. Stuffs.

Mr. Watts said, That the said Parke)' senior used to keep Company with a Brother of his, who worked for the Patentees; and that the said Parker w'as to give his said Brother 3/. to learn him his Art; Thirty Shillings whereof was in Hand paid, and the other Thirty Shillings is still due; and that he himself did use the Art a Twelvemonth before ever Parker pretended to it: And further said, That Parkers Wife promised him, That, if he would not contradict her Husband, before the Committee, in what lie should say, it should be the better for him.

Mr. Hancock, Clerk of the Cloth to the New East India Company, said, about Three Years ago, a Piece of embossed Cloth, done by the Patentees, was sent to India; which was very well approved of there; and that there has been, since, several Patterns sent for from thence:

And further said, That he hath likewise sent Cloth to the said Parker, the Petitioner, to be wrought, who hath spoiled him several Pieces thereof; but whatever Pieces he hath sent to the Patentees hath always been veil done, and well approved of; and at about 6d. per Yard more than the common Dye.

Mr. Blanch was produced as Evidence for the said Mr. Parker: Who alleged, That he has done something of the same Nature, above 30 Years ago, both at Gloucester, and other Places; but allowed, he could not strike it as the Patentees do; and has left off his Trade for above Seven Years.

5. And that, upon the Petition of the Governor and Company of Merchants trading to the Levant Seas;

The Governor of the Company, being examined to their Petition, said, That the Invention is new, and ought to be encouraged; but all that he does object against, and insist upon, is, That it may not be engrossed in a few Peoples Hands; which will be a Hindrance to the Improvement of the same.

6. And that, upon the Petition of the Leather Guilders;

The Patentees have agreed, That the Word Leather

should be struck out of their Bill; and that they should have any Clause whatever, to save their Right.

Ordered, That the said Committee have Leave to proceed upon the said Bill.

Translation of the Treaty between his Majesty and the States General, and the King of Prussia.

ALTH OUGH there arealreadv particular Alliances Treaty between his Majesty the King of Great Britain, his Prussia. Majesty the King of Prussia, and their High and Mighty Lordships the States General of the United Provinces; yet the presentand dangerous Conjuncture, particularly as to the grand Aflair of the Succession to the Monarchy of Spain, and the Consequences thereof; and likewise the due Consideration of the Security and mutual Conveniencies of their Kingdoms and States, which may depend thereon; together with the publick Good of Europe in general, which is so much concerned therein; have given them Occasion to enter into stricter Engagements: For which Purpose, there have been commissioned and authorized, on one Part, by his Majesty the King of Great Britain, John Earl of Marlborough, Baron Churchill of Sandridge, General of his Foot, and Commander in Chief of his said Majesty's Forces in the Lozv Countries, and his Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary; and by their High and Mighty Lordships the States General, the Sieurs John Van Essen, Burgomaster of the Town of Zutphen, Curator of the U niversityof liar demy k\ Frederick Baron de Rhcede,

Lord of Lier, St. Antony, and Ter-Lee, of the Order of the Nobility of the Province of Holland and Westfriseland;

First Noble, and Representative of the Nobility in the States, and in the Council of Zeeland; Everhard de Weede, Lord of Weede, Dykvclt, Rctcles, &c. Lord Proprietor of the Manor of the Town of Oudcxvater, Dean and Rector of the Imperial Chapter of St. Mary at Utrecht, Dykgrave of the River Rhine, in the Province of Utrecht, and President of the States of the same Province; David Constantin du Tour, Lord of Aveincs} la Pamerede, Maleret\ Arnold Lamhcr, Burgomaster of the Town of Deventer; and Indols Gockinga; respectively Deputies in the Assembly of the Lords the States General from the Provinces of Guelder land, Holland, and Westfriscland, Zeeland, Utretcht, Friseland, Overyssell, and Groningen, and Ommeland; and, oh the other Part, by his Majesty the King of Prussia, the Sieurs Ezechiel Baron of Spanheim, Privy Counsellor, and Counsellor of State, and Envoy Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary from his said Majesty; and Wolfgang Baron of Schmettau, Lord of Koningsrvalde and Kehrberg, likewise Privy Counsellor, and Counsellor of State, and Plenipotentiary from his Majesty the King of Prussia: And in Pursuance of the full Powers produced to this Effect on one Side, and on the other, it hath been agreed as follows:

1.

That there shall be an entire and perfect Intelligence between these Three Powers, for the Security, Advantage, and mutual Defence, of their Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, against all Sorts of Aggressors; and, above all,

on account of this present Convention.

2.

That for this Purpose, they shall, on each Side, employ their utmost Endeavours for the Establishment and Continuance of a good and secure general Peace, and the settling thereupon the particular Security of their Kingdoms, States, and Commerce.

3.

That, to this End, there shall be a strict and sincere Communication, between these Three Pow ers, of all that may be negotiated in relation thereunto; that so nothing may be treated of, and concluded, but by common Consent, and with the Satisfaction, Security, and Guaranty, of their said Kingdoms and States.

4-

And whereas the above-mentioned Affair of the Succession to the Spanish Monarchy, in the Condition to which it is at present reduced, to the great and notable Prejudice of the Rights and Pretensions of his Imperial Majesty to the said Succession, and of the Security and Liberty of Europe in general, and, in particular, of the neighbouring Powers, who are the most interested therein, hath given Occasion to a Treaty of Alliance, made and concluded at iha Hague, the 7th of September last, between his Imperial Majesty, his Britannick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships; it is therefore, and in pursuance of the Communication and Requisition, which hath been made on the Part of his said Majesty the King of Great Britain, and of their High and Mighty Lordships, to his Majesty the King of Prussia, that his said Majesty hath been induced to enter into the above-mentioned Alliance; and his Britannick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, do, on their Part, likewise declare, That they admit his Prussian Majesty into the said Alliance: Wherefore, separate Acts shall be made by the above-mentioned Powers, with the Insertion of the said Alliance, which shall be exchanged at the same time with the Ratification of the present Treaty.

5-

And seeing that as well his Britannick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, as his Majesty the King of Prussia, have great and clear Pretensions to considerable Sums of Money, which are due to them respectively from the Crown of Spain, they have agreed mutually to aid and assist one another for obtaining Satisfaction for the said Pretensions, and likew ise hereafter to concert the proper and convenient Means for this Purpose: And,

moreover, the particular Guafarity given by his nick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, to keep the Fort of St. Mary as a Security for one Part of the above-mentioned Pretensions of his Majesty the King of Prussia, shall continue to have its full and entire Effect 6.

That, furthermore, it is promised, on the Part of his said Britannick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, to come to no Conclusion of Peace with France and Spain, without his abovesaid Majesty's concurring therein as King of Prussia, and being owned and treated as King by those Two Crowns.

7*

That, in case these Three Powers jointly, or any One of them, should be attacked by France or Spain, on account of this present Treaty, or of the above-mentioned Alliance with his Imperial Majesty, they promise and oblige themselves, mutually to assist each other, pursuant to what is agreed by the 11th Article of the above-mentioned Treaty of Alliance with his Imperial Majesty, and also by the former Treaties and Alliances of his Britannict Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, with his Majesty the King of Prussia; which are renewed and continued by the 1 ith Article of this present Treaty.

8.

That, furthermore, in case, as abovesaid, of a Rupture and War, if Contributions should be raised in the Enemy's Country by the Troops of his Majesty the King of Prussia, or of his Territories and Dominions, or by their Assistance; especially if the Territories and Subjects of the said King were obliged to pay Contributions to the Enemy; there shall then be made an equitable Agreement concerning the Reparation of the said Contribution.

. 9- '

That in case, with the Consent of his Imperial Majesty, the Eight thousand Men, which his Majesty the King of Prussia has agreed to furnish him, the Conditions mentioned in the # Article of his Treaty with his said Imperial Majesty, made in the Year 1700, should remain all, or in Part, for the Defence of the Countries of the Lower Rhine, or of those between the Meuse and the Moselle; or for acting offensively against the Enemy; it shall be concerted on each Side w here they are to be employed: And, in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, should draw the said Troops out of the Countries and Dominions w here the Money of the Empire is current, they shall account with his Majesty the King of Prussia for the Exchange, or Difference, in respect to the Money: And, in the same case, they shall allow Forage to the said Troops out of the Magazines of the K'mgoi Great Britain, and the States, when the Country cannot furnish them with any; and, in like manner, Bread, according to w^hat was observed in the last War, Half on this Side the Meuse, and the w hole on the other bide.

10.

That, upon the Offer made by his Majesty the King of Prussia, to furnish his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, immediately, without demanding any Levy-money, a Body of Five thousand Men, of good old Troops, well cloathed, and well armed, and the Cavalry provided with good Horses, to be taken into their Service; and the same having beeu well received, and agreed unto, on their Part; a particular Convention hath been made and concluded for the same betw een their respective Ministers, having full Power for that Purpose: And, in case a Peace should be settled in the Countries neighbouring to Prussia, and that his Said Majesty the King of Prussia should have nothing to fear on that Side, his said Majesty declares he is ready, and disposed, to furnish a considerable Number of Troops, at least Seven thousand Men, for the Good of... common Cause, and to be employed on such a Foot, as shall be agreed on with his Britannick Majesty and their High and Mighty Lordships.

11.

Lastly, the former Treaties shall continue in their full and entire Force; that is to say, that of a perpetual and

Translation of the Convention with the King of Prussia, about Troops to be put into the Service of his Majesty and the States General.

HIS Majesty the King of Prussia having offered his Majesty the King of Great , and their High and Mighty Lordships the States General, to put into their Service a Body of Five thousand Men, of good and old Troops; and this Offer having been well received; an Agreement hath been made for the same on the following Conditions:

1.

This Body shall consist, according to the List annexed, in Two Regiments of Horse, making, together with the Field and Staff Officers, and the Officers of each Troop, Eight hundred and Seventy-four Men; and in Five Regiments of Foot, each of Twelve Companies, making, together with their Field and Staff Officers, and the Officers of each Company, Four thousand Two hundred and Fifty-five Men; and, in the whole, both Horse and Foot, Five thousand One hundred and Twenty-nine Men.

2.

These Troops shall be well cloathed, and well armed; and the Cavalry shall be furnished with good Horses; and they shall be, in all respects, treated and paid on the same Foot as the States treat their own Troops.

3-

The said Troops shall be paid, one Half by his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and the other Half by their High and Mighty lordships. This Payment shall be as Speedy, and on the same Foot, with the Troops of His Majesty the King of Prussia, which were in the Service of their High and Mighty Lordships during the ,last War.

4-

This Body shall receive a Month's Pay for Carriage-tboney, as soon as they shall be actually on their March.

5-

His Majesty the King of Prussia shall cause the said Body of Troops to leave their Quarters, and begin their March, Fifteen Days after the signing of this Treaty; and sooner, if it be possible.

6.

The Pay of these Troops shall not commence but from the Day they shall enter upon the Borders of the Domi-Vox. 13.

nions of their High and Mighty Lordships; and they Treaty with shall then he received by the Commissaries of his Britan- Prussia. nick Majesty, and of their High and Mighty Lordships:

And the said Troops shall take an Oath to the King of Great Britain, and to the States.

7-

As for the Recruits of the said Troops, they shall be upon the same F'oot as their High and Mighty Lordships treat their own Troops; and the said Troops shall likewise be left to their Liberty to raise their Recruits where it shall be most convenient for them, as well in the Dominions of His Majesty the King of Prussia, as in those of their High and Mighty Lordships.

8.

In time of War, there shall be paid to these Troops, in Money, for Waggons, and other Equipage, what is paid by their High and Mighty Lordships to their own Troops; and the said Troops shall be treated equally, iu all respects, according to what is practised towards the Troops of their High and Mighty Lordships.

In case that, after an Accommodation or Peace be made with the Crowns of France and his Majesty

the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, should have a. mind to send back the said Body of Troops, his Majesty the King of Prussia shall have Notice thereof Two Months before they begin their March, in order to their Return.

10.

If his Majesty the King of Prussia should happen to be attacked in his own Dominions-, far distant from the Rhine; and should be obliged, thereupon, to demand back his said Troops; they shall be sent him immediately, and without any Contradiction.

11.

Wrhen his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and theiik-High and Mighty Lordships, shall send back the said Body of Troops; in this Case they shall have One Month's Pay for their Return and Carriage-money: But, in case his Majesty the King of Prussia recalls them, they shall be paid no more than the Remainder of the Month's Pay wherein they are recalled.

12.

In case of these Troops being sent back, or recalled, his Majesty the King of Great Britai7i, and their High and Mightinesses, shall neither pay for, nor fill up, the private Soldiers that may then be wanting; and it shall lie upon the Officers of the said Body to answer for the same to his Majesty the King of Prussia.

13-

In case, as abovesaid, of the sending back, or recalling, of the said Troops, they shall be paid what shall appear to be then due to them, speedily; and, if possible, before they begin their March, in order to their Return.

14-

The present Convention shall be ratified, and the Ratifications shall be exchanged, on each Side, within the Space of Six Weeks, to be reckoned from the Day of its being signed.

In Witness whereof, we the underwritten Plenipotentiaries of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, his Majesty the King of Prussia, and the Lords the States General, by virtue of our full Powers, have concluded, signed, and sealed with the Seals of our Arms, the present Convention; that is to say, I the Earl of Marlborough, on the Part of his Britannick Majesty, at London, the 29<h of January ^ojn.s!* we Baron of Spanheim, and the Baron of Schmettau, on the Part of his Majesty the King of Prussia; the First at London, the 290Ih of January 5 an<* the Second at the Hague, the 30th

Translation of the separate Articles, relating to the Convention with the King of Prussia, about Troops.

Separate Articles.

1.

WHILE the Body of Troops of his Majesty the King of Prussia, concerning which an Agreement bath this Day been made, shall continue in the Service of his Bri-tannick Majesty, and their High and Mighty Lordships, his Majesty the King of Prussia shall fill up the vacant Places of the Officers, according to what was practised between his Majesty and their High and Mighty Lordships in the last War, which was ended by the Peace of Ryswick; but, upon the filling up of every Vacancy, Notice shall be given, by the Minister of the King of Prussia, to the Person whom the King of Great Britain shall appoint, and the Council of State, of the Name of the Officer to succeed; to the end that the IAsts may be kept in good Order: His Majesty the King of Prussia shall likewise have all possible Regard to the Recommendation of those Officers, which his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships^ would have made.

2,

For the Preservation of this Body of Troops, and for the observing good Order and Discipline among them, the same shall be commanded by a Major General, who shall be paid upon the same Foot as their High and Mighty Lordships allow to their own: And, in case his Prussian Majesty should give the Command to his Royal Highness the Margrave Albert his Brother, it shall be then in Quality of Lieutenant General, and likewise on the same Foot as their High and Mighty Lordships allow to their own.

These separate Articles shall have the same Force and Vigour, as if they were inserted in the principal Convention made this Day.

In Witness whereof, we have, in like manner, signed, and sealed them' with the Seals of our Arms. Done at London, the ^Qih of January > an<^at &e Hague,

the 30th of December 1701. N.S.

Translation of the Convention with the Landgrave of Hesse Cassell, for 9,000 Men, to be put into the Service of his Majesty and the States.

CONVENTION made between his Majesty the King of Great Britain and their High and Mighty Lordships the States General, on one Part; and his most Serene Highness the Landgrave of Hesse Cassel, on the other Part; touching a Body of 9,000 Men, which his said Highness h£s promised to give for the good of the Common Cause. 1.

First, His Highness shall furnish the said King of Great Britain, and the said Lords the States General, with Six thousand Men; which shall consist, according to the List which shall be made thereof, in One Regiment of Horse,

A. 1701

of Six Companies; Two Regiments of Dragoons, each of Eight Companies; and Five Regiments of Foot* each Of Twelve Companies; each Regiment having its Field and Staff Officers; and making together, in the Whole, the Number of Six thousand Men.

2.

These Six thousand Men shall be good Troops, well exercised, cloathed, and armed; and they shall have good Horses; and shall be provided with all that shall be necessary for them.

3.

The said Six thousand Men shall be paid regularly, according to the abovesaid List; one Half by his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and the other Half by their High and Mighty Lordships; on the same Foot the said States General pay their own Troops, and as soon as the other foreign Troops of other Princes; and they shall not, at any time, be more than Three Months in Ar-rear.

4-

The Pay of these Troops shall commence Two fiill Monfhs before the Day they shall enter upon the Borders of the State of their High and Mighty Lordships, or oa the Place whither they shall be required to cortie, whether it be for Action, or otherwise; where they shall be immediately received by the Commissaries of his Rritamiick Majesty, and of their High and Mighty Lordships: And they shall take an Oath of Fidelity to the said King, and to the said States General.

5-

For what relates to the Recruits of the said Six thousand Men, they shall be upon the same Foot as their High and Mighty Lordships treat their own Troops: And, moreover, it shall be left, on their Part, to the liberty of the said Six thousand Men to rpise their Recruits where it shall be most convenient for them, as well in the Territories of his Highness, as in those of their High and Mighty Lordships.

6.

In time of War, these 6,000 Men shall be paid n Money, for Waggons, and other Equipage, what (heir High and Mighty Lordships pay their own Troops: And, in short, they shall enjoy all the same Advantages in general, that the said Troops of their High and Mighty Lordships do enjoy.

7.

In case that, after an Accommodation, or Peace, bt made, his Majesty of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, should have a mind to send back the said Six thousand Men; his said Highness shall have Notice of it Two Months before they begin their March, in order to their Return.

8;

In case, as abovesaid, that these Troops be sent back, or recalled, his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, shall pay to the said Troops what shall be due to them, as well on account of their Pay, as for Waggons.

It shall be left to the Disposal of his Highness, incase of any great and evident Danger; or, if he shall happen to be attacked in his own Dominions; thereupon to recal the said Troops; and they shall be sent him back immediately, and without any Contradiction.

10.

When his Majesty the King of Great Britain, and their High and Mighty Lordships, after the War is ended, shall send back the said Six thousand Mbn; in that Case, they shall have One full Month's Pay for their Return and Carriage-money: But, in case his Highness recalls them before the Ratification of the Treaty of Peace, then they shall be paid no more than the Remainder of the Month's Pay wherein they are recalled.

11.

In case of the sending back, or Recall, of the said Six thousand Men, neither the said King, nor the said Lords the States General,- shall pay for, or fill up, the private Soldiers

- WHElREAS, sihee' the Treaty of Alliance between toe his Sacred Imperial Majesty, his Sacred Royal Majesty the King of Great Britain, lately deceased, and the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces, was made, and signed at the 'Bay

of September in the Year 1701, the 'most Christian King has so far taken upon him as to own arid declare the prer tended Prince of Wales King of England, Scotland, and Ireland; and has thereby offered a very great Injury and Indignity to the said late King, to the Queen ot Great Britain, and to the whole British Nation:

It is therefore agreed and concluded between the said Confederates, his Sacred Imperial Majesty, her Sacred Royal Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, and the High and Mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces, by this present Article, which shall have the same Force, Virtue, and Vigour, as if it had been originally inserted in the aforesaid Treaty of Alliance; That no Peace shall be concluded with France, until Reparation be made to her Sacred Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, for the said signal Injury and Indignity.

Sir RozvlandGwynn reported, from the Committee appointee! to view the Galleries and Seats in Westminster Hall and Westminster Abbey, and the Passages thither, in order to attend the Solemnity of her Majesty's Coronation, and the best Way to come to the House, on Thursday next, the Matter, as it appeared to them; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That, the Committee having been to view the Scaffolds in Westminster Hall\ and the Abbey, as also the Ta? bles for the Members in the Exchequer Court, and the Passages through which the Members are to come to Westminster Hall, and from thence to the Abbey;

They find the Scaffolds in the Abbey made very convenient to receive the Members; and that there is Room enough for the whole House, and the Tables in the Court of Exchequer large enough to entertain near Four hundred Members:

But the Seats appointed for the House in Westminster

Imp-1

DcOt.

Hall are made very 'narrow and inconvenient,__________

not receive above Two hundred and Fifty Persons; because, at each End of the Hall, a Part of the Seats are separated for other Company; whereby the Members must be obliged to go through a "long, narrow, dark Passage, to their Seats.

The Committee are of Opinion, That the best Way to come to the House upon Thursday next, will be, for the Members to come by Water to Sir John Cottorih Stairs; and so, through his House, up to the House of Commons; whence they may go through the Hall to their Seats; and thence through the Exchequer Court, by a Back Passage, through St. Margaret's Lane, into St. Margaret's Church; and thence, through the North Isle of the Abbey, to their Seats there; and they are to return the same Way to Westminster Hall: All which Passages will be raised in.

The Committee have also viewed the Scaffolds, and believe they are well built; and the Surveyor General does assure them, that the same are strong and safe.

The Committee do humbly conceive, That all those Seats on the Right-hand, coming into Westminster Hall, ought to be set apart for the Use of the House only.

And also he acquainted the House, That there are Scaffolds built upon the Roof of the Exchequer, where the Members are to dine, to the endangering the Roof thereof.

Ordered, That the Surveyor of her Majesty's Works do take care, that the Seats for the Members in Westminster Hall be inlarged, and made more easy for the Accommodation of the Members: And that the Partitions in the Gallery be removed.

Ordered, That the Surveyor of her Majesty's Works do likewise take care, that there be no Scaffolds over the Exchequer Chamber, and Place where the Members are to dine.

ORDERED, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, to whom the Bill for the Encouragement of an Invention of damasking, striking, and fixing, Colours into all Sorts of Stuff and Cloth; and raising and embossing Flowers of various Colours on the same; was committed; That they have Power to receive a Clause, That, in case of seizing of Wool to be exported, the Matter may be tried in an adjacent County.

A Petition of several Clothiers of divers Counties of England, met at Salisbury Fair, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Clothiers of England, was presented

to the House, and read; setting forth,.....they, being

apprehensive of the great Decay of their Trader which is fallen, and will hereafter fall, on all the Traders in W ool in the Kingdom, by reason of the vast Quantities sent into foreign Parts; and, if not prevented, will utterly ruin the Trade thereof, and cause many Thousands, w ho live thereby, to starve: That the Petitioners found Advantage by several Officers sent into the Country, under the Commissioners of Wool, who prevented the Exportation of a great deal of their Wool: They have withdrawn themselves, having no Allowance for such their Service And now having no Persons that w ill undertake the same, do pray, That there may be Persons sent into all the maritime Towns of this Kingdom, as well as in Kent and Sussex, to hinder the Exportation of Wool.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Island of Sicily, w as referred, to examine the Matter of Fact; and report the same to the House; That they had examined the same accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; Which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee do find, That, by the Act of the Second Year of the late King and Queen, all Thrown Silk, of the Island of Sicily, is prohibited to be brought into this Kingdom, but in English Ships, directly from the said Island.

And, in order to prove the remaining Allegations of the said Petition:

Mr. Slanyer, Mr. Hopegood, Mr. Leigh, and Mr. Thorole, testified, That, upon the Apprehensions of an approaching War, and for the Security of their Effects abroad,... were necessitated to order the samp to be sent to Legm'ne in Thrown Silk; whereby they have suffered a Loss of 25 per Cent.

That the whole Quantity of Silk does not exceed 120,000 Ounces; which amounts in Value, to about 80,060/.; whereof between 20 and 30 Bales of Silk are brought into this Kingdom directly from Messina to the Valup of 8,000l.;

That the Petitioners other Effects, of the Manufacture of this Kingdom, undisposed of, upon the first Apprehension of the War, amounted to the like Sum of 80,000l. or thereabouts.
