And they read a Letter to the House, as followeth; viz.

Chichester-house March 24th 1761.

Gentlemen,

WE think ourselves obliged, in Justice, to* recommend to you the unfortunate Case of Mr. Abel Butler Alderman of the City of Kilkenny; and do most heartily and unanimously make it our Request to you, if you think it proper, to lay it before the Parliament: It is the only Case of this or any other kind that we have thought fit to represent to you, though frequently importuned to that Purpose: And, indeed, we think it the most worthy of Compassion of any that has come to our Knowledge. It is as follow s: He has laid out his whole Substance, since the

VOL 13.

Year 1695, in lending Money, in paying a Fine for a Irish For-Lease, in purchasing in Incumbrances, and in making Im- feitures, provements on Part of the Estate of John Grace of Courts-towney in the County of Kilkenny: This he was induced to, by reason the said Grace was adjudged within Articles, was in the quiet Possession of his Estate, and recovered it from the King, by Petition of Right. Since the War, the said Grace claimed his whole Estate, before us, by virtue of a Settlement. We shall not trouble you with the several Points of Law, nor the other suspected Circumstances, upon hearing his Claim; but Only acquaint you with One bare Matter of Fact: Three Witnesses, which the Claimant produced to prove his Deed of Settlement, all swore positively, That DonoghEds\of Clancarthy, who was Trustee named in the said.....was present at the Execution

of it in Dublin, at the Time it bears Date, and gave several Directions about it. They being often severally asked,

Whether they were certain as to this Part of the Evidence, they all persevered in it: Counter to which, it was proved to us by the Lady Clanrickard, the said Earl's Sister, who appeared an unwilling Evidence; by his Nephew, one Mr. Donogh Carthy; and by an old Man, w ho was his Coachman at, and long before, his Death; That the said Earl was in London at the Time the said Deed bears Date, and near Twelve Months before. This was so evident, that even his own Counsel had toothing to object against it; and therefore the Trustees dismissed his Claim: Consequently, Mr. Butler is deprived of the Benefit of his Mortgage, his Purchase, his Lease, and his Improvements, they being all since the Forfeiture; by which Means he will be a Sufferer very near to the Value of 3,000l. if not relieved by the Parliament. And now you know his Case, w>e hope you need no other Inducement to do him all the Service you can; w*hich is the only Hopes he hath in repairing the Loss, which he could not avoid bringing upon him; and of maintaining himself* his Wile, and several small Children. We are,

Gentlemen,

Your humble Servants,

Cyril/ Wich, Tho. Baulins,

H. Shere, Wm. Fellmves,

J. Baggs, H. Longford,

John Trenchard, T. Harrison*

John Ishaniy To the Honourable Francis Annesly and James Hooper Esquires, Two of the Trustees for the Irishforfeitures, in London.

And then they withdrew.

A Petition of divers Clothiers in the County of Gloucester was presented to the House and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners perceiving, by the Votes, that there is a Bill brought into the House to confirm and prolong the Time of a Patent, granted to a few Persons, for Flowering and Embossing of Cloth: That the Art of Flowering Cloth was not first found out by any Person concerned in the said Patent, but by some of the Petitioners in the County of Gloucester: That the Embossing of Cloth, and Raising of Flowers, is, in some respects, rather a Prejudice, than an Improvement, of the said Art; viz. In hanging of Rooms, the Raising of Flowers will soon collect Dust, and thereby eclipse the Beauty of the Flower: And praying, no such. Bill may pass into a Law, to the Prejudice of the First Inventors of the said Art, or any other, who may, in any respect, improve the Woollen Manufactures.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the said Bill was committed.

That the Committee, looking into the Contracts made between the Committee for the Fabrick of the said Hospital, and their Master Workmen, do find, That, in the Years 1696, and 1697, they contracted with Mr. rlho. Hughes, for new Brick-work, well and workman-like performed, with good Bond, handsome Joints, and carefully wrought, being reduced to Brick and Half, 1 /. 7 s. per Rod; and to be allowed 15/. and 301 for Scaffolding: That, by another Contract made with the said Mr. Hughes, 14th March 1694, he was then allowed 30$. and 32 s. per Rod, and 30/.' for Scaffolding, for the same sort of Work:

But that, upon one Mr. Richard Billinghurst's being brought into Part of the Bricklayers Work, as some of the Commissioners said, to beat down Hughes' high Prices, they, the 12th of March 1700, contracted with the said ' Billinghurst to do the same Work for 25, 26, and 28*. per Rod, and he to find Scaffolding; as Mr. Hughes was. to have 30.9. and 32 s. per Rod, with an Allowance of 15 and 301: for Scaffolding:

Upon which, it appeared, that Mr. Hughes, rather than leave the Work, by another Contract, made the 2d of VOL.13.

April 1701, which was the Day when Mr. Billinghurst's Contract was signed, did undertake to do the same Work, that he had before received 30 and 32* per Rod for, at Mr. Billinghurst's Prices; viz. 25, 26, and 28 s. per Rod, without any Allowance for Scaffolding:

Whereas the Committee was informed, That, in private Contracts, it was customary to allow 20 s. and 22$. per Rod for Brick-work; and, the thicker the Work, the cheaper it may be performed.

That the Reason of the Differences in the said Contracts being inquired into by the Committee, it was answered by some of the Contractors, That, at the First Beginning of the Work, there was publick Notice given, in 1696, for Undertakers to come in, and once in 1698; which Publication was put'into the Gazette, For Masons; and that they beat them down as low in their Prices as they could: The reason of Mr. Hughes s high Prices in 1694 was upon building the Hall, which w as a very high Building, without any Ilooring, as is in the other Building every 12 Foot:

Mr. Comptroller acquainted the House, That he was convention commanded, by her Majesty, to lay before this House a with the Convention between her Majesty, the Emperor, and the Emperor and States General, about declaring War against France and ^ou*de'clar-Spain, with a Translation thereof: jug War.

And he presented the same to the House:

And the said Translation was read; and is as follow eth; viz.

WHEREAS, in the Third Article of the Alliance between him Imperial Majesty, his Majesty,

and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces of the Low Countries, concluded the Seventh of September in the Year One thousand Seven hundred and One, it was stipulated, That they should employ Two Months to endeavour to obtain, in an amicable Way, a reasonable Satisfaction for his Imperial Majesty, in relation to the Spanish Succession; and for his Britannick Majesty, and the said Lords the States General, a particular and sufficient Security for their Kingdoms, Dominions, and Provinces:

That these Two Months are long since elapsed, without seeing the least Appearance of an Accommodation: That, on the contrary, the most Christian King continues resolved to keep the whole Monarchy of Spain intirely for his Grandson, and to unite it closely with the Monarchy of France: That, to this End, these Two Powers join their Arms in Italy, and in the Netherlands: That the Troops of France have since invaded, and seized, all the Country of Cologne and Leige; and they fortify themselves there, in like manner as they do in all the Spanish Low Countries: That, by these means, the keep they United Provinces blocked up: And, moreover, the French King threatens to attack them with his numerous Armies, unless the said Lords the States General do what he desires;

Now, the said Allies, not judging it convenient to suffer themselves to be deluded any longer, have agreed, pursuant to the Fourth Article of the said Alliance, to join their Forces, and to declare War, by Sea and by Land,

In Witness whereof, Six Copies have been made of this Convention; Two of which are signed by the Plenipo*-tentiaries of his Imperial Majesty, One at London, and the other at the Hague; Two others by the Plenipotentiary of her Majesty the Queen of Great Britain, at London; and the remaining Two by the under-written Deputies of the States General, at the Hague: And the Plenipotentiaries and Deputies have set their Seals thereunto. Done atthe Hague, the 18th of April 1702*

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That, upon their Aum Address being presented to her Majesty Yesterday, returning her Majesty the Thanks of this House, for communicating to this House her Royal Intentions of declaring War, in Conjunction with her Majesty's Allies, against the French King, and his Grandson, her Majesty was pleased to give this gracious Answer \ viz.

Gentlemen,

I am extremely pleased with the Assurances of your Resolution to assist and support Me in this War: I make no Doubt but your Unanimity, upon this Occasion, will have a very good Effect, for the Encouragement of our Allies.

THE House took into Consideration the Amendments, made by the Lords, to the Bill, intituled, An Act to declare the Alteration in the Oath appointed to be taken by the Act, intituled, An Act for the further Security of his Majesty's Person, and the Succession of the Crown in the Protestant Line; and for extinguishing the Hopes of the pretended Prince of Wales, and all other Pretenders, and their open and secret Abettors; and for -declaring the Association to be determined*

Vol. i.j. y

And the same, being read, are as follow J viz.

Clause A: That the Test and Oaths to be taken pursuant to the Statute i° Willielmi et Marice; and making and subscribing the Declaration, pursuant to the Statute 250 Car. II.; may be in the Courts of Common Pleas and Exchequer; and for lengthening the Time for Officers to do the same in.

Clause B: That whereas Dissenters, called Quaker's, scruple to swear, or take an Oath, in any Case, it enacts.

That they shall be exempted from the said Oath; but, instead thereof, that they shall make a solemn Declaration, prescribed, in the Clause, in the same Words as the Oath, leaving out only the Word swear, abjure, Abjuration; and, upon the true Faith of a Christian. So help me God:

And further enacting* That those People shall be subject and liable to the like Pains and Penalties, Forfeitures and Disabilities, for neglecting or refusing to make and subscribe the said Affirmation, as other Persons refusing or neglecting the Oath,

Clause A being thrice read;

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Amendment;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put, That the House do agree with the Lords in the said Amendment.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Thomas Hodges Esquire w as referred.

And the said Report w as read; and is as followeth; viz.

That the Petitioner, in order to prove his Allegations in his Petition, and the Articles thereunto annexed, containing divers Accusations against the Lord Grey, late Governor of Barbadoes, and the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, delivered in to the Committee a List, a great Number of Memorials, Answers, Replies, and other Papers, the which he desired might be laid before the Committee, by the said Commissioners of Trade, for him to have recourse to the same, in making good his Charge: Which w'as ordered by die Committee; and the said Papers were laid before them accordingly; and Mr. Hodges was, at his Request, permitted to have Copies of such of those Papers he thought fit to ask for, and Perusal of the rest.

In the Preface of the said Articles, the Petitioner alleges, That, in the Island of Barbadoes, the Custom and Usage . is, that the Court of Chancery should be held monthly, and continue to sit as many successive Days as the Business before them requires: And the said Court should be called or summoned by the Governor's Order; and that, without his Presence and Assistance therein, no Court should be held: And the Court of Errors hi that Island is, in like manner, to be called and held by the said Governor and Council:

That the late Governor, the Lord Grey, landed in that Island on or about the 26th Day of July; and, during the time of his Government, there were several Hundred Causes depending in the said Court of Chancery, as appears to the Petitioner by the Information in Writing of Mr. John Knap ton, delivered, by him, to the Lords Commissioners of Trade, on the 3d of January 1700; and by a Letter from Edward Chilton Esquire, Attorney General of the said Island:

To prove which, the Petitioner referred to his late Majesty's Instructions to the Lord Gray, as Governor; whereby it appeared to be Part of the Instructions, for the Governor not to displace any of the Judges, Justices, or other Officers, without Cause to he signified to his Majesty, and to the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations:

That the Petitioner also referred to his late Majesty's Commission to the Lord Gray, as Governor; whereby it appeared, the Governor had full Power given him to suspend any of the Members of the said Council from sitting, voting, or assisting the rein, if he should find just Cause; and also to susj end any of the said Deputy Governors of the said Island from the Execution of their Commands, and to appoint Others in their stead, till his Majesty's Pleasure should be known:

As also, the said Governor had Power, with the Advice and Consent of the Council, to erect, constitute, and establish, such and so many Courts of Judicature, and publick Justice, within the respective Islands, as he should think fit, for the Hearing and Determining of all Causes, as well criminal as civil, according to Law and Equity; and for Awarding of Execution thereupon:

That the Petitioner referred likewise to the Answer of the Commissioners of Trade, concerning Courts of Justice, pursuant to an Order of the House of Commons, of the 2d of April 1701; whereby it appeared, That, to the end a strict and continual Care might be taken in all Matters relating to the Administration of Justice in that Island, the Governor was required to send to the said Commissioners a Copy of the Register and Minutes of the Court of Chancery, and of the Minutes and Business done as a Court of Errors, since his Arrival in that Island; as also, a particular Account of all Causes, Injunctions, and Decrees, made in the Chancery; and a particular Account of all the Days of that Court, and all other Courts sitting in that Island; and that all Courts should be held, for the Dispatch of Business, as Occasion should require; and that sudi Account should be returned by the Register, or other proper Officer, upon Oath, as by the Paper marked (A) will more fully appear; which Paper is as follows; viz.

To which First Article it was answered for the Lord Grey, That the Reason why the Court of Chancery did not sit from the said 10th of August 1698, till the 25th January following, was from the Sickness of the Governor, Sickness of the Place, Unwillingness of the Lawyers and the People to attend: That it was Vacation-time for other Courts; and that no Person complained of any Injury done thereby.

To prove which;

Major Garth was examined: Who said, That he was in Barbadoes when the Lord Grey arrived there; and that, soon after his Lordship's Arrival, he was seized with the Sickness of the Country; inso much that they had great Apprehensions of his Life; and, upon his Recovery from the Sickness, he broke out with Boyls, which seemed to be little less contagious than the Plague: That he did not see the Lord Grey at any publick Entertainment, but the Cockneys Feast, which was about the 20th of August, from the 10th of August 1698, to the 25 January following; and that he did not hear of any Complaints, that the Chancery did not sit during that time: And that though the Lord Grey was sick, yet the Island w'as, as to Health, much as it used to be at other times.

Mr. Gibbs said, That he was in Barbadoes when the Lord Grey arrived there; and that his Lordship, soon after his Arrival, was taken with the Sickness, and broke out in Boyls; whereby his Life was in Danger: That he saw him Three or Four times between August and January 1698; once at the President's House, once at Colonel's Scott's, and twice at his Lordship's own House;

and that he did not hear of any Complaint, that the (Chancery did not sit at that time.

Mr. Eyles said, That he is one of the Agents for Barbadoes; and was ordered by the Assembly there, they hearing that Complaints were made to his Majesty against the Lord Grey, and, as he believes, by Mr. Hodges, to justify their Proceedings, and his Lordship's Government; and that they were entirely satisfied with his Lordship's Conduct therein:

' That being acquainted with several Persons who came from Barbadoes, he inquired of them concerning his Lordship's Behaviour in his Government; and they all gave him a very good Character; and said, there was not then any Complaint in the Island for want of Administration of Justice; and produced an Address to his Majesty from the Council, and General Assembly; which was read; and is as followeth; viz.

WE, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Members of Your Majesty's Council and General Assembly of Your Island of Barbadoes, humbly implore Your Royal Leave, by this Opportunity of our Governor, the Right Honourable Ralph Lord Grey Baron of JVarke, to prostrate ourselves at Your Feet with our dutiful Acknowlegements, and Thankfulness for the great Care and Tenderness which Your Majesty hath, at all times, extended to these Your remote Dominions; not only rendering us safe against our Enemies hitherto, but happy in all other Circumstances; especially in that of sending that noble Lord to govern us, whose Wisdom, Moderation, and due Administration of our Laws, have made all Your Subjects here happy, during his Government over us.

And though his Lordship, on his private and weighty Affairs, hath obtained Your Majesty's Leave to come for Englandwe hope, and most humbly pray Your Majesty, that, if it may consist with Your Majesty's Royal Wisdom and Pleasure, it may not be the Occasion of our losing his mild and good Government over us for the future.

And that Your Majesty will be graciously pleased to receive from his Lordship in Favour of this Your poor Colony, a Memorial of such Matters which w>e have thought our Duty to lay before Your Majesty, for the Welfare and Safety of it.

That Your Majesty's sacred Life, and Reign, which is the greatest Security of Your Subjects, the strongest Bul-

of the Liberties of all Europe, may be long and t and that You may, at all times, triumph over all Your Enemies, in all Places, and be safe in Your Royal Person, against the private Machinations of all wicked designing Men; are the most ferventand zealous Prayers to Almighty God of,

May it please your Majesty,

Your Majesty's most loyal and most dutiful Subjects and Servants.

Mr. Turner, Solicitor General in the Barbadoes, said, That he went thither some time before the Lord Grey, and staid there till September last; and that, during his Stay there, according to his Observation, his Lordship did administer Justice according to the known Laws of the Island; and that his Lordship was sick for some time; and there were some Persons, who said, it was hard that the Courts were not held; but no Complaint was lodged.

Mr. Brookes said, That in February was Twelve-months, he went to Barbadoes, and carried with him an Account of the Complaint, made by Mr. Hodges to the House of Commons, against the Lord Grey: That he is acquainted with the most considerable Men in the Island; and they did blame Mr. Hodges; and said, he had no Reason to make any Complaint: That they did generally declare they were satisfied with the Lord Greys Government; and that he did not hear of any Complaint there against his Lordship for his Administration of Justice: But, as an Instance of the Dispatch of Business there, said, That he having a Bill in Chancery brought against him, to procure an Injunction to stay Proceedings at Law; which was granted; as also a Ne exeat Insulam, till he should answer; and, upon his the said Brooks' putting in his Answer, he obtained a Dismission of the Plaintiffs Bill in Two Days time from the granting the Injunction.

Dr. Parsons said, That the Lord Grey, soon after he came to the Island, broke out with Sores; which, he thought, were pestilential: That he had, at one time, about Thirty upon him, and that, as one Set dried up, another did rise, till towards January; and that his Lordship was reduced to great Weakness, and not fit for Business: That he often persuaded the Lord Grey not to ;o to the Town, for fear the Heat there should increase is Distemper; but his Lordship did sometimes reply, with some Passion, That he came there to do his Duty, and no Danger should fright him from it: That he never heard the Complaint against his Lordship, for not holding the Court of Chancery; and believes, there was not any one Person dissatisfied in the Island with his Government; and that, wheu his Lordship was so weak as not to be able to go to the Town, the Council sometimes met at his House, for Dispatch of Business: That his Lordship fell ill about Five Weeks after he came to the Island; and that between the Time of his Arrival and January following, he used to go Three or Four Times a Week to the President's House, which was about a Mile from his own, to take the Air, when he was able to do it; and that, when he came first to the Island, he lodged at the President's House.

Mr. Devoid Davis said, That, about Five Weeks after the Lord Grey came to the Island, he broke out with Boyls, which continued upon him, from time to time, till towards the Middle of January, and was not fit for Business during that time; for that he could not bear any Croud or Noise; and was often confined to his House a Week or more at a time, by reason of his Iudisposition.

The Petitioner, in his Second Article, alleges, That from the 26 January 1698, to the 5th of July 1699, which is Five Months and Nine Days, the Chancery sat but Two Days; so that in the First Year of his Government, there were Eleven Months, wanting Six Days in which the Court of Chancery sat but Four Days.

To prove which; the Petitioner referred to the Minutes of the Orders taken in the Chancery; whereby it appeared, that the Court of Chancery sat but Two Days, from the 26 January to the $ July following.

To which Second Article it was ahsw^red for the Lord Grey, That though the Petitioner had picked out the Two Days between which there was the longest Recess of that Courts Sitting; yet by the same Minutes of Chancery, to which it was referred, it appeared that Court was held Six times in the Five Months the Petitioner mentions but twice, by his making the Days exclusive; for that the said Court was held 25, 26 January, 22d March, 19th of April, 17 May, and the said 5th July 1699.

The Petitioner, in his Third Article, alleges, That, in the Second Year of his Government, the Court of Chancery sat to hear Causes, and make final Decrees, but One Day in Eleven Months; and that it is, from the 7th September 1699, to the 7th of August 1700; and there is no just Excuse for more than Two Months of his Time.

To prove which he referred to the List of the Business heard and determined in Chancery, attested by the Register of that Court, upon Oath, and so certified to the Commissioners of Trade; whereby it appeared that Court sat but One Day, from the 7th of September 1699, to the 7th of August following.

And the Petitioner alleged the Sickness was over the 9th July; for that, upon that Day, it appeared, by the Minutes of Council, that a Thanksgiving was ordered to be upon the 25th of that Month, for their Deliverance from the Sickness:

And the Court of Common Pleas sat to do Business the 24th, 25th, and 26th of April 1700; as appeared, by the Proceedings of that Court, to which the Petitioner referred.

To which Third Article it was answered, for the Lord Grey, That it would, and did, appear by the Registers Certificate, that tho' the Chancery sat but One Day upon Causes after September till the Sickness in April, yet the Court sat, in most of those Months, upon Pleas, Demurrers, Petitions, Exceptions, Special Reports, and Motions.

And it appeared, that, in the Months of December and February, the stated Day in December happened to be a Holy-day; and, upon the stated Day in February, the Governor was sick.

And, to prove the Sickness began in April, and continued till August, Witnesses were examined; viz.

Mr. Beddingfeild: Who said, That, for the Months of April, May, June, and July, he several times passed through the Town, and met but very few People in the Streets, by reason of the Sickness; and most of the Shops were shut up those Months.

Mr. Chamberlaine said, That he did not live in the Town; but had Business to come thither very often during the said Months of April, May, June, and July, and saw scarce any Country Gentlemen in the Town, and met few in the Streets, but Corps carrying to be buried, and Doctors and Apothecaries; and most of the Shops were shut up, by reason of the Contagion.

The Petitioner, in the Fourth Article, alleges, That, from the time of the said Lord Grey's entering upon the Government of that Island, in July 1698, to the time when the Petitioner complained to his Majesty, which was in December 1700, the said Court of Chancery sat very seldom, and did very little Business on many of the Days on which they sat: On the 1 ith of September 1699, it sat, and heard but Two Common Motions, though so much Business was depending in that Court: The next Day it sat, was on the 4th of October 1699; and there were but Two Motions, or Demurrers, heard that Day; and then the Court adjourned for a Month; and, on several other Days, there were but a small Number of Motions, and many of them have been put off to other Courts; and sometimes more have been put off than have been heard, though the Court did commonly adjourn for a Month, and often for a longer Time; and many other great and unreasonable Delays were put upon Suitors by that Court.

To prove which he referred to the Minutes in Chancery; whereby it appeared,

That on the 1 ith of Septempher 99, the Court heard One Petition, and One Motion.

Colonel Cteland was examined on Behalf of the Petitioner: Who said, That there hath not been a free current Court of Justice in the Island of Barbadoes since Colonel Kendall's Government:

That he hath heard great Complaints there, of the Delay of Justice; and also from several in England; but knows not the Cause:

That the Courts were held constantly in Colonel Kendall's Time; and a Judge was turned out, upon Complaint to the Governor for neglecting his Duty in Holding of Courts: That he does not know of any Complaint made to the Lord Grey, of Delay of Justice in any of the Courts: That the Delay of Holding of Courts w as not greater in the Lord Greys Time than in the preceding Governments:

That in the Case of Bayly against Bayly, there was a Writ of Error depending in the said Island about a Year before the Lord Grey came to the Government there; and many of the Negroes were possessed by the Creditors, by several Decrees obtained before his coming thither; so that, had the Writ of Error been tried, the said Negroes could not have been restored, unless it had been before those Decrees were obtained:

That the said Writ of Error was not determined while he staid there; which was till April 1700; though such Writs were usually determined in Three Months time:

That he never did hear of any Complaints against the Lord Grey, in relation to Injunctions either unduly granted, or unjustly kept on foot.

To which Fourth Article it was answered, for the Lord Grey, That the Petitioner hath Cunningly picked out of the Register's Book only those Days on which the least Business came on; and it appears there were but Two Days, wherein the Court did not clear all the Business that came before them.

And that in 1697, and 1699, there were several Injunctions granted the same Day the Bill was filed:

(C).

SIR, Whitehall, January 27th, 170^.

HAVING, in pursuance of his Majesty's Order in Council, upon the Petition of John Loder Esquire, Mary Ciofts, and Martha Frederick Widow, whereof we send you here inclosed a Copy, considered the Matter therein complained of; and finding, that, by the great Neglect there has been in holding Courts of Chancery in Barbadoes, and by the Want of Dispatch of Business, there are more than Three hundred Causes depending in that Court, many of which are of several Years Standing, to the very great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and other Suitors; we are, in his Majesty's Name, to require you, for the future, to be more careiul in the Expediting of Justice, and to hold Courts of Chancery, until all the Causes depending the re be determined; to the End that no more Occasion he given for Complaints in Matters of this Nature, which are so grievous to the Subject: And we do further direct, That Entry be made of this Letter in the Council Books, for the Sasisfaction of all Persons therein concerned; and that you return us an Account of your Proceedings herein, and in Answer to our Letter of the 16th October last So we bid you heartily farewel.

Your very loving Friends,

Stamford, JVm. Blaithwait,

Abr. Hill, Mat. Prior,

Ph. Meadows, John Polleafen.

Geo. Stepney,

Barbadoes

Government.

TRUSTY and Well-beloved, We greet you well. Whereas John Lod6r> Isaac Hawkins, and Thomas Hodges, Esquires, in behalf of themselves, and others, have, by their humble Petitions severally laid before Us divers Complaints of great Delays, and undue Proceedings, in Our Courts of Justice in Our Island of Barbadoes; in the Setting forth whereof, they offered to prove, that there were lately above Eight hundred Causes, depending at one time, in Two of the Courts of Common Pleas in that Island, besides what more might be depending in the Three other Courts of the same Kind, whereof they had not yet been informed; and have imputed this Disorder, amongst other Causes, to the Partiality of some Persons appointed to sit in the Judica^ tories of the said Island, who are themselves much indebted; have many Suits depending against them; and are thereby frequently interested, either directly, or by Consequence, in the Issue of the Suits that are brought before them: And whereas it has been further represented by the said Petitioners, That the Method practised in the Courts of Chancery, in determining Controversies, and pronouncing Decrees, is very irregular; and that the Neglect in holding those Courts, and the Want of Dispatch of Business there, have been such, that there has been sometimes but One Court held in the Space of Eight or Nine Months, and very little done in it since your entering upon that Government; so that there are more than Three hundred Causes depending in the said Court, many of which are of several Years standing; and also, that, since your being the re, not any Court of Errors did sit in Two Years time; by which means, all Judgments at Common Law, whereon Writs of Error have been brought, were staid from Execution: All which Delays, and undue Proceedings, do tend to the very £rcat Prejudice of the Petitioners, and other Suitors: And it being highly necessary, that all Irregularities of this Nature, which are so grievous to Our Subjects, be reformed, and that the Grounds of all such Complaints being thoroughly inquired into, effectual Care be taken, that they be, for the future, intirely removed: We have, in order thereunto, directed Our Commissioners for Trade and Plantations to transmit unto you the Copies of the aforesaid Petitions, and of the Memorials offered thereupon, for your Answers not only to the particular Cases of the Petitioners, but also. to the more general Complaints afore-mentioned.

And we do hereby will and require you to take especial Care, that no Person, interested in the Suits depending in any of the Courts of Our said Island, be appointed or permitted to sit as Judge in the Causes w herein they are concerned; that Justice be every where duly and speedily administered; that the Complainants have such Redress as is agreeable to Law; and that you do yourself constantly hold Courts of Chancery, until all the Causes there be determined: We do likewise declare Our Royal Will and Pleasure, That no Members of our Council in that Island be exempted from any Prosecution, in Law or Equity, for the Payment of their just Debts, except only during the Time that the General Assembly of Our said Island shall be sitting; which you are accordingly to declare unto them. And, for the better Observance of Our Directions in all this Matter, as well as for the Satisfaction of all Persons concerned, you are to cause Entry to be made of this Letter in Our Council Books. So We bid you farewel.

Given at Our Court at Kensington, the 16th Day of March 170^, in the 13th Year of Our Reign.

By His Majesty's Command,

James Vernon.

SIR, (F). Whitehall, March 25th, 1701.

(G). To the Kings most Excellent Majesty*

May it please Your Majesty,

SEVERAL Petitions having been laid before Your Majesty the last Winter, complaining of Delays, and other Irregularities, in the Administration of Justice ia Barbadoes, which Your Majesty was then pleased to refer to our Consideration, and to require us to report what we conceived fit to be done therein; and, in pursuance thereof- several Memorials, and other Papers, having been delivered unto us by Mr. Thomas Hodges, One of the Petitioners; all of which Petitions, Memorials, and other Papers, we accordingly considered, and did thereupon humbly report to Your Majesty, the Sixth of February last, to the following Effect; viz. That Copies of all the said Petitions, and other Papers, might be transmitted to the Governor of that Island; and a Letter writ, to require him to take especial Care, that no Persons, interested in the Suits depending in any of the Courts of that Island, be appointed or permitted to sit as Judges in the Causes wherein they are concerned; that Justice be every where duly and speedily administered; and thathe do also himself constantly hold Courts of Chancery, until alftlie Causes there be determined: And, in relation to the particular Case of Mr. Hodges, upon which he desired, that the Court of Chancery of the said Island might be directed to set aside certain Agreements, which he conceives to have been made in his Wrong; we further added, that it has not been usual for Your Majesty, or Your Predecessors to interpose the Royal Authority in judicial Proceedings in the Plantations, otherwise than by receiving Appeals to Your Majesty ia Council for Your Royal Determination, as to Right shall appertain:

All which Your Majesty was pleased to approve; and a Letter thereupon, prepared, by us, having accordingly been dispatched, under Your Royal Signature, the 16th of March last, and sent thither, together with Copies of all the forementioned Papers; we now humbly crave Leave to lay before Your Majesty an Account of the further Progress of that Matter:

The Governor and Council of Barbadoes have transmitted to us a large and particular Answer to the several Heads of Complaint exhibited by Mr. Hodges against the Proceedings of the Court of Chancery, and other Courts of Justice, in that Island; wherein they set forth, That the said Courts did sit more frequently than had been suggested by Mr. Hodges; appealing, for Proof of what they say, to the Copies of their Journals, and Certificate of the publick Register; *by which they also shew, that all the Causes, ripened for hearing in the Court of Chancery sines the present Governor's Arrival, being in the Whole but Seventy-eight, and Fifteen thereof having been upon the List before his Arrival, were finished in March last: And 1 when

when the Interval between their Sittings happened to be longer than usual; they offer divers Reasons for it; as the Governor's Sickness; the Sickness of the Island; the necessary Forms and Methods of their Proceedings, &c.: They likewise vindicate themselves from some other Imputations, by denying directly what Mr. Hodges asserts; particularly in relation to the Circumstances of the Judges of that Island, as if they were Persons much in Debt; disc* in relation to the Authority of some great Men amongst them, as if it were made use of to deter Witnesses concerning declaring their Knowledge of the Maladministration of Justice: And they, in like manner, contradict him in several other Points; challenging hint withal tb prove, by particular Instances, wherein Justice has beefl perverted, either through Bribery, or any other unwarrantable Consideration: And, in further Testimony of the Governor's good Conduct, they appeal to the Addresses that have been made by the Inhabitants to Y6ift Majesty, and to him the Governor, acknowledging his impartial Administration of Justice amongst them: in reference whereunto, they likewise observe, That, amongst the Seventy-eight Causes, which have been determined by him, there have been but Two Appeals made to Your Majesty in Council here. These are the principal Heads whereof their Answer consists.

Upon the Receipt hereof, Mr. Hodges, who is the only Person who appears to us to concern himself in the Prosecution of these Matters, desiring that the same might be communicated to him, together with all the Papers therein referred to, we complied with him therein; and he has thereupon delivered to us a long Reply, in which he endeavours to disprove what the Governor and Council have alleged, and to invalidate the Reasons, which they have offered from the Consideration of Sickness, and otherwise, for the extraordinary Intervals that have sometimes happened: And this he does by Observations upon their Journals; by offering some Grounds of doubting, whether the Certificate of their Register was made upon Oath, as is pretended; together with other particular Objections.

He complains of the Governor's Neglect to inspect the Management of the Courts of Common Pleas; particularly that of St. Andrews, whose Negligence was such, that, as he says, they sat but One Day in Fourteen Months: He instances an Obstruction in the Course of Justice, by the Governor's not filling up a Judge Assistant's Place in the Court of St. Michael for about Sik Months after the Death of Mr. Gardiner, who had been in that Place; by means whereof all Proceedings in that Court were so long stopped: He likewise complains of the great Hindrance, w'hich his, and other Mens, Common Law Proceedings had received from the Court of Chancery, by Injunctions irregularly granted, and long continued; and instances particularly in Two Cases of his own; the one carried on in the Names of Coates and Spry, his Trustees, against Sadler; the other in the Name of Holdipy his Trustee, against Downes; each of which, he says, had been suspended, by Injunction out of Chancery, for above Two Years.

Tie further asserts, That no Court of Errors was held by the Governor, or, at least, that no Writ of Error was heard, and determined, by that Court, from his Arrival there in July 1698, until the 24th January 1700, which is about Two Years and a Half; and he names Mi*. Sharp and Mr. Sadler as Persons much in Debt; and therefore unfit to sit in any of the Judicatories of that Island: Whereas the Governor and Council have certified. That all Cases, ripe for a Hearing in Chancery were finished in March last.

He does not deny but that extraordinary Diligence was used a little before that Time; but this he attributes to the particular Directions given to the Governor by our Letter of the 16th October 1700, for sending home attested Copies of the Proceedings of all their Courts. He does not instance in any Delay or Denial of Justice, either since the Receipt of Your Majesty's Letter of the 16th March last, or of Your Letter of the 16th of October before; nor has he produced to us any Affidavits Vql. 13.

We now humbly offer, That, considering the Expence which the Lord Grey has been obliged to make in supporting the Dignity of that Government, has exceeded his Salary; and there not appearing to us any sufficient Cause to hinder him of the Benefit intended him in this manner by the Inhabitants of that Island: Your Majesty would be graciously pleased to permit him the said Lord Grey to receive the said Sums of Two thousand Pounds current Money of Barbadoes, and Tw o thousand Pounds Sterling, according to the Contents of the aforesaid Acts.

And the said Commissioners did further allege, That the Occasion of Mr. Hodges's Displeasure and Complaint against them was, that, upon his Request to that Board, that he might have an Order from his late Majesty to the Chancery of Barbadoes, directing them to set aside an Agreement made by Mr. Pilgrim, Mr. Hodges' Attorney, with Mr. Hei ne, although the same should have been passed into a Decree; and that the Suit against Mr. Hodges should be put into the same Condition, in all respects, as it was before the making the same Agreement; which Request of Mr. Hodges appears under his own Hand; the said Commissioners did thereupon report to his late Majesty, That it bad not been usual for his Majesty, or his Predecessors, to interpose the Royal Authority in judicial Proceedings in the Plantations, otherwise than by receiving Appeals to his Majesty in Council for his Royal Determination, as to Right should appertain; w'hich, the said Commissioners humbly conceive, they were in Duty obliged to represent to his late Majesty, although to the Dissatisfaction of Mr. Hodges; and that, if they had done otherwise, they would have deserved as severe a Censure, as Mr. Hodges has, by his Petition and Articles, most unjustly laid upon them.

Resolved, That Thomas Hodges Esquire hath not made good his Petition, or any of the Particulars of Maladministration complained of by the said Mr. Hodges against Ralph Lord Grey, late Governor of Barbadoes, or the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations.

Resolved, That the said Petition, and Complaint, is vexatious and scandalous.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for laying a Duty upon buying, selling, or bargaining for, Shares in any joint Stocks of Corporations, after the Committee of the whole House upon the Bill for regulating the Frauds and Abuses in the Salt Duties.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee, to whom the Bill to prevent the Making of unwholesome and unmerchantable Brandies from Corn; and for preventing the clandestine Importation of French Brandies; was committed; be made upon Friday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine a Clock.

Ditto. A Petition of divers Weavers of London, Norwich, and

Canterbury, and other Dealers in the Silk, and Silk and Worsted, Manufactures, in behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Bringing of Thrown Silk of the Growth of Italy, Sicily, and Naples, was prohibited by an Act of Parliament of the Second of William and Mary, unless imported in such manner as is directed by another Act of the Twelfth of King Charles the Second: And it being found, that the Importation of such Silk, in the manner prescribed by the last mentioned Act, in regard of the Difficulties and Hazard occasioned by the late War with France, was so prejudicial, as that the Silk Manufacture w as in great Danger of being lost; for Prevention whereof, an Act passed in the Fifth Year of the said King and Queen, for the Importation of the said Silk from any Place, unless the Ports of France, during that War: And, in regard the same, or greater, Hazards will now happen, if not prevented, they pray, That the said Thrown Silk may be imported from any Port or Place, except of France and Spaine, during the present War.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the importing Thrown Silk, according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Colonel Lee, Mr. Sayers, and Mr. Brewer, do prepare, and bring in, the said Bill.

Ditto. Colonel Lee, according to Order, presented to the House a Bill for the Importation of fine Italian Thrown Silk; And the same was received.

The Lord Marquis of Hartington reported the Conference; and that it was managed by the I^ord Privy Seal; who acquainted them, That the}- have, for the preventing all Correspondence with France and agreed upon an Address to her Majesty: To which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And the said Address, being read, is as follows; viz.

WE, Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects# the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to represent to Your Majesty, as our Opinion, that nothing will more contribute to the effectual carrying on the just and necessary War, w herein You are engaged; to the interrupting the Trade of Your Enemies; to the depriving them of intelligence; and reducing them to the greatest Streights; than an intire Prohibition of all Correspondence with France and Spain, on the Part of the Allies: And we do therefore humbly advise Your Majesty, That You would be pleased, so soon as may be, to engage the Emperor, the Mates General, and Your other Allies, to join with Your Majesty in prohibiting, in the strictest manner, and under the severest Penalties, all Intercourse by Letters, or otherwise, between the Subjects of Your Majesty, and Your AHies, and the Subjects of France and Spain.

Ordered, That the Consideration of the said Report he adjourned talll Tomorrow Morning.

Sir Rowland Gwyn reported from the Committee ap- Privateer*, pointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered at a Conference with the Lords, for disagreeing to the Amendments, made by their Lordships, to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of Privateers, That they had drawn up the same accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House; and are as follow; viz.

That the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Encouragement of Privateers, doth alter several Duties granted to the Crown; and doth likewise dispose of several Sums of Money arising therefrom, and of other publick Monies:

The Commons do therefore disagree to all your Lordships Amendments to the Bill: For the Altering of Duties, and the Granting and Disposing of all publick Monies, is the undoubted Right of the Commons alone, and an essential Part of their Constitution.

Ordered, That a Conference be desired with the Lords Conference upon the Subject-matter of the said Amendments. desired witt

MR. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the Answer to House, That, their Address having been pre- Address, sented to her Majesty, That her Majesty would be graciously pleased to give all necessary Encouragement for making Captures on the Enemy; and particularly, that she will grant Commissions or Charters to such of her Subjects that shall endeavour to make Acquisitions in the East ox West Indies; with such Directions, Instructions, ' and Limitations, as her Majesty shall think best in her great Wisdom; her Majesty was pleased to give Answer,

That her Majesty will take care the Address shall be complied with, so far as it is in her Power.

Mr. Secretary Hedges acquainted the House, That Ditto, their Address, relating to Dr. Gastrell, Chaplain to this House, having been presented to her Majesty, her Majesty was pleased to give Answer, That her Majesty, having always a Regard to the Recommendation of this House, will bestow on Dr. Gastrell some considerable Dignity in the Church.

Mr. Speaker,

The Queen commands this Honourable House to attend her Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend her Majesty:

Where her Majesty was pleased to give the Royal Royal Am Assent to several publick and private Bills; and afterwards to Bills, to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses,

And afterwards the Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, by her Majesty's Command, prorogued the Parliament prorogue until Tuesday the Seventh Day of July next.
